New Jersey was one, and miles of homes and businesses were devastated in a series of towns. Some remained inundated with water or sand washed up by the storm. The neighboring state of New York had the highest death toll in the storm. - The state got personal attention from the White House, as Obama toured storm-damaged areas Wednesday. New Jersey coastal town turned to "devastation" - Sandy killed at least six people in the state, said Gov. Chris Christie, who warned people in low-lying areas to evacuate. "We're lucky that more people didn't die as a result of folks ignoring those warnings." - "When it comes to getting things done, I don't care what party somebody's in," the Republican governor said after touring the disaster area with Obama, a Democrat. "I'm aware of all the atmospherics. I'm not in a coma. But the fact is, I don't care." - Some 500,000 gallons of diesel fuel will be delivered to the state by Thursday night to run trucks and generators at nursing homes, hospitals and other high-priority locations, he said. - State offices will be open Thursday. - "We'll be ready for Election Day, one way or another," Christie said. - Residents not cleaning up damage to their property spent much of their time Wednesday standing in line - at gasoline stations, stores and restaurants. - Transportation is coming back on line, the governor's office said. The majority of major closed roads have been cleared, Gov. Chris Christie said. By Thursday, all airports should reopen, but service in some is limited. Air Train service to Newark International is running again but is still down to JFK. All but one tunnel into New York City are open. Only the Holland Tunnel is still closed. Ferry service to New York has also resumed. Buses hit the streets again on 86 routes Thursday, according to NJ Transit. But light rail resumes on only one route and major rail service is down until further notice. The transit authority has posted dramatic photos of storm damage on its rail lines to its website. - Amtrak said it would provide Northeast Regional service on Thursday between Boston and New Haven, Connecticut, and between Newark and points south. - PATH train service, which typically ferries 245,000 people under the Hudson River to New York City each weekday, is suspended until further notice. NEW YORK. - With at least 28 killed, the state had the most fatalities, most of them in New York City. - Bellevue Hospital was evacuating its remaining 700 patients, some of them critically ill, in a process that could take two days, a source familiar with the evacuation plan told CNN. - Coney Island Hospital and Manhattan Veterans Affairs Hospital were also evacuated.

'Why, don't you see that fellow yonder? That is the very chap who fired the shot which broke the blackfellow's leg.' And then he told me how the fellow had been employed to work at the punt, but had taken the first opportunity of deserting his employer, and joining the hostile tribe, who were now encamped on the opposite side of the river. I have thought it necessary to give these details, as they explain what follows. It seems that after leaving the scene of the skirmish above mentioned, the war-party had made their way down to the Murray, where they remained concealed until an opportunity presented itself of crossing over to the other side, where they had friends, and where they knew they could obtain food and shelter. They had not long to wait before the man alluded to deserted his master, and joined them. He was, as I afterwards found out, the chief instigator of the attack on the sheep-station, which shortly followed. This man had lived for several years among the whites, and spoke English fluently. His own people were those with whom he had now cast in his lot; but although born on the banks of the river, he had never visited his native place since he left it, many years ago, to go to Sydney. He had no doubt heard from time to time accounts of the country around the Murray, and had probably seen some of its natives when they visited Melbourne, or Swan Hill, where he resided during the latter part of his stay among the settlers. He had therefore acquired a knowledge of the habits and customs of his countrymen, and was consequently able to advise them as to the best method of carrying on hostilities against the whites. He had already, as I have shown, planned two attacks on the sheep-stations; but both had failed. Still, he had not given up the idea of making another attempt. The mere fact of his being present among them, and inciting them to deeds of violence, rendered the position of the settlers extremely insecure; for even if they succeeded in driving off one party, there was always a chance of others coming down from the interior. They could not be kept away by force, because there was no one to oppose them. It was true that the police were stationed at Swan Hill; but they were few in number, and besides, they had other duties to perform. So the settlers determined to take the law into their own hands, and to put a stop to these marauders once and for ever. A meeting was held at the inn, and it was decided that a party should proceed across the river, and attack the enemy in their own quarters. To carry out this plan, however, required some caution; for the blacks might easily be alarmed, and escape. It was therefore arranged that the attack should be made early in the morning, while the natives were still asleep. Accordingly, on the appointed day, a party consisting of five white men and six friendly blacks crossed the river, and proceeded towards the camp. They reached it just as daylight appeared, and rushed in amongst the sleepers. Some of the latter tried to defend themselves, but without success. Others attempted to escape, but were pursued and killed. Only three managed to get away, and these were hotly chased by the avenging party. Two of them were overtaken and despatched; the third succeeded in reaching the river, and plunging in, swam across to the other side. Here he was met by a white man named Thompson, who happened to be passing at the time. Seeing that the black was unarmed, and evidently terrified, Thompson took pity on him, and offered him protection.

The ticket agent tells us the time of our standby flight. 6am....6am? You mean as in TOMORROW? NooooooOOOOOOO!!! So we accept the standby tickets and all disperse to different ticket counters to try our luck at landing another (cheap) flight for tonight...no luck. I finally ascend out of the depths of denial and realize that I am in fact NOT going to make it to Miami tonight. I also try to grasp the concept of not making it at all since it's a very busy travel weekend. A ray of hope did come from the ticket agent at Southwest airlines. She tipped me off that many people miss that first flight out in the morning because it's so early. My chances are good that several seats will be available. My ticket counter (American)opens at 4am. I have to be there then. I checked into the Red Roof Inn very close to the airport for the night. There's no way I'm going back home and risking missing it again. I didn't even move my car because I didn't want to deal with that god forsaken airport shuttle either. The hotel van will be leaving at 4am for the hotel and you better believe I'll be on it. I suppose the fear of missing my flight grabbed me because I didn't sleep well at all that night. I got in the bed around 10:30 and slept lightly for 2 hours. By the time 12:30am hit, I was WIDE awake. I watched TV for a few hours, roamed down to the vending machines and waited for 4:00 to arrive. Around 3:40am I go down and check out and load my bags into the van. To my surprise the van was full of other travelers. Long story short, I made it on my flight. I arrived in Miami around 8:30am and the airport already looked like a party. When my friend LJ and I first decided to do this, we didn't know that Memorial Day weekend in South Beach was HUGE for black folks. It was basically an all Hip Hop weekend packed full of parties, pool parties, basketball tournaments, concerts, club events etc. I've heard it referred to as the "new Freaknic". Well we didn't know, but it sure looked like everyone else did. Girls were decked out in their best club gear at 8:30 am!! Heels, short skirts, tight pants, and hair in place. They weren't playing. The fellas just enjoyed taking all the sights in. The funny thing was that I knew the view would only get worse as the weekend went on. My first celebrity sighting was as soon as I arrived at the airport. Biz Markie was standing around waiting for his bags I guess. Nobody seemed to notice him, or really care. He was standing in the middle of everything not being bothered at all.

As I settled into my new home in Handong, I couldn't help but feel a sense of belonging. The ocean air, the scent of pine and salt, the sound of the waves crashing against the shore - it was all so familiar, so comforting. I felt like I had finally found my own little slice of heaven on earth. And yet, as I looked out at the vast expanse of the ocean, I couldn't help but feel a twinge of longing for the city. The bright lights, the bustling streets, the endless possibilities - it was all so intoxicating. I missed the thrill of exploring new places, trying new foods, and experiencing new cultures. But as I gazed out at the ocean, I knew that I had made the right decision. This was where I was meant to be. As I walked along the beach, the sand between my toes and the wind in my hair, I felt a sense of peace wash over me. It was as if the world had slowed down, and all that mattered was the present moment. I closed my eyes and breathed in deeply, feeling the salty air fill my lungs. I felt grateful for this new chapter in my life, for the opportunity to start anew in a place that felt like home. As I walked, I stumbled upon a small cafe perched on the edge of the cliff, overlooking the ocean. I decided to stop and grab a cup of coffee, and as I sat down at a small table by the window, I felt a sense of contentment wash over me. The sun was setting, casting a golden glow over the ocean, and I felt like I was exactly where I was meant to be. I pulled out my journal and began to write, the words flowing easily onto the page as I poured out my thoughts and feelings. As the sun dipped below the horizon, I closed my journal and gazed out at the ocean, feeling a sense of peace and contentment wash over me. I knew that this was where I was meant to be, and I was grateful for this new chapter in my life.

The first thing to note is that in Wheaton, when you want to talk about an action that started and finished in the past, you use the helping verb "di" with the main verb in the past tense. For example, "I di go to the store yesterday" or "She di finish her homework last night". This is similar to English, where you would say "I went to the store yesterday" or "She finished her homework last night". However, things get a bit more complicated when you want to talk about an action that started before another action in the past. In this case, you use the helping verb "da" with the main verb in the past tense. For example, "I da study English before I move to London" or "They da live in Paris before they come to New York". This is different from English, where you would say "I had studied English before I moved to London" or "They had lived in Paris before they came to New York". Another important thing to note is that when you want to talk about an action that was ongoing at a specific point in the past, you use the helping verb "sta" with the main verb in the present tense. For example, "I sta watch TV when my friend call me" or "They sta work on the project when the boss come in". This is similar to English, where you would say "I was watching TV when my friend called me" or "They were working on the project when the boss came in". Now, let's talk about the exceptions. In Wheaton, there are some verbs that don't follow the general rules. For example, the verb "to be" is a bit tricky. When you want to talk about a permanent or temporary state in the past, you use the verb "bi" instead of "di" or "da". For example, "I bi a student at that time" or "She bi very happy when she was a child". This is different from English, where you would say "I was a student at that time" or "She was very happy when she was a child". Another exception is the verb "to have". When you want to talk about possession or relationship in the past, you use the verb "ha" instead of "di" or "da". For example, "I ha a car when I was 20" or "They ha a big house in the countryside". This is similar to English, where you would say "I had a car when I was 20" or "They had a big house in the countryside". So, to summarize, the helping verbs in the past in Wheaton are "di" for completed actions, "da" for actions that started before another action, and "sta" for ongoing actions. The seizures were relentless, tearing through his fragile body like a tempest that wouldn't abate, leaving everyone around him in a state of perpetual vigil. At first, there was hope-hope that each seizure would be the last, hope that the doctors would find a way to quell the storm raging within him. But as days bled into weeks, that flicker of optimism began to wane, overshadowed by the grim reality of his condition. Eve spoke in hushed tones, her voice trembling with each syllable. She recounted the daily visits, the endless hours spent by his bedside, clutching his hand, whispering words of encouragement that felt increasingly hollow against the stark backdrop of medical machines. It was as if their relentless whirrs and beeps synchronized with the pulse of dread that thudded through her veins. "I kept thinking, if I just hold on a little longer, if I just pray a little harder, maybe he'll come back to us," Eve said, her eyes distant, as though she were peering into a world only she could see. "But faith can be such a fragile thing, can't it? I wanted so desperately to believe." Her words hung heavy, a testament to the buoyancy of human hope even in the face of despair. It was a reminder of the delicate dance between acceptance and denial, a tightrope walk that leaves one teetering on the brink of both lucidity and madness. As Eve spoke, I found myself lost in reflection, my mind wandering back to the Rick I had known-a vibrant soul whose laughter could light up a room, whose generosity knew no bounds. It was difficult to reconcile that memory with the image of the man she described, battered and broken, fighting a battle he never saw coming. "Every day I would look into his eyes and see glimpses of recognition," Eve continued, her voice cracking under the weight of emotion. "It was like he was trapped inside himself, trying to find a way out. And I couldn't do anything except hold his hand." The helplessness that comes when those we love are suffering is a unique kind of torture. It strips us of our illusion of control, leaving us naked and vulnerable before the caprices of fate. All the while, the world outside spins on, indifferent to the private hell unraveling in hospital rooms and homes across the globe. Eve paused, drawing a shaky breath. It seemed, in that moment, as though the words clung to her throat, unwilling to be birthed into the open. There was more to this story; a conclusion that remained unspoken, waiting in the shadows like a specter refusing to be acknowledged fully. "In the end, it wasn't the seizures or the blindness or any of the physical pain that claimed him," she finally admitted, eyes glistening with unshed tears. "It was as if, piece by piece, part of what made Rick 'Rick' just faded away, leaving behind-" Her voice broke there, and we sat in silence, unified in our grief, bound together by the threads of memory and loss. Whatever was left of Rick seemed less a presence and more an echo now, a whisper of a once lively spirit now lost to time and tragedy.

That evening, as the sterile lights above flickered, my mind began replaying the day's events. Disturbance seeped into my bones, whispering a truth I wasn't ready to fully grasp. It was something that gnawed at me, a feeling that was just out of reach, but I couldn't shake the sensation that I had been violated. My thoughts were a jumble, yet there was an unsettling clarity in that one moment. It echoed loudly now, deafening in the silence of my hospital room. My heart thudded in my chest, a raw drumbeat that refused to let me rest. When my husband visited, I hesitated, words catching in my throat, unsure if I was imagining things or if he would even believe me. After everything we had been through, I didn't know if I wanted to burden him-or if he would just try to brush it off as a misunderstanding. But the shock and distress weighed heavily on my conscience. My lips trembled, and the resolve formed to quietly tell him what occurred. He listened, eyes widening, his brow furrowing with a storm of emotions I couldn't quite read. Anger was there, yes, but also something protective, as if he was ready to shield me from the world. "You've got to tell someone," he urged quietly, squeezing my hand until our knuckles were white between the sheets. "This isn't something you can let slide." The hospital staff buzzed around us, a flurry of scrubs and medical jargon, while I felt like a stone sinking in water. I knew then that I must speak up. The decision settled like a slowly forming bruise, painful but necessary to confront. The next morning would bring a series of whispered conversations, a report submitted to the hospital administration, and a promise from them to investigate the matter further. I hoped this wasn't all lip service, a placation to soothe a patient's distress. I had seen how the system sometimes faltered, but I clung to a fragile trust that they would act. Days blurred into one another as I recuperated. The familiarity of my family's visits brought some comfort, grounding me amidst the chaos of recovery. My strength was slowly returning, an ember gradually fanned into a flame, but psychologically, shadows still lingered. I waited with bated breath for any development from the complaint but heard only the ticking clock and rustling papers. Finally, word came that the hospital had suspended the phlebotomist pending a full investigation. A part of me sighed with relief. I wasn't merely a number lost in the shuffle; my voice had resonated somehow. They promised to keep me updated, and I clung to that promise like a lifeline. As I prepared for discharge, there was a bittersweet twinge. Leaving the hospital meant returning to normalcy, a chance to heal without the constant reminder of those sterile walls and lingering glances. Yet I also knew that out there, I'd have to confront the world anew, wary but determined. I wouldn't let that moment define me, but it would make me more vigilant, more aware. This ordeal had marked me, yes, but it had also sparked a resilience I didn't know I possessed.

These techniques have been successfully applied to measure the distortion of glass plates after they have been processed using roller bending machines. However, there are no reports of their application to monitor the deformation of the glass plate during the bending process. Therefore, the aim of this paper was to evaluate the effectiveness of these techniques in monitoring the deformation of glass plates during the roller bending process. Monitoring the deformation of glass plates during roller bending J. F. Silva The demand for flat glass is high and increasing significantly. Since 2009 float glass production has increased by 5% per annum to meet this demand. The building industry has by far the largest share of this market, and accounts for around 80% of all the flat glass produced [1]. This increase is a direct result of the recent architectural requirements for additional lightness, transparency and natural light in new buildings, leading to an increased demand for larger glass panels. In addition, architectural trends increasingly require the use of glass in curvilinear forms to produce smooth free-form facades [2]. The processes available for producing curved glass can be divided in two categories based on whether heat is involved in the process. Static mould bending and roller bending are the two most common techniques used to create curved glass and involve heating the glass above the transition temperature (550 C), so that it becomes viscous. In the static mould bending method (also known as sag bending), the desired curvature of the glass is obtained by allowing the heated flat plate to sag under its self-weight, onto a mould. However, different moulds are required for plates of different curvature therefore, this method is neither energy nor cost efficient. Furthermore, the optical quality of the curved glass plate is very sensitive to imperfections in the mould. An alternative technique that also requires the glass to be heated above its transition temperature is roller bending which can be performed either horizontally or by vertical toughening bending. The former is performed in a horizontal bending toughener during the toughening process of glass; wherein adjustable tilting rollers are used to form the desired shape of the heated glass plate. The glass is then submitted to jets of cold air to create the favourable residual stress profile of toughened glass. On the other hand, in vertical toughening bending, the glass is lowered into the furnace in a vertical position and is pressed onto the mould before being toughened. Roller bending methods therefore have adjustable and re-usable "moulds", but the optical quality of the glass plate is affected by the straightness of the rollers, their position relative to one another and more commonly by roller wave distortion. The optical quality of glass can be assessed qualitatively with the use of a zebra board plate (consisting of black and white stripes). The waviness of the reflected image on the surface of the glass plate is used to assess whether the level of distortion is acceptable. However, this method is subjective as it relies on the experience of the inspector. More recent quantitative methods include: (i) in-contact with the glass gauges (flat bottom or 3-way-contact gauge) that are conveyed along the direction of the distortion while measuring peak to valley height [3,4]; (ii) non-contact distortion measuring systems involving the use of computer vision and high-resolution cameras [5]. These techniques have been successfully applied to measure the distortion of glass plates after they have been processed using roller bending machines. However, there are no reports of their application to monitor the deformation of the glass plate during the bending process. Therefore, the aim of this paper was to evaluate the effectiveness of these techniques in monitoring the deformation of glass plates during the roller bending process.

Snowden told the Morning Post that he felt U.S. officials were pressuring his family and also accused them of "trying to bully" Hong Kong into extraditing him to prevent the release of more damaging information. He vowed to resist extradition efforts if it comes to that, saying he "would rather stay and fight the United States government in the courts, because I have faith in Hong Kong's rule of law." "My intention is to ask the courts and people of Hong Kong to decide my fate," the South China Morning Post quoted Snowden as saying. "I have been given no reason to doubt your system." But Hong Kong lawmaker Regina Ip, a former secretary of security for the territory, said Tuesday that while any extradition process could take months, Snowden isn't necessarily beyond the reach of the United States. "If he thought there was a legal vacuum in Hong Kong which renders him safe from U.S. jurisdiction, that is unlikely to be the case," she said. The newspaper said Snowden has been hiding in undisclosed locations inside the semi-autonomous Chinese territory since checking out of his hotel room Monday - a day after he revealed his identity in an interview with The Guardian. Snowden told the Morning Post he is not trying to evade U.S. authorities. "People who think I made a mistake in picking Hong Kong as a location misunderstand my intentions," the newspaper quoted him as saying. "I am not here to hide from justice; I am here to reveal criminality." The NSA and the National Intelligence director did not immediately respond to a CNN request for comment. Asked during a media briefing on Wednesday for comment on Snowden's latest claims, U.S. State Department spokeswoman Jennifer Psaki declined. She said she had not seen the latest Morning Post report. On the defensive. The revelations have renewed debate over surveillance in the United States and overseas in the name of fighting terrorism, with supporters saying the programs revealed by Snowden are legal and have helped stop terror plots. Civil liberties advocates, however, call the measures dangerous and unacceptable intrusions. Such criticisms have put Obama and his allies on the issue - both Democrats and Republicans - on the defensive against mounting criticisms from a similarly bipartisan group of critics demanding changes to rein in the programs. There also is a sharp division among Americans over the issue. A Gallup poll released Wednesday found that 44% of Americans believe Snowden did the right thing by releasing details about the classified surveillance programs, while 42% said it was wrong and 14% said they were unsure. The poll for that question had a 6% margin of error. It also found that more Americans disapprove than approve of the government's surveillance programs, 53% to 37%. Ten percent had no opinion. The poll for that question had a 4% margin of error.

Eaves were dripping and she heard the beat of the drops upon the tin roof of a porch outside. Eyes the color of brighter skies considered thoughtfully the prospect till the sound of an opening door made them turn in another direction. Quickly Janet stepped to the floor, rounding the newel by catching hold of it and swinging herself around it. At the second door, down the hall to her right, she presented herself. It was Miss Hilliard, principal of this small school for girls to whom Janet curtsied prettily. "Allie May said that you wanted to see me. Miss Hilliard," she said. "Yes, Janet. There is a package here in the office that must be meant for you, yet the address is peculiar, to say the least. It is about the size of the usual box that comes for the girls, - come in to see it for yourself." Miss Hilliard drew back from the door, admitting Janet, who went to the table by the big desk. There a box of medium size reposed, a square package, wrapped in heavy paper and well tied with cord. "You will notice that the return address is with initials only, from some hotel in Albany, New York," Miss Hilliard continued. Janet stood close to the table, looking with interest at the package, saying first, as she had said to Allie May, that there was "probably some mistake". But she caught her breath as she looked at the address. "Why - " she began. "Why, how queer!" "Yes, isn't it? Rather pretty, though. Could that be your name, Janet? There is no one else here, - there has never been any one here by the name of Eldon; and you will observe that the name of the school is given, the correct address." "I see." Janet looked again in the upper left hand corner. The initials were P.V.M. But it was the address which filled her with surprise. The package was addressed to Miss Jannetje Jan Van Meter Eldon! The longer she looked at it, the stranger it seemed. "Why, Miss Hilliard, I don't understand it at all. Could it be some joke? Oh, I just imagine that there is some mistake in addresses. Shall we open it?" "Yes, Janet. But I shall be very busy for a while and have no time for this. I will have it taken to your room and you may do the investigating. I need not tell you to preserve the treasure intact if it should be full of diamonds." Janet looked up at the tall, slender woman beside her and laughed at the suggestion. She was not afraid of Miss Hilliard, though many of the girls were. Had not Janet been in this school since her sixth year? The older woman's arm now drew her close and her cheek was laid for a moment against Janet's hair. "Now run along, child. Get back to your lessons and I will have this sent upstairs by Oliver.

Those years following my return home were clouded with a sense of turmoil, a cacophony of emotions that often left me drained. The guilt of leaving my husband, only to return battered by love's complexities, was a heavy cloak I wore. My self-esteem, once bolstered by familial affection and childhood achievements, felt fragile against the harshness of reality. Yet, in the midst of this internal chaos, I longed to reclaim the joy that had once filled my days. I began to seek solace in the things that had once brought me happiness. I immersed myself in my love for dance, rediscovering it as a form of expression far beyond just a physical activity. Each practice session became a little rebellion against my feelings of entrapment and regret. It was a sacred space where my body could move freely, and my mind could find respite from the echoes of disappointment. Dance took me to places where my heart could skip and soar, where worries momentarily melted away. In parallel, I dove into the depths of literature, losing myself in stories that painted sweeping canvases of love, loss, and self-discovery. The words of poets and authors became my companions, their tales resonating with my desire to find meaning amid the tumult. After all, how often do we reflect on our lives through the lens of others, finding threads of connection that bind us all together? It was a revelation that both soothed and stirred a longing for transformation. That spring, I initiated what I came to call my "Mindfulness Journey." I began practicing meditation, carving out moments in my day to simply be-allowing my thoughts to drift and settle like leaves on the surface of a calm pond. It was an exercise in patience and self-acceptance, a way to confront the shadows that loomed over my heart. Sometimes, I would sit quietly, tears streaming down my cheeks, but other times, a gentle smile would break through, whispering promises of better tomorrows. The process was not without challenges. The emotional weight of my choices lingered, begging for acknowledgment. I grappled with the questions that arose: What does it mean to be true to oneself? How do we reconcile desire with obligations? The answers didn't unfold neatly; rather, they brushed against me like the brush of grass beneath my feet, reminding me to revel in the process of exploration. Slowly, I began to foster patience with my journey. I found that joy doesn't dwell in a singular moment or within a person; it resides within the fabric of our experiences-the good, the messy, and the beautiful. Eventually, I healed, not by erasing the past, but by honoring it-recognizing the lessons embedded within all my ups and downs. As time marched forward, my laughter returned, and I became attuned to the subtle joys of everyday life: the way the morning light danced through the trees, the rich aroma of freshly brewed coffee, and the effortless connection shared with friends and family. My brother and I grew even closer, bonded by the laughter of children as we became co-conspirators in their joy. And through all this, I realized my capacity for love-boundless and evolving, like the deep blue sea. It was a journey, indeed, but it was mine-a tapestry sewn together with threads of resilience, heartache, and love that continued to warm my spirit. And as I sit here today, reflecting on those moments, it strikes me how far I've come-and how the road ahead is painted with new opportunities, waiting for me to embrace them with open arms.

That Rosa Lee and her family were sinned against is evident in Dashs tracing of the familys roots (the discovery, for instance, that Rosa Lees older sister was conceived when her sharecropper mother was raped by a white overseer). Yet equally clear is that Rosa Lee also bears responsibility for her choices. As our understanding of Rosa Lee as a human being deepens, the inevitable questions come. We interviewed Leon Dash and asked him some of these questions. Did your greatest shock come over Rosa involving her own children in crime? Well, I was familiar with the oldest child in an underclass family becoming part of the parents criminal activity, or providing money for the family by some illegal means with no questions asked by the parents. But all of Rosa Lees children were brought into her criminal activity. It was for what she always called survival. Rosa, for instance, would buy a brick of marijuana and her children, right on down to the youngest, would sit around the kitchen table and cut this brick into what is called dime bags. And you found this to be true of other families, this passing on of criminal behavior? Yes. Its part of the Urban Institutes definition of the underclass, that the criminal behavior is generational. But you say Rosa Lee would call this her way to survive. Did her government assistance fall short? I knew from a past project I had done on teen pregnancy that welfare assistance is not enough to cover the necessities of life. I had seen firsthand that these families on welfare would regularly have no food in the house by the end of the month. This was also true for Rosa Lee and her family. If the government made you poverty czar with full authority to change things from the ground up, what would be the first thing you would change? Education is the single most important thing. It has not been working and this is not just a blip in history. Rosa Lee went to school in the 1940s. She, her children, grandchildren, and now her great-grandchildren have not gotten an education that would help them. Three of her five grandchildren cant read. Cationization and metalation of photosensitizers improved PDI of microorganisms [7,28,29]. For instance, cationic zinc pyridinium phthalocyanine [30] and cationic N-methylpyridinium porphyrins [31] were among the examples of photosensitizers capable of photoinactivating both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. These pioneer studies helped to realize that effective PDI of Gram-negative bacteria required a photosensitizer with a pronounced cationic charge. The quest for cationic photosensitizers with stronger light absorption in the near-infrared motivated the development of cationic chlorins [32,33], bacteriochlorins [34,35], porphycenes [36] and phthalocyanines [37,38], and the characterization of their PDI effect. Zn(II) cationic anilinium phthalocyanines are among the best examples of cationic metallophthalocyanines: 0.1 1/2M concentrations and 5 min irradiation with 600-700 nm light (50 mW/cm2) led to a 5 logs reduction of S. aureus colonies [39]. Although the inactivation of Gram-negative bacteria is more challenging, PDI using phthalocyanines with different structural motifs were reported [40-48]. Dei et al. used cationic phthalocyanines bearing trialkylammonium groups and were able to reduce E. coli colonies by 6 log units with 1 1/2M photosensitizer concentration and red light irradiation (50 mW/cm2) for 10 min [49]. Cationic phthalocyanines can also inactivate fungi [50-53]. The family of phthalocyanines mentioned above achieved a 6 log reduction of C. albicans at photosensitizer concentrations of 1 1/2M under red light irradiation (50 mW/cm2) for 10 min [49]. A good disinfection consists in decreasing the number of bacteria colonies by 5 or 6 log units. The photosensitizers currently employed in PDI require micromolar concentrations to meet this goal [54]. Attempts to increase the potency of phthalocyanines for PDI should consider the following factors: i) adding cationic groups to increase electrostatic interaction with the outer membrane improves PDI of Gram-negative bacteria and increases hydrophilicity [8,49]; ii) increasing of the size of cationizing alkyl chain favours photosensitizer uptake [50] and may result in enhanced antimicrobial activity [55,56]. The role of differences in cell wall thickness between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (20-80 nm for Gram-positive bacteria and 10-15 nm for Gram-negative species) was investigated using crystal violet-based photosensitizers. The depth of the modified derivative in the bacterial cell walls plays a key role in its PDI selectivity, which in turns is controlled by the positive charges of the photosensitizer [57]. It must be realized that PDI in vivo adds the problem that increased phototoxicity is often correlated with damage to normal tissue [58], and is still unclear how to favour PDI of microorganisms without phototoxicity towards human cells. Structure-activity relationships and formulations for PDI must also consider cytotoxicity towards eukaryotic cells. It came to our attention that imidazole-containing metallophthalocyanines showed good photosensitizing results towards cancer cells [59], but their use in PDI of bacteria was overlooked.

However, when the decision maker is concerned about perceptions of the entire stakeholder group instead of only the respondents in a sample, it becomes necessary to admit uncertainty about the mean of the entire population of stakeholders. This uncertainty depends on the prior knowledge about the stakeholder preferences, but also on sample size and variation among respondents. Although the variability between the individual values in a group has been studied earlier in the context of MCDA (Scala et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2017), probabilistic approaches to combine perceptions and quantify the uncertainty about the group consensus from a diverse set of participants to be used in formal decision-making models are lacking. We propose a sequential Bayesian Belief Network (BBN) approach (Korb and Nicholson, 2010) to analyse and acknowledge the uncertainty about the group mean as part of the MCDA. The approach consist of two stages: (1) a continuous model for estimating the stakeholder group-specific parameters and the related uncertainties, and (2) a discrete state graphical element for more interactive and visual analysis. The latter can be connected to an influence diagram (ID) - an extension of a BBN for solving decision analytic problems under uncertainty (Nielsen and Jensen, 2009) - where it serves as a multi-criteria utility function in probabilistic evaluation of alternative management strategies, enabling the search of jointly optimal solution. The present approach allows transparent analysis of estimated variability between and within the stakeholder groups selected, as well as providing insights regarding whether listening to one group instead of another would actually change the formally optimal management strategy. Bayesian inference has been widely utilized in population analyses and fisheries stock assessments to evaluate the uncertainty about unknown population parameters (Mantyniemi and Romakkaniemi, 2002; Mantyniemi et al., 2005; Michielsens et al., 2006; Mantyniemi et al., 2015). Here we suggest to use the approach to estimate the opinions of the stakeholder populations. The estimation of uncertainty about population mean can be achieved using the Bayesian approach, whereas frequentist approaches, such as bootstrapping, only provide measures of uncertainty about potential values of point estimators of the population mean under assumed true value (e.g. standard error of the sample mean). They do not measure uncertainty about the population mean itself. Even if the population mean was known exactly, potential point estimators still have non-zero variance. The approach works even for small sample sizes, as Bayesian statistics provide probabilistic expression of uncertainty about parameters of interest for the given sample size (Hox et al., 2012, 2014; McNeish, 2016). Graphical BBN is an efficient approach when modelling uncertain and complex issues associated with stakeholder involvement (Maskrey et al., 2016; Salliou et al., 2017; Xue et al., 2017) as it provides a transparent system to engage stakeholders in complex management and decision-making processes (Xue et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2018).

He was a tiny man of elegant proportions: so tiny, so elegant, that one felt inclined to put him under a glass case and stick him on a mantelpiece. He leant his small arms upon the parapet of a wall as they were approaching Zell, shifted the knapsack on his back with sylph-like grace, and murmured ecstatically, with a side glance at the stalwart peasant-women carrying basketfuls of fodder in huge creels on their backs in the field close by, "How delicious! How charming! How essentially picturesque! How characteristically Tyrolean!" His companion scanned him up and down with an air of some passing amusement. "Why, I didn't know you'd ever been in the Tyrol before," he objected, bluntly. And, in point of fact, when they started together from Munich that morning on their autumn tour, Florian Wood had never yet crossed the Austrian frontier. But what of that? He had got out of the train some five hours back at Jenbach station, and walked the sixteen miles from there to Zell; and in the course of the tramp he had matured his views on the characteristics of the Tyrol. But he waved one lily-white hand over the earth none the less with airy dismissal of his friend's implied criticism. "How often shall I have to tell you, my dear Deverill," he said blandly, in his lofty didactic tone-the tone which, as often happens with very small men, came most familiarly of all to him-"that you unduly subordinate the ideal to the real, where you ought rather to subordinate the real to the ideal. This, you say, is the Tyrol-the solid, uncompromising, geographically definite Tyrol of the tax-gatherer, the post-master, and the commercial traveller-bounded on the north by Bavaria, on the south by Italy, on the east by the rude Carinthian boor, and on the west by the collection of hotels and pensions marked down on the map as the Swiss Republic. Very well then; let me see if there's anything Tyrolese at all to be found in it. I have instinctive within me a picture of the true, the ideal Tyrol. I know well its green pastures, its upland slopes, its innocent peasantry, its fearless chamois-hunters, its beautiful, guileless, fair-haired maidens. Arriving by rail to-day in this its prosaic prototype-cast up, as it were, from the train on the sea-coast of this Bohemia-I turn my eyes with interest upon the imitation Tyrol of real life, and strive earnestly to discover some faint points of resemblance, if such there be, with the genuine article as immediately revealed to me." "And you find none?" Deverill put in, smiling. Florian waved that dainty Dresden china hand expansively once more over the landscape before him, as if it belonged to him. "Pardon me," he said, sententiously; "in many things, I admit, the reality might be improved upon.

The processes underlying smoltification are not merely mechanical but rather complex biochemical cascades that reflect the fish's remarkable adaptability to environmental shifts. These physiological transformations ensure that anadromous salmonids transition from a freshwater habitat-characterized by a relatively stable osmotic environment-to the harsher and more variable conditions of marine ecosystems. Critical to this adaptability is the hormonal interplay initiated by the aforementioned environmental triggers, notably the increase in photoperiod which acts as a primary signal to stimulate the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. This interaction elicits the release of growth hormone and prolactin, followed by an elevation in cortisol levels, which ultimately promotes osmoregulatory adaptations necessary for survival in a saline environment (Sumpter and Penn, 1994). As the salinity levels rise, the physiological response includes heightened production of the ion transport proteins, particularly NKA 1b and NKCC1a, with an attendant increase in the gill surface area due to cellular hypertrophy. This augmentation enhances the fish's capacity to excrete the excess salts that accumulate in the body as it adapts to seawater. Furthermore, the transformation also includes a shift in metabolic pathways to accommodate the increased energy demands during migration and adaptation. Enhanced gill permeability is facilitated by aquatic calcium uptake as fish establish a delicate equilibrium within their internal environments, underscoring the intricate relationship between ion regulation and energy metabolism. More than merely a physiological rite of passage, smoltification embodies evolutionary sophistication, underscoring the idea of an adaptive strategy that has persisted through countless generations of salmonids. A hallmark of this evolution lies in the diverse genetic underpinnings that shape smoltification across various species and populations. Recent genomic studies are shedding light on the polymorphisms associated with these critical physiological processes. Variability in genes linked to osmoregulation and smolt development has been documented, suggesting a strong selective pressure related to differing environmental conditions faced by salmonids during their life cycles (Hassanin et al., 2018). Moreover, these insights highlight the role of epigenetic influence in smoltification, where changes in gene expression occur without alterations to the underlying DNA sequence. Epigenetic modifications, triggered by environmental cues such as temperature fluctuations and photoperiod variations, can lead to heritable changes in smoltification timelines across generations. This phenomenon suggests a capacity for populations to rapidly adjust to shifting climates or habitat destruction, albeit with potential costs associated with reduced diversity or increased susceptibility to disease due to a narrowed genetic pool. In light of climate change, these adaptive traits are under significant scrutiny, as shifting temperatures and altered freshwater flow patterns affect habitat availability and the timing of migration cycles (Petersen et al., 2016). Consequently, aquaculture practices must evolve to accommodate these changes, ensuring that the environmental parameters of hatcheries mirror those of the wild to guarantee the survival of smolts released back into natural waterways. By aligning aquaculture practices with the natural rhythms of salmonid biology, we might forge pathways that sustainably connect commercial interests with ecological integrity, paving the way for future generations of this remarkable species. The understanding gained from salmonid research not only deepens our appreciation of their life history strategies but also reinforces the importance of preserving the delicate interplay between these migratory fish and the ecosystems they inhabit, ensuring their persistence amidst the challenges posed by an ever-changing environment.

When we had taken our last look, he tucked my hand under his arm and told me that one day he and I should take a trip abroad.... Owing to the shortage in our money supply, we had decided to go to a theatrical boarding house. Will was depending on his father to send him an allowance throughout the summer, and while it would be sufficient for his needs, now that he was married - well, we should have a chance to test the saying that two can live as cheaply as one. Our marriage had been a secret one - besides the "star" and one or two members of the company, we had taken no one into our confidence. Will's family - his father, a sister and brother - his mother having died about the time I came into his life - all were intolerant of the stage and its people. Though I was not yet a "really truly" actress, the fact that Will had met me "in the profession" would have prejudiced them against me; added to this was the fact that Will, himself a tyro, taking a wife at the very threshold of his career would not be looked at through our love-coloured glasses. The effect my marriage might have upon my own relatives never troubled me; my father and mother belonged to that great class of incompetent parenthood which brings children into the world without any actual love for them. Never questioning their fitness for child-rearing, they divine no greater responsibility than providing bodily necessities and a more or less superficial education. When, at the restless age of sixteen, I announced my determination to become an actress, there was some surface opposition, but no effort was made to enquire into my fitness for the dramatic profession, or the fitness of the dramatic profession as a career for any innocent and unprotected young girl. I had been highly successful as an amateur, and, as it was not necessary that I earn my own living, the stage appeared to their insapient minds an interesting playground for a dilettante daughter.... One week in a theatrical boarding-house was all we could endure. I wonder why it is that the rank and file of the theatrical profession are at such pains to impress one another with their importance. The flippant familiarity with which they referred to "Charley" or "Dan" Frohman; the coarse criticism of their fellow-actors, which Will called "knocking"; their easy disregard of the conventions, especially between the sexes; a bombastic retailing of their own exploits, as "how I jumped on and saved the show, with only one rehearsal"; talking "shop" to the exclusion of every other subject in the world. I overheard one of the actresses at the next table say we were "very up-stage," which Will interpreted as "not sociable, and having too good an opinion of one's self."

The new leaders simply can't face the reality that traditional reference services are being eclipsed by Google and Yahoo. Ginnie Cooper, director at Brooklyn Public Library and chair of the committee, talked about how most of the top companies in the US at the turn of the 20th century no longer existed at the turn of the 21st. The few that are still around have drastically changed their businesses. She specifically noted that GE made and sold light bulbs in 1900; today they still sell bulbs, but now, they outsource the manufacture and just put them in GE-branded boxes. Instead, GE makes its money on finance and medical imaging technologies, business models that didn't even exist in 1900. This made me think that the library of the future may have automated and hidden their finding services so completely and so effectively that the public face of the service will be utterly different. After an hour of stimulating discussion and a 20-minute break full of lots of smaller, equally intriguing conversations, I gave an overview of the Scan, focusing on the landscapes, the dominant trends (decrease in guided access to content, disaggregation, and collaboration and context), and the three themes (self-sufficiency, satisfaction, and seamlessness). I hit a couple of the major factors as they apply to public libraries: the "third place," the changes in the profession, the collections grid (Lorcan and Eric Childress would disavow the grid if they knew how quickly and shallowly I covered their brilliant concepts), and I wrapped up by saying that if we never ask the unaskable, if we refuse to think the unthinkable, we will never reach beyond our current reality. Increasing the system's complexity, these receptors are expressed in brain regions influencing HPA activity such that the binding of corticosterone can inhibit HPA-activity (i.e., negative feedback) regardless of the continued presence of a stressor or stimulus (de Kloet, 2014; Joels et al., 2008; Sapolsky et al., 2000). Ultimately the amount of corticosterone circulating in the blood stream is controlled by the neural networks that stimulate corticosterone release and those that regulate negative feedback - both of which can be influenced by the two corticosterone receptors: the high affinity mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) and the low affinity glucocorticoid receptor (GR) (Breuner and Orchinik, 2009; Lattin et al., 2012). MR is predominately expressed in the hippocampus in birds and mammals (Baugh et al., 2017; de Kloet, 2014; Dickens et al., 2009; Hodgson et al., 2007; Joels et al., 2008; J. Krause et al., 2015; Senft et al., 2016; Zimmer and Spencer, 2014). In the rodent brain MR are activated by basal concentrations of corticosterone and are thought to regulate basal levels of corticosterone with an overall inhibitory tone (Reddy et al., 2009; Zilliacus et al., 1995). Studies in rodents further indicate that MR can be targeted for insertion in the cellular membrane and this form is thought to act similarly to the low affinity GR receptor to help facilitate the stress response by promoting rapid behavioral responses to elevated plasma corticosterone (Joels et al., 2008). The low-affinity GR is a nuclear receptor with transcriptional activity that is predominately expressed in the paraventricular nucleus, amygdala, cerebral cortex and the hippocampus in rodents (de Kloet, 2014; Joels et al., 2008; Sapolsky et al., 2000). Similar patterns of GR exist in birds except for expression in the hippocampus, which seems more variable across species (Baugh et al., 2017; Hodgson et al., 2007; J. Krause et al., 2015; Senft et al., 2016; Zimmer and Spencer, 2014). GR becomes activated in mammals when corticosterone levels rise during the circadian peak, during a stress response or when metabolic demands rise (Reddy et al., 2009; Reul and de Kloet, 1985; Zilliacus et al., 1995). Changes in MR and GR expression in the avian brain have been correlated with seasonal changes in hormone profiles, selection for high stress responsiveness, and under chronic stress (Dickens et al., 2009; Hodgson et al., 2007; J. Krause et al., 2015). More importantly, food restriction in rodents has been shown to reduce receptor expression in the brain leading to reduced negative feedback and elevated levels of corticosterone (Lee et al., 2000). The interaction between circulating levels of corticosterone, MR and GR expression in the brain and social information to regulate physiology and decision-making processes, however, remain completely unexplored in any taxa. Cornelius et al. (2010) previously demonstrated that social information can alter corticosterone secretion in a bird that is highly adapted to coping with unpredictable food resources.

In Oklahoma, executions are carried out by a series of injections - considered the most humane method. Robert Patton, the director of the Oklahoma Department of Corrections, later revealed what had gone wrong. 'We've had a vein failure in which the chemicals did not make it into the offender,' he said. 'His vein exploded.' Although the precise details are still not clear, it appears that the authorities had to administer the sedative via a catheter into Lockett's groin, after which they were finally able to inject him with the second and third drugs. Mary Fallin, Oklahoma's Governor, immediately ordered a halt to 54 planned executions, and demanded 'an independent review' into how the state executes those on Death Row. Around the world, opinion was divided, as it always is with the death penalty. 'Why should we give him a humane death when he didn't give his victim a humane death?' asked one Oklahoma defence lawyer. 'I think that's a basic instinct.' On the other side of the debate was the United Nations. A spokesman for the High Commissioner for Human Rights declared that the execution process may have amounted to 'cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment' under international human rights law. Also adding their voice to those who condemned the execution was a London-based organisation called Reprieve UK, which campaigns worldwide for the abolition of capital punishment. 'States need to stop conducting secretive, experimental executions,' said Maya Foa, head of Reprieve's Death Penalty team. Ms Foa, a 30-year-old former teacher, then launched an attack on companies that supplied the drugs used for executions. 'It is a clear demonstration of why no responsible pharmaceutical firm or pharmacy wants to get involved in selling drugs to executioners,' she said. 'How many more of these horrifying events will it take before the authorities in Oklahoma and elsewhere get the message?' However, what Ms Foa - unsurprisingly - failed to mention was that Lockett's execution might never have been botched had it not been for Reprieve. Mary Fallin Govenor of Oklahoma ordered to halt the executions - demanding an independent review. For the past four years, Reprieve has been vigorously lobbying governments and pharmaceutical companies to stop supplying the U.S. Department of Corrections with drugs for executions. The campaign has been so successful that it has brought near chaos to the U.S. justice system, as it has been denied supplies of the tried and tested drugs. As a direct consequence, the authorities have had to test new 'protocols' on their condemned prisoners - some of which have produced agonising and unnecessarily drawn-out deaths.

Stayed up late once more, unable to shake the restlessness that seemed to cling to my skin. Through the darkened hours, I scrolled through the headlines on my phone, absorbing bits of chaos from around the globe. I found myself buried in articles, one after another, with links leading me deeper into a labyrinth of disquieting stories about climate change, economic instability, and political strife. The barrage of information was overwhelming, and yet, I couldn't look away. As dawn broke, I finally pulled myself from the glow of screens to draw a hot bath, the steam rising and curling like ghosts around me. I sank into the water, seeking solace in the quiet of the morning. There, suspended in liquid calm, I reflected on the growing disconnect I felt with the world outside my door. It seemed everyone was shouting to be heard, their voices amplified and entangled in a digital chorus that I struggled to decipher. I wished for a moment of clarity, a sliver of peace in a cacophonous landscape. The hours slipped by as I read through fearless prose from authors who dissected society with surgical precision, analyzing the world's problems with a clarity I envied. I found some comfort in the lines of a short story buried in an anthology, each word crafted with care, drawing me momentarily away from the noise. The heroine within was navigating her own tumultuous path, and I felt a kinship with her battle for understanding and authenticity. Afternoon came, and with it, my regular sojourn to the local bookshop. It had become an almost ritualistic escape, ingrained within the framework of my weeks. The familiarity of the place offered a sanctuary of sorts, a place where I could delve into other minds and worlds, even if for just a fleeting moment. Inside, I traced the spines of countless books with the tips of my fingers, my eyes searching for treasures among the shelves. I inhaled the distinctive scent of paper and ink, letting it ground me, reconnect me to a tactile reality that too often felt distant. Serendipitously, I stumbled upon a memoir by a writer I had long admired for her unapologetic exploration of the human condition. The pages whispered promises of untold stories, and I clutched it with an eagerness that cracked through my malaise. Settled into a worn armchair with a steaming cup of coffee beside me, I was struck by a wave of latent hope. With each page turned, I felt a piece of myself awaken, the words reviving dormant curiosities and a thirst for genuine connection. This book became a lifeline, a reminder that however shredded the world appeared, it was important to find beauty in unexpected places and strength in the stories we share. As evening descended, casting the city in hues of gold and shadow, I walked home, mindful of the shifting light. My thoughts lingered on the need to disengage from the perpetual din, to find moments of stillness in an ever-churning world. I resolved to do so, to cultivate quiet spaces where I could listen, not just to the noise, but to the subtler, often overlooked whirring of life. Perhaps through this simplicity, I might reforge my connection to the world, one silent, intent footstep at a time.

I was caught in this endless loop of comparison, feeling like I was drowning in a sea of inadequacy. Each day, I opened my social media feed, and there they were-the beautiful lives, the pristine homes, the neatly curated feeds that screamed perfection. I felt like I was living in grayscale while they were bathed in vibrant color. But what I've come to realize is that the highlight reels we see are often just that-reels of highlights that fail to capture the behind-the-scenes chaos that many women, including myself, navigate daily. It wasn't until I stumbled upon a community of women who were brave enough to share their messy, unfiltered lives that I truly started to shift my perspective. They were talking about the chaos of motherhood, the days filled with tantrums, laundry, and the occasional meltdown over a forgotten snack. Their vulnerability dismantled the facade I had built around my own perceived flaws. I began to understand that everyone was wrestling with their internal battles, even those I had held up on a pedestal. This is crucial: we are all human, and humanity carries imperfection as part of its DNA. When I began to embrace my messiness, my insecurities softened. I implemented changes in how I viewed myself and my life. I stopped checking my social media to see what others were doing and began honing in on what made me feel fulfilled. I discovered the importance of gratitude-grateful for my home, my children, and yes, even those quirky imperfections that once felt so unbearable. Over time, I became aware that my worth wasn't dictated by likes or followers or the pristine lifestyle I compared myself against. I carved out pockets of time in my day for self-care, for my passions, and for reflection. Journaling became a lifeline, a space where I could unload the heavy expectations I held onto for far too long. I wrote down my achievements, no matter how small, and celebrated them. But let's talk about those comparisons. We all know they creep in, right? When you are scrolling through an idealized version of reality, it's easy to slip back into that familiar mindset. Yet, it's essential to recognize when those feelings arise. When I feel that twinge of envy surfacing, I stop and ask myself, "What is the root of this feeling?" More often than not, it's not about the other person's success but a reflection of some insecurity within myself. And then I pivot. Instead of wallowing, I choose to reach out and connect. I either celebrate their success or find a way to incorporate some of their strengths into my own life without a tinge of jealousy, rather with inspiration. It's about building each other up. By shifting the focus from competition to camaraderie, I thrive within a supportive network of women. This journey of self-discovery and self-acceptance has not been easy, and it's one I still navigate each day. However, those moments of comparison still serve as opportunities-opportunities for growth, for connection, and ultimately for a deeper understanding of myself. It's a continuous process, one I am committed to fostering not just for myself but for you, too. It's time to discard the exhausting notion that we must measure up to anyone else and instead celebrate our unique journeys. Here's to our imperfect paths, intertwined and beautiful just as they are!

Neil Young joined in seamlessly, adding another layer of depth. Their set ended with "Suite: Judy Blue Eyes," and it felt like being part of something truly special. The variety of performances made the whole experience diverse and engaging. Each band brought their unique energy to the stage, combining to make a memorable event that highlighted the essence of live music. It's concerts like these that remind me why I love music so much. The Bridge School Benefit is one for the books, going beyond expectations and delivering something extraordinary. Can't wait for next year!

Tripoli, Libya (CNN) - As the sun dipped below the horizon, casting long shadows over the battered streets of Tripoli, a palpable sense of despair enveloped the city. The sirens that had become a common backdrop to daily life pierced through the thick air, serving as a grim reminder of the chaos that had befallen the capital. Residents scavenged for basic necessities, their faces etched with fatigue and hopelessness. "It's as if the world has forgotten us," lamented Fatima, a community organizer, clutching her child close as she navigated through the debris-strewn alleyways. With dwindling supplies and no consistent means of sustenance or hydration, families resorted to desperate measures. Reports of looting increased as hunger set in. The rebel's Front Line Emergency Response Team struggled to maintain order, tasked with distributing rations and water wherever possible. Yet the need was far greater than the supply, leaving many to go hungry. "We can only help those on the brink of survival," a spokesperson for the team, Khaled Ameer, stated, frustration evident in his eyes. "Every day, I'm confronted with people who should not have to endure this." Beyond the immediate human suffering lay a grim political reality. The standoff between the rebel forces and Gadhafi loyalists threatened to escalate, compounding the already critical humanitarian crisis. The streets of certain neighborhoods buzzed with rumors of imminent skirmishes. Families huddled together in dimly lit basements, listening intently for the sounds of conflict. "This is our life now," murmured Omar, a local shopkeeper, gesturing towards his boarded-up store. "All I want is for my children to feel safe again." Internationally, calls for intervention grew louder, with world leaders scrambling to find a diplomatic solution to the escalating violence. The U.N. Security Council convened for an emergency session, yet divisions remained evident as member states voiced differing opinions on how best to assist Libya. "We cannot afford to let this situation spiral further out of control," emphasized French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius, pressing for a coordinated humanitarian response. But the language of compassion was often drowned out by the cacophony of military strategy, as nations weighed their options on a geopolitical chessboard fraught with risks. Amidst this turmoil, the resilience of the Libyan people shone through. Community kitchens sprang up to feed the hungry, and volunteers risked their safety to distribute water. Hope flickered in the eyes of those whom adversity had tried to extinguish. "We will endure," declared Aisha, a teacher who had turned her home into a shelter. "Our spirit cannot be broken." Yet the specter of violence loomed large, as nighttime curfews forced citizens to retreat into the shadows. Explosions echoed in the distance, punctuating the night air, while families nestled together, soaking in moments of warmth amid the chaos. The situation remained uncertain, balances of power shifted with each passing hour, leaving all of Tripoli on a knife's edge. "We are waiting," said Hisham, a young artist whose canvases confronted the realities of war. "Waiting for change, for hope...but for now, we must endure." In the heart of the city, the once vibrant markets stood eerily silent, save for the whispers of those who dared to dream of a better tomorrow. The road ahead was treacherous, but the determination of the Libyan people-scarred yet unyielding-served as a testament to their resilience, a beacon of possibility amid the shadows of despair.

Charley shrugged off Evil Ed's taunts, trying to focus on the notes scrawled haphazardly in his math textbook. The buzzing voices of classmates flowed around him like a river he struggled to wade through, their energy too vibrant, too alive for his current mood. Amy's absence weighed on him. He knew she'd meant it last night when she said she was ready, and yet, just as they found themselves teetering on the edge of something significant, he'd hesitated, his attention caught by the shadowed figures next door. His mind kept replaying the scene, those two men carrying what he swore was a coffin. Could that be a trick of the light, an overactive imagination spurred by late-night horror shows and too many tales of the undead? Or was his neighborhood hiding a sinister secret? His gaze drifted to the window, where sunlight bounced off the leaves of the oak trees lining the street. The ordinary charm of the suburban scene only deepened his unease. He couldn't shake the feeling that something unnatural had settled into the bones of every house on their quiet block. "Attention! Earth to Charley!" Evil Ed waved a hand in front of his face, snapping him back to reality. The classroom felt too bright, too real, after the shadows of his thoughts. "What, Ed?" Charley replied tersely, gripping the desk's edge as if to anchor himself there. "You've got that look again," Ed said, arching an eyebrow with mock curiosity. "Like you're expecting Dracula to waltz in and offer to make you his sidekick." "Very funny," Charley retorted, rolling his eyes, but Ed's words hit closer to home than either of them expected. A chill crept up Charley's spine, and he shook it off, forcing a casual tone. "I'm fine. Just thinking." Ed smirked. "Sure you are. Which is why you've been staring at the window like you expect it to bite you. Just admit it, man. You were watching another Peter Vincent marathon, weren't you?" "Drop it, Ed," Charley snapped, wishing more than anything to shut down the conversation about last night. The truth was, he hadn't told anyone, not even Amy, about the strange things he'd seen. He wanted to handle it himself, unravel whatever oddity had caught his imagination or-more worryingly-whether his imagination had begun unraveling. Just then, the bell rang, a clamor of sound that signaled freedom and distraction, at least temporarily. Charley gathered his things, trying to mask his eagerness to leave the confines of the classroom and head towards something - anything - that felt like progress. He just needed to figure out what that was. The school corridor was an ebb and flow of students' conversations, laughter, and feet shuffling to the next class. Charley sidestepped a couple arguing by the lockers and shoved his books into his backpack, finally making his way to the main doors. The thought of what he might discover next door consumed him. He had to know if the night shadows held truths wrapped in fear or if he'd simply woven stories as a child might, scared of the dark. He pushed through the crowd, stepping out into the bright, almost blinding daylight, and headed home, determined to uncover whatever was hiding just beyond the apparent normalcy of his world.

When the Brookville Hotel, the home of famous, affordable and hearty fried chicken dinners, was forced to move locations in 2000 due to a sewage issue, the owners decided to make an exact replica of their former home, one their loyal regulars would recognize. The new version, located 40 miles away from Brookville in Abilene, Kansas, includes a rebuilt facade and as many of the old doors and fixtures from the original hotel restaurant, with origins dating back to 1870, as possible. Brookville Hotel stopped welcoming overnight guests decades ago, but the name lives on. The chicken dinner, served since the current owners' great-grandmother originated it in 1915, includes coleslaw, half a fried chicken, mashed potatoes, creamed corn, biscuits and ice cream, all for $15. 105 E. Lafayette, Abilene, Kansas (785) 263-2244. Shady Glen, 1948. Manchester, Connecticut, institution Shady Glen began back in 1948 as a classic soda fountain and ice cream maker, the offshoot of a dairy farm. When the original owners, John and Bernice Rieg, decided to branch out to lure business in the colder months, they added savory diner staples to their menu - including a special take on the classic griddle-top cheeseburger featuring a giant crown (using four slices) of crispy cheese. Burgers and homemade ice cream are still served in the old diner today, which was enlarged and renovated over the decades but has kept the same look since 1978. 840 Middle Turnpike E, Manchester, Connecticut (860) 649-4245. Cold Springs Tavern, 1886. Cold Springs Tavern, founded in 1886 on a site established as a stagecoach stop in the 1860s, is located 20 minutes north of Santa Barbara, California, nestled on a mountainside off a winding road. Its buildings, a group of low log cabins outfitted with fireplaces, taxidermy and animal hides, have been preserved through the decades, making this a local destination, even without much signage or promotion. The place is big with bikers, especially on Sundays when live music is offered and the Log Cabin Bar offers their locally famous tri-tip steak sandwiches. 5995 Stagecoach Rd., Santa Barbara, California (805) 967-0066. It was in this valley that lived a solitary old man whose name was Harney. He was a hunter by profession, and for thirty years had roamed through the vast forests of the far west, seeking food for himself and his family. In the prime of life he had married a young girl who came with him from the Atlantic states, and together they had lived happily in the solitude of nature. The children of the marriage were three sons and four daughters. The eldest son, a lad of sixteen, was called Tom; the second, William, was fifteen; while the youngest, Harry, was only ten years of age. The girls were Mary, Sarah, Jane, and Ellen. All these children, excepting the last named, were tall and finely formed, and of a complexion so clear and bright that they might have passed for Spaniards, although their features were decidedly Saxon. Their father and mother, however, were both of a fairer hue, and possessed the fine blue eyes and light hair characteristic of the people of northern Europe. It was in the year 18 - that a party of five hunters, consisting of Mr Harney and his four elder children, started forth on a hunting expedition which was to occupy them for several weeks. They were mounted on ponies, and each carried a rifle slung across his shoulders. With the exception of Tom, the eldest boy, none of the party had ever been on a similar expedition, but under the guidance of their father, who knew every foot of the country, they felt no doubt of being successful. They rode along merrily, chatting gaily as they went, until they reached a point about half-way between their home and the distant mountains, when they halted beneath the shade of a large tree, and sat down to rest themselves. As soon as the halt was made, the younger boys began to look out for game, and they were rewarded by seeing a herd of antelopes grazing close at hand. These animals, though timid enough at ordinary times, are sometimes known to approach quite near to human beings, especially if they are disturbed by dogs. A small pack of hounds, belonging to the family, had accompanied the party, and, finding that their masters had stopped, they scampered off in search of prey. Seeing that the antelopes were likely to escape, Tom spurred forward, followed by his brothers and sisters. In a few minutes the whole party were galloping furiously after the fleet-footed creatures, and in another moment the antelopes turned upon them in a body, and began to fight for their lives. The hounds were soon engaged with the foremost of the band, and the riders were hard pressed by the remainder, which darted furiously to right and left, charging the horses with their sharp horns, and tossing their heads defiantly in the air. The conflict continued for some time, during which the hunters fired repeatedly, killing a number of the animals. At length, however, the hounds, who were almost exhausted, gave way, and the antelopes, turning suddenly, charged back upon their assailants, who were just about to renew the contest. One of the beasts rushed directly at Tom, who raised his rifle, took deliberate aim, and fired. The animal fell dead, and the rest of the herd disappeared in the distance. Having secured his trophy, Tom dismounted, and, taking the knife from his belt, proceeded to cut off the head of the antelope, intending to carry it home. The rest of the party also dismounted, and commenced skinning the bodies of the animals.

He had already curried her thoroughly, and now he was hard at work with brush and comb. She stood perfectly quiet, save when the touch came upon some specially ticklish part, and then she would stretch out her neck, draw in her breath, and tremble. Her master would stop a moment, pat her, speak kindly to her, and proceed. But ever and anon his hand would drop to his side, and he would stand gazing up at the sky, whence the light fell through a rift in the clouds, ruddy and warm as if it came direct from the bosom of the sun. His face wore a look of expectation. Was there something about to happen? Or did he only feel that this was one of the mornings on which anything might happen? He resumed his task, and finished one side of the mare, then walked round her head to begin the other. At the same moment the sun went down behind the cloud-rift. The flush faded from the dial, and the cold blue of a winter-day filled the sky. Malcolm dropped his brushes, and, turning his face upward, stood once more gazing into the heaven. A shadow crossed his countenance. He turned away, led the mare back to her stall, gave her corn, and left her. Then he took his way to the stables, and thence to the harness-room. There he busied himself with various matters until noon. When he returned to the yard, the sun was shining again, and the wind had changed. He drew his watch from his pocket, looked at it, and put it back with a sigh. He then entered the house by a side-door. The kitchen regions were deserted. All the servants were at their dinner except Jeannie, the cook's daughter, who was waiting at table, and who had just carried a huge sirloin to the dining parlour, where sat Mr. Soutar, the steward, and Miss Horn, the governess, making what haste they could over their meal, for the former wanted to get to the stables, and the latter to finish a letter to her mother. "What are ye wantin', Ma'colm?" said Jeannie, appearing suddenly before him, with her arms bare, and her apron tucked up. "I want my dinner, Jeannie," answered Malcolm. "Ye're ower late for that, Ma'colm." "I'll take pot-luck." "There's nae luck aboot the pot the day. It's jist stock." "That'll do." "Weel, ye can gang ben to the hoosekeeper's room, and sit doon. Ye'll get yer denner there." Malcolm went to Mrs. Courthope's sitting-room, and found the housekeeper seated at her daintily spread table, with a plateful of roast beef and greens before her. She was a tall woman, with a large nose, a small mouth, and a long chin, which somehow suggested that she kept her lips together that the better to hold her tongue between her teeth. She wore a black silk gown, and a clean white cap bordered with muslin lace. She received Malcolm respectfully, but without cordiality. "Sit ye doon, Ma'colm," she said; "ye're welcome to what there is." "Thank you, mem," returned Malcolm. "It looks very nice." And he drew in his chair. "If ye please, mem," he added, "will you ask Jeannie to bring me a glass of beer?"
