Winds from the Ural mountains, winds from the Atlantic celebrated Walpurgis-night on the lawn of Plasencia; and, on such occasions, to look through the riven garden, the swaying flowers and grasses, the tossing birch saplings, at the tranced fields of the view was to experience the same aesthetic emotion as when one looks at the picture of a great painter. But the back of Plasencia had another glory-its superb herbaceous border, which, waving banners of the same hues, only brighter, marched boldly into the view, and became one with it. Now in September it was stiffened by annuals: dahlias, astors, snapdragon, sunflowers; Californian poppies whose whiteness-at any rate in the red poppyland of East Anglia-always seems exotic, miraculous, suggesting the paradoxical chemical action of the Blood of the Lamb. There were also great clumps of violas, with petals of so faint a shade of blue or yellow that every line of their black tracery stood out clear and distinct, and which might have been the handiwork of some delicate-minded and deft-fingered old maid, expressing her dreams and heart's ease in a Cathedral city a hundred years ago. As to herbaceous things proper, there was St. John's wort, catmint, borrage, sage; their stalks grown so long and thick, their blossoms so big and brave, that old Gerard would have been hard put to see in them his familiars-the herbs that, like guardian angels, drew down from the stars the virtue for the homely offices of easing the plough-boy's toothache, the beldame's ague. A great lawn spread between the border and the house; it was still very threadbare owing to the patriotic pasturage that, during the last years of the War, it had afforded to half a dozen sheep, but it was darned in so many places by the rich, dark silk of clover leaves as almost to be turned into a new fabric. Well, then, the view and border lay simmering in the late sunshine. A horse was dragging a plough against the sky-line, and here and there thin streams of smoke were rising from heaps of smouldering weeds. In the nearer fields, Teresa could discern small, moving objects of a dazzling whiteness-white leghorns gleaning the stubble; and from time to time there reached her the noise of a distant shot, heralding a supper of roast hare or partridge in some secluded farm-house. Then, like a Danish vessel bound for pillage in Mercia, white, swift, compact, a flock of wood pigeons would flash through the air to alight in a far away field and rifle the corn.

But the Markenmores, easily as they allowed their butler to rule them in certain things, were folk who would not permit interference with time-honoured custom and arrangement, and so gold cups and silver salvers, meticulously polished and carefully dusted, glittered in careless profusion on the massive oak sideboards, and rare ivories and priceless china stood on the open presses and ancient cabinets-as if, said Braxfield plaintively, they were of no more value than the trumpery things arranged in the museum of the neighbouring market-town. And therefore he locked up the house at eight o'clock every night, and carried the keys of some baker's dozen of doors to his butler's pantry: whoever, master or man, maid or mistress, desired to walk out of Markenmore Court, after that hour, had to apply to Braxfield for the means of egress. On a certain evening in the third week of April, in the year 1912, Braxfield, the simple dinner to which Mr. Harry Markenmore and his sister Valencia sat down every night at seven o'clock, being well over, set out on his usual round of the doors. He always began with the smaller ones and ended up with the great triple door that opened on the terrace. And here came in another of his fads-before finally locking and bolting that door, Braxfield invariably stepped out on the terrace, crossed it to the balustrade which fenced it in from the widespreading park that stretched in front, and took a view of all that lay before him: he did this irrespective of the seasons; sometimes, therefore, as in the case of dark winter evenings, he saw nothing but gloom: in summer he saw a great deal of beauty. On this particular occasion he saw the twilight settling upon the old elms and beeches, and over the undulating meadows which lay between Markenmore and the level lands to the southward. The twilight was settling fast, then: within the few minutes during which Braxfield stood there, looking about him, he saw it through the dusk; the woods and coverts became blurred and indistinct shapes, and beyond them, a mile away, the lights of the village began to twinkle in the darkness. At that he turned towards the door-and then suddenly stopped. Somewhere behind him, a man, taking long rapid strides, was advancing across the lawn beneath the terrace. There was a powerful lamp just within the big doorway: its rays spread fanwise across the terrace and over the steps which led to the lawn. As Braxfield lingered, wondering who it was that approached (for visitors of any sort were rare at Markenmore Court in those days) a tall figure strode into this arc of light and moved hurriedly up the steps, making for the door-the figure of a big, athletic man, whose evening clothes were only partly concealed by a light, unbuttoned overcoat.

What's going on with me? Well, I suppose it's time to dive into the chaos that has been my week. First, let me clue you in on the nitty-gritty of the day-to-day madness that keeps my brain swirling like the currents in a reef tank. You know, trying to keep those nutrient levels stable is a mind game of its own, but that's a discussion for another day, you know what I mean? It's been one of those weeks where every moment feels like I'm juggling fire torches blindfolded on a unicycle. I finally managed to upgrade my lighting setup-oh, how the corals are beaming now! You never really realize how crucial lighting is until you see the fluorescent beauty of your softies and SPS just bloom under the right conditions. It's like watching a symphony unfold in chromatic bursts of life. I swear, those LEDs are smarter than me, and I'm convinced they're plotting something in secret Morse code when I'm not looking. And let's not forget the torrential rain that tried to reenact the Great Flood. You'd think after living all these years by the coast, I'd have a better relationship with water that isn't encased in acrylic, but alas, nature always finds a way to humble us. My commute was like navigating through a waterpark, except with less fun and more exasperation. On a lighter note, the new fish shipment came in, and it was like Christmas morning unwrapping those treasures. Just imagine unboxing these vibrant swimmers, each with its own personality, ready to explore the new aquatic kingdom. Watching them take to their new environment is a joy-seeing them glide around the live rock like acrobats performing for an audience of one. The blennies and gobies are particularly amusing; they're like the clowns of the reef, always finding the weirdest nook to squish into, as if in some sort of fishy game of peek-a-boo. Speaking of clowns, did I mention the bizarre escapade involving my cat and the neighbors' Halloween decorations? Yeah, she decided to make friends with an inflatable ghost. Watching that play out from my window was better than any sitcom I'd ever binged. Maybe she was just trying to learn the secret to their eerie luminescence to pass on to her finned companions-a feline-reef conspiracy in the making! I'm also knee-deep in planning my next big DIY project. There's something truly rewarding about building your own sump or custom refugium. The creativity and ingenuity that goes into crafting the ideal filtration system can be a therapy of sorts, grounding my scattered thoughts into a focused flow, much like the steady current I've perfected in my tanks. Next week, who knows? Maybe I'll even dabble in some aqua-scaping workshops. You never stop learning in this hobby; that's what keeps the passion burning. And yet, as we sit here, our discussions ricocheting like hyperactive ping-pong balls, I realize the essence of what makes this all worthwhile. It's not just the corals or the clownfish or even the perfect pH balance-it's these conversations, these shared stories, that make each day feel like an episode in our own peculiar series. Whether it's reef-keeping or life, we're all just trying to keep our tanks from crashing, right? And with that, dear friends, let's venture once more into the depths of The Reef Keeping World.

For example, you said that your work focuses on identifying novel non-invasive biomarkers of aging in human subjects and also that your recent research has shown that obesity is associated with accelerated aging at the cellular level. These are big claims. Can you explain to us what you mean by these two statements and how they relate to each other? Yeah, absolutely. So essentially my main area of interest is trying to understand why some people develop chronic diseases like type 2 diabetes cardiovascular disease and cancer and others don't and what we're interested in is the role of metabolic health and specifically obesity. And so one of the things that we found is that when you look at somebody who's obese compared to someone who isn't they actually appear to be older on a cellular level. So when you look at the cells, they seem to be aged prematurely and we think that this may be contributing to their increased risk of developing these chronic diseases and ultimately Premature mortality. Okay, so can you give us some examples of these non-invasive markers that you're measuring? Yes, sure. So one of the main ones that we use is called telomere length and what these are is they're basically the protective caps on the end of your chromosomes. And what happens is every time your cell divides. This cap gets shorter and shorter until eventually it reaches a point where it can no longer divide anymore and it dies off and this is one of the mechanisms by which we age so if you can imagine somebody who's overweight or obese who might have premature aging at the cellular level. What we see is that their telomeres are shorter and so we can measure those using blood samples. That's quite interesting because I remember from school biology classes that the telomeres are often described as being similar to the plastic tip on a shoelace. But then I was reading that actually it's not entirely clear whether the telomeres themselves are the cause of aging or if they are just kind of the symptom of something else that's going on inside our cells. What's your opinion on this? Is there any consensus within the research community? No, it's definitely not clear and I think that's probably the reason why we haven't seen a massive uptake in clinical practice yet because we don't know whether the telomeres are driving this process of aging or whether they're simply a consequence of aging and therefore whether intervening to try and change them will actually make any difference. There's certainly lots of evidence now that they're linked to various different diseases. So for example, we know that individuals who have shorter telomeres tend to have higher rates of heart disease and cancer and stroke and dementia and all sorts of things. But again, we don't know whether that's causative or whether it's just that they're sort of both happening at the same time. And so it's something that needs further investigation. But certainly there seems to be a link between the telomeres and aging. I think the other thing that we should say is that although we've been talking about telomeres as a marker of aging. It's not necessarily the case that everybody who has short telomeres is unhealthy and vice versa. It's not the case that everyone who has long telomeres is necessarily Healthy. So it's not necessarily a direct relationship. But what we do find is that when you compare groups of people that there does seem to be this relationship between telomere length and aging. That's super interesting. Do you think that this means that in the future we'll be able to calculate our biological age based on these markers? And if so, what would we do with that information? Yeah, absolutely.

A comprehensive study conducted by Hale et al. (2012) found that the PAH concentrations in biochars pyrolyzed at 250-900 C ranged from 0.07 to 45 mg/ kg. A more recent study revealed that the total concentrations of 16 USEPA-priority PAHs in 43 biochars produced at 400-750 C varied from 0.4 to 2000 mg/kg (Hilber et al., 2017). According to Hilber et al. (2012), the dominant PAHs in biochars produced from wood, elephant grass, and coniferous/deciduous wood residues (pyrolyzed at 600-750 C) include naphthalene (40%-60%) and phenanthrene (10%-30%). To ensure the production of high-quality biochars, organizations such as the International Biochar Initiative (IBI) and the European Biochar Certificate (EBC) have developed numeric criteria for biochar-borne PAHs. IBI initially set the limit value for PAHs in biochars at 6-20 mg/kg (IBI, 2013), but the maximum allowable thresholds were increased from 20 mg/kg to 300 mg/kg (IBI, 2015). Meanwhile, the limit for PAHs in biochars set by EBC was under 12 mg/kg and 4 mg/kg for basic-grade and premium-grade biochars, respectively (EBC, 2012). Given the difference in guidelines on biochar-borne PAHs, there is currently no standardized value on the allowable PAH concentrations in biochars. Therefore, this study may provide some insights into developing product standards for biochars. It was previously pointed out that the application of biochars into farmland soils can release PAHs and result in elevated PAH concentrations in soils (Quilliam et al., 2013; Rombola et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018). After the release of biochar-borne PAHs into soils, plants can absorb PAHs via roots and transport to the edible portions (Gao and Collins, 2009). Consequently, the accumulation of PAHs in food crops grown in biochar-amended soils has been reported as elevated (Khan et al., 2015). In a previous combined greenhouse and field study by Wang et al., they found that biochar application in loam soils increased the concentrations of PAHs in root and leaf vegetable roots and leaves (Wang et al., 2018). Therefore, the potential health risks of PAHs released from biochars should be assessed before agricultural adoption. However, to the best of our knowledge, no study has been undertaken to evaluate food safety and human health risks of biochar-borne PAHs by using extensive datasets available in the literature. The United States Environmental Protection Agency (US-EPA) developed a five-step method, namely data collection, toxicity assessment, exposure pathway, risk characterization, and management in the toxicity assessment of hazardous compounds (Mirsadeghi et al., 2011). The contamination risks of hazardous compounds have potentially adverse impacts on both ecological and human health (Nikolaou et al., 2009). Humans are exposed to PAHs in soils via skin contact, ingestion of contaminated soils, or consumption of contaminated food, thus quantifying their human health risks would require a quantitative assessment of their exposure intensity, frequency, and duration (US EPA, 1991; Mallika et al., 2008).

In addition to the aforementioned barriers, parents may also face difficulties in finding a treatment that aligns with their cultural background and values. Cultural competence is a crucial aspect of effective parent training, as parents from diverse cultural backgrounds may have different parenting styles and expectations that may not be taken into account in traditional therapist-led programs. Moreover, parents from low socioeconomic backgrounds may face additional challenges in accessing parent training due to limited financial resources, transportation issues, and lack of access to healthcare services. Therefore, it is essential to develop parent training programs that are culturally sensitive and tailored to the needs of diverse populations. Furthermore, the lack of flexibility in traditional parent training programs can be a significant barrier for parents. Parents may have conflicting schedules, work or school commitments, and other responsibilities that make it difficult to attend sessions at a fixed time and location. Self-directed interventions, on the other hand, offer more flexibility and convenience, allowing parents to access the program at their own pace and in the comfort of their own home. This can be particularly beneficial for parents who are struggling to balance multiple responsibilities and may not have the time or energy to attend traditional sessions. Despite the potential benefits of self-directed interventions, there are concerns about the quality and effectiveness of these programs. Without the guidance of a trained therapist, parents may not receive the support and feedback they need to implement the parenting strategies effectively. Additionally, the lack of human interaction and social support may lead to feelings of isolation and disconnection, which can negatively impact parental well-being and child outcomes. Therefore, it is essential to develop self-directed interventions that incorporate elements of human interaction and social support, such as online support groups or phone coaching. In conclusion, parent training is a crucial component of treatment for children with ADHD, but it is not without its challenges. Dropout rates are high, and parents may face numerous barriers to participation, including lack of time, resources, and cultural sensitivity. Self-directed interventions offer a promising alternative, but more research is needed to determine their effectiveness and potential benefits. By developing culturally sensitive and flexible parent training programs, we can increase access to effective treatment for children with ADHD and improve parental well-being and child outcomes.

Prior research indicates that the function of basal plane orientation is important in dwell fatigue for dual-phase Ti alloys [9-13]; yet fundamental deformation mechanisms within each hard and soft grain (i.e. contributions of individual slip systems) are still unknown. One hypothesis on time sensitive dwell fatigue is that strain rate sensitivity (SRS) is a crucial factor governing the load shedding phenomenon. As titanium alloys are typically more elastically and plastically anisotropic at the grain scale [14-16], there are likely to be differences in the SRS of different grain orientations due to variable rate sensitivities of the different slip systems [17]. These slip systems are a dislocations on prismatic planes; a dislocations on basal planes; and c+a slip systems on pyramidal slip planes. Each slip system has a different critical resolved shear stresses, where their ratio is likely to be 1/23:4:9 [18,19]. Even though the c+a deformation mode has a significantly higher CRSS value it is still likely to activate, as slip with a type dislocations only does not provide 5 independent deformation modes which are required to accommodate an arbitrary shape change. Nanoindentation has been previously used to study the mechanical response of single grains in titanium alloys. Quasistatic nanoindentation, combined with TEM of Ti-7Al, reveals that indentation into different grain orientations activates different slip systems [20]. In particular indentation into the basal plane activated both c+a type dislocations and a type dislocations. The a type dislocations were of opposite sign to the a component of the c+a dislocations to enable local deformation and support the local curvature around the indent. This supports a prior demonstration [21] that indentation into grains of Ti-6Al-4V revealed clearly that these mechanisms also happen in dual-phase microstructures and in particular that c+a type dislocations are geometrically required if twinning does not activate. This change in plastic deformation mechanism, when indenting into grains of different crystallographic orientation, results in significant anisotropic hardness measurements. Additionally indentation, combined with EBSD, has been used to systematically study grains of different orientations and confirmed that the anisotropic mechanical performance is consistently observed across a range of Ti alloys [14,16,22,23]. Furthermore, experimental data has been fitted with crystal plasticity models has enabled extraction of the critical resolved shear stress for different dislocation types [14,16]. The nanoindentation approach is insightful and relatively inexpensive to undertake, but precise mechanistic analysis is fraught with complications, as the stress state around the indention is complex and there are likely to be significant lengthscale contributions due to the indentation size effect for small indentation depths. Often these effects are considered for relatively isotropic materials, yet in HCP alloys ignoring the effect of orientation is likely to be problematic. This does not diminish from the potential use of nanoindentation to elucidate mechanisms and highlight opportunities for further study.

The use of HSI in the infrared spectral range has also helped to reveal features of artists' techniques such as their preparatory drawing [22,25]. Due to the very broad range of wavelengths available for hyperspectral systems, the transmittance and reflectance response of different layers of paintings and drawings is frequently observed during data analysis. When material that is transparent at a specific wavelength range (but opaque at others) covers material that is reflective within the same spectral range, the underlying material can be detected by the HSI system and is hence revealed in the data acquired. Empowered by signal processing techniques this facilitates a detailed study of the artwork creation process and enables identification of the materials used [26]. Spectral selectivity of HSI data was also used on various occasions to analyse texts of historic value [27-29]. Identification of pigments and inks facilitated by HSI has also been used to aid in dating of manuscripts [27]. Furthermore, HSI technology empowers the recovery of erased and overwritten scripts as well as allowing the determination of appropriate bands for monitoring laser and non-laser cleaning processes [28]. Alongside the aforementioned benefits for art conservation, the potential of hyperspectral imaging in forgery detection has also been recognised. The application of HSI to address the challenge of forensic analysis of documents was successfully applied in the past [30-32]. Classification of different inks after obliteration of the text and the 'crossing lines problem' [30] were studied and analysed with chemometrics-based tools. These techniques applied to HSI data have had a significant impact on forgery recognition and provided objective results compared to traditional visual inspection based judgments [30]. Other forensic applications of HSI were also reported, such as fingerprint detection [33] and for blood stain dating at crime scenes [34]. The implementation of hyperspectral imaging in the aforementioned applications gave access to the rich dataset, however the conclusions drawn from this data were based on subsequent signal processing making it difficult to use by non-experts. In some cases the use of pure spectroscopic techniques achieved sufficient results [25], while in others, more advanced algorithms were applied in order to analyse the data [23,24,26]. It was also recognised that full diagnostic potential of HSI may be improved by implementation of robust data processing algorithms [28]. It is clear that HSI technology combined with advanced signal processing techniques have already found various application in the art world. However, to date these have focused on supporting various aspects of conservation and have allowed researchers to better understand paintings by allowing them to observe materials below the surface of the completed work. In this paper, we illustrate a novel combination of near- and mid-infrared hyperspectral imaging with state-of-the-art signal processing algorithms and background information from experts in the field of art analysis to provide HSI data based classification of paints and artwork for the purposes of authentication.

Therefore, Haverman and Brondel (2013) approach relies on a manipulation to the potential availability of uneaten foods in the first half of a meal and the subsequent detection of this effect at the end of the meal. Since the second half of the meal was essentially identical in both conditions (participants were equally aware that the uneaten foods were unavailable) this paradigm may not be optimized to detect the specific phenomenon of interest. The 'decision making' literature provides a theoretical framework within which to explore this idea. 'Commodity Theory' (Brock, 1968) describes the process that takes place when an individual evaluates a range of products that may or may not be available to them (Lynn, 1991). Specifically, a 'commodity' is valued in its level of unavailability. For example, Fromkin, Olson, Dipboye, and Barnaby (1971) found the rated value of a nylon hose was significantly higher if it was presented as having low availability (as opposed to high) and if participants thought they would be unable to take ownership of the hose. We note that this approach may be particularly relevant to the study of SSS because protocols tend to involve asking participants to evaluate both a food that is available to them eaten (the 'eaten food') and other foods that are not (the 'uneaten food') (e.g., Rolls et al., 1981). The primary aim of this study was to investigate whether effects akin to those described by commodity theory can account for SSS. We reasoned that since the uneaten foods are unavailable, their relative value may increase. This causes a contrast with the eaten food, producing a relative decrease in its value. In other words, an eaten food becomes relatively less appealing because other unavailable uneaten foods increase in their value. In Study 1 we explored this idea by manipulating the perceived availability of uneaten foods. This between-subjects study comprised the following conditions; in the 'available uneaten foods' condition, the participants initially tasted and rated a set of foods. They were then told that they would be given one of these foods to eat ad libitum and that they could switch to another food afterwards. In an 'unavailable uneaten foods' condition, participants initially tasted and rated a set of foods and were then told they would receive one of the foods to eat ad libitum but that they would not be permitted to switch to a different food. Following commodity theory, it was hypothesised that greater SSS should be evident in the unavailable uneaten food condition compared to the available food condition. The second aim of this study was to address a related and fundamental question about whether the mere presence of uneaten foods influences the evaluation of the eaten food (i.e., a participant is given a single food to taste and rate, and no mention is made about the uneaten foods or their availability).

Despite the importance of coastal lowland strata in preserving a record of natural hazard events, the examination of these areas has become increasingly challenging due to extensive human disturbance. In Japan, for instance, the Pacific coast is characterized by narrow tidal flats, which are distributed in coastal areas where subduction has created coastal mountain ranges. These areas are expected to preserve a record of natural hazard events, such as storm surges, tsunamis, and earthquakes. The depositional environments and sedimentary facies in these tidal flats have been examined using geochemical, geological, and paleontological approaches. In a geochemical approach, the total sulfur content (TS) and the ratio of total organic carbon (TOC) to TS (i.e., the C/S ratio) have been used to distinguish between ancient marine and freshwater sedimentary deposits. Berner and Raiswell (1984) analyzed the TS and TOC contents of modern sediments in Chesapeake Bay, United States, and reported that in sediments with >1 wt% TOC, the C/S ratios of marine sediments were between 0.5 and 5.0, with a mean value of 2.8 +/- 1.5. Freshwater sediments yielded ratios of >10. However, further studies indicated that the C/S ratio and TS content of sediments exhibit considerable geographical variation (e.g., Terashima et al., 1983; Koma, 1992; Tanigawa et al., 2013; Sheng et al., 2015). In the context of coastal lowland strata, the examination of sedimentary facies and depositional environments is crucial for understanding the evolution of coastal systems and the impact of natural hazards. The sedimentary facies in tidal flats can provide valuable information on the paleo-environmental conditions, such as sea-level changes, sediment supply, and ocean currents. Moreover, the geochemical analysis of sedimentary facies can help identify the sources of sediment and the processes that controlled sediment deposition. In Japan, the Pacific coast is characterized by a complex geological history, with multiple phases of tectonic activity and changes in sea level. The sedimentary facies in tidal flats along this coast have been influenced by these geological processes, resulting in a diverse range of sedimentary deposits. For example, the sedimentary facies in the tidal flats of the Pacific coast of Japan are characterized by a mixture of marine and terrestrial sediments, with a dominance of sand and silt deposits. The C/S ratio and TS content of these sediments vary significantly, reflecting the complex geological history of the area. In conclusion, the examination of coastal lowland strata is crucial for understanding the evolution of coastal systems and the impact of natural hazards. The sedimentary facies and depositional environments in tidal flats can provide valuable information on paleo-environmental conditions, sediment sources, and deposition processes. The geochemical analysis of sedimentary facies can help identify the sources of sediment and the processes that controlled sediment deposition. Further studies are needed to better understand the geological history of coastal lowland areas and the impact of natural hazards on these systems.

I dived headfirst into developing a platform specifically designed to aid international students during their first year-guiding them through the academic rigors and cultural adjustments. The idea was to create a digital space where students could access resources, seek guidance, and find community support, all designed to ease their transition. I named the startup "Bridge," symbolizing the connection between students and opportunity. I soon connected with a few like-minded individuals, also passionate about this cause. We were a diverse group, hailing from various backgrounds, and each of us brought different skills to the table-marketing, design, even a bit of finance-creating a well-rounded team. As we navigated the startup landscape, we quickly learned that product management was at the core of everything we were building. We needed to channel our efforts efficiently, ensuring that we met the needs of our user base-students like us. The early days of our startup were truly a rollercoaster. There was the thrill of brainstorming sessions filled with creative ideas, but there were also potential pitfalls-ensuring we were adhering to university regulations, securing funding, and, most importantly, validating our concept. We reached out to our peers, conducting surveys and focus groups to gather insights. This feedback was golden; it informed our product iterations and helped us pivot when something wasn't resonating. One of the most enlightening moments for me was realizing that product management isn't merely about overseeing development; it's about advocating for users. We became tireless champions for the students we aimed to support. For instance, we discovered that many students sought mental health resources but felt uncomfortable reaching out-so, we worked to incorporate chat functionality into our platform, allowing them to connect anonymously with counselors. It was a pivotal feature and one that emerged directly from user feedback. After months of hard work, we launched "Bridge" at the beginning of the academic year. The response was overwhelmingly positive; students began utilizing the platform, sharing their experiences, helping one another, and ultimately creating a vibrant community. But even with this success, I understood that our journey was just beginning. We faced constant challenges-scalability issues, fostering engagement, and adapting to the ever-evolving needs of our users. Listening to that feedback became an ongoing part of our philosophy as a team. We began implementing quarterly user feedback sessions, which was a game-changer. Not only did these sessions allow us to strengthen our product, but they also created a poignant reminder of why we started this venture in the first place. While balancing my studies and startup life was daunting, it became clear that every late night spent coding or strategizing was worthwhile. I was learning invaluable lessons in teamwork, leadership, and most importantly, empathy in product management. Understanding the user's perspective became second nature, and it helped shape the narrative we were creating with our product. As I wrap up my time at UW, I'm just as passionate about product management as when I first started my journey. Although my technical foundation is crucial, I've come to understand that the core of successful product management lies within genuine user connection. I now wish to take these experiences into the professional world, ideally landing a role where I can keep creating impactful solutions for real-world problems. But enough about me; I'm keen to hear from our guests who have their own tales and insights on this exciting field of product management. Let's dig deeper into their stories and perspectives.

What he remembers best isn't the frivolity of those carefree days but the darker undertows slowly drawing them all under-every laugh hiding a potential tragedy. The world outside beckons. A surge of restlessness propels CHARLIE out of bed, and he pulls on a worn leather jacket that still carries the scent of cologne and remnants of past escapades. He hesitates momentarily, catching his reflection in the mirror once more. The boy staring back carries the weight of ghosts unseen, eyes tinged with shadows of remorse. Outside, the city breathes a different rhythm-footsteps echoing down empty alleys, distant sirens shrilling like some cosmic alarm. The bar is a beacon, glowing defiantly against the backdrop of the night, its allure undeniable. As he steps down the staircase, every creak resounds like a heartbeat, a reminder of the life coursing just beneath surfaces. In the bar, the atmosphere is thick, a swirl of tension mingling with laughter. TONY is at the center, surrounded by familiar faces caught between loyalty and vice. Their lives weave into a tapestry of reckless abandon, and CHARLIE steps into that familiar chaos. He wants to drown out the noise of his own uneasy mind, to engage with the vibrant hum of nightlife. For a moment, he forgets-the fear, the anxiety, all wrapped in the euphoria of camaraderie. As he settles in, glass raised, he can't shake a sense that-somewhere deep down-the party is coming to an end, and the cards are about to be dealt.

Shorts, you know, I don't need to make any decisions on what am I going to wear? I've made my decision. It's already been made and it makes life easier. I know for myself, I've been doing a little bit of reading on this and I was watching a video recently with a doctor who was talking about this and she said something really interesting. She talked about how people with dyslexia tend to be very creative thinkers and people without dyslexia tend to be linear thinkers. So if you think about the difference between the two, you know, you might have a project and you might have 10 steps to complete that project. If you're a linear thinker, you would naturally think step one step two step three step four step five step six step seven step eight step nine step ten done. That's the way you would think if you're a creative thinker, you may start at step one then jump to step four then jump to step two then jump to step six and you may actually even skip a few steps because you're jumping ahead and thinking about the next thing. You're thinking about the overall outcome rather than each individual step and that's where we run into problems. Sometimes we forget to do certain steps because we're focused on the overall outcome rather than each individual step and when you've got a task that has multiple steps. There's a higher chance of forgetting one of those steps. So you could say well, you know, if I'm a creative thinker, how do I overcome this? Well, one of the ways I found that helps me is using checklists. So if you think about a checklist, it's a list of every single step that needs to be completed. So if you're going on holiday, for example, you'd have a checklist of all the different things that you need to take, you know, your clothes, your toiletries, your passport, your money, etcetera, etcetera. All these different items that need to be checked off and ticked off and once you've done that you've done it. So that's an example of a checklist. Another example is in business. I use checklists for all my processes. So when I have a new client come on board, I've got a checklist of all the things that I need to do to set them up. When I have a new podcast episode come out. I've got a checklist of all the different things that I need to do to publish that podcast episode and promote it and send it to the right people and all that sort of stuff. So I use checklists to break down all these steps and then I can work through them one at a time and tick them off and then I know I haven't missed anything. So that's one way to deal with that issue. The other thing is you may have heard me talk about the idea of batching tasks. So rather than doing one item at a time or one task at a time. You batch similar tasks together and do them all in one hit. So for example, if you're making a meal and you've got a couple of meals that you want to cook for the week, you might choose to cook both of them at once. So rather than cooking one tonight and one tomorrow night, you might cook both tonight and save yourself some time. So you're batching those tasks together. This is also a really effective way to manage your time.

Recent advances in neuroimaging techniques have shed light on the neural mechanisms underlying anorexia nervosa (AN), a severe mental disorder characterized by self-induced starvation and a distorted body image. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have identified altered functional activations in various brain regions, including cognitive control areas, ventral anterior cingulate-striato-thalamic areas, and posterior parietal areas, in response to food-related, body-related, and reward-related stimuli. These findings suggest that AN may be associated with abnormalities in neural circuits involved in appetite regulation, somatosensory perception, and executive control. Structural neuroimaging studies have also revealed decreases in global gray and white matter and increases in cerebrospinal fluid in AN patients, as well as regional gray matter decreases in specific areas, such as the left hypothalamus, left inferior parietal lobe, right lentiform nucleus, and right caudate. These findings are consistent with the idea that AN may be associated with neurobiological changes in brain regions involved in appetite regulation, body perception, and executive control. The neurobiological model of AN suggests that childhood temperament and personality traits, such as anxiety, cognitive inflexibility, obsessionality, and perfectionism, may be risk factors for the development of AN. Additionally, altered eating patterns in AN patients may be a means of decreasing negative mood brought about by altered interactions between the serotoninergic and dopaminergic systems. The serotoninergic system is involved in regulating appetite and satiety, while the dopaminergic system is involved in reward processing. Altered interactions between these systems may lead to the development of AN symptoms, such as food avoidance and restriction. Recent studies have also investigated the role of genetic factors in the development of AN. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified several genetic variants associated with AN, including variants in genes involved in appetite regulation, such as the melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R) gene. Additionally, epigenetic studies have found altered DNA methylation patterns in AN patients, which may contribute to the development of AN symptoms. The neurobiological model of AN also suggests that environmental factors, such as societal pressure to be thin and cultural beauty standards, may contribute to the development of AN symptoms. The model proposes that individuals with certain personality traits, such as perfectionism and low self-esteem, may be more susceptible to the influence of these environmental factors and may be more likely to develop AN. In conclusion, recent advances in neuroimaging and genetic research have provided important insights into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying anorexia nervosa. The neurobiological model of AN suggests that AN is a complex disorder with multiple risk factors, including neurobiological, genetic, and environmental factors. Further research is needed to fully understand the underlying mechanisms of AN and to develop effective treatments for this disorder.

And, while she worked hard and long - and sometimes anxiously - she managed to extract a good deal of enjoyment from her life. She was working hard this morning, packing her trunk and bundling her bedding, preparatory to the departure on the morrow. But, nevertheless, she was enjoying herself hugely. For she was thinking of what she should wear when she reached Boston. The question of clothes had troubled her greatly ever since the plan to go to the city had been formed. It is true that, in the course of her conversation with Mr. Hezekiah Cahoon, the Wellmouth furniture dealer, who had offered to take charge of her belongings until they could be sold, she had mentioned that there were some of her dresses which she intended to keep and carry with her. But those dresses, which she had worn to church and to funerals, were, she realized, quite unsuited to her needs in Boston. They were black, somber, and plain. They had been made for a Trumet seamstress, and not for a sewing woman in a great city factory. When the idea first occurred to her that perhaps she might alter and refashion these garments, making them less severely plain, and therefore better suited to her altered station, she dismissed it promptly and scornfully. To cut, stitch, and sew in order to make a living was one thing; to do those same things merely to gratify personal vanity was quite another. Vanity was a sin, and Keziah was a consistent member of the Come-Outer Church. Then, after the dismissal of the idea, it returned again, and yet again. It came to her as she sat in the little chapel Sunday afternoon, listening to the sermon preached by Deacon Zelotes Richardson. She looked about her at the congregation, the women in particular, and wondered if any of them wore dresses which they themselves had remodeled. There were many bright colors in the pews; there were silks and velvets and flowered muslin. Keziah's eyes rested upon the gown of Miss Marietta Hoag, the schoolmistress. Miss Hoag was an earnest Come-Outer, and a devout Christian, but she dressed very stylishly indeed. Her gown was blue silk, trimmed with lace, and, although its wearer was stout, she carried it off very well. Keziah knew that Marietta had designed that dress herself. She had heard her tell how she did it. Could there be anything wrong in altering a perfectly respectable garment in order to look nice? Wasn't looking nice a duty? Of course, there were limits beyond which it was sinful to go. If one went to extremes, then it became vanity. But simple alterations, such as changing the collar and sleeves and adding a bit of trimming here and there - could they be wicked? Keziah wrestled with the problem during the week following. On Saturday evening she made up her mind to consult someone else. That person must be a woman, of course, because no man understood such things. It must be a sensible, discreet woman, whose judgment could be trusted. After much thought, she decided to talk with Mrs. Thankful Atkins. Mrs. Atkins lived next door to the Halls. She was a widow, and the mother of two children, a boy of twelve and a girl of eight. She took in washing, and Keziah often helped her when the rush of work was more than she could handle unaided. The two women were friends, and Keziah believed she could rely upon her neighbor's advice.

[30] tested jatropha oil methyl esters (JME) in a single cylinder diesel engine and observed ignition characteristics similar to palm methyl ester, though elevated emissions of nucleation mode particles were observed, attributed to the presence of long chain and high boiling point lignoceric methyl esters (C24:0). Similar durations of ignition delay of JME relative to PME and SME were also observed in a constant volume combustion chamber [31], and lifecycle analysis suggests that the possible reductions in global warming potential (GWP) with biodiesel production from jatropha are also comparable to that achieved with production from edible crops such as sunflower, soy and rapeseed [32,33]. A further alternative to use of oils from food crops for the production of biodiesel is the utilisation of waste edible cooking oils [34,35]. While the composition of such waste oils varies with source [36], several researchers have found these to contain elevated levels of free fatty acids (FFA) [37-39], necessitating a two-step transesterification process and resulting in reduced ester yields relative to unused oils [38]. In engine tests of waste cooking oil methyl esters relative to those from food crops, Wu et al. [40] found the waste cooking oil biodiesel to exhibit similar ignition characteristics, but a decreased reduction in particulate matter emissions relative to a fossil diesel. The recovery of lipids suitable for biodiesel manufacture from solid waste materials and residues produced by food industries has also been considered, such as spent coffee grounds [41-43] and date pits (or seeds) [44-48]. Date palm is mostly farmed in hot arid regions, with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) member states the largest producers [49,50], cultivating an estimated 2.34 million tons of dates per year for human and animal consumption, up to 11.47% of which consists of pits which are not consumed or widely utilised [47]. Using various methods of solvent extraction, maximum oil yields from dried and powdered date pits of between 10.36% and 16.5 % on a dry weight basis have been reported [45,46]. Methyl ester yields of up to 85% following esterification of the extracted date pit oils have been found [47], with the physical properties of date pit biodiesel found to be broadly within the range required by legislation [46]. Chapagain et al. [44] undertook oil extractions from desert date oil kernels and esterification to both methyl and ethyl fatty acid esters. The fatty acid profile of the resultant biodiesel was found to be similar to that from soybean oil (composed primarily of fatty acids in the range C16:0 to C18:2) and tested alongside a reference fossil diesel, and a B5 blend of the two fuels, in a light-duty diesel engine.

As I stood at the base of the Statue of Liberty, gazing up at its imposing figure, I couldn't help but feel a sense of disillusionment. The grandeur of the steps, once a symbol of hope and freedom, now seemed diminished by the restrictions that had been imposed. The officials' words echoed in my mind: "Most of you may think you have gone all the way up, but you really haven't." It was a hollow victory, a hollow reopening. I remembered my own experience, climbing those steps with my parents in 1978. We had arrived in the United States by air, and my parents had been awestruck by the sight of the Statue of Liberty. They had not been overcome with emotion, but they had felt a sense of respect for what the statue represented: a beacon of hope for those seeking a better life. But now, the statue seemed to be a symbol of something else entirely. It was a symbol of fear, of the cowardice and xenophobia that had taken hold of our society. The screening, the metal detectors, the baggage restrictions - all of it was a reminder that we were no longer a nation of freedom and opportunity, but a nation of fear and control. I thought about the Sikh community, and the way they had been targeted and mistreated since 9/11. The turban, once a symbol of their faith and culture, had become a symbol of suspicion and mistrust. I thought about the way they were often mistaken for Muslims, and the way they were treated as a result. It was a sad and disturbing reality, one that seemed to be perpetuated by the media and the government. As I walked away from the Statue of Liberty, I couldn't help but wonder what the future held. Would we continue to let fear guide our decisions, or would we find a way to overcome it? Would we continue to let our differences divide us, or would we find a way to come together and build a more just and compassionate society? I didn't have the answers, but I knew that I couldn't give up. I knew that I had to keep fighting for what I believed in, even in the face of adversity. And so, I walked away from the Statue of Liberty, determined to make a difference, one step at a time.

During a sojourn in this vicinity last season, it was one of our greatest pleasures to spend an evening with the old gentleman, listening to legends of the Indians, reminiscences of the Revolution, and pithy remarks on the present age, with which he loved to entertain us, while we occasionally interrupted him by comparing knitting-work with the kind old lady, his wife, or by the praises of a sweet little grandchild, who would cling about his knees and play with the silver buckles on his shoes as he talked. That tall, stately old man, and the sweet child made a beautiful picture of "age at play with infancy," when the fire-light flickered over them, to the ancient family pictures, painted in Holland, hanging on the wall behind us, in the old-fashioned oval frames, which, with the heavy Dutch Bible, which lay on the stand, secured with hasps and brass hinges, ponderous as the fastenings of a prison-door, were family relics precious to the old gentleman from antiquity and association. Yes, the picture was pleasant to look upon; but there was pleasure in listening to his legends and stories. If the one here related is not exactly as he told it, he will not fail to recognize the beautiful young Indian girl, whom he described to us, in the character of Malaeska. At the time of our story, the beautiful expanse of country which stretches from the foot of the Catskill mountains to the Hudson was one dense wilderness. The noble stream glided on in the solemn stillness of nature, shadowed with trees that had battled with storms for centuries, its surface as yet unbroken, save by the light prow of the Indian's canoe. The lofty rampart of mountains frowned against the sky as they do now, but rendered more gloomy by the thick growth of timber which clothed them at the base; they loomed up from the dense sea of foliage like the outposts of a darker world. Of all the cultivated acres which at the present day sustain thousands with their products, one little clearing alone smiled up from the heart of the wilderness. A few hundred acres had been cleared by a hardy band of settlers, and a cluster of log-houses was erected in the heart of the little valley which now contains Catskill village. Although in the neighborhood of a savage Indian tribe, the little band of pioneers remained unmolested in their humble occupations, gradually clearing the land around their settlement, and sustaining their families on the game which was found in abundance in the mountains. They held little intercourse with the Indians, but hitherto no act of hostility on either side had aroused discontent between the settlers and the savages. It was early in May, about a year after the first settlement of the whites, when some six or eight of the stoutest men started for the woods in search of game.

Due to the apparent redundancy of having two signaling proteins (GlnB and GlnK) relaying the glutamine state of the cell, previous models (9-12) have ignored GlnK regulation of AT/AR, it being less potent than GlnB. This simplification is supported by mutational studies of the receptor interaction domains of GlnB and GlnK (13) and by in vitro studies (14). From this viewpoint, the role of GlnK is mostly circumscribed to regulating the membrane-bound channel protein AmtB, whose gene (amtB) lies in the same operon as glnK, causing glnK and amtB expression to be directly correlated (15-17). However, various experiments suggest that GlnK also acts as an effective regulator of AT/AR. For instance, GlnB-deficient strains (i.e., glnB mutants) exhibit unimpaired growth (18) with regulated GS (de)adenylylation (19), suggesting that GlnK can substitute for GlnB. It has also been found that GlnK does interact with AT/AR in vitro (14), albeit relatively weakly, and binds -KG, ATP, and ADP similarly to GlnB (20,21). Importantly, glnK expression is induced during nitrogen limitation, whereas glnB is expressed constitutively (19). Taken together, these observations raise questions about the in vivo regulation of AT/AR and about a complementary role for GlnK in nitrogen assimilation to provide not only added redundancy but also a flexible and rapid response to the consequences of variations in external ammonium levels. To establish the relevance of GlnK in nitrogen regulation during external nitrogen variations, we combined experiment with modeling. We measured the growth rate (Fig. 2) and the in vivo temporal response of relevant metabolites, proteins, and posttranslational modification (PTM) protein states during ammonium run-out, starvation, and a subsequent ammonium shock (Fig. 3). Measurements of the wild-type (WT) strain were complemented with experiments with two genetic knock-outs: glnB (no GlnB) and glnK (no GlnK), as shown in Fig. 5. Our experiments show that growth rate and ammonium uptake are not impaired by the removal of either GlnB or GlnK (Fig. 2), suggesting that GlnB and GlnK form two complementary branches of nitrogen signal transduction regulating AT/AR. We also find that GlnK plays a limited role in regulating GS expression and adenylylation during ammonium run-out and starvation. However, GlnK levels rise steeply during run-out, exceeding those of GlnB fourfold during starvation (Fig. 3). This suggests a functional role of GlnK, poststarvation, until normal ammonium conditions are restored. To confirm this hypothesis, we developed a concise, mechanistic model of GS regulation (Fig. 1). We show that competition between GlnB and GlnK for UT/UR active sites and AT/AR allosteric sites, as well as functional sequestration of GlnK, are necessary to explain the in vivo uridylylation and adenylylation dynamics in the WT and to predict those in the two mutants. Our model predicts the dynamic response of GS adenylylation levels in the mutants, indicating that GlnK can substitute for GlnB.

I found myself mesmerized by the precision and passion of the Toronto-based ensemble, the soaring harmonies of the San Francisco Gay Men's Chorus, and the sultry rhythms of the Miami Gay Men's Chorus. And then, of course, there were the performances that made me want to weep with joy. The women's ensemble from Los Angeles, with their lush harmonies and heartfelt lyrics, left me breathless. I was particularly moved by their rendition of a song about the struggles and triumphs of the LGBTQ+ community, sung in a language I didn't understand but felt deeply in my bones. As the days went by, I found myself getting more and more swept up in the magic of the festival. I started to feel like I was part of a global community, connected to these talented performers and their music in a way that transcended language and culture. And, of course, there were the parties - oh, the parties! - where we'd dance the night away with our new friends from around the world. But even in the midst of all this revelry, I couldn't help but notice the little things that made the festival truly special. Like the way the sound technicians would pause the music to let the audience applaud for a full minute, or the way the performers would take the time to chat with us after the show and share their stories. It was clear that this was more than just a festival - it was a celebration of the human spirit, and all its beauty and complexity. And yet, as much as I loved every moment of it, I couldn't help but feel a pang of sadness when it was all over. I didn't want to leave this magical world, where music and love and community came together in perfect harmony. But, of course, I knew I had to return to my own reality, where the only music was the sound of my own heartbeat, and the only love was the love I had for myself. As I made my way back to the airport, I couldn't help but feel grateful for the experience, and a little bit wistful for what could never be. But I knew that the memories I'd made, and the music that still echoed in my ears, would stay with me forever. And who knows? Furthermore, the development of targeted fertilizer recommendations necessitates a comprehensive understanding of the nutrient dynamics in specific soils across the Northern Nigerian Savanna. Integrated soil fertility management practices must be adopted, combining chemical fertilizers with organic amendments such as compost and green manures (Fowler et al., 2017). This holistic approach can enhance the bioavailability of nutrients while improving soil structure and microbial activity, thus fostering a more resilient agroecosystem. The significance of soil microbial communities cannot be overstated, as they play a crucial role in nutrient cycling and organic matter decomposition (Muller et al., 2016). Current fluctuations in organic matter levels often hinder nutrient mobilization, necessitating a greater emphasis on biological soil health alongside traditional agronomic practices. Studies indicate that soils enriched with diverse organic inputs exhibit improved fertility and yield responses, particularly when addressing maize production (Mwafulirwa et al., 2017). Empowering local farmers with knowledge and resources to implement integrated soil fertility management can lead to improved crop rotations and diversification, ultimately enhancing food security in the region. To further bolster maize productivity, the introduction of improved maize varieties that are resilient to biotic and abiotic stresses should be emphasized. Breeding programs targeting drought-resistant and pest-resistant maize varieties can significantly mitigate the risks associated with climate variability and pest outbreaks (Wing et al., 2018). The adoption of diverse and adaptive cultivars is imperative, enabling farmers to better withstand climatic shocks and thus sustain production levels across varied environmental conditions. This aligns with broader agricultural resilience frameworks that call for cultivars attuned to local agronomic and climatic contexts (Lobell et al., 2011). Moreover, it is essential to enhance farmer education and access to extension services. Many farmers lack information regarding modern agricultural techniques and best management practices, which contributes to conservative yield outcomes (Obi et al., 2019). Implementing community-based learning programs that facilitate knowledge exchange and practical demonstrations can empower farmers to experiment with new technologies and practices in a low-risk environment, thereby fostering innovation and boosting maize yields. The role of digital agriculture cannot be overlooked in this context. Harnessing mobile technology and digital platforms to disseminate real-time weather information, market prices, and agronomic advice can bridge information gaps and facilitate better decision-making among farmers (Aker, 2011). Such technological interventions can enhance market access and foster stronger value chains, ultimately contributing to improved livelihoods and reduced food insecurity. In conclusion, addressing the intricate challenges of maize production in the Northern Nigerian Savanna requires a multi-faceted approach that emphasizes soil health, varietal improvement, farmer education, and the integration of technology. By developing tailored fertilizer recommendations, promoting sustainable practices, and empowering farmers with knowledge and resources, it is feasible to significantly narrow the existing maize yield gap. This holistic strategy not only aims to elevate maize productivity but also contributes to broader food security and economic stability for millions of individuals in Nigeria and beyond, ensuring a resilient agricultural future. Such systemic improvement is pivotal, as the trajectory of food security will significantly hinge upon sustainable agricultural intensification and equitable resource distribution in the coming decades.

The film takes a deftling humorous yet poignant route as it dives deeper into the trials and tribulations of its characters. The heart of the narrative revolves around Mary's turbulent journey-a journey that endeavors to reconcile her burgeoning identity with the suffocating expectations of her environment. In the blistering heat of judgment at American Eagle Christian High School, Mary finds herself in a whirlwind of contradictions, yearning for acceptance while grappling with the realities of her situation. Humor serves as both armor and weaponry, brilliantly employed to defuse tension while highlighting the absurdity of rigid moral dogmas. As Mary begins to free herself from the gilded cage constructed by Hilary Faye and her zealous followers, the camaraderie she finds with Cassandra, Roland, and Dean deepens. Cassandra, the unapologetically outspoken Jew, quickly becomes a foil to Hilary, embodying the spirit of rebellion with a knack for wit that could slice through the thickest of pretensions. Her disdain for hyper-religiosity is palpable; she often comments on the irony of piety being so selectively applied among their peers. "I thought Jesus was supposed to love everyone, even those who, you know, don't share his hair gel..." she quips with a sardonic grin, reminding the audience-and Mary-that there can be vastly differing interpretations of faith. Roland, wise beyond his years despite his physical challenges, embodies resilience, challenging the social norms surrounding him with every calculated move. His relationship with Cassandra not only subverts Hilary Faye's ideal but also redefines the conventional romantic archetypes portrayed in teen comedies. Together, they become advocates for those who exist on the periphery of "normalcy"-championing the mantra that love defies the limitations imposed by societal constructs. Meanwhile, as Mary wrestles with shame-encapsulated by the pressure to conform to the ideals of her community-her interactions become a tapestry of exquisite comedy rooted in tragedy. The surprisingly spirited scenes where she envisions Jesus as the pool maintenance man serve as a clever metaphor for her misguided attempts at redemption. When she eventually confides in her eclectic group of friends, their acceptance reflects a stark contrast to the intolerance she experiences from the mainstream circles, adorned with their pious proclamations. Things escalate when Mary decides to confront her unplanned pregnancy. The sequence where she musters the courage to inform her mother is a comedic tour de force; the scene is drenched in sitcom-like absurdity, oscillating between sincere emotional gravitas and slapstick humor. "Mom, you wanted to be a single unwed Christian mom-meet your daughter!" she exclaims, though she knows the tone belies the gravity of what she must confess. The film crescendos as the characters band together to challenge the hateful rhetoric espoused by Hilary Faye and her follows. This culminates in a hilariously chaotic climax during the school's annual talent show, where shadowed truths are juxtaposed against the garishness of ostentatious performances. Every awkward moment, every misstep fuel their narrative-a call to arms against the walls of prejudice and misunderstanding. Just as it entangles itself in this darker sentiment, the film delicately balances laugh-out-loud moments, leading us to consider that the heart of faith lies not in strict adherence to dogma but in the capacity for love, acceptance, and, ultimately, the courage to be true to oneself. In a landscape dominated by caricatures and cliches, the unfolding narrative promises to challenge the status quo and elevate the voices of all individuals-no matter how different from the norm they may be.

This finding suggests that the pSTS response to social interactions may reflect the detection of specific cues, or computations that are shared across many different kinds of stimuli. However, it is unclear what those cues might be, since the stimuli used in previous experiments vary widely along several dimensions. To investigate this question, we conducted three fMRI experiments using point-light displays (PLDs) of human motion. PLDs were first developed by Johansson (1973) to isolate the role of biological motion in social perception. They consist of dots placed at key points of articulation on the body (e.g. shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles) and can depict isolated individuals or groups performing various actions. PLDs provide a unique opportunity to study the neural basis of social interaction processing because they allow us to control for low-level stimulus properties while manipulating higher-order variables related to social interactions. We manipulated one variable in particular: contingency. Contingency refers to the degree to which the actions of one agent depend on the actions of another. It plays an important role in social cognition, allowing observers to infer agency and causality in social scenes (Michotte, 1946/1963; Saxe et al., 2004; Woodward, 1998). Recent work in developmental psychology has shown that infants as young as 10 months old are sensitive to contingencies between the actions of two agents, suggesting that contingency detection may play an important role in the development of social cognition (Frankenhuis et al., 2013). In Experiment 1, we examined how contingency affects univariate activity levels in the pSTS and other brain regions. Participants viewed short clips of PLDs displaying two agents performing either highly contingent or minimally contingent actions. We predicted that the pSTS would show greater activity for highly contingent interactions than for minimally contingent ones. In Experiments 2 and 3, we tested whether the pSTS represents the degree of contingency present in a scene in a graded manner. Participants viewed clips of PLDs displaying varying degrees of contingency between the actions of two agents. We predicted that the pSTS would respond parametrically to increasing levels of contingency, with greater activity for more contingent interactions. Finally, we used representational similarity analysis (RSA) to test for a relationship between contingency ratings provided by participants outside the scanner and the pattern of neural activity elicited by each clip inside the scanner. We predicted that the patterns of activity evoked by each clip would be correlated with the contingency ratings provided for those clips. A growing body of research indicates that the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) responds preferentially to observed social interactions. However, little is known about the precise nature of this response. Here, we investigated the effect of contingency on pSTS activity during the observation of social interactions. Participants viewed point-light displays depicting two agents performing highly contingent, moderately contingent or minimally contingent actions. Using univariate analyses, we found that the pSTS responded most strongly to highly contingent actions, followed by moderately contingent and then minimally contingent actions. Representational similarity analysis revealed that the patterns of activity elicited by each video clip were correlated with participants' judgments of the contingency between the two agents. Together, these results suggest that the pSTS represents the degree of contingency present in a given scene.

This was not only a battle between Saxon and Briton, it was also a battle between Christian and Heathen; and yet the woman, on the Christian side, from time to time broke forth into the Druidical incantations of early British days; this she did in moments of savage passion as she stood upright in her car dealing forth death from the sheaf of arrows at her side. In one corner of the battle-field the mist-cloud lifted wholly for a few minutes, and the sun shone on the thinned ranks of the Britons showing them woefully hindered in their movements by fallen warriors and horses; a mere sprinkling of young and strong remained; here and there a wounded man raised himself and still tried to use his bow. Old men and women fought on desperately. The war-dogs were still numerous - a veritable phalanx armed with spiked collars and goaded into savage rage, strangely horrible with their red, hanging tongues and bloodshot eyes. In the sudden gleam of sunshine the boy saw that the woman leader was in extreme peril. She had driven her chariot so quickly over the grass - slippery with dew and blood - that her horse had fallen. The boy galloped over dead and dying to her side - as he rode he saw a javelin, aimed at the woman, pierce the side of the struggling horse. At a sign from his friend, the youth, with rare dexterity, harnessed his own horse to her chariot, in place of hers. She pointed to a gap in the ranks of a small band of Saxons; and, mounting again on his steed, the boy galloped with her to the spot - the sharp knives of the chariots doing desperate work among a body of Saxon soldiers through which they ploughed. It was the ancient method of warfare, which the woman by instinct had followed. At just such a gap in the ranks of the foe as she had chosen it was the custom to leap from the chariot and charge on foot; but now she remained standing in her car and, suddenly cutting the traces, set her companion free to charge furiously on the surprised enemy - whilst she aided him by a quick shower of arrows. Her artifice succeeded; the boy bounded forward causing such havoc among a little band of Saxons that they - taken off their guard - turned and fled. In the panic of the moment the enemy did not see that the boy's gallant horse had received his death-wound. With a last frantic attempt to obey his master's onward signal, the animal raised itself on its hinder limbs, pawed wildly in the air, gave one long, whistling breath and, with throat and nostrils choked with blood, fell back dead - and, in falling, fell upon his master. It was the last act of the long, stubborn, futile resistance.

Yet, amidst this historical tumult and the disillusionment surrounding the promises made and the seeming absence of their fulfillment, we find ourselves in the tension of expectation. As we navigate the complex realities of our world, the question remains: how do we reconcile our faith in the promises of God with the brokenness we witness around us? The Advent season beckons us not merely to observe a festival of waiting but to delve into the depths of longing for something more profound-something transformative. The prophet Jeremiah, standing in the midst of a society grappling with despair, extends a flicker of hope. This hope is neither a naive optimism nor a disregard for reality; it is a radical expectancy that arises from the unwavering character of God. For Jeremiah, the promise of a righteous branch is not simply about political restoration, but it is inherently tied to the divine commitment to justice, equity, and peace. The righteous Branch signifies a restoration not only of a throne but signifies a new way of being, a new covenant that transcends the limitations of human governance. That is where the intersection of the Jewish understanding of messianic fulfillment and our Christian interpretation becomes poignant. While Andrew's perspective highlights an essential truth about the nature of kingship, as Christians, we embrace a different layer-that of a spiritual kingdom inaugurated in an unexpected manner. Jesus, the One who walks among the marginalized and oppressed, embodies the very essence of the just King. His writings echo the deep cries of the prophets, calling for justice, mercy, and loving-kindness. The reign of Christ is not confined within the territorial borders or political machinations; rather, it permeates every barrier, directing us to extend love and grace to our neighbors and even our enemies. Yet, this realization poses a challenge. How do we invite ourselves to participate in this Kingdom that is both here and still to come? As we await the consummation of God's promises, we are not called to a passive waiting but to an active engagement. The righteous Branch invites us to be agents of justice, to stand alongside the widows, orphans, and aliens, embodying the very heart of Christ's mission. Our waiting is active; it demands from us a profound commitment to live into the values of the kingdom we profess to believe. As we navigate this season of Advent, we might ask ourselves: in what ways are we called to uphold righteousness in our communities? Where are the injustices hidden from view that require our voice and our actions? Are we willing to extend the reaches of our compassion beyond the familiar confines of our comfort zones? It is in answering these questions that we breach the gap between the prophetic promise and our contemporary reality, seeking to embody the hope of restoration that Jeremiah proclaims. When we engage with these questions, we affirm that the promise remains alive, sustained by the very Spirit that breathes into existence a future filled with hope. Our collective waiting is not in vain; it is a powerful act of remembrance-a tethering to the conviction that God is present, working steadfastly towards a day when all will be made whole. So in this Advent season, may we cling to the promise with courage and resolve, anticipating the unfolding of God's salvation in our midst, as we remain ever vigilant for the holy arrival of the righteous Branch.

This versatility allows synthetic biologists the intriguing prospect of repurposing BMCs to construct novel biosynthetic modules. By co-opting the innate functionality of these empty shells, researchers can engineer bespoke reaction environments, tailoring them to facilitate diverse metabolic pathways beyond their naturally occurring configurations (Parsons et al., 2010). This innovative approach beckons a future where metabolic pathways can be reimagined and optimized for industrial applications, offering a robust platform for the production of value-added compounds. The significance of this advancement lies in the customizable nature of BMCs, where shell proteins can be altered or recombined to chamber specific enzymes, thereby creating a microenvironment conducive to specialized reactions. This holds immense promise for optimizing the synthesis of complex molecules, offering unprecedented control over reaction pathways and minimizing undesirable side reactions (Lawrence et al., 2014). Synthetic biologists can, thus, mitigate the detrimental effects of volatile or toxic intermediates by isolating them within these confined spaces, thereby enhancing both reaction efficiency and yield. Moreover, the incorporation of synthetic biology in BMC research facilitates the expansion of their applicability beyond natural confines. Through precise genetic manipulation, pathways for pharmaceuticals, biofuels, and other industrially relevant chemicals could be encapsulated within redesigned BMCs, potentially transforming the landscape of microbial biotechnology. While formidable challenges remain in optimizing the specificity and efficiency of transport across BMC shells, advances in protein engineering and bioinformatics provide encouraging avenues to surmount these barriers. The potential of BMCs extends into sustainable practices, particularly noteworthy in the wake of global environmental concerns. By enhancing the bacterial production of natural compounds, industries can reduce reliance on fossil-fuel-derived chemicals, thus decreasing their environmental footprint. This application underscores the potential of metabolically engineered bacteria, augmented by BMC technology, to contribute substantively to the development of green chemistry and sustainable manufacturing processes. Furthermore, understanding the regulatory mechanisms that control BMC assembly and disassembly remains an essential area for ongoing research. Insights into these processes will be crucial for developing systems with improved performance and control over metabolic fluxes. Advances in this field hold the potential to reveal novel methodologies by which BMCs could be synchronized with host cellular machinery, optimizing the integration of synthetic pathways and enhancing metabolic balance within engineered organisms. As research unfolds, a holistic approach encompassing systems biology, protein engineering, and computational modeling will be instrumental in driving forward the successful implementation of engineered BMCs. These collective efforts signify a paradigm shift in our capacity to harness biological systems for innovative applications, with BMC technology standing as a keystone in the future of metabolic engineering. In summary, bacterial microcompartments offer a transformative potential for synthetic biology, essentially revolutionizing the field of metabolic engineering. Their ability to act as customizable microreactors presents an exciting frontier for the production of a myriad of compounds, from biofuels to pharmaceuticals, while addressing some of the most pressing challenges in industrial biotechnology. As research progresses, the evolution and adaptation of these structures promise to bolster the sustainable production of chemicals, heralding a new epoch in biotechnological innovation.
