There was a sudden noise outside, and then a loud knocking at the door. Father Adrian started to his feet, and stood listening. The dying man opened his eyes, and spoke feebly: - "Let him enter." "My son, my son," murmured the priest, "it is too late! Too late! You cannot receive another visitor to-night." The sick man's lips moved, and the words they framed were faint but distinct: - "It is he! Let him enter." Again the knocking sounded through the house, dull and solemn like a death-knell. The priest crossed the room, and admitted the intruder. Gomez rose also, and stood watching the new-comer with a scowl upon his swarthy face. Father Adrian held up his hand with a warning gesture. "Hush! My son, you are too late. He is passing away even now. You cannot speak with him." The stranger stepped forward into the full glare of the candlelight, and fixed his dark, piercing eyes upon the bed. "I must speak with him. I must and shall! Stand aside, all of you!" The priest fell back before the imperious gesture and flashing glance. Gomez followed his example, and the stranger bent over the dying man. "Ralph, Ralph!" he cried, in thrilling accents, "look upon me ere you go hence! Look upon me! Do you know me?" The white face upon the pillow was suddenly convulsed. The glazed eyes opened wide, and stared upward with an awful look. "Yes, yes!" gasped the dying man. "Speak quickly!" "Your time grows shorter! Answer me one question, and I spare you. Where is she?" "Dead these twenty years." "She lives! She lives! Tell me where she is, or you go hence unabsolved. Confess your sin, and I will pardon it. Speak!" The dying man groaned aloud. "Mercy, mercy! O God, have mercy upon me! Take him away! Let me die in peace!" "Answer me, and I go. Refuse, and I denounce you to the world. Where is she?" The voice that uttered the words rang through the house, and echoed from wall to wall. All was silent. Only the pattering of the rain, and the moaning of the wind broke the awful stillness. "Where is she?" "Curse you! Would you hunt me down even to the grave? Go to the devil, and leave me in peace! Leave me, I say! Avaunt!" The stranger's form dilated, his eyes flashed fire, he threw his arms above his head, and cursed the dying wretch with fearful words. Slowly, and with pain unspeakable, the sick man dragged himself into a kneeling posture, and holding out his skeleton arms towards the crucifix, his fleshless fingers working horribly in the dim light, he called upon God to witness that he spoke the truth. As the last word quivered on his lips, the final change passed over his face. The lines faded away, the lips ceased to twitch, the eyelids dropped. He fell backward amongst the pillows like a log, and all was over. The stranger stood for a moment looking down upon him. Then he raised his eyes to heaven, and extending his arms cried in a voice of thrilling anguish, "Cursed! Cursed! Cursed!" Father Adrian caught hold of his arm, and tried to lead him from the room; but he flung him off with such violence that the slight form of the priest went down before him.

However, DNS is too computationally expensive, requiring supercomputing to simulate systems of reasonable size (Xiong et al., 2012). DEM-CFD has been a powerful tool for understanding physical phenomena in gas-solid flows. Since DEM-CFD models individual particles, it has been used to calculate particle velocity and granular temperature (He et al., 2012; Muller et al., 2008) as well as particle mixing (Bokkers, van Sint Annaland, & Kuipers, 2004; Liu, Xiao, Chen, & Bu, 2012). Additionally, since discrete element modelling can account for a variety of particle sizes, DEM-CFD has been used to model two phase granular flow in polydisperse systems of particles (Beetstra, van der Hoef, & Kuipers, 2007b; Tagami, Mujumdar, & Horio, 2009; Zeilstra, van der Hoef, & Kuipers, 2008). Since DEM-CFD can also model the flow of either liquid or gas through fluidized beds, DEM-CFD has also been able to provide insight on the differences, and transition, between homogeneous and bubbling fluidisation (Di Renzo & Di Maio, 2007). Originally, almost all DEM-CFD simulations were limited to modelling essentially 2D fluidized beds with rectangular fluid grids, owing to computational limitations (Bokkers et al., 2004; Di Renzo & Di Maio, 2007; He et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012; Muller et al., 2008, 2009; Tagami et al., 2009; Zeilstra et al., 2008). Since most fluidized beds used in experiments and industry have cylindrical or more complicated geometries, new DEM-CFD models for simulating beds with these geometries have recently emerged (e.g. Chu & Yu, 2008; Guo, Wu, & Thornton, 2013; Liu, Bu, & Chen, 2013). Fluidized beds with complicated geometries have been directly modelled using one of two techniques: (1) a rectangular fluid grid with immersed boundaries (Guo et al., 2013) or (2) an unstructured fluid grid, typically generated by a commercial CFD package (Chu & Yu, 2008). A difficulty associated with both these techniques is that it is impossible to keep the fluid cells similar in size and shape. Since the volume-averaged fluid equations (Anderson & Jackson, 1967) used in DEM-CFD models require the fluid cells to cover regions which would not change in macroscopic physical properties if slightly changed in size (Crowe, Sommerfeld, & Tsuji, 1998), having cells too small or with oblong shapes could cause these equations to break down, thereby corrupting the results. Conversely, having fluid cells too large will cause the simulation to miss important features of the flow. A commonly used method for calculating voidage on rectangular grids, described in full by Khawaja et al. (2012), involves treating each particle as if it is encapsulated by a cube, with side length equal to the diameter of the particle. The fraction of the volume of the cube which lies in different fluid cells is then calculated, and the corresponding fraction of the particle's volume is assigned to the fluid cells which contain a portion of the volume of the encapsulating cube.

She told Dolly everything about the college, and advised her what to buy, and showed her how to make her bed and where to hang her clothes. She told her all about the different classes, and said that she need not worry, because the instructors were always ready to help anyone who really tried to learn. "But don't study too hard, dearie," she warned. "If you do, you'll get sick. And then, of course, you won't enjoy yourself. It isn't supposed to be work, anyway. Just fun, you know." Dolly was tired enough by now, so she went to sleep almost as soon as she got into bed, and slept soundly till morning. She awoke to find the sun shining through the window, and Margery bustling about the room, getting breakfast. "What time is it?" asked Dolly, rubbing her eyes. She felt stiff and sore, and her head ached slightly. "It is eight o'clock. I thought you'd sleep longer, after your long ride yesterday. Why, didn't you sleep last night?" "No," confessed Dolly. "I lay awake nearly all night, thinking of home." "Oh, yes, that would be natural enough. It was the first night you've ever spent away from home, wasn't it? But why didn't you tell me? I should have helped you to go to sleep." "I'm afraid it wouldn't have done any good, even if I had told you," laughed Dolly. "I was homesick. I wanted to be with Mother and Father, and the babies. Oh, I guess I shall never get over being homesick!" "You'll forget all about it in no time. Don't think about it any more. We'll have lots of fun today, and you'll see. Come along, now. Breakfast is waiting." Breakfast was delicious. There was a hot cake with maple syrup, and buttered toast and coffee. Dolly ate ravenously, for she was hungry indeed, and afterwards she dressed quickly and ran downstairs to the assembly hall. There she met Margery, who introduced her to some of her friends. They all greeted her warmly, and made her feel glad that she had come. After assembly, she went to class with Margery, and found that she enjoyed the lessons thoroughly. One of the girls in her class was studying French, and she helped Dolly with the grammar lesson. By noon, Dolly was beginning to realize that she was having a splendid time, and that she ought to be ashamed of herself for ever having been homesick. But she had learned one thing. If she ever came to college again, she would bring her mother with her, and stay at home during vacations. That would take care of the homesickness.

The next morning we continued on to Amarillo Texas, stopping briefly in Tucumcari. It's an interesting town that has lots of murals and some nice architecture, including a Spanish style Catholic church. You should stop there too if you get the chance. In Amarillo we visited the Cadillac Ranch (see photos), which consists of ten Cadillacs buried nose-down in the ground. They were originally installed in the early 70s as part of an art project. The cars have since moved several miles west of their original location due to development. They are now on private land, but people still come to spray paint them. The original owners of the cars wanted people to vandalize them, so it seems fitting that people continue to do so. We also visited Palo Duro Canyon State Park (see photos). It's a beautiful canyon formed by the Prairie Dog Town Fork of the Red River. It reminded me a lot of the Grand Canyon, only much smaller. It was the site of a battle between the U.S. Army and the Kiowa, Cheyenne, Arapaho and Comanche tribes in 1874. There are many trails in the park, and we chose to hike the Lighthouse trail. The Lighthouse is a rock formation that looks like a lighthouse. We didn't make it all the way out to the Lighthouse, but we did get far enough to get a good view of it. The trail follows a creek bed, and it was quite hot the day we went. However, the rocks provided shade in spots, and there were water faucets at intervals along the trail. One thing that struck me was how flat the plains around the canyon were. From the top of the rim, all you could see were prairie dogs and cows. The next day we arrived in Springfield MO. We stayed in a hotel near the airport, which is pretty far from the city itself. We spent most of our time visiting my wife's family, who live nearby. We did manage to visit Wilson's Creek Battlefield, which was the site of the first major Civil War battle fought west of the Mississippi river. The Union army lost the battle, and General Nathaniel Lyon died in the fighting. He was the first general killed in action during the war. We also visited Fantastic Caverns, which is a cave system near Springfield. What makes this cave unique is that they drive you through the cave instead of walking through it. They claim that this is the only ride-through cave in America. The cave was discovered in 1862 by John Knox and his hunting dog. His dog chased an animal into a small hole in the side of a hill. When the dog refused to leave the hole, John sent five women from a nearby farm to explore the cave. He figured that if the cave was dangerous or contained hostile forces, then the women would probably survive. It turned out to be safe, and the women explored the cave using ropes and lanterns. The cave is full of stalactites and stalagmites, and other formations. It contains several large rooms and passages, and it extends under a highway. We left Springfield and headed home via Tulsa OK. We drove past the Gilcrease Museum, but we didn't have time to stop. We also stopped briefly in Clinton OK. We walked across Route 66 to eat lunch at a restaurant called the Golden Corral. While we were eating, we noticed a woman sitting alone at the table behind us. She looked like she was trying to attract attention. She kept making faces at the waitresses and at us, and she even tried to talk to us.

"Can you believe a father asking his son to take his joy and happiness somewhere else?" But the pair were determined to have a party. "If we gave up our dream, it would equal defeat," says Ziad. First, the couple kept the guest list to about 100 and settled for an early afternoon reception. Ziad spent days driving around the city checking out hotels and banquet halls for the reception. He found that nearly all the nice halls were shut down or located in unsafe neighborhoods. All the good hotels in Baghdad have been taken over by foreigners - mainly journalists and contractors - and have been turned into fortresses encircled with concrete blast barriers and machine-gun-toting guards. At hotels, wedding guests would be required to pass through checkpoints and endure body searches. They would have to leave their cars outside and walk through hundreds of yards of labyrinthine barbed-wire passageways to reach the party. A second option was to have the reception at Ziad's parents' house. The home, a beautiful old two-story house with a big well-tended garden, is in many ways perfect for the occasion. They worried that one of the frequent U.S. military raids or an attack on U.S. troops might occur in their neighborhood during the reception. They also worried a noisy party could attract kidnappers or robbers who might follow guests when they left. At last, the couple found a bland hall in an obscure alley in central Baghdad. It wasn't pretty, but it was just what they were looking for: no heavy fortifications, no armed guards, no foreigners and a banquet hall with a large generator to provide electricity in case of a blackout. "It's almost normal," joked Ziad. To minimize the risk to guests of driving around Baghdad, the couple picked a church near the reception hall for the ceremony.

Most recent models calculate NH3 fluxes using Henry's Law, i.e. the dissociation reactions of ammonium and NH3 in solution is used to calculate the NH3 gas on the surface, with the flux estimated using a resistance-based approach (e.g. Sutton et al., 1998; Cooter et al., 2010; Massad et al., 2010; Flechard et al., 2013). For instance, Cooter et al. (2010) used a process-based model to predict measured diurnal variation and daily means of NH3 emissions from agricultural soils. Even though Henry's Law has been used to calculate NH3 emissions from Nr sources, these models have not been explicitly validated with high resolution empirical measurements from a range of meteorological conditions. For example, Massad et al. (2010) reviewed existing measurements to compile a comprehensive dataset and derived generalized parameterizations for a range of fertilizers and ecosystems to be used in large-scale chemical transport and earth system models. Flechard et al. (2013) synthesized data from a range of studies to generate consistent parameterizations that can be used to calculate NH3 emissions on the regional and global scale. Cooter et al. (2010) used their model to calculate NH3 emissions at the field scale and compared their model output to fertilizer application at a site in North Carolina, USA. In an initial approach to modelling NH3 emissions from seabirds, only the bioenergetics part of the GUANO model was used, linked to empirical estimates of the percentage volatilized (Wilson et al., 2004; Blackall et al., 2007). This approach provided an adequate description of the spatial differences in NH3 emissions on a regional and country scale. However, it meant that there was a high uncertainty in the estimates in the extrapolations to a global scale by Blackall et al. (2007). A first approach to address this uncertainty was provided by Riddick et al. (2012) who used an empirical temperature correction, with uncertainty ranges of estimates based on a) no temperature dependence and b) full solubility dependence according to the thermodynamics of Henry's Law and ammonium dissociation. If, like Blackall et al. (2007), they ignored the possible effect of temperature, then they found total global NH3 emissions from seabirds of 442 Gg NH3 year-1 (where penguins contributed 83%, due to improved bird statistics). By contrast, if NH3 emissions were proportional to the thermodynamic effect of temperature, they found total global NH3 emission from seabirds to be only 97 Gg NH3 year-1 (where penguins contributed 63%). According to a mid-range estimate of the temperature dependence, they estimated 270 Gg NH3 year-1 (with 80% from penguins). Penguins were thus estimated to be the main source of NH3 emissions from seabird colonies globally under all three scenarios, while this clearly shows the importance of addressing the temperature dependence of emissions. The main limitation of Riddick et al. (2012) was the wide uncertainty range of their estimates and the need to constrain these by measurements, ideally using a process-based approach.

The limbus, a narrow region where the cornea and conjunctiva meet, is a critical zone that plays a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the ocular surface. The limbal epithelial stem cells, which reside in the limbal niche, are responsible for the regeneration of the corneal epithelium and the maintenance of its homeostasis. These stem cells have the ability to differentiate into transient amplifying cells, which then give rise to post-mitotic daughter cells that migrate towards the central cornea to replace senescent or damaged cells. The limbal epithelial stem cells are also capable of self-renewal, ensuring a continuous supply of new cells to maintain the corneal epithelial layer. The corneal epithelium, in turn, is supported by the underlying stroma, a thick, collagenous layer that provides mechanical strength and structural integrity to the cornea. The stroma is composed of a network of collagen fibrils, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins, which are produced by the stromal keratocytes. The keratocytes, a type of fibroblast, are responsible for the synthesis and degradation of the stromal matrix, and play a critical role in maintaining the transparency and refractive power of the cornea. The corneal endothelium, a single layer of cells lining the inner surface of the cornea, is responsible for maintaining the corneal hydration and transparency. The endothelial cells have a unique morphology, with a high density of mitochondria and a well-developed endoplasmic reticulum, which enables them to pump ions and water out of the cornea, thereby maintaining its deturgescence. The endothelial cells also produce a variety of growth factors and cytokines that regulate the proliferation and differentiation of the corneal epithelial cells. The corneal epithelium, stroma, and endothelium are intimately connected through a complex network of cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, which are essential for maintaining the integrity and function of the cornea. Disruption of these interactions can lead to a range of corneal disorders, including epithelial defects, stromal opacification, and endothelial dysfunction. Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying these interactions is crucial for the development of effective therapeutic strategies for the treatment of corneal diseases. In addition to its structural and functional importance, the cornea also plays a critical role in the immune response, serving as a barrier against external pathogens and allergens. The corneal epithelium and stroma contain a range of immune cells, including dendritic cells, macrophages, and T cells, which are responsible for recognizing and responding to foreign antigens. The cornea also produces a variety of antimicrobial peptides and cytokines, which help to combat infection and inflammation. In conclusion, the cornea is a complex and highly specialized tissue that plays a critical role in vision and ocular health. Its unique structure and function are maintained through a delicate balance of cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, which are essential for maintaining its transparency, refractive power, and immune function. Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying these interactions is crucial for the development of effective therapeutic strategies for the treatment of corneal diseases and the preservation of vision.

As the mate and the chief engineer sat with Carr, the air grew heavier and more oppressive, the heat seeming to press down upon them like a physical weight. The native boy, still fanning Carr's face, looked up at the two men with wide, curious eyes, his dark skin glistening with sweat. The flies buzzed lazily around them, and the only sound was the creaking of the steamer's wooden hull and the distant chanting of the native women in the village. Morrison, the chief engineer, poured a long drink of beer into a glass and handed it to Carr, who grasped it eagerly, his eyes shining with a mixture of desperation and relief. He drained the glass in one long swallow, then lay back on his bed of mats, his chest heaving with exhaustion. "Ah, that's better," he said, his voice low and husky. "I feel a bit more human now. But I'm afraid I'm going to be a long time getting over this fever, Oliver. I've had it before, but never so bad as this." The mate, Oliver, nodded sympathetically. "You've been working too hard, Carr," he said. "You should have taken a break sooner. We've got a good crew, and I can handle things for a bit. Just rest and get your strength back." Carr smiled weakly. "I know, Oliver. But I've got to get this cargo offloaded and get the Motutapu back to port. We can't stay here much longer. The weather's going to break soon, and I don't want to be caught in a storm." Morrison, who had been watching the two men with a concerned expression, spoke up. "Captain, I think you should consider putting in at the next port we come to. You're not fit to be in charge of the ship in your condition." Carr's eyes flashed with anger, but then his face relaxed, and he nodded slowly. "You're right, Morrison. I know I'm not fit. But I've got to get this cargo offloaded, and then I'll take a break. I promise." As the three men sat in silence, the sounds of the native village grew louder, and the air grew heavier and more oppressive. The sun was setting, casting a golden glow over the steamer and the village, and the sea was beginning to stir, as if sensing the approaching storm.

There were speaking-tubes in the porter's lodge, communicating with each floor of the great Conti palace, but the porter did not move. "I cannot go upstairs and leave the door," he said. "You can speak to the servant through the tube, I suppose!" The porter slowly shook his massive head, and his long grey beard wagged from side to side. "There are no servants upstairs," he said. "There is only the family." "No servants? Are you crazy?" "Oh, no!" answered the man meditatively. "I do not think I am mad. The servants all went away last night after dinner, with their belongings. There were only sixteen left, men and women, for I counted them." "Do you mean to say - " The Baroness stopped in the middle of her question, staring in amazement. The porter now nodded, as solemnly as he had before shaken his head. "Yes. This is the end of the house of Conti." Then he looked at her as if he wished to be questioned, for he knew that she was not really a great lady, and guessed that in spite of her magnificent superiority and coldness she was not above talking to a servant about her friends. "But they must have somebody," she said. "They must eat, I suppose! Somebody must cook for them. They cannot starve!" "Who knows? Who knows? Perhaps they will starve." The porter evidently took a gloomy view of the case. "But why did the servants go away in a body?" asked the Baroness, descending from her social perch by the inviting ladder of curiosity. "They never were paid. None of us ever got our wages. For some time the family has paid nobody. The day before yesterday, the telephone company sent a man to take away the instrument. Then the electric light was cut off. When that happens, it is all over." The man had heard of the phenomenon from a colleague. "And there is nobody? They have nobody at all?" The Baroness had always been rich, and was really trying to guess what would happen to people who had no servants. "There is my wife," said the porter. "But she is old," he added apologetically, "and the palace is big. Can she sweep out three hundred rooms, cook for two families of masters and dress the Princess's hair? She cannot do it." This was stated with gloomy gravity. The Baroness also shook her head in sympathy. "There were sixteen servants in the house yesterday," continued the porter. "I remember when there were thirty, in the times of the old Prince." "There would be still, if the family had been wise," said the Baroness severely. "Is your wife upstairs?" "Who knows where she is?" enquired the porter by way of answer, and with the air of a man who fears that he may never see his wife again. "There are three hundred rooms. Who knows where she is?"

However, it is not clear yet which specific angular configuration provides the best results when retrieving vegetation parameters. Additionally, it remains unclear whether including more than two viewing angles would still provide further improvements. In this study we investigated the effect of different configurations of multi-angular input data on the inversion performance of the PROSAIL model. We compared the results obtained from a single-viewing angle to those obtained from three different multi-angular configurations: (1) two viewing angles, (2) three viewing angles, and (3) four viewing angles. These configurations were selected because they represent typical sensor designs of satellite missions such as EnMAP, Sentinel-2, Sentinel-3, Landsat and Hyperion. Furthermore, all these sensors have a nadir view angle (0 ) and one forward-looking view angle (30 -60 ). In addition, Sentinel-3 has a backward-looking view angle (-60 ), while EnMAP, Hyperion and Landsat have a second backward-looking view angle (-45 ). The objective of this study was twofold: First, we aimed to investigate if the inclusion of multi-angular information improves the inversion performance of the PROSAIL model, specifically in terms of the root mean square error (RMSE) between retrieved and reference values of the parameters. Second, we wanted to assess which multi-angular configuration yields the highest retrieval accuracies. We performed a Monte Carlo simulation to obtain statistically robust results. A total of 1000 simulations were conducted per parameter configuration. Each simulation consisted of an inversion of the PROSAIL model for each pixel of a Sentinel-2 image, where the input was a simulated hyperspectral signal. From the retrieved parameters, we calculated the RMSE between the estimated and reference value for each parameter. The RMSE was then averaged over the entire image and across the simulations for each parameter configuration. To simulate the multi-angular reflectance signals, we used the PROSAIL model in combination with the Monte Carlo code developed by Duan et al. (2014). This code allows us to simulate the reflectance signal at any viewing and illumination geometry. In our simulations, we considered the following parameters: the leaf chlorophyll content (LCC), the leaf dry matter content (LDMC), the leaf internal transmittance (T), the leaf mesophyll structure parameter (N), the leaf structure parameter (SID), the leaf equivalent water thickness (EWT), the leaf stomatal conductance (GSC), the leaf specular component (SPAR), the LAI, the soil brightness (SB), the hot spot parameter (HOTP), the hotspot position (PHOTP), and the hotspot shape (SHAP). For the soil parameters SB, HOTP, PHOTP, and SHAP, fixed values were used throughout the simulations (Table 1). For the other parameters, values were sampled randomly from their respective distributions (Table 1). Note that we only used the leaf parameters T, N, SID, EWT, GSC, SPAR and LCC as inputs for the PROSAIL model, since the remaining parameters could be derived from these parameters. The resulting distribution of parameter values was then used to simulate the reflectance at six different view zenith angles: 0, -45, -60, 30, 40 and 50. All simulations were conducted for a constant solar zenith angle of 30. To simulate the noise associated with real-world measurements, Gaussian noise was added to the simulated reflectance spectra. The noise level was adjusted such that the standard deviation of the simulated reflectance spectra equals the standard deviation of the Sentinel-2 bands at 10 m spatial resolution.

This is a rare moment, and even Mokwami, who was born in the Delta, is thrilled to see the dogs. African wild dogs, also called Cape hunting dogs, are officially endangered. Conservationists say shrinking habitat and farmers, hunters and rangers who poison and shoot them to protect livestock are eroding their number. The dogs roam small swaths of forest, desert and savanna in southern Africa. They hunt whatever they can catch: antelope, small wildebeest, warthogs, rodents and even birds. Tonight, they are after impala. Suddenly, they are on the move, first as an unorganized group, then in a line, first walking, now trotting. We haven't seen the impala, but Mokwami knows the dogs have their scent. "The impala are that way (he points to the right), but the dogs will go that way, then up there (he points to about 11 o'clock), they will turn right. They always follow the line of the bush. Then they will run." He turns his outstretched arm to 2 o'clock. "We need to be there to see the chase." "How do you know that?" I ask incredulously. "These are dogs," he says. "I know these dogs. I have seen dogs before." The dogs pick up the pace. We start bushwhack-driving toward 2 o'clock, pacing the dogs along the track. We reach a point, and now see the impala through the bush to the right, maybe 600 meters off. The dogs slow, they turn to the right and accelerating, leap into the bushes just behind us. We have a difficult time seeing them, but Mokwami knows where they are heading and we turn right, directly toward the impala along the outside of the bushes that are giving the dogs cover. Suddenly we see a dog through the bushes, then another, then another. They are sprinting. They are making their move. We accelerate, blasting and bouncing through the uneven grass. The impala are on high alert, watching the bush, watching us, perceiving a threat but not yet knowing what it is. Suddenly, the dogs streak out of the bush straight for the impala, and the chase is on. On level, unobstructed ground, Mokwami explains as we dash in pursuit, a dog can catch an impala. An impala's high step can kick up dirt, and if it can gain ground, the flying dirt will confuse the dog's scent. But there they are! From behind a bush, an impala flies in full sprint, and at most two seconds behind, the dogs are ripping after it like a stiff evening wind. The speed and focus of the predator and the prey are razor-sharp. We race along on a parallel track. The dogs are going to get him, I'm sure of it. Mokwami isn't so certain. "Mayyyybe, mayyybe," he says. What I have yet to learn is that the impala isn't just running from something, it's running toward something. This isn't a chase. It's a race.

Victoria: So, you know, I've always been a runner, even as a kid. I mean, I was one of those weirdos who loved running. I ran cross-country and track in high school, and I was actually pretty decent. I mean, I wasn't the best, but I was solid. And then I got to college, and that's when things started to get really serious for me. I went to the University of St. Thomas, and that's where I really started to develop my skills and learn how to train properly. But even in high school, I was always a bit of a rebel. I didn't really follow the traditional training methods. I mean, I didn't do a lot of structured workouts, and I didn't really pay attention to my pace or my heart rate or any of that stuff. I just kind of ran by feel, you know? And it worked for me, I guess. I mean, I was able to get decent times and stuff. But when I got to college, that's when I started to realize that there was more to running than just showing up and running. I mean, I started to learn about periodization, and I started to learn about different types of workouts, and I started to learn about how to fuel my body properly. And that's when things started to click for me. I mean, I started to see improvements in my times, and I started to feel like I was getting stronger and more efficient. And then, of course, I got to the Olympics, and that's when things really took off. I mean, I was able to train with some of the best coaches and athletes in the world, and I was able to learn from them and pick up some new techniques and strategies. And that's when I started to see some really big improvements. I mean, I was able to go from running 15-minute miles to running 6-minute miles, and that's when I knew that I had really made it. But even now, as a professional runner, I still don't use a GPS watch for most of my runs. I mean, I know some people swear by them, and I'm sure they're great for some people. But for me, I just like to run by feel. I like to listen to my body and trust my instincts. And I think that's one of the things that's helped me to be successful. I mean, I'm not a robot, and I don't need to be told exactly how fast to run or exactly how far to go. I can just kind of feel it, you know? Victoria: So, what do you think is the biggest misconception about running? I mean, people always think that running is just about putting one foot in front of the other, but there's so much more to it than that. What do you think is the biggest misconception? Victoria: Oh, definitely. I think the biggest misconception is that running is just about the physical act of running. I mean, people think that if you can just put one foot in front of the other, you're a runner. But running is so much more than that. It's about the mental game, it's about the strategy, it's about the fueling and the recovery, it's about the whole package. And I think that's what people don't realize. They think that running is just about going out there and running, but it's so much more than that. And I think that's why I don't use a GPS watch for most of my runs. I mean, I know some people love them, but for me, I just don't need that level of precision.

As Burns delved deeper into the world of infectious diseases, he became increasingly fascinated by the intricate web of connections that exist between humans, animals, and the environment. He spent hours discussing with Lipkin the concept of zoonosis, where diseases can jump from animals to humans, and the alarming rate at which this is happening. "Ian would tell me about the latest outbreak of avian flu in Indonesia, and how it was only a matter of time before it mutated into something that could be transmitted human-to-human," Burns says. "It was like hearing a ticking time bomb, and I knew I had to get this story out there." Lipkin, who has spent his career tracking down the sources of mysterious outbreaks, was instrumental in helping Burns create a fictional virus that was both plausible and terrifying. "We wanted to create a scenario that was grounded in reality, but also had the potential to be catastrophic," Lipkin explains. "We drew inspiration from real-life outbreaks like SARS and H1N1, and then extrapolated to create something that could potentially bring the world to its knees." The result is the MEV-1 virus, a highly contagious and deadly pathogen that spreads rapidly across the globe, leaving a trail of death and destruction in its wake. As the virus spreads, the film's characters - including Winslet's Dr. Erin Mears, a determined epidemiologist, and Damon's Mitch Emhoff, a grieving father - struggle to contain the outbreak and find a cure. One of the most striking aspects of "Contagion" is its attention to detail when it comes to the science behind the outbreak. From the way the virus is transmitted to the methods used to track its spread, the film is meticulous in its portrayal of the complexities of epidemiology. "We wanted to make sure that everything in the film was accurate, from the way the CDC responds to an outbreak to the language that scientists use when discussing the virus," Burns says. Lipkin, who was on set throughout the filming, was impressed by the cast's willingness to learn about the science behind the story. "Kate Winslet was particularly dedicated to getting it right," he says. "She spent hours with me, asking questions and learning about the procedures and protocols that epidemiologists follow during an outbreak." The film's commitment to accuracy has already paid off, with many in the scientific community praising its portrayal of the complexities of infectious disease outbreaks. "Contagion" has also sparked a national conversation about the importance of preparedness and global cooperation in the face of pandemics. As Burns notes, "The film is not just a thriller - it's a wake-up call. We're not just telling a story; we're trying to raise awareness about the very real threats that we face as a global community."

Marriage had certainly complicated life for Mr. Pett, as it frequently does for the man who waits fifty years before trying it. In addition to the geniuses, Mrs. Pett had brought with her to her new home her only son, Ogden, a fourteen-year-old boy of a singularly unloveable type. Years of grown-up society and the absence of anything approaching discipline had given him a precocity on which the earnest efforts of a series of private tutors had expended themselves in vain. They came, full of optimism and self-confidence, to retire after a brief interval, shattered by the boy's stodgy resistance to education in any form or shape. To Mr. Pett, never at his ease with boys, Ogden Ford was a constant irritant. He disliked his stepson's personality, and he more than suspected him of stealing his cigarettes. It was an additional annoyance that he was fully aware of the impossibility of ever catching him at it. Mr. Pett resumed his journey. He had interrupted it for a moment to listen at the door of the morning-room, but, a remark in a high tenor voice about the essential Christianity of the poet Shelley filtering through the oak, he had moved on. Silence from behind another door farther down the passage encouraged him to place his fingers on the handle, but a crashing chord from an unseen piano made him remove them swiftly. He roamed on, and a few minutes later the process of elimination had brought him to what was technically his own private library - a large, soothing room full of old books, of which his father had been a great collector. Mr. Pett did not read old books himself, but he liked to be among them, and it is proof of his pessimism that he had not tried the library first. To his depressed mind it had seemed hardly possible that there could be nobody there. He stood outside the door, listening tensely. He could hear nothing. He went in, and for an instant experienced that ecstatic thrill which only comes to elderly gentlemen of solitary habit who in a house full of their juniors find themselves alone at last. Then a voice spoke, shattering his dream of solitude. "Hello, pop!" Ogden Ford was sprawling in a deep chair in the shadows. "Come in, pop, come in. Lots of room." Mr. Pett stood in the doorway, regarding his step-son with a sombre eye. He resented the boy's tone of easy patronage, all the harder to endure with philosophic calm at the present moment from the fact that the latter was lounging in his favourite chair. Even from an aesthetic point of view the sight of the bulging child offended him. Ogden Ford was round and blobby and looked overfed. He had the plethoric habit of one to whom wholesome exercise is a stranger and the sallow complexion of the confirmed candy-fiend.

The USSR had 27,000 strategic nuclear warheads and another 15,000 smaller ones; some 40 percent were in what became four other countries after 1991 - Belarus, Kazakhstan, Ukraine and Georgia. In addition, there were thousands more tons of weapons-grade uranium and plutonium, enough for tens of thousands of bombs. At the same time, the Soviet Union's nuclear custodianship system began breaking down, the KGB lost its monopoly on information and the Russian economy plunged into free fall. For the United States, the priority was to get rid of any non-Russian nuclear arsenals, which would complicate arms control efforts and might lead to a dangerous regional competition. The White House sent William Perry, then deputy secretary of defense, to Kiev in May 1994 to persuade Ukraine to give up its nukes. He found a receptive audience. 'The Ukrainians didn't want them. They knew that having those nuclear weapons was going to make them a pariah state. It was going to make it very hard for them to get Western economic assistance,' recalled Rose Gottemoeller, who worked alongside Perry in the Pentagon and later negotiated nuclear issues with Russia at the State Department. The last strategic missile was removed from Ukraine in June 1996, ahead of schedule. Belarus and Kazakhstan also gave up their nukes. The United States and Russia agreed on a framework for securing the weapons in June 1992, and Washington spent $8 billion through 2011 on a broad range of programs aimed at helping Russia keep track of its nuclear materials and prevent theft. One early success came with the Cooperative Threat Reduction Program, which provided funding for the safe destruction of 7,600 nuclear warheads, 900 intercontinental ballistic missiles, 700 submarine-launched ballistic missiles and 155 bombers. The effort included scrapping nuclear-capable bombers and missiles in Belarus, Kazakhstan and Ukraine. Another initiative involved buying highly enriched uranium from dismantled Russian warheads, turning it into low-enriched uranium for peaceful purposes and selling it to power plants in the United States. Russia also received financial help to improve security around nuclear sites, including building fences, installing sensors and hiring guards. 'There are people who have been critical of these programs, saying we're paying the Russians to take care of their own nuclear stockpile,' said Matthew Bunn, a Harvard expert on nuclear terrorism. 'But the question is, how much worse off would we be today without this? I think the answer is quite a lot.' As the Russian economy collapsed in the 1990s, concern grew that impoverished nuclear scientists could sell secrets or materials to rogue regimes or terrorist groups. So the U.S. government launched a series of programs to find them well-paid employment in Russia and elsewhere. The biggest such effort, the International Science and Technology Center, spent $1 billion between 1993 and 2011 to support research projects involving more than 70,000 scientists from Russia and other ex-Soviet republics. The center says it has no evidence that any of its scientists transferred sensitive technology to third parties. The most recent U.S. intelligence assessment, conducted in 2005, concluded that the risk of a Russian nuclear weapon being stolen was small. It noted that Moscow had made progress in improving security since the 1990s, and added that Russia's nuclear command-and-control system was reliable enough to ensure that only authorized personnel could launch a strike. The assessment did acknowledge, however, that there was an increased chance of insiders stealing bomb-making material because of corruption and inadequate screening procedures. Some doubt remains.

The significance of teaching-focused I-A collaborations in emerging countries cannot be overstated, particularly in the context of R&D offshoring. The existing literature on I-A collaborations has primarily focused on research and entrepreneurship-focused alliances, neglecting the critical role of teaching-focused collaborations in enhancing the quality of E&T graduates (Perkmann et al., 2013). This oversight is surprising, given the substantial investments made by MNCs in R&D offshoring to emerging countries. The scarcity of E&T talent in developed countries has led to a shift in the global R&D landscape, with emerging countries becoming increasingly attractive destinations for MNCs seeking to establish R&D subsidiaries (Gassmann and Han, 2004; Jha et al., 2018; Lewin et al., 2009). However, the quality of E&T graduates in emerging countries remains a major concern for MNCs. Studies have consistently shown that a significant proportion of E&T graduates in emerging economies lack the necessary skills and competencies required for R&D positions (Aspiring Minds, 2019; Blom and Saeki, 2011; Farrell et al., 2005). This skills gap has significant implications for MNCs, which must invest substantial resources in on-the-job training to bring these graduates up to speed. Teaching-focused I-A collaborations offer a potential solution to this problem, by providing E&T students with the necessary skills and competencies during their formal education. Despite the potential benefits of teaching-focused I-A collaborations, there is a dearth of research on this topic. Existing studies have primarily focused on the benefits of research and entrepreneurship-focused alliances, neglecting the critical role of teaching-focused collaborations in enhancing the quality of E&T graduates (Perkmann et al., 2013). This oversight is particularly surprising, given the significance of teaching-focused collaborations in addressing the talent recruitment challenge faced by MNCs in emerging countries. To address this knowledge gap, further research is needed to explore the impact of teaching-focused I-A collaborations on the quality of E&T graduates in emerging countries. This research should examine the effectiveness of these collaborations in enhancing the skills and competencies of E&T students, as well as the benefits and challenges associated with these collaborations. Furthermore, research should investigate the factors that influence the success of teaching-focused I-A collaborations, including the role of university-industry partnerships, curriculum design, and faculty development. The implications of this research are far-reaching, with significant consequences for MNCs, universities, and policymakers. By examining the role of teaching-focused I-A collaborations in enhancing the quality of E&T graduates, this research can inform strategies for addressing the talent recruitment challenge faced by MNCs in emerging countries. Furthermore, this research can provide insights into the development of effective university-industry partnerships, which are critical for addressing the skills gap in emerging economies. Ultimately, this research has the potential to contribute to the development of a more skilled and competitive workforce in emerging countries, which is essential for driving economic growth and development.

At about seven-forty-five on the evening of June seventeenth, four years ago, Patrolman Matthew Clabby was on duty - fixed post duty - at the corner of Thirty-fourth Street and Second Avenue. According to the report made by him at the time to his immediate superior and subsequently repeated by him under oath before the grand jury and still later at the trial, his attention was attracted - to use the common formula - by a disturbance occurring on a crosstown trolley car, eastward bound, which had halted just west of the corner. Patrolman Clabby boarded the car to find a small, shabby man endeavouring to break away from a larger and better-dressed man, who held him fast by the collar. In reply to the officer's questions the large man stated that he had detected the small one in the act of picking his pocket. He had waited, he said, until the other lifted his watch and chain and then had seized him and held him fast and called for help. At least three citizens, passengers on the car, confirmed the main points of the accuser's story. For added proof there were the watch and chain. They were in the thief's side coat pocket. With his own large firm hands Patrolman Clabby fished them out from there and confiscated them for purposes of evidence. As for the prisoner, he said nothing at all. The policeman totted down in his little book the names and addresses of the eyewitnesses. This done, he took the small man and led him off afoot to the East Thirty-fifth Street Station, the owner of the watch going along to make a formal charge. Before the desk in the station house this latter person said he was named Hartigan - Charles Edward Hartigan, a private detective by occupation; and he repeated his account of the robbery, with amplifications. The pickpocket gave his name as James Williams and his age as thirty-eight, but declined to tell where he lived, what occupation he followed, or what excuse he had for angling after other people's personal property on a crosstown car. At this juncture Clabby grabbed one of his prisoner's hands and ran a finger over its inner surface, seeking for callosities of the palm; then he nodded meaningly to the desk lieutenant. "I guess he's a dip all right, Loot," said Clabby; "the inside of his hand is as soft as a baby's." "Take him back!" said the lieutenant briefly. Before obeying, Clabby faced the man about and searched him, the search revealing a small amount of money but no objects that might serve for the prisoner's better identification.

The molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of collective behavior in social insects are complex and multifaceted, involving the interplay of various genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors. Recent advances in high-throughput sequencing technologies have enabled the identification of genetic and transcriptomic differences among social insect species, providing valuable insights into the evolutionary pressures shaping the evolution of collective behavior. For example, studies have revealed that ants and honeybees exhibit distinct genomic and transcriptomic profiles, reflecting their unique ecological niches and social structures (Boomsma et al., 2017; Favreau et al., 2018; Toth and Rehan, 2017). Furthermore, molecular studies have characterized the role of specific genes and gene networks in regulating division of labor among workers within social insect colonies (Friedman and Gordon, 2016; Kamhi and Traniello, 2013; Linksvayer, 2015; Simola et al., 2016). In addition to genetic differences, epigenetic mechanisms also play a crucial role in regulating collective behavior in social insects. Epigenetic marks, such as DNA methylation and histone modifications, can influence gene expression and contribute to the development of distinct behavioral phenotypes (Chandra et al., 2018; Gordon, 2016a; Jeanne, 2016; Johnson and Linksvayer, 2010; Toth and Dolezal, 2017). For example, studies have shown that epigenetic marks can influence the expression of genes involved in brain development and function, which in turn affect behavior (Gordon, 2016a; Jeanne, 2016). The regulation of collective behavior in social insects is also influenced by environmental factors, such as food availability and social interactions. For example, changes in food availability can induce changes in gene expression and behavior in social insects, allowing them to adapt to changing environmental conditions (Gordon, 1989; Gordon and Mehdiabadi, 1999). Social interactions, such as communication and cooperation, also play a critical role in regulating collective behavior, and can be influenced by genetic and epigenetic factors (Bengston and Jandt, 2014; Jandt et al., 2014; Jandt and Gordon, 2016). In conclusion, the regulation of collective behavior in social insects is a complex process involving the interplay of genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors. Further research is needed to fully understand the molecular mechanisms underlying this process and to identify the specific genes and gene networks involved. However, the recent advances in high-throughput sequencing technologies and molecular biology have provided valuable insights into the evolution of collective behavior in social insects, and have opened up new avenues for the study of this fascinating phenomenon.

The door of common humanity being closed against him, he made up his mind to continue his journey, let the dangers and privations be what they might. An angel seemed to whisper, "I will lead thee in the way in which thou shalt go;" so he took courage. Being thirsty, he ventured to ask for a drink of water. But George, a lad of about ten years, and Mary, a little flower of seven summers, had looked on and listened with the curiosity common to children. Their hearts were filled with pity toward the poor man; and, when even a drink of water was denied him, the inherent kindness, implanted in all our natures, was instantly awakened. In a moment, as the missionary turned the corner of the yard, the two children met him each with "a cup of cold water." "Here is good fresh water, please drink," said the little ones. When saving for a deposit, it is easy to forget that there are a whole range of other fees that you need to think about. Money Advice Service has compiled a list of extra costs to help This Is Money readers, which need to be factored in to your overall buying or moving budget before you take out a mortgage. Fees vary by lender, value of property and mortgage size. Deposit - mortgage providers will need you to save at least 5 per cent of the cost of the home you want to buy. So if you want to buy a home costing 150,000, you'll need to save 7,500.Mortgage set-up fees - some lenders charge a mortgage booking fee (or equivalent), usually to reserve funds on a fixed or capped rate product. The typical cost is between 99 and 250 and may be refundable if the mortgage application falls through before completion (check this before you pay for it).Mortgage arrangement fee - some mortgage products will incur an upfront fee, which some lenders call an 'arrangement fee'. This may be in addition to a separate booking fee. It can cost up to 2,000 and is added to your mortgage amount. You will have to pay interest on the amount if you decide to do this.Valuation fee - this is charged by a mortgage lender to value the property you are buying. It costs between 150 and 1,500, depending on value of the property. Some lenders will pay this for you so try and negotiate this into your contract.Mortgage account fee - this is a single fee charged by the lender when you take out your mortgage to cover set up, maintenance and closing down costs of your account. You won't have to pay a separate exit administration fee when you repay your mortgage. It's typically 100 to 300.

The country is divided into three main geographical zones: 1) the Ferghana Valley with intensive irrigated agriculture and the largest share of cotton cultivation; 2) the Kyzylkum Desert with traditional rainfed farming systems; and 3) the Aral Sea Depression with intensive livestock grazing and pastoralism (Kopylov and Yuldashev, 2012). The majority of the population live in the Ferghana Valley, where the highest concentration of irrigated lands is located. Irrigated agriculture is the basis of national economy, contributing 25-30% of gross domestic product (GDP), and providing employment to about 40% of the labour force (Government of Uzbekistan, 2015). However, the development of irrigated agriculture was not without consequences for the environment. Overuse of water resources, especially during the Soviet era, resulted in severe environmental degradation, including salinization, soil erosion, air pollution and loss of biodiversity (UNEP, 2002). These effects were even more pronounced in the Aral Sea Basin, where a large part of the water supply of the Aral Sea was diverted for agricultural purposes (Micklin, 2007). To mitigate the negative impacts of unsustainable water management, new water saving technologies and land management approaches have been developed. The main focus of the current paper is on those techniques which can potentially contribute to improve water productivity and reduce water consumption in Uzbekistan. We start with an overview of the existing water saving technologies in the region, followed by a discussion on how these technologies can help to increase water productivity. Finally we propose a methodology to select the most suitable ones for implementation. Monsieur le Cure made the sign of the cross and looked very grave. There was every reason why he should, for the Baron D'Ucelles had shot himself through the head five years ago - two years after his wife's death. It was natural that he should regret her. She had spent six months in giving him what he wanted, and thirteen years in not giving him what he didn't want. She would have made an ideal wife for any man. Still it was not altogether on her account that he had followed her to the grave. The late Baron had been a little extravagant both with his money and with his life, and when he had at length discovered that he would shortly become a helpless paralytic on a very small income, he had decided to take the only means left him to avoid these issues. He had left behind him only Ucelles itself and two small farms, which was all that could be saved for his son out of his once handsome inheritance. His family said that this was what came of having married an English woman without a dot. "There is one thing," said the Cure, after a pause, "that I have never quite understood, and this is why Monsieur Jean should have been brought up by this English relation?" The doctor shrugged his shoulders. "I too have wondered," he said. "But what will you? The activation of NPR-B has been shown to have a protective effect on the optic nerve and retinal ganglion cells, which are the primary targets of POAG. This is achieved through the activation of the guanylyl cyclase domain of NPR-B, leading to an increase in the intracellular concentration of cyclic GMP (cGMP) (Lajmi et al., 2017). cGMP is a potent vasodilator and has been shown to have neuroprotective effects in various models of retinal disease (Bucci et al., 2015; Kielbass et al., 2013). The activation of NPR-B has also been shown to reduce the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and to increase the expression of anti-inflammatory cytokines, which may contribute to the neuroprotective effects of this receptor (Lajmi et al., 2017). In addition to its potential neuroprotective effects, the activation of NPR-B may also have a role in the regulation of IOP. CNP, the natural agonist of NPR-B, has been shown to reduce IOP in animal models of glaucoma (Takashima et al., 1998). This may be due to the ability of CNP to increase the outflow of aqueous humor through the uveoscleral pathway, which is an important route for the drainage of aqueous humor in the eye (Lajmi et al., 2017). The potential therapeutic benefits of activating NPR-B in POAG are promising, and several studies have investigated the use of NPR-B agonists as a potential treatment for the disease. One study used a NPR-B agonist to reduce IOP and prevent the progression of POAG in a rat model of the disease (Lajmi et al., 2017). Another study used a NPR-B agonist to protect retinal ganglion cells from damage in a model of chronic ocular hypertension (Kielbass et al., 2013). While the results of these studies are promising, there are still several challenges that must be overcome before NPR-B agonists can be used as a treatment for POAG. One of the main challenges is the development of a NPR-B agonist that can selectively target the eye and avoid systemic side effects. Another challenge is the determination of the optimal dose and duration of treatment required to achieve the desired therapeutic effects. In conclusion, the activation of NPR-B has been shown to have potential therapeutic benefits in POAG, including the reduction of IOP and the protection of retinal ganglion cells. While there are still several challenges that must be overcome before NPR-B agonists can be used as a treatment for POAG, the results of these studies suggest that this may be a promising new direction for the treatment of this disease. Further research is needed to fully explore the potential of NPR-B agonists as a treatment for POAG and to determine their safety and efficacy in humans.

Strain mismatch within a substrate is the driving force for many of the transformations in nature as well as for many synthetic actuators upon activation by the stimuli. Swelling is one of the simplest way to realise strain differential in a substrate. Combined with the morphing response of cellulose to stimulus (e.g. water), a time-dependant transformation of a printed 3D shape could be triggered, to produce a "4D" printed structure. This approach is analogous to the "4D printing" concepts developed and demonstrated at MIT [16], which utilise materials with shape memory and volumetric expansion properties to achieve micro to macroscopic actuation responses [17-20]. The use of 3D printing to achieve shear-alignment of cellulosic fibrils to preferentially control the swelling of an embedding matrix would further emulate the macroscopic response demonstrated in the hierarchical structure of natural 4D materials, such as the pinecones described above [2,21]. While cellulose, as a potential 4D printing feedstock, has benefits such as environmental friendliness, biodegradability and low cost [22-24], in its native form, cellulose is not compatible with current commercial 3D printing/additive layer manufacturing systems as it cannot be melted and extruded in a similar manner to existing 3D printing polymer feedstocks, nor sintered with a laser, such as is commonly done with ceramic/metal/polymer beads. Commercial 3D printing filaments comprised of cellulosic materials systems do exist where the cellulose is in the form of sawdust or recycled wood forming fillers ( 30%) hosted within a polymer matrix such as PLA (polylactic acid) [25,26]. However, this method limits the exposure of cellulosic components to the environment/stimuli and hence such approaches are not appropriate for 4D morphing applications. Markstedt et al. 3D printed cellulose by dissolving three different types of cellulose (namely bacterial nanocellulose, Avicel-PH-1-1 and dissolving pulp) in ionic liquids (IL) followed by coagulation, resulting in 2D and multilayer 3D gel structures on a coagulating bed, allowing ionic solutions with cellulose concentrations of 1%, 2% and 4% to be 3D printed [27]. Composite bio-inks have also been prepared by combining cellulose nanofibril (NFC) dispersions in an alginate-based hydrogel consisting of 95-99% water, crosslinked by immersion in calcium chloride (CaCl2) solution [28]. However, the cellulosic content of the reported bio-ink was very modest (1.5%-2.3% w/v). Hakansson et al. reported similar bio-inks where the 3D dry state shape was achieved by means of freeze drying the bio-ink print [29], with similar approaches in cellulose printing also being reported by researchers at Aalto University (Finland) and VTT research (Finland) as part of their joint DWOC (Design Driven Value Chains in the World of Cellulose) program [30]. Leppiniemi et al. reported a nanocellulose-alginate hydrogel with good tissue compatibility for 3D printing [31]. The nanocellulose content within printable hydrogel formulations varied from 0.5%-1.3% w/w.

The purpose of these is to elongate the nose-entry wavefront sufficiently to ensure that, even after steepening during propagation along the tunnel, it is not too steep when it reaches the exit portal. This has proved to be a highly effective counter-measure, but it has some important limitations. First, the required length of the modified entrance region typically increases approximately with the cube of the train speed. Second, the required length increases with the length of the tunnel. Third, entrance region counter-measures have no influence at all on wavefronts that are generated further along the tunnel, notably when a train crosses an airshaft or other branch feature in a tunnel. When these limitations are relevant, it is logical to consider counter-measures further along the tunnel. One possibility that has been considered, but found to be less effective than expected is the provision of baffle plates along a tunnel [10]. Greater success has been obtained with measures that can be applied at outlets from which unacceptable disturbances must be prevented. This paper focuses on the most important of these locations, namely the main tunnel exit portal. Several exit portal countermeasures have been studied. Passive methods include chambers that are loosely analogous to gun-silencers or automobile exhaust silencer boxes [11,12]. Typically, these include some form of baffle plates, possibly in a helical formation [13]. However, all such devices have a fundamental disadvantage of requiring a large structure in the affected region - which is contrary to the usual wishes of designers to minimise the visual impact of tunnels. This particular disadvantage can be avoided by employing active measures to generate so-called anti-noise, namely a second set of MPWs that, ideally, is equal to the train-generated MPWs, but opposite in sign [12,14,15]. An obvious disadvantage of such techniques - apart from the technical difficulties involved in their design - is that they are not fail-safe. That is, in the event of a power failure, they would provide no relief at all and, in the event of malfunction, they could even increase the disturbance. In this paper, attention is focussed on a tunnel exit counter-measure comprising an extended region of tunnel with holes/slots along its length leading directly to the atmosphere (Fig. 1a). This is geometrically similar to one form of existing tunnel entrance regions (which automatically become exit regions when the direction of train travel is reversed). In a nutshell, the objective is to cause the incident wavefront to elongate as it propagates along the extension, thereby greatly reducing its steepness and hence reducing the MPW emission through the final outlet portal. However, there is a price to pay for this, namely the creation of additional MPWs from the slots along the tunnel roof. The latter have been assessed in an experimental and numerical investigation of a related geometry, namely snow sheds between adjacent tunnels in a mountainous region of Japan [16].

The persistence of smoking behavior, encapsulated within the concept of state dependence, implies that past habits are an influential predictor of future behavior. This has profound implications for public health policy, as interventions aimed at mitigating smoking must consider not only the immediate deterrents but also the entrenched patterns of behavior that perpetuate smoking across time. In conjunction with the rational addiction model, the concept of state dependence provides a framework for understanding how smokers assess the balance of present enjoyment against future risk, often reinforcing a cycle that proves challenging to disrupt. Policy measures that merely increase the cost of smoking might not suffice in compelling change, especially for entrenched smokers displaying high state dependence. These individuals may possess deep-seated attachments to smoking rituals and patterns, which economic deterrents alone are unlikely to disrupt. Comprehensive strategies should therefore be multifaceted, incorporating economic, psychological, and social dimensions. These strategies might include not only raising tobacco taxes but also providing support systems such as counseling, cessation programs, and community support to address the multifactorial aspects of smoking. Moreover, the endogenous time preference model implies that interventions could be directed towards altering individuals' time preferences. Tailored programs that promote long-term thinking and planning, perhaps integrated into educational curriculums or workplace incentives, could potentially influence individuals' assessments of future consequences, thereby reducing smoking behavior. Individuals better educated on the long-term impacts of smoking might recalibrate their internal discount rates, leading to more conscientious decisions regarding their health. This theoretical framework underscores the necessity of early intervention. Given that time preferences and smoking habits are shaped over an individual's life course, targeting younger populations could yield substantial benefits. Educational initiatives that instill the value of future-oriented thinking, alongside awareness campaigns about smoking's health risks, may preempt the development of adverse smoking habits. Embedding these concepts into a broader societal narrative about health and wellness can contribute to shifting norms and reducing the social acceptability of smoking. Furthermore, empirical studies highlight the role of life shocks in altering time preferences and, consequently, smoking behavior. Traumatic events or significant life changes can prompt individuals to reevaluate their priorities and health behaviors. Public health strategies could leverage such moments of reflection, offering targeted support and resources for smoking cessation to those undergoing life transitions or dealing with stressors that might otherwise reinforce negative behaviors. Advancing our understanding of the interplay between time preferences, state dependence, and smoking behavior could also inform the creation of predictive models. These models, employing data analytics and machine learning, could identify individuals at high risk of persistent smoking. This would enable more precise targeting of interventions, optimizing resource allocation and increasing the interventions' cost-effectiveness. Ultimately, a nuanced comprehension of the intertemporal decision-making processes behind smoking behavior fosters more effective policy implementation. By integrating economic theories with insights from psychology and sociology, policymakers can design comprehensive approaches that acknowledge the complexity of smoking behavior. As researchers continue to explore these dynamics, the insights gathered will be instrumental in crafting innovative strategies to curb the prevalence of smoking and improve public health outcomes overall.

The next morning was damp, and grey, and mild, no autumn wind stirring the long sweeping branches of the cedars on the lawn, the dead leaves falling silently, the world all sad and solemn, clad in universal greyness. Christabel was up early, with her boy, in the nursery - watching him as he splashed about his bath, and emerged rosy and joyous, like an infant river-god sporting among the rushes; early at family prayers in the dining room, a ceremony at which Mr. Tregonell rarely assisted, and to which Dopsy and Mopsy came flushed and breathless with hurry, anxious to pay all due respect to a hostess whom they hoped to visit again, but inwardly revolting against the unreasonableness of eight-o'clock prayers. Angus, who was generally about the gardens before eight, did not appear at all this morning. The other men were habitually late - breakfasting together in a free-and-easy manner when the ladies had left the dining-room - so Christabel, Miss Bridgeman, and the Miss Vandeleurs sat down to breakfast alone, Dopsy giving little furtive glances at the door every now and then, expectant of Mr. Hamleigh's entrance. That expectancy became too painful for the damsel's patience, by-and-by, as the meal advanced. "I wonder what has become of Mr. Hamleigh," she said. "This is the first time he has been late at breakfast." "Perhaps he is seeing to the packing of his portmanteau," said Miss Bridgeman. "Some valets are bad packers, and want superintendence." "Packing!" cried Dopsy, aghast. "Packing! What for?" "He is going to London this afternoon. Didn't you know?" Dopsy grew pale as ashes. The shock was evidently terrible, and even Jessie pitied her. "Poor silly Dop," she thought. "Could she actually suppose that she stood the faintest chance of bringing down her bird?" "Going away? For good?" murmured Miss Vandeleur faintly - all the flavour gone out of the dried salmon, the Cornish butter, the sweet home-baked bread. "I hope so. He is going to the South of France for the winter. Of course, you know that he is consumptive, and has not many years to live," answered Miss Bridgeman. "Poor fellow!" sighed Dopsy, with tears glittering upon her lowered eyelids. She had begun the chase moved chiefly by sordid instincts; her tenderest emotions had been hacked and vulgarized by long experience in flirtation - but at this moment she believed that never in her life had she loved before, and that never in her life could she love again. "And if he dies unmarried what will become of his property?" inquired Mopsy, whose feelings were not engaged. "I haven't the faintest idea," answered Miss Bridgeman. "He has no near relations. I hope he will leave his money to some charitable institution." "What time does he go?" faltered Dopsy, swallowing her tears. "Mr. Hamleigh left an hour ago, Madam," said the butler, who had been carving at the side-board during this conversation. "He has gone shooting. His man has taken his luggage to the station."

As one ventured deeper into this labyrinthine quarter, the cacophony of sounds and aromas intensified, a symphony of clanging hammers, rattling chains, and the constant din of human voices, punctuated by the occasional shrill cry of a street vendor or the mournful lowing of a dray horse. The air was thick with the smells of coal smoke, hot metal, and the sweet, pungent aroma of freshly baked bread wafting from the ovens of the nearby bakery. Here, amidst the chaos, the denizens of this forgotten corner of London went about their daily lives, each one a thread in the intricate tapestry of this vibrant, if somewhat tattered, community. In the midst of this bustling throng, a few stalwart establishments stood out, beacons of stability in a sea of flux. There was old Mr. Jenkins' chandler's shop, its windows a riot of colour, with coils of rope, lanterns, and gleaming brass fixtures spilling out onto the pavement. Next door, the venerable sign of the "Sailor's Rest" creaked in the gentle breeze, a haven for weary mariners and dockworkers seeking solace in a foaming mug of ale and a warm fire. Across the way, the imposing bulk of the "Riverbank Warehouse" loomed, its stone facade bearing the scars of countless storms and the weight of generations of commerce. Yet, despite the apparent vitality of this quarter, there existed an undercurrent of unease, a sense of impermanence that hung in the air like the acrid tang of smoke from the nearby factories. It was a place where fortunes were made and lost with equal rapidity, where the line between prosperity and penury was perilously thin, and where the whispered rumour of a dock strike or a shipwreck could send shockwaves through the entire community. In this precarious world, the inhabitants of the street had developed a unique dialect, a patois of nautical slang, Cockney rhyming, and Music Hall patter, which served as a badge of identity and a means of communication in a world where outsiders were viewed with suspicion. It was a language that was both colorful and cryptic, capable of conveying a wealth of information in a few, well-chosen words, and one that was spoken with a speed and fluency that left the uninitiated bewildered. As the day wore on, the street began to take on a more subdued aspect, the bustle and clamour of the morning giving way to a more languid, afternoon air. The sun, a burning copper disk in the sky, cast long shadows across the pavement, and the smell of cooking wafted from the open windows of the tenements, mingling with the cries of children playing in the narrow alleys. It was a time of day when the street's inhabitants paused to draw breath, to reflect on the morning's events, and to prepare for the long, uncertain night ahead. And yet, even in this moment of relative tranquility, the street remained alive, a pulsing, vibrant entity, its rhythms and cadences woven into the very fabric of the city itself.
