Beyond the parapet of the terrace, the garden, with its apple and walnut trees, its beeches, its lawn, its beds of tulips, its lilac and laburnum and may and all sorts of other pleasant things, slopes lazily upwards to a horizon of iron railings separating the garden from a meadow where now and then a cow, when she desires to be peculiarly agreeable to the sight, poses herself in silhouette against the sky. I like to gaze on that adventitious cow. Her ruminatory attitude falls in with mine.... But I digress.... I glanced up at the obscuring human form and recognized my wife. She looked, I must confess, remarkably pretty, with her fair hair blond comme les bles, and her mocking cornflower blue eyes, and her mutinous mouth, which has never yet (after all these years) assumed a responsible parent's austerity. She wore a fresh white dress with coquettish bits of blue about the bodice. In her hand she grasped a dilapidated newspaper, the Daily Telegraph, which looked as if she had been to bed in it. "Am I disturbing you, Hilary?" She was. She knew she was. But she looked so charming, a petal of spring, a quick incarnation of pink may and forget-me-not and laburnum, that I put down my pen and I smiled. "You are, my dear," said I, "but it doesn't matter." "What are you doing?" She remained on the threshold. "I am writing my presidential address," said I, "for the Grand Meeting, next month, of the Hafiz Society." "I wonder," said Barbara, "why Hafiz always makes me think of sherbet." I remonstrated, waving a dismissing hand. "If that's all you've got to say - " "But it isn't." She crossed the threshold, stepped in, swished round the end of my long oak table and took possession of my library. I wheeled round politely in my chair. "Then, what is it?" I asked. "Have you read the paper this morning?" "I've glanced through the Times," said I. She patted her handful of bedclothing and let fall a blanket and a bed-spread or two - ("Look at my beautifully, orderly folded Times," said I, with an indicatory gesture) She looked and sniffed - and shed Vallombrosa leaves of the Daily Telegraph about the library until she had discovered the page for which she was searching. Then she held a mangled sheet before my eyes. "There!" she cried, "what do you think of that?" "What do I think of what?" I asked, regarding the acre of print. "Adrian Boldero has written a novel!" "Adrian?" said I. "Well, my dear, what of it? Poor old Adrian is capable of anything. Nothing he did would ever surprise me. He might write a sonnet to a Royal Princess's first set of false teeth or steal the tin cup from a blind beggar's dog, and he would be still the same beautiful, charming, futile Adrian." Barbara pished and insisted.

Now the grand-daughter of that Wigod, whom we will not call traitor to his country - although some might deem him so - in default of male issue, became the wife of Brian Fitz-Count. The only son of Wigod, who might have passed on the inheritance to a line of English lords - Tokig of Wallingford - died in defence of William the Conqueror[2] at the battle of Archenbrai, waged between the father and his son Robert Courthose. To build the new castle,[3] Robert d'Oyley, who succeeded to the lordship on the death of Wigod, destroyed eight houses, which furnished space for the enlargement, and material for the builders. We are not told whether he made compensation - it is doubtful. The castle was built within the ancient walls in the north-east quarter of the town, occupying a space of some twenty or thirty acres, and its defence on the eastern side was the Thames. Within the precincts rose one of those vast mounds thrown up by Ethelfleda, lady of the Mercians, and daughter of the great Alfred, a century and a half earlier. It formed the kernel of the new stronghold, and surmounted by a lofty tower, commanded a wondrous view of the country around, from a height of some two hundred feet. On the north-east lay the long line of the Chilterns; on the south-west, the Berkshire downs stretching towards Cwichelm's Hlawe, and the White Horse Hill; between the two lay the gorge of the Thames, and in the angle the fertile alluvial plain, chiefly filled at that time by a vast park or chase, or by forest or marsh land. The Chilterns were covered with vast beech forests, the Berkshire downs were more bare. There were three bastions to the north and two on the south; within the inner dyke or moat on the east was the "glacis," which sloped abruptly towards the river: the main entrance, on the west, was approached by a series of drawbridges, while beneath the tower a heavy portcullis defended the gateway. Upon the keep stood two sentinels, who from the summit of their lofty tower scrutinised the roads and open country all day long, until they were relieved by those who watched by night. Beneath them lay the town with its moat, and earthen rampart in compass a good mile and more, joining the river at each extremity. Within the compass were eleven parishes, "well and sufficiently built," with one parish church in each of them, well constructed, and with chaplains and clerks daily officiating, so that people had no lack of spiritual provision. Beyond, the roads stretched in all directions: the Lower Icknield Street ran by woody Ewelme along the base of the downs, towards distant Stokenchurch and Wycombe; while on the opposite side, it ran across the wild moor land through Aston and Blewbery to the Berkshire downs, where it joined the upper way again, and continued its course for Devizes.

Hank's thoughts swirl like the flurries outside, the December wind carrying the chill of unwelcome memories. It was supposed to be simple, this muted New Year's Day; a quiet retreat from the chaos of the holidays, the mounting expectations of life. Not today. Not with Lou - his brother's sometimes-sullen presence lingering like a shadow across the threshold of his door. HANK (clearly uncomfortable) I thought you were staying at Mom's longer. LOU (shrugging) Yeah well, thought I'd come check up on you, little brother. Mom had too many people over. Needed some air. Hank forces a tight-lipped smile, the politeness pressing against him like the layers of his overcoat. He glances up and down the street, hoping to glean something from the icy silence. The neighborhood was a ghost town; sounds swallowed by the frost-laden ground-conversations muffled, laughter stifled. It seeped into him, the stark abandonment making his heart clench tighter against that uncomfortable familiarity. LOU (noticing Hank's hesitance) You expecting someone? HANK (distracted) No. Just-nothing. Just thought maybe we could have some time alone...you know? LOU (chuckling softly) Good luck with that. Can't hide from what's out there, Hank. It'll always find you. With a stiff nod, Hank steps aside, allowing Lou into the house. He hitches his coat closer around him and glances again at the door leading to the rest of their home. Warmth tugs at him from the kitchen, promising the scent of freshly brewed coffee, the kind Sarah made countless mornings, wrapping time around them like a comforting blanket. INT. MITCHELL KITCHEN - MOMENTS LATER Sarah stands in front of the stove, the glow of the gas flames dancing against her silhouette. She hums softly to herself, the tune a tender echo of the earlier song. A steaming pot bubbles, filling the space with inviting aromas, but today it feels different, as though the warmth of what was once refuge now mingles with anticipation of what's to come. Hank wanders over, intent to grasp brief moments of solace. She looks up, a smile blooming on her face-a flower pushing through the winter's frost. SARAH (playfully) You look like you've seen a ghost. HANK (half-smiling) It's just Lou. SARAH (feigning shock) Oh, that ghost! Should I prepare the exorcism kit? Hank chuckles softly, the laughter swelling in his chest before it wilts beneath the briefness of it. He becomes conscious of Lou's heavy footsteps thumping in from the living room-a tangible reminder of the fragility encasing their reality. LOU (leaning against the doorframe) Smells good in here. What are we having-ghost stew? SARAH (rolling her eyes affectionately) It's a surprise. Family tradition and all that. HANK (trying to steer the mood) We weren't expecting company. LOU (deflecting) Just came to check in on the home fires! Didn't you say you needed someone to liven up the place? A tense silence drapes over them like a shroud. Nobody acknowledges the subplot beneath Lou's words-the unspoken past that drags like a faded tapestry through their interactions. The kettle whistles, a sharp, teeth-clenching sound that slices through the tension, drawing Hank's focus back to Sarah. He meets her eyes, searching for a semblance of understanding that wasn't yet lost. SARAH (serving mugs) Here we go-nothing like a hot cup to warm a cold day. Hank takes a mug, his fingers lingering against the tiny cracks in the ceramic. They're all cracked, he thinks: his own facade hiding a depths he doesn't speak about and Lou's unapologetic, overshadowing presence. HANK (softly) It's not as simple as that, is it? Lou shrugs, sipping the coffee, and the flicker in his eyes suggests he knows the collision they're pushing toward, even if he pretends otherwise. LOU (quietly) No, it never is. And against the backdrop of muted conversation, a quiet yet resounding realization settles among them, abruptly heavy. This New Year's Day was merely another chapter in a saga that seemed endlessly unresolved-, echoing through the room, like the hymn sung through the mist.

"I don't think they should be banned," she says. "They're like any other dog." Sullivan isn't alone in her views. A recent poll commissioned by the American Veterinary Medical Association found that 54 percent of respondents believe there is no evidence that certain types of dogs pose more of a threat to public safety than others. Despite the high number of pit bulls being trained in HSUS's Pets for Life program, the organization does not take a stance on breed-specific legislation. Instead, it promotes programs that focus on individual dogs rather than whole breeds. For example, HSUS supports laws that require dogs to be licensed regardless of breed. It also advocates for mandatory spaying and neutering of animals. And the organization works with local animal shelters to educate staff about how to handle specific breeds during intake and adoption. While the Maryland Court of Appeals ruling may be bad news for pit bulls, some experts say the decision could ultimately benefit them. In 2002, San Francisco became the first U.S. city to pass a law banning pit bulls and other so-called aggressive breeds. Since then, many other cities have passed similar ordinances. Some studies show that such bans fail to reduce attacks by targeted breeds; instead, they increase the likelihood of attacks by non-banned breeds. One study published in the Journal of Urban Health found that after the passage of a breed-specific ordinance in Denver, fatal dog bites increased by 50 percent. Others claim breed-specific legislation does nothing to address the underlying problem. "Breed-specific legislation will not solve the issue of dog bite prevention," Dr. Ron Hines writes in an article for PetMD. "It just shifts the focus from education and training to the breed of the dog involved."

Just relax! You're going to look amazing!" I shout, hoping my enthusiasm might seep through her walls of worry. She glances at me skeptically, fingers nervously twisting a lock of her hair. "Doesn't sound like it's going to be fine to me," she huffs back, eyeing her reflection one more time. "And don't even get me started on the food! What if there's nothing to eat? I can't survive a night without popcorn!" "Did you say popcorn?" And suddenly I feel like I'm being pulled into her whirlpool of insecurities. I know she's just joking, but deep down, I think she means it. Isn't that the odd truth about fears? Sometimes they manifest in the most absurd ways-like the fear of not having a snack at the prom. A lingering silence hangs between us as the clock ticks closer to the event. Even though the atmosphere is thick with apprehension, the images of dancing lights and laughter rumble in my mind. How magical it all seems! But somewhere in the background, sneering doubts claw at my heart. Could I be brave enough to talk to Nick? "Hey, what's the worst that could happen?" I try to muster a comforting smile as I suggest, "It's only a dance. Just picture it as one big chance to meet people and have fun. Just let it go!" Kim shrugs, her brows furrowing as she considers my words but ultimately shakes her head. "Easy for you to say. You're not the one who has to deal with the dance floor... or people looking at you... and the embarrassing moments!" "Except for the fact I'm losing my mind too." It's difficult not to laugh, but her face is so sincere I just can't. "We're a mess together, huh?" "Yeah, a beautiful mess." She cracks a smile, softening just a fraction. My heart swells because I know at least that spark of connection remains. Every fear clouds our emotions in a way that makes us wonder if we can ever truly face the world.

We've been encouraged in our society to do what I call worst-first thinking, which is come up with the worst-case scenario first and proceed as if it's likely to happen, and that's what happened with the Meitivs," Skenazy said. "Someone sees two children alone, and they leap to 'Oh, my God, they're neglected. What if they're run over by a Mack truck? What if they're kidnapped? There are predators all around.' " Crime rates are way down from when many of us were kids in the '70s; rape, murder, burglary and arson are all down, said Skenazy, so it's not exactly true to think today's world is scarier than when I walked four blocks to the candy store when I was in the first grade. "And if we are going to say, 'Oh, my God, I would never let my kid walk outside; something bad could happen,' well, I hope you're saying that 'Oh, my God, I would never put my kid in the car, something bad could happen,' because the No. 1 way children die in America is as car passengers, and yet we seem to keep that 'danger' in perspective, but we can't keep the same perspective when it comes to letting our children walk outside," she added. Alexander Meitiv was not arrested, but a few hours later, someone from Child Protective Services arrived and said the family needed to agree not to let the children be unsupervised until the matter was resolved within the agency, or the children would be taken into the custody of Child Protective Services.

Father took me, and-oh, Dave, you should have seen the way they moved-it was like watching the wind play with the autumn leaves!" Dave chuckled softly, the sound a rumble that came from deep in his chest. "Sounds like quite the spectacle. And I suppose their skin was tanned just the same as Tom and Harry's?" "Perhaps even more so," Belle admitted with a teasing twinkle in her eye. "But you must remember, your friends have spent considerable time under the harsh sun of the Southwest. They've taken to their new life out there quite enthusiastically." "It's good to hear," Dave said with genuine warmth. "Hard to picture them away from the old crowd, but it's comforting to know they're doing well." Belle nodded in agreement, her gaze drifting momentarily to the small, framed photograph on the side table. It was a picture of Dave in his plebe summer, the proud square shoulders and determined expression so very typical of him. "I suppose we all have our own paths to follow," she mused softly, just as the grandfather clock in the corner began to chime the hour. "You, too, are setting sail on your own course, Dave," she continued, her tone turning reflective. "There you are in your sharp uniform aboard the naval vessels, sailing to who-knows-where. I sometimes wonder whether you ever feel adrift." Dave considered her words seriously, his brow furrowed slightly with thought. "There's a structure to our wanderings, Belle. We navigate by the stars and the maps, by orders handed down in true naval fashion. But yes, there are moments when the entire world feels vast and uncertain, and I am just a small part of it. Yet that's the nature of the sea, isn't it? It reminds you of your smallness, but also of the endless possibilities." Belle leaned forward slightly, looking at him with tender concern. "And do visions of those possibilities guide you, Dave? Do they give you solace when the waves are high and the nights are long?" His eyes met hers, the sincerity in them unmistakable. "They do, Belle. And so does the thought of you. Knowing you're here, waiting, well-it makes the long nights less daunting." Her cheeks flushed, a delicate pink brushing over her skin. "Oh, Dave," she murmured, her voice barely above a whisper. The air between them settled into a comfortable quietude, where words seemed redundant but the shared understanding was profound. Outside, the evening shadows grew longer as the day prepared to hand over its watch to the night. Belle's gaze shifted to the window, where the first stars were already daring to prick the twilight canopy. "In all the grand expanse," she mused aloud, "do you think of those stars as guides too, Dave?" "In a way, yes," he admitted, a thoughtful smile on his lips. "Guides, reminders, old companions. And perhaps, themselves, small dreams burning brightly in the night sky-just like our hopes and aspirations."

As I sat in the dimly lit cabin of the Arrow, surrounded by the familiar scent of tar and saltwater, I couldn't help but feel a sense of defeat wash over me. The memory of the Southern Cross, my pride and joy, lying broken and battered on the Irish coast, still lingered in my mind like an open wound. I thought of the crew, my friends and comrades, who had stood by me through thick and thin, and how I had let them down. The weight of my failure hung heavy on my shoulders, and for the first time in my life, I felt like a man without a purpose. But as I gazed out into the darkness, I knew I couldn't stay stuck in the past. I had to find a way to move forward, to prove to myself and others that I still had what it took to be a master of the sea. And so, I threw myself into my work, taking on every task with a renewed sense of determination and grit. I worked tirelessly, day and night, until my body ached and my eyes burned with fatigue. But I didn't stop. I couldn't stop. The Arrow's captain, a gruff old salt named Jenkins, took notice of my efforts and began to take me under his wing. He taught me new tricks and shared stories of his own struggles and triumphs on the high seas. Slowly but surely, I began to rebuild my confidence, and with it, my reputation. I started to see the sea in a new light, as a force to be respected and harnessed, rather than a foe to be conquered. As the months passed, I found myself growing into my new role, earning the respect of the crew and the trust of Captain Jenkins. I learned to navigate by the stars, to read the winds and the waves, and to anticipate the unexpected. I became a student of the sea, and it taught me more about myself than I ever could have imagined. But even as I found my footing on the Arrow, I knew I couldn't stay there forever. I had to have my own ship, my own command. I had to prove to myself and the world that I was more than just a failed captain, that I was a master of the sea. And so, I began to make plans, to save and scheme, to dream of the day when I would once again stand on the bridge of my own ship, the wind in my hair and the spray of the sea on my face. It was a dream that drove me, a fire that burned deep within me. And I knew that no matter what lay ahead, I would stop at nothing to make it a reality. For I was a sailor, rough and weathered, but unbroken. And I would not rest until I had claimed my rightful place on the waves.

We study the role of smallholder farmers' participation in market-oriented agricultural value chains in reducing food insecurity in sub-Saharan Africa. We construct an index of market integration from household surveys in six African countries: Cameroon, Ethiopia, Ghana, Malawi, Tanzania and Uganda. Using this measure, we show that there is a negative association between household market integration and food insecurity. We find that market integration reduces food insecurity directly by increasing income and indirectly by changing the composition of consumption toward non-staple foods. These results suggest that efforts to integrate smallholders into market-oriented agriculture can reduce food insecurity. This entry was posted in Uncategorized on October 5, 2018 by admin. The social cost of carbon (SCC) is an increasingly important metric for evaluating climate change mitigation policies. Yet, despite its growing prominence, there remains substantial uncertainty about the SCC. Some have argued that the SCC should be based on the marginal abatement costs (MACs) of reducing greenhouse gas emissions, while others have suggested that the SCC should be based on the net benefits of mitigating climate change. Here we propose a framework for comparing the SCC derived from MACs and the SCC derived from net benefits. Our approach is based on three principles. First, we assume that the SCC is defined as the present discounted value of the net benefits of mitigating climate change over time. Second, we focus on the SCC under different assumptions about the rate of discounting. Third, we evaluate the SCC using a range of alternative models of the economy and climate. Based on simulations using our integrated assessment model, we conclude that the SCC derived from MACs is higher than the SCC derived from net benefits, and the difference increases with the discount rate. This finding suggests that estimates of the SCC derived from MACs may substantially overstate the true social costs of carbon. This entry was posted in Uncategorized on September 28, 2018 by admin. How do agricultural subsidies affect consumers? We address this question empirically by studying the introduction of price controls on wheat flour in Kenya in 2014. We develop a new methodology for analyzing supply-side shocks to consumer prices, which allows us to estimate both the short-run and long-run pass-through of price changes to retail prices. We find that the immediate pass-through of the subsidy is almost complete, but the long-run pass-through is only partial. We attribute the incomplete pass-through to differences in the degree of competition among retailers, and show that supermarkets pass through most of the subsidy, while informal retailers pass through none. We then explore the welfare implications of the subsidy. On average, the subsidy raises real incomes by $15 per year, but the gains are concentrated among poor households who spend a larger share of their budget on bread. Finally, we analyze the political economy of the policy. We show that the subsidy increased voter turnout in the national elections held shortly after its implementation, suggesting that politicians may target price interventions strategically. Now comes the fun part: driving through the town of Cotati. It has a major intersection where US-101 meets Rtes. 116 & 116W. The light turns green and we start across. I'm doing about 30mph when suddenly we hear a loud bang and the van starts shaking violently. A tire blew! We pull off to the side of the road and try to figure out what to do. I call AAA Roadside Assistance and they tell me someone will be by shortly. They have us wait until a tow truck arrives, since the tire cannot be replaced on site. It's about 10pm so we're waiting outside the vehicle. Luckily it's warm enough to not need a jacket and we have a flashlight. The tow truck arrives about twenty minutes later and the driver tells me that he can't take the van because his truck isn't high enough to lift it. He also says that the place that does flat repairs won't open until 7am. I ask him if he knows of any other repair places nearby and he points me to one just down the street. This is great news. I thank the tow guy and head to the shop. It's still early, like 11pm, so there's nobody there. I go inside and see that the front door is locked. There is a phone number posted on the glass. I call and am told that the owner is on vacation but that his son would be there in the morning to help me out. What? Vacation? That's fine but why couldn't you leave your cell phone number for people who might be stranded? I don't know. Anyway, I get back in the van and sit outside the shop until about 1am. In order to navigate the complex landscape of stakeholder engagement, it becomes essential to employ strategies that facilitate constructive dialogue and collaboration (Burgess et al., 2017). This dialogue must not only encompass the perspectives of diverse stakeholders, but also emphasize the inherent uncertainties and trade-offs that accompany ecosystem-based management (EBM) processes (Brown and Carr, 2010; Pahl-Wostl et al., 2008). Consequently, effective communication strategies are paramount, fostering a shared understanding of the multifaceted challenges that stakeholders face while elucidating the potential consequences of various management decisions (Romer et al., 2017). This, in turn, promotes a sense of shared responsibility and collective ownership of the management outcomes, thus enhancing the legitimacy of the decision-making process (Muro and Jeffrey, 2017). Furthermore, the integration of scientific knowledge and local expertise cannot be overstated. Local stakeholders often possess invaluable insights gleaned from years of living and working in the affected areas, providing a rich context that can fill the gaps left by conventional scientific assessments (Berkes, 2017). Thus, embracing a co-learning approach allows for the fusion of traditional ecological knowledge and contemporary scientific practices, broadening the understanding of ecosystem dynamics and enriching the participatory modelling exercises (Turner et al., 2016). It is critical that this synthesis of knowledge is not merely anecdotal but is rigorously documented and integrated into the decision-making framework (Bennett et al., 2016). Additionally, the continual evolution of socio-ecological systems necessitates that the policies derived from participatory modelling remain dynamic and adaptable (Folke et al., 2010). Static models can quickly become obsolete, as they fail to account for rapid environmental changes, shifts in stakeholder priorities, and technological advancements. To combat this, adaptive management frameworks should be in place, allowing for periodic reassessment of both assumptions and outcomes in light of new information and experiences (Williams et al., 2011). This adaptive approach not only enhances resilience but also cultivates a culture of learning, emphasizing the importance of iterative processes in managing ecosystems. Moreover, the importance of equitable stakeholder representation within these frameworks cannot be overlooked. Power imbalances often hinder effective participation, with marginalized groups frequently underrepresented in decision-making processes (Probst et al., 2016). To counteract this, targeted efforts must be made to empower all stakeholders, ensuring that local voices are not only heard but actively influence the direction of management initiatives (Fischer et al., 2016). Such empowerment can be facilitated through capacity-building initiatives, providing stakeholders with the tools necessary to engage meaningfully in the dialogue surrounding ecosystem management (Alder et al., 2019). Ultimately, the pursuit of effective ecosystem-based management is a complex endeavor, requiring a delicate balancing act between the competing interests of various stakeholders (Jansson et al., 2017). Emphasizing transparency, trust, and mutual respect will be crucial in fostering an environment conducive to collaboration. Moreover, recognizing the ongoing nature of environmental decision-making-where feedback loops are inherent and outcomes are subject to change-can bolster stakeholder resilience and commitment to collective goals. As we continue to grapple with the intricacies of human-nature interactions, the principles of participatory modelling, collaborative governance, and adaptive management will serve as cornerstones for fostering sustainable ecological systems, ensuring that they thrive for generations to come (Daw et al., 2015).

"You must know, doctor," continued the captain, "that although I've been all my life at sea, and sailed among savages many a day, I'm not what you may call a sailor in the strict sense o' the word. My father was a merchant, and I've always been in command of merchant vessels. In course o' time I've learned how to handle a craft pretty well, and can do anything that most men can do aboard ship. But I've got no great notion o' navigation, an' I never could make head nor tail o' the figures that are used in the nautical almanac. Now, my mate here is just the opposite of me. He's a regular blue-jacket - can steer by the stars, work out his reckonings, and navigate a ship wherever she goes. But he don't understand handling a craft in bad weather, an' I've had to show him more'n once or twice how to get her out o' scrapes." "Well," said Will, somewhat impatiently, "what has all this to do with your ship coming to grief?" "Everything," answered the captain, with a sigh. "You see, when the Foam came a wreck, I found myself in a fix. I couldn't afford to buy another ship, so I went into partnership with my mate, who bought the Rover, and we agreed that I should navigate her and act as supercargo, while he should manage the sailing. We started on a trading voyage to the South Seas, and, as you know, took you aboard at Port Jackson, in New South Wales. When we reached the islands, we fell in with these missionaries, who wanted to go to the Friendly Islands, and they agreed to pay us handsomely if we would take them there. So far so good. But when we got to the Friendly Islands, we found that the natives there had taken a dislike to white men, because a wicked trader had treated 'em badly, and cheated 'em. They wouldn't let us land, so we had to put back to Tahiti again. Of course the missionaries didn't want to go to Tahiti, so I told 'em that we'd take 'em to Tonga, which is near the Friendly Islands, and they might easily get a passage from thence to their destination. This they agreed to do, and we're bound now for Tonga. But here's the rub: since we left Tahiti I've noticed a change in the conduct of my mate. He's not quite so free with me as formerly, and he keeps company altogether with the crew. You know that sailors are naturally suspicious. Well, I've observed that whenever I pass near a group of 'em, they stop talking, and begin to hum, or whistle, or sing. Besides, they don't treat me with the same respect as they used to do. I believe that my mate has been putting stories into their heads about me, and turning their minds against me, though why he should do so passes my comprehension. However, I'm certain that mischief of some sort is brewing. I don't know whether you have remarked it, but several times during the past week I have seen the men in groups, holding earnest conversation with each other, and glancing furtively towards me when I passed near them. Of course, knowing that my mate is capable of navigating the ship, I am unable to interfere in such matters as these. And now, having given you the whole state of affairs, what think ye? Am I right in suspecting mischief, or am I mistaken?"

While such modified cell lines will need to undergo extensive testing to address questions regarding (1) genetic stability, and (2) the compatibility of modified cell line traits (e.g. doubling time, cell viability) with current vaccine manufacturing processes, this amalgam of technologies may enhance the production of both vaccines and biotherapeutic molecules. The work presented here is a follow-up to a study performed by Van der Sanden et al. in 2016 [1]. In that report a genome-wide RNA interference (RNAi) screen identified multiple host gene knockdown events that enhanced the production of Sabin and wild type poliovirus (PV). These gene knockdown-mediated increases were dramatic, with 20- to 60-fold increases in viral titers observed in two unrelated cell lines (Vero and Hep-2C). Moreover, the overall effects (i) varied with virus serotype, (ii) were demonstrated to exhibit additive properties, and in some cases, (iii) facilitated the production of closely related viruses (e.g., EV-71). Importantly, the authors created stable Vero knockout cell lines of the top gene candidates using clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR; Ran et al., [11]) technology and, using plaque assays, demonstrated that stable KO clones could dramatically improve PV vaccine strain production. In a separate study that examined gene targets that enhanced rotavirus (RV) production, the same group recently reported that 7- to 18-fold increases could be achieved through knockout of a single Vero cell host gene (Wu et al. [2]). With the reported dramatic yield increases for multiple viral vaccines, these discoveries could address the challenges currently facing governments and vaccine manufacturers. In this manuscript, we investigated this approach further by evaluating the gene targets identified in the van der Sanden and Wu publications to determine whether stably engineered single and double knockout cell lines with greatly increased viral production of PV and RV could be created in the WHO 10-87 GMP Vero cell line currently employed in industry. Focusing attention on these vaccines is essential to address the economic and disease burden these two pathogens impose on the developing world. While significant progress has been made towards eradication of polio since the introduction of the Sabin live oral polio vaccine (OPV) in the 1950's and the Salk inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) in the 1960's, complete eradication requires that OPV, because it can result in rare cases of vaccine associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP), be phased out and replaced with IPV. Such a change has a challenging price and supply impact. OPV is typically sold for less than $0.20 per dose (compared to IPV, which is sold in different price tiers based on the financial resources of the country; from under $1 per dose for the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization (GAVI) countries up to $2.40 per dose for middle-income countries(web 1, web 2). In addition, since IPV is an inactivated virus formulation, it requires nearly ten times greater amount of viral antigen to achieve equivalent levels of protection.

Lantana camara L. (Verbenaceae) is one of the most problematic invasive plants in South Africa, where it has been listed as a Category 1 weed (Poynton, 2009). It is considered to be the world's third worst invasive plant species after Mimosa pigra Linn. and Prosopis juliflora (Sw.) DC. (Richardson and van Wilgen, 2004). The species was first introduced to South Africa in 1818 as an ornamental garden shrub and quickly escaped cultivation (van Wyk, 1984; Richardson and van Wilgen, 2004). Lantana camara is now found throughout most of the country and is particularly prevalent along roadsides and river banks (Richardson and van Wilgen, 2004). There are currently three recognised subspecies of L. camara: ssp. camara, ssp. aculeata (Roxb.) Borhidi and ssp. mucronata (Cav.) Borhidi (van Wyk, 1984; Richardson and van Wilgen, 2004). Of these, ssp. camara is the only one found in South Africa (van Wyk, 1984). Lantana camara is a perennial evergreen shrub with erect branches that grow up to 3 m tall (van Wyk, 1984). Leaves are simple, alternate, oval shaped and 3-10 cm long (van Wyk, 1984). Flowers are small (1-2 mm) and arranged in clusters of 3-12 at the ends of shoots (van Wyk, 1984). Fruits are globose berries approximately 5 mm in diameter and ripen to red or black (van Wyk, 1984). Each berry contains many seeds that are attached to the fruit flesh by a thin layer of aril tissue (van Wyk, 1984). Although L. camara reproduces sexually, vegetative propagation via stem cuttings is common (van Wyk, 1984). The species is adapted to a wide variety of environments and its ability to form dense thickets makes it difficult to control (van Wyk, 1984; Richardson and van Wilgen, 2004). Lantana camara produces large quantities of flowers and fruits, and rapidly spreads across disturbed areas, outcompeting native vegetation (van Wyk, 1984). The species is known to suppress herbaceous plant growth and reduce grass biomass (Ferreira et al., 2003). As a result, animal grazing and browsing are reduced, leading to decreased productivity in agricultural lands and rangelands (van Wyk, 1984; Ferreira et al., 2003). Furthermore, L. camara alters fire regimes and changes the nutrient cycling dynamics of invaded ecosystems (Ferreira et al., 2003). The species is allelopathic and releases toxins into the soil which negatively affect surrounding plants (van Wyk, 1984; Richardson and van Wilgen, 2004). The toxicity of L. camara is thought to be derived from several chemicals including pyrrolizidine alkaloids (Richardson and van Wilgen, 2004).

To overcome these limitations, researchers have been exploring alternative methods for producing high-quality CCA or HEA coatings with minimal defects and optimal properties. One promising approach is the use of cold spraying (CS), which has gained significant attention in recent years due to its ability to deposit thick, dense coatings with minimal thermal input and oxidation [21-23]. In CS, the powder particles are accelerated to high velocities using a high-pressure gas stream, and upon impact, they undergo plastic deformation and bonding with the substrate, resulting in a dense and adherent coating [24]. The low temperature and high velocity of the particles in CS minimize the risk of oxidation and thermal degradation, making it an attractive method for depositing high-performance CCA or HEA coatings [25]. Moreover, CS allows for the use of a wide range of powder morphologies, including irregular shapes, which can be more cost-effective than spherical powders [26]. However, the deposition efficiency and coating quality of CS are highly dependent on the powder characteristics, such as particle size, shape, and surface roughness, as well as the process parameters, including gas pressure, temperature, and standoff distance [27-29]. Therefore, optimizing the CS process parameters and powder properties is crucial for achieving high-quality CCA or HEA coatings with desired microstructures and properties. Another approach that has been explored for producing high-performance CCA or HEA coatings is electrochemical deposition (ECD), which involves the reduction of metal ions from a solution onto a substrate [30-32]. ECD offers several advantages, including low cost, high deposition rates, and the ability to control the coating composition and microstructure [33]. However, the electrochemical reactions involved in ECD can be complex, and the coating quality is highly dependent on the solution chemistry, electrode design, and operating conditions [34-36]. Moreover, the deposition of thick, dense coatings with good metallurgical bonding to the substrate remains a challenge in ECD [37]. To address these limitations, researchers have been investigating the use of pulse electrodeposition, which involves the application of a pulsed current to the electrode to control the deposition process and improve the coating quality [38-40]. In addition to CS and ECD, other methods, such as magnetron sputtering and atomic layer deposition, have also been explored for producing high-performance CCA or HEA coatings [41-43]. These methods offer high deposition rates, good coating uniformity, and the ability to control the coating composition and microstructure. However, they often require complex and expensive equipment, and the deposition of thick, dense coatings with good metallurgical bonding to the substrate remains a challenge [44-46]. Furthermore, the high vacuum environment required for these methods can be a limitation for large-scale industrial applications. In conclusion, the development of high-performance CCA or HEA coatings with optimal properties and minimal defects is a complex task that requires careful selection of the deposition method and optimization of the process parameters and powder properties. While CS, ECD, and other methods have shown promising results, further research is needed to overcome the limitations and challenges associated with each method. The development of high-performance CCA or HEA coatings with good metallurgical bonding to the substrate and optimal properties will have significant implications for various industrial applications, including aerospace, energy, and biomedical industries.

In contrast to such prominent facultatively anaerobic "workhorses" of biotechnology as E. coli and B. subtilis, and even to Lactococcus lactis (which bears an inducible electron transport chain with low coupling efficiency, resembling the major electron pathway in Z. mobilis; Brooijmans et al., 2007), aeration does not improve Zymomonas biomass yield (Belaich and Senez, 1965; Kalnenieks, 2006). Yet, it lowers the ethanol yield, since respiration withdraws the reducing equivalents from the alcohol dehydrogenase reaction and causes accumulation of the inhibitory metabolic precursor of ethanol, acetaldehyde. Due to accumulation of acetaldehyde, aerobic conditions tend to inhibit Z. mobilis growth. However, Z. mobilis in the presence of respiratory inhibitors (cyanide), and more specifically, its Ndh-deficient mutant strains under aerobic conditions grow better than the wild type. They produce more ethanol, without accumulation of acetaldehyde (Kalnenieks et al., 2000, 2008; Hayashi et al., 2011, 2012). Although in general the Ndh-deficient Z. mobilis looks promising for aerobic bioprocess applications, our basic understanding of its catabolism is insufficient. Quantitative data on its aerobic product spectrum and yield values are lacking. Furthermore, our previous study indicated that inactivation of ndh elicited certain adaptive response at the level of the electron transport chain and oxidative stress protection (Strazdina et al., 2012). In particular, the Ndh-deficient Z. mobilis strain showed increased activity of the respiratory D-lactate oxidase (Ldh). This finding posed further questions, concerning the general relation of Ldh activity to the aerobic physiology of the mutant - its growth, aerobic persistence, and metabolism. Z. mobilis possesses two distinct enzymatic activities of lactate dehydrogenase: the cytoplasmic NAD+-dependent lactate dehydrogenase (Lawford and Rousseau, 2002) and the membrane-bound FAD-dependent respiratory lactate dehydrogenase (Kalnenieks et al., 1998). In the Ndh-deficient phenotype, these lactate dehydrogenase enzymes may function in tandem, forming the so called respiratory lactate bypass. The cytoplasmic NAD+-dependent enzyme produces lactate by reducing pyruvate, while the respiratory lactate dehydrogenase reoxidizes lactate, regenerating pyruvate. The net result of this shunt is oxidizing of NADH and transferring reducing equivalents to the respiratory chain. Lactate bypass has been shown to operate in an NADH dehydrogenase - deficient strain of the bacterium Corynebacterium glutamicum (Nantapong et al., 2004), where its supposed function is to fuel the electron transport chain with electrons, and hence, to maintain the respiratory ATP yields comparable to those of the wild type. In the present work our aim was to carry out a quantitative study of the product spectrum and carbon balance in aerobically growing Z. mobilis with an Ndh-deficient background, as well as to examine the putative role of the respiratory lactate bypass for growth and production in these strains. In our previous study and in the works of Hayashi et al. (2011, 2012), Z. mobilis ZM6 (ATCC 29191) was chosen for construction of Ndh-deficient mutants, so here we used the existing ZM6 Ndh-deficient strain as the background for further Ldh mutant derivatives.

Now, I'm not opposed to a good dance party, but this guy is doing some sort of bizarre, spastic movement that's making everyone around us uncomfortable. I mean, The Benders are playing some great tunes, but Ben's dance moves are stealing the show - and not in a good way. Jamie's mortified, Becky's giggling, and I'm just trying to ignore him. My uncle, bless his heart, is trying to be polite and clap along, but even he looks like he's about to cringe. So, Ben finally sits back down, and we're all relieved. But then, he starts yelling out requests to the band. Now, I'm all for audience participation, but this guy is shouting out song titles that The Benders don't even play. I mean, come on, dude, you've been listening to their music for all of five minutes, and you think you know their set list better than they do? The band's being super gracious about it, but you can tell they're getting annoyed. I'm just sitting there, trying to enjoy the music, and this guy's ruining it for everyone. And then, the piece de resistance: Ben decides to try to impress us all by doing a little banjo solo. Let me tell you, it was like nails on a chalkboard. I mean, I've heard cats in heat that sounded more in tune. The Benders' banjo player, bless his heart, was trying not to laugh, but I could see the corners of his mouth twitching. I was just sitting there, thinking, "Please, for the love of all things bluegrass, stop." After the show, we're all chatting with the band, and Ben's trying to impress them with his "musician skills." I'm just standing there, rolling my eyes, and trying not to laugh. Jamie's looking mortified, and Becky's just shaking her head. My uncle's being his usual charming self, chatting with the band and buying them beers. And I'm just thinking, "Well, that was an experience." But hey, at least The Benders were amazing, as always. And I got a good story out of it.

But we also have to consider how the gameplay itself shapes our understanding of these majestic yet menacing creatures. So let's shift our gaze to the diverse tapestry of vampire clans woven throughout the Elder Scrolls series. Each clan not only occupies a unique niche but also offers distinct perspectives on vampirism, culture, and survival. Starting with the Vvardenfell's labyrinthine caves, the Quarra Clan dwells-ferocious and unmatched in physical combat prowess. These vampires embody a raw warrior spirit, eschewing subtlety for might and brawn. Led by Kjeld, their belligerence often paints them in a hostile light. Preferring stealth and magic over brute strength, they value sophistication and intellect, embracing a lifestyle reminiscent of noble sorcery. Then we wander into the depths of Cyrodiil, where the Cyrodiilic Vampire Clan demonstrates a unique adaptation-they blend seamlessly into society, an ominous haze of deception clouding the capital. Unlike their brethren in Morrowind, these vampires are masters of charm and persuasion, living amongst mortals, unseen and unsuspected. Their ability to walk in daylight represents a divergence from the typical vulnerabilities vampires face, challenging our traditional perceptions and adding layers to the enigma that is vampiric existence. In the frozen expanses of Skyrim dwells the Volkihar Clan, a lineage shrouded in both ice and legend. Known for their necromantic prowess and terrifying ability to protrude from frozen waters, the Volkihar vampires occupy a dreaded chapter in Nordic tales. Their castle, hidden amidst the icy wilderness, stands a testament to their ancient heritage and formidable power. This clan's story intertwines inexorably with the tale of Serana, a tragic figure trapped within the gothic splendor of her family's ambitions. What is fascinating about these clans is not only their varied abilities and philosophies but also how these aspects echo the landscapes they inhabit. The environment sculpts their existence, with each clan adopting strategies and powers that harmonize-or clash-with the world around them. Cultural echoes, historical shifts, and environmental interactions all enrich their unique stories, painting a grand mosaic of blood, power, and allure across Tamriel. Finally, the story of vampires in the Elder Scrolls is not complete without understanding the moral and ethical undertones they present. Vampires serve as mirrors, reflecting the fears and desires of mortals; their immortality is as much a blessing as it is a curse, encapsulating the eternal struggle between power and its inherent cost. The choice to embrace the vampiric path is laden with consequences, questioning the very essence of life and identity. Now, as we close today's exploration, consider the vast depth beneath the vampiric surface. Embrace the shadows and ponder: What clan-or destiny-calls to you? Whether you're drawn by the allure of the aristocratic Aundae, the combative spirit of the Quarra, or the mysterious cold of the Volkihar, understanding these intricacies enriches not just the game, but our broader perspectives on lore and legend. As always, stay curious, stay sharp, and until next time, may your paths be free of shadows... or filled with adventure, depending on your chosen side.

He laid down the canvas on his lap and looked in a puzzled way at the fire. Then he raised it nearer to his eyes for further examination. "This is really very dreadful," he said at last, looking at his daughter. "Something will have to be done soon," replied the latter. "It is so horribly vulgar, Grace," said the old man; "look at that boy's nose - and that drunken man - his face is a nightmare of evil. I really must begin to talk seriously to Clytie." Mrs. Blather smiled somewhat pityingly. Since the earliest days of her long widowhood she had undertaken the charge of her father's house and the care of her two younger sisters, Janet and Clytie. Her familiarity, therefore, with the seamy side of Clytie's nature had been of long duration. "You might as well talk to that fender, papa," she said. "Clytie has got it into her head that she is going to be an artist, and no amount of talking will get it out." "It's all through her visiting those friends of hers, the Farquharsons. They are not nice people for her to know. I shall not let her go there again." "If she goes on like this there is no knowing what will happen." "Where did the child get these repulsive and ungirlish notions from?" the old man asked querulously. The conception of the picture was not that of a young girl, and though the execution was crude and untrained, there was a bold cruelty of touch that saved it from being amateurish. The canvas was divided into two panels. On the one was painted a tiny bully of a boy with his arm rounded across his throat, about to strike a weakly, poverty-stricken little girl. They were children of the poorest classes, the boy realistically, offensively dirty - the petit morveux in its absolute sense. Behind them was the open doorway of a red-brick, jerry-built cottage, showing a strip of torn and dirty matting along the passage that lost itself in the gloom beyond. On the other panel was the corner of a public house in a low slum, the window lights and a gas-lamp throwing a lurid glare upon wet pavement and the figures of a woman and a drunken man. The faces were those of the children in the first picture, and the eternal tragedy was repeating itself. The man's face was loathsome in its sodden ferocity; the woman, with a child in her arms, was reeling from the blow. The evident haste in which the panels had been painted, the glaring, unsoftened colouring, heightened as if by impressionist design the coarse realism of the effect. Above was written the legend, "La joie de vivre" and in the left-hand bottom corner, "Clytie Davenant pinxit." "She has certainly grown much worse of late," sighed Mrs. Blather, holding out her thin, short hand to shield her face from the fire.

Magda played an amazing set. It was full of deep minimal tracks, many of them unreleased, most of them sounding like they could easily be released on Perlon or one of the other minimal labels. Her mixing was flawless and her track selection was superb. The crowd was very receptive to the sounds she threw down. Afterwards we headed back to the hotel room and I passed out. Saturday morning arrived and I woke up feeling as though I hadn't slept. I showered and then went off to get breakfast and coffee. A nap followed this and then it was off to the Piknik Electronik. Unfortunately the weather did not cooperate and there were torrential downpours all day long. Luckily, the organizers of the festival had planned ahead and arranged for tents to be erected over the dance floor and stage area. The rain was still getting through, but it wasn't too bad. The lineup was great, but I have to say that the highlight for me was seeing Mike Shannon play. His style is similar to Ricardo Villalobos, Luciano, Akufen, etc. Very minimal, lots of percussion, lots of odd samples. His mixing was tight and his song selection was perfect. I picked up a copy of his new CD "Possible Conclusions To Stories That Never End" after his performance and have been listening to it non-stop since I returned home. I highly recommend it. Another highlight was seeing Tomas Jirku perform live. I saw him open for Richie Hawtin at Stereo last year and thought it was pretty good. This time around he blew me away. It was totally different from anything I heard before. Very glitchy and experimental, but with a definite beat. It sounded as though he was using samples of records skipping and scratching and making those noises into beats. It was awesome. Again, unfortunately, I didn't pick up any CDs by him. I'm going to have to hunt down some copies online somewhere. The rest of the night was spent wandering around the city and doing what people do at festivals... partying. Sunday was a total write-off. I didn't wake up until 5pm. I showered and went to dinner with my friend, her boyfriend and another couple. After that we went back to their hotel room and watched TV. Now I'm sitting here writing this and trying to figure out how to stop the cycle of destruction I seem to put myself through every weekend. I guess I should just accept that I'm a fuck-up and leave it at that. Mutek was a blast, but I'm glad it's over. I'm tired and hungover and sore. More details will follow soon.

My fingers trembled slightly as I turned the pages of my safety guide, the paper crinkling under the pressure of my grip. It was heavier than I expected, and the smell of the ink was strangely comforting, like the hint of a new beginning. I caught a glimpse of myself in the reflection of the window-pale, slightly awkward, completely lost. I quickly averted my gaze, hoping that no one else noticed. Just keep your head down. With each passing moment, the classroom filled with the sound of chatter, laughter, and the occasional teasing toward unsuspecting freshmen. I was aware of the ripple of social dynamics unfolding around me, each glance and giggle a reminder that I was like a fish out of water, floundering in an ocean of social hierarchies I had yet to comprehend. Through the din, my gaze landed on Patrick again, the kid who was brave enough to crack a joke in a room full of more fortified souls. He seemed like a soft light cutting through the hazy fog of high school life-a flicker of hope in this sea of uncertainty. As the bell rang, reverberating through the hall and announcing the start of my new reality, I felt dread prickling at my skin. The teacher-a stone-faced figure with an imposing presence-entered the room with an air of authority that sent an almost palpable silence washing over us, kinking the noise like air escaping a punctured balloon. The introduction was swift and blunt, without much fanfare. It was the kind of authority that made kids shrink back and wish they had worn invisibility cloaks. "Welcome to shop class. I expect you all to pay attention and follow the rules. If you want a passable grade, I suggest you leave your antics at the door. Safety is my priority." His voice was rough, each syllable dripping with a weight that left no room for dissent. An ex-soldier, no doubt, from experiences he related in gruff tales buried deep under layers of chipboard and sawdust. I felt a slight shiver pass through me; perhaps the hope I grasped onto a second ago was in vain. My heart sank a little lower as my mind raced with the embarrassing memories of middle school mishaps. I could feel the judgment from those around me, like a heavyweight on my chest. What if they all knew the truth? The story behind the weird kid in the hospital-the one who had to explain the scars with nervous laughter and quick changes in subject. What if, instead of casting off their judgments, it only fed their amusement? And that's when I remembered: the plan. The vision of a future not yet lived. Days spent in the sun, eyes bright with joy, friendships blooming like wildflowers-lush, vibrant, alive. I had to believe it was waiting for me, a little further down the stretch of this long road. I needed to focus on the two things on my plate-survival and transformation. Kid Pat, the freshman, was not the end but a chapter in my unwritten saga. Perhaps, just perhaps, tomorrow I might muster enough courage to sit next to Patrick during lunch. Save that seat for the kid who would befriend the outcast, and together we could redefine what it meant to belong. If there was one thing that I learned already, it was that even a single, simple act of kindness could feel like a lifeline. A compass guiding me through the woods of high school, leading me toward myself. Each day, I told myself, it could be the day things changed. So today, I would take the first step-one foot in front of the other, one sentence spoken, one laugh shared. The next time the bell rang, I could be ready.

The deployment of the Argo network marked a transition in physical operational oceanography, as it has provided publicly available observations of the interior of the global ocean in near real time (Le Traon, 2013). Recently, a biogeochemical equivalent of Argo, the BGC-Argo programme, has been established (Johnson and Claustre, 2016). The BGC-Argo network is rapidly growing, although the density of operational floats is still scarce compared to Argo. However, at regional scale, specific activities might provide a sufficient number of floats to both contribute to the improvement of ocean biogeochemical models (Brasseur et al., 2009) and to be used in operational modeling frameworks (Le Traon et al., 2017). The Mediterranean Sea has one of the first BGC-Argo networks with a sufficient density of floats (deployed in framework of the NAOS French initiative and of the Argo-Italy BGC-Argo programme) to test and validate assimilation systems. Thirty-nine BGC-Argo floats equipped with biogeochemical sensors were deployed from 2012 to 2017, thus making the Mediterranean BGC-Argo network one of the densest (in terms of the number of profiles per unit surface area) of the global ocean. The Mediterranean BGC-Argo float data also contributed to develop the quality control methods for the BGC-Argo chlorophyll observations that are presently endorsed at the international level (Schmechtig et al., 2016). Moreover, specific methods for nitrate sensor calibration have been derived for the Mediterranean (Pasqueron de Fommervault et al. 2015; D' Ortenzio et al. 2014) to account for the biogeochemical characteristics of the basin. In this work, an innovative BGC-Argo data assimilation framework is discussed, and its feasibility within a realistic model is demonstrated. The framework is intended to be integrated into the operational Mediterranean biogeochemistry model (MedBFM) of the CMEMS system (Bolzon et al., 2017). The MedBFM model features the off-line coupling of NEMO3.6 (Clementi et al., 2017) and OGSTM-BFM (Lazzari et al., 2012, 2016; Cossarini et al., 2015) and includes separate physical (Dobricic and Pinardi, 2008; Farina et al., 2015; Storto et al., 2014) and biogeochemical (Teruzzi et al., 2014) variational data assimilation schemes. The 3DVarBio variational assimilation scheme has already been shown to be suited for biogeochemical data assimilation, due to its modularity (Teruzzi et al., 2014, 2018a). A new upgrade of the 3DVarBio has been developed to assimilate the vertical chlorophyll profiles and update the phytoplankton state variables of OGSTM-BFM model. The Mediterranean Sea is characterized by peculiar vertical phytoplankton characteristics; it displays a marked seasonal cycle of surface and deep chlorophyll maxima (Lavigne et al., 2015; Mignot et al., 2014) and a noticeable west-east deepening of the deep chlorophyll maximum and trophic gradient (Lavigne et al., 2015). Thus, the BGC-Argo float assimilation is discussed with the aim of showing its capability to correct the vertical structure of modelled chlorophyll. Furthermore, we propose a tuning procedure based on the analysis of the a posteriori observation and background errors (Desroziers et al., 2005) to define the observation error.

At night, or when the evening glooms are falling, nothing can be more startling than to stray into the presence of this huge thing, which is not a habitation, and which seems, all complete yet so incomplete, to have strayed into regions quite uncongenial and out of sympathy with it, where it stands as much out of its element as a stranded boat. But all the same there is nothing ghostly or terrible about Murkley Castle. It involves no particular mystery of any kind - nothing but the folly of a man who built a house without counting the cost, and who found himself without means to complete, far less enjoy, the palace he had constructed. Not the less is it a strange feature in the landscape, and it would be still stranger if popular superstition did not see sights and bear sounds in it of nights, for which the wiser persons in the country declared they could not account, though of course they did not believe in anything supernatural. This was the reason given by the driver of the gig from the "George" at Kilmorley for the round he wanted to make on a certain June night in the lingering daylight, as he conducted the gentleman reckoned as No. 5 in the books at the 'George' to Murkley village, where this ill-advised person, not knowing when he was well off, as the "George" was of opinion, meant to establish himself at the village inn, which was no better than a public-house. "It's no from ony superstition," the driver said. "I'm no a man, I hope, to be feared for ghosts; I'm mair feared for flesh and blood. I've a good watch in my pocket, and life's sweet, and if it's tramps, as is maist likely, that have a howff in the auld castle, and mak' a' thae noises to frichten the countryside, the mair reason, say I, to gi'e the auld castle a wide berth." "But it's daylight," said the traveller; for, after all, as in the days of Mr. G. P. E. James, it is a traveller of whose early impressions the historian avails himself; "and there are two of us; and that beast of yours could surely show a clean pair of heels - " He spoke with a slight accent which was foreign, but which the countryman took to be "high English:" and had certain little foreign ways, which Duncan was not clever enough to understand. He responded, cautiously, "Oh, ay; she'll gang weel enough - but a mare ye see's a flighty creature - they're mair nervous than a fine leddy - and, if they think they see something they canna account for - " "But, man alive!" cried the stranger, "you're not afraid of ghosts in broad daylight." "I'm no speaking about ghosts - and ye ca' this braid daylicht! It's just the eeriest licht I ever saw. Do you ken what o'clock it is?

ASB temperature distributions are known to be highly transient, with short range spatial periodicity in the direction of their growth (Guduru et al., 2001a). The temperature has been measured by Ranc et al. (2008) separately for initiation and propagation of ASBs in Ti-6Al-4V during dynamic torsion testing. With a global strain rate from 1000 s-1 to 2000 s-1, the low temperature range for ASB initiation is found to be from 50 C to 300 C and the high temperature range for ASB propagation from 800 C to 1700 C. Temperature heterogeneity, i.e. highly non-uniform with discrete regions of high temperature, is observed along the formation length of ASBs. This has also been found by Guduru et al. (2001b) based on high-speed infrared camera measurement. It has been noted by Ranc et al. (2008) that the difficulty of accurately capturing the ASB formation lay in achieving simultaneously high resolutions in time, space and temperature measurement. For instance, it is difficult to simultaneously maintain a temporal resolution of about 1 1/2s and spatial resolution of 43 1/2m for low temperature ranges and 10 1/2s and 2 1/2m respectively for the high temperature range. Continuous and high-speed temperature measurement from 50 C to 1670 C (melting point of Ti-6Al-4V) remains very difficult for a single pyrometer. This has hindered a better understanding of the onset mechanisms in shear localization and formation of ASBs. The mechanisms of ASB formation remains controversial (Medyanik et al., 2007; Peirs et al., 2013; Rittel, 2009). Conventional criteria for the initiation of ASBs are to define a critical shear strain (Zhou et al., 1996a). Nevertheless, for a given shear stress, the critical strain decreases with increasing strain rate (Lindholm, 1974) and this is attributed to the increase in strength at high strain rates (Meyers, 1994). Weak strain-rate sensitivity characterised by small rate hardening exponent reduces the strain necessary for the onset of shear bands (Clifton et al., 1984). On the other hand, shear localization can be delayed by the effects of strain hardening (Clifton et al., 1984). Nonetheless, ASBs are commonly considered as an instability resulting from thermal softening effects (Bai and Dodd, 2012; Wright, 2002). In order to understand the emergence of an adiabatic shear band, Zener and Hollomon (1944) proposed to consider the competing influence of strain-rate hardening and thermal softening effects, the latter generating conditions where the material can no longer harden, thus losing its stability and allowing the formation of a localized failure mode. Internal heat generation is recognized to be important for nucleation of adiabatic shear banding, and has been considered in the classical Johnson-Cook model (Chen and Ghosh, 2012; Dolinski et al., 2010; Khan et al., 2004), the Kocks-Mecking model (Chichili et al., 1998; Follansbee and Gray, 1989), continuum viscoplasticity models (Rosakis et al., 2000; Zhou et al., 1996a, 1996), and crystal plasticity models (Austin and McDowell, 2011; Clayton, 2005; Lloyd et al., 2014a, 2014b).

After this enlightening introduction to the tapestry that is Welton Academy, our story unfolds with the young men embarking on the academic journey that shapes their futures. Eager fresh faces, timid yet bursting with potential, align in neat rows of importance. In the eyes of the elders, they are fledglings poised to make great leaps under the vigilant watch of tradition's ever-seeing gaze. As the assembly disperses, the hallowed corridors hum with anticipation, the air filled with whispers of legends past and promises of dreams yet to come. Anderson, bearing the weight of expectation, navigates the winding halls. His gaze catches the portraits of stalwart graduates, their accomplishments etched into the annals of Welton's proud narrative. He wonders which path will be his own, traversing between the echoes of history and the aspirations awaiting him. In the hallowed library, where knowledge lounges in stately tomes, Anderson finds refuge. It's here that John Keating first makes his impression. His presence announced by a quiet enthusiasm rather than the loud proclamations of tradition, Keating enters with an aura of gentle rebellion. Elegantly mismatched with the world of conformity around him, he carries an aura that appears both modern and timeless. "Ah, literature's sanctuary," Keating muses, eyes twinkling with a mischief untouched by age, as Anderson nervously thumbs through Emerson. "Tell me, how must a reader greet a book - as friend or foe?" Anderson, caught off guard, fumbles for words. "A friend, I suppose. Or perhaps a guide." Keating chuckles softly, an ally to youthful inquiry. "Indeed, a guide - and yet sometimes the best guides challenge, even provoke. Remember, Mr. Anderson, words offer the rarest opportunities to forge one's destiny. Seize them." The induction into English Literature unfolds not as a march through dusty relics but as a vibrant exploration. Keating's creed is one of unexpected juxtapositions, bringing poetry to life not as relics, but as living breaths. He charges his students not to merely read, but to truly see. "Carpe diem!" he exclaims one afternoon, thrusting the motto into the consciousness of those before him. "Seize the day!" The declaration hangs in the air, intoxicating, hinting at freedoms unbound by rules and expectations. Dalton, possessing a daring nature, is the first to leap into Keating's challenge with vigor. "Seize it and make it our own." A ripple of amusement and discomfort pulses through the class. With Keating's lessons as silent accomplices, Dalton and his peers begin their quest to claim more than just academic success. By autumn's end, Anderson, Dalton, and their compatriots stumble upon whispers of an ancient student society - the Dead Poets Society. Intrigued and inspired, they seek to rekindle its spark, meeting clandestinely in the cavernous quarters of the boarding house attic. Through poetry read by candlelight-the words alive on their lips-they find segments of themselves long overshadowed by societal dictates. With verse both sacred and profane, the boys craft emotions into verse, releasing the dormant spirits of aspiration and rebellion. In these dalliances with ink and paper, on the cusp of winter's breath, they begin not just to inhabit Welton's traditions, but to redefine them. With Keating as their guide, they unlock the power to question, dream, and transcend the boundaries once thought unyielding.

The optimization of the HVOF process parameters is crucial to achieve the desired coating properties and microstructure. The CFD models can provide valuable insights into the complex flow physics and combustion chemistry involved in the process. For instance, the simulation of the gas flow, particle dynamics, and heat transfer can help in understanding the breakup of the suspension droplets, evaporation, and melting of the nanoparticles, and their subsequent deposition onto the substrate. The CFD models can also be used to optimize the torch design, injection parameters, and operating conditions to achieve the desired coating properties. One of the key challenges in the HVOF process is the control of the particle size and distribution within the coating. The CFD models can be used to study the effect of various parameters such as suspension concentration, viscosity, and surface tension on the particle size and distribution. The simulation results can be validated through experimental measurements, and the optimal parameters can be determined to achieve the desired coating properties. In addition to the CFD models, experimental techniques such as scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) can be used to characterize the microstructure and properties of the coatings. The SEM and TEM can provide information on the particle size, morphology, and distribution, while the XRD can be used to determine the phase composition and crystal structure of the coatings. The HVOF process has also been used to deposit coatings with unique properties such as self-healing and self-lubricating properties. The incorporation of nanoparticles with specific properties such as graphene, carbon nanotubes, and nanoparticles with catalytic activity can enhance the performance of the coatings. The HVOF process can be used to deposit coatings with complex geometries and shapes, making it suitable for a wide range of applications including aerospace, biomedical, and energy industries. Furthermore, the HVOF process can be combined with other deposition techniques such as electroplating, sol-gel, and chemical vapor deposition (CVD) to achieve coatings with unique properties. The hybrid deposition techniques can be used to deposit coatings with multiple layers, each with specific properties, to achieve the desired performance. In conclusion, the HVOF process is a versatile technique that can be used to deposit coatings with unique properties and microstructure. The optimization of the process parameters using CFD models and experimental techniques can help in achieving the desired coating properties. The incorporation of nanoparticles with specific properties and the combination of HVOF with other deposition techniques can further enhance the performance of the coatings. The HVOF process has the potential to revolutionize various industries, and further research is needed to fully explore its capabilities.

Wednesday was a bit of a blur, but I think we started the day with a late breakfast at the Bellagio's Cafe Gelato. I had a ridiculous amount of pancakes, and Nelly had some sort of omelette. We then decided to take a stroll along the Strip, taking in the sights and sounds of the various hotels and casinos. We stopped at the Mirage to see the volcano outside, which was pretty impressive, even in the daylight. After that, we headed over to the Venetian, where we took a romantic gondola ride through the indoor canals. It was a bit cheesy, but we both enjoyed it. Our gondolier was quite the character, singing and making jokes the whole time. That evening, we had reservations at Le Cirque, one of the fancier restaurants in the Bellagio. The food was incredible, and the service was top-notch. I had some sort of seafood dish, and Nelly had a filet mignon. We both had the chocolate souffle for dessert, which was to die for. After dinner, we headed back to the room to relax for a bit before heading out to the Cosmopolitan to see the Chandelier Bar. It's this massive, three-story bar surrounded by a chandelier made up of thousands of lights. We had a few drinks and took in the views of the Strip from the top floor. Thursday was our last full day in Vegas, so we decided to make the most of it. We started the day with a visit to the High Roller observation wheel at the Linq Promenade. It was a bit pricey, but the views from the top were stunning. We could see the entire Strip and even the surrounding mountains. After that, we headed over to the LINQ to check out the Fountains of Bellagio. We grabbed a spot right up front and watched the show, which was absolutely breathtaking. The music, the water, the whole thing was just amazing. That evening, we had tickets to see Zumanity, the Cirque du Soleil show at New York-New York. I wasn't really sure what to expect, but it was actually really good. It was a lot more sensual and erotic than I thought it would be, but it was still a great show. The acrobats and performers were all incredibly talented, and the music was great. After the show, we headed back to the Bellagio to pack up and get ready to leave the next morning. Friday morning, we checked out of the Bellagio and headed back to the airport to catch our flight home. I was a bit sad to leave Vegas behind, but I was also exhausted. We'd packed so much into our five days, and I was ready to collapse. The flight home was uneventful, and we landed back in Fort Smith around 7 pm. It was great to be home, but I was already thinking about when we could go back to Vegas.

As he stood there, erect as a soldier, with his fine athletic figure revealed, and the bronze on his face seemingly inches deep, Tom Reade looked what he was - every inch a man though still a boy in years. "Do you think you look as healthy as I do?" Tom repeated. "No-o-o-o," admitted Alf. "But you're older'n me." "Not so much, as years go," Tom rejoined. "For that matter, if you go on with your cigarettes you'll be an old man before I get through with being a young man. Fill up your chest, Alf; expand it - like this." As he expanded his chest Reade looked a good deal more like some Greek god of old than a twentieth century civil engineer. Alf puffed and squirmed in his efforts to show "some chest." "That isn't the right way," Tom informed him. "Breathe deeply and steadily. Draw in your stomach and expand your chest. Fill up the upper part of your lungs with air. Watch! Right here at the top of the chest." Alf watched. For that matter he seemed unable to remove his gaze from the splendid chest development that young Reade displayed so easily. Then the boy tried to fill the upper portions of his own lungs in the same manner. The attempt ended in a spasm of coughing. "Fine, isn't it?" queried Tom Reade, scornfully. "The upper parts of your lungs are affected already, and you'll carry the work of destruction on rapidly. Alf, if you ever live to be twenty you'll be a wreck at best. Don't you know that?" "I - I have heard folks say so," nodded the boy. "And you didn't believe them?" "I - I don't know." "Why did you ever take up smoking?" "All men smoke," argued Alf Drew. "Lie number one. All men don't smoke," Tom corrected him. "But I think I catch the drift of your idea. If you smoke you think men will look upon you as being more manly. That's it, it?" "It must be manly, if men do it," Alf argued. "You funny little shaver," laughed Tom, good-humoredly. "So you think that, when men see you smoking cigarettes, they immediately imagine you to be one of them? Cigarette-smoking, for a boy of fourteen, is the short cut to manhood, I suppose."
