Then there are the results. Despite winning four La Liga titles and two Champions Leagues under Guardiola and Tito Vilanova, the club has only finished above Real Madrid once since the 2009-10 campaign. In fact, they have failed to win a trophy in either of the past two seasons. All of these factors combined to create a sense of malaise within the club, and a growing feeling among some supporters that the board and management had lost touch with what makes Barca special. This frustration boiled over when the news broke that Neymar would be leaving for PSG. The club responded by announcing a series of measures aimed at placating disgruntled fans. They included the appointment of former player Gerard Pique as vice-president of the football area; the creation of a new position called director of institutional relations; and the formation of a new social media department, which will include the appointment of a social media manager. The club also announced plans to open a fan consultation centre, where supporters can air their views on how the club is run. "We need to know what our fans think," said Bartomeu. "It is vital that we hear them." But while such measures might help to rebuild bridges between the club and its followers, they do nothing to address the underlying problems. If anything, the response could be seen as confirmation that the club does indeed believe itself to be 'more than a club', or at least that it sees itself as one of the world's most important institutions. It is a philosophy which has already caused controversy in the past, notably when club president Joan Laporta claimed that Barca were worth more than Spain itself. Some feel that the club's obsession with its status has led to a disconnect with reality. "Barcelona have become obsessed with being 'the greatest'," wrote Guillem Balague in The Guardian earlier this week. "They are constantly referring to themselves as the best, the greatest, the most beautiful club in the world. Even if it is true, they should stop saying it out loud because it sounds arrogant." For others, though, the club's lofty ambitions are entirely justified. "I don't see any reason to change our philosophy," said former Barca defender Albert Ferrer. "We are the most popular team in the world, and we have to act like it." Neymar has finally made his decision to leave Barcelona - but even now it remains unclear exactly why. The Brazil forward's move to Paris Saint-Germain was confirmed by the Ligue 1 champions on Thursday, despite Barcelona claiming they had received no official offer from the French club. The announcement ends weeks of speculation over Neymar's future, with reports suggesting he had agreed terms with PSG in principle as far back as June. However, neither party has provided a definitive explanation for the sudden U-turn, although the 25-year-old is understood to have fallen out with the club over a number of issues. One potential problem point is Neymar's relationship with star team-mate Lionel Messi, who reportedly warned the Brazilian against moving to PSG amid fears it would ruin his chances of success at international level. Messi has also come under fire for his own actions in recent months, including an alleged attempt to force his way out of the club last summer, while his current contract expires next summer and talks over a renewal remain deadlocked. PSG's financial muscle may have played a part too, with Neymar set to earn around 30m ( 27m) per season in France compared to around 20m ( 18m) at Camp Nou.

We were running before a fine fresh breeze, under courses and topsails, with our fore-topmast studding-sails set, and were carrying a good deal of weather helm, owing to the fact that we had our windlass, together with its gear, taken out of the forecastle-head, to make room for some extra cargo. The decks were wet with spray, and everything was working perfectly well; but suddenly the mainyard broke adrift from the heel, and fell overboard, carrying away the main-topsail-yard with it, and, consequently, bringing down both those sails into the sea. The main-topsail-halyards parted at the same time, and the whole of this damage occurred within about five minutes after Mr Moore had gone below for his dinner. He had left the quarterdeck in charge of Midshipman Dutton, who was acting as officer-of-the-watch, and who, having heard the crash of the yards, came aft immediately, and reported to me what had happened. The chief mate, Mr Drake, hearing the alarm, came up from the cabin, and, seeing the disaster, gave orders to get the main-topsail yard reeved again, and the sail bent to it, whilst he himself went forward to see what could be done with the broken mainyard. I sent Dutton forward to assist him, and remained myself on the poop-deck, in order to keep a look-out ahead. The sky was clear overhead, and the sun shining brightly, but the horizon was obscured by thick clouds, and I could see nothing beyond them, except a bank of fog, which stretched away right across the sea. Presently, however, I observed a vessel coming up through the fog, apparently right on our course, though she was still too far off for us to distinguish her. She appeared to be heading straight for us, and I knew that she must either alter her course, or else run foul of us. I therefore went down the companion-ladder, and called to the captain to come up on deck. When he reached the poop, I told him that there was a strange vessel bearing down upon us, and that she must either change her course or else collide with us. He looked at the ship through his glass, and then handed it back to me, saying, "She's a big barkentine, with her sails set, and her head right to windward of us. She'll pass us at least two miles astern." "Yes," I replied; "but she'll pass us much nearer than that if she don't alter her course. Look!" And I pointed to where she was now approaching us, almost directly on our beam. The captain took another look, and then went forward to give instructions for getting the spare topgallant-mast rigged out in place of the mainyard. I followed him, and found him giving orders to get the main-topsail yard reeved again, and the sail bent to it. At the same moment, I saw the stranger pass directly abreast of us, at the distance of less than half-a-mile, without altering her course in any way. As soon as she had passed, I ran to the break of the poop, and shouted to the captain to look out, for the stranger was coming straight for us. But he did not hear me, and was engaged in issuing further orders, when the next instant the Salamis struck the stranger with a tremendous shock. The collision threw the captain flat on his face, and knocked me completely overboard. I was picked up almost instantly by a boat belonging to the stranger, and taken on board.

It sometimes seems as if the Olympic Winter Games were created to remind the world just how many outstanding winter athletes come from Norway. (No country has won more medals in the Winter Olympic Games.) So when you're in Oslo, it's no surprise that the Holmenkollen ski jump is still the biggest thing in town. Ski jumping has been part of the action here since 1892, and the jump has been redeveloped more than a dozen times. The latest structure, which opened in 2010, is made of steel and stretches nearly 97 meters (318 feet). The Ski Simulator at the top of the hill is a virtual reality experience that will leave you breathless and more awestruck by ski-jumpers than ever. The arena next to the ski jump was used for cross-country skiing and biathlon competitions in 1952, and might be again should Oslo win its bid to host the 2022 Winter Olympics. Blood Falls and other natural oddities. Innsbruck, Austria (1964 and 1976) The Tyrolean Alps were a picture-perfect backdrop for Olympic skiing competition in 1976 as Austrian favorite Franz Klammer seemed to gobble up the terrain on his way to a gold medal in the men's downhill and West Germany's Rosi Mittermaier took two golds and a silver in the women's downhill and slalom events. You'll want more than the 1 minute 45 seconds or so that Klammer and Mittermaier spent on the mountain. Take your time to soak in the scenery on an evening lantern hike that takes you past the Olympic ski slopes and ends with singing and beverages at a friendly inn. Sapporo, Japan (1972) The double lift takes just five minutes to carry you to the top of the Okurayama 90-meter ski jump hill where, in 1972, 19-year-old Wojciech Fortuna became the first and only Polish man to win an Olympic ski-jumping gold medal. (In 1972, transport to the top took 20 minutes; the trip down for Fortuna, less than 20 seconds.) The viewing lounge at 300 meters allows you to peer down at the city and at the ski jump starting line. At the Sapporo Winter Sports Museum, simulators in the "Sensation/Experience Zone" replicate the ski jump experience. Calgary, Canada (1988) The Olympic spirit has never left Calgary, where Katarina Witt won a gold medal in figure skating for East Germany and curling resurfaced as a demonstration sport after an absence of more than 50 years. In addition to marking the Olympic debut of American speed skater Bonnie Blair, the Calgary Olympics also introduced the world to the Jamaican Bobsleigh Team (later immortalized in the 1993 film "Cool Runnings"). Today, visitors with just slightly less bobsleigh training than those four gentlemen can slide down the very same track at speeds of up to 75 miles per hour (120 km/h) in a bobsleigh driven by a professional pilot.

Sir Evelyn drove more slowly than ever. His face grew red, his hands trembled on the steering wheel. Suddenly the road curved sharply round a projecting bank of rock. A char-a-banc, coming up the hill, appeared in front of him. It was crowded with men and women. They were singing. The driver saw Sir Evelyn and stopped his horses. Sir Evelyn stopped too. The two vehicles confronted each other, almost touching. The char-a-banc filled the whole width of the road. On either side were high banks. There was not the slightest possibility of passing it. Sir Evelyn felt that he must back out into the open country above. That would be easy enough, but how was he to turn? The char-a-banc blocked the way. "You'll have to get your people out," said Sir Evelyn. The char-a-banc driver nodded. He did not seem to mind being stopped. He was quite ready to get his people out. But why should he do so? Why should Sir Evelyn not get out instead? Sir Evelyn was not inclined to argue. He got out. So did the char-a-banc passengers. They formed a circle round him, laughing and talking cheerfully. Some of them knew who he was. One of them recognised him as the man who used to sit on the Treasury bench beside the Prime Minister. He was pointed out to the others. Then they began to sing: "We want eight hours and we won't work more." Sir Evelyn, though frightened, was determined to keep cool. He smiled pleasantly at the crowd. They took no notice of him. They went on singing. Their song was evidently intended as a taunt, but Sir Evelyn could not see why. He was not a mill-owner nor a factory manager. He was not responsible for the number of hours worked by anyone. The crowd finished its song and stood staring at him. He stared back. It seemed to him that the situation was ridiculous. He wanted to laugh, but dared not. Then someone threw a stone. It struck Sir Evelyn on the forehead. The blood spurted out over his eyes. He staggered backwards, half blinded. A second stone hit him on the temple. He fell, stunned and unconscious. CHAPTER I The char-a-banc party dispersed. No one remained to help Sir Evelyn. The driver whipped up his horses and rattled away towards Hailey Compton. Sir Evelyn lay on the grass by the roadside. In less than ten minutes he recovered consciousness. He sat up, feeling dazed and bewildered. Blood trickled down his cheek. He put his hand to his head and found a lump the size of a walnut swelling under his fingers. He tried to remember what had happened. He remembered leaving home, driving through the country lanes, turning into the lane which led to Hailey Compton. He remembered nothing else. How did he come to be lying there on the grass? Where was his car? He looked round. The car was nowhere to be seen. What had become of it? Had he run off the road and crashed? He could not understand. He got up and walked shakily along the lane. At the first bend he saw his car. It was standing by the wayside, quite uninjured. He could not imagine how it came to be there. He climbed into it and drove slowly up the hill. When he reached his own house he called the doctor. "I've hurt my head somehow," he said. "I don't know exactly how it happened."

As Moore dilates on the intersection of societal behaviors and government actions, he stirs a cesspool of complex nuances, blurring the line between artistic expression and social culpability. For every sensational headline linking violent crimes to the music of Marilyn Manson or the films of Quentin Tarantino, there exists a multitude of layers - cultural, socioeconomic, and historical - that beg for examination rather than mere condemnation. It is within this context that Moore's selective interviews often veer out of moral integrity, crafting a narrative that serves his thesis at the expense of a more holistic understanding of gun ownership. Take, for instance, the unwavering portrayal of the American psyche as a gun-crazed entity, seemingly lacking in empathy or reason. This characterization ignores the substantial segment of Americans who not only advocate for responsible ownership but also actively engage in community service, youth mentorship, and public safety programs. Moore's decision to spotlight the fringe elements of gun culture draws away from the reality of gun safety courses, hunting traditions, and the historical significance of firearms in American life, which have often played roles beyond mere violence - as tools for personal protection, recreation, and bonding across generations. Moreover, Moore tends to gloss over the historical contexts that have shaped the national conversation around guns. The legacies of violence, both governmental and civilian, wind through our streets and neighborhoods, imbuing events with far greater significance than simply their immediate aftermath. To implicate the NRA and gun manufacturers as the primary architects of this violence, while neglecting to address systemic issues like poverty, social dislocation, and mental health crises, is not only myopic but irresponsible. A true documentary requires the courage to confront uncomfortable truths, rather than seeking to vilify an entire demographic based primarily on its loudest, least representative voices. Moreover, Moore's narrative risks enabling a cycle of blame that is as counterproductive as it is potent. For every shocking anecdote he presents, another perspective remains unexplored. The urban teen growing up in a crime-ridden neighborhood faces an entirely different set of choices and pressures than the suburban enthusiast at a gun club. Ignoring these disparities obscures the broader dialogue about violence in America and detracts from the urgent need for multifaceted solutions. Then there's Moore's tendency to evoke emotional responses that displace analytical discourse. His stylized emotionalism risks alienating potential allies who might otherwise engage in constructive debate. By framing gun ownership as an abomination based solely on the periphery of violence, he constructs barriers to dialogue with responsible owners who could contribute to efforts in shaping more constructive policies around gun control rather than stoking the fire of divisiveness. When combativeness replaces conversation, the real issues often become overshadowed by indignation, ultimately yielding a hollow exchange devoid of actionable solutions. As the film progresses, the mosaic of viewpoints continues to expand. Interviews, visuals, and anecdotes sway across the spectrum of thought, but without a thoughtful synthesis, they threaten to unravel into incoherence. Moore's dexterity in weaving a narrative is commendable, yet the responsibility that accompanies such influence mandates a more thorough examination of the issues at stake. His portrayal has the power to ignite fervor, sparking demonstrations and conversations that desperately need to occur - yet it must also wield the temperance that comes from recognizing the complexity of America's relationship with guns. Only then can we hope to emerge from this quagmire, possibly reaching some palatable form of understanding that builds bridges rather than erects walls. In the deep veins of discussion around violence and responsibility, it becomes imperative that we elevate the discourse - delving into the intricacies of culture, legislation, and the myriad factors contributing to this visceral issue. To shape a future where the mantra of "never again" resonates beyond rhetorical bombs, we must transform this dialogue from explosive anger into a comprehensive examination of systemic truths. Perhaps it's in this examination, rather than selective outrage, that we might find a semblance of clarity - one that will guide us toward a more secure, empathetic society.

As obesity rates have increased faster in poor communities, a likely driver has been the lowering cost of food calories (Mattson et al., 2014; Mullan et al., 2017), including sugar-sweetened beverages (Basu et al., 2013a; Hu and Malik, 2010; Johnson et al., 2007, 2016; Malik et al., 2006; Shang et al., 2012; Song et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2008). Since 1970, when high-fructose corn syrup (HCFS) was introduced at commercial scale into processed foods and sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs), consumption of HFCS increased from virtually zero in 1970 to over 60 pounds per capita annually in 2000 (Gerrior et al., 2004). Overall, the consumption of added sugars increased from about 70 pounds per person annually in 1970 (340 cal/day) to almost 90 pounds per capita (440 cal/day) by the late 1990s (Fig. 1b). By the 2000s, the top 20% of consumers of caloric sweeteners were ingesting over 300 kcal from HFCS per day (Bray et al., 2004). Much of the rise in total added sugar consumption between 1970 and 2000 is attributable to HFCS (Fig. 1b), often in SSBs that contribute additional calories without suppressing appetite for the intake of other foods (Almiron-Roig et al., 2013; Mattes and Campbell, 2009). The correlation between the increased consumption of added sugars in U.S. foods and the rise of obesity (Fig. 1b) has been recognized (Bray et al., 2004; Basu et al., 2013b; Lustig et al., 2015), even by the sweetener industry (Corn Refiners Association, 2006). Consequently, sugar consumption has been hypothesized to be a primary driver of the recent obesity increase (Basu et al., 2013a,b; Bray et al., 2004; Bray, 2007; Lustig et al., 2015; Nielsen et al., 2002; Nielsen and Popkin, 2004; Popkin and Hawkes, 2016). So, if Russell Brand was implying, as I infer from his remarks, that Hugo Boss created the Nazi uniforms, he is plain wrong. Perhaps Brand meant that Boss simply manufactured them. In which case he's right. But there's more to it than that. To answer the question fully, it is vital to know a little more about Hugo Boss himself. Boss was born in 1885, to parents who owned a lingerie and linen shop in the small town of Metzingen, 20 miles south of Stuttgart. After serving in World War I, Boss established his own clothes factory in 1924, which produced traditional outfits. It was certainly not designing couture, and its clothes, such as raincoats and sportswear, were functional. Among one of Boss's earliest clients was a textiles distributor called Rudolf Born, which commissioned Hugo Boss to produce some brown shirts for an organisation called the 'National Socialist Party', later, to become better known as the Nazis. Style: Hugo Boss is now a global fashion powerhouse. By the late Twenties, the growing Nazi Party had become a good client. And when the Party supplied Hugo Boss (as it did other manufacturers) the production templates for its uniforms, it appears that Boss did not see the relationship in anything but commercial terms. After all, Boss produced uniforms for many organisations, including the police and the postal service, and the apparently apolitical Boss was happy to make clothes for whoever paid their bills. However, on April 1, 1931, Boss took a step that would see his name - and brand - forever associated with Nazism. He joined the Nazi Party and was given the relatively low membership number of 508,889. Boss's reasons for becoming a Nazi comparatively early were twofold. First, as a businessman, it made commercial sense, as it made it easier for Boss to win contracts from the Nazis who were increasingly coming to dominate every aspect of German life. Second, Boss believed that Hitler was the only man who could lift Germany out of its economic doldrums. Such a businesslike attitude was not exceptional. There were certainly better men who refused to do business with the Party, but though Boss was happy to sign contracts with them, he was not a rabid Nazi. He was simply a pragmatist. Dubious: Boss became a Nazi as it made it easier for him to win contracts. Partly thanks to his membership of the party, the Nazis were good to Boss. By 1933, he was able to advertise that he made clothes not only for the SS, but also for the Hitler Youth and the Brownshirts - the paramilitary wing of the Nazi Party. Then in 1938, business skyrocketed when Boss won contracts to make army uniforms. By 1940, the company was turning over some 1,000,000 Reichsmarks, compared to 200,000 Reichsmarks in 1936. However, it was still far from being a major manufacturer. In 1940, Boss was employing some 250 workers, which made it a small to medium-sized firm.

One cognitive factor that has been implicated in the development and maintenance of depression is rumination, which refers to the tendency to repetitively think about and dwell on negative thoughts, feelings, and experiences (Nolen-Hoeksema, 2000). Research has consistently shown that rumination is a key predictor of depression onset, severity, and duration (Nolen-Hoeksema et al., 2008). Furthermore, rumination has been found to be a robust predictor of treatment response, with individuals high in rumination being less likely to respond to treatment and more likely to experience relapse (Segal et al., 2006). However, little is known about whether rumination differs between individuals with a more chronic versus episodic course of depression. One possibility is that individuals with a more chronic course of depression may exhibit higher levels of rumination, which in turn contributes to the persistence of symptoms. Alternatively, it is possible that rumination is a transdiagnostic feature of depression, present across different course configurations. Another cognitive factor that may be relevant to the differentiation of chronic and episodic depression is cognitive flexibility, which refers to the ability to switch between different mental sets and adapt to changing situations (Dennis and Vander Wal, 2010). Cognitive flexibility has been found to be impaired in individuals with depression, and has been linked to the development and maintenance of depressive symptoms (Kashdan and Ciarrochi, 2013). However, it is unclear whether cognitive flexibility differs between individuals with a more chronic versus episodic course of depression. One possibility is that individuals with a more chronic course of depression may exhibit reduced cognitive flexibility, which in turn contributes to the persistence of symptoms. Additionally, the current study aimed to investigate the role of self-compassion, which refers to the ability to treat oneself with kindness, understanding, and acceptance in times of suffering or failure (Neff, 2003). Self-compassion has been found to be a robust predictor of mental health outcomes, including depression (MacBeth and Gumley, 2012). However, little is known about whether self-compassion differs between individuals with a more chronic versus episodic course of depression. One possibility is that individuals with a more chronic course of depression may exhibit lower levels of self-compassion, which in turn contributes to the persistence of symptoms. To address these questions, the current study employed a cross-sectional design, recruiting individuals with a diagnosis of major depressive disorder who had experienced either a chronic or episodic course of depression. Participants completed a range of self-report measures assessing rumination, cognitive flexibility, and self-compassion, as well as a range of demographic and clinical variables. The results of this study will provide important insights into the cognitive factors that differentiate individuals with a more chronic versus episodic course of depression, and will inform the development of more effective treatments for this debilitating disorder.

The newcomer, wrapped in a thick, dark cloak, moved with an air of preoccupied elegance, every footstep careful against the heaving deck. The early light unveiled a countenance marked by sharp features and eyes that darted over the sea like a hawk's, appraising and calculating. He halted momentarily, taking in the sea's vastness and the ship's altered course, before addressing the nearest crew member with a quiet command to fetch him a spyglass. The spyglass was brought promptly, and he raised it to his eye, scrutinizing the distant horizon with a furrowed brow. Though spoken softly, his observations were pointedly directed toward the crew's interests. "A steamer on the horizon," he noted, lowering the instrument. "And, perhaps, an opportunity for those with foresight." The crew exchanged furtive glances, their faces expressing a mix of intrigue and suspicion. The passenger, undeterred by their silence, continued, "We must be nimble, we must be cautious. The sea grants few favors to the hesitant or the unwary." His words struck a chord, echoed by the persistent crash of waves against the Excelsior's bow. In the steady rhythm of the ocean's growl, an understanding seemed to ripple among the men. The promise of something significant loomed, couched in the guise of fortune or peril, neither fully knowable beyond the horizon's seam. Meanwhile, back at the helm, the two shadows maintained their silent vigil over the wheel. The wind whipped a spray of salt air around them, chilling their bones as they steered the ship further from the Mexican coast. The third mate, returning to their side, added with a note of urgency, "Keep it steady. Once past Cape San Lucas, we break for the open sea, avoiding any unkind eyes." "And the Senor?" queried one of the helmsmen, nodding towards the figure looking out to sea. "He knows his business. For now, best keep our thoughts to ourselves and our hands at work. Any talk could earn us more than we bargained for." A long silence followed, punctuated only by the groaning of wood and sighing of sails. Each sailor occupied with private conjectures, aware of the whisper of change carried on the ocean breeze. In the distance, small dots began to appear, forming the feathery silhouettes of seabirds dancing above the waves. An albatross sailed gracefully, unaffected by the complexity below. To those aboard, even this ethereal presence seemed a harbinger of mysteries yet uncovered or courses yet uncharted. The sun climbed higher, bleaching the heavens with swathes of morning hue, as the Excelsior plowed purposefully on. Its crew now joined in the shared anticipation of whatever lay northward-beyond promises, beyond charts, and into the unregimented theater of man's ambition. Around them, the vastness of the Pacific yawned-a space where secrets and tales intermingled, awaiting the bold. Adventure's clock ticked steadily, its echoes resounding across timeworn decks, imbued with destinies lined and intertwined. To the heart of such uncertainty, the Excelsior and her reluctant travelers bore their calculated path, against the sunlit expanses and the weaving shadows of surf and sail.

A meticulous devotion to detail featured prominently in Bannino's compositions, with every object meticulously chosen and expertly placed to convey the peculiarities and extravagance inherent in these dietary philosophies. His work explores not just the contents of these diets, but the broader cultural obsession with health, appearance, and status that fuels them. Through Bannino's lens, Gwyneth Paltrow's meals transform into an ascetic tableau, where humble kale and quinoa assume a regal posture against a backdrop reminiscent of the Dutch Golden Age. The sumptuous edges of a lemon are softened by the chiaroscuro lighting that nods to Caravaggio himself, almost whispering to the viewer a reminder of indulgence's seductive power cloaked in the guise of discipline. In stark contrast, the barren table of Kate Moss speaks volumes of an aesthetic war that rages on, where invisible barriers define beauty and sustenance takes a backseat to the alluring call of an unattainable image. Exploring further into the eccentric gastronomic world of his subjects, Bannino paints a wet, citrusy sheen across dreamlike lemons and maple syrup-infused elixirs, which together form Beyonce's controversial liquid cleanse. The harsh juxtaposition of cayenne pepper nestled amidst golden-yellow hues conjures the paradox of the diet itself: a stark simplicity belying the challenge of its intimidating rigor. This modern concoction adopts an almost alchemical presence within the painterly setting, its ingredients seeming both transformational and aloof. Behind the scenes, Bannino delves into a parallel world where digital craftsmanship remains untouched. His process is a testament to an authentic artistry that leans heavily on the forgotten virtues of patience and precision. Hours are poured into the crafting of each composition, where every shadow is coaxed and every highlight rendered with an eye as sharp and discerning as the masters who inspire him. Here, Caravaggio's legacy finds renewal-shadow and light dance intimately across Bannino's canvas, breathing life into the static and granting depth to his commentary on contemporary society's dietary peculiarities. In his portrayal of Simon Cowell's indulgences, Bannino orchestrates a delicate symphony of airfreighted fruits captured within a gleaming halo of their natural splendor. These seemingly opulent details elevate the mundane into the realm of luxury, taking quotidian nourishment and adorning it with the aura of decadence. The voluptuous bath of milk becomes a fountain of youth, swirling beneath the subtle luminescence reminiscent of marble statues swathed in creamy textures. Then there's the portrayal of Bill Clinton's patriotic cabbage diet, an intersection of humble produce and stoic resolve. The spread's vibrant greens and earthy reds capture the simplicity and dignity of a return to nature, symbolizing Clinton's journey from indulgence to moderation. Bannino masterfully encapsulates the essence of this transformative narrative, presenting raw vegetables arrayed as a magnificent tapestry that challenges the viewer to reevaluate their understanding of luxury and necessity. Bannino's collection is not merely an exploration of dietary eccentricities; it is a profound and provocative reflection on the broader societal relationship with consumption, shedding light on the cravings that bind us to our historical roots and the myths that compel us toward new age traditions. Each image, a paradoxical blend of abundance and restraint, communicates a story both timeless and acutely relevant, inviting an introspection of our culinary choices and the cultural narratives they weave.

A celebrated method is to use a multiple drain system, where more than one outlet are used at appropriate locations, to achieve desired flow conditions in the tank. In a dual-drain system with an elevated wall-drain, the solids can quickly be discharged out of the tank and improve the water quality. Also, such wall drain can reduce the flow velocity downstream and hence control the flow pattern as desired. Although octagonal tanks are the best alternative for circular tanks with an advantage of better space management and shared sidewalls, it is important to note that there is a considerable difference between the two tank shapes as the flow velocity and water quality is concerned (Gorle et al., 2018). For instance, dead zones can be created in the near-corner wall region in the octagonal tanks, which does not happen in case of circular tanks. Circular-type culture tanks sometimes use dual-drain to create two advantages over a single drain tank, i.e., to concentrate a majority of settleable solids into a relatively small tank underflow (as in a swirl separator) and/or to shift the impulse force associated with outlet flows in a manner that can be used to help optimize water rotational velocities located in the annular region about the center of the tank (Davidson and Summerfelt, 2004; Gorle et al., 2018). Water rotational velocities, particularly within the annular region about the tank center, are critically important to create a self-cleaning tank and when trying to maintain more optimum swimming speeds for the fish. At least one drain is always located to draw flow off the bottom center of the tank. However, the second drain is typically located above the bottom-drawing drain at the tank's center (Terjesen et al., 2013) or part-way up the tank's side wall (Davidson and Summerfelt, 2004; Summerfelt et al., 2004; Despres and Couturier, 2006; Summerfelt et al., 2006; Summerfelt et al., 2009a, 2009b; Wolters et al., 2009; Pfeiffer and Riche, 2011; Carvalhoa et al., 2013; Terjesen et al., 2013; Summerfelt et al., 2016). The second drain is elevated in order to withdraw flow out of the tank in a location where it should contain minimal settleable solids, because the settleable solids tend to concentrate on the tank floor as they are moved by the tank's primary rotating and radial flows to the bottom-center drain. However, the lack of knowledge on the effect of elevated wall drain on the overall flow behavior leads to uncertain flow split ratio in the commercial as well as research facilities, which describes the paucity of research on culture tanks with dual-drain systems. Only three studies have described empirical water velocity data collected in sidewall-type dual-drain circular tanks (Davidson and Summerfelt, 2004; Summerfelt et al., 2006; Summerfelt et al., 2009a). This results in a trial-error flow-split between multiple outlets, or sometimes uncertain operating conditions in the commercial farms.

My husband was living in Arizona and had just gotten a new job there. He asked me to move out there with him and our son and we agreed. I found another job in San Diego and began to look for apartments. When I told my boss I needed to leave she said she couldn't afford to keep paying me while I searched for a place to live and she let me go. The apartment complex where I lived was bought out by another company and they wanted us to sign a new lease. I didn't have any money left over from the month before when I paid rent, so I signed the lease and gave them my credit card number. When I received the bill I was shocked. They charged me for two months worth of rent plus a $1000 security deposit. I had no idea I was responsible for two months rent. So now I was broke and had to move within the next two weeks. My husband was getting a divorce settlement and we were supposed to receive the money in early December. We figured we would use the money to pay off bills and save enough to put down on a house in Arizona. Then the economy crashed. Our mortgage company filed bankruptcy and my husbands lawyer said he wouldn't see any money until April. By this point I was down to my last hundred dollars. I called my mom and told her I was coming home. She offered to help me find an apartment and I took her up on the offer. I found a small studio apartment in Chula Vista and moved in. I had been unemployed for almost three months at this point and was running out of food stamps. I was making about half of what I made at my previous job and my husband had yet to send me any money. On top of that I was trying to buy groceries for a four year old who was used to having plenty of food. I was buying only the bare necessities and sometimes I would skip meals. I was losing weight rapidly. Then I received a call from my husband saying he had finally sold his car and was sending me a check for $800. I was thrilled! I immediately went to the grocery store and bought as much food as I could carry. The next day I got a phone call from my mom asking how I was doing. I told her I was great and that I had a bunch of food in the fridge. She asked if I was sure and I said yes. She said ok and hung up. About thirty minutes later I received a call from her telling me to come right away. I ran over to her house and she showed me my bank statement. My husband had sent me a check for $80 instead of $800. At this point I was crying hysterically and my mom was trying to comfort me. I was completely humiliated. My mom asked if I wanted to eat and I said no. I told her I was fine and walked back to my apartment. Once inside I locked the door and cried. I threw up everything I had eaten earlier that morning and sat on the floor sobbing. I couldn't stop. I was hungry and ashamed and alone. I cried until I fell asleep. The next morning I woke up feeling physically sick. I hadn't eaten anything since I threw up the night before and I was still hungry. I opened the refrigerator and saw nothing but condiments. I closed the door and sat on the couch. I knew I should eat something but I didn't want to. I stared at the door for twenty minutes before walking into the kitchen and opening the cupboard. I pulled out a box of cereal and poured a bowl full. I sat down at the table and ate every bite. I washed the dishes and then walked into the bathroom.

You want to start in a space where your dog can focus on you, and you can focus on your dog. And I think that's one of the biggest mistakes people make, is they try to start training their dog in a high-distraction area, like a busy street or a dog park, and it's just too much for the dog to handle. So, by starting in a quiet space, you can really focus on building that connection with your dog, and teaching them to walk beside you without pulling on the leash. And I think another important factor is to start with short sessions, you know, 5-10 minutes, and gradually build up the duration as your dog becomes more comfortable and more focused. Now, one of the tips I mentioned in my blog post is to use a harness instead of a collar. And I think this is a game-changer for a lot of people. When you're using a collar, the leash is attached to your dog's neck, and that can be uncomfortable for them, especially if they're pulling hard. But with a harness, the leash is attached to their chest or their back, and it distributes the force more evenly, making it much more comfortable for your dog. And I think another key factor is to avoid pulling back on the leash when your dog pulls. I know it's tempting, because it feels like you're trying to correct them, but really, you're just creating a tug-of-war situation. Instead, when your dog starts to pull, stop moving forward, and wait for them to come back to your side before you start walking again. This teaches your dog that pulling on the leash doesn't get them where they want to go faster, but rather, it slows them down. And then, of course, there's the importance of rewards and reinforcement. When your dog is walking beside you without pulling, be sure to reward them with treats, praise, and affection. This positive reinforcement will help them associate walking on a loose leash with good behavior, and they'll be more likely to repeat it in the future. Now, I know some people might be thinking, "But Shannon, my dog is really strong, and they're going to pull me down the street no matter what." And I get it, some dogs are definitely more powerful than others. But the thing is, it's not about physical strength, it's about mental focus. If you can teach your dog to focus on you, and to walk beside you without pulling, they'll be much more manageable, even if they are strong. And finally, I think it's important to be patient and consistent. Teaching your dog to walk on a loose leash takes time, and it takes practice. Don't expect to see results overnight, but with consistent effort and positive reinforcement, you can get there. Ken: That's really great advice, Shannon. Sir Evelyn ventured from time to time to raise his strained eyes from the road immediately in front of him and glance at the roofs of the houses which lay below, and the sea, blue and sparkling, below them. Each time he looked the roofs and the sea seemed a little nearer, which cheered him; but the descent still twisted before him. He began to wonder whether his nerves would remain under control until he reached the bottom. Sweat broke out on his forehead and trickled into his eyes, cold sweat. His hands on the wheel were moist and cold. On the other hand - such are the compensations which nature arranges - the inside of his mouth became perfectly dry, so that it was painful to swallow. Yet he had to swallow each time he crawled round one of the blind corners and found nothing on the other side. There was much excuse for Sir Evelyn's nervousness. A highly skilled driver would have disliked the hill. Sir Evelyn was a novice. A reckless youth would have hesitated over it. Sir Evelyn was sixty-five and most unwilling to throw away the few years of life remaining to him. It is greatly to his credit and a proof of the fine qualities which had raised him to the position of Cabinet Minister that he reached the bottom of the hill safely. Passing a row of fishermen's cottages, he crawled, not daring to change gear, till he came to the Anchor Inn. There he stopped. A board, either new or newly painted, announced that James Hinton was licensed to sell beer, spirits and tobacco. Sir Evelyn passed the tip of a dry tongue across a dry lip. At the moment it seemed to him that beer, even the poorest, thinnest beer, any beer at all, was the best thing the world contained. He left his car and went into the tap-room. Had Sir Evelyn been capable for the moment of any feeling except a desire for beer he would have been surprised at the tap-room of the Anchor Inn in Hailey Compton. Instead of reeking stuffily of stale beer, the place was fresh, cool and pleasant. Instead of a soiled floor, were clean polished boards. Instead of a messy counter and stained tables there was shining cleanliness. Not such are English inns in remote villages. Though thirsty Sir Evelyn could not help noticing the landlord when he came in. He was not in the least the landlord who might have been expected in such a village. He came from an inner room and greeted Sir Evelyn with respectful courtesy. He was a tall, slim man, neatly dressed, cleanly shaved. He might still have been, what indeed he once was, the valet of a wealthy peer. "A glass of beer," said Sir Evelyn. "In fact a jug of beer." The landlord, the James Hinton of the newly painted board, spread out apologetic hands. "Very sorry sir," he said.

Disengagement of protein molecules and subsequent mass transfer to the bulk of the wash solution (boundary layer) were considered to be the rate limiting stages. The initial swelling stage was constrained to occur before a 'reptation time' was reached and no cleaning was observed during this period. The 'reptation time' is linked to the initial time required for the first molecules to disengage. A first-order equation was proposed to characterise the removal rate and a disengagement rate constant introduced. This constant was considered as a function of the volume fraction of the disengaged protein molecules at the soil-solution interface. As the rate limiting stage is the movement of these molecules to the interface and their subsequent detachment, a critical concentration would be reached in this area and a constant removal rate obtained. This agreed with the results seen in experiments. Finally, the decay stage was modelled as a function of the surface area of the remaining film. By integrating the three steps, good correlations (no error given) were obtained with experimental data. Extensive research has been done to study swelling and dissolution mechanisms on simple protein soil deposits such as -lactoglobulin ( -lg). Studies performed (Mercade-Prieto et al., 2007a) showed the presence of a dissolution threshold below which the gel swelled but did not dissolve. This threshold is a function of pH and the volume fraction available inside the protein network. It establishes the limit for the stability of the gels formed. An increase of pH increased the degree of swelling observed. Particularly, significant swelling occurred above pH 10. However, the addition of salts to increase of the ionic strength produced a screening effect between cations from solution and the polymer network. Thus, at a certain level the degree of swelling decreased. Dissolution occurred when pH was high enough (pH threshold) (Mercade-Prieto et al., 2007b) and a certain swelling ratio was achieved (volume fraction threshold) (Mercade-Prieto et al., 2009, 2007c). Dissolution rates varied for different alkalinities and solution ionic strengths. A sharp transition in the dissolution rate was found between pH 11 and 12. The disruption of non-covalent intermolecular bonds due to alkali denaturation was established as the main dissolution mechanism. This disengagement was favoured by the repulsion produced due to the increase in the number of charges and the subsequent unfolding of the protein structure. As the collectivist movement gained momentum, it began to permeate the fabric of Western societies, masquerading as a benevolent force aimed at rectifying the perceived ills of industrialization. Lippmann argues that this movement was, in reality, a thinly veiled attempt to concentrate power in the hands of the state, under the guise of promoting the greater good. The proponents of collectivism, he asserts, were driven by a fundamental mistrust of individual liberty and a belief that the state was the sole arbiter of progress. The consequences of this shift were far-reaching and devastating. As the state's power grew, so too did its propensity for coercion and control. The individual, once hailed as the cornerstone of liberal democracy, was gradually reduced to a mere cog in the machine of the state. The rights and freedoms that had been painstakingly won over the centuries were slowly eroded, as the state assumed an increasingly paternalistic role. Lippmann contends that this phenomenon was not unique to totalitarian regimes, but was, in fact, a pervasive trend that had infected even the most ostensibly democratic nations. The New Deal in America, for instance, was touted as a bold experiment in progressive governance, but Lippmann saw it as a thinly veiled attempt to consolidate power in the hands of the state. The proliferation of government agencies, the expansion of bureaucratic control, and the erosion of individual liberties were all hallmarks of this creeping collectivism. The good society, Lippmann argues, is not one in which the state exercises total control, but rather one in which the individual is free to flourish, unencumbered by the shackles of authoritarianism. He advocates for a return to the liberal principles of the 18th and 19th centuries, which recognized the inherent value of individual liberty and the dangers of concentrated power. The state, he believes, should be a servant of the people, not their master. In this sense, Lippmann's work can be seen as a clarion call to arms, a warning against the dangers of unchecked state power and the erosion of individual freedom. Written against the backdrop of a world teetering on the brink of war, The Good Society is a powerful indictment of the authoritarian collectivism that had come to define the era. It is a testament to Lippmann's prescience that his warnings remain as relevant today as they were in 1937, serving as a powerful reminder of the importance of vigilance in the face of encroaching state power. As we reflect on the tumultuous events of the 20th century, it is clear that Lippmann's warnings fell on deaf ears. The totalitarian regimes of Europe and Asia, which he so astutely critiqued, went on to commit some of the most heinous atrocities in human history. The New Deal, meanwhile, paved the way for an era of unprecedented government intervention in the economy, setting the stage for the welfare state and its attendant ills. And yet, despite the catastrophic consequences of authoritarian collectivism, its allure remains strong. The siren song of state power continues to entice, promising a utopian future of equality and prosperity, but delivering only misery and despair. Lippmann's The Good Society stands as a powerful rebuke to this false promise, a testament to the enduring power of individual liberty and the importance of limiting state power. As we navigate the complexities of the 21st century, his work remains a beacon of hope, illuminating the path to a brighter, freer future.

A number of death sentences were converted to life sentences in 1983 when a military appeals court found the death penalty was unconstitutional because of problems with the armed forces' sentencing guidelines. Unlike in civilian courts where prosecutors decide charges, a commanding general - who has other duties - decides whether a military defendant will face the death penalty. That general also can reduce a sentence. It's one of the biggest differences with the civilian system and it leads to one of the major criticisms of the decentralized nature of the military judicial system, where each branch operates independently. "Even if you have two identical cases, one being prosecuted by one commander at one base and other being prosecuted by a commander at another base, you may have different outcomes because the commanders may have different philosophies," said Dwight Sullivan, a former Marine prosecutor and judge who now works as a civilian attorney specializing in military death penalty appeals. The strong synergy between AMP and A769662 in allosteric activation of AMPK in cell-free assays (Scott et al., 2014a) is also observed in vivo (Ducommun et al., 2014; Foretz et al., 2010; Timmermans et al., 2014). We recently reported that salicylate is a direct activator of AMPK and that it binds the same site as A769662 (Hawley et al., 2012). The relentless sun bore down with an unyielding ferocity, as if taking delight in the desolation it wrought upon the land. The man, now fully absorbed in his task, allowed the rhythmic blows of the hammer to drown out the cacophony of his own thoughts. Each strike sent tiny fragments of rock spiraling into the air, where they disappeared into the dust and heat that cloaked the surroundings. His brow, furrowed beneath the intensity of concentration, gleamed with beads of perspiration that glistened like precious dew in the merciless glow of midday. Around him, the silence of the Veldt was a living thing, a palpable entity that wrapped itself around the landscape: heavy and oppressive, yet strangely comforting in its familiar weight. He could hear the faint whisper of the wind as it surreptitiously navigated through the cracks in the rocky earth, carrying with it the scent of parched sagebrush and the acrid tang of sun-bleached soil. Every breath he inhaled filled his lungs with the history of the land, a tapestry woven from ancient stories that seemed to echo from the very stones beneath him. To the untrained eye, the landscape might appear lifeless, a sprawling canvas of muted ochres and browns bereft of any sign of vitality. Yet he knew better. The Veldt, with its rough-hewn beauty and austere grandeur, teemed with prospects for those willing to search. Gems lay hidden beneath the surface, waiting for an eye keen enough to discern their worth. His restless spirit had drawn him to this forsaken domain; he was a seeker of secrets, a pursuer of nature's hidden treasures. As he chipped away, his mind drifted to thoughts of home-or what was left of it. Like this unforgiving land, the memories of his past were marred by difficulties and trials. He had ventured far from the comforts of civilization, leaving behind the bustling towns where laughter resonated and voices mingled in vibrant harmony. Here, there was only the solitude of rock and dry grasses, an existence punctuated by the occasional bleating of a goat echoing from a distant kraal, or the sudden flap of a bird taking flight from the ground. The sun had reached its zenith, and the shadows that danced beneath the scattered stones grew shorter, almost reluctant to announce the end of another day. Yet the heat seemed as insufferable as ever, pressing down upon him like a physical weight. He paused to wipe the perspiration from his brow. The hammer rested against his thigh, and he surveyed the horizon. In the distance, a dust cloud twirled, a fleeting mirage humorously intermingling with the heat waves. He squinted against the glare. It could be nothing, a mere figment of the oppressive atmosphere, or it could herald the arrival of someone else - perhaps a wandering traveler or a fellow sojourner enticed by the same silent call of the earth. With a sudden surge of optimism, he stood taller, brushing dirt from his legs as he prepared to greet whatever fortune had sent his way. As he focused his gaze, it became clearer. A figure emerged from the billowing haze, a silhouette against the impossible brightness, its form growing more defined with each passing moment. The landscape's stillness trembled with anticipation, whispering promises of new encounters and dusty tales yet to unfold. Each heartbeat echoed within him, matching the rhythm of the approaching footsteps; unfamiliar yet beckoning with the allure of possibility. His hand tightened on the hammer, not in defense, but as a ready companion to greet whatever fortune awaited. And as the figure drew nearer, so did the dawning realization that perhaps this arid land still had surprises to reveal.

In terms of communicating my ideas and developing my ideas, I work on a drawing board - as opposed to all my colleagues now, who are obviously on computer-aided design (CAD) systems. I guess I'm the last dinosaur in the industry. I view it simply as a language. It's the way of taking an idea in the head - typically I'll take an idea, sketch it on a bit of paper and then develop it on the drawing board. Now, of course, as everything has to go onto the CAD system, I'm lucky enough to have a team of two or three people who take my drawings and convert them into electronic images. But whether you use a drawing board or go straight to the CAD I think it's really a personal preference. That's the way I grew up and I'm afraid I'm getting a bit too much of a creature of habit to change. Have you ever been forced to try the newer design technology? When CAD first came in during the early 1990s, then various people - particularly when I was at Williams - said I ought to really be changing. Perhaps at that time when I was still in my 30s, I should have done. But I like the freedom of drawing, the fact that you can sketch very easily, you can rub out, you can change, you can freehand. When I watch people on the CAD system now, that's still a weakness to me of the CAD system - the freehand ability and the ability to change things very quickly and easily with a rubber is not there. What are the things that you are most proud of? Certainly the first Formula One cars - I was involved in the Leyton House/March team from 1988. We were a very small team. It was only two aerodynamicists I think, including myself, on the car. The total engineering team was five or six people. We were stuck with an abnormally aspirated engine which had far less power than the turbocharged engines of the era. So we set out to build an as aerodynamically-efficient car as we could. That car I think genuinely changed the direction of F1 at the time. The cars had become quite big and clumsy and our little March was, despite being well done on power, was able to get ahead of McLaren and Ferrari and Williams, just by being aerodynamically efficient. Of course other people recognized that and over the coming years increasingly cars became a clone of the 1988 car. Which of your innovations do you think have stood the test of time? Certainly my route has always been to try to put aerodynamics first and foremost in the design of the car because that's the biggest performance differentiator. And that really is something now that is generally accepted - everybody does that. But in the 1980s when I first started that wasn't the norm.

Also, it would be open to show, by contemporaneous history, that this mode of alluding to slaves and slavery, instead of speaking of them, was employed on purpose to exclude from the Constitution the idea that there could be property in man. To show all this, is easy and certain. Industrial interest on this phenotype arises from the need to diversify production and the possibility to expand on-growing production sites to low salinity locations, which are more suitable for rainbow trout smolts than for Atlantic salmon (Altinok and Grizzle, 2001) and are less prone to salmon louse (Lepeophtheirus salmonis) infestations. However, our understanding of the environmental control of rainbow trout smoltification is insufficient and there is a need for appropriate tools to assess rainbow trout seawater-readiness. In the absence of a rainbow trout specific all-season production protocol, most hatcheries are rearing rainbow trout at continuous light (LL) and natural temperature while seawater-readiness is regarded exclusively as size-dependent. Under these conditions, high mortalities and high numbers of fish that experience sub-optimal growth (growth-stunted phenotype) upon seawater transfer, especially in summer post-smolts, have been reported by the industry. While LL has been compared to other photoperiod regimes and has been shown to be an appropriate option for rainbow trout smoltification (Morro et al., 2019), the effect of temperature and its interaction with photoperiod remain untested. In order to reduce the incidence of growth-stunted fish, optimizing rearing conditions for rainbow trout smoltification, as well as identifying and implementing biomarkers of seawater-readiness and biomarkers for the early detection of growth-stunted fish are all crucial. In this sense, insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-I is a peptide hormone that promotes growth of fish (Wood et al., 2005). The activity of circulating IGF-I is stabilized and regulated by the presence of multiple IGF-binding proteins (IGFBPs). In salmonids and other teleost species, plasma IGF-I is positively correlated with growth rate and can be used as a positive marker of growth (Beckman, 2011; Picha et al., 2008). On the other hand, IGFBP-1b, one of three major circulating forms of IGFBP, is negatively correlated with growth rate and may be useful as a negative marker of growth in salmonids (Kaneko et al., 2019; Kawaguchi et al., 2013; Shimizu et al., 2006). Another factor to take into consideration during production is disease, which remains as one of the main threats (Asche et al., 2009; Dale et al., 2009; Kristoffersen et al., 2009). Therefore, immune capacity is a key factor to take into consideration when optimising new production protocols. Since blood cells constitute the main line of defence against pathogens and non-self particles, haematopoiesis has been used as a proxy of immune capacity (Martin et al., 2012).

For ground based measurements, SIF is estimated from spectral measurements taken around the O2B feature using the FLUXNET standardised protocol, which has been successfully employed to retrieve SIF from sunlit and shaded conditions (Sun et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2018b). In recent years, spaceborne SIF retrievals have become available through instruments onboard NASA's Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2) satellite launched in July 2014, and the European Space Agency's Fluorescence EXplorer (FLEX) mission currently scheduled for launch in 2021. Ground-based SIF retrievals are now also possible using portable spectrometers such as the FLUXSCAPE sensor, which was first deployed in 2014 (Sun et al., 2018a). To date, SIF has been used extensively to explore the physiological basis of variability in photosynthesis in both controlled and field experiments (e.g. Botta-Dukat et al., 2017; Porcar-Castell et al., 2014; Walter et al., 2018). There is also growing interest in how SIF may be used to improve our understanding of terrestrial CO2 fluxes at larger scales. Studies to date indicate that SIF may provide a better proxy for GPP than traditional VIs, although many questions remain regarding the relationship between SIF and GPP, including the spatial and temporal scales of measurement needed to accurately capture these relationships (e.g. Jeong et al., 2017; Frankenberg and Berry, 2017). Despite the increasing availability of SIF data, the lack of coordinated and consistent approaches to their use is a major barrier to their widespread application (Porcar-Castell et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018a). In particular, the sensitivity of SIF retrieval methods to ambient environmental conditions needs to be considered carefully, particularly as it relates to the use of SIF in models designed to simulate photosynthetic processes (e.g. the JULES land-surface model). As part of the UK Earth System Model (UKESM) development effort, we investigated the impact of varying SIF retrieval parameters on the simulated photosynthetic behaviour of the JULES land-surface model. The JULES land-surface model (Best et al., 2011) is one component of the Unified Model (UM) weather forecast system, and is used in the Met Office's Earth System Model (EM). It simulates exchanges of heat, water vapour, momentum and carbon between the land and atmosphere, and includes parameterisations of snow, soil freeze-thaw cycles and vegetation phenology (Clark et al., 2011; Harper et al., 2014). The most recent version of JULES used in the UM is v4.6, which includes a number of new developments relating to the simulation of vegetation photosynthesis, namely: (1) improved representation of stomatal conductance, (2) inclusion of a coupled nitrogen-carbon cycle, (3) addition of the explicit photosynthetic responses of C4 plants, (4) incorporation of the dynamic light use efficiency (LUE) framework, and (5) implementation of a new model for the estimation of gross primary production (GPP). All of these developments were included in the EM1.0 configuration of the UM, which was released in February 2018. In this paper we focus on the LUE framework and GPP scheme in JULES v4.6. Hereafter we refer to JULES v4.6 simply as JULES.

Jack, who had been watching the exchange with interest, spoke up for the first time. "Now, now, boys, let's not get too worked up. We're all friends here, ain't we?" Bud turned to him, his eyes narrowing. "You're a mighty quiet one, Jack," he said. "I reckon you're waiting for something to happen, but I don't rightly know what it is." Jack's eyes flickered, and he looked away, his face a mask of indifference. Bissell, however, seemed to find his voice. "I'll tell you what I want, Larkin," he growled. "I want you to get out of here, and take your sheep with you. You're a trespasser, and I won't stand for it." Bud's smile was cold and hard. "I reckon I'll do no such thing," he said. Her name was Lucy, and she lay with a pallid face framed by a cascade of auburn curls. I remembered feeling a peculiar chill as I watched her chest rise and fall with fragile breaths, the sound like the whisper of wind against autumn leaves. She was the catalyst, the beginning of what would unravel beyond that wall-an invisible thread weaving silently between our lives, connecting us inextricably to realms both known and unknown. Her mother, a wraith-like figure hovering beside the bed, caught my sleeve, her eyes glistening with desperation. "Doctor," she implored, her voice barely more than a rustle, "I trust you'll do what you can." I nodded gravely, compelled by forces I couldn't name, beyond the tangible science that had become my creed. Here, amidst the opulence, lay the stark simplicity of human fear, a reminder of our mortality. Lucy's condition required expertise I couldn't claim, but I was ensnared by a sense of obligation-a need to render aid, though the path was unclear. Days dripped by, poignant, filled with fleeting successes and lingering anxieties. I visited Lucy daily, a ritual that became fraught with strange occurrences. The air grew thick with a restless energy; an imperceptible hum seemed to resonate through the rooms and settle, like dust, upon my skin. And then, subtly at first, I became aware of how porous walls could be. It flared one evening as I returned homeward along a dimly lit street, the familiar facade of buildings blending into shadows. My thoughts were on Lucy, on the jaundiced pallor of her cheeks and the glazed absence in her gaze when, without warning, a vivid vision struck me. It lingered-as if I had glimpsed something through a doorway abruptly ajar. In this vision, Lucy was playing in a garden, a sunlit realm thriving beyond those barriers of brick and mortar. She laughed, free of the burdens she bore in reality, but I knew this garden was not local; it had no place along the city's grid nor was it scribed in maps. It dwelled somewhere deeper, somewhere hidden, perhaps behind that elusive wall. The vision ended, leaving behind a residue of wonder and disquiet. I shivered, realizing this was no mere remnant of a stressed mind. Was the boundary-so sturdily conceived by our senses-more pliable than I had ever imagined? Were these the tremors of the intangible, brushing against our world like the fleeting stroke of fingers on a string? I resolved to confide in Evelyn Marbury, Lucy's mother, sharing these glimpses, these curious insights, hoping they might serve as balm for her troubled heart. Her response was unexpected; a flicker of recognition sparked in her eyes, and she whispered of dreams, vivid dreams that had visited her since that fateful day I took up her daughter's care. Dreams of Lucy dancing through meadows resplendent beyond this weary existence. As Evelyn spoke, a profound realization unfurled in my mind. This wall, this formidable construct we believed so unyielding, might be but a veil, thin and laced with mystery, parting subtly to reveal truths yet unseen. It suggested a connection, an overlay of realms where our influence, unseen and unknowable, might indeed intertwine, shaping destinies unbidden. Thus, what lay beyond the wall began to take shape, an echo of possibilities I could no longer dismiss, whispering of barriers transcended, realities intertwined, a saga written in the spaces betwixt, yearning, ever yearning, for discovery.

The smart and sensitive minx was a quiet one, often spending her time alone and in her own mind. She had gone through some difficult times and had lost herself in her explorations, and although she didn't know it at first, felt as if the ferret could bring her out of the dark places she had been. But Ariel did not mind this, although she realized it. It was wonderful, in its way, fascinating by strangeness. To tell the truth, Mrs. Nevin interested her more at the moment than the unknown, beautiful harbor at which she appeared to be gazing. And no aching longing for her father's sharing of this interest could turn it dreamlike, for her father could never share it, alive or dead. Fashionable women, even at a distance, bored him. But how did a woman like that feel, Ariel wondered, about her so finished and catered-to beauty, and her easy self-sufficiency? And how did it feel to have two burnished, curled children that were one's very own, to love, to live for, to play with? How wonderful if Ariel herself had had children of her own to play with and dance with on their beach, while her father was alive and she could still have gloried in them, before the sense of unreality had settled like a thin dust over unshared happiness! The Nevins and the nurse had come the length of the deck now, and were standing near her, but not taking their chairs, and oddly silent. Still, she would not look directly at them to discover the reason. If she looked into their faces she might become visible to them. So far, these two past days, Ariel had kept herself wrapped in a cloud of invisibility, she felt, merely by not meeting other eyes. She was shy of contacts, ever since her father's death; and the aching, hurting suspense at the back of her mind, which was caused by dread of the near approaching meeting with her father's friend, had only intensified her desire for invisibility. As for Mrs. Nevin, until this instant she had been nearly as unaware of Ariel as Ariel supposed her to be. She had looked at her once or twice in the beginning, to wonder whether it was a child, a girl or a woman who occupied the neighboring chair, but quickly decided that such speculation was waste of time since the one thing certain was that Ariel's age didn't matter, since she was obviously - nobody. From that decision she had returned to social obliviousness, lying back for hours at a time, wrapped up preciously by her eager cabin steward in two fur-lined rugs, which could not have been hired for the passage but must be her own expensive property, following with absorption the fine print of a thick novel by some one named Aldous Huxley. Now and then she would lift languid but brilliant eyes and gaze for a while at the flying sea. That was all, for after the first half hour on board she had not thought it worth her while to waste that brilliant languid gaze on any other fellow-passenger more than on Ariel.

The Roosters, for example, have a plethora of attacking options and playmakers who can step up when needed. When one of their stars is not at their best, someone else invariably rises to the occasion. Are there any features of EE that do not occur in Cockney? At present these questions cannot be answered unambiguously. The best way of proceeding is probably to take an individual speaker of EE, transcribe him/her into Cockney and into EE, and see if anything distinctive remains in the latter transcription. This has yet to be done. However, the question is complicated by the fact that Cockney itself is no longer homogeneous. There are, for instance, educated Cockneys whose pronunciation may differ from that of the uneducated. In fact, the educational level of the speaker is likely to be a major factor in determining how close to Cockney his/her pronunciation is. (This is presumably why Cockney rhyming slang is becoming so popular among people who have never heard of it.) To return to the original point, we can say that EE is a more formal version of Cockney. But we must remember that Cockney is itself a spectrum of varieties, ranging from the hypercorrect to the hypervernacular. These two extremes merge imperceptibly into RP and Broad. We need to know where EE falls on this scale. If it were just a matter of taking the lower end of the Cockney range and moving it up towards the RP pole, then we should expect to find all the features of Cockney still there, but in a less extreme form. However, some of them may disappear altogether. For example, the change of /s/ to /z/ before voiced consonants in Cockney is a feature of the vernacular end of the Cockney spectrum. We do not expect it to appear in EE. If it does, then EE is clearly not just a more formal version of Cockney. (But note that this feature is actually common in RP, though it is often said to be characteristic of Cockney.) Similarly, the change of /t/ to [?] is also typically found only in the vernacular end of the spectrum. It too is not expected in EE, though again it occurs in RP. The same goes for the reduction of unstressed syllables in polysyllabic words (dih-krih-tuh-riz-um 'dictionary'). This is typical of the vernacular end of the spectrum, but it also occurs in RP. The only sure way of telling whether a feature belongs to the vernacular end of the spectrum is to compare the vernacular with the formal style of a given speaker. This has yet to be done. It is also worth noting that the whole idea of the Cockney spectrum is problematical. What is the basis of the division between the hypercorrect and the hypervernacular? We need to consider such things as the age of the speaker, his/her social background, and the extent to which he/she has been exposed to the formal style. All this needs to be borne in mind when considering the relationship between EE and Cockney. Perhaps it is better to think of the Cockney spectrum as a single continuum, with the hypercorrect and hypervernacular ends merging into each other rather than being divided by a sharp boundary. Then the position of EE becomes clearer: it is the more formal end of the continuum.

Since the initial description of gametocytes in 1880, their morphology and metabolic profiles have been examined and there has been progress in identifying genes involved in their differentiation (reviewed in Alano, 2007; Dixon et al., 2008; Baker, 2010). However, many aspects of their biology remain unknown, including the initiation of their development. Intriguingly, only a small proportion of the parasites per erythrocytic cycle commit to gametocytogenesis (Ponnudurai et al., 1982; Graves et al., 1984). All merozoites from a sexually committed schizont develop into either male or female gametocytes, a developmental decision made at a point prior to the release of the committed merozoites (Silvestrini et al., 2000). Once committed, the P. falciparum gametocyte develops over 10-12 days through five distinct morphological stages (I-V), the last of which is taken up by the feeding mosquito (Josling and Llinas, 2015). Gametocytes of other Plasmodium spp. develop much more quickly, albeit typically slightly slower than the asexual stage (Galinski et al., 2013). The mechanism underlying commitment to sexual differentiation has until recently remained elusive, but there is now evidence that it is an epigenetically regulated process. Epigenetic regulation allows differential gene expression during development, the pattern of which can be inherited via DNA or histone post-translational modifications (PTMs), without alteration of the nucleotide sequence (Jaenisch and Bird, 2003). A Plasmodium genome has a typical nucleosomal organization (Fig. 1A) and epigenetic phenomena are indeed mediated by PTMs of histones, replacement of core histones by histone variants (H2A, H2B, H3, H4 by H2A.Z, H2B.Z, H3.3, CenH3, respectively) and chromatin remodelling (Fig. 1B) (Cui and Miao, 2010; Duffy et al., 2012; Voss et al., 2014). While the biological importance of DNA methylation as an epigenetic modification has been widely recognised, only recently has there been evidence provided that it is likely involved in regulating gene expression in Plasmodium, through the identification of a functional DNA cytosine methyltransferase and genome-wide mapping of methylated cytosines in P. falciparum (Ponts et al., 2013). Epigenetic regulation is critical in many processes in Plasmodium biology, including the demarcation of functional elements in the genome and life cycle progression (reviewed in Merrick and Duraisingh, 2010; Cortes et al., 2012). Control at the epigenetic level also regulates clonally variant gene expression, a process that results in transcriptional heterogeneity among a clonal parasite population. This spontaneous transcriptional switching of certain genes and gene families, also known as bet-hedging, offers a method of adaptation that is alternative to traditional gene regulation. It is key for the success of the parasite as it generates a phenotypically heterogeneous population, thus making the parasite fitter in response to varied environmental challenges, before these even present. Several genes are variantly transcribed and contribute to bet-hedging, including the main high-copy gene families and, most importantly, the var gene family (Rovira-Graells et al., 2012).
