In children chronically treated with glucocorticoids, complaints of families include stunting of growth, delay of puberty, weight gain, mood disturbances and brittle bones [12]. Increasing evidence has suggested that anti-inflammatory efficacy of glucocorticoid drugs is predominantly via non-genomic effects, whereas side effects are via genomic effects [13]. Dissociative steroidal drugs dissociate genomic and non-genomic effects, with the goal of retaining anti-inflammatory efficacy while reducing the burden of side effects. VBP-15 (generic name vamorolone) was developed as a dissociative steroid by synthesizing a series of compounds with a 9,11 steroidal scaffold, and testing of cell-based assays for retention of non-genomic anti-inflammatory activity (inhibition of TNF-induced NFKB activation; suppression of innate immunity pathways), and loss of genomic activity (GRE-mediated transcriptional reporters) [14,15]. Pre-clinical data has shown that vamorolone has potent binding to the glucocorticoid receptor and anti-inflammatory effects similar to traditional glucocorticoid drugs [15]. Testing of multiple mouse models of inflammatory states has shown efficacy similar to prednisolone, and dramatic improvements of side effect profiles, including loss of growth stunting and loss of bone fragility [15-19]. In addition to the dissociation of genomic (lost) and transrepression (retained) activities, vamorolone has changed additional sub-activities of traditional glucocorticoids. Cortisol and pharmacological glucocorticoids show high affinity for the mineralocorticoid receptor, similar to its physiological ligand, aldosterone. Glucocorticoids and aldosterone act as agonists for the mineralocorticoid receptor, and high circulating levels of pharmacological glucocorticoids result in salt imbalance and water weight gain (Cushingoid appearance) via the renin-angiotensin system. We used in vitro reporter assays for multiple steroid hormone receptors, in both agonist and antagonist modes, and showed that vamorolone is a potent antagonist for the mineralocorticoid receptor, in contrast to the agonist activity of glucocorticoids (unpublished observations). A pharmacological antagonist for the mineralocorticoid receptor, epleronone, has shown efficacy for improving heart function in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and many other cardiac disorders [20], suggesting that vamorolone may show benefit for cardiomyopathy in addition to its anti-inflammatory activity. Vamorolone can not be metabolized by 11 -Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11BHSD) isoforms, and thus should show greater stability in aldosterone-responsive cells (e.g. not inactivated as cortisol and glucocorticoids are). Another potential mechanism of action of glucocorticoids is via induction of mitotic synchrony in cells, which in turn reduces the pro-inflammatory state [21,22]. This mitotic synchronization activity may extend to regenerative synchronization and reduction of inflammation in tissues, including muscular dystrophy [23]. Vamorolone retains or improves this cell and tissue synchrony activity of glucocorticoids [23]. Finally, steroidal drugs may alter physicochemical properties of cell membrane systems when integrating and traversing lipid compartments. Vamorolone has been shown to impart stability to myogenic cell membranes, whereas prednisone de-stabilizes membranes [15]. This was anticipated because the C-ring of our delta 9,11 steroid has a lipophilic double bond rather than the hydrophilic hydroxy or ketone of glucocorticoids. Here, we report the initial clinical experience with vamorolone in healthy adult volunteers.

As he wandered through the sun-drenched streets of the French Riviera, Monte couldn't shake the feeling that something was amiss. The tennis courts, usually a source of joy and excitement, now seemed dull and uninviting. Even the prospect of the Grand Prix, which had once thrilled him, now held little appeal. The usual routine, which had sustained him for so long, was beginning to lose its luster. It wasn't until he arrived in Paris, however, that Monte began to grasp the true nature of his malaise. As he strolled along the Seine, taking in the city's familiar sights and sounds, he felt a sense of disconnection. The beauty of the city, once a source of inspiration, now seemed distant and unimportant. It was as if he was viewing it all through a veil of haze, as if he was observing his own life from afar. Monte's thoughts turned to his friends, the ones he had left behind in Cambridge. He wondered if they were experiencing similar feelings of restlessness. Were they, too, beginning to feel the pangs of disillusionment? The thought of returning to his old routine, of resuming his usual activities, filled him with a sense of dread. As he walked, Monte's mind wandered back to his childhood, to the days when life had been simpler, less complicated. He remembered the thrill of discovery, the excitement of exploration. But those days were behind him now, and he was left with the dull, monotonous routine of adulthood. The thought sent a shiver down his spine. Was this what lay ahead? A life of monotony, devoid of passion, devoid of purpose? Monte pushed the thought aside, telling himself he was being melodramatic. He was still young, still full of life. He would find a way to shake off this feeling, to rediscover the excitement and wonder of his youth. But as he continued to walk, the doubts lingered. What lay ahead? Would he find a way to recapture the magic of his youth, or was he doomed to trudge through the rest of his life in a state of listlessness and disconnection? Only time would tell.

The law, indeed, yet how stringent it can be, Elinor, when it so ruthlessly strips away the privileges that ought, by simple decency, to be distributed amongst us all. Yet here we stand, at the mercy of something so antiquated as tradition, while the very fabric of our lives is unraveled before our eyes. Can it be said that the delicate threads of our familial bonds are worth less than the clinking of coins in one's purse? One can only marvel at such oddities of society, a perplexing tapestry of duty and desire, where hearts weigh less in the balance than a ledger. But come, we must occupy our minds with something lighter than this dismal reality. Do you not see, Marianne? Next week brings forth the promise of a new assembly at the tavern! You shall wear the gown I made for you, the one of a soft lavender that dances upon your skin as if it were made of morning mist. I imagine you, standing in the light, captivating glances with every sway of your form. There shall be laughter, sweet music-oh! Such laughter that would almost drown the echoes of our troubles, if only for a brief reprieve. I cannot abide the thought of their arrival. Must we sit in silence while they feast upon our dismay? What if they arrive with their airs? What if Fanny brings her endless opinions on the management of our household? Prattle upon prattle, and then, my dear, we shall find the very walls of Norland closing in upon us like a noose. I can scarcely endure the anguish of it, and none but you would understand how such imaginary trifles take root in my mind and grow until they choke me! Yet, perhaps I am too hasty. Perhaps, in this moment of approaching dread, I ought to reserve judgment. John is charming in his own way, though he carries the weight of too many obligations upon his shoulders which might, by happenstance, render him less likable. And if Fanny's brow furrows in discontent, well, we shall simply call it a miscalculation of providence. Shall we not endeavor to meet this turn of events with grace? The air of expectation thickens by the moment, and with our spirits tempered by the thought of what might come to bear, we only serve to weaken our own resolve. You must promise me, dear sister, that you shall not give in to the bitter winds of fate that seek to invade our home. Think much of our sisterhood. Think of those fleeting hours shared by candlelight when we exchanged dreams, fears, and laughter. When did we last find joy together in the simplest of things? Perhaps it is in those whispers of warmth that we may yet sustain ourselves against the chill of circumstance. Let us summon our courage! We can withstand this storm. Margaret, little sprite, what mischief are you up to in the garden? Come now! We shall not send you hunting for strawberries while our world teeters on the brink. Share with us your delights, and then perhaps we, too, shall rediscover our mirth. For if all is to change, let us seize upon this moment, here and now, to inscribe our own narrative with laughter, before the arrival of those who would write over it with their calamities. Indeed, laughter, my dears-it is the very essence of our will to endure! Let us laugh heartily at what is to come, for in the end, they cannot take from us our spirits, nor can they rob us of our fondest memories. This is a truth I must cling to for it is the only reassurance I possess, amidst the mounting trials that astound!

Ten years ago to-day there was a grand wedding at the Oaks, and your mamma and I were there." "I too?" asked Eddie. "Yes, course, Eddie," spoke up five year old Violet, "grandpa would 'vite you and all of us; and I b'lieve I 'member a little about it." "Me too," piped the baby voice of Harold, "me sat on papa's knee." There was a general laugh, the two little prattlers joining in right merrily. "I really don't remember that part of it, Harold," said papa, while wee Elsie - as she was often called by way of distinguishing her from mamma, for whom she was named - shook her curly head at him with a merry "Oh, you dear little rogue, you don't know what you are talking about;" and mamma remarked, "Vi has perhaps a slight recollection of May Allison's wedding." "But this one at the Oaks must have been before I was born," said Elsie, "because you said it was ten years ago, and I'm only nine. O, mamma, was it your wedding?" "Yes, daughter. Shall we invite our friends for this evening, Edward?" "Yes, wife; suppose we make it a family party, inviting only relatives, connections and very intimate friends." After a little more discussion it was decided they would do so; also that the children should have a full holiday, and while their mother was giving orders and overseeing the necessary preparations for the entertainment, papa should take them all in the roomy family carriage and drive over to the Oaks, Roselands, Ashlands and Pinegrove to give the invitations. Beside these near friends only the minister and his wife were to be asked; but as Adelaide and her family were at this time paying a visit to Roselands, and Lucy Ross was doing the same at her old home, and all the younger generation except the mere babies, were to be included in the invitation, should all accept it would be by no means a small assemblage. Early hours were named for the sake of the little ones; guests to come at six, refreshments to be served at eight, and the Ion children, if each would take a nap in the afternoon, to be allowed to stay up till nine. How delighted they were: how the little eyes danced and sparkled, and how eagerly they engaged to fulfill the conditions, and not to fret or look cross when summoned at nine, to leave the drawing-room and be put to bed. "O, mamma, won't you wear your wedding dress?" cried little Elsie; "do, dear mamma, so that we may all see just how you looked when you were married." Elsie smiled, "You forget, daughter, that I am ten years older now, and the face cannot be quite the same." "The years have robbed it of none of its beauty," said Mr. Travilla.

In [21] a Fe-Ga harvester is coupled to a C closure yoke fitted by an excitation coil that varies the magnetic bias up to saturation. In [22] a stressed annealed galfenol harvester is studied through a three port equivalent circuit validated by experimental measurements. The last two studies present interesting results but only with few measurement points and a limited vibration frequency lower than 1 Hz. The study presented in this paper analyzes in detail the performance of a direct force harvester based on a polycrystalline galfenol sample (cubic grains with easy axes) by varying finely the magnetic and mechanical bias and electrical load. In this paper it was preferred to consider galfenol unannealed, so as to make the applied preload values clear and evident, although stress annealed galfenol is interesting for energy harvesting as it is possible to design a device that does not require an external preload. As in the case of the efficiency analysis of a Terfenol-D harvester performed in [23], the authors make use of an experimental setup mainly developed in [24], obtaining complete and clear characteristics of the harvester behavior. The study was performed in a laboratory setup, keeping the preload constant by means of a test machine. This provides clear and reproducible results. However, in real applications the dynamic chain (rod, plus springs, plus non perfectly rigid encasing, etc.) leads to fluctuations in mechanical quantities that should be taken into account during the design phase. The study clearly highlights the correlation existing between mechanical prestress and magnetic bias in the generation of the electrical power. This was possible by a laminated yoke designed to saturate the galfenol rod in dynamic conditions even at high prestress (up to 120 MPa). Another important feature of the present study is the use of excitation coils to produce the magnetic bias. Of course, the adoption of this solution, which requires an additional energy source, is not feasible in the actual harvesters, but it proves to be an essential tool for a detailed analysis because it allows a continuous regulation of the bias, in comparison with the stepped values provided by the permanent magnets. The choice of replacing the magnets with excitation coils has requested a verification that the results are not modified by this substitution. For such a purpose, two additional devices have been made by adopting yokes having the same size and the same laminations as in the yoke fitted with coils. The total length of galfenol rod is kept constant so that the laminated yokes of the external column are shortened to house two or four magnets respectively. It has been found out that, with a suitable tuning of the preload, the additional devices provide the same power obtained with the excitation coils. The values of electric power, bias and preload obtained with the permanent magnets are consistent with the values obtained by the yoke with coils and help one to better understand the behavior of the harvester.

It goes much better than before, but still not good enough. After breakfast we go to the regatta course and watch some races, and cheer on our fellow Americans. Then we go out for lunch. The whole team, coaches included, go to a local diner called the Muddy Waters Diner. We get in, and sit down, and wait for the waitress to take our orders. She comes back ten minutes later and takes our drink orders, another twenty minutes she comes back and takes our meal order. In the meantime, other people have come in after us, gotten served, and left. Forty-five minutes later she finally brings out our drinks. We wait another hour for our food. By this time we are all starving, and very pissed off. Some of the kids got their food right away, others waited longer than an hour. When I finally got mine, I gobbled it down, and asked for the check. At least she brought that fast. We paid her, tipped her, and got the hell out of there. If I ever see that bitch again I will beat her ass. Back to the race course, more cheering. We come back to the campsite, and practice again. Again we go out for dinner, this time to a pizza joint. It's pretty good, but I'm not feeling well. I feel sick to my stomach, and my head hurts. We come back to the campsite, and I lie down in the tent, and sleep until the next morning. Wednesday morning, I wake up at 6:00am, and immediately puke my guts out. I feel awful. I can't keep anything down. I get up and try to walk around a little bit. I try to eat something, but I can't keep it down. I try to sleep it off, but I can't do that either. I can't get any relief. I'm miserable. Finally I tell coach that I want to go home, and he agrees. We pack up the tents, and start to load the cars. We finish loading, and I get in the van. I can't sleep, I can't stay awake. Every bump in the road makes me wanna hurl. We cross the border without incident. We drive straight home. I lay down on my couch, and pass out. I slept for twelve hours. I woke up, ate a bowl of cereal, and went back to bed. I haven't been able to do anything since. I've missed work, I've missed school, I've missed everything. I hope I get better soon. I'm tired of laying around. Wow...that sucks. I'm sorry you're feeling bad.

The neural mechanisms underlying implicit MI during hand laterality tasks have been further explored using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electroencephalography (EEG). Studies have consistently shown that the same brain regions active during explicit MI, such as the primary motor cortex (M1), premotor cortex (PM), and supplementary motor area (SMA), are also active during implicit MI (Lotze & Halsband, 2006; Jeannerod, 2006). Additionally, the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), which is involved in error detection and conflict monitoring, has been found to be active during hand laterality tasks, suggesting that implicit MI is not a purely automatic process, but rather involves some level of cognitive control (Carter et al., 1998). Furthermore, the neural oscillations recorded during hand laterality tasks have been found to be similar to those recorded during explicit MI. For example, studies have shown that the mu rhythm, a neural oscillation typically associated with motor planning and execution, is desynchronized during hand laterality tasks, indicating that the motor system is actively engaged in the mental rotation process (Hari et al., 1998; Pfurtscheller & Lopes da Silva, 1999). The role of implicit MI in hand laterality tasks has also been investigated in individuals with motor impairments, such as stroke patients. Research has shown that these individuals exhibit impaired performance on hand laterality tasks, suggesting that the neural mechanisms underlying implicit MI are disrupted (Bonda et al., 1995; Parsons et al., 1995). Furthermore, studies have found that motor imagery training can improve hand function in individuals with motor impairments, highlighting the potential therapeutic applications of implicit MI (Lotze & Halsband, 2006). In addition to its role in hand laterality tasks, implicit MI has been found to play a role in other cognitive processes, such as spatial reasoning and problem-solving. For example, research has shown that individuals who are better at mentally rotating objects also perform better on spatial reasoning tasks, suggesting that implicit MI is involved in the mental manipulation of objects (Kosslyn et al., 2001). Furthermore, studies have found that implicit MI is involved in the planning and execution of complex movements, such as those required for sports or musical performance (Jeannerod, 2006). In conclusion, the research suggests that implicit MI plays a critical role in hand laterality tasks, and is supported by a network of brain regions involved in motor planning, execution, and control. The neural mechanisms underlying implicit MI are similar to those involved in explicit MI, and are disrupted in individuals with motor impairments. Furthermore, implicit MI has been found to play a role in other cognitive processes, such as spatial reasoning and problem-solving. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the neural basis of cognition and motor control, and highlight the potential therapeutic applications of implicit MI.

Moreover, natural hazards are expected to increase in frequency and severity due to climate change, population growth, and urbanization, leading to a rise in exposure and vulnerability of communities and infrastructure. The importance of proactive disaster risk reduction and management is therefore becoming increasingly evident. DSSs can play a crucial role in this context by providing decision-makers with a structured approach to identify, assess, and prioritize risks, as well as develop and evaluate strategies for mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery. In addition, the development of DSSs for NHRR is also driven by the need to address the complexity and uncertainty associated with natural hazards. Natural hazards are often characterized by nonlinear dynamics, multiple interacting factors, and high levels of uncertainty, making it challenging to predict their occurrence and impact. DSSs can help to address these challenges by integrating multiple data sources, models, and expert knowledge to provide a comprehensive understanding of the hazard, vulnerability, and risk. Furthermore, DSSs can facilitate the integration of multiple stakeholders and their perspectives, which is critical for effective NHRR. Natural hazard risk reduction requires the involvement of various stakeholders, including government agencies, emergency responders, local communities, and private sector organizations. DSSs can provide a platform for these stakeholders to collaborate, share knowledge, and make informed decisions. The development of DSSs for NHRR also requires the integration of multiple disciplines, including meteorology, hydrology, geology, ecology, economics, and social sciences. DSSs can facilitate this integration by providing a framework for combining data and models from different disciplines to assess the physical, social, and economic impacts of natural hazards. In terms of the technical requirements, DSSs for NHRR need to be able to handle large amounts of data, including spatial and temporal data, and perform complex simulations and analyses. They also need to be able to provide user-friendly interfaces for stakeholders to interact with the system and visualize the results. Moreover, DSSs need to be flexible and adaptable to accommodate changing user needs and new data sources. Several examples of DSSs for NHRR have been developed in recent years, including the Flood Early Warning System (FEWS) developed by the European Union (EU) (EU, 2016), the Natural Hazard Risk Assessment and Management System (NHRAMS) developed by the United States Geological Survey (USGS) (USGS, 2019), and the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management System (DRRMS) developed by the Asian Disaster Preparedness Center (ADPC) (ADPC, 2018). These systems demonstrate the potential of DSSs to support NHRR by providing decision-makers with timely and accurate information to make informed decisions. In conclusion, the development and use of DSSs for NHRR is critical for reducing the impact of natural hazards on communities and economies. DSSs can provide a structured approach to identify, assess, and prioritize risks, and develop and evaluate strategies for mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery. They can also facilitate the integration of multiple stakeholders and disciplines, and provide a platform for collaborative decision-making. As the frequency and severity of natural hazards continue to increase, the importance of DSSs for NHRR will only continue to grow.

In response to these gaps in our understanding, we set out to develop a conceptual model that outlines the antecedents and consequences of NIHS and provides guidance on how to overcome this bias. We hope that this article will inspire future research on overcoming NIHS. The Not-Invented-Here Syndrome: A Fundamental Threat to Open Innovation Antons D.;Piller F. T.;Salge T. O.;Drews M. C. Triggered by the growing popularity of open innovation and crowdsourcing, the VDMA (Verband Deutscher Maschinen- und Anlagenbau e.V.) - one of the largest industrial associations in Europe representing over 3100 member companies in the German engineering industry-set out to explore how its members could benefit from emerging forms of collaborative innovation. To evaluate the benefits from a more open approach to innovation, the association engaged with member companies to identify six unsolved technical challenges that were posted to solution providers in the machinery industry. This open and collaborative process yielded nearly 20 novel proposals from a global pool of solution providers for each technical problem posted. Many of the submitted proposals were well thought-out and provided feasible solutions to the identified problems. Much to the surprise of the VDMA team, not a single external solution proposal was adopted by its member organizations. Developers simply refused to integrate the external knowledge and insisted on developing their "own" in-house solutions instead (Luttgens et al., 2014). Given this persistent rejection of external input, the association eventually had to shelve its strategic initiative and leave important technical opportunities unsolved. The VDMA example above is not an isolated case. Indeed, the literature is replete with many reasons for why organizations struggle to internalize external knowledge, even when such input could have helped to solve the task at hand. These reasons include, but are not limited to, prohibitive absorption and transaction costs, intellectual property concerns, technological incompatibilities, or excessive risks associated with unproven ideas. Such explanations, however, do not fully account for the systematic individual rejection of external knowledge by internal research and development (R&D) employees as illustrated in the VDMA example. It is against this backdrop that a psychological phenomenon widely known as the Not-Invented-Here Syndrome (NIHS) moves into the foreground. NIHS can be formally defined as an individual's negative attitude towards knowledge that originates from a different field of expertise, from another organizational entity, or from another geography, and thus, is considered "outside" or "external" to the group(s) or organization(s), in which the individual is embedded (Antons and Piller, 2015). Due to this attitude, internal R&D employees are inclined to reject external knowledge during inbound open innovation, even though it might be beneficial to the development task at hand; as it was the case in the opening example. As such, NIHS hampers organizational learning, as it prevents the organization from absorbing external knowledge (Garvin, 1993). While examples of NIHS are frequently mentioned in open innovation research and practice (e.g., Laursen and Salter, 2006; Ter Wal et al., 2017), there is a notable scarcity of empirical evidence not only on its determinants and consequences (Agrawal et al., 2010; Kathoefer and Leker, 2012), but also - and arguably most importantly - on possible countermeasures. In response to these gaps in our understanding, we set out to develop a conceptual model that outlines the antecedents and consequences of NIHS and provides guidance on how to overcome this bias. We hope that this article will inspire future research on overcoming NIHS.

I noticed that sometimes these moments, those unexpected, raw flashes of humanity, have a way of revealing truths that lay dormant within us. As I sat next to him, engaging in casual conversation that meandered from the weather to our mutual love for the local baseball team, it was clear that he wasn't the only one benefiting from our little chat. I came to understand that making these connections, even if they're sparked by the gravity of circumstance, rekindles a warmth I had forgotten. It seemed so trivial, this exchange of words, yet it chipped away at the callouses cynicism had layered over my optimism. The hospital rooms, their sterile walls lined with muted colors meant to soothe but failing spectacularly, made me confront the quiet battles people face every day. Illness has a way of making everyday concerns appear trivial, and beneath the surface struggles, you find laughter still lingers, like bright spots in a cloudy sky. It hit me then, how sharing a moment with another person, undistracted by devices and the flimsy connections curated by social media, is an antidote to the detachment I'd let grow within myself. Rachel, who inspired this little venture, had remarked once about the importance of these visits, likening them to acts that stitch hidden gaps in the blanket of our community. I didn't fully understand then, but being there, in that small room, talking with a man who had just lost so much yet shared the air of someone wholly intact, made me appreciate the subtleties of her wisdom. He may have lost a limb, but his spirit filled the space around him, enveloping me with an aura of endurance and hope. It's curious how simple exchanges can refocus our understanding of contentment and purpose. After that visit, a lingering sense of fulfillment stayed with me, counteracting the cold emptiness I'd grown used to. I started to look forward to these weekly visits, using them as markers in my life, turning what could have been a passive existence into something active, something meaningful. Gradually, I began to feel the shift in myself, a renewal of purpose yawning broadly within the confines of my previous apathy. Regular visits expanded into friendships, conversations turning from polite to genuine, an unexpected brotherhood with those I had once only acknowledged with small nods at synagogue. It's funny how confronting hardship in others can turn into a life raft for oneself, pulling you from the depths of your own sorrow. Looking back, I've realized how these commitments brought about a subtle guidance, an invisible hand redirecting my path towards service, not just to others, but in service to my own soul. Because in the end, it wasn't only about being there for someone else; it was about understanding the shared human experience, recognizing that maybe, just maybe, the connections we forge illuminate our own shadows. And perhaps, these small gestures, these moments of genuine presence, might just be more than enough. Forward, I proceed with a less tangled heart and a sharper sense of belonging-all because I said yes to stepping out of my self-imposed solitude. And with these connections, a new journey unfolds.

Second in charge came Allan Hollister, a Maine boy, who had had considerable actual experience in wood's life, and to whom the rest of the patrol naturally turned whenever a knotty problem faced them during an outing. The exceedingly fat and good-natured youth was Bumpus Hawtree, bugler of the troop, even though just now he was minus the instrument on which he was accustomed to sound the various calls, such as "reveille," "assembly," "taps," and so on, the most popular being the second, as it was usually associated with meals. Bumpus had been looked upon as the real tenderfoot scout, up to recently; but having become lost in the big timber recently, he had acquitted himself so splendidly, as recorded in the preceding volume, that his mates now regarded him as one who had been keeping his light under a bushel. Then there was Bob White, otherwise Robert White Quail, a Southern boy, warm of heart, a faithful friend, and upon whom the leader could always depend in emergencies; Step Hen Bingham, whose real name of course was Stephen, but upon appearing at school for the first time he had insisted that it was pronounced as though made up of two syllables; Davy Jones, an athletic lad; Giraffe, really Conrad, Stedman, but given the significant nick-name because of a habit he had of stretching an exceedingly long neck most outrageously; and last but far from least, a dudish looking boy who at home answered when they called him Edmund Maurice Travers Smith; but among his playmates he was known simply as "Smithy." These Boy Scouts had seen some pretty lively times during the past year or so, down in the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina, where they visited the former home of Bob White, and found themselves mixed up with the moonshiners of that wild, inhospitable region; and later on up in Maine, where they had gone partly on business for Thad's adopted father and guardian, and to enjoy an outing, with a little hunting thrown in. It happened that here among the pine woods of Maine, they were instrumental in recovering some valuable bonds and other papers that had been stolen from a bank, and for which a large reward had been offered. With this money in the treasury of the troop, they were able to lay out a great trip to the Rocky Mountain region for the following summer. As the money really belonged to the eight lads individually, they felt justified in using it in this manner; for the second patrol had only been formed after the Cranford boys learned what glorious times the Silver Foxes were having right along.

Not only did I know, now, of whom they were talking, but I knew one of those who talked: a red-headed giant of a man I'd seen to-night for the first time, though he had annoyed Grandmother and me from a distance, for years. In fact, we'd left home and taken up the Red Cross industry in Rome, because of him. Indirectly it was his fault that I was married, since, if it hadn't been for him, I shouldn't have come to Italy or met Prince di Miramare. I did not stop, however, to think of all this. It just flashed through my subconscious mind, while I asked myself, "What has happened to Paolo? Has he been killed, or only wounded? And what do the brutes mean by a 'double blow'?" I had no longer the impulse to rush out. I waited, with hushed breath. I didn't care whether it were nice or not to eavesdrop. All I thought of was my intense desire to hear what those two would say next. "Like grandmother, like grand-daughter, I suppose," went on the ex-cowboy baronet, James Courtenaye. "A hard-hearted lot my only surviving female relatives seem to be! Her husband at the Front, liable to die at any minute; her grandmother dying at home, and our fair young Princess dances gaily to celebrate a small Italian victory!" "You forget what's happened to-night, Sir Jim, when you speak of your 'surviving' female relatives," said the woman. "By George, yes! I've got but one left now. And I expect, from what I hear, I shall be called upon to support her!" Then Grandmother was dead! - wonderful, indomitable Grandmother, who, only three hours ago, had said, "You must go to this dance, Elizabeth. I wish it!" Grandmother, whose last words had been, "You are worthy to be what I've made you: a Princess. You are exactly what I was at your age." Poor, magnificent Grandmother! She had often told me that she was the greatest beauty of her day. She had sent me away from her to-night, so that she might die alone. Or - had the news of the other blow come while I was gone, and killed her? Dazedly I stumbled to my feet, and in a second I should have pushed past the pair; but, just at this moment, footsteps came hurrying along the path. Those two moved out of the way with some murmured words I didn't catch: and then, the Marchese was with me again. I saw his plump figure silhouetted on the silvered blue dusk of moonlight. He had brought no ice! He flung out empty hands in a despairing gesture which told that he also knew. "My dear child - my poor little Princess - " he began in Italian; but I cut him short. "I've heard some people talking. Grandmother is dead. And - Paolo?" "His plane crashed. It was instant death - not painful.

What was wrong with that model? Well, I mean, they're not necessarily wrong. I think the problem is is that a lot of them were marketed as an investment opportunity and therefore you know, they were sold on the basis of well, you can buy one of these units and then you can sell it in five years time and make a profit. It's almost like buying a new car driving it out of the yard and then saying you'll sell it next year for more than you paid for it. It doesn't work like that. But I think also the reality is that we live longer today than we did 20-30 years ago. So you know, a retirement village is great. If you're happy to sit around play cards and bowls all day, but I think a lot of people would rather stay in their own home for as long as possible and then if they end up needing care they go into a rest home. Yeah, I agree with that. And certainly that's been my experience over the years. And I've seen a number of clients who have purchased units within retirement villages. The biggest issue is that they're normally very expensive to purchase and when you come to sell them, there's a limited market. And so you're selling to another person that wants to move into a retirement village. And the reality is most people want to stay in their family home until they absolutely have to move somewhere else. And so there's a limited market when you come to sell them. And I've seen a couple of clients who've actually lost money by moving into a retirement village and then having to sell after a short period of time and move elsewhere. Yeah, look, I think the key message is that people need to understand what they're getting themselves into. And I think that's true for any sort of investment. You need to understand what you're getting yourself into. And sometimes people get caught up in the emotion of oh, yeah, this looks really good. It's a nice unit. It's got lots of facilities and everything and you forget to ask the question. Okay. Well, what happens if I need to sell this and what are the costs involved in doing that? Because usually there's a fee payable to the operator of the retirement village. And that can be anywhere from 10% to 15%. But, although they continued to show great hostility towards each other, they both agreed that if anybody wanted to kill their respective offspring they should be allowed to do so. This was a matter of perfect indifference to the Philosophers who never liked the children anyway, and who had always regarded them as something like sores upon their persons. It was not long before the Grey Woman and the Thin Woman found somebody willing to help them to get rid of their children. There was a man named Tullagh O'Keeffe who lived in a village near by. He was a famous actor, and he used to come over often to the house of the Philosophers to rehearse his parts. His principal role was in the tragedy of 'The Death of Socrates,' and he had studied the part so well that he could repeat all Socrates's words without looking at his book. When he came to see the Philosophers he used to sit down beside the fire and read out of the book while he waited for them to appear. One day when he had nothing better to do he began to study the parts of the children, and he discovered that they were exactly alike. Then he thought of a plan. He went straight away to the Grey Woman and the Thin Woman and offered to murder their children in exchange for a certain sum of money. They were delighted to find that he knew all about the affair, and they gave him the money immediately. Then he took some poison and put it into a little bottle which he carried about with him. Next morning he went to the house of the Philosophers and sat down beside the fire. After waiting for some time the children appeared, and they sat down beside him. As soon as they were close enough he gave them the poison, and they died almost immediately. When the Philosophers heard of it they were furious, but they were obliged to admit that they themselves had been responsible for the deaths of their own children. For a whole year afterwards the Grey Woman and the Thin Woman were extremely ill-tempered, and they blamed everybody for the loss of their children. The Philosophers tried to make friends with them again, but they would not listen to reason. Finally they got tired of trying to please them, and they decided to go off together to live in another country where they would be free from their persecutions. They set out in the grey of the morning, and they walked till midday through the pine woods. At last they reached a place called the Giant's Graveyard. It was an open space surrounded by a high wall of stones, and it was full of huge piles of stones which the Giants had left behind them. As they entered the graveyard they saw a little cottage standing in the middle of the open space. It was built of turf and sticks, and it had a roof of straw. The door was open, and inside they could see an old woman sitting by the fire. She was spinning wool and singing to herself. The Philosophers were very surprised to see her there, and they went up to her to ask why she was in such a lonely place. "I am an old woman," she said, "and I am afraid of the people in the town. Every night they come out to hunt me, and if they catch me they will certainly kill me." "Why do they want to kill you?" asked the Philosophers. "Because I am a witch," she replied. "They say that I turn men into animals, and they are determined to destroy me. So I have come here to hide myself among the graves of the Giants, for I know that they will never harm me. If you will stay here with me I shall be safe."

Alternatively, one could adhere to the exact Jacobian matrix and solve the stiff adjoint equations more efficiently so that the resulting adjoint solution, and consequently the design gradient, remains accurate. To avoid the linear instability issue of any fixed-point iterative solver, Krylov solvers are usually preferred for solving the stiff and marginally stable adjoint equations. It is proposed that the Jacobian-free Newton-Krylov method is preferred for critical aerodynamic simulations and shape optimisation applications where numerical stiffness constantly causes convergence difficulties [20,21]. A few key aspects on the efficient implementation of the method are also highlighted to show that once properly implemented, superior efficiency and reliability can be achieved, compared with other more well-established solution methods such as multi-stage explicit schemes, point or block implicit procedure and implicit factorisation methods. The method has been successfully applied to solve adjoint equations arising from aerodynamic shape optimisaion [22] and error estimation [23]. Krylov solvers are also affected by the conditioning of the system matrix. For example, restarted GMRES could suffer from convergence stagnation for challenging problems unless m is sufficiently large, which would then result in prohibitively high memory overhead. An obvious remedy to alleviate the memory bottleneck of the Krylov solver for difficult cases is to use a stronger preconditioner. For example, a clean wing geometry for the common research model at cruise condition is studied in [24] using a mesh with 28 million points. For this case, incomplete lower-upper (ILU) factorisation with fill-in level of two, i.e., ILU(2), is necessary to effectively precondition GMRES, which is then able to converge with m of 200. Had a weaker preconditioner such as ILU(0) been used, the Krylov solver would have required many more vectors to converge. The fundamental reason for the convergence stagnation of GMRES(m) is that the restarted subspace is often close to the previous subspace. Generalised conjugate residual with optimal truncation (GCROT) [25], its simplified and flexible variant [26] and generalised conjugate residual with deflated restarting (GCRO-DR) [27] have been proposed to address this shortcoming by recycling a selected subspace from one cycle to the next. The subspace recycling technique allows the solvers to converge without stagnation with much lower memory requirement. GCRO-DR was shown to be effective in both lowering the stagnation memory threshold and accelerating the convergence for large scale linearised aerodynamics analysis [28]. In this paper, we replace the baseline GMRES solver within the DLR-TAU adjoint solver with GCRO-DR. The proposed method is applied to solve the adjoint equations to demonstrate its effectiveness in both reducing memory overhead and accelerating convergence for solving the adjoint equations arising from industry-relevant cases with complex geometries under both design and off-design flow conditions. Therefore, tapping into the capabilities of supercritical CO2-based cycles provides a unique avenue for enhancing energy efficiency and promoting sustainability. These systems not only harness available waste heat but also address the pressing challenges posed by climate change and resource scarcity. As industries worldwide increasingly turn to more rigorous regulations and voluntary carbon reduction commitments, implementing sCO2 technologies presents an opportunity for companies to improve their environmental footprint while simultaneously reaping economic benefits through increased efficiency. An essential aspect of sCO2 systems is their modular configuration, allowing for flexibility in integration within existing infrastructures. This adaptability enables diverse applications-from retrofitting existing power facilities to upgrading industrial thermal processes-thereby accommodating a wide array of operational scales. The industrial demands of sectors such as steel, cement, and even waste incineration, which typically generate significant high-temperature waste heat, stand to gain immensely from the application of sCO2 technology. With the conversion efficiency reaching significant levels, the potential for generating clean, renewable energy from waste heat becomes not only feasible but also imperative. Recent developments in the field have highlighted advances in sCO2 cycle modeling and component design, facilitating this technology's progression from theoretical research to commercial viability. Modular heat exchangers and turbine technology have undergone considerable enhancement, catering specifically to the unique operational parameters of supercritical CO2. Additionally, ongoing research into suitable materials that can withstand the harsh operational conditions enhances the reliability of sCO2 systems, making them increasingly attractive for both investors and end-users. Crucially, the implementation of sCO2 systems aligns seamlessly with broader energy transition strategies. In tandem with other renewable energy sources-be it solar thermal, biomass, or concentrated solar power-sCO2 technology paves the way for creating hybrid systems that utilize low- and high-grade energy inputs, thereby optimizing overall energy generation. This synergy not only boosts system reliability but also minimizes energy storage challenges associated with intermittent renewable sources. Moreover, as public and private sectors worldwide commit to transitioning towards a low-carbon economy, financial incentives for renewable technologies-including grants, tax rebates, and carbon credits-are anticipated to bolster the adoption of sCO2 systems. Policymakers have begun recognizing the critical role of waste heat recovery in achieving national and international climate goals, prompting the establishment of frameworks to support the deployment of such innovative technologies. Safety considerations are paramount, especially when dealing with supercritical fluids. Fortunately, CO2's favorable safety profile positions it as a superior choice for industrial applications. The advancements in carbon capture techniques further add to the versatility of sCO2, culminating in the potential for enhanced performance coupled with carbon neutrality initiatives. The captured carbon can be utilized or permanently sequestered, thus delivering substantial climate benefits. In conclusion, the integration of sCO2 technologies into waste heat recovery systems represents a pivotal strategy in the pursuit of enhanced energy efficiency and reduced greenhouse gas emissions. The synergy of innovation and sustainability within this domain unlocks vast potential for industries while contributing to a broader global effort to mitigate environmental impacts and foster a cleaner, more sustainable energy landscape. Embracing these developments is not merely a choice; it is an imperative for advancing environmental stewardship in the energy sector. As research continues to evolve and implementation strategies are refined, the path towards an energy-efficient future becomes increasingly tangible and achievable.

In a whirlwind of determination and a hint of superhero frenzy, I pulled on jeans that had seen better days, slipped on my somewhat scuffed sneakers that had become my trusty sidekicks over countless errands, and then, armed with a container of Oreos (you never know when a snack might be necessary), I dashed out the door. The anticipation hung in the air like the weight of a suspenseful movie plot twist. I was headed to an adventure-a realm where time bends, emotions run high, and fluorescent lights buzz overhead. Arriving at the hospital, I was greeted by the chaotic symphony only an ER can compose: the cacophony of beeping machines, the distant murmurs of concerned family members mingling with the sharp commands of medical personnel. As I walked through the sliding glass doors, I could feel the energy shift. I looked around, taking in the seriousness etched on the faces of those adults wearing scrubs and the restlessness of children who had learned far too early what "waiting" truly entailed. E was already waiting in the designated area, looking a bit pale but managing to strike the right balance between anxiousness and calmness-if one can indeed exist under those circumstances. C sat upright in her chair, her foot propped on a pile of jackets that E had hastily scavenged for comfort. She was trying to hold back tears, bravely mixing feigned strength with the reality of an imminent X-ray. "Hey, you," I said, kneeling beside C, who shot me a watery smile, "How's the ankle? Did it grow a dragon? Because it looks quite swollen!" C managed a weak chuckle, which was a good sign. Humor is a handy tool amid the storm of medical emergencies. "More like an elephant's foot," she replied, attempting to shift her tone back to a state of daring teenager bravado. I sensed a flicker of her usual spunk beneath the surface-a great omen for her spirit. "Alright, let's get through this together," I said, beckoning E to lean closer. "You'll be with us the whole time, and I brought snacks." I fished through my bag, revealing the Oreos with a flourish, half-expecting a standing ovation from both of them. Sweetening the deal brought a little light to an otherwise daunting experience. As we settled into reality, time warped oddly; minutes melded into hours-which, if you've ever visited an ER, is almost a universal rule. Someone with a marble history of the ER once told me that the clock ticks differently in such spaces. I looked around and observed the unfolding stories around us. A child in a bright red jacket rocked back and forth, clutching a toy dinosaur. A couple huddled close, whispering to each other as they awaited news from whatever ordeal they were facing. A nurse bustled past with purpose, her gait as determined as a character sprinting toward the climax of an epic tale. Finally, at 9:30, a nurse called C's name. "Time for your X-ray!" The wary anticipation in C's eyes mingled with traces of defiance, the kind that says, "I've got this." Holding E's hand tightly, they exchanged a long look as the nurse led them into the back. I trailed closely behind, the ever-curious sidekick peeking through the door as the drama unfolded, hoping to catch a glimpse of technology in action-who knew, maybe there was a real-life superhero vibe in the air?

When he found out the medical center was planning on building a cancer center and a children's justice center on the site, he said: "I think you are going to have a lot of graves." Part of his assessment hinged on history. The asylum drew residents from across the state, people who were committed for a variety of ailments. Many, according to records, were institutionalized for years. When residents died, few were claimed by families. Experts believe poverty may have also played a role - families could not afford to retrieve and transport the bodies. As a result, many were buried in unmarked graves in an area of the property believed designated as the asylum cemetery. Without headstones and markings to denote the outlines of the cemetery, it was swallowed up by time. So how do you determine that without digging up the grounds and, possibly, disturbing the dead? The answer: ground-penetrating radar. "When I saw the printout of that...property, it was mind-blowing," Mazurak said. The radar survey showed hundreds and hundreds of coffin-like outlines in tight rows. Many were believed to be just four or five feet below the surface. "As it turned out there were 800 to 1,000 graves on the southern piece of property, and another 1,000 graves on the north side of the property," Mazurak said. 'Living link' Almost immediately, construction plans on the site were put on hold. Already the university medical center was absorbing the cost to exhume and rebury the bodies found last year at a cost of about $3,000 each, Mazurak said. Removing 66 coffins from underneath a road was one thing. But removing hundreds of coffins from an unmarked graveyard was another thing entirely. "There is a living link to each grave," Mazurak said. Exhuming and reinterring upwards of 2,000 bodies would cost millions, a price the university can't afford. So for now, the medical center will leave the dead where they lie and look for alternatives for the expansion. As news of the find made headlines, people across the country reached out to the medical center. The questions, in many cases, were the same: Can you tell me if my family member is buried there? Unmarked graves bring their plight to light. Searching for answers. That's the question Jannie White posed when she stumbled upon the news of the unmarked graveyard at the medical center. White has spent years researching her family history, trying to piece together the path her family had taken from Mississippi north. She grew up hearing stories about a great-grandmother who had been institutionalized at the asylum. The details were sketchy, and nobody was sure where the woman was buried or even what name she was buried under.

The addition of inoculants, such as Al-Ti-B master alloys, to the molten metal triggers a series of events that ultimately lead to the formation of finer grains. The TiB2 particles, which are present in the inoculant, act as heterogeneous nucleation sites, providing a platform for the growth of new grains. The Al3Ti intermetallics, which are also present in the inoculant, dissolve into the molten aluminium, releasing titanium solute that enhances the nucleation process. The duplex nucleation theory, which is widely accepted, suggests that a layer of Al3Ti forms as a transition layer between the surface of the TiB2 particles and the nucleating aluminium grains. This layer facilitates the growth of new grains by providing a favourable lattice match between the Al3Ti and the aluminium. The resulting grains are finer and more uniform, leading to improved mechanical properties and formability. Despite the advantages of inoculation, there are still challenges and drawbacks associated with the process. One of the main challenges is the control of the inoculation process, which can be affected by factors such as the type and amount of inoculant, the temperature of the molten metal, and the stirring conditions. If the inoculation process is not properly controlled, it can lead to inconsistent grain refinement, which can result in variable mechanical properties. Another challenge is the potential for the formation of defects, such as porosity and inclusions, which can arise from the inoculation process. These defects can have a significant impact on the mechanical properties of the alloy, leading to reduced strength and ductility. In addition, the use of inoculants can also have an impact on the cost and sustainability of the alloy production process. The cost of the inoculants can be high, and the use of large quantities can increase the overall cost of production. Furthermore, the production of inoculants can have an environmental impact, particularly if the raw materials used are not sourced sustainably. Despite these challenges, the inoculation of Al alloys remains a widely used and effective method for grain refinement. The development of new inoculants and the optimization of the inoculation process can help to overcome some of the challenges associated with the process. For example, the use of nano-sized inoculants has been shown to improve the efficiency of the grain refinement process, while also reducing the amount of inoculant required. Furthermore, the development of new alloy compositions and processing techniques can also help to overcome some of the challenges associated with inoculation. For example, the use of alloys with higher solute contents can reduce the amount of inoculant required, while also improving the mechanical properties of the alloy. In conclusion, the inoculation of Al alloys is a complex process that requires careful control and optimization to achieve the desired grain refinement. While there are challenges and drawbacks associated with the process, the benefits of inoculation, including improved mechanical properties and formability, make it a widely used and effective method for the production of high-performance Al alloys.

Furthermore, myelin disturbance in HD may be related to the observed white matter microstructural changes. Myelin is composed of lipids and proteins, and its integrity is crucial for the proper functioning of neurons. Demyelination, or the loss of myelin, can lead to axonal damage and degeneration, which may contribute to the progressive decline in motor and cognitive functions seen in HD patients (Franklin and Ffrench-Constant, 2008). The elevated iron levels in the cortico-spinal tract and corpus callosum reported by Phillips et al. (2015) and Bartzokis et al. (2007), respectively, may indicate an attempt by the brain to compensate for myelin damage by increasing iron availability for myelin synthesis. However, this compensatory mechanism may ultimately fail, leading to further demyelination and axonal degeneration. In addition to myelin disturbance, other mechanisms may also contribute to white matter microstructural changes in HD. For example, inflammation and oxidative stress have been implicated in HD pathology (Browne et al., 1999; Jenkins et al., 2013). Activation of microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain, can lead to the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species, which can damage myelin and axons (Block et al., 2007). Moreover, the mutant Huntingtin protein has been shown to induce oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, which can also contribute to white matter damage (Oliveira et al., 2011). The use of advanced MRI techniques, such as magnetization transfer imaging (MTI) and diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), may provide further insights into the underlying mechanisms of white matter microstructural changes in HD. MTI is sensitive to myelin content and has been used to study demyelination in multiple sclerosis (Vavasour et al., 2011). DKI, on the other hand, can provide information on the complexity of white matter tracts and has been used to study white matter changes in Alzheimer's disease (Jensen et al., 2016). The combination of these techniques with DT-MRI and other modalities, such as magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), may provide a more comprehensive understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying white matter changes in HD. In conclusion, white matter microstructural changes are a hallmark of HD, and understanding the underlying mechanisms is crucial for the development of effective therapeutic strategies. The use of multi-modal MRI techniques, including DT-MRI, MTI, DKI, and MRS, may provide valuable insights into the pathophysiology of HD and help identify potential biomarkers for disease diagnosis and monitoring. Furthermore, the investigation of myelin disturbance, inflammation, and oxidative stress as potential mechanisms underlying white matter changes in HD may lead to the development of novel therapeutic targets for the treatment of this devastating disease.

Gas dynamics have a varied temperature, pressure, velocity, etc. depending on the type of fuel and fuel/oxygen ratio used for combustion. Particle dynamics is dependent on the injection mass flow rate, particle size and shape, injection velocity, the angle of spray and spray distance, etc. Moreover, the fuel/oxygen ratio plays a very important role in particle heating. [12] performed the first numerical modelling of angular injection in the HVSFS torch. Both liquid ethanol droplets (300 1/2m) and solid Titania particles (0.5-50 1/2m) are injected as discrete phases. The evaporation of ethanol droplets shows significant cooling of the combustion gases at a 0 angle of injection. Hence, the authors modified the injection phenomena by simulating the flow with an angle of injection of 30. They found that injection at an angle of 30 improves the rate of ethanol evaporation inside the combustion chamber (CC) and cooling is reduced. The disadvantage of angular injection is the impingement of droplets and particles to the CC walls and increase in the residence time of particles. Dongmo et al. [13] further analysed an optimized HVSFS torch, where the TopGun-G's is modified by designing a conical shape CC. Moreover, to improve the process efficiency of generating the dense nanosized coating, the atomization of droplets is essentially required for suspension carrying high concentrations of suspended particles. The atomization of liquid feedstock can be controlled by the atomizer nozzle design and its injection parameters [32-34]. Many researchers have studied the phenomenon of atomization and some specific work is highlighted here. The theory explained by Castleman in 1930 [35], states that atomization is due to the aerodynamic interaction between the liquid and gas leading to an unstable wave growth on the liquid jet surface. The fast moving air strikes the water jet. Hence, the portion of the liquid mass is drawn out into fine ligaments and turns into small droplets. The higher the air speed, the smaller the size of ligaments/droplets [35]. The atomization of liquid jet is a step-wise process [36]. The near field jet breakup process is dominated by the shedding of liquid sheets and ligaments. The far field has a secondary breakup phenomenon in which the disintegrated liquid lumps from the jet are fragmented by the high-velocity air jets.

Myelin insulates and protects axons and enables saltatory conduction, i.e., the process of action potentials moving in discrete jumps along a myelinated axon to speed up information transfer between neurons. In the central nervous system myelin is produced and repaired by oligodendrocyte glia cells, which are the cells with the highest iron concentration in the human brain (Koeppen, 1995). The view that myelin disturbance may play a critical role in HD is backed up by recent evidence from post-mortem and animal studies. Using a variety of techniques, including carbon dating, one post-mortem study of brain tissue from individuals with HD has suggested decreased proliferation of striatal oligodendrocyte lineage cells (Ernst et al., 2014). Furthermore, Teo et al. (2016) reported thinner myelin sheaths in fibers of the corpus callosum in HD knock-in mice at an early age before any striatal neuronal loss could be detected. Similarly, reduced levels of myelin regulatory factor and myelin basic protein and decreased numbers of myelinated axons in the corpus callosum were reported in other HD mice model studies (Huang et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2015). Together these results suggest that an early breakdown of myelination followed by homeostatic responses of increased levels of oligodendrocytes and iron may contribute to the pathogenesis of HD (Bartzokis et al., 2007). However, in vivo correlates of demyelination in human HD remain relatively unexplored compared to other neurodegenerative diseases such as multiple sclerosis, despite their potential in helping to better understand the pathogenesis of the disease and in providing biomarkers for the efficacy of therapeutics. The present study investigated HD-related differences in WM microstructure by utilizing both high angular resolution diffusion imaging (HARDI) (Tuch et al., 2002) and quantitative magnetization transfer imaging (qMT) (Henkelman et al., 1993, 2001) which provides improved myelin specificity compared to diffusion MRI. qMT estimates the liquid and semisolid constituents of tissue by applying an off-resonance radiofrequency pulse with time-varying amplitude to selectively saturate the macromolecular magnetization. This results in a reduction of the measured signal due to the magnetization transfer between saturated macromolecules and free water (Sled and Pike, 2000; Ramani et al., 2002). Molecules associated with myelin have been shown to dominate the magnetization transfer exchange process in WM (Koenig, 1991; Odrobina et al., 2005) and the relative density of the macromolecular pool, the macromolecular proton fraction (MMPF), has been found to be specific to myelin content of the optic nerve in shiverer versus control mice (Ou et al., 2009), to be sensitive to demyelination processes in multiple sclerosis (Levesque et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2015) and to depend on the myelin content of WM in post-mortem histology studies of human multiple sclerosis brains (Schmierer et al., 2007). Thus, although magnetization transfer will also be influenced by other processes such as inflammation and T1 changes, MMPF has been proposed as a proxy MRI marker of myelin (Serres et al., 2009b,a).

You never know who might be lurking out there. As I stepped a little closer to investigate, my heart raced slightly. My mind conjured scenarios that felt all too real. "But the question remains," I said, peering through the spare door that seemed to lead to what appeared to be an unassuming closet space. "Is it really necessary for a family home?" "My clients are looking for peace of mind, Sarah," Evan chimed in, forcing the mood back towards practicality. "I mean, if they can get it with a panic room included, why wouldn't they want it? At least it's not a bunker in the backyard." "Oh, that's reassuring," I replied, gesturing dismissively. The panic room had a strange allure, almost like a hidden treasure of sorts. But more than that, it felt intrusive. Wouldn't one just want to feel safe in one's home without the added weight of a fortress mentality? Aimless thoughts wandered while I continued to meander through the spacious layout. "Time's ticking," Evan reminded me, pacing over the polished wooden floor, his polished black shoes casting brief shadows in the overhead light. "I suggest we move on before they change their mind or before you go looking for the exit." "Mom!" Lydia chirped, shooting out of the master bedroom like a torpedo. "I'm going to see the backyard!" "Stay where I can see you!" I called out, but it was already too late. The child was off and sprinting through the rooms, her enthusiasm contagious. Evan shot me a sidelong glance. Was that the faintest smile on his lips? "Bright spirit, isn't she?" he remarked, his tone one of understanding mixed with professional detachment. "You both will definitely need room to breathe in here, escape from life's little messes." "I suppose you're right." I paused. "It wouldn't hurt to have a patch of green space, would it? In the city, even a sliver of grass feels like a miracle." "There is nothing else out there like this, Sarah," Evan continued, enthusiasm sparking back into his demeanor. "A unique opportunity, a piece of prime real estate in a market that doesn't know what to do with itself. Think of the potential!" I allowed his words to bounce around my mind, weighing them against my growing concerns about the impending deadline. The clock was ticking down, sealing my future beyond these walls. As I caught up with Lydia in the courtyard, the sunlight drenching her hair in golden highlights made everything seem possible, so vividly alive. "What do you think, sweetheart?" I asked, ruffling her hair. "Should we call this home?" She began to turn over rocks, little treasures from whatever had been cared for in this space before. "Where are the flowers?" she asked innocently, stooping low to perch on her knees. I smiled, but deep down, uncertainty thrummed like an engine. "We can plant them, my love. Make this place our own." "Do we have enough time to make it pretty?" she asked, her hope a fragile thing dancing in the sunlight. My heart clenched. "Just enough, kid. Just enough."

Scheduling requires selecting resource types (such as machineries, cranes, and workforce), determining the required number of each resource, and allocating them to simultaneously executed jobs (e.g., manufacturing a number of different components) over time to maximise productivity subject to the constraints (e.g., limited number of workforce, early start dates, late finish date). A sufficient number and type of resources is crucial for managing demand fluctuation, procurement processes and machine failures. Each sector can process a limited number of tasks at a time; each resource can execute at most one task at a time. Resource scheduling affects and is affected by the manufacturing factory, transportation options and the construction site. Nowadays, resource scheduling of a DfMA plan is not performed comprehensively: On the one hand, the available decision-making support tools do not cover the combined performance attributes of MtA sectors while evaluating prefabricated construction methods. On the other hand, they do not consider an optimal schedule for the combined MtA sectors before comparing conventional construction plan to prefabricated construction one. It is therefore essential to implement a decision support tool which considers all three MtA sectors as a unified system and acknowledges multiple objectives of the construction project. Hence, this paper proposes a Genetic Algorithm-based (GA-based) technique for solving a unified MtA construction system. The contributions are: The prefabrication scheduling problem has been considered as a holistic/unified MtA problem which needs to be solved. Due to the complexity of this unified MtA construction scheduling problem (which is equivalent to a complex extended Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem), a GA-based optimisation algorithm is applied for the first time. This non-exact model will return a good sub-optimal result in less time than exact methods. The presented GA-based technique is multi-objective with one dominant objective function. To evaluate the quality of the proposed GA for solving flexible job shop problems, the model is compared with other exact and non-exact models using instances from the literature and scenarios inspired by real data from precast construction projects. Section 2 provides a summary of the available prefabrication decision-making tools and construction scheduling models and identifies the issues of excising algorithms. The detailed description of the problem in the prefabricated construction, input/output decision variables, resource constrains, the optimisation objectives and the framework for resource scheduling a unified MtA system are described in Section 3. This leads to defining the MtA system in terms of a Resource-constrained Extended Flexible Job Shop Scheduling (REFJSS) problem with the aim of minimising the total completion time and cost. These types of problems are NP-complete problems and computationally demanding to solve [8]. Section 4 presents the MILP formulation for the REFJSS and the assumptions. Evolutionary algorithms such as the GA are suitable in finding a solution that is close to the optimal and satisfies the constraints of complex problems.

The condensate can return back to the evaporator by the effect of capillary force when the heat pipe is provided with a wick structure, or by the effect of the gravity force. The gravity assisted heat pipe is also known as thermosyphons [10]. Heat pipes heat exchangers have proven their advantages over conventional heat exchangers in many applications such as waste heat recovery, waste treatment, and solar applications [12]. The advantages of heat pipe heat exchangers include their size and cost reduction, ease of maintenance, uniform wall temperatures and the capability of transporting large heat fluxes. It is also a passive heat transfer device. Jouhara et al. has investigated a novel wraparound heat pipe heat exchanger for heat recovery in air handling units [13]. The heat pipe heat exchanger achieved an effectiveness of 30% and the pay-back period of the system was less than two months [14]. Delpech et al. [15] investigated the application of HPHE in enhancing the energy efficiency in the ceramic industry. The effect of the HPHE on the kiln was conducted by numerical modelling. It was concluded that utilising the HPHE in waste heat recovery in the kiln will results in significant saving of energy cost. Delpech et al. [16] Investigated experimentally a radiative heat pipe in a lab-scale kiln for waste heat recovery by radiation in ceramic industry. The radiative heat pipe was tested at different heaters temperature which were used to simulate the hot ceramic and at difference water flow rate. It was noted that the radiant heat recovery is dominant over natural convection heat recovery at heaters temperature above 300 C. Heat pipes cannot only be in cylindrical shell case design, but also they can be in a flat shape or a flat evaporator with a cylindrical condenser. A flat heat pipe (FHP) utilises the features of heat pipes and additionally it maximises the heat transfer area and transforms a flat surface into an isothermal surface. Flat heat pipe expands the range of applications of heat pipes especially in thermal management applications. Flat heat pipes have been applied mainly in electrical and electronic devices cooling. Ye et al. [17] conducted an experimental study on a micro flat heat pipe array (MHPA) used to cool lithium-ion battery packs. The battery temperature during charging and discharging cycles was measured with and without utilising the heat pipe system. The results indicated that the temperature difference between the battery cells was uniform with less than a 6.5 C difference by cooling the cells using the MHPA. In solar applications, a flat heat pipe increases the heat transfer area which is exposed to the solar radiation.

The boy, Pete, sighed, trying to muster patience as he studied his younger sister. 'I'm fetchin' mushrooms, ain't I?' he replied, tipping his chin toward the basket swinging from his arm. 'Food for the table. You're just wanderin' about with none the wiser and likely to get growled at.' Nancy stomped a foot, damp earth rising around her ankle. 'Mushrooms or no mushrooms, those young ladies don't need you nosin' about neither! You're no more helpful than me, sneakin' about for a peek!' Pete chuckled, setting his basket down and sitting beside it on the garden's low stone wall. 'Aye, but I'm not peepin' at nobody,' he said, his tone softening. 'I'd say that's the difference between the two of us, Nance. Besides, you know Miss Clara and Miss Louisa've had a hard time of it since their father passed. Best leave 'em be.' Nancy's shoulders sank, and her expression turned sheepish. 'I was only worried,' she muttered, glancing towards the shuttered windows, the mist clinging to them like a protective veil. 'No one sees 'em out no more. Not since the funeral.' Pete's face grew thoughtful, and he nodded slowly. 'Truth be told, it's none of our business, but...' He hesitated, then leaned forward with earnest eyes. 'You know as well as I do how grief holds on tight. Maybe they need time, or maybe they need somethin' else.' Nancy tilted her head, curiosity flaring once more, tempered now with genuine concern. 'Somethin' like what, Pete?' The young man looked up at the pale morning sky as if seeking answers in its depths. 'Companionship, perhaps? Folks who remember 'em. Comfort when the world's a cold place. We all need it sometimes, don't we?' Nancy fancied she understood. 'What can we do then? Can we leave somethin' for 'em? As a token, maybe. Just so they know they're not alone.' Pete pondered her suggestion, rubbing his chin thoughtfully. 'Perhaps a basket,' he mused aloud, 'filled with mushrooms and maybe some of Ma's preserves. Enough to warm the heart on a chilly mornin'.' Nancy's face brightened, and she clasped her hands together. 'Oh, yes! Do you think Ma'll mind? I can help make it, and you can leave it at their gate!' They lingered there a moment longer, the weight of grief lifting slightly in the shared anticipation of a small kindness. In the end, it was Nancy who broke the silence with a renewed fervor. 'I'll run back now and convince Ma,' she announced, cheeks flushed with a sense of purpose. 'You'll see, Pete. They'll smile again.' Pete watched her dart away, small feet hasty on the path back home. The morning mist was beginning to thin, revealing the first blush of sunlight gracing the autumn day. As he rose, capturing his basket once more, he caught a glimpse of pale light filtering through the cottage's shutters. With a final glance towards the house of grief and shadow, Pete hoped that their small gesture might whisper to the Misses in mourning that somewhere beyond their sorrow, warmth awaited. Perhaps, in the company of kind intentions, they could find solace in the simplest acts of neighborly love.
