The dorsal stream's vulnerability in individuals with developmental dyslexia has been a topic of significant interest in recent years. The idea that this stream is responsible for processing global motion and spatial cognition has led researchers to investigate its role in the development of reading skills. However, the relationship between dorsal stream function and reading ability is complex and not yet fully understood. One of the key challenges in studying the dorsal stream's role in reading is the difficulty in measuring its function. Unlike the ventral stream, which is responsible for processing visual form and object recognition, the dorsal stream's function is more difficult to quantify. This is because the dorsal stream is involved in processing motion and spatial information, which is more abstract and difficult to measure. Despite these challenges, researchers have used a variety of techniques to study the dorsal stream's function in individuals with developmental dyslexia. One common approach is to use random-dot kinematograms (RDKs), which are stimuli that contain a pattern of individual dots that move in a specific direction. By changing the proportion of dots that move in the same direction, researchers can vary the coherence of the stimulus and measure the individual's ability to detect the direction of motion. Several studies have used RDKs to investigate the dorsal stream's function in individuals with developmental dyslexia. For example, Cornelissen et al. (1995) found that poor readers with dyslexia had higher coherence thresholds than control readers, suggesting that they were less able to process global motion information. However, other studies have found no significant differences between dyslexic and control readers in their ability to process global motion (e.g., Grinter et al., 2010). The inconsistent findings across studies may be due to a number of factors, including the use of different stimuli and tasks, as well as the heterogeneity of the dyslexic population. Recent research has suggested that there may be a genetic component to dyslexia, which could contribute to the variability in dorsal stream function (Cicchini et al., 2015; Gori et al., 2014). In conclusion, the dorsal stream's role in reading is still not fully understood, and further research is needed to determine its precise contribution to reading ability. The use of RDKs and other visual stimuli may provide valuable insights into the neural mechanisms underlying reading and may help to identify new targets for intervention and treatment.

By varying the volume of air injected into the base of the apparatus, different lengths of Taylor bubbles were generated in the cell and it was possible to find the critical volume of bubble which can pass through the expansion without splitting by the necking of the bubble. Similar to approach of Danabalan [8], an exact value for the critical length could not be found, but only upper and lower bounds for it. The stimuli in the Cornelissen et al. (1995) study were spatially complex. To perform the task participants had to detect directional shearing between horizontal bands, rather than the direction of global motion per se. Thus one cannot determine whether poor readers have a difficulty processing visual motion in general or a difficulty detecting motion contrast. To address this issue, Raymond and Sorensen (1998) administered a simpler, conventional random-dot global motion task. A single RDK was presented on each trial, the participants had to judge the overall direction of the stimulus and motion coherence was varied. Poor readers coherence thresholds' were significantly higher (1.8 times) than those of controls. However, there was no group difference when the RDKs consisted of only two images (i.e. the dots underwent a single displacement). These results imply that poor readers have a particular difficulty integrating local motion signals over extended trajectories, rather than a general difficulty with motion detection. Talcott, Hansen, Assoku, and Stein (2000) sought to determine whether the perceptual deficit in poor readers reflects anomalous spatial or temporal integration. In two separate experiments, the mean dot density and exposure duration of random-dot stimuli, similar to those used by Raymond and Sorensen (1998) were manipulated. Results showed that overall poor readers' coherence thresholds were significantly higher than those of normal readers in both experiments and there was no significant interaction between subject group and dot density nor subject group and duration, demonstrating that the spatiotemporal manipulations had similar effects regardless of reading ability. However, at the highest dot density tested (12.2 dots/deg2) the performance of readers with dyslexia approached that of the controls, suggesting a marginal improvement perhaps as a consequence of the greater motion energy present in the denser RDKs facilitating the poor readers. Talcott et al. speculated that greater motion energy might be expected to facilitate performance if motion sensors have a relatively low response gain, more inherent noise or sparser spatial sampling but no firm conclusions could be drawn. An alternative hypothesis is that deficits on sensory tasks associated with poor reading and dyslexia are the result of impairments in external-noise exclusion (Sperling, Lu, Manis, & Seidenberg, 2005). Within this framework relatively poor performance on RDK tasks, in which coherence thresholds are used as a measure of sensitivity, is directly indicative of an underlying problem in segregating the signal dots from the noise dots. Although this noise-exclusion hypothesis has received support (e.g. Sperling, Lu, Manis, & Seidenberg, 2006) it fails to explain why some individuals with dyslexia often exhibit relatively normal performance on analogous static global form tasks that also contain high levels of visual noise. For example, Hansen, Stein, Orde, Winter, and Talcott (2001) administered two psychophysical tasks: a random-dot global motion task and a static global form task. The latter was devised by Atkinson et al. (1997) to investigate the processing of global form in individuals with Williams syndrome.

In addition to its major role in electron transfer to desaturases and hydroxylases, cytochrome b5 is also known to be involved in electron transfer to some CYP enzymes (Henderson et al., 2013; Gan et al., 2009), though the functional relationship between CYPs and the CBR-b5 pathway remains largely elusive. In addition to the microsomal CBR-b5 system there is also a mitochondrial CBR-b5 system (Hahne et al., 1994). Though the function of this system also remains largely elusive, it has been linked with metabolism of xenobiotics and lipid biosynthesis (Nikiforova et al., 2014; Neve et al., 2012; Glory and Thiruvenangdam, 2011). To date studies on microsomal CBR enzymes have been limited to the model yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the industrial arachidonic acid-producing fungus Mortierella alpina (Class: Zygomycota), the model white-rot fungus Phanerochaete chrysosporium (Order: Basidiomycota), and the filamentous fungus Mucor racemosus (Class: Zygomycota). In S. cerevisiae it was demonstrated that the sole microsomal CBR present in the fully sequenced genome is able to provide the reducing power necessary for the function of a CYP enzyme (albeit in a reconstituted system), CYP51, needed for biosynthesis of the main fungal sterol, ergosterol, rendering CPR dispensable (Lamb et al., 1999; Sutter and Loper, 1989). Similarly, studies in P. chrysosporium showed that the CBR-b5 system is able to efficiently provide electrons to the enzyme CYP63A2, a multifunctional CYP (Syed et al., 2011). These findings offered some insight into the potential overlap in function between the CPR and CBR systems in fungi. In M. alpina two CBRs were identified and cloned in the late 1990s. The first of these was heterologously expressed in Aspergillus oryzae leading to an increase in ferricyanide reduction activity (Sakuradani et al., 1999), though no analyses of the in situ function of this enzyme were carried out. The second of these was used in conjunction with the first in a phylogenetic analysis, which demonstrated evolutionary divergence of mammalian CBR enzymes from those of fungi and plants (Certik et al., 1999). In M. racemosus, CBR was cloned and expressed in E. coli (Mirzaei et al., 2010), though again no analyses of the biological function of the enzyme in the host organism were conducted. Whilst much research has been carried out on mammalian (Celik et al., 2013; Elahian et al., 2014) and plant CBRs (Wayne et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2006; Shockey et al., 2005; Bagnaresi et al., 2000), there have been no further investigations into the roles of these enzymes in fungi.

In the first place, he missed Edhart, the old maitre d'hotel who for a decade had catered to his primitive American tastes in the matter of foodstuffs with as much enthusiasm as if he had been a Parisian epicure. The passing of Edhart did more to call Monte's attention to the fact that in his own life a decade had also passed than anything else could possibly have done. Between birthdays there is only the lapse each time of a year; but between the coming and going of the maitre d'hotel there was a period of ten years, which with his disappearance seemed to vanish. Monte was twenty-two when he first came to Nice, and now he was thirty-two. He became thirty-two the moment he was forced to point out to the new management his own particular table in the corner, and to explain that, however barbarous the custom might appear, he always had for breakfast either a mutton chop or a beefsteak. Edhart had made him believe, even to last year, that in this matter and a hundred others he was merely expressing the light preferences of a young man. Now, because he was obliged to emphasize his wishes by explicit orders, they became the definite likes and dislikes of a man of middle age. For relief Monte turned to the tennis courts, and played so much in the next week that he went stale and in the club tournament put up the worst game of his life. That evening, in disgust, he boarded the train for Monte Carlo, and before eleven o'clock had lost five thousand francs at roulette - which was more than even he could afford for an evening's entertainment that did not entertain. Without waiting for the croupier to rake in his last note, Monte hurried out and, to clear his head, walked all the way back to Nice along the Cornice Road. Above him, the mountains; below, the blue Mediterranean; while the road hung suspended between them like a silver ribbon. Yet even here he did not find content. Monte visited the rooms every evening for the next three days; but, as he did not play again and found there nothing more interesting than the faces, or their counterparts, which he had seen for the past ten years, the programme grew stupid. So, really, he had no alternative but Paris, although it was several weeks ahead of his schedule. As a matter of fact, it was several weeks too early. The city was not quite ready for him. The trees in the Champs Elysees were in much the condition of a lady half an hour before an expected caller. The broad vista to the triumphal arches was merely the setting for a few nurses and their charges. The little iron tables were so deserted that they remained merely little iron tables.

An interesting characteristic of IL-33 is that it belongs to a special subset of cytokines, including IL-1 and HMGB1 (high-mobility group box 1), which lead a "double-life" active both in their secreted and non-secreted (intracellular) forms, differentially involved in the induction and modulation of inflammatory responses [15,17,34]. The unique feature of IL-33 is however about its seemingly opposing pro-inflammatory versus anti-inflammatory properties. In contrast to its IL-1 counterpart which drives pro-inflammatory gene expression [35], the IL-33 intracellular precursor protein has been found to act instead as a co-repressor of pro-inflammatory genes, and its intra-nuclear binding could result in an anti-inflammatory phenotype [17]. It has also been shown that ST2 can dimerize with an alternative coreceptor of the IL-1R family, SIGIRR (single Ig IL-1R related molecule), acting as a negative regulator of the IL-33/ST2 signalling pathway [36]. While its ligation by IL-33 may result in the activation of MyD88, NFkB and MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinases) in Th2 and mast cells leading to a preferential induction of Th2 cytokines (IL-5, IL-13), it may alternatively under certain condition also suppress IFN- (Th1) production via a hitherto unknown mechanism [15]. The immunological mechanism underlying such dichotomous functions and complex regulatory properties of IL-33 remains therefore to be understood. This may first depend on its molecular processing, release and the associated cellular compartments of the cytokine. It is now believed that, similar to the chromatin-associated nuclear factor HMGB1, the mature form of IL-33 can be released by cells undergoing necrosis. As a result of cell damage, it alerts the immune system of 'danger' ('alarmins') but otherwise remains in the nucleus of living cells where it limits immune responses [37]. IL-33 may also further exert its effects on different cell types which in return regulate each other by releasing soluble factors, as part of the immunological regulatory network or polarisation process [16]. We have recently demonstrated how necrotic cells or necrotic cell-derived factors, and their complex interactions with dendritic cells, could be directly involved in the induction of a lupus-like disease in susceptible mouse strains [38,39]. Most importantly, we showed that difference in susceptibility versus resistance to the disease induction was critically depending on the presence or absence of certain immune regulatory mechanism, and IL-10 appeared to be a crucial protective factor against the disease induction. By using IL-10 gene-knockout (IL-10-/-) mice, we demonstrated recently that, in the absence of IL-10 even the resistant strain could be rendered susceptible to the induction of a typical lupus-like renal disease [39]. These IL-10-/- mice also develop spontaneously a Th1-mediated chronic enterocolitis, and have been widely used as an animal model of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) [40-42].

A 'return' provides a larger conceptual canvas that allows us to include a variety of non-monetary and intangible entities observed in our analysis. Moreover, the concept of 'return' has an established discourse in anthropology (see [34-37]). We prefix 'peer-to-peer' (p2p) to 'return' to indicate specific structural elements of the returns discussed in this article, i.e., these are mutually structured, negotiated, and organized by energy-givers and energy-receivers. In the existing energy literature on off-grid energy systems, there are two main knowledge gaps about peer-to-peer returns that this article attempts to address. First, an emerging body of energy literature sees a local, social, and cultural understanding of various aspects of off-grid systems as crucial for their success and adoption by people [16,17,38-41]. However, the existing discussion on returns in such energy systems is mostly rooted in a techno-economic analysis [14,20,23,42-44] and lacks an understanding of the sociocultural embedding of the returns, i.e. how these returns are grounded in the social and cultural reality of people's life. Second, the existing energy literature on such returns in off-grid settings is primarily limited to discussion on monetary returns (fiat money) and lacks an understanding of different types of monetary and non-monetary returns possible and people's preferences for these. Moreover, the contemporary understanding of p2p returns in limited to a 'rational market' paradigm that presumes universal and exclusive preference for fiat money and primacy of logic of market where the householders engage in competitive buying and selling of energy in return for fiat money. Such an understanding does not take social and cultural variations and particularities, and diversity in logics into account. To respond to these above-mentioned knowledge gaps, in this article, we bring a perspective from the discipline of anthropology to develop a sociocultural understanding of p2p returns. To the best of our knowledge, p2p returns in off-grid energy systems have not yet been explored from an anthropological perspective. In a broad sense, an anthropological perspective focuses on two types of understandings. First, a holistic, bottom-up, and embedded understanding of a (sociocultural) phenomenon which starts by building and analyzing 'emic' (insider's or internal) viewpoints, i.e., people's multiple realities, perceptions, and logics. Second, translating the 'emic' understanding to 'etic' (external) concepts, i.e., an analytical and conceptual description of the phenomenon (for more on 'etic' and 'emic perspectives see [45,46]). Hence, this anthropological perspective attempts to ground the understanding of a phenomenon in everyday realities of peoples' social life. This article is based on an ethnographic 'research intervention' study conducted at two off-grid villages Rampur and Manpur in rural India for 11 months (1 February 2016-31 December 2016).7 The study started with the installation of an off-grid energy distribution infrastructure to enable exchanges of solar-lighting in the villages.

Florian Wood, a man of slippery identities and elusive truths, meandered through the quaint streets of Zell, whistling a tune that seemed to blend seamlessly with the melodies of the bustling marketplace. The air was filled with the rich aroma of freshly baked bread and the faint notes of a zither played by a weathered musician sitting beneath a canopy of vibrant tulips. Here, in this enchanting valley, Florian fancied himself a connoisseur of the art of disguise, a chameleon who could blend effortlessly with the scenes unfolding before him-a troubadour of his own making. He paused to observe the intricate dance of the villagers, their understated attire a stark contrast to the flamboyant myths that surrounded them in distant lands. Still, there was a beauty in their simplicity, a rustic charm that owed nothing to the stage or to the expectations of cosmopolitan onlookers. They moved with a grace born of generations spent in the shadow of the Alps, and Florian couldn't help but feel a small pang of envy for the seamless integration of their identities into the landscape they called home. Not one to remain a passive observer for long, Florian soon joined an impromptu gathering around an aged storyteller, his voice carrying tales as old as the valley itself. The crowd, captivated by the sagas of heroic deeds and whispered secrets of the mountains, ebbed and flowed like the gentle rivers cutting through the meadows. Florian, with his curious mixture of cynicism and awe, considered the power of such tales to shape reality, to transform the mundane features of everyday life into something bordering on the mythical. As the sun set behind the craggy peaks, casting long shadows that seemed to echo the day's events, Florian continued his wandering through the narrow lanes, past weather-beaten cottages adorned with climbing ivy and timbered charm. The soft, golden glow of lamp-lit windows beckoned with promises of warmth and camaraderie, yet still, he wandered, content in his solitude, a lone minstrel casting his thoughts to the wind. In his pocket, Florian carried only a worn journal, its pages filled with musings and mercurial thoughts, scribbled in crowded ink. Among its tattered leaves were the reflections of a man in search of authenticity, a pilgrim seeking truth in the kaleidoscope of human existence. He wondered if perhaps, beneath his practiced apathy, there lay a yearning as profound as that of the Zillerthal singers embarking on their journeys-a desire not for fame or fortune, but for meaning in a world that so often seemed devoid of it. The night carried a cool breeze, hinting at the crisp promise of morning. Picking a path that led to the emerald slopes above the valley, Florian climbed steadily, his mind drifting back to the image of the minstrel in the marketplace. How much of life, he pondered, was performance? And could even the most skilled actors deceive themselves into believing the roles they played? With a sigh and a smile that was almost wistful, Florian took a seat upon a moss-covered rock, overlooking the vast expanse of the Zillerthal beneath a sky spangled with stars. Here, enveloped by the ancient calm of the mountains, he sought answers in the silence, where everything and nothing existed in perfect harmony-a fitting backdrop for a seeker of truths, both real and imagined.

At lunchtime, Hazel took a few minutes to sit with the children, eating her own simple meal of bread and cheese, and listening to their chatter and laughter. She felt a sense of peace wash over her as she watched them, and for a moment, she forgot about her worries and troubles. But as the afternoon wore on, her thoughts returned to her mother, and she felt a pang of anxiety. As the children left the schoolroom, Hazel stood up, her mind racing with thoughts of what she could do. She knew that she couldn't just sit back and do nothing, not when her mother was suffering so much. She took a deep breath, squared her shoulders, and made a decision. She would talk to Mr. Lambent, the local doctor, and ask for his advice. Maybe he could help her find a way to ease her mother's suffering, and help them both to find a way out of their difficult situation. With a sense of determination, Hazel Thorne walked out of the schoolroom, ready to face whatever challenges lay ahead.

My wife and son were right in front of me, just steps away from safety, and then they weren't. I heard the shattering glass, the roar of the explosion, but all I could focus on was the absence-the absence of their life, their laughter, the love they filled my days with. The people around me must have been talking, but it was like they were underwater, their voices distorted and incomprehensible. All I could see was the way the sunlight gleamed off the shards of broken glass strewn across the street, glinting like stars on a sidewalk in a cruel echo of hope. Someone took me by the arm, guiding me gently away from the chaos, away from the images that would haunt me for a lifetime. Mike's voice cut through the fog like a lifeline. "Gordo," he said, his voice steady and grounding, "we're gonna find out who did this. We're not letting this slide." I nodded, not fully comprehending, just needing something, anything, to hold onto. I stumbled through the questions they asked, words falling from my lips without thought. "It happened so fast," I heard myself say. "I-there was no time." Hours, maybe days later, I found myself in a room that felt unfamiliar despite its well-worn comforts: the dusty couch, the faded quilt over the back of the recliner, all the little things that were parts of a life now reduced to memories. "Mr. Pitt," someone called softly. A voice at the edge of the periphery, slowly drawing me back to the present. Sound sharp, reality harsh. I turned to face him, the detective, and noticed the threads of gray weaving through his dark hair, a sign of battles fought and witnessed. "We need to talk about what comes next," he said, regret shading his words. My heart was a spent engine running on the fumes of grief and disbelief. "What comes next?" I echoed hollowly. I couldn't process the notion of a future, not without Anne and Luis. He put a hand on my shoulder, heavy with shared loss. "Gordo, you've got a fire in you," he insisted. "Use it. Remember them by fighting for the truth, by helping us catch those bastards. Every second counts." The fire, he said. A conflagration tearing through my insides, fed by sorrow and saturated with rage. My family was a casualty in a war that had no faces, no boundaries, just devastation that seeped into every pore. I wasn't alone. Others had suffered in similar ways, their names marked with sorrow across a map of the city, the world. And yet, private's scars were woven through a shared tapestry of loss. Through grief, I stood numbly as the detective continued, words like embers settling in the ashes of our departed dreams. "We need you, Gordo," he said again. "You knew the streets, the runs. We've got leads, and we'll keep pushing. You said goodbye today, but tomorrow you could help." Help? Maybe. A small word, weighed down with meaning. The water of their laughter still rippled in my mind, even in the absence. But from those ashes, something new might rise, carrying forward the legacy of their love.

Priebus cautioned his comments are not set in stone and he described his ideas in "hypothetical" terms. One idea he mentioned was instituting a penalty system in which candidates for the nomination would lose a percentage of delegates if they participated in a debate not sanctioned by the RNC. Dark horse candidates hungry for media attention would likely oppose such a move, but it's unclear if they would have the power to prevent a change in the rules. The idea of handpicking moderators would also face stiff opposition from the media organizations who foot the bill to stage and broadcast the debates. Primary calendar needs to be condensed. In an ideal world, he said, the intra-party fight would start later and finish sooner, with the Republican National Convention possibly being held as early as June. But he doesn't talk about changing the order of the four leadoff primary and caucus states - Iowa, New Hampshire, Nevada and South Carolina - that have traditionally kicked off the nomination process. "I think that the carve-out states have served us well, but I think the timing of the calendar and the rest of the calendar issue should be looked at," he said. Priebus rejected the notion of the RNC becoming involved in presidential primaries to assist the strongest candidate, but he was quick to point out that state Republican parties can choose to play in primaries if they want. "State parties can decide for themselves," he said. "It's their choice." In terms of outreach to minorities, Priebus said the GOP failed to pass a very basic test. Attracting minority voters a key GOP goal as Obama begins second term. "Well, for one thing, we have to ask for the vote," he said. "You have to ask for it and I don't think that we've been doing a very good job of that." Priebus said a glaring organizational flaw for Republicans is that there have been no long-term investments made in human capital to help sell the GOP message on a neighborhood to neighborhood level.

In light of this knowledge gap, it becomes evident that efficient strategies must be developed to facilitate the collection, management, and dissemination of information pertinent to construction components. Such strategies would not only enhance the understanding of the lifecycle of materials but also enable practitioners to make informed decisions regarding refurbishment and reusability. The digital era offers a multitude of tools that can be harnessed to bridge this chasm; for instance, Building Information Modelling (BIM) technologies present a powerful mechanism for capturing and sharing detailed characteristics of construction components throughout their lifespan. By integrating various layers of data-ranging from design specifications to performance history-BIM can act as a comprehensive repository that supports decision-making processes related to reuse and recycling. In addition to technological advancements, the importance of regulatory frameworks cannot be overstated. Policymakers have a crucial role in shaping the landscape for CDW management. The European Union, through its Circular Economy Action Plan, seeks not only to enhance recycling rates but also to foster an environment conducive to reuse practices within the construction sector. Regulations that incentivise reusability, such as tax breaks for buildings employing reclaimed materials or penalties for excessive waste generation, could stimulate a shift in industry practices. Such economic mechanisms could encourage stakeholders to prioritise reuse over mere recycling, thereby amplifying the lifetime value of materials used in construction and ultimately contributing to environmental sustainability. Moreover, the involvement of stakeholders across the supply chain is paramount. Construction projects often involve multiple parties-from architects and engineers to contractors and end-users-each possessing unique knowledge that, if effectively synthesised, could enhance the identification and recovery of reusable components. Collaborative platforms and workshops that bring together these stakeholders can help to educate them on the benefits of reuse and the importance of proper documentation. Such initiatives can also cultivate a culture of circularity, wherein reuse becomes a standard consideration in project planning rather than an afterthought. Furthermore, addressing the market barriers that presently restrict the flow of reclaimed materials is essential. This includes establishing predictable supply chains for reused construction components, which can often be hindered by inconsistency in quality and availability. Standardising the assessment criteria and certification processes for reclaimed materials would bolster confidence among builders and developers, making reused components a more attractive option in project specifications. By guaranteeing quality and reliability through certification, reclaimed materials can begin to occupy a more prominent position in the marketplace. Lastly, it is vital to foster a cultural shift within the construction industry that embraces innovation and sustainability at its core. Educational programs focused on sustainable design practices, coupled with active encouragement from industry leaders for adopting reuse methodologies, could initiate a broader transformation in thinking. As younger generations of architects, engineers, and builders enter the workforce, instilling principles of circular economy and resource conservation can help shape a new paradigm in construction. Ultimately, developing a cohesive strategy that integrates technical knowledge, regulatory frameworks, stakeholder collaboration, market facilitation, and cultural transformation is essential to realising the full potential of construction and demolition waste reutilisation. Only then can the industry effectively secure a sustainable future that not only mitigates waste but also celebrates the inherent value of materials through reuse.

The detection of outcome switching is a crucial task in ensuring the integrity of clinical trials, and it relies heavily on the ability to compare and match outcomes across different sources. This process can be challenging due to the variability in outcome definitions, terminology, and reporting styles used in trial registries, protocols, and medical research articles. To address this issue, it is essential to develop a systematic approach to identify and normalize outcome concepts across different sources. One potential approach is to use natural language processing (NLP) techniques to extract and analyze outcome-related information from unstructured text data. By applying NLP algorithms to medical articles, protocols, and trial registries, researchers can identify and extract outcome-related concepts, such as outcome names, definitions, and measurement scales. These extracted concepts can then be normalized and standardized using ontologies and controlled vocabularies, such as the Clinical Trials Ontology (CTO) or the Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) thesaurus. Another approach is to use machine learning algorithms to classify outcomes into predefined categories or to identify patterns and relationships between outcomes. For instance, machine learning models can be trained to distinguish between primary and secondary outcomes, or to identify outcomes that are related to specific disease domains or interventions. By applying these algorithms to large datasets of trial outcomes, researchers can identify trends and patterns that may indicate outcome switching or other forms of reporting bias. In addition to these technical approaches, it is also essential to develop guidelines and standards for outcome reporting and to promote transparency and accountability in clinical trial reporting. For example, the CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) statement provides guidelines for reporting randomized controlled trials, including the reporting of outcomes. Similarly, the SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) statement provides guidelines for reporting clinical trial protocols, including the definition and reporting of outcomes. Ultimately, the detection and prevention of outcome switching require a multifaceted approach that involves both technical and non-technical solutions. By developing and applying advanced NLP and machine learning algorithms, promoting transparency and accountability in clinical trial reporting, and establishing guidelines and standards for outcome reporting, researchers can ensure the integrity and reliability of clinical trial results and promote evidence-based decision-making in healthcare.

The information available to different agents in terms of (private and social) benefits, and cost will greatly influence the market outcomes both in terms of resource allocation and in terms of what households consume as household inputs for daily activities. The outcome of a (wrong) household decision in the presence of imperfect information will be costly and households will bear negative consequences, leading to the loss of social welfare. One option for solving this inefficient market outcome is to design a policy by which the market participants are well informed and ensure that decisions are made in light of perfect information. The literature on fuel adoption suggests that education, income, accessibility and price play an important role in the adoption of cooking fuel (e.g. Rahut et al., 2016; Hanna et al., 2015; Jeuland et al., 2015; Heltberg, 2005; Israel, 2002). In addition, there is the consensus on the role of information in adopting cooking fuel and ICS. To the best of our knowledge, however, there is no evidence regarding how information disseminated through television affects the adoption of clean cooking fuels, and our study is an attempt to fill this knowledge gap. Considerable, evidence shows that individuals or agents behave differently when information is made available to them. For instance, the energy consumption of households decreases when households are treated with information about energy price increase (Jessoe and Rapson, 2014), disclosing the quality (state of the art) of automobiles helps the bidder participation decision in auctions (Tadelis and Zettelmeyer, 2015), information about the benefits of a tax deferred account increase the take-up rate (Duflo and Saez, 2003), and scientific information increases the approval of a supply organ (Elias et al., 2015). The effects of information on the abatement of environmental risk in developing countries are mixed. When information about level of arsenic in drinking water is provided households switch the drinking water source (Barnwal et al., 2017), early governmental warnings (information) about an approaching tsunami and mangrove trees reduced the death tolls during the tsunami in India (Das and Vincent, 2009) and exposure to newspaper and radio increased the probability of purifying drinking water (Jalan et al., 2009). However, Dupas (2009) report that the households do not respond to health and financial information in terms of mosquito net purchase decision by cash constraint households in Kenya. There are many channels through which households may acquire information or knowledge about the harmful effects of IAP, and television is one of the most important sources of information and knowledge. In developing countries, households generally acquire information through television, radio, interactions with others (phone or in person) and from various government awareness programs. In high-literacy areas, households may also acquire information from reading materials such as newspapers or books. In rural Bhutan, the literacy rate is relatively low. According to the Bhutan Living Standard Survey (BLSS) 2017 (NSB, 2017) report, the rural literacy rate is 58%, indicating that approximately half of the population cannot read and write.

These climatic shifts pose profound challenges, necessitating a comprehensive reevaluation of policies aimed at fostering sustainable development. The agriculture sector, being the backbone of many economies in the region, is experiencing heightened vulnerability. With the majority of farmers relying on rain-fed agriculture, erratic weather patterns diminish crop yields, exacerbating food insecurity. Farmers, often employing traditional farming methods, lack the adaptive strategies to cope with the fluctuations wrought by climate change. Furthermore, the cyclical nature of droughts and floods threatens not only food production but also livelihoods, pushing millions further into poverty. In light of these challenges, sustainable agricultural practices emerge as a potential remedy. Integrating methods such as agroecology and conservation agriculture can enhance resilience among farming communities. These approaches encourage biodiversity, improve soil health, and optimize water usage, providing a buffer against climatic anomalies. Moreover, investment in agricultural research and technology could facilitate the development of climate-resilient crops, providing farmers with viable alternatives to traditional staples. Access to innovations, however, will necessitate strong policy frameworks and infrastructure investments that ensure rural communities are not left behind. The challenge of climate change is further compounded by weak governance systems and limited institutional capacity in many SSA countries. The interplay of socio-economic factors creates an environment where policy implementation often falls short of desired objectives. Corruption, lack of transparency, and insufficient political will hinder effective responses to these pressing issues. Therefore, it is imperative to strengthen governance structures to create an enabling environment for coherence among policy sectors, particularly those focused on economic development and climate resilience. Public awareness and community engagement are vital elements in addressing the interrelated issues of climate change and poverty reduction. Educating communities about sustainable practices and the importance of environmental stewardship can catalyze collective action. Empowering local leaders and stakeholders to drive change can ensure that interventions are contextually relevant and culturally sensitive. Moreover, fostering partnerships between governments, non-governmental organizations, and private sectors can mobilize the resources and expertise required to implement effective climate adaptation strategies. Financing remains a critical aspect of climate adaptation and mitigation efforts. Mobilizing both domestic and international financial resources will be essential for achieving the sustainable development goals (SDGs) that many SSA countries have committed to. Innovative financing mechanisms such as climate bonds and green financing offer pathways for securing the necessary funds. However, these approaches must be complemented by sound fiscal policies that prioritize investments in climate-resilient infrastructure and renewable energy initiatives. Transitioning to sustainable energy sources not only mitigates climate impacts but also enhances energy security and creates job opportunities in the process. In conclusion, while sub-Saharan Africa grapples with the daunting challenges posed by climate change, there exists a unique opportunity for transformative change. By prioritizing sustainability, fostering resilience within agricultural practices, and enhancing institutional capacities, the region can mitigate the adverse effects of climate change. This multifaceted approach, supported by a strong commitment to governance and collaboration, holds promise for a more equitable and prosperous future. Yet, urgent action must be taken to avert the impending crises that loom on the horizon; the time for decisive leadership and innovative solutions is now. Without such efforts, the repercussions of climate change will continue to overshadow the progress made in the realm of development and well-being for the people of SSA.

His findings resulted in an upgrading of the 'sleep environment' in the Team GB boxing training base in Sheffield - 37 single beds replaced by 33 double and four extra-long singles; sheets, duvets and pillows switched to breathable, quick drying fabrics; materials selected to create a hypo-allergenic barrier to allergens in each bedroom. In track cycling, GB physio Phil Burt and team doctor Richard Freeman realised saddle sores were keeping some female riders out of training. Their response? Totems and flags, while visually stunning, can obstruct views, especially for those who aren't tall enough to see over or around them. There's nothing more frustrating than having your view blocked during your favorite set. The debate is all about finding that balance between expressing oneself and being respectful to others in the crowd. So, how can we practice good etiquette when bringing a flag or totem to a festival? Here are a few tips. First, be mindful of the location and timing. When you're at the back of a massive crowd, waving your flag high is less likely to obstruct anyone's view, as opposed to being right up front and center. During a headliner's set, maybe bring it down a notch so that the folks behind you get a chance to enjoy the performance too. Next, think about the design and structure. A cleverly compact or telescopic design means it can be easily lowered or packed when not in use, reducing the intrusion on others. Lightweight materials also ensure it's easier for you to handle without fatigue. Additionally, consider collaborating with your group to avoid a clutter of multiple banners, which can minimize the crowd footprint. Embodying the spirit of community within rave culture means being considerate and spreading positivity. Communicate with those around you. A simple, "Hey, is this blocking your view?" can make a world of difference. Most people appreciate the thoughtfulness, and it often leads to friendly exchanges and shared enjoyment. It's all about the people, the energy, and the music that unites us. Whether you're a flag bearer or someone who prefers unobstructed views, let's keep the harmony going, showing kindness and consideration in every beat and bass drop. Until next week, keep the conversations alive, keep dancing, and keep spreading that PLUR-loving vibe, my friends!

Throughout the album, you can hear the Stooges' signature sound, which is equal parts silly, irreverent, and just plain fun. It's an album that's guaranteed to put a smile on your face, and maybe even make you laugh out loud. So if you're looking for a holiday album that's a little bit different, a little bit silly, and a whole lot of fun, then "Christmas Time With The Three Stooges" is the album for you. She plopped down at the kitchen table, a chorus of children echoing faintly from the living room as they started a new game. Sara smiled softly, but the weight of the past months still lingered behind her eyes. She felt it every time she looked at Matt, every time she coaxed him out of restless dreams, every time another doctor told her there was little left they could do except hope. "How's the kid?" Wendy asked, leaning back in her chair, stretching out her long legs the way only teenagers do, defiant of space and boundaries. Sara shrugged, the gesture carrying more weight than her words. "He's...hanging in there. Doctor Gregory thinks this new treatment might help, though." Wendy nodded, though she had heard this all before. They all had-the family, this close-knit group of survivors clinging to each other in the uncertainty of Sara's kitchen. Yet they continued with the routine: the false optimism, the cautious belief, the dam against a constant surge of despair. "Hey, Aunt Sara," Wendy's voice pulled her back from thoughts she visited too often, "remember when we went to the beach, and Matt spent the whole time trying to dig to China?" Sara chuckled at the memory. He was just a child then, filled with dreams and boundless energy. She could still picture him-sunburnt and determined, wielding a plastic shovel as though it were his ticket to a grand adventure. "Yeah, he believed if he dug deep enough, he'd find treasure," Sara replied, a soft smile settling on her lips despite herself. "Still waiting on that treasure," Wendy teased, her gaze flicking to the hallway where Matt rested. They let the moment linger, a shared memory knitting over the fractures the recent months had forged. Sara allowed herself these brief respites, these whispers of the past, even as they flitted away like shadows chased by light. The rear door creaked open, admitting a gust of morning air along with Sara's husband, Peter. He donned the weary look of one accustomed to nights spent worrying, fiercely protective of the fragile peace within their home. "Morning," he greeted, placing a gentle kiss on Sara's forehead before glancing at Wendy, grinning like someone years younger. "Breakfast today or is it more of an excuse to see chaos manifested in child form?" "Cereal and chaos," Wendy returned, laughing. "Best kind of breakfast." He slouched into a chair, allowing himself a fleeting pause. Familiar clinks and clanks filled the kitchen, a symphony of normalcy that defied the tumult just outside their suburban bubble. Later, the children barreled in, their exuberant greetings wrapping around the adults like buoyant life rafts. For a moment, the kitchen seemed to expand with life, pushing against the heavier shadows of uncertainty. Under it all, the promise Sara had made to herself-spoken into the night where only hope could hear-remained steadfast: whatever time they had, they would make it count. They would live, despite whatever reality or headline dared to tell them otherwise. And somewhere beneath this resolve, like a buried ember, flickered the undying wish that things would be alright, that their fragmented lives still held room for unexpected fortune.

But then something shifted. It was about eight years ago, as I mentioned, when I realized that this cycle of quitting was not serving me. I sat down one evening, exhausted from yet another failed fitness attempt, and I started reflecting on what I truly wanted-not just in fitness but in life. Was I really ready to give up on the things I desired most? Absolutely not. The first revelation was acknowledging that my lack of consistency didn't define me; it merely described a phase of my life. This realization was liberating. I began to understand that consistency is not an inherent trait but rather a skill that can be cultivated like any other. Yes, I would continue to face hurdles, distractions, and moments of weakness, but that didn't dictate my ability to forge ahead. From that point on, I took a new approach. Instead of setting grandiose and overwhelming goals, I opted for small, incremental changes. I remember sitting down and crafting a list-simple and actionable items that I could commit to. I chose to focus on one small fitness goal at a time. For instance, I would commit to a daily ten-minute workout. At first, it felt trivial; I had spent years believing that if my efforts weren't monumental, they weren't worthwhile. But slowly, those ten minutes transformed into something much more significant. Instead of overwhelming myself with daunting expectations, I embraced the power of habit. I adopted a focus on accountability as well, telling friends and family about my new goals. Sharing my journey made me feel less isolated in my struggle. It was as if I had created my own little support network who cheered me on, and it worked wonders for my motivation. I began to show up, not just for them but for myself. Within months, I noticed a transformation-not just in my body, but in my mindset. The scales began to tip in my favor, both literally and metaphorically. I was no longer that girl who quit almost out of instinct; I was now a woman who could pick herself up, dust herself off, and try again even when the going got tough. But here's the kicker: throughout this journey, I found that consistency was not purely about discipline. It was about grace. It was about allowing myself the space to stumble and acknowledging that imperfection is part of the human experience. I realized that every day is not going to be perfect and that setbacks wouldn't erase the progress I had made; instead, they would simply be markers on the road of life. Now, even as I stand before you and share my experiences, there are days when I falter. The truth is, consistency isn't a straight line-it's winding and unpredictable. And despite the setbacks, each time I fall off the horse, I get back on with a renewed sense of purpose. I started to understand that being consistent means showing up for myself, time and time again, no matter the circumstances. This mental shift proved to be my superpower. It empowered me to tackle my ambitions head-on, to push against self-doubt, and to encourage others to do the same. What was once my greatest weakness morphed into my greatest strength. I could now talk about my journey-not just to inspire others, but to remind myself that consistency, with just a bit of grace and forgiveness, is within everyone's reach. So here we are, transformed together, ready to own our stories, embrace our imperfections, and emerge as the best versions of ourselves, one consistent step at a time. Remember, achieving greatness is not about perfection but the willingness to show up, brush yourself off, and keep moving forward.

In general, there are two types of corticosteroid receptors: mineralocorticoid receptors (MR) and glucocorticoid receptors (GR). MR have high affinity for corticosterone and are responsible for basal regulation of the HPA axis, whereas GR have lower affinity for corticosterone and are thought to mediate more acute responses to stressors (Reul and de Kloet, 1985). These receptors are found throughout the central nervous system and periphery (de Kloet et al., 1998) and have been shown to vary in expression across tissue type and life history stage (Breuner et al., 2003; Breuner and Orchinik, 2002). Additionally, recent work has suggested that changes in receptor density may play an important role in altering organismal sensitivity to corticosterone (Jenni-Eiermann et al., 2014). The goal of this dissertation was to investigate how physiological systems (specifically, the HPA axis) integrate multiple sources of information about environmental conditions to influence behavioral decision making. I examined the extent to which food availability and social cues interacted to affect both corticosterone release and corticosterone receptor densities in white-crowned sparrows ( Zonotrichia leucophrys ). Specifically, I conducted three experiments designed to test whether food availability and social cues independently affected corticosterone release and receptor density in the liver and brain of white-crowned sparrows. I first tested whether food restriction and social isolation affected corticosterone release in captive white-crowned sparrows. Second, I examined the effect of food restriction and social cues on corticosterone release and corticosterone receptor density in captive white-crowned sparrows. Finally, I measured baseline corticosterone concentrations and corticosterone receptor density in free-living white-crowned sparrows exposed to varying degrees of food abundance and sociality. I found that both food availability and social cues influenced corticosterone secretion patterns in captive white-crowned sparrows. Food restricted birds had higher baseline corticosterone concentrations than fed birds. Food-restricted birds also showed a greater increase in corticosterone after handling compared to fed birds, indicating that food restriction resulted in increased responsiveness of the HPA axis. Furthermore, socially isolated birds had higher baseline corticosterone concentrations than group-housed birds, but did not differ in their response to handling. In addition to affecting corticosterone secretion, food restriction and social cues altered corticosterone receptor density in the liver and brain of captive white-crowned sparrows. Fed birds had higher hepatic GR density than food restricted birds, while socially housed birds had higher hippocampal GR density than socially isolated birds. There were no differences in MR density in either tissue type. Lastly, baseline corticosterone concentrations and corticosterone receptor density in the liver and brain of free-living white-crowned sparrows varied depending on food availability and sociality. Baseline corticosterone concentrations were negatively related to food availability and positively related to sociality. Hepatic GR density was positively associated with baseline corticosterone concentration, while hippocampal GR density was negatively associated with baseline corticosterone concentration. Hippocampal MR density was positively related to food availability, while hepatic MR density was unrelated to any measure of food availability or sociality. Taken together, my results suggest that food availability and social cues both influence corticosterone secretion and corticosterone receptor density in captive and free-living white-crowned sparrows. These data support previous findings that food availability alters corticosterone release and receptor density, but also demonstrate that social cues alone can alter corticosterone secretion and receptor density.

Lastly, the LC equipment is usually expensive, and some of the required precision components are easily damaged. Hence, there is an urgent demand for new, effective, and economical methods for the fabrication of CCA or HEA coatings with enhanced mechanical properties. Spark plasma sintering (SPS), a promising method to fabricate high-performance materials, can rapidly consolidate powders to high density by applying pressure and passing an electric pulse current within a short soaking time; therefore, SPS has recently become a widespread approach for preparing HEA and CCA bulk materials [21-24]. However, to date, there are almost no reports concerning the investigation of CCA coatings prepared by SPS. The hypothetical advantages for fabricating CCA coatings by SPS can be summarized as follows. First, SPS is applicable to an extensive number of powder types (such as mechanically alloyed powders [12,21,22] and dry mixed powders [23,24]). Second, the features of quick heating and solid-phase sintering can ensure a low dilution ratio in the coatings, and a sound diffusional and metallurgical bond can be formed at the interface of the clad layer/substrate under the combined effects of the spark discharge, electric field/current, and high temperature/pressure, which results in the fast and efficient diffusion of various elements in the SPS process [25,26]. Third, the oxidation of the powders can be effectively avoided because the whole sintering process is performed in a vacuum, which ensures the designed coating compositions are obtained. Fourth, the SPS equipment is relatively inexpensive and easy to maintain. Furthermore, it is important to note that the combined effects of the spark discharge and high temperature/pressure during SPS, resulting in the fast and efficient diffusion of various elements, can facilitate the precipitation of fine-scale second phases, which can fully ensure the realization of precipitation strengthening in the CCA coatings. AlxCoCrCuFeNi was one of the first reported HEA systems [27-29], in which the Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi (further termed Al0.5) HEA with moderate properties has received particular attention [30-35]. Several original studies have shown that the Al0.5 HEA contained only two simple FCC solid solution phases in the as-cast state under the effect of high mixing entropy and sluggish cooperative diffusion [27,29,32]. However, an increasing number of recent studies have shown that the configurational entropy of the Al0.5 HEA was insufficient to fully stabilize the disordered solid solution phases against enthalpic effects, which resulted in the occurrence of phase decomposition and intermetallic phase precipitation, even when the material was quickly cooled to room temperature [36-40]. Therefore, the Al0.5 alloy is more appropriated classified as a CCA rather than an HEA. In addition, the formation nature of the L12 phase in the Al0.5 CCA is still disputed. One of the original studies suggested that the formation of the L12 phase resulted from the complete ordering of the dendritic FCC phase [27].

In practice, detection probability varies between observers and with environmental conditions. Therefore, line transects must be sampled repeatedly across space and time to obtain sufficient sightings for reliable estimates. This requires extensive resources. Despite these limitations, line transects have been widely adopted for estimating wildlife abundance because the associated software (Distance, http://www.distancemodelling.com/) is relatively easy to use, has no inherent bias, and provides a wide array of statistical options to accommodate different study designs and objectives. Line transects are also highly adaptable to ground-based surveys and a variety of sampling regimes. They are therefore favored by many practitioners, even though the resulting estimates may be more variable than those obtained from traditional aerial surveys (Robinson and Buckland, 2009). Finally, the technique can be applied to any animal species for which individuals can be distinguished, but is best suited to large mammals (Buckland et al., 2001). Tracking is the art of following spoor or other evidence of passage by animals, usually for hunting purposes. It has been practiced since prehistory and is still widely employed today. While tracking skills have evolved through experience rather than formal training, the underlying principles are easily taught and learned. Tracking is a powerful tool for understanding animal behavior and ecology, and is increasingly being recognized as an effective means of studying elusive species in wild environments (Kruuk, 1993; Kays et al., 2010). The technique is particularly well-suited to large carnivores, small ungulates, and primates, although it can be adapted to a wider range of taxa depending on the quality of available sign. Tracking is becoming increasingly popular among researchers working in developing countries, as it offers several advantages over conventional methods such as capture-recapture studies and direct observations (Ruggiero et al., 2010). First, it is non-invasive, meaning that there is no need to disturb animals or their habitats. Second, it can be done remotely, allowing for greater flexibility in study design and implementation. Third, it can be used to track multiple individuals simultaneously, providing valuable insights into social dynamics and group composition. Fourth, it can be used to assess habitat suitability and resource selection, helping to inform management decisions. And finally, it is relatively inexpensive compared to other techniques, making it accessible to researchers working on tight budgets (Feldhamer et al., 2015). In short, tracking offers a unique set of advantages that make it an attractive option for researchers interested in studying wildlife populations in developing countries. However, its potential remains largely untapped, and further research is needed to better understand how tracking can be used to advance knowledge about the ecology and conservation of threatened species. The socioeconomic gradient in obesity prevalence is particularly striking when examining the relationship between county-level poverty rates and obesity rates. In the United States, the correlation between county-level poverty rates and obesity rates is strong and inverse, meaning that counties with higher poverty rates tend to have higher obesity rates (Bentley et al., 2018). This is not unique to the United States, as similar patterns have been observed in other developed countries (Hruschka, 2012; Smith, 2017). The mechanisms underlying this relationship are complex and multifaceted, but several factors are thought to contribute, including limited access to healthy food options, lack of access to safe and affordable physical activity opportunities, and higher levels of stress and socioeconomic disadvantage (Hruby and Hu, 2015). Another important factor contributing to the rise in obesity is the changing food environment. Over the past several decades, the availability and marketing of unhealthy foods has increased, particularly in low-income and minority communities (Guthrie et al., 2013; Powell et al., 2013). The proliferation of fast food restaurants, convenience stores, and other retailers selling unhealthy foods has made it easier for individuals to access and consume high-calorie, high-fat, and high-sugar foods (Powell et al., 2013). Additionally, the rise of online food delivery and meal kit services has made it easier for individuals to have unhealthy foods delivered directly to their doors (Katz et al., 2014). The built environment also plays a critical role in shaping physical activity levels and obesity rates. Communities with limited access to safe and accessible parks, sidewalks, and bike lanes, as well as those with high levels of traffic congestion and air pollution, are more likely to have higher obesity rates (Sallis et al., 2016). The lack of walkability and bikeability in many communities, particularly in low-income and minority neighborhoods, can make it difficult for individuals to engage in regular physical activity, contributing to higher obesity rates (Frank et al., 2012). Furthermore, the rise of screen-based entertainment and sedentary behaviors has also contributed to the increase in obesity. The proliferation of smartphones, tablets, and other devices has led to increased screen time, which is associated with decreased physical activity and increased risk of obesity (Hinkley et al., 2012). In conclusion, the rise in obesity is a complex issue with multiple contributing factors. And there was old Simon, the piper, waiting for them on the bank, fuming and raging, not because the water was running high, but because he couldn't get across to give the young laird what for. And then he remembered how this little girlie had saved him from getting thrashed, and how she had boxed his ears herself instead. It all came back to him now: how he had caught sight of some of the big fellows of the village school fishing in his pool; how he had rushed off to drive them away; how they had taken no notice of his orders; and how he had hurled himself upon them, and how they had scattered before his fury. But one of them had struck him from behind, and he would have been beaten up badly but for the appearance of this wee girlie, who had taken the side of the big boys against him, and had laid about her right and left with a hazel stick till the enemy took to their heels. Then she had proceeded to deal with the young laird in the same fashion, calling him names in the vernacular which he could never afterwards remember without a blush of shame. She had threatened to report him to his mother and to his father, and had only let him go after extracting from him a solemn promise to fish no more alone in the dangerous waters of the burn. That was the day he had begun to admire the pluck and spirit of this little daughter of his father's retainer, and to seek her company whenever he could. Now, however, he had come back to find her grown into a young woman, and apparently determined to keep him at arm's length. Yet he felt sure that if he only knew how to set about it, he could win her over again, and they would resume their friendship where they had left off so long ago. So he began to laugh, and held out his hand, saying, "Come along, Marrion, don't be stiff. You are quite right to teach me manners, but it's rather late in the day to begin." She did not take his hand or smile. Instead, she said quietly, "You will excuse me, sir; I am busy here just now, and must ask you to wait until I am free." Her eyes met his steadily, and something in their expression made him feel uncomfortable. He had never seen her like this before. There had always been a certain reserve in her manner, but it had been due to shyness rather than pride. This was different. As he looked at her, he wondered if he had offended her somehow. Certainly he had spoken lightly enough, but he had meant nothing by it except friendliness. Perhaps he had gone too far in addressing her by her Christian name. He resolved to make amends. "I am sorry, Miss Marrion," he said humbly; "I didn't mean to offend you. I thought perhaps that as we used to be great friends when we were children, you wouldn't mind my speaking to you as I did. If I have done wrong, please forgive me." She was mollified, but still suspicious. "It's a lang time since we played thegither," she replied guardedly. "Things are different now." He smiled pleasantly. "Not so very different," he answered. "We're older certainly, and perhaps wiser, but I hope not much worse. We can still be friends, I suppose?" She eyed him warily. "Friends, yes," she assented; "but not playfellows any more." His face clouded. "Why not?" he asked quickly.

Simulations within our study, suggested the minimum required structural change that allowed access to the S2 site was the 'unplugging' of the linker between the first two LNR modules (LNRA and LNRB) from a position over the S2 site in the HD domain. However, deletion of the LNRA and the LNRA:B linker region was not sufficient to allow cleavage in vitro; removal of the LNRB was also required for S2 cleavage within these experiments [21]. The heterodimerization domain is so-called due to an initial cleavage event carried out by a furin-like convertase at an S1 site located in an exposed loop of the domain. This S1 cleavage occurs during processing and transport of the Notch receptor to the cell membrane and, whilst it does not disrupt the core structure of the HD domain (or play any role in receptor signal activation), the domain is effectively divided into two non-covalently associated N- and C-terminal subunits, HD-N and HD-C. The stable core structure of the HD domain comprises a kinked 1-helix and the 4-strand [27], structural elements that actually derive from the different HD-N and HD-C subunits. Mutations that lie within these structural elements or nearby, known for their activating status within the hN1 associated disease T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) [6], have been shown to increase heterodimer dissociation (relative to wild-type) in native or mildly denaturing conditions [28]. Interestingly, in the context of hN2, these mutated constructs failed to increase heterodimer dissociation upon EDTA treatment [40]. This highlights crucial differences between the hN1 and hN2 receptors. However, whilst these differences in chemical stability of the mutations within hN1 and hN2 are clear, little is known about their effect on mechanical stability, which is key if the mechanotransduction hypothesis is true. Given the increasing evidence for a role for mechanical force in the Notch signal activation mechanism, we investigate the effect of six mutations, related to those shown previously to destabilise the HD domain within hN1, [6,39] on the mechanical stability of recombinant hN2-NRR (hN2 residues 1425-1672). Five of the six mutations are within the core region of the HD domain (Fig. 1A; made up of the 4 strand and 1 helix) which has previously been shown to be a critical region for HD domain stability [27] and at the interface between the HD-N and HD-C. Since our model is the hN2 protein, mutations were chosen based on the sequence homology between hN1 and hN2, ensuring mutation at conserved positions (Fig. 1B). The mutated recombinant hN2-NRR proteins generated are hence: F1565S, L1566P, L1573P, V1623D, I1627N and A1647P (equivalent to the F1593S, L1594P, L1601P, V1677D, I1681N and A1702P in hN1; Fig. 1C). Three of these mutations (L1566P, V1623D and I1627N) have recently been biochemically analysed, revealing fundamental differences between the N1 and N2 NRR [40].

The moment I stepped through the towering gates of the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library, I was filled with a profound sense of nostalgia and appreciation. The air was thick with history, carrying the weight of ideals and decisions that shaped a nation. It is a place where one comes not just to learn about a former president, but to relive the triumphs and trials of an era defined by resilience and optimism. The meticulously kept grounds, overlooking the spectacular Thousand Oaks, are a testament to not only Reagan's legacy but also to the spirit of America. As I roamed through the exhibits, each artifact seemed to whisper stories of yesteryear. The beautifully restored Air Force One fuselage stood majestic, a tangible representation of Reagan's globetrotting efforts to bolster democracy and fend off the clouds of tyranny. Standing inside that aircraft, I could almost feel the pulse of a world leader navigating through turbulent times. The photographs lining the walls captured defining moments-the fall of the Berlin Wall, the cheers of crowds, the unity of purpose that gripped the nation during his presidency. I was particularly struck by the section dedicated to the era's remarkable advancements in technology and how they were harnessed for the greater good. The "Star Wars" initiative, while debated by many, showed us the ambitious drive to protect our homeland. How invigorating to witness the vision of a future unfettered from the grasp of fear! The ideas and dreams brought forth during those years were audacious, but they invigorated a country hungry for a sense of purpose. What resonated with me most, however, were the speeches-those iconic words filled with hope and determination. I stood transfixed by the audio stations playing snippets of Reagan's addresses. His voice, calm yet firm, spoke of "A Shining City on a Hill," a metaphor that still serves as a beacon for those seeking freedom and prosperity. It was a reminder that, no matter how dark the times appear, hope persists. Indeed, it was these very speeches that rallied a generation and instilled in them a faith in their country and its boundless potential. Reflecting on the current political landscape, I can't help but feel a disheartening contrast between those ideals and the continuous bickering we now witness within our own government. The sense of unity that characterized the 1980s seems more elusive than ever. President Reagan understood the importance of collaboration and teamwork, something that's often lost in today's hyperpartisan climate. Perhaps, we need to revisit those principles that governed his presidency, allowing empathy to bridge the chasms that separate us. The lessons from his time loom large and are as relevant now as they were then. And yet, as I walked back through the picturesque gardens, I felt a renewed spark of inspiration. The fight for liberty and justice persists; the echoes of Reagan's words remind us that this endeavor is neither easy nor completed. Each one of us has a role to play in shaping future narratives, ensuring that the ideals of freedom, opportunity, and compassion endure. America stands strong on the principles it was built upon, but it takes courageous hearts to keep the flame alive. In conclusion, visiting the Reagan Library was not simply a journey through the past, but a clarion call for our present and future. Let us draw upon that spirit of unwavering resolve and together forge ahead, remembering that we are all stewards of this great legacy that we now share as citizens of this vibrant nation.

Then, the moving mirror of the interferometer is relocated at a next position and the whole process of excitation and measuring is repeated. The shaft of the spear snaps short across, as the thick unwieldy body turns slowly over, and the boar shivers out his life on the smooth sward, soft and green as velvet, that exists nowhere but in Britain. The dream changes. The boar has disappeared, and the woodland gives place to a fair and smiling plain. Vast herds of shaggy red cattle are browsing contentedly, with their wide-horned heads to the breeze; flocks of sheep dot the green undulating pastures, that stretch away towards the sea. A gull turns its white wing against the clear blue sky; there is a hum of insects in the air, mingled with the barking of dogs, the lowing of kine, the laughter of women, and other sounds of peace, abundance, and content. A child is playing round its mother's knee - a child with frank bold brow and golden curls, and large blue fearless eyes, sturdy of limb, quick of gesture, fond, imperious, and wilful. The mother, a tall woman, with a beautiful but mournful face, is gazing steadfastly at the sea, and seems unconscious of her boy's caresses, who is fondling and kissing the white hand he holds in both his own. Her large shapely figure is draped in snowy robes that trail upon the ground, and massive ornaments of gold encircle arms and ankles. At intervals she looks fondly down upon the child; but ever her face resumes its wistful expression, as she fixes her eyes again upon the sea. There is nothing of actual sorrow in that steadfast gaze - still less of impatience, or anger, or discontent. Memory is the prevailing sentiment portrayed - memory, tender, absorbing, irresistible, without a ray of hope, but without a shadow of self-reproach. There is a statue of Mnemosyne at one of the entrances to the Forum that carries on its marble brow the same crushing weight of thought; that wears on its delicate features, graven into the saddest of beauty by the Athenian's chisel, just such a weary and despondent look. Where can the British child have seen those tasteful spoils of Greece that deck her imperial mistress? And yet he thinks of that statue as he looks up in his mother's face. But the fair tall woman shivers and draws her robe closer about her, and taking the child in her arms, nestles his head against her bosom and covers him over with her draperies, for the wind blows moist and chill, the summer air is white with driving mist, huge shapeless forms loom through the haze, and the busy sounds of life and laughter have subsided into the stillness of a vast and dreary plain. The child and its mother have disappeared, but a tall, strong youth, just entering upon manhood, with the same blue eyes and fearless brow, is present in their stead. He is armed for the first time with the weapons of a warrior.

Given our existing knowledge of the exquisite region-specific patterns of brain atrophy, glucose hypometabolism, spread of tau and amyloid burden in AD progression, we asked whether the ApoE mu 4 allele, as the largest genetic determinant of AD risk, also elicits similar brain-region specific changes in MCI which often precedes Alzheimer's (Chan et al., 2003; Cope et al., 2018; Drzezga et al., 2005; Grijalva-Eternod et al., 2012; Knopman et al., 2014; Mecca et al., 2018; Misra et al., 2009; Mosconi et al., 2009). Functional neuroimaging is a valuable non-invasive tool to monitor disease progression and brain metabolic changes in various neurodegenerative disease, including AD, Parkinson's disease and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (Chen et al., 2016; Dickens et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2016; Niethammer et al., 2012). In particular, FDG-PET imaging allows for the characterization of ApoE mu 4-mediated phenotypic changes in AD and MCI, including its association with glucose hypometabolism (Rosen et al., 2013). Cross sectional studies including work by Reiman et al. have used FDG imaging to establish the dose-dependent effect of ApoE mu 4 on hypometabolism in non-demented adults (Reiman et al., 1996). Longitudinal studies such as work by Thambisetty et al. used oxygen-15 PET to compare changes in cerebral blood flow in 29 non-demented ApoE mu 4 carriers and 65 non-carriers (Thambisetty et al., 2010a). They found greater longitudinal decline in cerebral blood flow in ApoE mu 4 carriers compared to non-carriers in the temporal, parietal, and frontal cortices. While these studies are important in establishing the association of the ApoE mu 4 allele with increased glucose hypometabolism, these studies were performed in the context of normal aging. These existing studies, including work by Thambisetty and Reiman, have helped to show ApoE mu 4 dose-dependent associations between cerebral blood flow decline and hypometabolism, both validated readouts of AD (Reiman et al., 1996; Thambisetty et al., 2010a). However, there exists a clear lack of >4 years longitudinal FDG studies, which are critical for studying the role of ApoE mu 4 in increasing the risk of disease over time. In contrast to previous studies, a up to 84 month (median 72 month) follow up period was used in the present study with partial volume correction (PVC) to minimize inaccuracies in PET measurement due to changes in tissue volume or low spatial resolution. Partial volume effect is particularly a concern in small brain regions or in longitudinal studies in which atrophy can lead to an underestimation or overestimation of the true changes in quantitative PET (Jonasson et al., 2017). Several recent analyses have highlighted the importance of correcting for partial volume effects in longitudinal brain PET studies (Dukart and Bertolino, 2014; Fouquet et al., 2009).
