Sato et al. [4] melted single layers of Ti-6Al-4V powder on to stainless steel substrates at 50 nbar. At a very low scan speed of 10 mm/s, they observed a surface roughness (Ra = 0.40 1/2m) which was significantly lower than the most abundant powder diameter of 35 1/2m and the largest powder diameter of 88 1/2m. Imaging at 60 frames per second (fps) revealed that no spatter was produced from the melt pool at this low scan speed. At 100 mm/s, the surface roughness (Ra = 25 1/2m) and spatter had both increased to resemble the PBF process more closely. The authors concluded that, at sub-atmospheric pressures, the sputter free process at low laser scan speeds improves the surface roughness. Matthews et al. [5] investigated the depletion of metal powder particles (denudation) in the zone immediately surrounding the solidified track, which can affect the porosity and surface roughness of built parts. The width of the denuded region was measured after scanning laser tracks across layers of Ti-6Al-4V powder in a vacuum chamber. The width increased as the pressure was reduced from 1 bar down to 13 mbar, and was attributed to the increased velocity of the evaporation plume from the melt pool and the associated increase in particles entrained towards the melted track by the inward flow of the ambient gas. The width then decreased from 13 mbar to a local minimum at 3 mbar, before increasing again as the pressure was further reduced to 660 1/2bar. The decrease and subsequent increase in the denuded zone width was attributed to the onset of molecular (or rarified) flow and the outward expansion of the evaporation plume counter-acting and eventually dominating any inward flow of the ambient gas. An alternative explanation involved asymmetrical heating of particles close to the laser spot which were then propelled away by the vapour flux generated, transferring momentum to remove adjacent powder particles. However, this second explanation was not preferred because smaller diameter particles were preferentially removed below 3 mbar, whereas asymmetrical heating should affect particles of all diameters equally. High-speed images were recorded close to the melt pool at atmospheric pressure using a localized jet of inert gas, and so this mechanism at lower pressures was not confirmed. Laser welding at sub-atmospheric pressure is well established in the literature [6] and has received increased attention recently for joining thick materials using solid state fibre and disk lasers. The penetration of a keyhole weld is typically twice that achieved at atmospheric pressure, with an associated reduction in voids in the weld seam and an increase in weld pool stability. The deep, narrow weld is similar to that achieved with electron beam welding but without the production of harmful x-rays associated with that technique.

"I seek shelter from this coming storm," the traveler began, his voice even and sure, yet carrying the weight of untold miles and unending vigilance. "The night is cruel and offers no kindness to those without a hearth." The host nodded, gesturing to the ember-glow of a nearby hearth, where flames danced languidly upon aged logs of yew and ash. "It's a bitter wind, true enough. You're welcome to share what warmth we have, though there's little else to give," came the reply, each word carrying the cadence of cautious hospitality. "More than enough," remarked the traveler with a grateful inclination of the head. He settled himself near the fire, allowing the warmth to permeate weary bones and soothe the chill that had seeped beneath his skin. Though words were few and they sat in the quiet company of their own thoughts, an unspoken understanding passed between them-the silent comradery of those who carried the heavy burden of living midst tumult and want. Yet as the storm grew in ferocity, rattling the shutters and sending torrents against the wooden walls of that solitary refuge, the traveler knew that in the morning he would resume his journey. The path ahead remained fraught with uncertainty, his mission ever bound by duty and the unseen threads of loyalty that wove him inexorably into the fabric of this land.

Though stretched and distorted by the technique used to spot them (an intervening galaxy cluster was used as a "gravitational lens"), the newfound galaxies, Windhorst's team assures us, resemble our own Milky Way. They are seen as they existed more than 13 billion years ago, within 1 billion years of the Big Bang.Practically side-by-side in time, discovered in separate observations made as part of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, are compact but bright objects known as quasars. These galaxies-to-be shine brilliantly because, researchers believe, each has a gargantuan black hole at its core, whose mass is equal to a billion suns or more, all packed into a region perhaps smaller than our solar system. The resulting gravity pulls in nearby gas. The material is accelerated to nearly the speed of light, superheated, and swallowed. The process is not entirely efficient, and there is a byproduct: An enormous amount of energy - radio waves, X-rays and regular light - hyper-illuminates the whole scene. Quasars also seem to be surrounded by halos of dark matter, a cryptic and unseen component of all galaxies. Co-existing around and amongst all this, researchers are coming to realize, is a collapsing region of stars and gas as big or larger than our galaxy.It was no coincidence that the announcements of the two findings - distant quasars and normal galaxies - were made together at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society (AAS) Jan. 9. Co-evolution was on the minds of the discoverers.Among co-evolution's significant impacts is its ability to render mostly moot a longstanding chicken-and-egg question in astronomy: Which came first, the galaxy or the black hole?"How about both?" Windhorst asks. "You could actually have the galaxy form simultaneously around a growing black hole."Urry, who was not involved in either finding but was asked to analyze them, explained it this way: "We believe that galaxies and quasars are very intimately connected, that in fact quasars are a phase of galaxy evolution. In our current picture, as every galaxy forms and collapses, it has a brief quasar phase." So when a quasar goes dormant, what's left are the things we associate with a normal galaxy - stars and gas swirling around a central and hidden pit of matter. Quasars are cagey characters, however. (The term is short for quasi-stellar radio source; astronomers first mistook the objects for stars within our galaxy in the early 1960s.) When one is firing, its brightness can exceed a thousand normal galaxies. The quasar outshines its entire host galaxy so significantly that scientists have not been able to see what's really causing all the commotion. That veil is lifting as you read this, however, as telescopic vision extends ever backward in time and data is fed into powerful new computer models.

To claim that rock has died would mean that we could find no evidence of life left within it, and that seems to be an impossible task. There is always going to be someone somewhere who is playing rock music that is new, exciting, fresh and meaningful. It may be harder to find, it may be less popular, it may be less profitable, but it exists nonetheless. Take Radiohead, for example. When they first came out, their debut album was pretty good, but nothing spectacular. They had a few hits, and were considered by some to be one-hit wonders. Then they released "OK Computer." This album blew everyone away. It was a landmark record, and still remains one of the best records of the 90s, if not the entire history of rock. A band that was once dismissed as another British pop group suddenly became the toast of the town. With their next release, "Kid A," they took an even bigger risk, releasing an album that was entirely electronic and ambient, and contained very little rock at all. This was a huge gamble, and it paid off. People loved it. Even people who hated it loved it because it meant that a band had taken such a big chance. They followed that up with "Amnesiac," which was basically a bunch of songs that didn't fit onto Kid A. It wasn't quite as successful, but it still got rave reviews and sold well. Their latest album, Hail to the Thief, was a return to rock and roll. It is more guitar driven, and contains more songs with vocals. It too was hailed as a great work, and continues to sell well. What makes this important? It shows us that bands CAN take risks. Bands CAN do whatever they want. If they are true artists, they can follow their muse wherever she leads them, and they will be rewarded for it. Radiohead are now considered one of the best bands in the world, and rightly so. They have shown us that you don't need to write formulaic pop songs to be successful, and that you can push boundaries without losing credibility or sales. Radiohead is just one example. There are many others, including Wilco, The White Stripes, Beck, Bjork, Sigur Ros, Coldplay, Muse, Travis, Gomez, Ben Harper, Death Cab For Cutie, etc. These are all bands that are pushing the envelope in some way, and are being rewarded for it. They are selling records, getting airplay, winning awards, and gaining critical acclaim. So while it may be harder to find good music these days, it is still out there. You just have to look a little harder. And when you do find it, it is all the more rewarding. Now, let's talk about irony, sarcasm, wit and kitsch. These are all things that have become increasingly prevalent in our culture, and especially in our music. I think that this is a direct result of the postmodern condition. We live in a world where everything has been done before, and there is nothing new under the sun. As a result, we have become cynical and jaded. We can no longer take anything seriously, because we know that it has all been done before. This has led to a rise in irony, sarcasm, wit and kitsch. Irony is when you say one thing but mean the opposite. Sarcasm is when you use irony to mock someone or something. Wit is when you use irony or sarcasm in a clever way. Kitsch is when you use irony or sarcasm in a tacky or tasteless way.

"Nanny," mused Grandma, "there's a good many years difference in our ages but there's only one woman I ever loved as I love you. I think I might have loved your mother but she died the very first year your father brought her here. And she was ailing when she came. The other woman that meant so much to me used to go traveling too. I always helped her with her packing. Then one day she packed and went away, never to come back." "Was that Cynthia Churchill?" Nan asked gently. "Yes - Cynthia. She was dearer than a sister to me, and neither of us dreamed that a whole wide world would divide us." "Why did she go, Grandma?" "Because a Green Valley man well-nigh broke her heart." "A Green Valley man did - that? Oh, dear! And here I have been hoping that some day I might marry a Green Valley man myself." "Nanny, I expect I'm old and foolish but I've been hoping and hoping that you'd marry a home boy and fearing you'd meet up with some one on your travels who would take you away from us forever. It would be hard to see you go." The last sunbeam had faded away and golden twilight filled the room. Outside little day noises were dying out. "Grandma dear, don't you worry about me. I intend to marry a Green Valley man if possible. But even if I didn't I'd always come back to Green Valley." "No, you wouldn't. You couldn't, any more than Cynthia could. Cynthia loved this town better even than you love it. Yet she is lying under strange stars in a foreign land, far from her old home. Her father, they say, is dying in California. I suppose the old Churchill place will go now unless Cynthia's son comes back to take it over. But that isn't likely." "Why - did Cynthia Churchill leave a son?" wondered Nanny. "Yes. He must be a few years older than you. He was born and raised in India. 'Tisn't likely he'd come to Green Valley now that he's a man grown. Still, if Joshua Churchill dies out there in California, that boy will come into all his grandfather's property." "Well," Nanny stood up and walked to the window from which she could see the fine old home of the Churchills, "if any one willed me a lovely old place like that Churchill homestead I'd come from the moon to claim it, let alone India."

The development of a robust and computationally-efficient method for fibre profile extraction is crucial for the characterization of CFRC microstructures. In recent years, various image processing techniques have been employed for fibre profile extraction, including thresholding, edge detection, and feature extraction algorithms. However, these techniques often struggle to accurately identify fibre cross-sections in the presence of noise, artefacts, and fibre overlap. Moreover, the complexity of CFRC microstructures, characterized by varying fibre orientations, diameters, and coating thicknesses, further exacerbates the challenge of fibre profile extraction. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel approach that leverages the strengths of machine learning algorithms in image analysis. Specifically, a deep learning-based approach is developed to segment individual fibre cross-sections in each image of the sequence. The proposed approach utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, which has been shown to be effective in image segmentation tasks. The CNN is trained on a dataset of labelled images, where each image is annotated with fibre cross-sections. The trained CNN is then used to segment fibre cross-sections in the entire image sequence. Once fibre cross-sections are identified, the next step is to link individual fibre cross-sections through the sequence of images to construct 3D fibre profiles. This is achieved by developing a novel fibre tracking algorithm that utilizes the segmented fibre cross-sections as input. The algorithm employs a combination of spatial and intensity-based features to link fibre cross-sections across adjacent images. The fibre tracking algorithm is designed to be robust to fibre overlap, noise, and artefacts, ensuring accurate reconstruction of 3D fibre profiles. The proposed method is validated using a dataset of CFRC specimens imaged using automated mechanical polishing-based serial sectioning. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in extracting accurate 3D fibre profiles, even in the presence of complex fibre orientations and overlap. The extracted fibre profiles are then used to quantify fibre misalignment, which is a critical parameter in predicting the mechanical properties of CFRCs. Furthermore, the proposed method is compared with existing fibre profile extraction techniques, including thresholding and edge detection algorithms. The results show that the proposed approach outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. The proposed method is also shown to be robust to variations in image quality, noise, and artefacts, making it a reliable tool for characterizing CFRC microstructures. In conclusion, this study presents a novel approach for extracting 3D fibre profiles from a sequence of greyscale images of CFRC specimens. The proposed method leverages the strengths of machine learning algorithms in image analysis and fibre tracking to accurately extract fibre profiles. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in characterizing CFRC microstructures and quantifying fibre misalignment. The proposed method has the potential to accelerate the development of stronger and more consistent microstructures for next-generation CFRCs.

Such reflections lay heavy on the hearts of those few souls who, amid the rush of progress, paused to consider the implications of their relentless march. Yet, humanity's endeavors rarely heed such moral deliberations when animated by the potent allure of empire and prosperity. Thus, the pioneers, in their resolute drive westward, regarded their actions not as transgressions but as a noble part of a divinely ordained expansion. They perceived themselves as bearers of civilization, adventurers taming untamed lands, and establishing realms where commerce, industry, and culture could flourish unchecked by the antiquity of wild existence. Across the once-silent wilderness now arose a new clamor-the persistent clamour of saw and hammer, mingled with the shouts of men forging futures with their toil. The solitary screech of the eagle was supplanted by the whistle of locomotives, heralding the ingenious encroachment of steel rails that cut the land with enterprise's keen edge. Smoke pillars rose from settlements like offerings to modernity, their factories spewing forth both goods and the acrid breath of transformation. Nature, humbled but unyielding, surrendered its treasures grudgingly. Fortunes lay embedded within the soil, luring multitudes with promises of riches wrested from its depths. The varied lands, from fertile plains to mineral-rich mountains, proffered their bounty. As forests dwindled, rivers, too, changed their courses, constrained by man's designs, channeling power to growing cities that glittered like new constellations across the continental expanse. Yet, amid the triumphant progress, echoes of what was lost lingered-a mere whisper of winds through ghostly groves and the rustling of leaves carried to lands where memories of their existence will fade into myth. The poignant legacy of those who once roamed freely now became inscribed in legends that future storytellers might recount by the fireside, their tales filtered through generations. Nevertheless, these movements of change crept inevitably across time, shifting societies as a river shapes the canyon. The new settlers brought their cultures, their customs, irrevocably altering the social landscape. Churches and schools rose amid the burgeoning towns, promising enlightenment and moral guidance, yet also fostering an immutable sense of separation from those whose lands they claimed. Though the pioneers envisioned a destiny manifest in unending growth and prosperity, the spectres of reckoning lay entwined with this vision. Could they reconcile the advance of one civilization with the quiet erasure of another? Would their descendents grasp the complexities of such an inheritance, woven with both glory and grave wrongs? Amidst these questions, life continued its relentless march. Children played in streets hewn from the wilderness, their laughter ringing where once only silence reigned. Farmers tilled fields under vast skies that had watched the passage of a thousand seasons, indifferent to the players below. The winds surged anew, scattering both seeds and stories, blending past and present into an inextricable tapestry of humanity's rise and nature's relentless endurance. Thus, the land, though forever altered, remained witness to the unfolding saga of existence-a testament to both human striving and the enduring spirit of the vanquished wild.

'I'm innocent until proven guilty, and I am innocent,' Salim told the AP during an interview at his home in January. Salim was arrested in October after authorities said DNA taken from under Ballman's fingernails matched his. Investigators believe Salim lured Ballman to his house with a fake. Craigslist ad soliciting a masseuse. Authorities say Ballman, who was desperate for money, responded to the ad because she wanted to buy a crib for her soon-to-be born child. A coroner determined Ballman died of a drug overdose, but it's unclear if she willingly took the heroin or if someone injected it into her body. Salim says he met Ballman only once, when she stopped by his house for just minutes to inquire about a painting. He says she never mentioned anything about being pregnant. 'She looked like a teenager, not somebody who could have children,' he said. 'That's why it shocked me.' Salim grew up in Karachi, Pakistan, and moved to the United States in 1998, where he received his medical degree from West Virginia University School of Medicine. He completed his residency at Akron General Medical Center in 2004 and started working as an emergency room physician at Knox Community Hospital in Mount Vernon in 2005. At the time of Ballman's death, Salim had worked for more than six years at Knox Community Hospital, where he was known for his affable personality. 'Ali always had a smile on his face, always seemed happy-go-lucky,' said Scott Bowman, a hospital paramedic. 'Everybody liked him.' But there were signs of trouble. Salim was fired in June 2012 after failing to show up for work several times, said Bruce Whitehead, chief executive officer of Knox Community Hospital. Whitehead said he didn't know whether Salim's absences were related to Ballman's disappearance, since police hadn't yet identified Salim as a suspect. Salim had other issues. On Aug. 30, 2011, he was pulled over by the State Highway Patrol for driving erratically. To cherish someone so deeply that you have to release them, to step back and allow them to walk their own journey, even if it terrifies you and brings your own world crashing down. As I stood by the window, watching the delicate dance of the autumn leaves falling to the earth, I realized the gravity of my decision. Each leaf twirling down was a reflection of my heart letting go, piece by piece, of the dreams and promises that we had spun together in the tapestry of our lives. Yet, I found solace in knowing that in doing so, I was loving him in the purest form I knew: unconditionally. Steven was my light, my muse, the very essence of my happiness, and yet I was seeing him dim before me like a candle flickering in the wind. We had built a life together on shared dreams and whispered secrets under moonlit skies. But now, as I looked at him, I saw a man wrestling with phantoms I could not chase away. Often, I pondered whether love, by its very nature, was meant to be eternal, or if it should be free to transform, shift, and evolve, even if it meant parting ways. The thought was like a jagged stone in my heart but necessary. True love, I have come to understand, is not possessive. It is brave and selfless, a force that rises above personal desire. Steven, in all his enigmatic grace, deserved to explore the depths of his soul, to conquer the shadows lurking within, free from the weight of my expectations and dreams. I owed him the freedom to rediscover himself, to emerge anew, even if it meant our paths would no longer converge as they once did. The echoes of our laughter, the moments we cherished, and the dreams we nurtured would remain as a testament to a love that was real, that was powerful beyond words. In time, perhaps, he would come to see that my decision had come from a place of profound adoration and respect for the person he was and the person he might yet become. I penned a letter, each word carefully chosen, a farewell not of sorrow but of gratitude. Gratitude for having known him, for having been loved by him, and for having shared in the wild, breathtaking adventure of our joined lives, even for a little while. I included a reminder, a silent wish, that he might find peace and clarity, that his battles would fade as dawn kissed the horizon, leaving only warmth and light in their wake. Steven Michael, my true love, my light, it is time to set you free. As I lay the letter down, I felt a strange sense of peace descend upon me. Love, after all, is not about clinging to what is familiar but about having the courage to embrace the unknown. It is about the release-the most poignant and profound act of love I could offer.

For example, the amount of knowledge that diffuses to a firm from its suppliers may vary depending on whether the suppliers are in the same closed firm group or are connected with different types of firms. However, the previous literature ignores such detailed characteristics of whole supply chain networks in the economy and instead identifies supply chain relations only through firms' engagement in trade (Kimura and Kiyota, 2006; Loof and Andersson, 2010; Van Biesebroeck, 2005), firms' subjective perceptions (Crespi et al., 2008a; Flynn et al., 2010), input-output tables at the industry level (Javorcik, 2004; Piermartini and Rubinova, 2014), or - at best - firms' direct supply chain partners (Belderbos et al., 2015; Bernard et al., 2014; Isaksson et al., 2016). The literature on social networks has emphasized the importance of considering the overall structure of networks (Granovetter, 2005). For example, Burt (1992) finds that actors who create bridging links between otherwise disconnected groups of actors - or across structural holes - have superior access to diverse information. This finding is related to the argument of Granovetter (1973) that weak ties to relatively less frequently met partners are instrumental for accessing new information because such links frequently extend beyond the immediate circle of densely interconnected strong ties among similar partners with similar shared information. In other words, network density may prevent active knowledge diffusion due to knowledge overlaps and redundancy among partners. However, structural holes and weak ties may not always be the key to knowledge diffusion. Other studies have found that dense networks within an organization in which actors are closely connected with one another but are not closely connected with outsiders can promote knowledge diffusion. The positive effect of dense networks most likely emerges in these studies because actors in these networks know one another well and thus trust new knowledge from each other (Ahuja, 2000; Phelps, 2010). This study adopts methods from social network analysis to examine how the structure of the entire supply chain network affects the knowledge diffusion manifested in innovations and productivity increases using a large firm-level panel dataset for the Japanese manufacturing sector that covers most firms within the country and major buyer-supplier relations. Following the literature, we test for knowledge diffusion by estimating whether the structure of supply chain networks positively affects productivity and innovation capability, as measured by sales per worker and the number of registered patents respectively. More specifically, we investigate how the density of a firm's ego network - or how frequently its supply chain partners transact with one another - affects its performance, which is the first time this subject has been addressed in the literature on knowledge diffusion through supply chain networks. The effects of ego network density have been studied by Ahuja (2000) and Phelps (2010) in research collaboration networks but not in supply chain networks. Ego network density may have both positive and negative effects on knowledge diffusion, as we argued above. Therefore, the net effect of the network density should be empirically examined.

As rain was falling, he turned up his pantaloons, turned up his coat collar, raised the umbrella, and joined the throng of hurrying pedestrians, homeward bound. Home! John had no home in the city. He had left his home behind - the modest, cheaply builded, scantily furnished and illy appointed home of his parents in the mountains - to come to the city to make his fortune. His home now was a "room" - merely a room among a multiplicity of similar rooms, in between the four angles of plastered walls. His remuneration as the lowest bookkeeper in the line of such functionaries was insufficient to purchase more than the most meager accommodations in a cheap boarding house up Diamond Alley way. This room in question was in an ancient brick and timber building, that, in its earlier days, was an architectural ornament in its stateliness compared to other business blocks; but by reason of the rapid striding of modern prosperity, it was long ago left in the vast shades that great fortunes had reared into iron and concrete, standing by. There were only two sides open to the light and air in this low and aged building - one in front and one on top. In between were three tiers of small dark rooms, one tier above the other, resembling very much the little cubes of a concentrated egg case. Two small paned windows looked drearily into them from the street, on each floor, with a smaller time-stained window in each resounding hallway. The inner rooms were lighted by abbreviated wells dug in from a skylight on the side adjoining the blank walls of a dizzy skyscraper. And cloudy and shadowy and dim and cheerless, indeed, was the light let in on the brightest of days, while on dull days it was nothing more than the semblance of a waning twilight; so that, if used in day time at all, a light were needed to make out and clearly discern any object within. In one of these dark and inodorous rooms, John Winthrope had his temporary abiding place. There were in it a cheap iron bed, with musty smelling tick, sheet and coverlets; a small oak-grained pine washstand, with such a wavy little mirror hanging over it, that one could not tell, in looking at himself in it, whether he were a Chinaman, a Greaser, or a crooked-faced Irishman toiling in the streets; a small bowl, for washing, and a correspondingly small pitcher, with water in it, sat upon the shaky stand; a cheap chair, a weak imitation of quartered oak, with many marks of usage all over it, stood by a little table, also with many marks of usage on it; a flowered carpet, faded, worn and fretted by the sure hand of wearing time, covered the floor, with here and there ragged spots of bareness to enhance the room's impoverishment.

Bird and Fryer (1991) used a similar approach to describe the decay stage of the cleaning process. They defined a specific time constant as the time required to reduce the mass of soil present by one-half. This constant was related to the flow rate and the nature of the soil. Theoretical models were also developed to describe the cleaning phenomenon. Nienow (1983) developed a simple model for describing the cleaning of particulate matter in turbulent stirred vessels. He assumed that the residence time distribution function of the solid particles follows a first-order kinetics. The overall removal rate was thus equal to the sum of the rates of each particle size fraction. However, this model only considers the erosion stage of the removal process. It does not consider the swelling step and the influence of chemical agents. Nienow's model was later extended by Sarioglu et al. (2010) who considered the impact of the swelling and decay stages of the cleaning process. They assumed that the swelling process was completed before the onset of the erosion stage. Moreover, they hypothesized that the decay stage did not affect the removal rate during the erosion period. The authors compared the predictions of their model with experimental data obtained using three different cleaning solutions. Good agreement between theory and experiments was observed. However, the model requires several fitting parameters and the hypothesis made on the swelling and decay stages might not always hold. More recently, a theoretical model considering all the steps involved in the cleaning process has been presented by Di Serio et al. (2014). The authors proposed a description of the whole cleaning process based on the balance of mass and momentum equations. They assumed that the erosion step is the controlling step of the cleaning process and that it occurs simultaneously with the swelling phase. Their model showed good agreement with experimental data for the removal of starch and egg white proteins. However, its predictive capabilities for other types of soils remain unknown. The aim of this work is to develop a comprehensive model for predicting the behaviour of any kind of soil under cleaning conditions. The objective is to provide a general framework that could be used to study the cleaning of any kind of soil without the need of having a detailed knowledge of the underlying mechanisms. In particular, the focus will be placed on the use of enzymes for the removal of protein-based soils. Enzymes are highly selective towards specific substrates and therefore may play a key role in the design of cleaning strategies. Moreover, they are biodegradable and therefore environmentally friendly. The proposed model is based on the balance of mass and momentum equations and considers the simultaneous occurrence of the swelling, erosion and decay phases of the cleaning process. The model includes terms accounting for the diffusive fluxes of the enzyme across the soil layers and for the irreversible adsorption/desorption of the enzyme onto/away from the soil particles. The model is validated against available literature data for the removal of bovine serum albumin (BSA) and ovalbumin (OVA) under different operating conditions. This paper presents the development of a comprehensive model for the prediction of the behaviour of any kind of soil under cleaning conditions. The model is able to predict the removal of any kind of soil and its validation is supported by available literature data for the removal of BSA and OVA under different operating conditions.

Although NDMMs are broadly conserved (Choe et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2018; Markov et al., 2016), inter- and intraspecific competition have driven the evolution of distinct response regimes (different levels of sensitivity to the same pheromone, or sensitivity to different pheromones) for the same phenotypes (Bose et al., 2014; Choe et al., 2012; Diaz et al., 2014; Falcke et al., 2018; Greene et al., 2016). In addition, distinct plastic phenotypes have evolved that are regulated by more complex ascaroside structures (Bose et al., 2012). In Pristionchus pacificus, a soil-associated nematode that is reliably found on scarab beetles (Figure 1A) (Herrmann et al., 2006, 2007; Sommer and McGaughran, 2013), an ascaroside dimer (dasc#1) that is not found in C. elegans regulates the development of a predatory mouth form (Bento et al., 2010; Bose et al., 2012; Sommer et al., 2017). Mouth-form plasticity represents an example of a morphological novelty that results in predatory behavior to exploit additional resources and kill competitors. Specifically, adult P. pacificus exhibit either a narrow stenostomatous (St) mouth (Figure 1B), which is restricted to bacterial feeding, or a wide eurystomatous (Eu) mouth with an extra denticle (Figure 1C), which allows for feeding on bacteria and fungi (Sanghvi et al., 2016), and predation on other nematodes (Wilecki et al., 2015). This type of phenotypic plasticity is distinct between direct, non-arrested development and indirect (dauer) development because the mouth form decision results in two alternative life history strategies in the adult (for review, see Sommer & Mayer, 2015). Recent studies in P. pacificus have begun to investigate the dynamics and succession of nematodes on decomposing beetle carcasses to better understand the ecological significance of mouth-form plasticity (Meyer et al., 2017). These studies revealed that on a carcass (Figure 1D), P. pacificus exits the dauer diapause to feed on microbes, and then re-enters dauer after food sources have been exhausted, displaying a "boom-and-bust" ecology (Meyer et al., 2017; Sommer and McGaughran, 2013). Presumably different stages of this succession comprise different ratios of juveniles and adults, and recognizing the age structure of a population as a juvenile could provide predictive value for adulthood. However, it is unknown whether the mouth-form decision is sensitive to crowding by different age classes (example of crowding by different age groups, Figure 1E). More broadly, whereas age classes are known to be important for population growth and density-dependent selection (Hastings, 2013; Charlesworth, 1994; 1972), their role in phenotypic plasticity has thus far been largely unexplored. Although nematodes have many experimental advantages, including easy laboratory culture and advanced genetic, genomic, and the aforementioned chemical tools, their small size has made investigations at the organismal level and in experimental ecology challenging. For example, no in vivo methodologies are currently available to label distinct populations without the need for transgenics, which is only available in select model organisms such as C. elegans, P. pacificus, and some of their relatives.

Canada was now in the possession of the British, and the settlers in our colonies along the great Atlantic seacoast, and on the frontier westward, were looking for a long spell of peace in which they might regain that which had been lost, or establish themselves in new localities which promised well. As already mentioned, Dave and Henry Morris were cousins, Henry being the older by several years. They lived in the little settlement of Will's Creek, Virginia, close to where the town of Cumberland stands to-day. The Morris household consisted of Dave's father, Mr. James Morris, who was a widower, and Mr. Joseph Morris, his wife Lucy, and their children, Rodney, several years older than Henry, who came next, and Nell, a girl of about six, who was the household pet. In years gone by Rodney had been a good deal of a cripple, but a surgical operation had done wonders for him and now he was almost as strong as any of the others. James Morris was a natural born trapper and fur trader, and when his wife died he left his son Dave in the care of his brother Joseph and wandered to the west, where he established a trading-post on the Kinotah, a small stream flowing into the Ohio River. This was at the time that George Washington, the future President of our country, was a young surveyor, and in the first volume of this series, entitled "With Washington in the West," I related how Dave fell in with Washington and became his assistant, and how, later on, Dave became a soldier to march under Washington during the disastrous Braddock campaign against Fort Duquesne. General Braddock's failure to bring the French to submission cost James Morris dearly. His trading-post was attacked and he barely escaped with his life. Dave likewise became a prisoner of the enemy, and it was only through the efforts of a friendly Indian named White Buffalo, and an old frontier acquaintance named Sam Barringford, that the pair escaped to a place of safety. War between France and England had then become a certainty. France was aided greatly by the Indians, and it was felt by the colonists that a strong blow must be struck and without delay. Expeditions against the French were organized, and in the second volume of the series, called "Marching on Niagara," are given the particulars of another campaign against Fort Duquesne (located where the city of Pittsburg, Penn., now stands) and then of the long and hard campaign against Fort Niagara. Dave and Henry were both in the contest, for they had joined the ranks of the Royal Americans, as the Colonial troops were called. With the fall of Fort Niagara the English came once again into possession of all the territory lying between the Great Lakes and the lower Mississippi.

Today's vote distracts us from our shared goal of direct negotiations that results in a secure Israel and an independent Palestine living side by side in peace and security." Palestinian leaders celebrated the vote. "This is a significant victory and sends a clear message to those who are trying to hold history and deny the rights of Palestinians that there are a majority of nations with conscience who refuse to be intimidated and blackmailed," said Hanan Ashrawi, a member of the Palestine Liberation Organization's Executive Committee, speaking by phone from Ramallah, in the West Bank. "The ones who voted negatively are isolating themselves along with Israel on the wrong side of justice and the law. And if the U.S. continues to threaten to boycott or withdrawal from organizations that recognizes Palestine it might find itself outside most global institutions with diminishing influence and standing," she said. Sabri Saidam, adviser to Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas, said, "This is a historic moment, a moment of jubilation on route to full recognition of Palestinian independence and self-determination, that's equally a call for reconsideration of positions to those wavering on the Security Council vote. "It is also a foundation stone for what's to come at the (Security Council) and other international organizations. Today's experience is a manifestation of ability of the international community to defy occupation and practically work towards ending it." The Israeli representative, Nimrod Barkan, addressing the meeting after the vote, called the decision "a tragedy for UNESCO" and "a great disservice to international law." UNESCO has now "adopted the science fiction version of reality by admitting a nonexistent state to the science organization," he said. In a statement, Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said, "This is a unilateral Palestinian maneuver which will bring no change on the ground but further removes the possibility for a peace agreement. This decision will not turn the Palestinian Authority into an actual state yet places unnecessary burdens on the route to renewing negotiations. Israel believes that the correct and only way to make progress in the diplomatic process with the Palestinians is through direct negotiations without preconditions." Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu referred to the vote during remarks at the start of the Knesset winter session. "Instead of sitting around the negotiating table," Netanyahu said, Palestinian leaders "have decided to make an alliance with Hamas and are carrying out one-sided endeavors in the U.N., including today. We will not sit with folded arms against these measures which are hurting Israel and are violating bluntly the most basic obligations the parties took in the peace process, to solve the conflict between us through negotiations. Sadly, during the time we are trying to form a Palestinian state with a peace agreement they are trying to form a state without an agreement."

There is no harm in wishing that, Michael; but it's as well that you should know the real state of the case, and as I cannot say what may happen to me, I do not wish to put off telling you any longer. I am not as strong and young as I once was, and maybe God will think fit to take me away before I have reached the threescore years and ten which He allows some to live. We should not put off doing to another time what can be done now, and so you see I wish to say what has been on my mind to tell you for many a day past, though I have not liked to say it, lest it should in any way grieve you. You promise me, Michael, you won't let it do that? You know how much I and granny and Nelly love you, and will go on loving you as much as ever." "I know you do, father, and so do granny and Nelly; I am sure they love me," said the boy gazing earnestly into Paul's face, with wonder and a shade of sorrow depicted on his own countenance. "That's true," said Paul. "But about what I was going to say to you. "My wife, who is gone to heaven, Nelly's mother, and I, never had another child but her. Your father, Michael, as true-hearted a seaman as ever stepped, had been my friend and shipmate for many a long year. We were bred together, and had belonged to the same boat fishing off this coast till we were grown men, when at last we took it into our heads to wish to visit foreign climes, and so we went to sea together. After knocking about for some years, and going to all parts of the world, we returned home, and both fell in love, and married. Your mother was an orphan, without kith or kin, that your father could hear of - a good, pretty girl she was, and worthy of him. "We made up our minds that we would stay on shore and follow our old calling and look after our wives and families. We had saved some money, but it did not go as far as we thought it would, and we agreed that if we could make just one more trip to sea, we should gain enough for what we wanted. "You were about two years old, and my Nelly was just born. "We went to Falmouth, where ships often put in, wanting hands, and masters are ready to pay good wages to obtain them. We hadn't been there a day, when we engaged on board a ship bound out to the West Indies. As she was not likely to be long absent, this just suited us. Your father got a berth as third mate, for he was the best scholar, and I shipped as boatswain.

"Iss dat a woif? Py Krismas, vot shall we do, mates?" "We'll land here, anyway," decided Matt. "The girl may need us." He glanced at the sky. There was still a good hour of daylight left, but the sun was sinking fast, and darkness would soon come on with a rush. Matt swung the Hawk around until she was heading straight toward the trees. Then he lowered her till she skimmed only a few feet above the branches. "See der light!" shouted Carl, pointing downward. A little clump of bushes, close to the edge of a narrow stream, showed a bright red glow, which shone through the leaves like a beacon. "Dat iss a fire!" cried Carl, "und de woif vill be dar near, py Kipperdick." "Right-o," agreed Dick. "There's a boat tied up to the bank, and the firelight shows up the smoke curling out of the chimney." "If we get her aboard," Matt declared, "we'll take her to New Orleans, and leave her at the hospital. She'll get all right treatment there." "But suppose she vill not let us haf her, Matt?" queried Carl. "She vill fight mit her fingars, dot woif." "She won't fight," Matt assured him. "She needs help, and she'll know better than to resist when she sees what kind of a craft we're in. Besides, she's probably sick, or she wouldn't be crying for help. Let her alone, Carl; just hold your horses, and don't try to grab her before we get her on board." "Goot!" said Carl. "Ve vill be vaiting fur her." As Matt spoke, he brought the Hawk down lower and lower, until she was skimming along only a couple of feet above the water. But even at this height, Matt had difficulty in keeping the ship under control. The wind was blowing strongly, and the current in the narrow channel was swift. The Hawk lurched and dipped, and once she nearly went over on her side. However, Matt held her steady, and finally brought her to rest within ten yards of the boat. At the same moment, two figures came running out of the brush, and stood peering intently at the strange-looking machine that hovered over the water. One of them was a young woman, clad in a long dress, and wearing a broad-brimmed hat, such as southern women affect during the hot weather. Her hair was loose about her shoulders, and her face was white and haggard. In her hand she carried a torch made of pine boughs, which she waved wildly as she ran. The other figure was a man, apparently a negro, who wore a straw hat and a pair of blue overalls. He carried a heavy ax, and he looked surly and ill-tempered. "She's in bad shape, fellows," said Dick. "What do you think of it, Matt?" "She looks like a ghost," replied Matt. "And the fellow with her doesn't look much better. He seems to be drunk, or crazy. We'd better land and get her aboard." "Vot you say, Matt?" asked Carl. "Vill you land mit de woif?" "Certainly, Carl. You stay where you are, and keep a watch on things. We'll land, and take care of the girl ourselves." "All right," nodded Dick. "I'll stand by you, old man." Matt opened the throttle wide, and sent the Hawk darting toward the boat.

The feeling of homeliness, of chumship with my surroundings, washes over me once more, and I am filled with a deep sense of gratitude for this small, ordinary room, which has held so much significance in my life.

Yet beyond the horizon, where doom seemingly loomed, the sparse lights of campfires flickered like fireflies caught in a web of night and mist. Each flame, steadfast yet ephemeral, whispered tales of valor and dread, tales of the men who had marched boldly northward beneath the banner of a cause now plagued by doubt. The air, thick with rain and the smell of churned earth, seemed to stifle even the whispers of the wind, which carried the drumming sounds of progress as if reluctant to let them fade into silence. Harry Kenton, soaked to the skin, tightened his grip upon the bridle as he pulled the collar of his greatcoat closer to stave off the chill. His horse moved with a weary gait, its head bobbing low, ears twitching at the occasional gust that rattled through the sparse trees. Each step resounded with resignation, echoing the rhythm of weariness that beat within the breast of every man in their long and arduous procession. Harry's mind wandered back to the day's grim endeavors, to the unfolding of fates and fortunes, and he could hardly separate his own thoughts from those of the men around him. Somewhere ahead, the rhythmic clanking of a wagon axle momentarily disrupted the monotony, only to blend once again into the encompassing soundscape of night. A soldier, wrapped in a sodden blanket, shivered as he sat against a bundle of supplies, eyes glazed with fever but flickering now and then with the spirit of defiance. And through the shadow of evening, the specter of absent comrades lingered, silently marching in lockstep with those who remained. Harry could nearly sense the presence of Stonewall Jackson himself, a ghostly figure urging them onward, toward a dawn shrouded in uncertainty. An older sergeant rode up alongside Harry, tipping his cap. His voice, though gruff, bore the deep-seated resolve that age and experience seemed to hone in men like him. "Captain Kenton, if yeh don't mind me askin', what's the General's next move? It seems we're not heading toward Richmond." Harry met his eyes, recognizing a need for reassurance that words could scarcely fill. "I reckon General Lee has his sights set on Virginia yet," Harry said, "but our immediate concern is to reforge our strength and spirit." The sergeant nodded, accepting the answer and understanding the layers beneath it. The horizon, however obscured by darkness, served as their compass, leading them stubbornly back toward the heart of a Confederacy now embattled both in flesh and in soul. They rode on, Harry scanning the path behind for any shimmer of torches marking pursuit. The enemy, it seemed, was content for now to focus on the cost of their own tenuous victory. The sky began to shift above them, yielding to a lighter greyness as night conceded its reign to day. With the change of light came a change in sound-cooing doves intermingling mournfully with the rasp and clatter of the retreating column. Harry straightened in his saddle, a mere silhouette against the muted dawn, and urged his steed forward once more. Resolute, yet never alone, he rode southward, along with the myriad hopes and fears entwined within him and his brethren. The path extended endlessly ahead, disappearing into the haunting morning mist, shrouding both fortune and misfortune alike.

The osmoregulatory function of CS is thought to be mediated by the generation of glycine betaine, a compatible solute that helps maintain cellular osmotic balance. This is achieved through the conversion of choline-O-sulfate to glycine betaine via a series of enzyme-catalyzed reactions involving CS, betaine aldehyde dehydrogenase, and betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase [23]. The regulation of CS activity is crucial for the bacterium's survival in environments with fluctuating osmotic conditions. In addition to its role in sulfur metabolism and osmoregulation, CS has been implicated in the virulence of certain bacterial pathogens. For instance, a CS-deficient mutant of the plant pathogen Pseudomonas syringae was shown to be attenuated in its ability to cause disease in Arabidopsis thaliana [39]. The exact mechanism by which CS contributes to virulence is unclear, but it is thought to involve the modulation of host-pathogen interactions. Studies on the structural and biochemical properties of CS have provided valuable insights into its catalytic mechanism and substrate specificity. The crystal structure of CS from Pseudomonas aeruginosa revealed a tetrameric enzyme with a unique active site architecture, featuring a binuclear metal center and a flexible loop that facilitates substrate binding [40]. Kinetic analysis of CS from Sinorhizobium meliloti demonstrated a high degree of substrate specificity for choline-O-sulfate, with a Km value in the low micromolar range [41]. The enzyme's high affinity for its substrate is thought to be essential for its physiological function, as it allows the bacterium to efficiently scavenge choline-O-sulfate from its environment. The discovery of CS in diverse microbial species has sparked interest in its potential applications in biotechnology and bioremediation. For example, CS-expressing bacteria could be used to clean up choline-O-sulfate-contaminated environments, or to produce glycine betaine as a valuable commodity chemical [42]. Furthermore, the development of CS-based biosensors could enable the rapid detection of choline-O-sulfate in environmental samples, facilitating the monitoring of ecosystem health. As research on CS continues to uncover its intricate roles in microbial physiology and ecology, it is clear that this enzyme will remain an important area of study in the years to come.

Agee said his group has independently confirmed Humayun's results regarding the age. What accounts for this discrepancy? Agee said his first result may have been for the bulk rock - that is, an average age of all of the rock types embedded within it. It's likely that the earliest formation of the meteorite was at 4.4 billion years, Agee said, but it continued to be shaped by geological processes for another 2 billion years before it blasted off into space. Agee and Humayun continue working on different Black Beauty samples separately, but not as rivals, said Agee. In fact, they are good friends. "Two labs working completely independently coming up with similar conclusions is much more convincing than if you're all part of the same gang," Agee said. Different than other meteorites. NASA's most powerful and sophisticated rover on Mars, the 2-ton Curiosity, has given plenty of insight into the planet's former habitability since it landed there last year. But even it cannot do a great job of dating rocks. On Earth, scientists can better estimate ages because they can measure the amount of trace elements in rocks, not just the most common elements. The trace elements - those that are present in tiny quantities in a particular sample - can be more indicative of the processes that led to the formation of meteorites than common elements, Humayun said. The trace element iridium, present in this meteorite, indicates that it came from a mysterious area of Mars called the southern highlands. That makes Black Beauty the first known resident of the southern highlands to get to Earth. Other samples from Mars that have reached Earth have been coming from the Martian Northern Hemisphere, which has low, flat plains. The Southern Hemisphere, by contrast, has a lot of craters, Agee said, meaning it's about 3.8 billion years old or older. Given its newly confirmed age, Black Beauty is one of the oldest samples scientists have seen from Mars. The other possible contender for that title is the famous Allan Hills meteorite, which has been dated to a similar time frame. NASA announced in 1996 that the Allan Hills meteorite, discovered in Antarctica, contained evidence of primitive life, but that conclusion has since been disputed. Agee noted futher that the Allan Hills sample is a chunk of bedrock, and would not have interacted with water and the surface environment the way that Black Beauty did. In the meantime, scientists are also probing Black Beauty for ancient Martian fossils. So far none have turned up, Agee said, but there could still be chemical byproducts of primitive life hidden in the rock samples. Clues to Martian history. Mars had a lot of volcanic activity when Black Beauty's zircons formed 4.4 billion years ago, Humayun said.

These complications have led to ongoing efforts in the scientific community to develop therapeutic regimens that maximize anti-inflammatory efficacy while minimizing adverse effects. As researchers strive to delineate the molecular intricacies behind genomic and non-genomic pathways, they also explore innovative drug design strategies that target distinct signaling cascades. For instance, selective glucocorticoid receptor agonists (SEGRAs) represent a promising class of compounds. SEGRAs aim to preferentially activate the glucocorticoid receptor-mediated transrepression pathways-which inhibit pro-inflammatory gene expression-without significantly engaging transactivation pathways responsible for many adverse metabolic consequences [12]. This distinction may attenuate deleterious effects like hyperglycemia and muscle wasting while preserving desirable anti-inflammatory properties. Another strategy involves the modulation of 11 -Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase enzymes, which regulate local glucocorticoid concentrations within tissues. Inhibitors of 11 -HSD1, an enzyme that converts inactive cortisone to active cortisol, could potentiate anti-inflammatory effects locally in tissues with high inflammation. Conversely, inhibitors targeting 11 -HSD2 enhance the inactivation of cortisol to cortisone within mineralocorticoid-sensitive tissues, potentially mitigating adverse sodium and fluid retention effects seen with glucocorticoid therapy [13]. In developing synthetic analogues, researchers also consider the interaction of these molecules with plasma carrier proteins. Binding of corticoids to carrier proteins like cortisol binding globulin (CBG) can influence their free, bioactive concentrations in the bloodstream. Alterations in carrier protein affinity may thus modulate drug distribution and availability, impacting therapeutic efficacy and side effect profiles [14]. Beyond pharmacologic interventions, lifestyle modifications such as dietary changes and regular physical activity are recommended to mitigate metabolic disturbances associated with chronic glucocorticoid use. These strategies may help manage weight gain, hyperglycemia, and hypertension, thereby reducing cardiovascular risk in patients undergoing long-term treatment [15]. Psychological interventions and support services are also emphasized, given the adverse neuropsychiatric effects of glucocorticoids, including mood swings, cognitive changes, and increased risk of depression or anxiety [16]. The dynamic interplay between genomic and non-genomic effects, drug development innovations, enzymatic modulation, and lifestyle strategies encapsulates the multifaceted approach necessary to optimize glucocorticoid therapy. Ongoing research and clinical trials continue to elucidate these pathways and refine therapeutic protocols. As our understanding deepens, the goal remains to harness the potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects of glucocorticoid hormones and their analogues, while minimizing the spectrum of potential adverse effects that can significantly impact patient quality of life. In summary, advances in glucocorticoid research hold exciting promise for more precise and individualized therapeutic approaches. By better understanding the mechanistic actions and optimizing treatment regimens, healthcare providers may enhance the benefit-risk ratio for patients with varying inflammatory and autoimmune conditions. Continued collaboration between researchers, clinicians, and the pharmaceutical industry is critical in achieving these objectives, ultimately leading to improved outcomes and patient satisfaction in managing these complex and chronic conditions.

The human genome contains two genes coding for ACC proteins: ACC1, located on chromosome 17q22, and ACC2, located on chromosome 17p13 (Savage et al., 1985). Both ACCs are expressed ubiquitously but differentially regulated in various tissues. ACC1 expression levels are relatively constant across all tissues, whereas ACC2 expression is highest in liver and adipose tissue (Braun et al., 1990). ACC1 has been shown to be primarily responsible for intracellular synthesis of malonyl CoA in vivo, whereas ACC2 regulates the rate-limiting step in fatty acid biosynthesis and controls mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation (Wakil et al., 1964). Mammals have two distinct ACC enzymes, ACC1 and ACC2, which differ in their regulation and localization. ACC1 is highly expressed in proliferative tissues such as adipocytes and hepatocytes, where it generates malonyl CoA for fatty acid biosynthesis (Haemmerle et al., 2002; McGarry and Brown, 1997). On the other hand, ACC2 is predominantly expressed in mitochondria-rich tissues such as brown adipose tissue, heart, and skeletal muscle, where it controls the flux of fatty acids into the mitochondrion (McGarry and Brown, 1997; Park et al., 2008; Winder and Hardie, 1999). Thus, ACC2 plays a crucial role in regulating fatty acid oxidation. ACC2 is subject to multiple posttranslational modifications including phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitylation, sumoylation, and methylation (Chen et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2007). Phosphorylation of Ser79 and Ser212 in ACC2 by AMPK inhibits its enzymatic activity, thus promoting fatty acid oxidation (Kim et al., 2004; Merrill et al., 1997). Acetylation of lysines K586 and K588 in ACC2 by SIRT1 promotes its enzymatic activity, thereby stimulating fatty acid synthesis (Lu et al., 2009). Ubiquitylation of ACC2 by SCF -TrCP promotes proteasomal degradation, thus reducing fatty acid oxidation (Sun et al., 2007). Sumoylation of ACC2 by PIAS and SUMO-1 inhibits its enzymatic activity, thereby reducing fatty acid oxidation (Zhou et al., 2007). Methylation of ACC2 by CARM1 stimulates its enzymatic activity, thus enhancing fatty acid synthesis (Liu et al., 2009). In this study, we report that AMPK phosphorylates ACC2 at Ser40. We show that this phosphorylation event occurs in response to AICAR treatment and exercise. Furthermore, this phosphorylation event inhibits ACC2 activity, which ultimately enhances fatty acid oxidation. These findings demonstrate that AMPK-mediated phosphorylation of ACC2 at Ser40 represents another mechanism by which AMPK regulates fatty acid oxidation. ACC2 was cloned from mouse skeletal muscle and then subcloned into pET28a vector (Novagen) with a His tag at the N terminus.

The aragonite skeletons of cold-water corals are composed of calcium carbonate, which is precipitated from seawater through a complex interplay of biological and geochemical processes. The rate of precipitation is influenced by factors such as seawater chemistry, temperature, and the presence of organic matter (Falkowski et al., 1984; Porter et al., 1984). The incorporation of magnesium and strontium into the coral skeleton is also thought to be influenced by the seawater chemistry, with higher concentrations of these elements in the skeleton reflecting higher concentrations in the seawater (Barker et al., 2005; Rueggeberg et al., 2008). In order to develop a proxy that is not affected by biological mediation, it is necessary to identify a geochemical component of the coral skeleton that is not influenced by the biological processes controlling calcification. One potential candidate is the concentration of rare earth elements (REEs) in the coral skeleton. REEs are a suite of 17 elements with similar chemical properties that are not readily incorporated into the coral skeleton through biological processes (Rollion-Bard et al., 2003, 2010). The concentration of REEs in the coral skeleton is thought to be controlled by the concentration of these elements in the seawater, making them a potential proxy for seawater chemistry (Mortensen and Rapp, 1998; Smith et al., 2000). However, the use of REEs as a proxy is not without its challenges. The concentration of REEs in the coral skeleton can be influenced by a range of factors, including the type of coral species, the age of the coral, and the environmental conditions under which the coral grew (Lutringer et al., 2005; Marali et al., 2013). Furthermore, the REE composition of the coral skeleton can vary even within a single coral colony, making it necessary to collect multiple samples from different locations within the colony to obtain a representative record of the seawater chemistry (Adkins et al., 2003). In order to overcome these challenges, it is necessary to develop a detailed understanding of the geochemical processes controlling the incorporation of REEs into the coral skeleton. This can be achieved through a combination of laboratory experiments and field observations. Laboratory experiments can be used to simulate the conditions under which REEs are incorporated into the coral skeleton, allowing researchers to test the effects of different environmental factors on the REE composition of the skeleton. Field observations can be used to collect data on the REE composition of coral skeletons from different locations and to identify any patterns or trends in the data that can be used to reconstruct past seawater chemistry. In conclusion, the development of a proxy that is not affected by biological mediation requires a fundamental understanding of the geochemical processes controlling the formation of cold-water coral skeletons. The concentration of REEs in the coral skeleton is a potential candidate for a proxy, but the use of this proxy is not without its challenges. Further research is needed to develop a detailed understanding of the geochemical processes controlling the incorporation of REEs into the coral skeleton and to identify any patterns or trends in the data that can be used to reconstruct past seawater chemistry.

Unsuspecting, the trusting little boy allowed himself to be led into a nearby storeroom - and a horrific sex attack ensued. 'I was inquisitive and followed him in there like a little sheep,' he says ruefully. 'I could have been a headstone by now. That's how it could have ended.' Luckily, Mr Williamson was allowed to go. He ran home and kept what had happened to him secret, never telling anyone what had taken place. Lonely existence: James as a toddler. He says he spent much of his early years with a child minder. 'At the time, I thought: "What was that? I can't tell anyone". I knew it was wrong.' Heartbreakingly, he was also convinced that should his parents find out, they might blame him instead. 'What I was most concerned about was that if I told my parents, they might be angry and maybe put me in a home. 'I thought they might think they'd adopted a duff one. So I just carried on and a year later, I joined the Scouts.' His decision to join the Scouts was to prove a fateful one and what came next left him with mental scars that have lasted all his life. 'The first thing I thought when I saw him was that he was smart,' says Mr Williamson of the moment he was introduced to his Scoutmaster, a man named Tom. 'He was well-presented. His trousers had real nice creases on the front. He came to the meeting because our Scoutmaster was leaving. 'In the end, it was announced that Skip [former Scoutmaster] was going and Tom would be taking over. I didn't think he was good looking because he wasn't.' The meeting, when Mr Williamson was aged 10, signalled the start of what would turn into almost a decade of sexual abuse. Showered with attention and affection, the lonely little boy was easily groomed and, when Tom offered to take him to the cinema and said he could stay the night afterwards, the relationship became a sexual one. Unable to tell anyone, in particular his parents, Mr Williamson felt trapped and unable to sound the alarm. Even today, he is unwilling to condemn his attacker and calls what passed between them 'conditional kindness'. 'My father had a violent and unpredictable temper and Tom's place was a place of tranquillity and safety,' he explains. 'I felt that I was being offered something - a trade. I called it conditional kindness.' Heartbreakingly, he still feels disloyal by talking about what transpired between him and Tom. 'I sort of feel that I'm betraying someone who helped me,' he admits. 'There's a sort of mixed feeling. I also feel disloyal in some way.' Escape finally came when he left the Scouts aged 18, although he reveals he had tried to escape Tom's attentions many times before. Scout: James aged 10, proudly wearing a poppy and his Robertson's Jam Boy Scout Golly.

And that is a truth complicated by the fact that medicine - when it concerns the cutting-edge treatment of terminally-ill children - is as much an art as a science, with issues rarely being straightforwardly black or white. Or as one of the consultants told me when my elder daughter Ellie was treated for leukaemia: 'Being a good doctor is as much like being a good cook as anything. You have to feel your way.' When a child is diagnosed with something as serious as cancer, the usual procedure is to start with the treatment protocols agreed by specialists all over the world. Some children respond well straight away. Others don't. Cancer is not just one disease but many hundreds of diseases under one heading, and something that looks like other similar cases may respond very differently. I have been that parent, the one repeatedly called in to hear the consultant say: 'It hasn't turned out as we hoped,' which is how they tell you when treatment hasn't worked and they are thinking of trying something else. So you return to the ward, where other children may be packing their bags to go home and your child is getting sicker for reasons you can't fully understand without years of medical training and maybe not even then. Not only that but, without a full understanding of what is happening, you are required to sign consent forms for operations that don't seem to be helping and, worse, calm your child while they have injections and painful procedures which they beg you to stop. When every fibre of your being is telling you to protect your child, the medical world orders you to over-ride those feelings over and over again in the interests of something that doesn't appear to be having much effect. And, to compound this nightmarish scenario, you are probably sleeping - if it can be called that - on a fold-up bed next to your child; washing in the hospital's visitors' loos and living on a diet of chips from the canteen, not having breathed fresh air or had a night off since the dreadful day of diagnosis. If you have other children, they will be distraught, missing both their unwell sibling and you. And if you have a partner, your relationship will almost certainly be suffering as you take your understandable anxiety out on each other. Asyha, who underwent an operation on a brain tumour last month, in hospital with his mother Naghmeh in a photo posted on Facebook by a relative. It's a recipe for disaster and to me the only surprise is that runaways like this don't happen more often. I spent eight months with Ellie in hospital before she died aged nine. And at 3am every night, every other parent there was, like me, awake but face-down on the pillow, shoulders shaking with sobs that couldn't be shed during the day.

The language was still Spanish, but Hickman's ear, attuned to the rhythms of the city, began to pick up the cadence, the musicality of the speech. He felt a pang of regret that he couldn't understand the words, but the emotions, the passion, and the intensity were universal, transcending language barriers. The platform, once a bustling, chaotic scene, receded into the background as Hickman's attention focused on the duo. He found himself wondering about their story, their relationship, the secrets they shared in their native tongue. Were they lovers, friends, or simply fellow travelers bound together by chance? As he reached the end of the platform, Hickman turned, his eyes seeking out the red-haired girl once more. The man was still talking, his hands weaving an intricate pattern in the air, but the girl's gaze had shifted, her eyes meeting Hickman's with a hint of mischief, a spark of connection that left him breathless. In that fleeting moment, the world narrowed to the two of them, the sounds of the station, the calls of the vendors, and the rumble of the train fading into insignificance.

I could hear the buzzing of the clippers, a sound so menacing it could easily double as a horror soundtrack, and that was enough for me to feel my anxiety bubble. Who would willingly submit themselves to a contraption that grounds hair into little bits of food for the vacuum cleaner? Only someone with a sick sense of humor-oh wait, that might be my mom. "C'mon, don't be a wuss," she chirped. "You've gotta look decent for picture day. Gotta give the camera something to work with, right?" Her voice was so normal and cheerful, contrasting painfully against the backdrop of my dread. It was as if a perky jingle was playing just for me. I shot her the best glare I could muster, but the short people on the waiting couch, absorbed in their own electronic gadgets, likely didn't notice. After a moment, I sighed, resigned to my fate of being trimmed and shaped by some skillful harbinger of hair loss. It was either that or subject myself to a life of 'mophead' as my peers would likely brand it. As we approached the stylist, who looked suspiciously too cheerful-was she secretly an executioner disguised as a beautician?-I noticed her name tag: "Cathy." Next to it was an oversized smile that screamed "I love cutting hair!" If my life were a cartoon, this is where the ominous music would thrive. "Alright, big guy, what are we doing today?" Cathy asked, brandishing those scissors like some ninja weapon. With all the enthusiasm of a puppy, she whipped around to face me, her hair in a perfect, bouncy bob, as if she were the poster child for 'Trust Me; I Know What I'm Doing.' "Uh, just a trim," I muttered, wishing there was a way to convey my silent protest without resorting to something as dramatic as throwing a tantrum. My mom, oblivious to the grave predicament unfolding before our eyes, piped in, "Make him look fabulous! He has his pictures tomorrow!" As if "fabulous" was a word that belonged in my vocabulary. I imagined my future self: bouncy hair styled perfectly, while I, in a parallel universe, posed awkwardly in front of a camera that captured my every flaw. Yep, that was precisely how I envisioned the event rolling out. "Alright, let's get started!" Cathy chirped again like a bird high on energy drinks. My heart sank. Before I could protest, she popped on an apron that looked like it had survived an apocalypse-snags and stains told tales of haircuts past, probably dating back to the '80s. Just like that, I was trapped. I sunk into the chair, feeling that familiar tingling of panic well up in my throat. There's a special kind of betrayal when you trust someone with your hair. Trust is a fickle thing-it's like the last slice of pizza; everyone wants a piece, but no one wants to be the one to take it. And in that moment, with the reflection of scissors gleaming dangerously close, I wondered if I would search for the bravery to actually survive this.

The semi-arid savannas of Africa are particularly vulnerable to water scarcity, as they are characterized by a distinct dry season with no rain and high temperatures. Droughts are a natural occurrence in these ecosystems, and the impact of climate change has only exacerbated the situation. The frequency and severity of droughts are expected to increase in the coming years, further threatening the resilience of these ecosystems. To address this issue, it is essential to develop effective management strategies that take into account the complex interactions between vegetation, water availability, and climate. One approach is to use Earth Observation data to monitor water use and stress in African savannas at fine scales. This can be achieved by combining data from low to high spatial resolution sensors, such as satellite imagery and airborne LiDAR. The use of Earth Observation data has several advantages in this context. Firstly, it provides a synoptic view of the ecosystem, allowing for the detection of subtle changes in vegetation health and water availability. Secondly, it enables the monitoring of large areas over time, providing valuable insights into the dynamics of the ecosystem. Finally, it can be used to identify areas of high water stress and prioritize management efforts. In this study, we used a novel tool to account for water use and stress in African savannas. The tool combines data from the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR) and the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) sensors, which provide data on vegetation health and water availability at fine scales. The tool was applied to a study area in South Africa, where it was used to identify areas of high water stress and prioritize management efforts. The results of the study showed that the tool was effective in identifying areas of high water stress, and that the management efforts prioritized by the tool were successful in reducing water stress and improving ecosystem resilience. The study also highlighted the importance of considering the complex interactions between vegetation, water availability, and climate in management decisions. The findings of this study have important implications for the management of African savannas. Firstly, they highlight the need for a more nuanced understanding of the complex interactions between vegetation, water availability, and climate. Secondly, they emphasize the importance of using Earth Observation data to monitor water use and stress in these ecosystems. Finally, they demonstrate the effectiveness of using a novel tool to account for water use and stress in African savannas. The study also has implications for the development of climate-resilient agriculture in Africa. The findings suggest that the use of Earth Observation data and novel tools can help to identify areas of high water stress and prioritize management efforts. This can help to reduce the vulnerability of agricultural systems to climate change and improve food security. In conclusion, the study demonstrates the potential of Earth Observation data and novel tools to support the management of African savannas. The tool used in this study provides a valuable framework for monitoring water use and stress in these ecosystems, and can be used to prioritize management efforts and improve ecosystem resilience. The study highlights the importance of considering the complex interactions between vegetation, water availability, and climate in management decisions, and demonstrates the effectiveness of using a novel tool to account for water use and stress in African savannas.

And though I might appear composed and aloof to those who only see the surface, there exists an inner tempest of feelings. The thrill of running fingers through emotions, dancing around vulnerability, digging into the depths of what makes us feel alive. Those little moments of connection-where words start to blur and laughter stitches gaps in understanding-are what I cherish. I often find myself lost in daydreams of what could be, entertained by the notion that there's more to see and feel than the ordinary.
