In conclusion, the integration of PV systems into building infrastructure is a complex task that requires careful consideration of various factors, including the building's energy demand, the availability of renewable energy sources, and the energy storage and grid infrastructure. Researchers have made significant progress in optimizing the design and operation of PV systems, TES systems, EV charging infrastructure, and hybrid DER systems to maximize the energy savings and reduce the energy costs. However, further research is needed to address the challenges associated with the integration of PV systems into building infrastructure and to develop more efficient and sustainable energy systems. I can still visualize the afternoons spent in that sunlit garden, the air heavy with the scent of summer blooms as the laughter of young faces echoed against the hedgerows. I was but a humble witness to their childhood joys, yet somehow, my heart grew attached to the gentle rhythms of their lives. As the years danced by, that laughter turned into the sound of dreams yet to be fulfilled. The young ladies had transformed into competent, elegant versions of the girls I once knew, yet the underlying spirit of their youth remained, flickering just beneath the surface like embers waiting for a gust of wind. At lunch, Mr. Hillier attempted to inject some levity. He offered half-hearted jokes about the French and their propensity for strange cuisine, but they fell flat, the humor lost on Miss Muriel, who had taken to sulking. I cleared the table in silence, careful to avoid any clatter that might disturb the saturated atmosphere. That was the unspoken code of our household-maintain balance, not rock the boat, and certainly don't draw attention to overcast sentiments. But Mrs. Hillier, ever perceptive, sensed the burden hanging heavy on her family's shoulders. Once I returned to the kitchen to prepare tea, soft murmurs reached me through the half-closed door as she leaned forward, a hand gesturing earnestly. What wisdom flowed from that beloved matriarch! She spoke of resilience, of navigating uncertainty, and of the importance of mutual support, her voice steady like a lighthouse guiding ships through fog. I finished with the china and gathered my thoughts sharper than ever, reflecting on my own peculiar position. I was not merely a servant; I had woven myself into the very fabric of this household, a patchwork of care extended over years. From the first awkward moments of formation, assisting with each small triumph or tragic tear, my attachment had grown; my affection for each of them, especially for Miss Katherine, had deepened as she matured into an enviable blend of grace and resolve. Once the dishes were cleared away and I caught a moment of quiet solitude, I considered their upcoming journey with a subtle melancholy. To pack one's life into blue labels and a trunk seemed banal yet so rife with emotion. The thought of an impending separation, however brief, stung more than I anticipated. Mrs. Hillier would return, of course, but in her absence, a silence would blanket the once vibrant abode. I could already foresee how the afternoons would stretch into long shadows without their joyful noises filling the rooms. I returned to the dining room to find Miss Katherine silently-yet somewhat animatedly-attempting to persuade her sister of the wonders that awaited them across the water. "But Muriel," she insisted, her brown eyes sparkling with idealism, "think of the markets in Nice! The oranges! And the sunlight! It will be darling, I promise you." Yet Miss Muriel scoffed, folding her arms, her resistance a stony barrier against her sister's optimism. In quiet moments like these, I understood a sense of duty beyond the realm of my position. I was determined to ensure their memories of this trip would not be colored by resentment or dread, even if they seemed at loggerheads with one another. Perhaps, after spending hours consuming foreign delights and basking in laughter with new acquaintances, they might return, transformed by experience, their bond fortified anew. I held onto that thought tightly as I wiped down the last plate, wishing for a glimmer of clarity among the clouds of uncertainty that shrouded us all.

Since savannas are highly influenced by human activities, private and institutional practices play a key role in their conservation, while also improving people's living standards and providing employment opportunities. This implies that integrated management strategies for savannas are required, which explicitly consider water resources management in an holistic manner and take the multifunctionality of the ecosystem and needs of all stakeholders into account (Lal, 2015; Schwarzel et al., 2016). There is then a need to develop a mechanism for monitoring water availability and vegetation dynamics in savannas, at both the regional and local scales. Earth Observation (EO) data, particularly data provided by Sentinel 2 and Sentinel 3 satellites, new missions developed by European Space Agency (ESA), allow us to map the water use, and water stress, and the vegetation distribution across the African savannas, as well as to monitor seasonal and long-term temporal variations. Although monitoring programs for savanna water use have been established in certain areas, most of them are largely restricted to point based/small scale measurements, which are not capable of providing distributed timely and up-to-date information for water resources management and planning purposes. African savanna ecosystem management, with natural vegetation susceptible to water stress, should take advantage of remote sensing advances for estimating water use applying ET as a proxy. The transferability of the findings to African ecosystem remains uncertain and should be tested in-situ. Ramoelo et al. (2014) and Majozi et al. (2016) have evaluated MOD16 global ET product and different ET algorithms over South African savanna sites (equipped with eddy covariance towers). Their results demonstrated the usefulness and potential of EO data for savanna water monitoring. In addition to these results, which used MODIS products with a spatial resolution of 1 km2 and that did not constrain vegetation water stress, there is a need to downscale ET estimates to farm/plot levels integrating high and coarse resolution images. The strength of the modelling framework presented here is its suitability to cover the different layers of rangeland management, improving the understanding of ET evolution on the complex Southern African context (with mosaics of heterogeneous, partially cover landscapes and land uses). Our hypothesis is that the Ecosystem Stress Index (ESI), applied with the new generation sensors of Sentinel 2 (S2) and 3 (S3) satellites, is a valuable tool to downscale timely estimates of actual ET derived at coarse resolution to fine scale. Therefore, the main objective of this paper was to model and validate the water used (actual evapotranspiration) by African savanna ecosystem at fine scale (meters), integrating water stress effects. To monitor savanna water fluxes in a semi-continuous way this paper integrates two different ET-estimation approaches, with different conceptual/operational capabilities and limitations.

The girl launched some verbal javelin at the man who gripped her wrist, at the same instant looking down at the clamping fingers as if to emphasize what must have been a command to release her. No answer but a flash of white teeth beneath a toy moustache. The girl's free hand shot to a great coil of hair over the nape of her neck, came away with twin prongs of thin steel - anchorage of some hair ornament - showing below her clenched fingers. A lightning jab downward, and the Spanish-speaking man dropped the imprisoned hand to whip his own to his mouth. He snarled something in sharp falsetto. The girl with the red hair tilted her chin at him, and the laugh that slipped between her grudging little teeth was thin and sharp as the double dagger points she had used. She turned, took three steps to a stool below the Pullman's steps, mounted with a quick swirl of skirts and was gone. Grant thought he saw a half-formed determination to follow flash into the Spaniard's eyes. Without knowing why he did it, the New Yorker hastily put one foot upon the lower Pullman step and bent his body so as to block access to it. Very painstakingly he unloosed the knot on his low shoe, straightened the tongue in place and began taking in slack on every loop of the strings. A grunt of exasperation from behind Grant. When at last he straightened himself and looked around the Spanish gentleman was gone. He chuckled. "Now that, senor, should teach you not to play rough with a red-head." He walked down to the Pullman his ticket called for and climbed aboard. Just as the conductor's bellow, "Bo-oa-rd," sounded, Grant, looking through the glass of the vestibule, saw the Spanish gentleman with a grip flying for the train out of the baggage room of the station. Passing into the body of the car he found his bags piled upon a seat midway of its length. As he seated himself he was the least bit startled to see flaming coils of hair above the top of the seat across the aisle and one beyond his. Grant was not displeased.

On the floor of the House honourable members might stretch themselves and doze; they might wander about St. Stephen's Hall with prominent constituents who sought admission to the Strangers' Gallery, entertain them in the dining-room, or take their ease across the way at St. Stephen's Club, ready to return by the underground passage on the ringing of the division-bell; but that gallery above the Speaker, the eye and ear of the world, was never anything else but a hive of industry from the moment after prayers until the House rose. Ever watchful, ever scribbling its hieroglyphics and deciphering them; ever covering ream upon ream of paper with the verbose and vapid utterances of ambitious but unimportant members, its telegraphs clicked on incessantly hour after hour, transmitting reports of the business accomplished to the farthermost recesses of the King's Empire. Truly, a strange life is that of both legislator and journalist within those sombre walls at Westminster. On this night a full House was occupied with serious business. Within St. Stephen's men collected in groups, talked anxiously, and awaited the doom of the Government; for the political horizon was black, and the storm, long threatened, was now to burst. Contrary to the usual course of things, the small band of Irish obstructionists, fluent orators, whose heckling of Ministers caused so many scenes, were silent, for a matter of foreign policy of the most vital importance had been debated ever since the dinner-hour. Member after member had risen from the Opposition Benches and beneath the soft glow of the electric light shining through the glass roof had, before a crowded and excited House, supported the vote of censure, denouncing the Government for its apathy, its neglect of warnings, and the failure of its diplomacy abroad. The scene would have been an ordinary one were it not for the fact that a five-line whip had been sent out. An important division was hourly expected, and as the defeat of the Government was believed to be close at hand, the excitement had risen to fever heat. The calmest man in the whole of that versatile House was, perhaps, he who was at that moment replying from the Treasury Bench. "Strangers" in the gallery were struck by his youthful appearance, for he did not seem to be much over thirty. Tall, dark-haired, with slightly aquiline features and a small black moustache, his face was refined, studious, and full of keen intelligence. Standing beside the clerk's table, upon the very spot where the late Mr. Gladstone had so often stood when delivering his masterpieces of oratory, he leaned easily upon his right hand while he addressed the House calmly and clearly in defence of Her Majesty's Government. All the world knew that the Right Honourable Dudley Waldegrave Chisholm, member for the Albury Division of Surrey and Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, was a coming man.

Compounds that increase cellular concentrations of cyclic GMP are known to lower IOP (Becker, 1990; Nathanson, 1992; Nathanson and Hunnicutt, 1988; Stein and Clack, 1994). As the natriuretic peptides activate the guanylyl cyclases to stimulate cyclic GMP production, they are potential IOP-lowering agents. The presence of NPRs in ocular tissues, especially those involved in the regulation of IOP, have been demonstrated in a number of species. For example, in rat and rabbit eyes, NPR-A, -B, and -C mRNA were found in the ciliary processes, where aqueous humor is produced (Fernandez-Durango et al., 1995). All three natriuretic peptides increase guanylyl cyclase activity in the rabbit ciliary processes, with CNP being the most potent, indicating that NPR-B is the major receptor subtype (Lajmi et al., 2017; Mittag et al., 1987; Nathanson, 1987). Similar results were found in bovine ciliary processes and cultured bovine ciliary epithelial cells (Millar et al., 1997; Shahidullah and Wilson, 1999). The natriuretic peptide-induced elevation of cyclic GMP in these cells activates various cell signaling pathways and more importantly, inhibits Na+/H+ exchanger activity, which is involved in aqueous humor production (Fidzinski et al., 2004). In addition to the ciliary processes, NPRs were also found in tissues associated with aqueous humor outflow (Samuelsson-Almen et al., 1991). In cultured human TM and ciliary muscle cells, CNP is the most potent and efficacious natriuretic peptide in stimulating the production of cyclic GMP, indicating the presence of functional NPR-B (Pang et al., 1996; Zhong et al., 2003). Activation of this receptor reduces carbachol-induced calcium influx, which predicts that activation of NPR-B should cause relaxation of these tissues (Pang et al., 1996). Indeed, CNP significantly decreases the carbachol-induced contraction of monkey and human ciliary muscle (Ding and Abdel-Latif, 1997). Change in contractility in the TM and ciliary muscle is expected to affect the outflow of aqueous humor. Various researchers have independently shown that intracameral or intravitreal injection of ANP or CNP in rabbits consistently and significantly lowers IOP (Korenfeld and Becker, 1989; Lajmi et al., 2017; Nathanson, 1987; Sugrue and Viader, 1986). The effect lasts for many hours or even days. Of the natriuretic peptides, CNP is the most efficacious for lowering IOP in the rabbit. A dose of 0.2 nmol (0.4 1/2g) of CNP lowered IOP by 13 mmHg from 3 to 8 h after injection; 2 nmol (4.4 1/2g) lowered IOP by 15 mmHg; and 20 nmol (44 1/2g) lowered IOP by 17 mmHg, lasting for up to 24 h (Takashima et al., 1996, 1998). These in vivo results corroborate the importance of NPR-B in the regulation of IOP. CNP, a 22 amino acid cyclic peptide, is an efficacious IOP-lowering agent in animal studies when injected into the eye (Korenfeld and Becker, 1989). Administered topically, it cannot penetrate the cornea and thus does not affect IOP.

The Energiewende, a pioneering initiative aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions and increasing the share of renewable energy in the energy mix, has led to a significant expansion of the electric grid. However, this expansion has been met with resistance from local communities, who are concerned about the environmental and visual impact of traditional transmission lines. In this context, superconducting transmission lines (SCTLs) offer a promising solution, as they can minimize the environmental and visual impact while increasing the public acceptance of transmission lines. One of the primary advantages of SCTLs is their ability to reduce the visual impact of transmission lines. Traditional overhead lines, with their tall towers and sprawling infrastructure, can be an eyesore for local residents. In contrast, SCTLs can be buried underground, reducing the visual impact to almost zero. This is particularly important in areas of high conservation value or scenic beauty, where the presence of traditional transmission lines can be detrimental to the local ecosystem and economy. Another significant advantage of SCTLs is their ability to reduce the environmental impact of transmission lines. Traditional transmission lines can have a significant impact on local ecosystems, particularly in areas where they intersect with sensitive habitats or wildlife corridors. SCTLs, on the other hand, can be designed to minimize their environmental footprint, reducing the risk of habitat disruption and fragmentation. In addition to their environmental and visual benefits, SCTLs also offer a number of technical advantages. They can operate at higher efficiencies than traditional transmission lines, reducing energy losses and increasing the overall reliability of the grid. They can also operate at lower voltages, reducing the risk of electrical interference and increasing the safety of the system. Despite these advantages, SCTLs are not without their challenges. One of the primary obstacles to their widespread adoption is the high upfront cost of development and deployment. However, as the technology continues to mature, costs are expected to decrease, making SCTLs a more competitive option for transmission system operators. Another challenge facing SCTLs is the need for advanced materials and manufacturing techniques. The production of superconducting materials requires specialized facilities and equipment, which can be a barrier to entry for some manufacturers. However, as the demand for SCTLs increases, it is likely that the manufacturing industry will respond with new and innovative solutions. In terms of existing and planned SCTL projects, there are a number of examples around the world. The AmpaCity project in Germany, for example, is a pioneering initiative that aims to develop and deploy SCTLs in urban areas. The project has already demonstrated the feasibility of SCTLs in real-world applications, and is expected to pave the way for further deployments in the future. In the US, the LIPA1 project is another example of a SCTL project that is pushing the boundaries of what is possible with this technology. The project aims to develop and deploy SCTLs in a variety of applications, including transmission and distribution systems. The project has already made significant progress, and is expected to provide valuable insights into the technical and economic feasibility of SCTLs. In conclusion, SCTLs offer a promising solution to the challenges facing the electric grid expansion. They can minimize the environmental and visual impact of transmission lines, while increasing the public acceptance and reducing the costs. While there are still challenges to be overcome, the benefits of SCTLs make them an attractive option for transmission system operators and policymakers around the world. As the technology continues to mature, it is likely that SCTLs will play an increasingly important role in the transition to a low-carbon energy system.

My parting with the family was very affecting; my mother cried bitterly, for, like all mothers, she liked the greatest fool which she had presented to my father, better than all the rest; my sisters cried because my mother cried; Tom roared for a short time more loudly than all the rest, having been chastised by my father for breaking his fourth window in that week. At last I tore myself away. I had blubbered till my eyes were so red and swollen, that the pupils were scarcely to be distinguished, and tears and dirt had veined my cheeks like the marble of the chimney-piece. My handkerchief was soaked through with wiping my eyes and blowing my nose, before the scene was over. My brother Tom, with a kindness which did honour to his heart, exchanged his for mine, saying, with fraternal regard, "Here, Peter, take mine, it's as dry as a bone." But my father would not wait for a second handkerchief to perform its duty. He led me away through the hall, when, having shaken hands with all the men, and kissed all the maids, who stood in a row with their aprons to their eyes, I quitted the paternal roof. The coachman accompanied me to the stage. Having seen me securely wedged between two fat old women, and having put my parcel inside, he took his leave, and in a few minutes I was on my road to London. I was too much depressed to take notice of any thing during my journey. When we arrived in London, they drove to the Blue Boar (in a street, the name of which I have forgotten). I had never seen or heard of such an animal, and certainly it did appear very formidable; its mouth was open and teeth very large. The coachman threw his whip to the ostler, and the reins upon the horses' back; he then dismounted, and calling to me, "Now, young gentleman, I'se waiting," he put a ladder up for me to get down by; then turning to a porter, he said to him, "Bill, you must take this here young gem'man and that ere parcel to this here direction. - Please to remember the coachman, sir." I replied that I certainly would, if he wished it, and walked off with the porter; the coachman observing as I went away, "Well, he is a fool - that's sartain." I arrived quite safe at St. Clement's Lane, when the porter received a shilling for his trouble from the maid who let me in, and I was shown up into a parlour, where I found myself in company with Mrs Handycock. Mrs Handycock was a little meagre woman, who did not speak very good English, and who appeared to me to employ the major part of her time in bawling out from the top of the stairs to the servants below.

Recent analyses have emphasized the importance of determining the PAH concentrations in biochars and developing strategies to mitigate potential risks to human health and the environment (Hale et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2015; Sohi et al., 2016). To address these concerns, various methodologies have been proposed, including optimizing pyrolysis conditions to minimize PAH formation and enhancing post-production treatments such as chemical washing or heat treatment to remove residual pollutants (Kaiser et al., 2012; Wen et al., 2014; Xia et al., 2019). Alongside these advancements, the research community has begun to explore the implications of biochar incorporation into urban landscapes, not merely limited to agrarian contexts. As urbanization accelerates globally, the cultivation of green spaces in cities is increasingly essential. Biochar's potential to augment soil quality while mitigating runoff and sequestering carbon could translate into healthier, more sustainable urban environments (Abel et al., 2013; Lehmann and Joseph, 2015). Projects integrating biochar into green infrastructure, such as community gardens and urban parks, are at the forefront of innovative environmental design (Cao et al., 2016; Beesley et al., 2017). Despite the glaring benefits, the implementation of biochar in urban or rural settings warrants careful management. Balancing the chemical characteristics of biochar with local soil conditions and crop requirements ensures maximum benefits without unintended negative effects. For example, excessive or inappropriate application can alter soil pH or disrupt nutrient availability to plants, necessitating targeted guidance for farmers and land managers (Chan et al., 2007; Major et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2012). As the landscape of biochar application evolves, collaborations between scientists, policymakers, and practitioners become pivotal. These partnerships foster a deeper understanding of biochar systems, integrating scientific advancements with practical applications and regulatory frameworks. Policy initiatives can provide incentives or subsidies for sustainable biochar production and use, aligning economic interests with environmental stewardship (Laird et al., 2009; Gaunt and Lehmann, 2012; Batjes, 2014). Further research into the long-term impacts and interactions of biochar in various ecological settings is crucial. Sustained investigations will elucidate pathways for optimizing biochar formulations to meet specific agricultural and environmental goals, such as enhanced nutrient retention, reduced pathogen load, or improved soil biodiversity (Novak et al., 2009; Jeffery et al., 2011; Bridle et al., 2017). In conclusion, biochar represents a promising, multifunctional innovation poised to address some of the pressing challenges of our time. Whether it's in promoting agricultural resilience, rehabilitating degraded lands, or contributing to urban sustainability, its role is underscored by a commitment to ecological harmony and resource efficiency. Yet, mindful stewardship and continued inquiry will ensure that biochar technologies evolve symbiotically with the ecosystems they seek to enhance, safeguarding both human and environmental health for future generations. By navigating the intersection of science, technology, and policy, we can harness the full potential of biochar in crafting a more sustainable world.

He asked me to please try and talk her into staying here in Florida, or at least returning after a year or two. He felt that this move was a bad idea and that she would regret it later. I assured him that I would talk to her about it, and that I would not push her either way. I thought it best to let her make up her own mind. If she decided to stay, great, but if she went anyway, then I couldnt stop her. Besides, I had already made plans to leave myself, and no matter which direction I took, it would be away from here. We left Pops place and headed back to the apartment. I had called ahead to the local U-Haul dealer and reserved a trailer. It was only a little after one when we got there and they were ready for us. We hooked it up and drove it around the block to make sure everything worked okay, then headed home to finish loading. It was three oclock now, and we still had a lot to load. We had been planning this move since March, and most of the stuff had been boxed up for months. All we really had to do was carry it downstairs and put it on the trailer. That and a few odds and ends. The TV stand, the stereo cabinet, the bed frame, etc. Nothing major, but still, it was an effort. Luckily for us, some friends showed up to help. I cant imagine trying to get all that done without them. By five thirty we were loaded and ready to go. I had planned on leaving around six oclock, but that wasnt happening. We decided to head over to the beach and have dinner with the girls parents. They wanted to spend as much time with her as possible before she left. They had planned on making the trip to California with us, but their car broke down and they werent able to go. They understood why she wanted to go, but they werent happy about it. Still, they supported her decision and wished her well. We arrived at the restaurant around seven. Dinner lasted about an hour, and then we said goodbye to her folks. I had been trying to get a hold of her brother all afternoon, but he never returned any calls. I was hoping to see him before we left. Her sister was working and wouldnt be available until ten oclock. The Princess had a couple of friends who had agreed to meet us at her house to say goodbye. I had seen everyone else except her brother, and I didnt think it right to leave without saying goodbye to him. I tried calling again, and finally he answered. He lived in a neighboring city, and I asked him to come by and see us. He promised he would. Around eight forty-five we left the restaurant and headed toward the apartment. We stopped at the store to pick up some last minute items, and then continued on our way. When we got there, I opened the door and walked inside. As soon as I stepped through the doorway I noticed that something was wrong. My heart sank as I realized what it was. Our front window was broken out. Someone had thrown a brick through it and stolen our computer system. It was brand new, and cost almost three thousand dollars. Now it was gone. I ran outside and looked around. I saw nothing suspicious. Just another beautiful Florida evening. The neighbors had heard nothing. I called the police and reported the crime. I asked them to send someone out immediately because we were getting ready to leave town. They sent someone right away. While we waited for them, The Princess went next door to tell her landlord. She came back crying.

Then I went across and unlocked the big leather kit-bag, turning its contents out upon the floor. At the bottom was something wrapped up in an old blanket, and this I drew forth. "That's it," he said. "Take care how you handle it." I removed the covering, and found myself gazing upon a great oblong slab of black basalt, carved with curious hieroglyphics, and measuring fully two feet six inches long by eighteen inches wide, and about eight inches thick. On each side was a ring of iron, and it seemed to be extremely heavy. "It weighs nearly three hundredweight," remarked the old man. "But carry it carefully - oh yes, carefully!" he urged, watching me closely as I raised it from the ground. "Ah! now you'll see!" he laughed in a low voice, his eyes shining strangely. "Place it on that chest of drawers yonder." I did as he directed, and then stood back to view it. "Now, go out - close the door behind you - leave me alone for ten minutes," he commanded. "Afterwards come back and unlock the door again." I left him lying there, with his blazing eyes fixed upon the mysterious stone. Outside in the corridor I waited, wondering if he had taken leave of his senses. A quarter of an hour later I entered the room, and found him lying stiff and cold, staring straight before him with glazed eyes. He was dead. That same night I buried the strange stone away in a locked trunk, and the next day saw poor Arnold consigned to mother earth in a quiet country churchyard, where the birds sang sweetly above his grave.

Snowden, who flew from Hawaii to Hong Kong before revealing himself, told the Morning Post he plans to stay in the city, rejecting speculation he might seek to flee elsewhere. "I am not here to hide from justice; I am here to reveal criminality," he said. He added, "I have had many opportunities to flee (Hong Kong), but I would rather stay and fight the United States government in the courts, because I have faith in (Hong Kong)'s rule of law." "The Morning Post said its interviews with Snowden were conducted in a "refuge co-ordinated by diplomats and human rights lawyers." Asked why he went to Hong Kong, he said that "they have a spirited commitment to free speech and the right of political dissent," according to the newspaper. He said he believed he was free from extradition under American accords because "the crime of espionage has never been publicly debated in Hong Kong court. The government could easily deny a vindictive prosecution, but it would sacrifice credibility and risk censure if it cooperated in one." "Hong Kong returned to Chinese control in 1997 after more than a century as a British colony. Beijing allows it a high degree of autonomy, but human-rights groups accuse the Chinese central government of frequently trying to exert pressure behind the scenes. Snowden told the newspaper he felt his presence in Hong Kong put American officials in a bind. "People who think I made a mistake in picking HK as a location misunderstand my intentions," he said. "I am not here to hide from justice; I am here to reveal criminality." But he said he expected Washington to act quickly against him. "On Thursday, the United States government itself vindicated my accuracy in claiming the 'NSA has weak hands,' when entirety of Congress ignored the fact that our spying programs are all based on a simple technical weakness in the law and reauthorized them for five more years," he said. "This is unconscionable, and The Washington Post editorial board understands that even if our representatives don't." "He was referring to a provision of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act that allows the NSA to collect records of Americans' phone calls. That provision, passed during the Bush administration, was up for renewal this year and won approval in the House of Representatives last week. Snowden said he hoped to apply for asylum in Iceland, which offers unique legal protections for whistleblowers. But he said he needs more time to secure his travel papers and work out other details. As a result, new or additional vulnerabilities can be created, such as low consumption levels resulting from either low incomes caused by excess labor supply, or rising food prices caused by output losses, or a combination of both. In a spatial environment, with multiple locations with independent but inter-connected markets, these transitions quickly become complex, and highly non-linear, as a result of the feedback loops between the micro individual-level decisions and the meso location-wise market decisions. To deal with these complex transitions, this paper presents an application of a spatially explicit agent-based model (ABM), or a "geo-simulation", of spatial non-linear short-run adjustment processes following a natural disaster-like shock scenario. The goal of this model is to allow policymakers to identify levels of post-shock displacement and spatial clusters of "food insecure" populations in low-income regions especially in the absence of reliable data. This leaps beyond the existing modeling efforts on natural disasters that usually deal with macro aggregated loss estimates in the long-run. Standard modeling tools, for example Input-Output models, CGE models, and Social Accounting Matrices (SAMs), lack the ability to analyze heterogeneous and spatial micro- and meso-level impact of shocks, and the short-run transitions where vulnerabilities can emerge in short time span. This paper builds on the agent-based model presented in Naqvi and Rehm (2014) where the interaction of six decision-making modules - Production, Wages, Consumption, Buying, Selling, Migration - form a complete economy with decentralized labor and goods markets with a focus on the decision making process of low-income workers. The original model is extended through two channels. First, market interactions are updated to allow for a more innovative search-and-match algorithm which allows supply networks to continuously adapt to a rapidly changing environment. Second, the model allows for a more dynamic migration decisions through endogenous location-wise probability assignments which go through several iterations to avoid completely arbitrary outcomes. In addition to updating the two behavioral rules, the model is extended to allow for incorporation of spatial data, bringing it one step closer to actual policy analysis. The model framework is applied to the 2005 earthquake in Pakistan which resulted in a massive loss of output and human life. A large fraction of the population was displaced while majority of the inhabitants in the region were left "food insecure" within weeks of the earthquake shock (ADB-WB, 2005; ERRA-UN, 2006). The region required immediate policy response to target vulnerable populations especially those facing food insecurity, but lacked reliable data for any type of evidence-based policy planning. This region is selected for two reasons. First, the region is fairly closed, both geographically and economically, comprising a large rural agrarian sector with simple economic dynamics and decision-making rules which are easy to implement in an agent-based modeling environment. Second, baseline data on population ratios, income, and consumption levels for pre-shock trends exist allowing for model calibration.

The Seamew was a marvel, its interior akin to the lavish spreads Mart had only ever glimpsed in magazines. They descended a polished staircase into the cabin, where they found Stephen Hollinger ensconced at a sturdy oak table cluttered with maps and machinery manuals, a testament to his thematic interests. The rugged, pioneering spirit was evident in every wrinkle and sun-crafted line on his face, suggesting tales untold, quests half-recounted. "Ah, Mart!" Hollinger's voice boomed with an unexpected joviality that shook Mart from his reverie. "Prompt as ever. We've got ourselves an opportunity. Just the man I need." He gestured to the array of intricate gadgets and blueprints splayed haphazardly. "Good to see you, sir." Mart nodded, navigating the transition from the formal to the familiar. His eyes danced over the papers, hungry for insight. "Bob, fetch us some orange soda or whatever's cold." Stephen waved a hand absently toward the mini-fridge in the corner, his attention firmly fixated on Mart now. "Mart, ever heard of the Quetzal?" "The Quetzal?" Mart repeated, intrigue tangling with wariness as he dug into his mental archives. "A shipwreck," Hollinger explained, eyes sparkling with the lift of a burgeoning exploit. The steward brought two bottles of lager beer, and Carr eagerly extended his thin, brown hand for the creamy, tempting liquid poured out for him by the mate. He drank it off and then laid down again. "When are we getting out of this beastly hole, Oliver?" he asked. "To night, I expect-that is, if the skipper comes aboard fairly sober. He doesn't often get too much grog aboard, but this island is one of the places where he is bound to get loaded up. The two traders ashore are countrymen of his, I believe, though they call themselves Britishers." Carr nodded. "Dutchmen of some kind, eh?" "Yes, like himself. He's a Dane, though if you told him so he'd get nasty over it." "He's a nasty brute, anyway," said Carr wearily. "I don't like that shifty eye of his. And I think he's a bit of a sneak." "You needn't think it; you can be sure of it. I'll prove it to you in a minute," said the mate. "Both he and that fat beast of a supercargo are a pair of sneaks, and they hate you like poison. What have you done to offend them?" "Nothing that I know of. But I have always suspected that neither of them are too fond of me. Hendry I consider a low-lived scoundrel. I met his wife and daughters in Sydney a year ago - went to his house with him. They think he's a perfect saint, and at the time I thought so too, considering he's been in the island trade for ten years. But I know what he is pretty well by now. He's not fit to be married to a decent white woman and have children." The mate assented. "You're right, Carr. He's a double-faced swab, and a thundering hypocrite as well. There's only one good point about him - he's a rattling good sailor man. As for Sam Chard, he's simply a drunken bully. I shall be glad to be quit of this hooker. I'm not a paragon of virtue, but this ship is a bit too rocky for me. Now I will show you what I meant just now when I said I'll prove that both Hendry and Chard are sneaks, and have their knives into you." He disappeared below for a few seconds, and then returned carrying a letter-book. "Now, Carr, my boy," he said, seating himself beside the sick trader again, "just cock your ears and listen. This is our esteemed supercargo's letter-book. I had to go into his cabin yesterday to look for the list of ship's stores, and I saw this letter-book lying on his table, opened at this particular page. I caught your name, and took the liberty of reading the letter. It is addressed to the owners in Sydney, and is dated May 5, 1889."

But the day's peculiarities did not conclude there. He wore a small reddish moustache which in the centre of his immense colourless face might remind a Biblical beholder of the Burning Bush in the desert of Sin, for he looked vaguely debauched (which he was not) and overfed (which was probable to the verge of certainty). His hands, of which he was exceedingly proud, were small and white and plump; they were carefully manicured and decorated with a couple of rings, each set with a large cabochon stone. When, as now, they were not otherwise occupied, he habitually used one of them to caress the side of this desert of Sin, as if to make sure that no whisker was surreptitiously sprouting there. In dress, though he was certainly old enough to know better, he affected the contemporary style of a fashionable young man, and his brown flannel suit had evidently the benediction of the tailor fresh upon it. His tie, in which was pinned a remarkably fine pearl, was slightly more vivid than his suit, but of the same colour as his socks, a smooth two inches of which appeared below his turned-up trousers, and his shirt had a stripe of the same colour as his tie. No watch-chain glittered on the amplitude where it would naturally repose, but on his left wrist he wore a narrow band of gold braid with a lady's watch set in it. A white straw hat and brown shoes were the alpha and omega of his costume. Though his face was singularly unwrinkled, except for rather heavy bags of loose skin below his eyes, it was quite evident that Arthur Craddock had left youth far behind him, but it would have been an imprudent man who would have wagered as to his ability to guess it within the limits of four or five years, for his corpulence was of the somewhat gross sort that may come early to an inactive man, in whose sedentary day dinner is something of an event. But it would not have required a very subtle physiognomist to conjecture for him an alert and athletic mind. His small grey eyes, which were unsurmounted by any hint of eyebrow, were, though a little red and moist, of a singular intensity in focus, and as active in poise and dart as a hovering dragon-fly, while even in repose they wore a notably watchful and observant look. His hands, too, which afforded him so constant a gratification, were undeniably the hands of an artist, long-fingered in proportion to the palms, and taper-nailed. Artist he was, too, to the very tips of those pink and shining triumphs of the manicurist, and though he neither painted nor played nor set forth on adventures in romance or poetry, his judgment and perception in all such achievements on the part of others was a marvel of unerring instinct, and was solidly based on an unrivalled knowledge of the arts.

Recent advances in fNIRS technology have significantly enhanced its applicability in diverse research and clinical settings, enabling a deeper understanding of brain function in complex environments. The integration of fNIRS with other neuroimaging modalities, such as EEG, can further enrich the data obtained, providing a more comprehensive view of neural activity. This multimodal approach allows researchers to capitalize on the strengths of each technique, facilitating the exploration of concurrent cortical and subcortical activities, and yielding insights that are both temporally and spatially precise (Cui et al., 2011). One of the key areas where fNIRS has shown remarkable promise is in pediatric neuroscience. Its non-invasive nature ensures that infants and young children, a population often challenging to study with conventional neuroimaging techniques, can be safely examined. By employing fNIRS, researchers can investigate early brain function and development, monitoring neural responses to various stimuli and identifying potential developmental disorders at an early stage (Lloyd-Fox et al., 2010). Beyond clinical and developmental contexts, fNIRS is being increasingly utilized in cognitive neuroscience to unravel the complexities of cognitive processes like decision making, language processing, and problem-solving. Its ability to record hemodynamic responses in the prefrontal cortex, a region heavily involved in higher-order cognitive functions, makes it an invaluable tool for elucidating the neural underpinnings of these processes (Ehlis et al., 2014). Researchers have employed fNIRS to study the neural correlates of cognitive load and multitasking, providing insights that have both theoretical implications and practical applications in fields such as education and human-computer interaction. Moreover, the portability and resilience to movement artifacts inherent in fNIRS devices make them ideal for field studies where participants engage in naturalistic tasks. This opens up exciting opportunities to study neural dynamics within real-world environments, such as athletic performance, workplace interactions, and social exchanges, providing a richer context for understanding how the brain functions in everyday life (Perrey, 2008). In the domain of neurorehabilitation, fNIRS has the potential to facilitate the development of personalized intervention strategies by monitoring brain activity in individuals undergoing therapy. This capability can guide the adjustment of therapeutic approaches in real-time, optimizing outcomes for conditions such as stroke, traumatic brain injury, and neurodegenerative diseases. By correlating patterns of brain activation with behavioral improvement, clinicians can tailor treatments to the unique neural profiles of their patients (Coyle et al., 2007). The realm of BCI also stands to benefit greatly from fNIRS advancements. By decoding brain activity patterns associated with specific cognitive or motor tasks, fNIRS-based BCIs can offer alternative communication and control methods for individuals with severe motor impairments. As the technology continues to evolve, it holds promise for enhancing the autonomy and quality of life for people with disabilities, fostering their independence and integration into society (Naseer and Hong, 2015). In conclusion, the rapid development of fNIRS technology is paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in neuroscience. Its versatility, non-invasiveness, and compatibility with real-world applications ensure that it will remain a pivotal tool in the exploration of brain function across a wide spectrum of contexts, from basic research to clinical interventions and beyond. As researchers continue to unlock its potential, fNIRS is poised to contribute significantly to our understanding and improvement of human health and cognition.

In essence, the journey towards a consolidated sense of self is intrinsically tied to various cognitive, emotional, and social developments observed in early childhood. Beyond basic physical self-recognition, there are nuanced layers of self-awareness that emerge as children engage with their surroundings and form social bonds with others (Meins et al., 2013). As children increasingly navigate their emotional landscapes, they inevitably encounter scenarios that prompt not only self-reflection but also the possibility of self-evaluation. It is in these contexts that the interplay of self-awareness and social cognition becomes particularly salient. At approximately two years of age, children begin to express themselves verbally, simultaneously marking a significant expansion in their cognitive capabilities. Language allows for more sophisticated internal dialogues, fostering the emergence of what researchers refer to as "narrative self" (Fivush, 1994). This narrative self enables individuals to weave their personal experiences into coherent stories, effectively integrating their perceptions of self with both temporal and situational contexts. The capacity to narrate one's experiences necessitates an understanding of continuity in life events-a hallmark of psychological self-awareness. Such skills further evolve through guided parental discussions about emotions and experiences, helping children to construct a nuanced understanding of themselves. As cognitive abilities progress, children not only become aware of their own psychological states but also develop an understanding of the mental states of others, a phenomenon referred to as theory of mind (Wellman, 1990). The convergence of self-awareness and the ability to infer the thoughts, feelings, and intentions of others is critical to forming meaningful social relationships. By realizing that others possess thoughts and motivations that may differ from their own, children undergo a transition that enhances their social interactions, leading to empathetic behaviors and cooperative play (Harris, 1992). Empathy and sociability are essential facets of self-awareness, serving as conduits for an individual's emotional experiences and social engagement. In the realm of developmental psychology, scholars debate the implications of these evolving self-concepts. Some suggest that self-awareness can be viewed as a linear developmental pathway, while others advocate for a more dynamic model, where self-concept is influenced by social contexts, cultural factors, and individual experiences (Rochat, 2009). The latter perspective acknowledges that the formation of self is not solely an individual endeavor but a relational one, emerging through interactions with caregivers, peers, and broader societal influences. For instance, cultural variances in self-construal can shape how children perceive and define themselves, leading to differing expressions of self in different environments (Markus and Kitayama, 1991). The developmental trajectory of self-awareness does not culminate in childhood; rather, it lays the foundation for ongoing self-reflective processes in adolescence and adulthood. As individuals age, their self-concept becomes increasingly multifaceted-intertwined with personal histories, relational dynamics, and existential queries about identity and purpose (Erikson, 1968). Adulthood may witness a reexamination of the self, spurred by life transitions such as career shifts, relationship changes, and parenthood, prompting individuals to recalibrate their understanding of self in light of new experiences. This ongoing evolution fundamentally suggests that our exploration of self-awareness should consider not only developmental stages but also the intricate web of interpersonal, cultural, and contextual influences that shape how individuals understand themselves across their lifespan. Employing an integrative approach, which acknowledges the complex interplay of cognitive, emotional, and social dimensions, may yield richer insights into the evolving tapestry of human self-awareness, allowing researchers to elucidate the breadth and depth of what it truly means to have a self.

Dr. King's eyes narrowed, reflecting a mix of disbelief and sorrow, like a window through which waves of history rushed forth. "It slays me to witness how far we seem to have drifted from the dream," he murmured, shaking his head gently. "When I spoke of freedom and dignity, I envisioned something more profound-a society wherein equality flourished, one where our voices would be celebrated and not caricatured. It causes my heart to ache knowing that our strides have been obscured by these images." He leaned forward, elbows resting on his knees, and I could see the weight of centuries pressing down on him. "These representations," he continued, "do more than entertain; they define who we are in the cultural lexicon. The young members of our community absorb these lessons, unaware that the language they adopt can suffocate the very essence of their heritage." As he sat there, the flickering light of the television bouncing off his stoic face, I pondered the breadth of his thoughts. "But Martin," I replied, attempting to provide some semblance of continuity in our conversation, "not everyone succumbs to those images. There are voices of resistance. Artists who counteract that narrative-are they not worthy of mention?" He nodded with cautious optimism. "Indeed, they deserve our attention and admiration, but they often remain overshadowed, walking in the shadows of a spectacle that so seductively captures the mainstream. The majority frequently overlooks the poets, the thinkers, the musicians who grapple with their experiences and transcend beyond mere survival. Their artistry sharpens our consciousness-reminding us of our legacy, our triumphs, and our tribulations." A sense of urgency filled the air; I felt the weight of our dialogue as if we were standing on the precipice of critical realization. "Martin," I pressed further, "what do you think could change this narrative? How do we bring those voices to the forefront?" "The answer," he said, pausing for effect, "lies in intentionality. We must cultivate spaces where our youth can engage with literature, music, and film that embrace complexity. Mentorship, it appears, is paramount. We must teach our values-values of empathy, introspection, and respect for all humanity. The more we can activate critical dialogues, the more likely our culture will thrive in richness rather than a hollow portrayal of brashness." His gaze drifted back to the colorful spectacle on the screen, a cacophony of sound and sight dimming the warmth of his eloquent revelations. "In my time, I sought to build bridges," he reflected. "Bridges of understanding that could lead us to reconciliation. Right now, there are too many chasms, widening with each passing moment. A society cannot thrive in division; instead, it must embrace its kaleidoscopic reality-with dignity and honor for every individual." As I listened, a sense of realization surged within me, igniting a desire for action. "So, what do we do?" I asked, feeling the weight of his wisdom distill down to a singular point of inquiry. Dr. King smiled faintly, that familiar glimmer of hope flickering in his eyes. "Extend your hand," he said earnestly. "Help others see the richness of their history and the nuances of our present. Engage not only in conversations but in actions that uplift, inspire, and educate. That, my friend, is the spirit of true progress." With those words hanging in the air, I felt a renewed sense of purpose and clarity-perhaps it was true; the journey towards change begins with the smallest of steps, like a ripple in a vast ocean, waiting to swell into waves of transformation.

Recently our political parties in a national conference declared the use of drones is not only a continued violation of our territorial integrity but also detrimental to our resolve at efforts in eliminating terrorism from our country," Sharif said. "This issue has become a major irritant in our bilateral relationship as well. I therefore would stress the need for an end to the drone attacks." Sharif has previously called for an end to the U.S. drone program in Pakistan, where it has stirred deep anger, and will raise the issue with Obama on Wednesday, said Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry, a spokesman for the Pakistani Foreign Ministry. "The government of Pakistan believes drone strikes are against international law and the sovereignty of Pakistan," Chaudhry told CNN. "Drone strikes are counterproductive to fighting terrorism." Pakistan wants to persuade the United States to stop using drones, he said. "International opinion is against drone strikes, not just here in Pakistan, but in the world," Chaudhry said. "This opinion is strengthening." Adding to the pressure, Human Rights Watch also released a report on U.S. drone attacks Tuesday - this one focusing on Yemen. Letta Taylor, a senior counterterrorism researcher for Human Rights Watch, said the group found at least two clear cases of violations of international laws of war, but those did not reach war crimes status. The group said four of the six attacks it had investigated "may have violated the laws of war." Sources: Drone strikes in Yemen kill 6, including senior AQAP leaders. Lack of U.S. disclosure. Based on extensive field research, the reports underlined the difficulties of gathering information on attacks in dangerous areas of Pakistan and Yemen. "We found that despite assurances from President Obama that (the U.S. government is) doing its utmost to protect civilians from harm, that in fact in many cases it is killing innocent civilians, even dozens of them, if not more," Taylor said. And both reports noted the U.S. government's unwillingness to talk about the cases. The lack of information from U.S. authorities, Amnesty said, makes it impossible "to reach firm conclusions about the context in which the U.S. drone attacks on Mamana Bibi and on the 18 laborers took place, and therefore their status under international law." White House Press Secretary Jay Carney rejected the idea that the United States has violated any laws. "To the extent these reports claim that the U.S. has acted contrary to international law we would strongly disagree," he said at a press briefing Tuesday. "The administration has repeatedly emphasized the extraordinary care that we take to make sure that counterterrorism actions are in accordance with all applicable law." The U.S. government has said strikes by the unmanned aircraft are a necessary part of the fight against militant groups. In May, Obama defended the drone program and disclosed the guidelines determining its use.

But two tired, brave, tough girls sat on a bench inside the hall of the ship, and painted their fingernails with bright red varnish and talked about wanting their mail and worried about their missing footlockers, their valuable footlockers which had in them the vital comfortable shoes and the unvital, probably never-to-be-worn evening dresses. One of the ship's British officers, who had been in the Merchant Marine since the beginning of the war but had never yet set forth in a white ship, came to talk with the girls. He looked tired, and he was vastly amused by their nail polish. "It would be nice," he said, "if we could take that nail polish to London tonight, instead of where we're going." The tall, pretty nurse held her hands out to see whether the job was well done. "No," she said. She was from Texas and spoke in a soft, slow voice. "'No. I'm glad to be going just where I'm going. Don't you know how happy those little old boys are going to be when they see us coming?" Pulling out of the harbour that night, we passed a Liberty ship going the same way. The ship was grey against the grey water and the grey sky, and standing on her decks, packed solidly together, khaki, silent and unmoving, were American troops. No one waved and no one called. The crowded grey ship and the empty white ship sailed slowly out of the harbour towards France. We crossed by daylight, and the morning seemed longer than other mornings. The captain never left the bridge and, all alone and beautifully white, we made our way through the mine-swept channel. Then we saw the coast of France. As we closed in, there was one LCT [landing craft, tank] near us, with washing hung up on a line, and between the loud explosions of mines being detonated on the beach, one could hear dance music coming from its radio. There were barrage balloons, looking like comic toy elephants, bouncing in the high wind above the massed ships, and you could hear invisible planes flying behind the grey ceiling of cloud. Troops were unloading from big ships to heavy barges or to light craft, and on the shore, moving up brown roads that scarred the hillside, our tanks clanked slowly and steadily forward. Then we stopped noticing the invasion, the ships, the ominous beach, because the first wounded had arrived. An LCT drew alongside our ship, pitching in the waves. A boy in a steel helmet shouted up to the crew at the aft rail, and a wooden box looking like a lidless coffin was lowered on a pulley, and with the greatest difficulty, bracing themselves against the movement of their boat, the men on the LCT laid a stretcher inside the box.

He said: 'It was a small-scale unit made up of 30 guys - one officer and two soldiers per patrol. We were all ex-paratroopers. The Army thought we were perfect for this type of work because we'd been trained in close-quarter combat. We wore civilian clothes. It was dangerous. You could be taken out at any moment. We were going out there to shoot people.' He added: 'We were given very little intelligence about targets but we were briefed on the kind of people we should expect to encounter. We knew our mission was to kill IRA members or those suspected of being involved in terrorism. There was no such thing as a warning shot. That would have been suicide. We would shoot to kill. When we heard a gun go off nearby we'd move in immediately. The idea was to stop the gunman escaping or firing another round.' Asked if he ever considered taking prisoners rather than killing them, Cursey replied: 'Not really. I didn't want to take the risk of getting captured. The idea was to kill them where they stood. It was kill or be killed.' He said the unit's operations were run from Thiepval Barracks in Lisburn, Co Antrim. The officers in charge gave orders via radio. They also kept records of the number of shots fired and the locations of engagements. Cursey said: 'When we came back we'd give a verbal account of what happened and then write it down. The details were recorded. At the end of each month we would receive 50 extra pay. I was paid 1,500 a year for my MRF duties. It was money well spent. We did a lot of good. It was worth every penny.' He added: 'There was no way you could have conducted the same operation openly. You couldn't do what we did while wearing uniforms. If the IRA realised what was happening they would have changed their tactics. They would have got rid of their weapons. That wasn't an option. We needed to carry on regardless.' Cursey served in the MRF from October 1973 until June 1974. He joined the Parachute Regiment in September 1968 and was posted to Belfast in April 1970. After leaving the Army he worked as a security consultant, running anti-terrorist training courses around the world. He also published two novels, The Thin Red Line and Storm Warning, both of which drew on his experiences in Northern Ireland. He now lives in Spain. Cursey is currently writing a third novel called Dead Man's Hand. He says it will contain further details of the MRF's operations.

As the hunter disappeared into the dense undergrowth, the forest seemed to swallow him whole, leaving behind only the faintest whisper of his presence. The trees, like sentinels of the wilderness, stood watchful and still, their branches creaking softly in the gentle breeze. The air was heavy with the scent of damp earth and decaying leaves, and the sound of crickets provided a soothing background hum. The sun, now dipping low in the sky, cast long shadows across the forest floor, making it seem as if the very trees themselves were stretching out to claim the land. The hunter's footsteps, muffled by the soft earth, were the only sound that broke the silence, and even those were quickly swallowed up by the dense foliage. As the darkness deepened, the forest began to take on a mystical quality, as if the very spirits of the land were stirring. The trees seemed to loom larger, their branches reaching out like skeletal fingers, and the wind whispered secrets through the leaves. The hunter, moving quietly through the underbrush, felt as if he was being drawn deeper into the heart of the forest, as if some ancient power was calling to him. And yet, despite the eerie atmosphere, the hunter felt a sense of peace, a sense of being one with the land and the creatures that inhabited it. He knew that he was not alone, that there were others out there, watching and waiting, but he was not afraid. For he was a hunter, a part of the forest, and he knew that he was home. As the moon rose high in the sky, casting a silver glow over the forest, the hunter came to a clearing. In the center of the clearing stood an ancient tree, its branches twisted and gnarled with age. The hunter approached the tree, feeling a sense of reverence wash over him. He reached out a hand and touched the trunk, feeling the rough bark beneath his fingers. And then, as if in response to his touch, the tree began to glow with a soft, ethereal light. The hunter felt a surge of energy run through him, and he knew that he was being called to something greater, something ancient and powerful. He closed his eyes and let the energy wash over him, feeling himself become one with the forest, one with the land and the creatures that inhabited it. The hunter opened his eyes to find that the forest had changed. The trees seemed taller, the shadows deeper, and the air was filled with a strange, pulsating energy. He knew that he had been changed, that he had been awakened to a new level of awareness, and he felt a sense of wonder and awe wash over him. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, everything was silent. The forest was still, the trees stood motionless, and the hunter was left standing alone in the clearing, feeling the weight of the forest's secrets upon him. He knew that he had been given a gift, a glimpse into the mysteries of the land, and he felt a sense of responsibility, a sense of duty to use that gift wisely.

Not a single person has testified that Milosevic ordered war crimes. Whole swaths of the indictment on Kosovo have been left unsubstantiated, even though Milosevic's command responsibility here is clearest. And when the prosecution did try to substantiate its charges, the result was often farce. Highlights include the Serbian "insider" who claimed to have worked in the presidential administration but who did not know what floor Milosevic's office was on; "Arkanas secretary", who turned out to have worked only as a temp for a few months in the same building as the notorious paramilitary; the testimony of the former federal prime minister, Ante Markovic, dramatically rumbled by Milosevic, who produced Markovic's own diary for the days when he claimed to have had meetings with him; the Kosovo Albanian peasant who said he had never heard of the KLA even though there is a monument to that terrorist organisation in his own village; and the former head of the Yugoslav secret services, Radomir Markovic, who not only claimed that he had been tortured by the new democratic government in Belgrade to testify against his former boss, but who also agreed, under cross-examination by Milosevic, that no orders had been given to expel the Kosovo Albanians and that, on the contrary, Milosevic had instructed the police and army to protect civilians. And these, note, were the prosecution witnesses. Serious doubt has also been cast on some of the most famous atrocity stories. Remember the refrigerator truck whose discovery in the Danube in 1999, full of bodies, was gleefully reported as Milosevic was transferred to The Hague in June 2001? The truck had allegedly been retrieved from the river and then driven to the outskirts of Belgrade, where its contents were interred in a mass grave. But cross-examination showed that there is no proof that the bodies exhumed were the ones in the truck, nor that any of them came from Kosovo. Instead, it is quite possible that the Batajnica mass grave dated from the second world war, while the refrigerator truck may have contained Kurds being smuggled to Western Europe, the victims of a grisly traffic accident. The realisation is now dawning that lies were peddled to justify the Kosovo war just as earnestly as they were to justify the attack on Iraq. The weakness of the prosecution case was underlined by the fact that its triumphant conclusion in February was to broadcast a TV documentary made several years ago. This suggests that its two-year marathon has not served to advance knowledge of the truth beyond the tall stories peddled by telly hacks at the time. Even professional supporters of the ICTY now admit that the only "proof" of Milosevic's guilt has been General Sir Rupert Smith's stated "impression" that Milosevic controlled the Bosnian Serbs, and Paddy Ashdown's statement that he "warned" the former Yugoslav head of state that war crimes were being committed in Kosovo.

Although now used routinely to retrieve terrestrial fluorescence from space, perhaps the main limitation of the SIF method is that although SIF is distributed across a relatively broad spectral range (~650-850 nm), fluorescence as measured by the FLD is observable only at the discreet intervals where light absorption occurs. Recent advances in spectral fitting methods address the above limitation by reconstructing the full emission spectrum by combining FLD measurements at multiple absorption features (Zhao et al., 2014, 2018; Cogliati et al., 2015). Such a reconstruction is desirable as it facilitates the scaling up of spectral parameters currently observable at the leaf scale to the canopy, such as the red far-red fluorescence peak ratio, which can be used to estimate leaf chlorophyll content (Hak et al., 1990; Buschmann, 2007). Further, the difference between canopy and leaf emission spectra provides insight into radiative transfer processes that occur at these scale intersections (Liu et al., 2017; Yang and Van Der Tol, 2018). Spectral reconstruction methods solve an inverse problem and rely on prior assumptions of the shape of the emission distribution to constrain the solution; this information is ultimately derived from simulations. In Zhao et al. (2014, 2018) and Cogliati et al. (2015) these simulations were generated by the Soil Canopy Observation Photochemistry and Energy (SCOPE) model (Van der Tol et al., 2009). Therefore although it is possible to predict and reconstruct canopy leaving fluorescence spectra, such predictions are un-validated due to the lack of any direct measurements of canopy scale spectra. Chlorophyll a fluorescence spectra are relatively easy to measure at the leaf scale in the laboratory (Hak et al., 1990; Magney et al., 2017; Rajewicz et al., 2019) and also in the field (Van Wittenberghe et al., 2013). Usually a low pass filter is employed to facilitate excitation but remove the contribution of reflected light from the measured signal. Once measured, SIF spectra can be statistically related to plant functional traits such as Specific Leaf Area or pigment contents (Van Wittenberghe et al., 2015; Atherton et al., 2017). However, as it is the canopy that is the typical target object in remote sensing, it is therefore the canopy emission spectrum that is of primary relevance. Of the little empirical work examining spectral fluorescence at the canopy scale, Zarco-Tejada et al. (2003) measured the superimposition of fluorescence spectra on canopy reflectance spectra for a small canopy and revealed a double-peak shape. More recently, Carstensen et al. (2016) developed a greenhouse-based system measuring fluorescence emitted from basil plant canopies using a multi-colour LED illumination system. Also recently, Romero et al. (2018) measured fluorescence spectra emitted by a small fig tree placed within a darkened wooden box. In this work Romero et al. (2018) developed a physically based set of equations to quantify the effect of light re-absorption at the leaf and whole tree scale, and therefore relate the canopy leaving fluorescence spectrum to the spectrum emitted from the chloroplasts within the leaf.

She would show the glittering arch of her upper third, occasionally, and scrape it along behind the comblike row; sometimes a pinnacle stood straight up, like a statuette of ebony, against that glittering white shield, then seemed to glide out of it by its own volition and power, and become a dim specter, while the next pinnacle glided into its place and blotted the spotless disk with the black exclamation-point of its presence. The top of one pinnacle took the shapely, clean-cut form of a rabbit's head, in the inkiest silhouette, while it rested against the moon. The unillumined peaks and minarets, hovering vague and phantom-like above us while the others were painfully white and strong with snow and moonlight, made a peculiar effect. But when the moon, having passed the line of pinnacles, was hidden behind the stupendous white swell of Mont Blanc, the masterpiece of the evening was flung on the canvas. A rich greenish radiance sprang into the sky from behind the mountain, and in this some airy shreds and ribbons of vapor floated about, and being flushed with that strange tint, went waving to and fro like pale green flames. After a while, radiating bars - vast broadening fan-shaped shadows - grew up and stretched away to the zenith from behind the mountain. It was a spectacle to take one's breath, for the wonder of it, and the sublimity. Indeed, those mighty bars of alternate light and shadow streaming up from behind that dark and prodigious form and occupying the half of the dull and opaque heavens, was the most imposing and impressive marvel I had ever looked upon. There is no simile for it, for nothing is like it. If a child had asked me what it was, I should have said, "Humble yourself, in this presence, it is the glory flowing from the hidden head of the Creator." One falls shorter of the truth than that, sometimes, in trying to explain mysteries to the little people. I could have found out the cause of this awe-compelling miracle by inquiring, for it is not infrequent at Mont Blanc, - but I did not wish to know. We have not the reverent feeling for the rainbow that a savage has, because we know how it is made. We have lost as much as we gained by prying into the matter. We took a walk down street, a block or two, and a place where four streets met and the principal shops were clustered, found the groups of men in the roadway thicker than ever - for this was the Exchange of Chamonix. These men were in the costumes of guides and porters, and were there to be hired. The office of that great personage, the Guide-in-Chief of the Chamonix Guild of Guides, was near by. This guild is a close corporation, and is governed by strict laws.

Here were the oriel windows of the best rooms, looking out on a grassplat, small enough in country eyes, but most extensive for the situation, with straight gravelled walks, and low lilac and laburnum trees, that came into profuse blossom long before their country cousins, but which, like the crocuses and snowdrops of the flower borders, had better be looked at than touched by such as dreaded sooty fingers. These shrubs veiled the garden from the great river thoroughfare, to which it sloped down, still showing traces of the handsome stone steps and balustrade that once had formed the access of the gold-chained alderman to his sumptuous barge. Along those paths paced, book in hand, a tall, well-grown maiden, of good straight features, and clear, pale skin, with eyes and rich luxuriant hair of the same colour, a peculiarly bright shade of auburn, such as painters of old had loved, and Owen Sandbrook called golden, while Humfrey Charlecote would declare he was always glad to see Honor's carrots. More than thirty years ago, personal teaching at a London parish school or personal visiting of the poor was less common than at present, but Honora had been bred up to be helpful, and she had newly come in from a diligent afternoon of looking at the needlework, and hearing Crossman's Catechism and Sellon's Abridgment from a demurely dressed race of little girls in tall white caps, bibs and tuckers, and very stout indigo-blue frocks. She had been working hard at the endeavour to make the little Cockneys, who had never seen a single ear of wheat, enter into Joseph's dreams, and was rather weary of their town sharpness coupled with their indifference and want of imagination, where any nature, save human nature, was concerned. 'I will bring an ear of Hiltonbury wheat home with me - some of the best girls shall see me sow it, and I will take them to watch it growing up - the blade, the ear, the full corn in the ear - poor dears, if they only had a Hiltonbury to give them some tastes that are not all for this hot, busy, eager world! If I could only see one with her lap full of bluebells; but though in this land of Cockaigne of ours, one does not actually pick up gold and silver, I am afraid they are our flowers, and the only ones we esteem worth the picking; and like old Mr. Sandbrook, we neither understand nor esteem those whose aims are otherwise! Oh! Owen, Owen, may you only not be withheld from your glorious career! May you show this hard, money-getting world that you do really, as well as only in word, esteem one soul to be reclaimed above all the wealth that can be laid at your feet!

As they entered the schoolroom, the girls took their seats at their respective desks, arranged in two rows facing each other. The teacher smiled warmly as she greeted her pupils, her eyes twinkling with a hint of mischief. "Good morning, my dears. I trust you are all ready for a busy day of learning?" she asked, her voice like music to the girls' ears. As Miss Patten began to review the previous day's lessons, Sylvia's thoughts drifted back to her mother, who would be delighted to hear about the song. People think I'm some kind of easy-going, laid-back guy because I'm from the Highlands. But let me tell you, I'm as competitive as they come. I just know how to channel it in a way that gets results." He pauses, taking a sip of his drink before continuing. "I mean, people think I'm this laid-back, affable guy, but I'm a winner.
