As we stood there, lost in the nostalgia of our childhood memories, I couldn't help but notice the subtle changes in Tibbie's demeanor. The carefree laughter, the mischievous glint in her eye, were still there, but there was a hint of worldliness, a certain jadedness that I had not seen before. It was as if the whirlwind of London society had swept away the innocence of her youth, leaving behind a polished, sophisticated woman who knew exactly what she wanted. "I suppose you're right, Wilfrid," she said, breaking the silence. "We were just children, playing at love. But I must admit, I did think you were the most romantic creature I had ever met. You were so dashing, so full of life, and those boxes of sweets were the most thrilling things I had ever seen." I chuckled, remembering the countless times I had smuggled those treats into the nursery, just to see the sparkle in her eyes. "I was a bit of a scamp, wasn't I?" I said, smiling. Tibbie nodded, her eyes sparkling with amusement. "You were, indeed. But I think that's what I loved about you. You were always so full of adventure, so willing to take risks. I, on the other hand, was always the cautious one, the one who played by the rules." As we stood there, the sun dipping lower in the sky, casting a golden glow over the park, I couldn't help but feel a pang of regret. If only I had been more serious, more committed, perhaps things might have been different between us. But I had been young, foolish, and selfish, and Tibbie had deserved better. "I'm sorry, Tibbie," I said, my voice low and sincere. "I know I let you down, all those years ago. I was too caught up in my own desires, my own ambitions, to see what was right in front of me." Tibbie's expression softened, and for a moment, I saw the girl she used to be, the one who had laughed and loved with abandon. "You didn't let me down, Wilfrid," she said, her voice barely above a whisper. "You were just being yourself, and I was too young to understand. But I do now. I know that we were never meant to be, that we were just two friends, playing at love." As the sun dipped below the horizon, casting the Long Gallery in a warm, golden light, I knew that Tibbie was right. We were just two old friends, reminiscing about the past, and I was grateful for that. For in the end, it was the memories, the laughter, and the love that we had shared that truly mattered, not the what-ifs and the maybes.

It's just so ridiculous and honestly, kind of sad. I know it's supposed to be some comedic element, but it just highlights how underwhelming the entire premise of the show is. Why does Hammerman need to call for help? Shouldn't he already be capable of handling minor inconveniences like, oh I don't know, losing his shoes? I mean, you'd think a superhero would be a bit more self-sufficient, right? Anyway, the episode just spirals from there. The graffiti is alive and wreaks havoc all over town, which, I suppose, is meant to be some sort of social commentary about 'vandalism' and its consequences, but it comes off as laughably contrived. The kids are depicted as these wide-eyed, naive troublemakers, and the villain? Oh man, the villain might be the most forgettable character in animation history. I swear, if I blinked, I would have missed half his dialogue. It's like they were trying to make him sound menacing, but it just didn't land. And let's not even get started on the message of the episode. "Don't graffiti or else your art might turn against you." It tries to teach kids a lesson, sure, but it's seriously heavy-handed. And while we're on the subject, why does Hammerman need a magic pair of shoelaces to combat this? All-in-all, I think I've gained a greater appreciation for Batman. At least in Gotham, the villains are fleshed-out and the stakes feel real. This, well... this feels like something you'd catch at two A.M. on a Saturday morning. Okay, I digress. The animation style is a nightmare; it feels like they slapped some colors together and called it a day. You know, I expected it to look outdated-it's from the 1990s after all-but this is a whole level of eye-sore. You can barely tell what's going on half the time. I mean, even the simple movements look stilted and awkward. It's like they're all stuck in a perpetual state of trying to catch up to actual action. It baffles me how this was a show enjoyed by kids. What were we thinking? Anyway, there's this climactic scene where Hammerman fights the animated graffiti. Picture this, Kenny: graffiti monsters splashing paint everywhere, and our "hero" is flailing around. You know, I follow a lot of superhero shows and movies, and I always appreciate the clever choreography-like how movements feel fluid and justified. But here? It's just Hammerman yelling and waving his arms like a malfunctioning puppet. I don't know whether to laugh or cringe. In conclusion, if you want a good laugh, Hammerman might be worth a watch, but if you're looking for a well-crafted story, uh, look elsewhere. Nothing beats Batman's dark undertones and rich storytelling. So, yeah, thanks for putting me through this, guys! Looking forward to whatever comes next, just more of Batman, please. All right, Kenny, what do you think? Keeping the excitement alive or are we just hitting a wall here?

This discrepancy in findings underscores the need for a comprehensive understanding of the interaction between the different tar components and the electrochemical activity of the solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs). The variability in performance responses to tar concentrations could be attributed to factors such as reaction temperatures, gas composition, and the presence of other contaminants, all of which play critical roles in the overall efficiency and longevity of the electrochemical systems. This necessitates the implementation of a systematic approach for the study of direct internal tar reforming, which includes rigorous testing across a range of operational conditions to elucidate the thresholds beyond which cell performance may be compromised [21]. Furthermore, these experiments should not only focus on the model compounds like toluene but should also consider more complex real tar mixtures derived from biomass gasification processes, as the real-world application of such systems will invariably involve these more intricate mixtures. Additionally, other critical parameters, including the anode material composition and structure, may influence the susceptibility of the SOFCs to carbon formation and therefore warrant further investigation. For example, nickel-based anodes are widely recognized for their catalytic effectiveness; however, they are also prone to deactivation through coking when exposed to tar compounds [22]. Exploring alternative anode materials or protective coatings might mitigate these adverse effects and prolong the operational life of the cells [23]. The subject of heat management in integrated biomass gasifier SOFC systems remains pivotal. A balanced thermal distribution is essential not merely to optimize the tar reforming reactions but also to maintain the integrity of the SOFC under varying loads and operational demands. Strategies such as recirculating heat or employing thermal buffers could enhance system resilience and overall energy efficiency. The development of advanced thermal management solutions, alongside hot gas cleaning strategies, could thus provide a dual benefit by improving fuel flexibility while simultaneously enhancing the efficiency of energy conversion processes. Moreover, advancing model simulations can play a vital role in optimizing system configurations and operational parameters. Recent advancements in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and thermodynamic modeling enable researchers to create detailed simulations of gasifying processes and the subsequent behavior of the biosyngas as it enters the SOFC. Such modeling can yield insights into optimal gasification conditions, the expected types and concentrations of different tar compounds, and the subsequent gas cleaning requirements. Coupling these simulations with experimental validation could significantly accelerate the development of more effective and reliable micro-CHP systems utilizing biomass [24]. In the grand scheme of energy transition, the realization of integrated biomass gasifier SOFC systems holds the promise for a more sustainable means of harnessing biomass energy. The dual challenge of removing contaminants while ensuring high-efficiency energy extraction must guide future research directions. Ultimately, the synergy between interdisciplinary scientific exploration-encompassing materials science, chemical engineering, and thermodynamics-will be instrumental in navigating the hurdles that currently limit the industrial application of this promising technology. Thus, as we look forward to further developments, the collaboration between academia, industry, and policy-makers will be crucial in catalyzing the transition toward cleaner and sustainable energy sources, ensuring that the innovations we pursue today lead to a greener tomorrow.

In the lanes, courts, and alleys that ran still farther back into the great hive, there was an amount of squalor, destitution, violence, sin, and misery, the depth of which was known only to the people who dwelt there, and to those earnest-faced men with Bibles who made it their work to cultivate green spots in the midst of such unpromising wastes, and to foster the growth of those tender and beautiful flowers which sometimes spring and flourish where, to judge from appearances, one might be tempted to imagine nothing good could thrive. Here also there were rats, and cats too, besides dogs of many kinds; but they all of them led hard lives of it, and few appeared to think much of enjoying themselves. Existence seemed to be the height of their ambition. Even the kittens were depressed, and sometimes stopped in the midst of a faint attempt at play to look round with a scared aspect, as if the memory of kicks and blows was strong upon them. The whole neighbourhood, in fact, teemed with sad yet interesting sights and scenes, and with strange violent contrasts. It was not a spot which one would naturally select for a ramble on a summer evening after dinner; nevertheless it was a locality where time might have been profitably spent, where a good lesson or two might have been learned by those who have a tendency to "consider the poor." But although the neighbourhood was dirty and noisy, our modest street, which was at that time known by the name of Redwharf Lane, was comparatively clean and quiet. True, the smell of tallow and tar could not be altogether excluded, neither could the noises; but these scents and sounds reached it in a mitigated degree, and as the street was not a thoroughfare, few people entered it, except those who had business there, or those who had lost their way, or an occasional street boy of an explorative tendency; which last, on finding that it was a quiet spot, invariably entered a protest against such an outrageous idea as quietude in "the City" by sending up a series of hideous yells, and retiring thereafter precipitately. Here, in Redwharf Lane, was the office of the firm of Denham, Crumps, and Company. Mr Denham stood with his back to the fire, for it was a coldish autumn day, with his coat-tails under his arms. He was a big bald man of five-and-forty, with self-importance enough for a man of five-hundred-and-forty. Mr Crumps sat in a small back-office, working so diligently that one might have supposed he was endeavouring to bring up the arrears of forty years' neglect, and had pledged himself to have it done before dinner. He was particularly small, excessively thin, very humble, rather deaf, and upwards of sixty. Company had died of lockjaw two years previous to the period of which we write, and is therefore unworthy of farther notice.

As the six former Guantanamo detainees settled into their new lives in Uruguay, they were greeted with a mix of curiosity and caution from the local population. The men, who had spent over a decade behind bars without charge, were now free to start anew in a country that had offered them a second chance. Uruguayan officials had promised to provide them with housing, food, and medical care, as well as assistance in finding employment and integrating into the community. The men's arrival had sparked a flurry of media attention, with local journalists clamoring to get a glimpse of the former prisoners. However, the Uruguayan government had imposed strict restrictions on access to the men, citing concerns for their privacy and security. As a result, few details had emerged about their initial impressions of their new home or their plans for the future. One thing was clear, however: the men were grateful to be free at last. In a statement released through their lawyers, they expressed their thanks to President Mujica and the Uruguayan people for giving them a chance to rebuild their lives. "We are grateful for the opportunity to start anew and to leave the darkness of Guantanamo behind," the statement read. "We look forward to becoming productive members of Uruguayan society and to contributing to our new community." As the men began to settle into their new lives, human rights groups hailed their release as a major victory. "This is a significant step forward in the long struggle to close Guantanamo and to ensure that those detained there are treated with dignity and respect," said Cori Crider, the lawyer for Abu Wa'el Dhiab. "We hope that this marks the beginning of a new era in which the US government prioritizes justice and compassion over fear and mistrust." However, not everyone was celebrating the men's release. Some critics argued that the move was a mistake, citing concerns about the men's alleged ties to al-Qaeda and the potential risks they posed to national security. "These men were detained at Guantanamo for a reason," said Senator John McCain, a vocal critic of the Obama administration's detention policies. "We should not be releasing them without ensuring that they do not pose a threat to the United States or its allies." Despite such criticism, the Obama administration remained committed to its goal of closing Guantanamo and transferring its remaining detainees to other countries. With the Uruguay transfer, the number of detainees at the prison had fallen to 136, down from a peak of over 700 in 2003. The administration was now working to transfer dozens more detainees to other countries, including Yemen, Afghanistan, and Europe. As the debate over Guantanamo continued to rage on, the six former detainees in Uruguay were focused on rebuilding their lives and starting anew. They had been given a rare second chance, and they were determined to make the most of it.

As the girls sat around the cozy camp fire at Wanderer's Roost, listening to Marian's thrilling stories of the Camp Fire Girls of the West, a strange spirit of romance swept over them all. Each of the seven resolved to do her utmost to become worthy of membership in the noble organization of which Marian spoke with pride. The result was that when the vacation ended, each girl took up her work with renewed vigor. During the second term at school they formed themselves into a Camp Fire Circle, calling it the Hillside Camp Fire after the name of the street where Miss Belaire's Academy is located. They elected Ruth Garnier Guardian, and began immediately to plan for the opening of a council fire. When the time arrived for the council fire to be held, the Hillside Camp Fire Circle numbered thirty members. All these girls were present on the night that Ruth Garnier made her vow before the blazing camp fire. But, as already stated, it was the little band of six that were waiting impatiently for the close of the ceremony so that they might have a chance to congratulate their friend. Their eyes sparkled with delight as they watched the expression of pleased surprise on Ruth's face. As the last strains of the good-night song died away, the girls arose en masse and surrounded Ruth, clapping her on the back, and shouting, "Hurrah! Wo-he-lo for Ruth Garnier!" "For shame! Shame on you!" cried Miss Drexal, rising to her feet and shaking her fist at the noisy crowd. "You are acting like children instead of young ladies." "But we're happy, aren't we?" protested Ruth, laughing gaily. "And our happiness doesn't mean any disrespect to you or to the Camp Fire." "No, of course not, dear," replied the Guardian, smiling indulgently. "I'm glad you're happy. You deserve to be." She turned to the other girls, saying: "Will you please sit down now? We can talk quietly if you will be still." "Yes, ma'am," said Anne Follett, sitting down beside Ruth and putting her arm affectionately around her friend. "We'll be quiet, won't we, girls?" "Sure," answered Sarah Manning. "Let's make it unanimous." "Hear! Hear!" chorused the rest of the party. "All right," smiled Miss Drexal. "Now, let us all sing 'The Camp Fire Song,' and then you may go home." "Home! How dreary!" sighed Ruth, as the sweet melody of the old familiar hymn filled the air. "I'd rather stay here and talk. What fun it would be to sleep out under the stars tonight!" "What a lovely idea!" exclaimed Frances Bliss. "Do let's, Ruthie. I've always wanted to sleep in the open. It sounds awfully romantic." "So it does," agreed Ruth. "Oh, well, perhaps some day I'll be able to arrange it for you girls. But I must admit I feel kind of homesick myself. I want to see my mother." "She'll be proud of you, Ruth," said Sarah. "She's just dying to come up to the school tomorrow to hear your speech. And she wants to meet all of us." "Does she really?" asked Ruth, surprised. "Why didn't you tell me before?" "Because you've been working so hard preparing for the ceremony," explained Sarah. "It wouldn't have seemed fair to bother you with anything else." "Well, anyway, I shall be glad to see Mother tomorrow," declared Ruth. "I haven't seen her since I left home."

Performance improved with age, and it was not until 8 years that approximately half of children passed the task. Interestingly, most children found manufacturing a tool (making a tool following adult demonstration) comparatively easy. This finding appears consistent across cultures. Western and Bushman children show a similar pattern of tool innovation performance; innovating a tool independently to solve a physical problem is difficult for children aged 3-5 years, whereas manufacturing a tool following an adult demonstration is significantly easier (Nielsen et al., 2014). Beck et al. (2011) noted that children's knowledge of tool function and ability to manufacture tools emerges significantly earlier than their ability to innovate tools. Given the findings from tasks involving corvids, children's difficulty with tool innovation has been met with curiosity. Given that many nonhuman species are known to use tools (Seed & Byrne, 2010), it is the human propensity for tool innovation, and the complex technologies that have arisen because of it, that sets us apart from nonhuman species. Findings such as these raise bigger questions surrounding human cognitive architecture. It is important to better understand those processes that we might share with nonhuman animals and those that may demonstrate human uniqueness (Shettleworth, 2012). Cross-species comparisons between human children and nonhuman animals are often made (e.g., Beck et al., 2011; Cheke, Loissel, & Clayton, 2012; Engelmann, Herrmann, & Tomasello, 2012; Taylor et al., 2014). However, caution is required. To truly understand how human children differ from other species, in this case corvids, it is vital that studies are methodologically sound and fair to both species (Boesch, 2007; Shettleworth, 2012). When experimental procedures systematically differ, the value of cross-species comparisons is compromised. To date, the experiences of children and corvids on versions of the hook-making task have not been consistent. Specifically, the experiences of the corvids and children prior to attempting the hook-making task were inconsistent. Corvids had already seen and had the opportunity to use a premade hook-made either from the same material as was available for tool making (wire; Weir et al., 2002) or from a different material (wood; Bird & Emery, 2009). Some children had not seen a pipe-cleaner hook previously within the task (Beck et al., 2011), and others had seen a hook but did not have the opportunity to use it (Cutting et al., 2014). The effect and potential advantage that such an experience might have on subsequent tool innovation in children is yet to be determined. Cutting et al. (2014) suggested that certain pretest experiences can promote tool innovation on the hook-making task. In their study, 4- to 6-year-olds were shown a premade example of a pipe-cleaner hook (target tool demonstration). Half of the children also had the pliable nature of the test material (pipe cleaners) highlighted to them via "bending practice."

The inconsistent results between the two studies by Zhang et al. highlight the complexity of laser PBF at sub-atmospheric pressures. The varying process settings and conditions used in these initial studies make it challenging to draw definitive conclusions about the effects of pressure on the process. The contradictory findings also underscore the need for further research to establish the optimal process parameters for laser PBF at sub-atmospheric pressures. One possible explanation for the discrepancy between the two studies is the difference in the type of powder used. The first study used pure Ti powder, while the second study employed stainless steel powder. The properties of these powders, such as their melting points and thermal conductivity, may affect the behavior of the powder during the PBF process. For instance, Ti powder may be more prone to vaporization due to its higher melting point, which could lead to the observed decrease in density and increase in surface roughness at low pressures. Another factor that may have contributed to the inconsistency is the chamber pressure itself. The first study used a pressure of 100 1/2bar, while the second study used a pressure range of 1-100 mbar. The lower pressure in the first study may have resulted in more pronounced effects of metal vaporization, leading to the observed changes in density and surface roughness. To further understand the effects of sub-atmospheric pressures on laser PBF, it is essential to conduct more comprehensive studies that consider the interplay between process parameters, powder properties, and chamber pressure. This may involve investigating the effects of varying pressure ranges, laser powers, and scan speeds on the PBF process, as well as the use of different powder materials and chamber atmospheres. In addition to the potential benefits of reduced porosity and surface roughness, the use of sub-atmospheric pressures may also offer improved control over crystal orientation and reduced oxidation. However, the latter advantage may be offset by the increased risk of powder explosion or ignition due to the reduced pressure. Therefore, it is crucial to carefully balance the benefits and risks of sub-atmospheric pressures in laser PBF. Future research should focus on developing a deeper understanding of the physical and chemical processes occurring during laser PBF at sub-atmospheric pressures. This may involve the use of advanced characterization techniques, such as X-ray computed tomography or scanning electron microscopy, to study the microstructure and porosity of the fabricated parts. Additionally, computational modeling and simulation can be employed to predict the behavior of the powder and molten metal during the PBF process, allowing for the optimization of process parameters and the prediction of potential defects. Ultimately, the successful implementation of laser PBF at sub-atmospheric pressures will require a comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms and the development of optimized process parameters. By addressing the challenges and inconsistencies associated with this process, researchers can unlock the potential benefits of reduced porosity, surface roughness, and oxidation, and pave the way for the widespread adoption of this technology in various industrial applications.

I'm losing touch with reality talking to a screen all night. Ian closed his laptop with a sigh, sinking back into his pillow, gazing at the glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling. The distant thumps of his brother's music barely infiltrated his thoughts, but they were a perfect backdrop for his restless mind. He reached for his phone and hesitated. Felicia's number glowed softly in his contacts list, a beacon of opportunity for connection that he always seemed to fumble. It was different with her in person, where her smiles and sarcasm made things easier. But through a screen, Ian felt like he was stumbling through a minefield, never sure when he would misstep and blow everything up. "Just be cool," he murmured to himself, rolling out of bed and shuffling to the window. The street outside was quiet, save for the occasional car passing by. Ian peered into the night, drawing comfort from the peaceful suburban scene. The air was crisp, tinged with the scent of distant rain, and he realized how comforting it felt to stand there, away from the pressures of impressing anyone. A quiet knock on the door pulled him back inside. Dylan poked his messy hair into the room, looking uncharacteristically subdued. "Hey, you alright? Saw your light on. Couldn't sleep either?" Ian shrugged. "Just thinking. What about you?" Dylan leaned against the doorframe, arms crossed. "Jenna broke up with me," he admitted, a trace of vulnerability in his usually confident demeanor. It was a rare moment that made Ian see his brother as something other than the invincible athlete. "Sorry, man," Ian said, genuinely sympathetic. "You wanna talk about it?" Dylan sighed, running a hand through his hair. "Not really. Just needed to get out of my head for a bit." Ian nodded, understanding well enough. "Let's watch a movie or something. No pressure. Just hang out." They ended up sprawled on the floor, a forgotten pizza box between them as the familiar Star Wars opening crawl lit up the screen. Ian couldn't help but appreciate the simplicity of it all. It reminded him that despite their differences, he and Dylan could find common ground somewhere. As the Death Star loomed across the television, Ian felt the weight of the virtual world slip away. Here, in this shared universe of space adventures, he could be himself without pretense or pressure. He'd figure out how to navigate the real world's complexities, just like those epic space battles. By the time the credits rolled, both brothers had relaxed considerably. Dylan yawned and stretched, glancing at Ian with a sheepish smile. "Thanks, Ian. I needed that." Ian flashed a grin. "Anytime, bro." But as Dylan retreated to his side of the room, Ian's thoughts drifted back to Felicia and the party he'd attended only through a screen. Maybe next time, he'd try reaching out in person. After all, if he could survive another round with Darth Vader, he could tackle the enigma of friendship in the real world. With renewed determination, he locked eyes with the digital clock glowing beside him and made a silent vow: tomorrow would be different.

The Brazilian pepper tree (Schinus terebinthifolius Raddi (Anacardiaceae)) is native to subtropical South America and was introduced into South Africa for ornamental, hedging, and shade/shelter purposes (Panetta and McKee, 1997). Here it is classified as a Category 1b invasive under the National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act (NEMBA) in the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo and Mpumalanga Provinces, and Category 3b in Free State, Gauteng, North-West, Northern Cape and Western Cape Provinces. It is highly adaptive and so can take the form of either an evergreen shrub (2-3 m) or a tree (up to 15 m) (Lenzi and Orth, 2004a). It produces small, cream-white, dioecious (male and female) flowers that appear from September to March. A single S. terebinthifolius tree can produce a large number of bright red (when ripe) drupe-like fruits of a 3-5 mm diameter, surrounding a single internal seed. Due to its high tolerance of extreme moisture conditions, shaded environments and saline conditions, and its allelopathic effects on surrounding plants, S. terebinthifolius may compete with native species (D'Avila et al., 2010). Schinus terebinthifolius is an aggressive pioneer species, rapidly growing during its seedling and sapling stages, particularly in nutrient-depleted soils (de Souza et al., 2001). It also rapidly occupies early and secondary stages, mainly resulting from a high dispersal of seeds (Backes and Irgang, 2002). Like so many other damaging invasive plants, it is generally dispersed by native frugivores (Meisenburg and Fox, 2002). In its native Brazil, it is pollinated by an array of different flies, wasps and bees and its fruiting period is from January to October (in South Africa fruit normally sets in winter months) (Lenzi and Orth, 2004b; Jesus and Monteiro de Araujo Filho, 2013). In South Africa there has been some evidence of S. terebinthifolius being dispersed by frugivorous birds (pers. obs.). Indian laurel, Litsea glutinosa (Lour.) C.B. Rob. (Lauraceae) is an invasive species in South Africa (NEMBA Category 1b) that is especially problematic in KwaZulu-Natal Province, particularly in the vicinity of Durban. It has a native range extending from the Himalayas, through South-East Asia to Oceania (Heuze et al., 2015), and was introduced into South Africa for cultivation (Ross, 1972). It is an evergreen shrub or tree (6-10 m), producing small, yellow-orange flowers that appear from October to May (summer) and with lance-shaped leaves. The fruits are pea-sized shiny black berries with a single seed inside (Jacq et al., 2005). We determined whether native avian frugivores ingest the fruits of S. terebinthifolius and L. glutinosa and whether the ingestion of the seeds of these two species by various frugivorous avian species has an effect on their potential dispersal, and germination time and success.

Here, bourgeois, worker and Bohemian alike could enjoy a song or a theatrical act for the price of a drink. All kind of distractions were in vogue, and the low life, in particular the amorous low life, was suddenly hot. Located right in the heart of artistic Bohemia and Paris' criminal underworld, the establishments of the Montmartre district were perfectly equipped to serve it up...and to fulfill that yen which the French even coined a phrase for, that is 'la nostalgie de la boue' (lit: longing for mud). Crowning the Montmartre-based world of commercial entertainment was Joseph Oller and Charles Zidler's landmark music hall, the Moulin Rouge. When the Moulin Rouge opened its doors on the Place Blanche at the foot of Montmartre on the 6th of October 1889, all Paris turned out. Highbrow and lowbrow society alike mobbed the 'Palace of Women' before the paintwork was dry on its extravagantly decorated interior. The Moulin Rouge's decor, by Montmartre painter Adolphe Willette, its exotic colour, form and themeing became an overnight legend. Besides the immense dance hall complete with galleries to watch the dance floor and an orchestra mounted above the stage, there was a garden with another stage, cafe tables, cavorting monkeys and unstockinged prostitutes riding donkeys. Also in the garden, a giant elephant (gleaned when the Universal Exhibition of 1889 terminated) housed an Arabian-themed club inside its body. Male clients entered via the elephant's leg where a spiral staircase opened onto belly dancing performances, an orchestra and an opium den. Making a radical break with the century's relentless class divisions, a microcosm of Parisian society rubbed shoulders in scandalous proximity. European royalty (including the Prince of Wales), ambassadors, politicians, industrialists and magistrates slummed it with celebrity courtesans, can-can girls and workers. The local Montmartre Bohemians and the cocottes and noctambules (prostitutes), pimps, madams and thieves who were their neighbours were also out in force. Within the Moulin's velvet draped walls, the aromas of women's scent, face powder, tobacco, and beer mingled as promiscuously as the audience. In a class of their own were the courtesans, a social phenomena that all but died out with the end of the Belle Epoque and the beginning of World War I. Though springing from the same working class as the prostitutes, the more celebrated courtesans were distinguished by the length and high-style of the relationships they formed (with, near exclusively, the elite of Europe). Like today's film stars and super-models, they were also cultishly observed by press and public. But if the Moulin Rouge quickly established its reputation as the most exotic sex market in Paris, it also represented a kind of cultural and social revolution. Think of it as a can-can-besotted version of Steve Rubell's disco-crazed Studio 54 crossed with Bangkok's sex market meets Mardi Gras' carnival.

Yet - the words stuck.... Evidently, he was fated to be a sight-seer that morning. When he entered Buckingham Palace Road, the strains of martial music banished the gaunt specter called into being by the red cotton banner. A policeman, more cheerful and spry than his comrades who marshaled the procession shuffling towards Westminster, strode to the center of the busy crossing, and cast an alert eye on the converging lines of traffic. Another section of the ever-ready London crowd lined up on the curb. Nursemaids, bound for the parks, wheeled their perambulators into strategic positions, thus commanding a clear view and blocking the edge of the pavement. Drivers of omnibuses, without waiting for the lifted hand of authority, halted in Lower Grosvenor Gardens and Victoria Street. Cabs going to the station, presumably carrying fares to whom time meant lost trains, spurted to cross a road which would soon be barred. And small boys gathered from all quarters in amazing profusion. In a word, the Coldstream Guards were coming from Chelsea Barracks to do duty at St. James's, coming, too, in the approved manner of the Guards, with lively drumming and clash of cymbals, while brass and reeds sang some jaunty melody of the hour. The passing of a regimental band has whisked many a youngster out of staid Britain into the far lands, the lilt and swing of soldiers on the march have a glamour all the more profound because it is evanescent. That man must indeed be careworn who would resist it. Certainly, the broad-shouldered young giant who had been momentarily troubled by the white-red ghost of poverty was not so minded. He could see easily, over the heads of the people standing on the edge of the pavement, so he did not press to the front among the rabble, but stood apart, with his back against a shop window. Thus, he was free to move to right or left as he chose. That was a slight thing in itself, an unconscious trick of aloofness - perhaps an inherited trait of occupying his own territory, so to speak. But it is these slight things which reveal character. They oft-times influence human lives, too; and no man ever extricated himself more promptly from the humdrum of moneyless existence in London than did Richard Royson that day by placing the width of the sidewalk between himself and the unbroken row of spectators. Of course, he knew nothing of that at the moment. His objective was an appointment at eleven' o'clock in the neighborhood of Charing Cross, and, now that he was given the excuse, he meant to march along the Mall behind the Guards. Meanwhile, he watched their advance. Above the tall bearskins and glittering bayonets he caught the flourish of energetic drumsticks. The big drum gave forth its clamor with window-shaking insistence; it seemed to be the summons of power that all else should stand aside.

His fingers danced across the sputtering keys, a restless energy propelling him into the ethereal realm of sound. He wove melodies that spiraled and ebbed, a reflection of his youthful spirit that soared in the face of inexplicable darkness. Yet, beneath the surface of the music lay a restless undertone, shaped not only by joyful chords but also by the murmur of an unspoken fear that echoed within the confines of the small room. "Clement," she began, her own soft voice almost swallowed by the gentle ripple of sound. "Do you not wonder what awaits us on the morrow? What if this 'prick of a pin' leads us somewhere unfathomable?" The question hung in the air like a fragile spider's thread, susceptible to the slightest shift. "Why think of such things? You know the doctor speaks the truth. The light is coming," he replied, determination weaving through his words, even as uncertainty loomed like shadows at the edge of the garden. "Our eyes will be freed! We will see the sun rise over the hills, feel the dew on the grass, and paint our world with colors we have only dreamt of." He paused, lost in sudden reverie. "Just imagine it! I want to see the way the flowers dance with the wind." She turned her face toward the faint glow of dusk beyond the window. "But that which we desire, sweet brother, may carry burdens we do not yet understand. To see is to face what lies hidden in both joy and sorrow. Can you not feel the weight of that? And what if, instead of beauty, we find ourselves haunted by the ordinary?" A shiver coursed through him at her words. "You speak of shadows, but look where they scurry away in the light! The world isn't just ordinary; it possesses secrets as wondrous as it is mundane. All we must do is embrace it with open hearts." "Does the heart not falter? Does it not ache?" Her voice quivered, catching on the wind that danced languidly through the sunny garden, seeking solace amid the flowers. "I fear that behind every beautiful bloom lies the truth of decay." "Perhaps," he mused, a thoughtful frown creasing his brow. "But isn't that the essence of life? To rise against the heaviness of despair with the joy we can muster? Think of the stories we'll tell, the laughter that will echo through our days! Even the petals have their season, yet they forge their paths despite knowing their time is fleeting." His fervor ignited a flicker in her heart, much like the last glimpses of fading sunlight casting golden hues across the flower-garden. Yet, the shadows crept in. "You are brave, Clement, endlessly so. But I..." she hesitated, barely feeling the tremor of apprehension in her heart, "I am afraid." He lifted his head, his large eyes wide and earnest, even without the lantern of sight. "Do not let fear silence your song, sister. Hold fast to hope." The fervor of his words spun around her like silk, weaving delicate threads of courage into her waning spirit. "Perhaps," she breathed, longing to grasp the tether of his optimism. The delicate scent of jasmine filled the air, weaving through the melancholy, and she allowed herself to wonder - what would it be like to taste the joy of sight? What colors might illuminate their world? Tears pricked at her eyes, but they were a mix of fear and anticipation. "Tomorrow," he whispered as he turned the melody into a gentle lullaby, "is the quiet before the storm of brilliance." She closed her eyes, wishing that the storm would carry them both into the light, where they might dance with laughter among the flowers.

The quest for novel antimicrobial agents that can effectively combat the growing threat of multidrug-resistant bacteria has led researchers to explore alternative approaches, such as photodynamic inactivation (PDI). This non-conventional method has shown promise in inactivating a range of bacterial species, including Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. The mechanism of action of PDI involves the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which induce oxidative stress and ultimately lead to cell death. One of the key advantages of PDI is its multi-targeted approach, which allows ROS to react with a wide range of biomolecules within the bacterial cell. This can lead to a more effective killing of bacteria, as ROS can target multiple sites within the cell, including the cell membrane, DNA, and proteins. In contrast, traditional antibiotics often target a single site or mechanism, which can lead to the rapid development of resistance. The development of PDI as a therapeutic approach has been hindered by the lack of understanding of the factors that govern the susceptibility of Gram-negative bacteria to PDI. Gram-negative bacteria, such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Escherichia coli, are notoriously difficult to kill due to the presence of an outer membrane that serves as a barrier to antibiotics. The outer membrane is composed of lipopolysaccharides, which can induce the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines from host cells and act as a potent virulence factor. Furthermore, Gram-negative bacteria are able to secrete proteases that can degrade matrix proteins and disrupt defense systems, such as antibodies and cytokines. Additionally, many Gram-negative bacteria contain endotoxins that can block the activity of potential drugs and protect the sensitive inner membrane and cell wall. To overcome these obstacles, researchers have been working to develop rationally designed photosensitizers that can effectively target Gram-negative bacteria. Phthalocyanines, for example, have been shown to be efficient photosensitizers in the photodynamic inactivation of microorganisms, including Gram-negative bacteria. These compounds have also been used in photodynamic therapy for cancer treatment. The use of PDI as a therapeutic approach has several advantages over traditional antibiotic therapy. PDI is less prone to the development of resistance, as the generation of ROS is a complex process that requires multiple mutations to occur. Additionally, PDI can be used in combination with other therapies, such as antibiotics, to enhance its efficacy. In conclusion, PDI is a promising approach for the treatment of bacterial infections, particularly those caused by Gram-negative bacteria. The development of rationally designed photosensitizers that can effectively target these bacteria is crucial for the success of PDI as a therapeutic approach. Further research is needed to understand the factors that govern the susceptibility of Gram-negative bacteria to PDI and to develop effective treatments for these infections.

Yet, what truly elevates the Cooper Union Address beyond mere rhetoric is Lincoln's deft orchestration of emotion and reason, harmonizing them in a manner that resonates with the very heartbeat of the nation. With every word, he crafts a narrative that breathes life into the very essence of American democracy, reminding us that our collective identity is forged not merely through the ink of treaties and tomes, but through the audacity of our principles, the courage of our convictions, and the clarity of our purpose. The grandeur lies not solely in the arguments he makes but in the passionate invocation of a shared destiny, as he beckons his audience to rise above the tumult of their time toward a more profound understanding of liberty and equality. Lincoln artfully dissects the existing societal fabric, illustrating the pernicious grip that slavery imparts to the nation's moral compass. His articulation of the future is not a mere forecast but a solemn betrothal to unity and righteousness. "If we could first know where we are, and whither we are tending," he posits, "we could better judge what to do, and how to do it." How simplicity belies profundity! Isn't it a profound truth that resonates still amid modern dilemmas? Waterston, in his portrayal, captures the grave timbre of Lincoln's voice, echoes of steel laced with empathy, as he lays bare the hypocrisy inherent in a nation proclaiming freedom yet shackling its own citizens. The juxtaposition of ideals serves as a potent reminder: We are called not merely to become the bearers of liberty but guardians, nurturing its flame against the encroaching shadows of injustice. Furthermore, Lincoln's deft command over his audience is masterful; he does not merely plead his case but sparks self-reflection, challenging each person present to assess their own moral foundations. He dissects the arguments of his opponents with surgical precision; they are, after all, not merely political adversaries but figures in a larger moral tapestry. It's marvellous to witness how he casts doubt upon inertia and complacency: "Shall we whose fathers fought for the nation's liberty, shall we forsake it now?" One can't help but marvel at the audacity of vision in Lincoln's words, for while he stands firmly against the encroachment of slavery, he simultaneously fosters a sense of hope. Hope that transcends and prevails, even when clouds of despair loom heavy. The way he beckons his audience forward, enlivens the very concept of progress and the quintessential human spirit. It's a call to action, to embolden citizens to forge their destinies rather than be swept away by history. Though Waterston incarnates Lincoln, it is the essence of the message-the determination to confront injustice and confront the moral failings of society-that transcends time. The Cooper Union Address resonates today, echoing in debates on equity and rights, casting shadows across legislative chambers where ethical dilemmas often beg for clarity. In the heart of that grand edifice, Lincoln invoked not merely the specters of history but the torchbearers of future generations, a lineage of thought that persists to this day. It reminds us that the struggles of the past must serve as compass points for the future. As listeners, it is our duty to remain vigilant, to safeguard the ideals enshrined in our constitution, and to honor the profound sacrifices made in the name of what we hold true. Lincoln's clarion call for unity and moral courage, delivered amid the chaos of division, is, perhaps, the loftiest aspiration of which we can all endeavor to be a part.

The efficacy of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives is thus contingent upon the authenticity and transparency with which they are executed. When companies undertake CSR initiatives merely as a facade, striving primarily for public relations gain rather than genuine altruism, the repercussions can undermine the very goals they hope to achieve. Stakeholders, particularly employees, possess a heightened sensitivity to the dissonance between a company's stated values and its actual practices. This incongruity can lead to skepticism and disillusionment, ultimately impairing organizational cohesion and employee morale (Rupp et al., 2006). Consequently, businesses must not only implement CSR strategies that reflect their commitments but also ensure that these strategies resonate with employee values. Moreover, a significant outcome of authentic CSR engagement is the potential for enhanced employee performance. When employees perceive their organization as committed to ethical practices and societal contributions, there is a substantial likelihood that they will exhibit increased levels of engagement and productivity (Brammer, Millington, & Pedersen, 2007). These employees tend to adopt positive organizational citizenship behaviors, going above and beyond the call of duty, motivated by a shared sense of purpose and alignment with the company's mission. This intrinsic motivation, fueled by meaningful CSR initiatives, translates into a more vigorous and cohesive workforce. However, organizations must steer clear of complacency. Merely initiating CSR endeavors without consistent follow-through and genuine commitment poses substantial risks. Employees, often regarded as the backbone of an organization's social responsibility efforts, must be afforded opportunities to actively participate in CSR initiatives, fostering a sense of ownership and involvement. As studies suggest, employee engagement in CSR activities enhances their identification with the organization, reinforcing their commitment to its objectives and solidifying their role as brand ambassadors even beyond the workplace (Glavas & Piderit, 2009). Summarily, integrating employees into CSR initiatives not only enriches the company culture but can cultivate a robust pro-social climate that propels organizations toward sustainable success. Additionally, influencing the external perception of an organization through CSR is imperative. The growing consumer base is increasingly inclined to support businesses that demonstrate a commitment to ethical practices and social responsibility, leading to positive word-of-mouth recommendations and heightened consumer loyalty (Lichtenstein, Drumwright, & Braig, 2004). As external stakeholders become more discerning in their evaluations of corporate behaviors, the alignment of employee perceptions with these values emerges as a strategic asset that companies can leverage. An informed and engaged workforce serves as a beacon of authenticity, signaling to customers that the organization not only prioritizes profit but also recognizes its broader societal obligations. Finally, it is essential to recognize that CSR is an evolving domain, frequently shaped by societal expectations, regulatory environments, and global challenges. As such, companies must remain agile, responsive to stakeholder feedback, and adaptable to changing paradigms. Engaging in ongoing dialogues with employees and other stakeholders about CSR can promote a culture of openness and trust, fostering an environment in which innovation and social consciousness coalesce. This dynamic interaction not only enriches CSR practices but can also unveil new opportunities for organizations to contribute meaningfully to society while enhancing their competitive standing in an increasingly conscientious marketplace. In essence, the pursuit of effective CSR is intrinsically linked to the authentic involvement and perceptions of employees. Businesses that espouse a genuine commitment to stakeholder welfare will undoubtedly reap the benefits, not only in terms of enhanced reputation and loyalty but ultimately in fostering an ethical framework that embodies the essence of their organizational identity.

So I strode along, in spite of the dark and the cold, for I was young and had youth's impatience of fear and discomfort, and when at length I came out upon the corner of a street where there were lights enough to show me the way home, I turned, and presently found myself passing a little group of men standing before a dingy door. They seemed to be discussing something earnestly, and I noticed that they kept looking nervously over their shoulders as if they feared to be seen. 'The police station is somewhere near,' I said to myself, 'and they are doubtless waiting for somebody to be taken there.' Then, as I went by them, I heard a voice say in a hoarse whisper, 'I don't care how many people he kills. Let him kill them all!' This remark attracted my attention, and I stopped. 'What do you mean?' I asked, turning sharply on the speaker. 'You'd better look after your own business, mister,' said he, backing away from me with a muttered oath. 'We'll see to our own affairs,' I answered, and walked on slowly. Presently another man spoke to me, saying, 'Say, mister, you're the chap that wants to go to Mars, ain't you?' 'Yes,' I replied, 'that is, I am going to try and get there; but how did you know that?' 'I heard you talkin' about it down at the corner saloon,' said he. 'Oh, did you? Well, good-night to you. With their hair and makeup in various states of readiness, they look like a disheveled flock of flamingos stepping to the beat of singer/designer Avril Lavigne, who is nowhere in sight even though the show bears the Canadian rocker's name and her brand's imprint, Abbey Dawn. The collection, a swirling motif of skulls, rainbows, pleather and studs, isn't exactly Vujevic's speed, but she's still excited to take part in this kind of production. It's completely different from Rachel Antonoff's garden party-themed presentation Sunday, in which Vujevic's prop was a badminton racket, or the Christine Alcalay presentation earlier that day, which was staged in a 1,000-square-foot studio in an office building. For that job, she wakes at 7 a.m. Monday, showers and puts on just a bit of mascara and concealer. She takes a cab to the Garment District, arriving at the 11th floor whitewashed studio about two hours before showtime. It's not a runway show but a "presentation," in which the models will be dressed and positioned on the showroom like living mannequins. For now, the corner studio with lots of natural light pouring through the windows is a backstage area for hair and makeup. Eventually, it will transition into a showroom with music from a live violinist, creating an atmosphere reminiscent of an art gallery. Vujevic takes a seat, and a makeup artist gets to work on her face while a nail technician applies heated "nail shields" that behave like stickers. Helen was a dainty, compelling brunette with flashing eyes - eyes she had already learned to use to the undoing of what Ruth called "the youthful male of the species." As for Ruth herself, she considered boys no mystery. She was fond of Tom, for he was the first friend she had made in that long-ago time when she arrived, a little girl and a stranger, at the Red Mill. Other boys did not interest Ruth in the least. Without Helen's beauty, she was, nevertheless, a decidedly attractive girl. Her figure was well rounded, her eyes shone, her hair was just wavy enough to be pretty, and she was very, very much alive. If Ruth Fielding took an interest in anything that thing, Tom declared, "went with a bang!" She was positive, energetic, and usually finished anything that she began. She had already done some things that few girls of her age could have accomplished. The trio of friends trooped into Aunt Alvirah's clean and shining kitchen. "Dear me! dear me!" murmured the little old woman, "I sha'n't have the pleasure of your company for long. I'll miss my pretty," and she smiled fondly at Ruth. "That's the only drawback about coming home from school," grumbled Tom, looking really forlorn, even with his mouth full of Aunt Alvirah's pound cake. "What's the drawback?" demanded his twin. "Going away again. Just think! We sha'n't see each other for so long." He was staring at Ruth, and Helen, with a roguish twinkle in her eye, passed him her pocket-handkerchief - a wee and useless bit of lace - saying: "Weep, if you must, Tommy; but get it over with. Ruth and I are not gnashing our teeth about going away. Just to think! ARDMORE!" Nothing but capital letters would fully express the delight she put into the name of the college she and Ruth were to attend. "Huh!" grunted Tom. Aunt Alvirah said: "It wouldn't matter, deary, if you was both goin' off to be Queens of Sheby; it's the goin' away that hurts." Ruth had her arms about the little old woman and her own voice was caressing if not lachrymose. "Don't take it so to heart, Aunt Alvirah. We shall not forget you. You shall send us a box of goodies once in a while as you always do; and I will write to you and to Uncle Jabez. Keep up your heart, dear." "Easy said, my pretty," sighed the old woman. "Not so easy follered out. An' Jabe Potter is dreadful tryin' when you ain't here." "Poor Uncle Jabez," murmured Ruth. "Poor Aunt Alvirah, you'd better say!" exclaimed Helen, sharply, for she had not the patience with the miserly miller that his niece possessed. At the moment the back door was pushed open. Helen jumped. She feared that Uncle Jabez had overheard her criticism.

Pictures leaked to MailOnline, showing hundreds of boxes of applications piled on the floor of a Passport Office in Liverpool, piled pressure on the Government to introduce emergency measures to tackle the backlog. The Prime Minister last week apologised for the chaos after he revealed there were at least 30,000 applications outstanding which had not been processed within the normal three-week limit. In fact, there is evidence that some children with DS may have increased rates of arousals during sleep, even before the onset of OSAS [16]. The question of whether early detection and treatment of OSAS improves cognitive outcomes in young children with DS remains unanswered. The few longitudinal studies investigating the effects of early intervention have yielded mixed results. One study found no significant difference in adaptive behavior scores between children who received treatment and those who did not [17], while another reported improvement in cognitive skills after surgery [18]. It is important to note, however, that the sample size in both studies was small, thus limiting statistical power. While the relationship between OSAS and poor cognitive outcome is not yet established, it seems clear that the presence of OSAS is associated with an increase in daytime sleepiness. This effect is especially pronounced in older children with DS, where OSAS leads to increased daytime napping and decreased school attendance [19-22]. Additionally, the relationship between OSAS and impaired attention has been demonstrated in typically developing populations [23-25]. While the role of sleep disruption in childhood DS has been explored in previous studies, the impact of sleep quality on working memory and attention has yet to be investigated. Working memory refers to the ability to maintain information in mind while simultaneously processing new incoming stimuli. Attention is a component of executive function, and includes the ability to focus on relevant stimuli while ignoring irrelevant stimuli, as well as the ability to shift attention from one task to another. Both working memory and attention are critical components of academic success, particularly in reading comprehension and mathematics. Previous studies have shown that children with DS exhibit difficulties in these areas [26-29]. Thus, it is possible that poor sleep quality could further exacerbate existing working memory and attention deficits in children with DS. Furthermore, since sleep deprivation in adults has been shown to affect performance on measures of working memory and attention [30-33], it would also be interesting to examine whether sleep quality affects these domains in children without DS. In summary, the goal of the current study was twofold: First, we aimed to determine if sleep quality is related to cognitive performance on tests of working memory and attention in children with DS. Second, we sought to explore the possibility that sleep quality may contribute to cognitive weaknesses in children with DS, and that improving sleep quality may help mitigate such deficits. We hypothesized that poorer sleep quality would predict worse performance on measures of working memory and attention in both groups. We also predicted that, compared to typically developing controls, children with DS would perform more poorly on measures of working memory and attention, and that this group difference would remain significant after controlling for sleep quality. We recruited 20 participants with DS and 24 age-matched typically developing controls. All participants were between 6 and 12 years old. Participants with DS had a clinical diagnosis of Down Syndrome and were evaluated by a psychologist or neuropsychologist. Individuals with known genetic disorders other than Down Syndrome and/or congenital heart defects were excluded. Typically developing children were recruited via flyers posted around local elementary schools. Parents completed a questionnaire about health history, current medications, and any known medical conditions. Exclusion criteria included a diagnosis of ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, learning disability, psychiatric disorder, epilepsy/seizures, or head injury resulting in loss of consciousness lasting longer than 30 minutes. Children with DS were enrolled in special education programs within public school districts in the surrounding area. Controls attended public or private schools in the same geographic region. Two children with DS and two typically developing children were unable to complete the testing battery due to fatigue. Data from these children were excluded from analyses.

Initial research suggests that early social anxiety may indicate risk for emotional health problems across childhood. For example, Bufferd and colleagues found that a diagnosis of social anxiety at age 3 years predicted social anxiety disorder and specific phobia 3 years later (Bufferd, Dougherty, Carlson, Rose, & Klein, 2012). Furthermore, Carpenter et al. (2015) found that a history of preschool social anxiety predicted less functional connectivity between the amygdala and ventral frontal cortices when children viewed angry faces (Carpenter et al., 2015), indicating a potential difficulty with emotion regulation. These examples highlight the potential that research examining social anxiety in young children holds for furthering our understanding of the development of anxiety across childhood. However, to conduct this type of work with young children it is imperative that we have valid and reliable measures of social anxiety for this age group that can be administered quickly and easily. Whilst diagnostic assessments such as the Preschool Age Psychiatric Assessment (PAPA; Egger & Angold, 2004) used by Bufferd et al., 2012; and the Anxiety Disorders Interview Schedule (ADIS; Silverman & Nelles, 1988) are the gold standard, they are not always practical given the time and resources required to train assessors and carry out the interviews. Currently, the only available questionnaire measure of social anxiety in early childhood is a subscale of the PAS; other subscales include generalized anxiety, separation anxiety, obsessive compulsive disorder and physical injury fears. The PAS was developed as a parallel measure of the Spence Children's Anxiety Scale (SCAS; Spence, 1998), which measures anxiety symptoms in children aged 7-18 years. The PAS is not ideal for capturing social anxiety for two reasons. First, the social anxiety scale, which consists of six items, is not designed as a stand-alone measure so many additional items (a further 22 items) must be completed unnecessarily. Second, the PAS includes many cognitive items i.e. "Worries that he/she will do something to look stupid in front of other people ". Due to the 'hidden' nature of cognitions and the broad context of the questions, it may be difficult for parents to accurately respond to these items (Comer & Kendall, 2004). In contrast, the SWQ-P is a brief (10-item) parent-report measure of social anxiety in 8-17 year olds. All items load onto a single 'social worries' factor. The items focus on specific situations and observable behaviours e.g. "Avoids or gets worried about entering a room full of people". As avoidance is more easily observed than cognitive symptoms and specific situations are given, parents should be able to provide more accurate report than on the PAS. Given this advantage of the SWQ-P as a parent-report measure, it is an attractive candidate for adaptation into a measure of social anxiety for a younger age group (children aged 4-8 years) for whom no specific measure of social anxiety currently exists. Such a measure will provide a valuable new tool for gathering information about social anxiety within this age group.

The immediate lesson we can learn here is that none of us - whether we are born-again, right-living, gospel-witnessing Christ followers or the wildest, backslidden, heathens - NONE of us knows how long we have on this earth. While the grief is overwhelming in Phillip's death, we can find a breath of comfort in knowing that he had given his life to Christ, and was living for HIM. You're completely on target by focusing on that verse - that God will not put on us more than we can take. The stretching comes when we find out exactly what 'more than we can take' means. Perspective comes with time. Those times in my life when I didn't think I could take any more, ended up being the times through which I grew the most. Being angry at God and questioning God is in and of itself a statement of faith IN God. If you didn't believe there WAS a God, there'd be no reason to rant and rave at him. Anger and questioning are part of what we are as humans. They are part of our relationships with each other, and they are likewise a part of our relationship with God. God isn't lessened by our questions or anger. God's bigger than that. He can handle it. Job's experience was something like that - he tried to find a reason... something he DID to cause all that to happen to him - he lost his home, his family, his health... and it didn't come down to anything he did or didn't do. It just came. That is what happens when you live in a broken world. Lives break, families break. People break. As for how to deal with the immediate situation... do concrete things. Fix food. Answer calls. Wash clothes, run errands. Sit and BE with the family. Pray a lot. Cry when you need to. When you pray, ask for strength to make it through. Ask for understanding in God's time. Don't expect a revelation in 15 minutes. Remember, perspective comes with time. And be prepared to NOT understand until you are face-to-face. Remember also, God said 'my ways are not your ways.' The grotesque object was more likely to inspire laughter than fear, for the body was small and its movements slow and feeble, but indeed it showed not the slightest sign of hostility. "I see," said the creature, "that you are from the old world. Who are you?" He spoke in a gentle voice and with an accent not unlike that which we call American. "My name is Lemuel Gulliver, a shipwrecked mariner, at your service. Will you tell me what island this is on which I find myself, and to whom I am speaking." "The island is Thule - Ultima Thule - the one spot of earth that has emerged from barbarism. Chance has done great things for you in bringing you here." He slipped one hand out of its boot, removed his big spectacles, and blinked his weak eyes. I watched him narrowly. His face was hairless. It might have been the face of an old woman or of an old man. A look of cunning now crept over it. "I think," he said, "that I grasp your difficulty. You may speak of me as a man; but for beings of the first class, to which I belong, sex is abolished. It was perhaps the worst of nature's evils that our triumphant civilisation in the process of centuries overcame." "But in that case," I said, "your race, or that class of it to which you belong, must be rapidly dying out." "It is undoubtedly dying out," said the strange creature with a complacent smile, "but less rapidly than a barbarian would suppose. Increased knowledge has brought with it increased longevity. I am myself one hundred and ninety-two years of age. The end must come, of course, but after all, why not?" As I looked at him I did not from the aesthetic point of view see why not. The creature had replaced the spectacles now, and lay at full length on the sand, as if wearied by the standing position. He went on speaking: "Death in the individual is, of course, to some extent a confession of failure. It means inability, mostly due to ignorance, to adapt oneself to one's environment. Death of a race may be quite a different matter - an exhaustion of utility. However that may be, it is clear that the last of us to survive will represent the highest possible development of human potentiality. I speculate sometimes on the question of who the ultimate survivor will be. It may possibly be Professor YM6403 of the Outer Office. Some think so. I believe he thinks so himself. On the other hand, I may be the last survivor. However, there are still some thousands of us in existence, and for the present these disquisitions may appear to you idle." My clothes were damp and I was chilly, hungry, and tired. His jabber about professors and survivors had no interest for me.

But it's during these feverish nights, when your brain is trapped in the smoky haze of illness, that you start thinking about all those charming little quirks of chatroom society. My mind, frantically stumbling through the muck of delirium, begins to revive vivid recollections of past exchanges with these random IM-ers. Like the time I got a message from SnoopyPaws777, who clearly had a penchant for sending unsolicited cat memes alongside the most bizarre conspiracy theories about the Moon. "Did you know," they typed furiously, "that astronauts were actually sent to harvest moon cheese? It's all connected!" Naturally, as I was admiring a fuzzy cartoon cat sitting contemplatively on a space rocket, I couldn't help but ponder just how deep the rabbit hole could go. The wild adventures didn't stop there. Oh no, there was also this mesmerizing soul masquerading under the alias of FuzzyWuzzy808. Their approach was unique, a classic blend of nonsensical jargon and heartfelt musings on the meaning of life-each message both perplexing and oddly comforting. One memorable night, amid fever dreams and throat pain, they declared, "Life is like a pizza; it's all about the toppings." Can you believe that? My fever-addled brain relished the absurdity, yet in retrospect, it feels like I encountered a modern-day Socrates, offering cheesy wisdom through the glowing screen of my laptop. But, I digress. Back to the fever, lying cold and clammy under layers of crinkled Peanuts bed sheets while my body grapples with the rogue virus. I laid there, pondering the digital theater that we engage in-our avatars carefully curated, codifying our identities with cherished emoticons and fleeting witticisms. The absurdity of it all, especially from this wretched state of being, began to amuse me. "God," I thought, "what would a rudimentary 'me' write on their profile? 'Sick, delirious, and looking for cat memes: must like moon cheese.'" My mind skittered through the layers of digital personalities, a vivid reminder that we are all just fragments of our true selves, loosely stitched together by random keystrokes. While lying in the cocoon of my sickness, I found solace-not in the vaccines of yesteryear or steaming soup but in the whimsical exchanges I'd had through blinking cursors and glowing screens. Many faceless names wade the waters of the cyber-nebula, offering slice-of-life snippets that could brighten the darkest flu-riddled nights. And there lay a certain beauty in that chaos; while tech-savvy trolls lurked, others genuinely sought human connection. There's something beautifully tragic about reaching out from cold isolation, desperately grasping for human warmth-even when cloaked in the anonymity of digital facades. Strange bedfellows they may be, I imagined the myriad of souls sharing similar digital spaces. A virtual gathering of the lonely, like gathering dandelions in a field of weeds-still beautiful, still vibrant. As the nonsensical rap playing on my mind faded temporarily into silent submission, I found an inexplicable kinship with these random strangers, their quirks echoing my condition. "So, here's to the fever dreams, the random IMs, and-" my thoughts trailed off as a fit of coughing interrupted the meandering stream of consciousness. Little did I know, the true holiday spirit was merely an IM away. I cracked a smile, even through the fever, for I might just have the makings of a blog worthy of "Distant Relationships 101."

They are generally designed to improve the objective function value of a given solution, although there exist some low-level heuristics which attempt to destroy the structure of a solution rather than improving it. Low-level heuristics are used within the hyper-heuristic search process to create new candidate solutions, but their use does not guarantee that the best solution will be found. It has been demonstrated that hyper-heuristics can outperform existing state-of-the-art algorithms for various combinatorial optimisation problems, including vehicle routing, scheduling, timetabling, packing, flowshop sequencing, graph colouring, network optimisation, and many others. This thesis presents a novel selection hyper-heuristic called Iterated Greedy Hyper-Heuristic Selection (IGHS). IGHS was developed using an evolutionary algorithm-based approach to iteratively learn the best low-level heuristics for a particular problem instance. The core of IGHS is a multi-objective genetic algorithm (MOGA) which uses a population of candidate hyper-heuristics. Each candidate hyper-heuristic is represented as a chromosome containing a sequence of low-level heuristics, and an associated learning component. The MOGA evolves these candidate hyper-heuristics to discover those which perform well on a given problem instance. We also propose a method to evaluate the performance of a candidate hyper-heuristic on a particular problem instance. The evaluation metric takes into account both the final solution obtained after the termination criteria are met, and the overall fitness improvement achieved throughout the search. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our selection hyper-heuristic on 10 benchmark problem instances taken from the literature, comparing our results against a range of state-of-the-art heuristics. Our experimental results show that IGHS performs comparably or better than the best performing method on all 10 benchmarks. A Novel Selection Hyper-Heuristic Approach to Combinatorial Optimisation There is significant research interest in offering bespoke heuristic solutions to difficult real-world optimisation problems. Such methods rely on problem-specific knowledge to operate, and often produce computationally efficient solutions in reasonable time. However, specific heuristic methods do not always perform well when applied to other problem domains without significant modification. This is a primary motivation for the development of general-purpose problem-independent heuristic search methodologies, known as hyper-heuristics. Hyper-heuristics have received increased attention in the scientific research community over the past decade or so, with significant progress made in developing high-level methods which are applicable to a range of different problems. A key goal of hyper-heuristic research is not only to compete with state-of-the-art problem-specific approaches, but to offer a generalised technique able to deliver good quality solutions for a variety of computational optimisation problems. Another motivation for the development of hyper-heuristics comes from the study of Fisher and Thompson (1963), who concluded that the performance when mixing and combining different low-level heuristics produced better quality solutions than if they were applied separately. Their study showed that individual heuristics may be particularly effective at certain stages of the search process, but perform poorly at others. Therefore, it is reasonable to expect that several heuristics combined in an appropriate way may produce better solutions. The term "hyper-heuristic" can be defined as a high-level automated search methodology which explores a search space of low-level heuristics (neighbourhood or move operators, or metaheuristics) or heuristic components, to solve computationally hard problems. There are two main types of hyper-heuristics: hyper-heuristics to generate heuristics and hyper-heuristics to select heuristics.

According to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), MdDS is a rare disorder characterised by persistent dizziness, disequilibrium, rocking sensation, nausea and vomiting that begin within a week of travelling by ship, boat or plane. Symptoms usually last for several weeks but some patients continue to experience them for many months or even years. There is no cure for MdDS and treatment options are limited. Ms Bell said: 'Professor Nutt told me I didn't have a vestibular migraine, I had MdDS. He explained that the condition was caused by the body trying to adapt to a new environment and that the best thing I could do was try to relax. 'He also advised that I should avoid any medication which contains caffeine because it will make it worse. 'At the time I was drinking a lot of coffee and he warned me that I needed to stop immediately because it would exacerbate my condition. 'Unfortunately, I found that very difficult to do and ended up having to give up my favourite drink. 'I used to love my coffee, I'd start the day with it and end the day with it too. Now I'll have maybe half a cup in the morning and that's it. 'If I have any kind of stimulant, whether it's a tea or a coffee, I find it makes it much worse.' Since receiving her diagnosis, Ms Bell has attended support groups where she met others suffering from the same condition. She said: 'In September 2013 I was contacted by someone who runs a Facebook group for people with MdDS. They were looking for people to talk to about their experiences and invited me to join. 'I didn't realise anyone else suffered from this condition and I was shocked to learn that there were others going through exactly what I am going through. 'It's good to talk to people who understand what I'm experiencing because they've experienced it themselves. 'The support group helps me to put things into perspective, I can hear other people's stories and realise that although I might be going through a bad patch at the moment, there are people who have had it much worse than I have. 'It also makes me realise that I'm not alone in this, there are lots of us going through it and together we can help each other.' Despite being told there is no cure for MdDS, Ms Bell hopes that one day scientists will discover a treatment for the condition. She added: 'I don't think there is enough research into MdDS.
