True story, I once met this punk guy down at CBGB's, the place where legends were born smothered under the layers of beer, sweat, and perhaps more beer. This guy had a mohawk taller than my future aspirations-seriously, it was practically speaking to the heavens. He was fiery, vibrant, and alive with this energy that could set the world ablaze. But towards the end of the night, when I chatted him up, between sips of Pabst and tales about his last DIY show, he had this resigned remark that echoed in my brain like a kick drum-"Punk isn't about how you look, it's about how you feel." And that, dear reader, was profound. So, okay, Wolverine's comment might sting harder than a leather-clad fist, but let's dig deeper than spiky haircuts and ripped jeans. What is this overblown notion that punk has perished, suffocated under the weight of emptier pop and corporate marketing schemes? I mean, sure, the mainstream is choking on watered-down, radio-friendly versions of what punk once was. But definitions-do we really want to constrain them to just safety pins and angst-ridden lyrics? I think not. Punk lives on, a ghost that pervades the very essence of rebellion-tangled in the chords of an unrelenting guitar riff; it breathes in the echo of protests that call for justice, in the veins of every artist who dares to push the envelope. Ah, the beautiful irony of mainstream's adoption of everything punk. Did we sell out or did they buy in? It feels like a paradox wrapped in a faux leather jacket. And yet, here we are, caught up in the culture clash. Walk down any street these days, and you'll see kids blasting punk in their earbuds, sporting their own brand of "subversion" through aesthetics that mean something completely different to each generation. From the fringes of society rises an entire ecosystem of artists, musicians, thinkers, and poets, ripping through the boundaries with ferocity that even Wolverine himself couldn't slice through. Sitting here, I envision a group of punk aficionados recruiting with sparks in their eyes, crafting zines with reckless abandon, or jamming to distorted guitars in basements that smell of spilled beer and defiance. There are those who still harken back to its roots, creating, breaking norms, and living the ethos in its rawest form. The spirit persists in the underground, where punk is not just relived but painstakingly reborn with every scream of rebellion, whether vocalized in a dingy venue or scribbled on the walls of the city. Consider the spoken word artists weaving tales of societal discontent. They ignite the same fires burning in the heart of 1970s CBGB's, connecting a thread across decades. Perhaps they don't fit the mold of leather jackets and band patches, but peel back the layers, and you'll find that they have just as much right to call themselves punk as the Dead Boys or Black Flag ever did. It's a kaleidoscopic notion that eludes the narrow definitions that our society tries to impose upon it. So if Wolverine thinks that changing one's hairstyle is tantamount to selling out, then perhaps he's just a tad bit out of touch. Punks are loud, chaotic, and most importantly, they are unapologetically *alive*. And as long as that spirit throbs in the pulse of rebellion-whether expressed through song, fashion, or ideology-then you better believe punk is not just alive; it's thriving. It's the flame that flickers defiantly in the faces of those who try to snuff it out, a relentless force that morphs, adapts, and survives. In conclusion, the punks gather, the revolution simmers, and trust me, the fight rages on.

In the context of Alzheimer's disease, various factors may contribute to the observed performance deficits in short-term memory tasks, particularly as they pertain to the binding and precision of stored information (Ma et al., 2014). One prominent hypothesis posits that these errors arise from a degradation of neural mechanisms implicated in maintaining integrated memory representations. This degradation is likely linked to the characteristic neurodegenerative processes that manifest in the brains of affected individuals, including the accumulation of amyloid plaques and tau tangles, which disrupt synaptic function and communication between critical brain regions (Selkoe, 2002; Sperling et al., 2011). Additionally, the reliance on feature-based binding in memory tasks amplifies the risk of confusion and misattribution among overlapping representations. Notably, studies investigating VSTM precision in individuals with Alzheimer's disease demonstrate that not only is the overall accuracy diminished, but the specific quality of remembered features is also compromised (Parra et al., 2010). For instance, when asked to recall the color of an object, patients might correctly identify that the object was presented but may struggle to recall the exact hue, indicating a shift from a purely qualitative to a qualitative deficit within their memory recall trajectories. This suggests that Alzheimer's patients may retain fragments of information, yet fail to accurately integrate them into coherent wholes-an observation that calls into question the traditional view of memory as strictly binary. Another pivotal consideration is the impact of cognitive load on memory performance in Alzheimer's disease. Increased complexity in tasks can exacerbate deficits in both maintenance and retrieval processes. Research indicates that as the number of items increases, individuals with Alzheimer's show a pronounced decline in their ability to maintain precise memories, which can be attributed to both a finite WM capacity and the added strain of binding multiple features together (Baddeley, 2003; Zokaei et al., 2014). This phenomenon elucidates potential mechanisms underlying memory errors, as the burden of multiple simultaneous representations can lead to confusion and interference. Furthermore, the temporal dynamics of memory encoding and retrieval are likely altered in Alzheimer's disease. The temporal sequencing of events is essential for creating meaningful narratives from disparate pieces of information; hence, disruptions in temporal processing can severely affect one's ability to accurately bind features together (Salthouse, 1991). Research has shown that Alzheimer's patients may experience impaired temporal order memory, which contributes not only to the accuracy of individual items but also to the coherent integration of various elements into a unified memory trace (Fleischman & Gabrieli, 1998). Thus, an exploration of how Alzheimer's disease inflicts its effects upon the integrity of temporal working memory could yield crucial insights into remedial strategies and therapeutic interventions. In summary, while the memory impairments associated with Alzheimer's disease are multifaceted and significant, a greater emphasis on the nuanced interactions between feature binding, item recall precision, and cognitive load reveals a complex landscape of memory dysfunction that extends beyond mere recognition without integration. The intersection of these factors presents a crucial focal point for ongoing research aimed at elucidating the mechanisms underlying short-term memory deficits, ultimately pointing toward a need for more sensitive and comprehensive assessment techniques. As we continue to uncover the intricate relationships inherent in memory processes, we may better equip ourselves to address the broader implications of these impairments, fostering a more nuanced understanding of Alzheimer's disease and its pervasive effects on cognition.

Oleogelators are soluble in the oil such that they can be dispersed but precipitate to form a network during gelation (Suzuki & Hanabusa, 2010). An ideal oleogel for edible application would have modifiable physicochemical properties, in order to match those of a fat being replaced or to achieve other desired functionalities, such as slowed release. Stability of the material over a given period of time is also important. For food or pharmaceutical applications, gelators should have 'generally recognized as safe' (GRAS) status or come from natural sources. Lipid structuring, by the formation of an oleogel or an alternatively structured system, can also have physiological implications. Food structure has a direct relationship with digestibility and nutrient bioaccessibility, as factors such as composition, molecular state, particle size and matrix all affect the fate of ingested materials (McClements, Decker, & Park, 2008; Norton, Gonzalez Espinosa, Watson, Spyropoulos, & Norton, 2015). In lipid systems, this relationship can be exploited to create materials with given levels of lipolysis, modifiable release profiles and increased bioaccessibility of lipid soluble molecules. The mechanism of lipid digestion and the effect of structure on lipolysis is therefore an important aspect to consider when designing oleogel systems. Different lipid-based systems for delivery, mainly emulsion-based, have been reviewed but these discussions have not included oleogels or other alternative structured lipids within their scope (Humberstone & Charman, 1997; Porter, Trevaskis, & Charman, 2007). The delivery of bioactive molecules is another possible application for oleogels, and has gained attention in recent years in the pharmaceuticals industry. In particular, their lipid medium is well suited for increasing the bioavailability of lipid soluble molecules and their gel matrix could offer benefits of sustained release and protection of the deliverable molecule. Several applications of edible oleogels have appeared in the literature for drug or nutraceutical delivery and offer interesting insights into the relationship of gel structure and delivery. Gelation has been shown to be successful at preventing precipitation of bioactives and slow lipolysis and release of nutraceuticals from crystalline and fibrillar oleogel networks (Duffy et al., 2009; Iwanaga, Sumizawa, Miyazaki, & Kakemi, 2010; Lupi et al., 2013; Murdan, Andrysek, & Son, 2005). Ethylcellulose oleogels, the only known food-grade polymer oleogel has been proposed as a material with delivery potential (Davidovich-Pinhas, 2015; Zetzl & Marangoni, 2012). Structure-functionality characteristics of the gel have been well researched, but polymer oleogels have never been explored for delivery applications. This review will begin with an overview of the mechanism of lipolysis and structural factors affecting lipolysis. Previous studies on lipid structuring and their effect on lipid digestion are also discussed. To explore the use of gels for oral delivery, lipid-soluble bioactive molecules will be introduced, with a focus on -carotene (BC). Challenges involved in the delivery of those lipid soluble molecules will be covered, leading to a discussion on current delivery strategies for these molecules and the use of novel oil-based gels for delivery.

Indeed, Sri Lanka and Myanmar have remarkable similarities as former British colonies overcoming decades of civil war through militant Buddhist regimes. In Oldmeadow's eyes he had always remained the "little Barney" he had then christened him - even Barney's mother had almost forgotten that his real name was Eustace - and he could not but know that Barney depended upon him more than upon anyone in the world. To Barney his negations were more potent than other people's affirmations, and though he had sometimes said indignantly, "You leave one nothing to agree about, Roger, except Plato and Church-music," he was never really happy or secure in his rebellions from what he felt or suspected to be Oldmeadow's tastes and judgments. Oldmeadow had seen him through many admirations, not only for books and pictures, but for original girls. Barney thought that he liked the unusual. He was a devotee of the ballet, and had in his rooms cushions and curtains from the Omega shop and a drawing by Wyndham Lewis. But Oldmeadow knew that he really preferred the photograph of a Burne-Jones, a survival from Oxford days, that still bravely, and irrelevantly, hung opposite it, and he waited to see the Wyndham Lewis replaced by a later portent. Barney could remain stubbornly faithful to old devotions, but he was easily drawn into new orbits; and it was a new star, evidently, that he had come to describe and justify. "What have I to do with charming American girls?" Oldmeadow inquired, turning his eyes on the blurred prospect of factory-chimneys and warehouses that the farther waterside of Chelsea affords. One had to go to the window and look out to see the grey and silver river flowing, in the placidity that revealed so little power. Oldmeadow lived in a flat on the Embankment; but he was not an admirer of Chelsea, just as he was not an admirer of Whistler nor - and Barney had always suspected it - of Burne-Jones. His flat gave him, at a reasonable cost, fresh air, boiling-hot water and a walk in Battersea Park; these, with his piano, were his fundamental needs; though he owned, for the mean little stream it was, that the Thames could look pretty enough by morning sunlight and - like any river - magical under stars. After Plato and Bach, Oldmeadow's passions were the rivers of France. "She'll have something to do with you," said Barney, and he seemed pleased with the retort. "I met her at the Lumleys. They think her the marvel of the age." "Well, that doesn't endear her to me," said Oldmeadow. "And I don't like Americans." "Come, you're not quite so hide-bound as all that," said Barney, vexed. "What about Mrs. Aldesey? I've heard you say she's the most charming woman you know." "Except Nancy," Oldmeadow amended. "No one could call Nancy a charming woman," said Barney, looking a little more vexed. "She's a dear, of course; but she's a mere girl. What do you know about Americans, anyway - except Mrs. Aldesey?"

Dr. Arnold, his brow furrowed, continues his ministrations with practiced ease, as though tending to an insignificant wound rather than a scrappy boy-a boy who had dared to think he was invincible, if only for a moment. "Just a tumble," Tom mutters, trying to brush off the incident, but the weight of embarrassment settles heavily on his shoulders. Mary's gentle hands pause, her eyes searching his for unspoken truths. "Why were you playing rough like that, Tom? You know it's not safe," she chides softly, her tone a mix of chastisement and effort to shield him from his own bravado. "It was just a bit of fun, Mary. I didn't mean..." His voice trails off as he glances sideways at Dr. Arnold, who is now searching for something in his desk. What did he mean? Did he intend to get hurt? Dr. Arnold finally pulls out a small white bandage and applies it with careful precision to the bruise forming just above Tom's brow. "A robust lad like you should know better than to willingly step into the lion's den," he remarks knowingly, an ember of firm wisdom lacing his voice. "Fitting in doesn't mean compromising your safety, Tom," Dr. Arnold interjects as he neatly ties the bandage. "Real courage lies not in the willingness to join reckless abandon but in the capacity to stand apart when one knows they should." The words echo, reverberating deep within Tom's consciousness, stitching together the frayed edges of his shame. A moment of silence envelops the room, the weight of the previous chaos and merriment now rendered irrelevant under the doctor's sagacious gaze. Mary squeezes his shoulder gently, grounding him to the present-a reminder that, amidst the tempest of foolish boyhood bravado, there exists an unwavering thread of kindness. "Will you promise us to be more careful?" Mary implores, her eyes shimmering with sincerity. Tom nods, feeling the warmth of their concern. It settles within him like a fleeting ember; fragile, yet hopeful. "I promise," he says, the assurance resonating within their shared space. As the winds outside howl ever so slightly, stirring the night to life, Tom feels a renewed sense of purpose. He would strive to blend his desire for belonging with the wisdom he's gleaned tonight, hoping to navigate the intricate web of friendship with newfound caution, and perhaps, a lightness that only understanding can bestow.

By applying CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing, researchers can achieve precise modifications that target specific genes responsible for limiting viral replication or influencing cell health, thereby improving overall vaccine yield and efficacy. Harnessing such tools not only enables the identification of critical genetic loci that govern these properties but also permits the reconfiguration of cellular pathways to favor the production of desired biopharmaceuticals. Furthermore, synthetic biology offers a platform for designing custom cell lines with optimized metabolic profiles, which can lead to reduced by-product accumulation and increased biomass growth (Jiang et al., [11]). In the quest to streamline vaccine production, the integration of automation and artificial intelligence into manufacturing workflows cannot be overlooked. Smart manufacturing systems equipped with machine learning algorithms have the potential to revolutionize the production landscape by enhancing process control, monitoring key performance indicators in real-time, and providing predictive analytics that can guide operational adjustments to maximize yield. These advanced operational strategies facilitate a more agile manufacturing process, reducing downtime and resource waste, contributing to overall cost-effectiveness (Li et al., [12]). Moreover, the development of point-of-care technologies represents an innovative stride towards decentralizing vaccine distribution. These portable devices offer the potential to administer vaccines in low-resource settings, thus overcoming significant barriers posed by infrastructure limitations. Through the miniaturization of cold chain storage solutions and rapid diagnostic tools, such technologies promise to effectively deliver life-saving vaccines to remote and underserved communities worldwide (Cheng et al., [13]). Such advancements are vital for ensuring that the benefits of vaccination reach all corners of the globe, particularly in areas where conventional healthcare systems struggle to function optimally. Additionally, the expansion of partnerships between public and private sectors plays a crucial role in addressing the multifaceted challenges of vaccine accessibility. Collaborative efforts, including those involving non-profit organizations, traditional pharmaceutical companies, and emerging biotechs, can lead to more innovative solutions tailored to the unique needs of developing regions. By pooling resources, expertise, and technology, these partnerships can help drive down manufacturing costs and expedite distribution, thereby improving global health outcomes significantly (GAVI, the Vaccine Alliance, 2020). Education and training for local healthcare workers must also be part of the solution. Empowering these professionals with the necessary skills to administer vaccines and manage logistics can lead to more sustainable healthcare practices. Initiatives focused on building local capacity not only enhance immediate health outcomes but also create a workforce ready to respond to future public health challenges. As the landscape of vaccine manufacturing and distribution continues to evolve, it becomes apparent that the quest for affordable and accessible vaccines is anchored in innovation, collaboration, and the commitment to health equity. The convergence of advanced biotechnologies, smart production practices, decentralized healthcare delivery, and robust educational initiatives holds the key to unlocking a future where life-saving vaccines are accessible to all, regardless of geographic or economic barriers. In this context, the efforts to reduce costs and enhance production capabilities signify a crucial investment in a healthier global society for generations to come.

These measures, similarly to financial ones, adopt a top-down approach to alleviate in the short-term some of the negative consequences associated to vulnerable individuals' inability to afford energy and pay the bills. Energy efficiency measures, on the other hand, enable the decrease of energy costs in the long-term by improving the efficiency of building materials, construction methods, and appliances. The high-energy costs in Europe are particularly due to the low refurbishment rate of buildings and the low rate of replacement of appliances [13]. Moreover, the share of income spent on energy costs is much higher for vulnerable individuals than for high-income ones [14]. Therefore, efficiency measures, like those that improve the insulation capacities of walls, might be effective at lowering energy bills [15]. This is especially true when the split incentive problem faced by vulnerable renters is sufficiently addressed [16]. In addition to energy cost savings, energy efficiency measures may result in numerous other positive externalities. In particular, living in deprived environments not only has adverse effects on health, but also on a community's capacity to develop the social capital [17] necessary to enforce desirable behaviors through informal social control [18]. Therefore, by improving the environment in which vulnerable individuals live, these structural measures might improve the quality of life of the whole neighborhood, by for example, reducing the crime rate [19]. Overall, energy efficiency measures offer enormous potential for addressing energy poverty. However, these may fail to reduce energy poverty [20], that is they might fail to achieve greater energy efficiency in buildings and related long-term energy savings [21]. This can occur due to reliance on wrong or invalid assumptions about individual behavior (i.e. energy efficiency gap [22]). What determines the efficacy of these measures is the behavior of the individuals who daily interface with those interventions [23]. Therefore, it is crucial to take into account the underlying factors that affect behaviors before these measures are implemented [24]. Information provision measures take into account the role of individual behavior. These measures play a significant role in improving not only vulnerable consumers' awareness of their rights and available market tariffs, but also in enhancing their understanding of energy-related problems in the context of everyday life and awareness of energy efficiency [25]. These measures are usually implemented in the form of information campaigns, advice provision, and increased information on bills and tariffs, by making billing more transparent, and by providing price comparisons or energy saving tips [9]. Similar to energy efficiency measures, information provision measures have the potential to bring economic benefits to vulnerable individuals. As an example, providing information on how to save energy might promote better energy consumption behaviors and, thus, cost savings [26].

Most players leave a game with the intention of keeping in touch with a handful of their "closest" friends from the game. They believe the rapport built up between them and their friends would help their friendships last over a long period of time. They are almost always wrong. Gamers who've recently quit soon realize that they've isolated all their real life friends by playing the on-line game, and have also lost all of their on-line friends by quitting. Sometimes the person who left the on-line game will grow tired of hearing about the latest raid of quest and eventually stop responding on their own. The effects of oxy-fuel atmosphere and O2 concentration in the oxy-fuel oxidant gas on pollutant emissions (NOx and CO) in fluidized bed systems firing different kinds of coal have been thoroughly investigated during the past years by a number of researchers. In general, the experimental results showed that NOx emissions in oxy-fuel combustion with low O2 concentrations are lower than those obtained under air-firing atmosphere, because of the lower temperatures as well as higher char and CO concentrations in the dense bed [10,11]. Furthermore, NOx emissions were found to increase with the increasing O2 concentrations in the oxy-fuel oxidant, which is as a result of i) the increase of the temperature in the furnace which elevates the concentrations of O and OH radicals and enhances NO formation and ii) the lower gas velocity in the riser and longer residence time of fuel particles in the combustor, which may promote the fuel-N conversion into NOx precursors [10-14]. In some studies an opposite trend was found, i.e. an decrease of NOx with the increasing O2 concentration in the oxy-fuel oxidant, as in the work of de las Obras-Loscertales et al. [15]. The authors explained this trend by means of the different operational procedure used, comparing with other investigations: in their work [15], an increase in the oxygen concentration was compensated with an increase of the coal flow rate fed to the reactor, keeping constant the total gas flow rate and excess oxygen coefficient in all tests. As a result, more unconverted char was present in the bed, favouring the NO reduction on the char surface. Regarding CO emissions, Duan et al. [16] observed a much lower CO emission in air than those in an oxy-fuel atmosphere with the same O2 concentration when firing two kind of coal in a 50 kWth CFB facility, due to the higher temperature achieved under the air combustion conditions. They also reported a decrease in CO emissions when the O2 concentration in the oxy-fuel oxidant gas increased; as the oxidation of carbon was more complete and therefore less CO was formed. On the other hand, Hofbauer et al. [14] observed similar CO emissions for air combustion and two oxy-fuel cases investigated (with 26 vol% and 36 vol% of O2 in the oxidant, respectively), firing bituminous coal in a 150 kWth CFB reactor. Jia et al. [17] performed a series of oxy-fuel tests with flue gas recycle in a 100 kWth CFB combustor firing bituminous coal. The CO emissions of oxy-fuel combustion were found to be equal or slightly lower than those of air firing, mainly due to the higher cyclone temperature achieved with oxy-fuel combustion. Biomass properties differ from those of coal in many important ways which results in different combustion behaviours [18]. For example, biomass generally has less carbon, more oxygen, higher hydrogen content and lower heating value.

When I was a little girl I did not, of course, understand that I was an important person, and I could not have realized the significance of being an heiress. I had always lived in the castle, and was used to its hugeness, of which I only knew corners. Until I was seven years old, I think, I imagined all but very poor people lived in castles and were saluted by every one they passed. It seemed probable that all little girls had a piper who strode up and down the terrace and played on the bagpipes when guests were served in the dining-hall. My piper's name was Feargus, and in time I found out that the guests from London could not endure the noise he made when he marched to and fro, proudly swinging his kilts and treading like a stag on a hillside. It was an insult to tell him to stop playing, because it was his religion to believe that The Muircarrie must be piped proudly to; and his ancestors had been pipers to the head of the clan for five generations. It was his duty to march round the dining-hall and play while the guests feasted, but I was obliged in the end to make him believe that he could be heard better from the terrace - because when he was outside his music was not spoiled by the sound of talking. It was very difficult, at first. But because I was his chieftainess, and had learned how to give orders in a rather proud, stern little voice, he knew he must obey. Even this kind of thing may show that my life was a peculiar one; but the strangest part of it was that, while I was at the head of so many people, I did not really belong to any one, and I did not know that this was unusual. One of my early memories is that I heard an under-nursemaid say to another this curious thing: "Both her father and mother were dead when she was born." I did not even know that was a remarkable thing to say until I was several years older and Jean Braidfute told me what had been meant. My father and mother had both been very young and beautiful and wonderful. It was said that my father was the handsomest chieftain in Scotland, and that his wife was as beautiful as he was. They came to Muircarrie as soon as they were married and lived a splendid year there together. Sometimes they were quite alone, and spent their days fishing or riding or wandering on the moor together, or reading by the fire in the library the ancient books Angus Macayre found for them. The library was a marvelous place, and Macayre knew every volume in it.

As we delve deeper into the fascinating history of tea in Britain, we find that its impact extends far beyond the realm of mere beverage consumption. Tea has woven itself into the very fabric of our society, influencing everything from our trade and industry to our culture and identity. The drink has been a constant companion to the British people, providing comfort, solace, and a sense of normalcy in times of turmoil. Take, for example, the role tea played during the tumultuous years of World War II. As the nation struggled to cope with the devastating effects of war, tea became a beacon of hope and unity. The Women's Land Army, comprised of women who took on the duties of their absent male counterparts, were often treated to a cup of tea as a token of appreciation for their hard work. Similarly, the iconic "Tea for the Troops" campaign, which saw tea packets and other provisions sent to soldiers fighting abroad, helped to boost morale and remind those serving their country of the comforts of home. Tea has also played a significant role in shaping British fashion and etiquette. The traditional afternoon tea, with its delicate china and dainty sandwiches, has been a staple of British society for centuries. And who can forget the iconic image of the "nippy" waitresses, clad in their crisp uniforms and aprons, serving tea to the masses in the grand tea rooms of the 1920s and '30s? But tea's influence extends beyond the realm of social niceties. The drink has played a significant role in shaping British industry and trade, with the East India Company's tea trade being a major factor in the country's economic growth. The Opium Wars, fought between Britain and China in the 19th century, were sparked in part by the British desire to secure a steady supply of tea and other Chinese goods. And then, of course, there's the matter of tea's impact on British health. While many of us rely on tea to help us wake up in the morning or to soothe our nerves, it's less well-known that the drink has been touted for its medicinal properties for centuries. In the 18th century, tea was believed to have the power to cure everything from headaches to indigestion, and its popularity as a health tonic was rivalled only by that of gin. As we continue to explore the fascinating history of tea in Britain, it becomes clear that this beloved beverage has played a far more significant role in shaping our nation than we ever could have imagined. From its humble origins in ancient China to its current status as a national institution, tea has been a constant companion to the British people, providing comfort, solace, and a sense of identity. So the next time you raise a cup to your lips, remember the rich history and cultural significance that lies behind that steaming cup of tea.

It is well known that clouds are among the largest sources of uncertainty in predictions of future climate (IPCC, 2014; Stephens, 2005). In fact, despite their importance in determining the radiative balance of the atmosphere, cloud processes are still not fully understood (Naud and Chen, 2010), especially considering the small-scale interactions between clouds and aerosols (Stephens, 2005). These uncertainties require more accurate cloud products from current and new generation sensors, which should include detailed information on cloud height and vertical structure (Baum et al., 1999; Winker et al., 2009). Over the last decades, several methods have been developed for the identification and classification of cloud types using multi/hyperspectral satellite data (Chen et al., 2002; Derrien et al., 2013; Devasthale et al., 2011; Di Girolamo and Davies, 1997; Heidinger et al., 2012; Jia et al., 2012; Lutz et al., 2003; Minnis et al., 2008; Rossow and Schiffer, 1999; Stubenrauch et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2013). Most of these algorithms were designed for specific sensors (e.g. MODIS, AVHRR, Meteosat, GOES, HIRS) and/or cloud types (e.g. cirrus, stratus, cumulus, etc.) and can hardly be transferred directly to other sensors. Moreover, most of them do not provide a comprehensive analysis of cloud physical characteristics (i.e. cloud optical thickness and effective particle radius). Indeed, most of these methods only provide a binary mask discriminating cloudy pixels from clear ones (Ackerman et al., 2008; Ackerman et al., 2010; Baum et al., 2005; Frey et al., 2008; Han et al., 2006; Hagolle et al., 2010; Martins et al., 2002; Martinez et al., 2009; Platnick et al., 2003; Simpson et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2011). Other approaches also provide cloud phase (ice/water) discrimination (Baum et al., 2012; Derrien et al., 2013; Di Noi et al., 2013; Frey et al., 2008; Gafurov and Bekenov, 2013; Hagolle et al., 2010; Han et al., 2006; Martins et al., 2002; Martinez et al., 2009; Platnick et al., 2003; Riedi et al., 2010; Simpson et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2011).

And so, the curtain rang down on the revelry, cloaked in somber disapproval, and the jubilant cheer was silenced. The Puritans, true to their austere nature, issued a decree that the Holy Day would not be a day of celebration but rather a time for reflection, shunning the carols and the festive gatherings. Their position, rooted in a fervent desire to uphold the sanctity of faith, inspired a methodical eradication of Christmas festivities, coupled with the belief that excesses of joy tarnished the spirit of piety. They were, somewhat paradoxically, the harbingers of a holiday war, not unlike the skirmishes that litter the annals of time. The clash over whether Christmas was a sacred observance or a simple opportunity for merriment persisted, bubbling to the surface repeatedly through epochs and cultures. Surges of traditionalists anguished over the commercialization of Christmas-an age-old debate that echoed through colonial America, where even the jolly presence of Saint Nicholas found itself ensnared in controversy. He, too, was borne aloft on laughter and joy, only to be reined in by the shadows of disapproving congregants who scowled at the raucous celebrations. Across the Atlantic, the arguments continued to unfurl. The Quakers, steadfast in their opposition to displays of revelry, rejected the notion of Christmas altogether, decrying it as "pagan." Yet, in the very same land, stores began to decorate their windows with tinsel and lights, diverging from the grim tones of Puritanism to embrace a kind of joyous revelry that would soon sweep the nation. The raucous clamor of Christmas curiously seeped into the fabric of lives, draped in garland and gleeful song, as if the rhythms of tradition had a will of their own. By the 19th century, America faced a critical crossroads-the virgin glory of Christmas was at stake. Writers such as Washington Irving sang the praises of a reformed Christmas, capturing the imaginations of readers who longed for a holiday pulsing with warmth and family connection rather than that rigid disbeliefs of Puritanical doctrine. The festive quilts began weaving themselves into the cultural consciousness-men clad in Santa suits, feasts with yams and eggnog, scenes of joy rather than melancholia. The holiday now seemed on the precipice of a rebirth, driven by romanticism and nostalgia, longing for a sacred return to unity amidst the chaos of modernization. From the far reaches of society, voices rang out, each a thread bound in a tapestry of belief and tradition. The Victorian Era embraced the holiday as an opportunity to reinforce social bonds. The publication of "A Christmas Carol" by Charles Dickens was a veritable call to arms in the ceaseless battle; a narrative guided by compassion and kindness, it urged readers to remember the poor, spurring charitable action that ignited the spirit of giving. Yet even then, beneath the whimsical spirit and the charitable heart, the wrestle persisted. As freshly cut trees adorned living rooms, as families gathered around dinner tables brimming with rich delicacies, another unseen strife simmered-one that always threatened to bubble over. The gap between those who celebrated in joyous unison and those who perceived such luxuriance as a betrayal of authenticity was a chasm that widened with each carol sung and gift exchanged. Ultimately, Christmas remained a multifaceted treasure-a topic still exchanged in fervent debates. Would it ever truly find peace? Or did the whispered disputes ensure its survival, anchoring Christmas in the struggle for cultural and spiritual identity? The answer danced on the edges of every festive moment, echoing through time, pulling on the threads of nostalgia, commerce, and reflection-a war without an end, perhaps, but for every heart willing to whisper, "Merry Christmas," a triumphant sword may find itself sheathed, if only for a season.

As the sun dipped below the horizon, casting a warm orange glow over the small town, Fanny and Grandma Wentworth sat on the porch, watching Nanny Ainslee disappear into the distance, her trunks and suitcases disappearing into the crowd at the station. The air was filled with the sweet scent of blooming flowers and the distant sound of crickets, a peaceful evening unfolding before them. "I declare, Grandma, I'm going to miss her something fierce," Fanny said, her voice tinged with a hint of wistfulness. Grandma Wentworth nodded, her eyes clouding over with a mix of sadness and pride. "I know, dear. I'll miss her too. But she's following her heart, and we can't blame her for that." Fanny nodded, her mind already racing with thoughts of the adventures Nanny would have in Japan. "I bet she'll be writing us letters from the most exotic places. I'll have to write back to her every week, I'll be so curious to hear about her travels." Grandma Wentworth smiled, her eyes twinkling with amusement. "You'll be writing to her every day, I reckon. You're as curious as a cat in a bird shop when it comes to Nanny's adventures." As they sat in comfortable silence, the sound of the crickets grew louder, and the stars began to twinkle in the night sky. Fanny leaned back in her chair, feeling the gentle rocking motion of the porch swing, and let her mind wander to all the places Nanny would visit, the people she would meet, and the stories she would tell when she returned. Just then, a faint sound of laughter and music drifted from the direction of the station, growing louder as the train pulled into town. Fanny's eyes lit up, and she jumped up from her chair. "That must be the train from Spring Road! I bet Uncle Tony's on it, and he'll have all the latest news about the wreck." Grandma Wentworth chuckled, her eyes sparkling with amusement. "You're as excited as a pup at a squirrel convention, Fanny. Go on, go see what's happened." Fanny didn't need to be told twice. She bounded off the porch, her long skirt fluttering behind her, and disappeared into the darkness, leaving Grandma Wentworth to sit alone, lost in thought, as the night wore on.

Corruption monitors say the issue of big money in politics pales in comparison to the abuse of government resources by the United Russia party of Prime Minister Vladimir Putin, who announced on March 04 he had won Russia's presidential election, returning the former KGB officer to the office he held from 2000 to 2008. While there are no limitations on the amount U.S. political parties can spend on televison ads, broadcast time in Russia is doled out on a limited basis, and is proportionate to the results of the last election. But as opposition parties prepare ads to maximize a limited amount of television time, nightly news broadcasts on state-run channels are filled with stories of United Russia politicians repairing hospitals, or opening new underground rail stations - officials benefitting politically from initiatives paid for with taxpayer money. "There are two sets of rules in Russia - one set for parties who are paying out of their own pockets, and another for the party and candidates with access to public resources," says Elena Panfilova, head of TI Russia. While opposition parties must finance campaign trips around the country during election season, incumbent politicians can campaign during official state-funded trips, according to Panfilova. Abuse of media and Russia's public resources may be time-tested tools of incumbents here, but that hasn't stopped United Russia from trying other ways to get a leg up on the competition. In November a crowd at a concert in Siberia rained down boos on veteran rock band Mashina Vremeni - Time Machine in English - when they were introduced by an emcee who announced that the concert was backed by United Russia and awarded them medals from the local governor. "The parties try to hijack whatever they can hijack in Russia," Panfilova told CNN. Brazil. Another country where big money and elections go hand in hand is Brazil, Latin America's largest country and one of the world's fastest growing economies. Roughly $2 billion was spent by parties and candidates in the 2010 presidential election, according to Claudio Weber Abramo, executive director of TI Brazil. Nearly 98% of winner Dilma Rouseff's campaign donations - and 95.5% of her main opponent's - came from corporations, says Abramo.

The obvious and targeted goal is the promotion of the formation of a great number of grains via heterogeneous nucleation in order to obtain a fine grain size but this also implies that the formation of the typical coarse columnar structure can be easily prevented. Intrinsic advantages of finer microstructural features are not only confined to mechanical properties such as higher yield strength (as per Hall-Petch relationship) and high impact toughness. Actually, technological and manufacturing benefits are really significant among which good formability (for extrusion and rolling processes), good surface finishing, lower propensity to hot tearing and better machinability as a consequence of the more uniform distribution of the second phases and of the shrinkage and gas porosity as well as the soundness of the castings are known. All these benefits are related to the fact that the inoculated melt fills more easily, faster and more efficiently mould cavities as well as allows the melt remaining in between the growing dendritic grains to move more freely enabling the filling of the cavities in the mushy zone of the solidifying metal (i.e., both mass and interdendritic feeding). Among the main concerns and problems relative to the employment of inoculants for the refinement of aluminium and its alloys, it can be named the fact that different manufacturing variables like reaction conditions, ratio of the chemicals, stirring conditions, etc. greatly influence the final refining efficiency. Coarse and agglomerated particles as well as impurities such as salt residues present in the grain refiner generate defect and can cause quality problems. Moreover, the efficiency can be lost by fading, which is either due to the dissolution/interaction of the potential nucleation substrates or the settling (or conversely floating) as a function of the density difference with the molten metal. Finally, impurities coming from the production of the alloy as well as the proper alloying elements have an impact (either enhancing or limiting the grain refining capability) on the refining efficiency and, eventually, can prevent the refinement such as in the case of the poisoning of Ti-based refiners from Zr. As indicated by Quested [20], although grain refinement is beneficial to the casting process, the inoculant particles are seen as unwanted inclusions in downstream processing of ingots. Because of their high efficiency in refining the grain size of wrought aluminium alloys, it was thought that the addition of Al-Ti-B master alloys to cast aluminium alloys would have the same effect. Nonetheless, from the many studies done it was found that the refinement of cast aluminium alloys, whose main alloying elements is silicon, cannot be efficiently performed by means of Al-Ti-B master alloys. This is due to the fact that silicon reacts with the titanium of the Al-Ti-B master alloys to form titanium silicides (i.e., poisoning [21]) depleting titanium in the melt and, thus, hindering the refinement.

And yet, there was a certain kinship between them. They all wanted work! He had been looking for work these last fourteen days, and had failed to find any. For weeks before that, he had been watching for opportunities, and had only succeeded in making himself thoroughly ill-tempered. All through the summer months he had been drifting along, doing nothing. He had been living on the income which came to him from a small trust fund; but it was not sufficient for his needs, and he had decided to seek a job. But how? What kind of employment could he take? He had no special qualifications. He had done no definite work since leaving school. At twenty-one he had joined the army, and served for three years in India, and then, returning home, he had taken up hunting and shooting, and roamed about the country, playing golf or cricket, and spending the rest of his time in reading and loafing. Occasionally he had gone abroad, and once he had spent three months in America. Now, suddenly, he had found himself penniless, and anxious to earn something for himself. But what? In the meantime, he had spent his money recklessly. That was why he was in debt. He had been obliged to sell his motor-car, his gun, his fishing tackle, his books, his golf clubs. He had sold everything except his clothes and his silver, and he was left with a thousand pounds. With that sum he had come to town, and had taken rooms in a big house in Belgrave Square, and here he was, still unemployed. Of course, he had tried various things. He had written to firms offering his services, but he had received no replies. He had called upon several people, including friends of his father's, and had made inquiries, but without success. He had tried the agency offices, and the employment bureaus, but nobody seemed to want him. And now, while he was thinking of these things, a young woman came running down the steps of one of the houses near the corner of Grosvenor Place, and, seeing him standing on the pavement, stopped short and looked at him curiously. She was tall and slim, and her face, framed in a mass of dark hair, was interesting, with its long, straight nose, its full lips, and its gray eyes, which were bright with intelligence and vivacity. Her dress was simple, but tastefully made, and she wore a hat of black straw trimmed with a bunch of violets. She glanced quickly at the sign-board over the door, and then looked back at Royson. He smiled at her, and raised his hat. "I beg your pardon," she said, "but I'm afraid I interrupted you." He bowed again. "Not at all. You didn't interrupt me. I was thinking." "Ah!" She laughed softly. "And dreaming?" "Perhaps."

Miles' eyes are fixed on his father's face, studying the lines and creases that have deepened with age. Jonathan's eyes, on the other hand, are cast downward, his gaze drifting toward the pavement. "I'm not sure what's going on, Miles," Jonathan says, his voice low and gravelly. "I just feel like I'm stuck in this rut. Like I'm just going through the motions." Miles nods, his eyes never leaving his father's face. "I know, Dad. I feel it too. Like we're just pretending to be adults or something." Jonathan's eyes flicker up, a glimmer of recognition in them. "Exactly! It's like we're just playing a role, you know? Like we're just pretending to be someone we're not." As they walk, the sounds of the city grow louder, the smells of food and exhaust and trash filling the air. Jonathan's mind begins to wander, his thoughts drifting back to the graduation ceremony, to the feeling of accomplishment and pride that had washed over him. But even that memory is tinged with a sense of emptiness, of uncertainty. Miles' voice brings him back to the present. "Hey, Dad? Can I ask you something?" Jonathan's eyes refocus, his gaze locking onto his son's. "What is it, buddy?" Miles hesitates, his eyes darting around the crowded street. "Do you ever feel like...like we're just going through the motions? Like we're just pretending to be happy or something?" Jonathan's face twists, a mix of emotions warring for dominance. "Yeah, Miles. I do. I feel like that all the time." As they continue walking, the sounds of the city swirling around them, Jonathan's thoughts turn to the pill bottle in his pocket, to the Oxycontin that was meant to dull the pain. But even that seemed hollow, a temporary fix for a deeper problem. He glanced down at his son, at the bright, shining eyes that seemed to hold a deep wisdom beyond his years. "You know, Miles," Jonathan says, his voice low and serious. "I think we're just trying to find our way. We're just trying to figure out who we are and what we want. And it's okay to not have all the answers right now. It's okay to not know." Miles nods, his eyes never leaving his father's face. "I know, Dad. I just wish it didn't have to hurt so much." Jonathan's eyes drop, his gaze drifting toward the pavement once more. "Me too, buddy. Me too."

Pedersen et al. (2009) found that batch addition of PAA to achieve 1 mg/L had minimal effect on nitrification compared to 2 and 3 mg/L PAA, which resulted in significant, prolonged increases of nitrite levels in freshwater RAS culturing rainbow trout Oncorhynchus mykiss. A later study determined that increased organic matter content significantly increased PAA decay and noted that biofilm and fish biomass also contributed to its dissipation rate (Pedersen et al., 2013). During another RAS-focused trial, Liu et al. (2017a) evaluated pulse applications of PAA delivered every three to four days over a 5-wk period to achieve a concentration of 2 mg/L PAA in a tank culturing common carp Cyprinus carpio. Fish were initially stressed by this procedure as measured by waterborne cortisol but appeared to adapt to subsequent treatments. There is still much to learn about the use of PAA in RAS and its potential benefits. In particular, a greater understanding of its ability to improve RAS water quality is lacking. The oxidizing capacity of PAA in RAS is of interest because PAA has been described as having properties similar to ozone (Pedersen et al., 2015), a powerful oxidant that is frequently used for RAS water treatment. Ozone improves the culture environment by enhancing water clarity, microflocculating fine solids, adding oxygen, and reducing dissolved metals, nitrite, and organic concentrations (Summerfelt and Hochheimer, 1997; Davidson et al., 2011; Gonclaves and Gagnon, 2011; Powell and Scolding, 2018). Antimicrobial effects can also be achieved when high ozone doses are applied to RAS water followed by ultraviolet (UV) irradiation (Liltved, 2002; Summerfelt, 2003; Sharrer and Summerfelt, 2007; Summerfelt et al., 2009), and improved growth performance, health, and survival of cultured species have been attributed to the enhanced culture environment created by ozone (Davidson et al., 2011; Good et al., 2011; Powell and Scolding, 2018). However, ozone is relatively expensive and complex to use (Summerfelt and Hochheimer, 1997; Gonclaves and Gagnon, 2011) and can present safety hazards for fish and human health (Gearhart and Summerfelt, 2007); therefore, an alternate water treatment method would be welcomed by the RAS industry. In addition, research evaluating the effect of PAA on the common off-flavor compounds geosmin and 2-methylisoborneol (MIB) in RAS has not been reported in peer-reviewed literature. The occurrence of off-flavors in RAS-produced finfish products continues to be detrimental to this industry sector (Schrader et al., 2013), as off-flavor can contribute to consumer dissatisfaction, result in a negative perception of aquaculture products, and inhibit future purchasing (Tucker, 2000). Yet, a proven method that immediately mitigates off-flavor in the primary fish production system (grow-out) has not been developed. Most RAS operations employ specific depuration/ "purging" protocols to remove off-flavors from fillets (Davidson et al., 2014a; Lindholm-Lehto and Vielma, 2018); however, this production step results in added capital, operating, and labor costs for the farmer.

The complexity of the ammonium assimilation system is underscored by the fact that it has been preserved throughout evolution from bacteria to humans, where it is known as the mammalian urea cycle (10). It is therefore not surprising that many questions remain about how this network functions. For instance, although it is clear that GlnB and GlnK act together to inhibit AT, it remains unclear whether they work synergistically or additively. Similarly, little is known about the role of GlnB and GlnK in the transcriptional regulation of GS. Here we show that the interaction between GlnB and GlnK is necessary and sufficient to account for the observed nonlinear activation of GS, and that this occurs through an allosteric mechanism. We propose that GlnB and GlnK are part of a molecular switch that controls the level of GS activity. The experimental approach taken here combines several techniques: biochemical characterization of purified components; analysis of mutant strains grown in batch culture; and single-cell measurements using fluorescence microscopy. First, we determined the kinetic parameters of GS and AT/AR and assessed the effects of uridylylation on GlnB and GlnK. Next, we measured the steady-state level of GS protein in wild-type cells and in mutants lacking GlnB, GlnK, or UT/UR. Finally, we quantified the behavior of individual cells expressing either GS alone or GS and GlnB/GlnK simultaneously, to determine the effect of GlnB/GlnK on GS activity. In vitro assays were performed with recombinant proteins expressed in E. coli and purified using standard methods (11). Kinetic data were obtained with GS and AT/AR purified from E. coli strain MG1655. Protein concentrations were determined using the Bio-Rad protein assay kit (Bio-Rad Laboratories Inc., Hercules, CA, USA) and bovine serum albumin as the standard. Glutamate synthase was assayed spectrophotometrically at 37 C by following the disappearance of -KG at 340 nm using a Cary 300 UV-visible spectrophotometer (Varian Medical Systems Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA). Reactions contained 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 100 mM NH4Cl, 0.1 mM NADH, 0.02 mM PLP, 20 mM MgCl2, 0.25 mg/ml BSA, 15 mM -KG, 35 mM L-glutamate, and 75 nM GS. Reactions contained 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 200 1/2M ATP, 60 1/2M AMP-PNP, and 150 nM AT/AR. Particularly considering neuroimaging findings, this neurobiological model suggests that AN patients may have an imbalance in information processing, linked to alterations of the ventral limbic circuits (which comprises amygdala, anterior insula, anterior ventral striatum, anterior cingulate cortex, and the orbito-frontal cortex), as well as the dorsal executive circuits (which particularly includes dorsal regions of the caudate, dorso-lateral prefrontal cortex, and parietal cortex). These two brain circuits are primarily implicated in inhibitory decision making processes and reward-related behaviours and their alteration might sustain AN symptomatology (Kaye et al., 2013). Other neurobiologically informed models of AN have pointed out the role of anxiety, stress, and fear, the gratifying nature of AN symptoms, and the consequent shift to habitual or compulsive behaviours as possible key factors in the persistence of AN (Zipfel et al., 2015; Treasure et al., 2015). During the last decade, several research groups have used a stimulus-free fMRI approach, defined as resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) (e.g. Fox and Greicius, 2010). In these studies, the participants are positioned in the scanner in an awake-state without performing any particular task. This method allows for making temporal correlations between brain areas, based on spontaneous task-independent fluctuations of the blood-oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signal in the brain (Biswal et al., 2010; Greicius et al., 2009). RsfMRI considers the functional connectivity of brain areas, whereas traditional, task-dependent fMRI concerns activity of particular brain areas in response to a stimulus. RsfMRI is a simple procedure, has a short scan time - on the order of minutes, and the reproducibility of results is robust within the same participant (Zuo et al., 2010). However, while rsfMRI is thought to reflect fundamental traits in personality or psychological function (Harmelech and Malach, 2013), some have criticized the ultimate usefulness of rsfMRI results (Morcom and Fletcher, 2007). Moreover, the debate on the role of unwanted thoughts in resting state functional connectivity is still open (Kuhn et al., 2014) and it could be a methodological concern in psychiatric disorders, due to the fact that several psychiatric disorders have intense forms of unwanted thoughts (e.g. obsessive compulsive disorder (Julien et al., 2007) and rumination on weight and body shape is present in AN (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). While generalities of the basic methodology in rsfMRI would benefit from further standardization and optimization (e.g. scan while eyes closed/open, or awake/asleep), rsfMRI has regardless emerged as a staple tool in neuroimaging studies - perhaps equal in utility to task-based fMRI (Fox and Greicius, 2010). A number of studies have used rsfMRI to investigate functional connectivity in patients with eating disorders. Several different approaches can be used in rsfMRI analysis. In particular, the most common are network-based and seed-based approaches (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Van Den Heuvel and Hulshoff Pol, 2010). Regarding the first approach, independent component analysis (ICA) is the most common analysis to investigate intrinsic neural networks, and it does not necessarily require an a priori hypothesis.

The dwelling was built by his grandfather, soon after he had emigrated from Holland. It was a favorite spot even then, although the Indian was still lurking among the hills, and the white man was not yet numerous enough to protect himself against the savage foe. The first settler of the place was a soldier in the army of William III., and he brought home with him a few trophies of war, which he placed in his new abode as mementoes of the past. A small brass cannon and two or three swords were among these relics, and they remained in the house until within the last twenty-five years, when the sword-blades were sold to some wandering pedlar. The cannon has gone too, and nothing now remains to remind the present generation of the warlike character of their ancestors. But there is another relic in the house which I have never seen equaled elsewhere. It is an ancient fire-place, such as we read of in old romances, and see represented in engravings of English castles. It occupies nearly the whole of one end of a large room, and looks as if it might once have served as a fireplace for the castle of Macbeth itself. There is space enough in it to roast an ox whole, and the ample chimney above spreads wide and far over head like the branches of a tree. When this venerable mansion was first occupied, the forest stood close around it, and the sound of the axe was heard daily ringing through the neighboring woods. The nearest neighbors were miles away, and the family lived almost alone in the midst of the wilderness. They were compelled to watch closely against surprise from the Indians, and often in the dead hours of night would they hear the stealthy tread of the savages prowling round the house. At times the tomahawk and scalping-knife would do their work among the scattered settlers, and many a fearful tragedy was enacted in the depths of those dark woods. The old people used to tell stories of Indian warfare and bloody strife, which made the hair of childhood stand erect, and sent the imagination back to the earliest periods of romance. It was related how, on a certain occasion, the Indians had surprised a party of whites, consisting of several families, while passing through the mountains. They succeeded in capturing every individual except two young women, who escaped to the woods, and concealed themselves during the massacre. After the Indians had departed, the poor girls came forth from their hiding-place, and found their friends weltering in their gore. Their brothers, fathers, mothers, and sisters lay stretched lifeless before them, and the whole scene presented a picture of horror indescribable. The survivors were so overcome with terror and dismay, that they knew not what course to pursue. Night was coming on, and they dreaded to remain amid the bodies of their slaughtered relatives, lest the savages should return. On the other hand, they feared to attempt making their way through the forest alone. In this emergency, one of the young women started off through the woods in search of assistance, leaving her companion to keep watch beside the dead. She traveled all that night, threading the tangled mazes of the wilderness, guided solely by the stars. Sometimes she lost her way, and wandered hither and thither without knowing whither she went. But morning dawned at length, and she reached a clearing, where stood the dwellings of white men. Assistance was immediately despatched to her friend, and both were rescued from their perilous situation. The poor girl who thus saved herself and companion from death, became afterward the wife of the founder of the homestead, and the great-grandmother of the present proprietor.

In recognizing this divergence, the inquiry must consider how generativity might inform and shape environmental actions within organizational contexts differently than in domestic settings. Generativity serves as a catalyst, spurring individuals to consider the legacy of their consumption and resource use, thus leading to more sustainable practices. This intrinsic motivation aligns with the notion that individuals who reflect on their generative potential are more likely to engage in behaviours that not only benefit them but, crucially, contribute positively to the community and environment (Urien & Kilbourne, 2011). When employees perceive their actions as part of a broader narrative that affects future generations, their engagement with pro-environmental behaviours may deepen. For example, initiatives designed to foster a culture of sustainability within the workplace can promote a sense of collective responsibility. Efforts such as recycling programs or energy-saving measures can serve as conduits for generative action, as they signal to employees that their contributions matter and are integral to a larger purpose. This sense of shared responsibility may instill a communal ethos, prompting employees to not only adopt these behaviours themselves but to encourage colleagues to follow suit, thereby amplifying the impact of individual actions. Moreover, the workplace provides unique opportunities for fostering generativity that are often absent in the home environment. The collaborative nature of many work settings can facilitate discussions about sustainability, allowing employees to share insights, strategies, and successes related to eco-friendly practices. These interactions can enhance the social learning element of pro-environmental behaviour, reinforcing the linkage between generativity and actionable commitment. Employees can witness firsthand the ripple effects of their colleagues' environmental choices, creating an atmosphere where eco-conscious behaviours are not only endorsed but celebrated, further eliminating barriers to engagement. Additionally, leadership plays a critical role in cultivating an organizational culture that promotes generativity and environmental stewardship. When management prioritizes sustainability and transparently communicates its importance, employees are more likely to internalize these values and incorporate them into their daily routines. Leaders who model sustainable behaviours - such as reducing waste, promoting the use of renewable resources, and advocating for responsible consumption - can inspire their teams to follow suit. By embedding generative values within organizational policies and practices, companies can not only signal the relevance of sustainability but can also empower employees to perceive their contributions as impactful within a broader generational context. However, while the potential for impact is significant, it is crucial to consider the implementation strategies that facilitate this transformation. A proactive approach that includes training sessions on sustainability, workshops that emphasize the importance of generative practices, and systems for recognizing and rewarding eco-friendly behaviours can serve as effective mechanisms for behaviour change. Such initiatives must be designed with the understanding that motivation can vary widely among employees, and therefore flexibility in approach is essential to address differing values and priorities. Ultimately, integrating generativity into the discourse surrounding pro-environmental behaviour expands the conversation beyond individual accountability and urges a collective approach to sustainability - one where the legacies of today's choices are linked to the well-being of future generations. This holistic perspective not only enriches our understanding of environmental behaviours within the workplace but also ushers in new possibilities for cultivating a culture of responsibility and care that transcends organizational confines, resonating into communities and, indeed, the world at large.

Between the sharp whizzing tones, peculiar to the instrument on which he played, rang the distant songs of home-returning peasants - a contrast, like that of their bright active life, with the dream-life of these blind children. The boy seemed to feel it. He rose quickly, walked with a firm step to the window - for he knew the room and all its furniture - and said, as he threw back his bright fair locks, "You are incomprehensible, Mary! Our parents and all the village congratulate us. Will it not be a gain after all? Until it was promised me I never asked much about it. We are blind, they say; I never understood what was wanting in us. When we sat without there by the wood, and travellers came by, and said, 'Poor children!' I felt angry, and thought, 'What have they to pity in us?' But that we are different from others, I know well enough. They often talked about things which I could not understand, yet which must be very beautiful. And now that we are going to know them too, the longing never leaves me day nor night." "I was contented as I was," said Mary, sadly, "I was so happy, and should have liked to be as happy all my life. It will all be different now! Have you never heard people complain that the world is full of sorrow and care - and did we know care?" "Because we did not know the world - and I will know it at all risks! I suffered myself to be pleased with groping about in the dark with you, and being obliged to do nothing, but not always! Often, when my father taught us history, and told us about heroes and bold deeds, I asked him if any of them had been blind? But whoever had done anything great could see. And then I often plagued myself all day long with thoughts about it. Then when I played on the spinet, or was allowed to play on the organ, in your father's place, I forgot my uneasiness for a time; but when it came back, I thought, 'Must you always play the organ, and go the few hundred paces up and down the village that you know; and must no one out of the village ever know you; and must none ever name you after you are dead?' Look you, Mary, - since the doctor has been at the castle, I hope that I yet may become a perfect man; and then I will go out into the world and take the path that pleases me, and I shall have nothing to ask any one!" "And not me, Clement?" She said it uncomplainingly and without reproach. But the boy answered vehemently, "Sister Mary, do not talk such nonsense - I cannot bear it! Do you think that I would leave you alone at home and steal away amongst strangers? Do you not trust me?"

It was not possible to establish whether the people driving the column and firing the artillery were Russian soldiers or separatist rebels. But there were strong indications that whoever it was doing those things operated out of Russian territory - something very unlikely to have happened without Moscow's consent. Ukrainian soldiers sit in a military camp near Luhansk, Ukraine. A Ukrainian soldier looks through his binoculars at a military camp near Luhansk, Ukraine. Fighting a civil war: Ukrainian soldiers eat at a military camp near Luhansk, Ukraine. The question of Russian involvement is at the core of Western governments' response to the Ukraine crisis, and could be crucial to how the conflict plays out. The European Union and United States have already imposed sanctions on Russia in part based on allegations Moscow is arming the rebels. The West has warned of more sanctions if Russia provides further help. A Ukrainian national guard unit stationed on the outskirts of Novoazovsk, on the road towards the Novoazovsk-Veselo-Voznesenka border crossing, showed a Reuters reporter a crater left by an exploding munition near their position. They said the artillery fire was coming from over the border inside Russia, about 10 km (six miles) to the east. 'There were about 500 salvos from Grad (multiple rocket system) and mortars. There have been and are no rebels here whatsoever. They're just firing straight from Russia,' Roman, the commander of a Ukrainian national guard unit, said on Sunday, before the armored column appeared in the same area. Reuters saw no direct evidence of this, and Russian officials have repeatedly denied that their military is in any way involved in the conflict in eastern Ukraine, between pro-Moscow separatist rebels and government forces. A spokesman for the Russian border guard service, when asked to comment, said: 'This is stupid. Russia doesn't fire at anyone.' The Russian defense ministry did not respond to a faxed request for comment. But with no rebel presence within range inside Ukraine, it was not clear what other source there could have been for the artillery fire. Even if rebels has somehow snuck into the area and fired the artillery, it seemed impossible they could have done that without using Russian territory to move about, given the distance from the nearest rebel-held locations. A Ukrainian soldier prepares a gun close to a military camp near Luhansk, Ukraine. The crater seen by the Reuters reporter on Sunday, before the clashes with rebels, was in the corner of a field behind a defensive trench dug by the Ukrainian national guard unit. A metal fragment that appeared to come from a munition was found in the hole. Reuters showed the photographs of the crater to four European weapons experts who said the crater was either made by an artillery rocket, most probably a Grad, or by a shell from a self-propelled 122 mm gun.

In recognizing the diversity of models and practices proliferating in the domain of local energy exchange, it becomes essential to explore the nuances and implications of such exchanges beyond the mere transactional. At the heart of these exchanges lie multifaceted relationships, intricately interwoven with cultural, social, and economic threads that demand a deeper understanding. When energy is traded within a community, it is not simply a matter of supply meeting demand; it is an opportunity to foster solidarity and resilience, echoing a communal ethos grounded in cooperation and mutual benefit. The exchange dynamics are driven by both necessity and ingenuity, particularly in resource-constrained environments. In rural areas where infrastructure might be lacking, communities have been observed to creatively adapt these energy models to serve not just as utility services but as platforms for community engagement and empowerment. This adaptive capacity reflects a broader trend of innovation at the grassroots level, challenging traditional notions of energy provision and hinting at a paradigm shift towards more localized, sustainable practices. For instance, in various African nations, energy hubs are being positioned not merely as service providers but as integrative community centers. These hubs become focal points around which community activities coalesce, from educational programs on sustainable energy practices to entrepreneurial ventures leveraging local resources. The emphasis on community ownership and management in many of these initiatives ensures sustainability by aligning operations with the specific needs and capabilities of the community, thereby enhancing the overall resilience of the energy system. In exploring the strategic frameworks that support these exchanges, there emerges a clear need for policy environments that are conducive to innovation and local adaptation. Policymakers are gradually recognizing the value of these decentralized models and are accordingly crafting regulatory landscapes that encourage rather than stifle local energy innovations. Creating spaces for dialogue among stakeholders-governmental bodies, NGOs, and local communities-is fundamental to fostering an ecosystem where energy exchanges can thrive and evolve. Moreover, a key area of interest lies in addressing the challenges of scalability and replicability of local energy exchange models. Successful pilots demonstrate the potential for broader application, yet each community presents unique challenges and opportunities that must be carefully navigated. Hybridizing models to fit specific contexts could enable the scaling of these solutions, drawing on lessons learned from early adopters while adapting to local socio-economic landscapes. Analyzing the technologies underpinning these systems reveals an evolving landscape where advancements in renewable energy generation and storage create new possibilities for local energy exchanges. The integration of technologies such as microgrids, blockchain for transaction recording, and mobile platforms for managing exchanges is opening up further dimensions of efficiency and transparency. Together, these technologies enhance the practical realization of peer-to-peer energy frameworks. Ultimately, the continued evolution and spread of local energy exchanges depend significantly on collaborative efforts at multiple levels. From the microtransactions between individuals within a community to larger cooperative networks that span regions, the successes of these initiatives highlight the potential of energy exchanges to redefine access to resources. This collaborative energy model aligns with a vision of a future wherein communities are not just passive consumers of energy but active participants in crafting sustainable and equitable energy solutions. These exploratory unfolding dynamics warrant further inquiry and will undoubtedly shape the contours of energy discourse in years to come.

In fact, when Knox first expressed interest in studying in Italy, her mother Edda Mellas thought it sounded like a great idea. She and her husband Curt Knox had raised their three daughters in Seattle, where Knox was born. A former high-school teacher, Mellas had taught her children to embrace different cultures through travel and world music. Her father, a civil engineer, had traveled extensively, and she took the girls with him whenever possible. When she learned of the program at the University of Washington, she encouraged her daughter to apply. By 17, Knox had become fluent in Spanish and was taking French classes. As soon as she got accepted into the University of Washington program, she started saving money. She worked as a hostess at a local restaurant and cleaned houses. She earned extra cash babysitting and teaching piano lessons. After graduating from high school, she spent her summers traveling around Europe and South America with her older sister, Deanna, who is now 28. They visited Peru, Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia and Ecuador. Knox also studied in Paris and Florence before landing in Perugia. Once she arrived in Italy, she found work at a bar, La Tazza d'Oro, where she met Sollecito. Their relationship began as a friendship but blossomed into something more within a month, according to Sollecito's lawyer Giulia Bongiorno. "She was very happy to meet someone who spoke English," Bongiorno said. Knox wrote back to her parents regularly, telling them how much she loved her life there. "I'm having a blast!" she wrote in October 2007. "I love this city." She signed off with a kissy face. Knox's mother recalls receiving a postcard from her daughter, written in Italian, thanking her for letting her go on the trip. "It was a beautiful letter," she said. "It was a very good letter. I can remember reading it and thinking what a wonderful time she must be having." Family close by. Knox's parents and her sister joined her in Italy over the Christmas break. "It was wonderful to spend time with my baby again," Mellas recalled. The couple returned to Italy in February for Knox's birthday. While there, they stayed with Knox and Sollecito. They were struck by his kindness and hospitality. He cooked dinner every night, and he and Knox seemed happy, they said. "He treated us like royalty," Mellas said. On Valentine's Day, Knox called her parents from a pay phone. She was too shy to call on her cell phone, Mellas said. "She was so embarrassed because she couldn't talk on the phone with me without stuttering," Mellas said. Knox was excited to tell them she'd received roses from Sollecito, she said. That same day, Knox and Sollecito went to the police station to report that someone had stolen her computer, a crime that remains unsolved. Sollecito's family remembers Knox as quiet, polite and well-mannered. His mother, Franca Sollecito, said Knox was a welcome guest in their home. "We liked her," she said. "She was a nice girl." Friends describe Knox as bright, ambitious and eager to learn. She was excited to share her knowledge with others. At one point, she wanted to open a language center in Italy. Her aunt, Jan Cassidy, said Knox was always looking for ways to make a difference in people's lives. She often volunteered with disabled children. When she came home for Thanksgiving in 2006, she talked about starting a nonprofit organization to help underprivileged kids in Seattle, Cassidy said.
