Nan, being the most tender-hearted among the trio, felt an immediate pang of guilt for not intervening sooner, although Gabriel and Cephas were quick to assure her that they had all done their best. The field mouse, perhaps sensing a certain kindness in the children's demeanor, hovered near but dared not come too close. It was a small tragedy, a microcosm of the world's infinite struggles, and yet it occupied their thoughts much more than any abstract idea of progress or civilization. "Maybe we can build something for her," Cephas suggested, his imagination already constructing a minute fortress where the mouse could find refuge. Gabriel, ever the pragmatist, nodded thoughtfully. "That's a good idea. We could use those sticks over there," he pointed, gesturing toward a haphazard pile of fallen branches at the edge of the hill where the trees cast elongated shadows in the late afternoon sun. With newfound purpose, they set to work, driven by an instinctive desire to reorder a world in which chaos had momentarily intruded. As they gathered materials, their serious discussion broke often into playful jests, the somber mood lifting like morning mist under the sun's persistence. Nan, who possessed a careful eye for detail, took charge of the decoration once the basic structure had taken shape. She adorned the tiny stick fortress with wildflowers and soft tufts of grass, humming a cheerful tune, a sound more like a babbling brook than music, the cadence of innocence itself. Mother Mouse, perhaps emboldened by the construction of her new realm, moved closer, her whiskers twitching with wary curiosity. The children retreated a few paces, sitting back on their haunches to watch the creature investigate their handiwork. The mouse entered, sniffing and exploring, at last settling into what would soon become her makeshift abode. "I think she likes it," Nan proclaimed, satisfaction lighting up her face. "Of course she does," Cephas added with a smile. "It's a palace for a mouse queen!" The sun crept further toward the horizon, casting golden light across the field, and the three companions, feeling the day had been somehow filled with significance beyond their understanding, leaned back to rest on the hill. There was magic in their togetherness, in the symphony of the evening crickets that rose around them, a balm for the world's harsher remedies. In this small corner of Shady Dale, away from the ponderous burdens of grown-up concerns, the children had found something that could not be easily labeled or contained, something that existed outside the ambit of civilization's relentless march. They felt, perhaps without knowing, that life was not only in the large and loud but also in the quiet and simple, in each small act of kindness. Thus, in building a sanctuary for a mouse, they had constructed something intangible for themselves-a memory, a shard of understanding, a glimpse of the possible warmth that lay hidden even in a world shadowed by inevitable complexities. The day waned, and they arose at last, leaving behind their play and setting off toward home, filled with a gentle contentment that no words could sufficiently describe.

He is happy with the support from advisers at his local job centre, who helped him get the voluntary work. But the lack of interviews frustrates him, as does the dearth of any feedback. Andrew is at the Dusty Forge, a converted pub, which is home to Action in Caerau and Ely (Ace). This provides training, drop-in support, a workshop and computer centre. The Communities First team there are looking into "up-skilling" Andrew to get over the hurdles and making him more employable, but share his frustration at the system. "He deserves employment, it's about getting him over the barrier," says training officer Simon Murray. "The biggest issues are finding credible, contracted jobs paying more than the minimum wage." Simon, who has worked in Ely for 10 years, said: "There's not enough decent work locally - there are supermarkets and retail, all offering - if you're lucky - eight or 16 hours contracts, predominantly minimum wage. It's cheaper to employ people that way. "There's no industry within the area, and people can be reluctant to travel. People will get one bus and travel across town. With people coming in here it's about skills and their CVs are a bit light, I think 89% of the local population will not go to university. Our schools are ranked low in terms of achievement. It's a classic scenario." Simon said: "It's depressing in some capacities but you get little victories along the way. We like the community a lot, when you watch people grow up and do well it's nice to see that. "It's the perception, perpetuated by programmes like Benefits Street that people are having a good time. They manage, but then you get people who prey on them and get them into debt." "People come in here in a terrible state, upset, last resort because they've been sanctioned or got mental health issues," said Simon. "We feel we're seeing more people and can do more for people, but then our remit's changed, we're losing staff. Communities First will be gone by next March. I don't want to just end up being a training organisation - I'd like to do stuff because we can, not because we have to. It's whether we can still deliver a service when we essentially become self-sustaining." Has it got better with unemployment falling? "It doesn't feel any better because Trussell Trust will report food banks are continuing to rise," said Simon. He picks up bread from a friend's bakery in Pontcanna to give out and they are also making their own mobile pizza ovens in the workshop, which are out in the community as part of outreach work, to talk to people about what they can offer. "It's not necessarily about people being in employment but it's about people being out of poverty - which are two different things."

For instance, individuals earning similar incomes might find themselves facing vastly different premiums and out-of-pocket expenses based on whether they purchase insurance through their employer or the exchanges. This disparity fosters frustration and distrust, eroding public confidence in the system. Moreover, the intricate web of regulations and mandates woven into the Affordable Care Act stifles competition. Insurers, bound by uniform standards, struggle to differentiate themselves through cost-saving innovations or custom-tailored plans. Instead, they focus on compliance, absorbing administrative costs that inevitably inflate premiums. Hence, consumers are left with limited choices, selecting from nearly indistinguishable plans, devoid of differentiation beyond superficial branding. The ACA's well-intentioned aim to reduce the uninsured population has also led, paradoxically, to the potential neglect of the system's financial sustainability. Subsidies designed to make coverage more affordable have placed significant fiscal strain on both federal and state budgets. Without substantive reforms, the long-term viability of these subsidies remains questionable, threatening a potential reckoning where funds dry up, and coverage becomes increasingly elusive once more. Compounding this issue is the continued presence and power of large, monopolistic medical providers. These giants dictate prices and stifle competition, ensuring that the cost of care remains prohibitive. While the ACA's architects envisioned marketplaces where insurers could negotiate better prices with these providers, the intransigent clout of medical conglomerates has largely thwarted such aspirations. Consequently, the anticipated downward pressure on healthcare costs has not materialized as hoped, leaving many Americans scraping by to afford essential care. The envisioned transformative effect of Obamacare, reliant on creating a nationwide tide lifting all boats, has instead revealed persistent divides. States opting out of Medicaid expansion harbor substantial pockets of uninsured, exacerbating the national disparity in healthcare access and quality. This patchy acceptance further fragments the landscape, ensuring that where you live often dictates the caliber of care you receive, an inequity unbefitting a nation striving for universal coverage. Critics like myself argue that a genuine reform should address these pervasive issues rooted deep within the system. A holistic approach requires tackling the structural impediments head-on-empowering consumers with greater transparency and choice, integrating competitive pressures to curtail prices, and ensuring equitable access regardless of geography. While the ACA planted seeds of change, its yield thus far demands a rigorous reassessment and nurturing, not merely maintenance. As I embark on my journey through New York's exchange, registering for coverage under a law I've vigilantly critiqued, I'm reminded that genuine, lasting change is forged in the crucible of trial and adaptivity. My sign-up was simultaneously an acceptance of the current reality and an assertion of my willingness to advocate for change from within. The pursuit of universal, equitable healthcare for all Americans is a noble aim, requiring broad shoulders to bear both its failures and successes. And as history has shown, it is often the critics who, compelled not by opposition but aspiration, usher in the most profound transformations.

As we navigate this brave new world, the importance of minimizing electromagnetic interference (EMI) and radio-frequency interference (RFI) cannot be overstated. The proliferation of wireless devices, computer networks, and sensitive electronic equipment has created an environment where the crude, high-frequency switching of SCR dimmers is no longer acceptable. The sine wave dimmer, on the other hand, offers a more refined approach to intensity control, one that is better suited to the demands of modern technology. Sine wave dimmers, also known as high-frequency dimmers or PWM (pulse-width modulation) dimmers, operate on a fundamentally different principle than their SCR counterparts. Instead of chopping the waveform, sine wave dimmers modulate the width of the AC waveform to achieve the desired intensity. This approach eliminates the high-frequency spikes and EMI associated with SCR dimming, resulting in a much cleaner and quieter operation. The benefits of sine wave dimming extend beyond just reduced EMI and RFI. Because they don't rely on the inertia of the filament to smooth out the output, sine wave dimmers can respond more quickly and accurately to changes in intensity. This makes them ideal for applications where precise control is critical, such as in film and television production. Additionally, sine wave dimmers can operate at much higher frequencies than SCR dimmers, allowing for faster switching times and reduced lamp flicker. Another significant advantage of sine wave dimmers is their ability to work with a wider range of lamp types. While SCR dimmers can struggle with certain lamp geometries, sine wave dimmers can handle even the most demanding loads with ease. This is particularly important in applications where lamp life is critical, such as in retail or hospitality environments. The increased sophistication of sine wave dimmers also enables advanced features like real-time monitoring and control, allowing for more efficient energy management and maintenance scheduling. This level of intelligence is simply not possible with traditional SCR dimmers, which are often limited to simple on/off and intensity control. As the world continues to evolve and our reliance on technology grows, it's clear that the humble SCR dimmer is no longer up to the task. The sine wave dimmer, with its cleaner, quieter, and more precise operation, is poised to take its place as the new standard in lighting control. It's a brave new world, indeed, and one that demands a more refined and sophisticated approach to lighting. The days of the SCR dimmer may be numbered, but the future of lighting has never looked brighter.

Then he saw Dick Elliott sent ahead to reconnoitre. Chippy looked over his shoulder, and measured the distance he would have to run down the alley before he could find cover. No go. If he ran, the scout of the other side would see him scuttling, and suspect something. Besides, Chippy was well known. He was a famous leader in this kind of warfare. So he curled himself up as round as a hedgehog, and lay hidden behind the box, with his eye at a crack. He gave a little grunt to himself as he saw Dick Elliott look carefully along the alley before he went on down the lane. Chippy was glad he hadn't run; he would certainly have been seen. But as soon as Dick had passed, he was up and away down the alley at full speed. He made a couple of turns along side-streets, and then Quay Flat lay before him. He put his fingers into his mouth and gave a long, shrill whistle. There was no answer, but Chippy was quite satisfied. He knew that his warriors would understand. From another carefully chosen spot he watched Dick Elliott come out on Quay Flat and look all about. But the braves of Skinner's Hole had caught their chief's whistle, and were lying hidden among piles of old cordage and rusty anchors which were heaped in one corner of the Flat. Dick ran back up the lane. 'I can't see anyone about,' he reported. 'The Flat looks as quiet as can be.' 'Come on!' said Arthur Graydon to the other boys. 'Keep together; and if the wharf-rats come out, we'll give 'em beans!' The band of Grammar School boys gained the Flat, and struck out for the bridge which crossed the river and led to the suburb in which lay their homes. All went quietly till they were well out in the open space, and then the wharf-rats set up a tremendous yell and darted from their ambush. A furious battle was started at once on the Flat. Stones flew like hail on both sides, and then the combatants came to close quarters, and the fray developed into a series of stand-up fights, with every boy yelling like mad. 'Slug 'em! slug 'em, Skinner's 'Ole!' howled the wharf-rats. 'Out 'em! Down 'em, Skinner's 'Ole!' 'Rally, School!' shouted Dick Elliott. 'Drive 'em into the river!' bellowed Arthur Graydon. The latter was fighting with a couple of heavy books buckled tightly into a long, stout strap, and he fetched a couple of his opponents down with swinging blows. Suddenly he was confronted with the rival chieftain, the redoubtable Chippy. Arthur swung his books at Chippy's head, but the latter was far too quick for so slowly delivered a stroke, and was inside his opponent's guard in a flash.

The sun hung low in the sky, casting long shadows upon the bustling port town of Port Royal. The chatter of merchants and sailors filled the air, a cacophony of bartering and laughter mingling with the salty breeze. Elizabeth felt the weight of the delicate necklace around her neck, a tangible reminder of her father's expectations, and the impending responsibilities of her station. Just then, a loud crash echoed from the nearby tavern, followed by the raucous yells of sailors fueled by rum and revelry. The sound drew Elizabeth's attention like a moth to a flame. "Come! Let us see what mischief they are up to," she urged, and with a glance shared, the two made their way toward the ruckus. As they approached, they found a scene well known to the seafaring folk-a card game spiraled into chaos. Coins flew, fists clenched, and laughter mingled with threats. At the center of it, a man with a weather-beaten face and a scar tracing down his cheek raised a tankard high in celebration. "A toast, to the bravest crew to sail the Caribbean! To the Black Pearl!" The name sent a shiver down Elizabeth's spine, tales of the infamous ship and its ghostly crew flooding back to her. Surely, such men were the embodiment of the very legends she adored. "Careful, lass. Those who sit at the edge of the abyss often find themselves drawn in... with no way back." "Perhaps the dangers of the abyss are where the true adventure lies," she tossed back, a defiant gleam sparking in her gaze. As the tavern crowd cheered again, Elizabeth felt an unwelcome thrill of excitement stir within her. This moment, alive with laughter and folly, tugged at the yearning in her heart. Could she truly step beyond the confines of expectations? "Don't venture too close," Will advised, yet he remained beside her, caught in the pull of her adventurous spirit. The rowdy laughter echoed around them, mingling with the evening mist rolling in from the sea, as if beckoning them closer to the horizon of the unknown. Caught between the world of decorum and the promise of adventure, Elizabeth's heart raced. Would she turn back, or embrace the call of the wild seas ahead? With heart alight, she glanced back at Will. "Shall we... join them?" As uncertainty hung heavy in the air, the allure of the pirate life pulled at her spirit, hinting at secrets just beneath the waves-waiting to be unraveled, waiting for those brave enough to dive into the depths...

As the controversy surrounding Russell Brand's remarks at the GQ Men of the Year Awards continued to simmer, it's worth noting that the comedian's own fashion choices have been called into question. Despite his criticism of Hugo Boss's Nazi ties, Brand has been spotted wearing the brand's clothing on multiple occasions. In February, he was photographed wearing a Hugo Boss jacket, which has sparked accusations of hypocrisy. But the real question is, what's the truth about Hugo Boss's Nazi past? While it's true that the company did produce uniforms for the Nazi Party, the extent of their involvement has been greatly exaggerated. The uniforms were not designed by Hugo Boss himself, but rather evolved from earlier Prussian styles. The infamous black uniform, which has become synonymous with the SS, was actually designed by an artist and senior SS officer named Karl Diebitsch, who worked with a graphic designer called Walter Heck. It's also worth noting that Hugo Boss himself was punished as a Nazi supporter after the war, and died in 1948. While the company's executives are no doubt furious about the recent bad publicity, it's clear that the brand's past is a complex and controversial topic. Rather than simply demonizing Hugo Boss, it's important to understand the historical context and the ways in which the company's designs were influenced by the era in which they were created. In the end, Brand's outburst may have been a bit of a publicity stunt, but it has also sparked an important conversation about the intersection of fashion and history. As we continue to grapple with the complexities of the past, it's essential that we approach these topics with nuance and sensitivity.

However, more complex heuristics such as metaheuristics can also be considered at the lower level. Over the past few years, a number of review papers and book chapters on hyper-heuristics have been published (Burke et al., 2003; 2010; 2009). Burke et al. (2013) provided an overview of the scientific literature on hyper-heuristics up until the end of 2012, also discussing the history of hyper-heuristics and the intellectual roots of hyper-heuristic methods. The authors introduced some related areas and discussed directions for future research, encouraging more interaction between related communities, especially those working in the fields of metaheuristics and machine learning. A tutorial article was later published by Ross (2014), which gave useful guidelines for implementing a hyper-heuristic approach, in addition to discussing a number of relevant research issues and identifying promising application domains. The chapter also gave a brief history of the area and discussed some representative examples published at the time in detail. A more recent publication by Branke, Nguyen, Pickardt, and Zhang (2016) provided a comprehensive review of recent developments in generation hyper-heuristics, with an emphasis on the design of construction heuristics in production scheduling optimisation problems. This paper presented three useful components in the design of hyper-heuristics for the generation of heuristics: (i) the representation of what they call candidate heuristics, which define the search space, (ii) the optimisation algorithm used to explore this search space, and (iii) the fitness function used to determine the quality of candidate heuristics. The authors classified hyper-heuristics according to the learning method they adopt (supervised or unsupervised). Another recent publication by Pillay (2016) presented an overview of hyper-heuristics for university examination timetabling, university course timetabling and school timetabling problems. The author emphasised one of the key objectives; namely, to produce reusable technologies to solve difficult real-world educational timetabling problems in a more general manner. General purpose heuristic search and optimisation methods have been studied in various fields, from Operational Research to Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence. Although this study focuses on selection hyper-heuristic approaches in particular, there are other strands of independent ongoing research using related approaches. A survey on 'Algorithm Selection' was presented by Kotthoff (2014). The key goal of the algorithm selection problem is to select the most suitable algorithm to solve a given problem instance, instead of developing new algorithms. This paper presented an overview of previous categorisations of algorithm selection approaches, providing a unified classification and definition that captures the work currently being undertaken in this field. The author also described the concept of 'Algorithm Portfolios', where the decision of which algorithm to use is decided on a case-by-case basis for each problem instance individually. The author distinguished two main classes of portfolios: Static Portfolios which are constructed offline before any problem instances are solved; and Dynamic Portfolios which change the composition and/or configuration of the constituent algorithms in an online manner, while solving a given instance problem.

Papurello et al. observed a large decrease in performance when a Ni-YSZ cell was fed with simulated biosyngas and an amount of toluene as low as 0.1 g/Nm3 [21,22]. This same model tar was used by Liu et al. with Ni-GDC cells. A toluene concentration of 20 g/Nm3 did not degrade a cell operating under current with simulated biosyngas [23]. Also Doyle et al. investigated the effect of toluene on Ni-GDC using simulated biosyngas. Despite the deposition of carbon, as discovered with post-mortem SEM-EDS analysis, 20 g/Nm3 actually increased the cell performance by decreasing the cell ASR and increasing the amount of fuel available due to the tar reforming. However, 32 g/Nm3 dramatically affected the ASR even with a fuel utilisation close to 70% [24]. Namioka et al. reported a tolerance limit of 3 g/Nm3 for a SOFC with Ni-ScSZ anode operated at 800 C and 500 mA/cm2 with humidified hydrogen and a steam to carbon ratio of 1. Interestingly, despite no carbon was observed at 10 g/Nm3, disappearance of Ni particles was detected with SEM-EDS analysis [25]. The authors ascribed the observation to metal dusting corrosion, as explained in [26]. Also the effect of HCl contamination on SOFC anodes has been investigated in the past years [11,27-31]. Recently, Kuramoto et al. found that Ni-YSZ cells operated at 900 C with a current density of 150 or 200 mA/cm2 were not affected by the presence of 10 ppmv HCl when fed with simulated post-CCS syngas (H2/N2/H2O = 70.9/23.6/5.5 vol%) [32]. Similar results were obtained by Li et al. and Blesznowski et al. [33,34]. However, concentrations higher than 100 ppmv were reported to increase the cell degradation, especially with methane as fuel gas [35]. Conversely, Madi et al. reported more sever degradation when the cell was fed with H2 rather than with syngas. They explained the observation by the decrease in HCl adsorption as due to competitive CO adsorption and oxidation. A degradation of 3.1% per 1000 h was observed already with 10 ppmv HCl in H2 [36]. Papurello et al. showed that below 20 ppmv a cell fed with biogas reformate does not suffer degradation. Above this concentration, the loss in performance is probably caused by HCl adsorption on Ni [21]. Despite the presence of scientific work, at present there is not yet general agreement on the fate of tar in the anode chamber. This is due to the different anode materials tested, the discrepancies in the operating conditions, and the various model tar compounds used. Moreover, different diagnosis methodologies and techniques, and evaluation criteria might affect the conclusions of a study [37]. Regarding HCl, results are somewhat more congruent. However, the cross influence of HCl with tar and its effect on direct internal tar reforming has not been studied yet.

There are over 30 secreted HpVALs which dominate the immune response in H. polygyrus infected mice (Hewitson et al., 2011b). As observed in human and canine hookworms, HpVALs are characterised by having either a single or double 15-25 kDa CAP domain. In infected mice, the antibody response primarily targets four HpVALs, the double-domain HpVAL-1, -2 and -3, and the single domain HpVAL-4. Following secondary infection of mice, antibodies are directed at the same four HpVALs as well as another single domain family member, HpVAL-7. Both HpVAL-1 and HpVAL-2 bear an immunodominant O-linked glycan which is exposed on the parasite surface (Hewitson et al., 2011a). Interestingly, each member of the HpVAL family has a distinct pattern of expression during the parasite life cycle with HpVAL-4 being expressed at high levels by all mammalian stages from day 3 and day 5p. i, L3s, L4s, and adult worms (Hewitson et al., 2013) Several structures of proteins having a single CAP domain and one structure of a hookworm ASP with two CAP domains have been reported (Fernandez et al., 1997; Serrano et al., 2004; Asojo et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2005; Shikamoto et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2005; Gibbs et al., 2008; Asojo, 2011; Xu et al., 2012; Borloo et al., 2013). Each CAP domain has a large central cavity (Serrano et al., 2004; Asojo et al., 2005, 2011; Gibbs et al., 2008; Suzuki et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010a; van Galen et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012; Mason et al., 2014; Darwiche et al., 2016; Baroni et al., 2017). The function of the cavity is unknown but in some SCP/TAPs proteins the cavity contains two histidine residues that have been shown to bind divalent cations including Zn2+ and Mg2+ (Gibbs and O'Bryan, 2007; Gibbs et al., 2008). The ability to bind Zn2+ is critical for heparin-sulphate dependent inflammatory mechanisms of the cobra SCP/TAPs protein natrin (Wang et al., 2010a). To make an oleogel, a low concentration of gelator molecule is added to oil, and with the appropriate processing, the molecules self-assemble to form 3-D networks, structuring the liquid oil. The assembly of these molecules is driven by various intermolecular forces, including Van der Waals forces, hydrogen bonding, stearic interactions, ionic interactions, or covalent bonding. In conclusion, oleogels have the potential to revolutionize the food industry by providing a novel and innovative way to create edible products that are both healthy and delicious. The analysis of benthic foraminiferal fauna is essential for reconstruction of changes in the sedimentary environment and elevation of tidal flats and coastal lowlands (e.g., Kosugi et al., 1991; Hayward et al., 2004; Takata et al., 2009; Hawkes et al., 2010; Engelhart et al., 2013). This is because the distribution of benthic foraminifera in tidal flats is usually a direct function of elevation relative to the tidal frame, with the duration and frequency of intertidal exposure being the most important controlling factors. In addition, foraminiferal estimates of paleomarsh surface elevation together with detailed lithostratigraphy and chronostratigraphy can be applied to develop predictive transfer functions capable of inferring the past elevation of a sediment sample relative to the tidal frame from its fossil foraminiferal content (e.g. Horton and Edwards, 2006). This study examines recent sediments deposited on a narrow, muddy tidal flat on Miura Peninsula, metropolitan Tokyo, which is located along the Sagami Trough, where the Philippine Sea Plate subducts beneath the Japanese islands (Fig. 1). Thus, this area has been severely damaged by megathrust earthquakes of magnitude 1/28 and the ensuing large tsunamis with a recurrence interval of 200-400 yr in the trough (e.g. Ando, 1971; Matsuda et al., 1978; Shimazaki et al., 2011; Shishikura, 2014). In addition, storm surges caused considerable damage to the Tokyo Metropolitan Area in 1979 and 2011 (Tsuji, 1981; Kanagawa Prefecture, 2015). The region was also severely damaged by river floods in 1910 and 1947 (e.g. Endo, 2009). More recently, the 2015 Kinu river flood disaster took place in the northern Tokyo Metropolitan Area (Sato et al., 2017). Thus, detection of past events from the study area is essential for improvement of the coastal hazard assessments of metropolitan Tokyo. Identification of fluid-mud deposits provides information on ancient river floods and storm surge events (Wells, 1995; Hill et al., 2007; Ichaso and Dalrymple, 2009). Abundant muddy sediment particles brought in by river floods and resuspended associated with storm surges result in high-density fluids known as fluid-mud (Kirby and Parker, 1983; Ross and Mehta, 1989; Lesourd et al., 2003; Nishida et al., 2013). Many studies have examined the criteria used to identify fluid-mud deposits in coastal and shallow-marine successions (e.g., Ichaso and Dalrymple, 2009; Macquaker et al., 2010; Mackay and Dalrymple, 2011). In tidal flat environments, Yamashita et al. (2011) and Nishida et al. (2013) proposed that the deposits are characterized by sharp lower and upper contacts and an absence of burrows. However, sufficient reference data on depositional environments and sedimentary facies are not currently available for this region. Therefore, the aim of this study is to establish multidisciplinary approaches combining C, N, and S elemental analysis, faunal analysis of benthic foraminifera and sedimentological analysis to identify sedimentary facies and natural hazard events in the study area. Particularly, the recognition of 'fluid mud' facies is important.

I, too, felt a sense of annoyance, but I was also intrigued by the writer's sheer audacity. Who was this man, with his weak lungs and his passion for the romantic and the unknown? His words painted vivid pictures in my mind: the open boat, the beautiful young wife, the mysterious arrival in a Samoan harbor. I could almost smell the salt air and feel the sun beating down on my skin as I listened. And Captain Shreve, too, seemed to be caught up in the tale, his eyes glinting with a hint of nostalgia as he nodded along, his voice interjecting occasional comments and questions. And Captain Shreve, too, seemed to sense it, his expression growing more guarded as the writer spoke. As the sun began to set, casting a golden glow over the deck, the writer finally wound down, his words trailing off into silence. Captain Shreve nodded thoughtfully, his eyes never leaving the horizon. "Ah, yes," he said, "I knew King Waldon. A remarkable man, in many ways. While these passive control methods could produce the desired flow patterns, they were limited to specific geometric configurations and had their own limitations. The most effective method to improve the hydrodynamics of the culture tank would be to actively control the flow at the boundaries using smart flow control devices. Smart flow control devices can adaptively alter the flow boundary conditions based on real-time feedback from the system. Smart flow control devices such as variable-frequency drive pumps, valves, and servo motors have been successfully employed in different applications including smart irrigation systems (Kamilaris et al., 2016), smart city drainage systems (Wu et al., 2018), and smart building heating ventilation air conditioning systems (Lee et al., 2010). Although the concept of active flow control has been extensively studied in the aerospace industry (Becker, 1979; Collis et al., 2004; Cattafesta and Sheplak, 2011), its application in the aquaculture industry remains largely unexplored. This paper proposes a novel design of a smart flow control device (SFCD) that can manipulate the flow boundary conditions in a circular-type tank. The SFCD consists of two main components: a flow actuator and a controller. The flow actuator controls the flow boundary condition at the inlet of the tank. The controller uses information from sensors measuring the flow field within the tank to determine the appropriate control action for the flow actuator. The proposed SFCD was implemented in a laboratory-scale experimental setup consisting of a cylindrical tank and a recirculation pump. The performance of the SFCD was evaluated by comparing the flow field inside the tank with and without the SFCD. Experimental results showed that the SFCD significantly reduced the nonuniformities in the flow field, thereby improving the hydrodynamics inside the tank. ## Materials and Methods ### Design of Smart Flow Control Device The schematic diagram of the SFCD is shown in Figure 1. It consists of a flow actuator and a controller. The flow actuator is connected to the inlet of the tank and controls the flow boundary conditions at the inlet. The controller receives input signals from sensors placed inside the tank and determines the control actions required to maintain the desired flow characteristics inside the tank. Based on this information, the controller sends commands to the flow actuator to adjust the flow boundary conditions accordingly. The flow actuator then modifies the flow entering the tank according to these commands. Figure 1: Schematic Diagram of the Proposed Smart Flow Control Device. ### Implementation of Smart Flow Control Device To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed SFCD, a laboratory-scale experimental setup was developed. The experimental setup consisted of a cylindrical tank with a diameter of 60 cm and height of 30 cm. Water was circulated through the tank using a recirculation pump. The SFCD was installed at the inlet of the tank. Two ultrasonic flow meters were mounted on either side of the tank to measure the volume flow rate entering and leaving the tank. These measurements were used as inputs to the controller of the SFCD. Four pressure transducers were also installed along the circumference of the tank to monitor the pressure gradient across the tank. Finally, a camera was positioned above the tank to capture images of the water surface during experiments. The SFCD was designed using SolidWorks software. The CAD model was then converted into G-code using CAM software and machined using a CNC machine. The final prototype of the SFCD is shown in Figure 2. The SFCD consists of three parts: a housing unit, a rotating disc, and a motorized shaft. The housing unit houses all other components of the SFCD.

Many of the reasons were heartbreaking: "Owner moved and couldn't keep," "Too many pets in the household," or the one that always hits me the hardest, "Unwanted." The look in their eyes as you read those cards is haunting. It's as if they understand they've been cast aside, left in a place where they rely on the kindness of strangers. Those piercing eyes stay with you long after you leave the shelter, a reminder of the cruelty they're subjected to by those who pledged to care for them. Since that first visit, my involvement has only deepened. I dedicate my weekends to volunteering there, ensuring the animals receive the attention and love they deserve. Grooming the scruffy ones, providing treats to the well-behaved, or simply sitting by the cage of the more reserved animals, offering nothing but silent companionship. Some react instantly, nudging me with their wet noses, while others require more time, still reeling from past betrayals. But patience is the key. It's incredibly rewarding to see them gradually warm up, their cautious tail wags and tentative purrs signifying trust regained. Yet, it's not all arduous. There are moments of pure joy when a family comes in and makes the decision to adopt. Watching a dog that had once seemed so forlorn leave with its new family, tail dynamically wagging, or a cat snuggly curled up in the arms of a young child, these are the moments that make all of the heartache worthwhile. You know that you've played a role, albeit small, in that happy ending. An animal finds its place in the world, a home, a family, and suddenly the gloomy reality of the shelter lightens just a bit. Each adoption means a spot opens up for another needy soul. Yet, the cycle almost seems endless. For every animal that finds a home, more fill their place. It's a battle that feels overwhelming at times, but giving up is simply not an option. Every creature deserves a chance, a slice of happiness in their lives, and I am committed to pursuing that unyielding vision of a world where no animal feels unwanted. As I drive home from the shelter each weekend, I carry both the weight of those I couldn't help and the joy for those I could. It's a complex mix of emotions that fuels my resolve. It's not always easy, but it's a mission of the heart, and those are often filled with the most profound rewards. My dedication to animals has even inspired others. Friends who once marveled at my commitment now come to volunteer themselves. Seeing them taking those first steps, petting a shy dog, or playing with an energetic kitten, fills me with immense pride. Our shared passion creates a small community of believers, striving to make a difference, one animal at a time. In this journey, I've learned much about humanity from creatures who lack the power to speak in words. Their resilience, gratitude, and unconditional love continue to teach me invaluable lessons every single day.

As the flames crackled and spat, casting flickering shadows on the surrounding darkness, Trooper Peter Halket's thoughts turned to his comrades, wondering if they would indeed find him before dawn. He had been so sure he knew the route, but the endless expanse of veld had played tricks on him, and now he was alone, with nothing but the fire to keep the night at bay. The chill in the air seemed to seep into his bones, and he wrapped his arms around himself, trying to retain what little warmth he had left. The fire danced and spat, casting eerie shadows on the rocks around him. Peter Halket's eyes felt heavy, and he rubbed them wearily, trying to shake off the fatigue that had been building all day. He had eaten nothing but a few scraps of bread and some dry, tasteless meat, and his stomach growled with hunger. The brandy in his flask was almost gone, and he knew he wouldn't be able to rely on it much longer. As he gazed into the flames, he felt a creeping sense of unease. The darkness seemed to press in on him from all sides, and he could almost hear the distant roar of lions, their eyes glowing like embers in the darkness. He shivered, despite the warmth of the fire, and his hand instinctively went to the rifle slung over his shoulder. He knew it was foolish, but he couldn't shake the feeling that something was watching him, waiting for its chance to strike. The fire crackled and spat again, and Peter Halket's gaze snapped back to the flames. He knew he had to keep himself awake, had to keep the fire burning, no matter what. He couldn't let his thoughts wander, couldn't let himself drift off into the darkness. He poked at the embers with a stick, sending sparks flying up into the night air. As the hours ticked by, the fire burned low, and Peter Halket's thoughts grew more and more disjointed. He saw visions of his comrades, their faces twisted with worry and fear. He saw the charred remains of the kraals, the burned-out fields, and the empty, trampled earth. He saw the lions, their eyes glowing like embers, their hot breath on the back of his neck. And then, just as he thought he was slipping into the darkness, he heard it - a faint rustling in the grass, a soft, scratching sound. Peter Halket's heart skipped a beat as he froze, his eyes fixed on the darkness beyond the fire's reach. He knew it was too late to run, too late to hide. All he could do was wait, and hope that his comrades would come before the night was over, and the darkness consumed him.

The challenge of modeling the economic impact of water buyback schemes grows more complex within regions lacking fully developed water markets. In such areas, the inefficiencies in water allocation persist, deeply entangled with historical entitlements and administratively set prices that fail to reflect the true scarcity and value of water resources. This situation complicates efforts to establish robust models like the Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) framework, which depends heavily on data that accurately mirrors market dynamics and resource valuation. Despite the hurdles, researchers continue to explore innovative methodologies to navigate these complexities. One promising approach involves the integration of localized case studies and participatory stakeholder analyses. By incorporating insights from local water users-such as farmers, industries, and municipal authorities-researchers can better understand the varied economic consequences of buyback programs across different sectors. This participatory approach aids in tailoring responses that mitigate adverse impacts while promoting sustainable practices, which is crucial for maintaining community support and achieving long-term objectives. Parallel to these localized studies, there's a growing emphasis on advancing policy frameworks that encourage the development of water markets. By transitioning from administratively-determined pricing to market-based mechanisms, regions can improve the efficiency of water allocation and incentivize conservation. This shift requires legal and institutional reforms that ensure the transparent and equitable distribution of water rights while safeguarding ecological needs. Another dimension of the research focuses on the broader ecological and social implications of water buybacks. Restoring water flows through buyback schemes not only aids environmental recovery but also enhances ecosystem services, such as improved water quality and habitat restoration. These ecological benefits, though challenging to quantify in economic terms, hold significant value for communities reliant on healthy ecosystems for their livelihoods and well-being. Moreover, social equity considerations are integral to the success of water buyback initiatives. Ensuring that buyback programs do not disproportionately affect marginalized groups is essential. Targeted compensation measures and investment in community-led development projects can help address these potential inequities. Enhanced agricultural practices, vocational training opportunities, and support for alternative livelihoods are critical components that accompany buyback schemes, fostering resilience and adaptability amidst the transition. Innovation in water conservation technologies also complements buyback efforts. Efficient irrigation systems, soil moisture monitoring technologies, and water-efficient crop varieties contribute to reducing water demand, thereby easing the pressure on water resources. These technological advancements, when coupled with buybacks, present a synergistic approach to sustainable water management. As water scarcity intensifies due to climate change and growing populations, the dynamics surrounding water buybacks and their economic, ecological, and social implications will demand continued attention and research. Policymakers, researchers, and stakeholders are called upon to collaborate across disciplines and regions, sharing insights and strategies to optimize water management frameworks. In conclusion, while challenges persist, the potential for adaptive and resilient water management systems offers a pathway toward balancing the needs of people and nature. Through strategic investments in research, policy development, and technological innovation, water buyback programs can play a crucial role in achieving sustainable water futures across diverse geographical and socio-economic landscapes.

But ultimately, it's a complex interplay of factors that determines whether or not we get bitten by mosquitoes. Two o'clock - two o'clock in the morning. The bells had just chimed the hour. Big Ben had boomed forth its deep and solemn note over sleeping London. The patient constable on point-duty at the foot of Westminster Bridge had stamped his feet for the last time, and had been relieved by his colleague, who gave him the usual password, "All right." The tumultuous roar of traffic, surging, beating, pulsating, had long ago ceased, but the crowd of smart broughams and private hansoms still stood in New Palace Yard, while from the summit of St. Stephen's tower the long ray of electricity streamed westward, showing that the House of Commons was still sitting. The giant Metropolis, the throbbing heart of the greatest empire the world has known, was silent. London, the city of varying moods, as easily pleased, as easily offended as a petted child; London, the dear, smoke-blackened old city, which every Englishman loves and every foreigner admires; London, that complex centre of the universe, humdrum and prosaic, yet ever mysterious, poetic and wonderful, the city full of the heart's secrets and of life's tragedies, slept calmly and in peace while her legislators discussed and decided the policy of the Empire. The long rows of light on the deserted terrace and along the opposite shore in front of St. Thomas's Hospital threw their shimmering reflection upon the black waters of the Thames; the cold wind swept roughly up the river, causing the gas-jets to flicker, so that the few shivering outcasts who had taken refuge on the steps of the closed doorway of Westminster Station murmured as they pulled their rags more tightly round them. Only the low rumbling of a country waggon bearing vegetables to Covent Garden, or the sharp clip-clap of a cab-horse's feet upon the asphalt, broke the quiet. Except for these occasional disturbances all else was as silent on that dark and cloudy night in late October as if the world were dead. Over in the far corner of New Palace Yard horses were champing their bits, and coachmen and police were waiting patiently, knowing that with the Twelve o'clock Rule suspended the length of the sitting was quite uncertain. Wearied journalists from the Press Gallery, having finished their "turns," came out singly or in pairs from their own little side door in the opposite corner of the yard, wished a cheery "good-night" to the portly sergeant and the two idling detectives who acted as janitors, and then hurried on through the chill night over the bridge towards their homes in Brixton or Clapham. An autumn session is a weary one, and weighs quite as heavily upon the Parliamentary journalist as upon the Leader of the House himself. As the shadows lengthened and the hour grew late, the streets of Westminster lay shrouded in silence, save for the soft flutter of a newspaper in the breeze and the occasional whisper of treetops swaying in the wind. The Thames, that age-old witness to the countless dramas of human ambition and folly, rolled gently beneath the arching bridges, reflecting the flickering lights as if they were stars brought down to earth. Each ripple seemed to bear a story, a fragment of dreams long-forgotten, or perhaps yet to unfold, while the lamplights flickered in a slow dance, casting shadows that elongated and writhed like the thoughts of those who wandered the depths of their own minds this early morning. In the distance, the faint chime of a clock reverberated through the air, marking the passage of time in a city that thrived on it. As the last of the evening's revelers departed from a nearby tavern, the distant sound of laughter and clinking glasses faded, leaving behind only remembrance of fleeting joy. The moon, a pallid specter, peeked through the veils of clouds, casting a silver glow over the damp cobblestones where echoes of footfalls once resounded, now lost to the whisper of the night. At this hour, when dreams winged their way across the sleeping city, few remained active within the labyrinth of Parliament's hallowed halls. On the fringes of that dormant political landscape, a figure emerged from the shadows, an inconspicuous silhouette against the grand backdrop. He moved with purpose, slipping into the sanctuary of a narrow alley, his intentions cloaked in secrecy, as if the very night conspired to safeguard his clandestine mission. The air grew heavier, thick with expectancy, as a distant murmur of voices reached his ears. Curiosity gnawed at him, urging him toward the source of the sound, a nudge that propelled him deeper into the heart of London's silence, where decision-makers formed and feasted on ideas, where futures could pivot with the mere stroke of a pen. Unbeknownst to him, the weight of history's gaze lingered heavily upon that shadowy alley, where dreams collided with the relentless march of reality, and choices made or lost shaped the world beyond the whispers of midnight.

As I walked out of BHS's Central London headquarters, I couldn't help but wonder if Sir Philip Green's aggressive new strategy was a deliberate attempt to blindside Marks & Spencer. The air was thick with the scent of freshly baked bread and the hum of conversation, as the once-maligned retailer seemed to be undergoing a radical transformation. Gone were the flammable tat and elasticated waists of yesteryear, replaced by a sleek, modern aesthetic that seemed to be targeting the very same demographic that M&S has long dominated. But as I delved deeper into the store, I began to notice subtle differences that set BHS apart from its High Street rival. The homeware, for instance, was decidedly more... British. The Union Jack-patterned throw pillows and tea towels seemed to scream "Middle England" in a way that M&S's more generic offerings did not. And the prices? Well, let's just say that 10 candle in a glass jar was a steal. As I made my way to the food hall, I spotted a familiar face - none other than Richard Price, the former managing director of M&S, now poached by BHS to lead the charge. He was busy chatting with a group of staff, his eyes shining with excitement as he gestured to a display of artisanal cheeses. "This is the future of food retail," he declared, as if trying to convince himself as much as anyone else. "People want quality, they want value, and they want it now." But as I watched the shoppers milling about, I couldn't help but feel a sense of unease. Was this really the future of retail, or was it just a desperate attempt to cling to the past? The prices, while reasonable, were hardly revolutionary, and the offerings - while nice - were hardly game-changing. And what of the customers, those Middle England mums who were supposed to be the target audience? Were they really going to flock to BHS in droves, abandoning their M&S loyalty for the sake of a slightly cheaper price tag? As I left the store, I couldn't help but wonder what the future held for both BHS and M&S. Would Sir Philip Green's bold new strategy pay off, or would it prove to be a costly mistake? Only time would tell, but one thing was certain - the battle for the hearts and wallets of Middle England was about to get very, very interesting.

Scarred and rent by the grinding of its prison-ice and weather-beaten by the rasping of wind-driven snow in a land where the snow never melts, still on the square stern of the vessel could be read the dimming letters which spelled "Yedda." Polaris unharnessed the pack, and man and dogs crept on board the hulk. It was but a timber shell. Much of the decking had been cut away, and everything movable had been taken from it for the building of the cabin and the shed, now in black ruins fifty miles to the south. In an angle of the ice-wall, a few yards from the ship, Polaris pitched his camp and built a fire with timbers from the wreck. He struck his flame with a rudely fashioned tinder-box, catching the spark in fine scrapings of wood and nursing it with his breath. He fed the dogs and toasted meat for his own meal at the fire. With a large robe from the sledge he bedded the team snugly beside the fire. With his own parka of furs he clambered aboard the ship, found a bunk in the forecastle, and curled up for the night. Several hours later hideous clamor broke his dreamless slumber. He started from the bunk and leaped from the ship's side into the ice-lane. Every dog of the pack was bristling and snarling with rage. Mixed with their uproar was a deeper, hoarser note of anger that came from the throat of no dog - a note which the man knew well. The team was bunched a few feet ahead of the fire as Polaris came over the rail of the ship. Almost shoulder to shoulder the seven crouched, every head pointed up the path. They were quivering from head to tail with anger, and seemed to be about to charge. Whipping the dogs back, the son of the snows ran forward to meet the danger alone. He could afford to lose no dogs. He had forgotten the guns, but he bore weapons with which he was better acquainted. With a long-hafted spear in his hand and the knife loosened in his belt he bounded up the pathway and stood, wary but unafraid, fronting an immense white bear. He was not a moment too soon. The huge animal had set himself for the charge, and in another instant would have hurled its enormous weight down on the dogs. The beast hesitated, confronted by this new enemy, and sat back on its haunches to consider. Knowing his foe aforetime, Polaris took that opportunity to deliver his own charge. He bounded forward and drove his tough spear with all his strength into the white chest below the throat. Balanced as it was on its haunches, the shock of the man's onset upset the bear, and it rolled backward, a jet of blood spurting over its shaggy coat and dyeing the snow. Like a flash the man followed his advantage.

This is surprising given the large body of cognitive research that has elucidated the role of depressive thinking in the maintenance of symptoms, both in terms of its content and process characteristics. On a content level, cognitive research has highlighted the role of enduring dysfunctional beliefs (Kovacs and Beck, 1978) and early maladaptive schemata (Young, 1995), with the latter assumed to represent a broader set of themes that have their origin in childhood. On a process level, research has demonstrated how maladaptive responses to negative mood such as rumination (Nolen-Hoeksema, 1991), suppression (Wenzlaff and Luxton, 2003), and experiential avoidance (Hayes et al., 1996) play an important role in maintaining negative mood with research on rumination also demonstrating effects on length of depressive episodes (Nolen-Hoeksema, 2000). Rumination undermines active attempts at problem-solving, reinforces negative biases and dysfunctional attitudes, and, in line with the idea that the above processes can be considered facets of a more encompassing maladaptive mode of processing (Williams, 2008), has been suggested to serve an avoidant function (Nolen-Hoeksema et al., 2008). Furthermore, research shows that depressed patients tend to frame their experience and thoughts in abstract and general terms. Autobiographical memory overgenerality has been found to be related to history of childhood adversity and abuse, rumination, deficits in interpersonal problem solving, and has been demonstrated to be a significant predictor of time to recovery in those who are currently depressed (for an overview see Williams et al., 2007). While these cognitive factors are clearly implicated in maintenance of negative mood, there are currently few studies that have investigated the extent to which these are distinguishing characteristics of patients with more or less persistent courses of depression. Riso et al. (2003) compared patients with chronic depression to patients with non-chronic Major Depression and found that, after controlling for current levels of depression, patients with chronic depression showed higher levels of maladaptive core beliefs relating to the themes of disconnection and rejection, impaired autonomy and overvigilance. However, there were no significant differences in ruminative tendencies, attributional style or dysfunctional attitudes, suggesting that chronically depressed patients may differ from others predominantly with regard to factors with a stronger developmental origin. In contrast, a more recent and larger study comparing patients with chronic and non-chronic depression categorized based on the course of the disorder during the last five years (Wiersma et al., 2011) found that chronically depressed patients reported significantly stronger tendencies to respond with ruminative thinking during times when they are feeling low. Additionally, chronically depressed patients showed lower levels of extraversion and higher external locus of control. One of the reasons for these inconsistencies might have been that these studies investigated patients who were currently suffering from high levels of symptoms.

Arizona GOP Sen. John McCain repeatedly challenged Hagel in the tense confirmation hearing over whether he still believed his 2007 statement that the Iraq war surge was the "most dangerous foreign policy blunder" since the Vietnam War.

The ApoE mu 4 allele has been consistently shown to accelerate the progression from MCI to AD, with studies suggesting that ApoE mu 4 carriers exhibit more rapid cognitive decline and hippocampal atrophy compared to non-carriers (Cruchaga et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2010). Furthermore, the presence of the ApoE mu 4 allele has been linked to increased amyloid- deposition, neuroinflammation, and synaptic dysfunction in individuals with MCI (Khan et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2013). The exact mechanisms by which ApoE mu 4 exerts its detrimental effects on cognitive function and AD risk remain unclear, although several theories have been proposed. One possibility is that ApoE mu 4 disrupts the normal functioning of the blood-brain barrier, leading to increased permeability and the influx of toxic substances into the brain (Bell et al., 2012). Another theory suggests that ApoE mu 4 alters the clearance of amyloid-, a hallmark protein of AD, leading to its accumulation and aggregation in the brain (Castellano et al., 2011). Additionally, ApoE mu 4 has been shown to modulate the immune response, with evidence suggesting that it may promote a pro-inflammatory environment that exacerbates AD pathology (Liu et al., 2013). The identification of ApoE mu 4 as a major genetic risk factor for AD has significant implications for the development of therapeutic strategies. Several ApoE-targeting therapies are currently being explored, including small molecule inhibitors of ApoE mu 4 and gene therapy approaches aimed at reducing ApoE mu 4 expression (Cramer et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). Furthermore, the use of ApoE mu 4 as a biomarker for AD risk has the potential to revolutionize the field of AD diagnosis and prevention. For example, genetic testing for ApoE mu 4 could identify individuals at high risk of developing AD, allowing for early intervention and potentially delaying or preventing disease onset (Reiman et al., 2010). In addition to its role in AD, the ApoE mu 4 allele has been implicated in other neurological disorders, including Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and multiple sclerosis (Elias-Sonnenschein et al., 2011; Feussner et al., 1998; Friedman et al., 1999). The mechanisms underlying ApoE mu 4's involvement in these disorders are likely to be complex and multifaceted, and further research is needed to fully elucidate its role. In conclusion, the ApoE mu 4 allele is a major genetic risk factor for AD, and its presence is associated with increased risk of cognitive decline and AD development. The precise mechanisms underlying ApoE mu 4-mediated AD risk remain unclear, although several theories have been proposed. Further research is needed to fully understand the role of ApoE mu 4 in AD and to develop effective therapeutic strategies for the prevention and treatment of this devastating disease.

The raiders had only 467 feet of runway to take off from - barely half the amount required for a normal B-25 takeoff - and had never practiced such short-distance flying before. They had to do so carrying enough fuel and bombs to fly 600 miles to Japan, drop their loads then fly another 600 miles to safety in China. The men knew that if the mission failed, they would be captured, tortured and executed as war criminals. Doolittle told them, 'If we fail, there will not be any hope of a pardon or early release because our country will be defeated.' But they succeeded. All but one of the planes made it to Japan where they dropped their bombloads, causing little physical damage but boosting U.S. morale tremendously. After dropping their bombs, the crews continued westward, knowing that they did not have enough fuel to reach their designated landing fields in China. By the time the raiders reached China, night was approaching and the weather had deteriorated. Most crewmen bailed out over eastern China and landed in Japanese-controlled territory. In all, three crewmen died as a result of being shot down, another three were killed while bailing out of their plane, and eight became prisoners of war. Of the eight POWs, three were executed and another died of disease. The remaining five were held captive until August 1945. Despite having lost all aircraft, 69 airmen survived the mission. A number of them went on to be decorated veterans, including Doolittle himself. The raid was credited with forcing Japan to recall top-line fighters back home for defense against further raids, leaving its fleet exposed to defeat at Midway Island just two months later. Although the mission was costly to the United States in terms of personnnel and equipment, and produced negligible material damage to Japan, American morale surged.

Tentatively, yes: there may well be speakers who avoid stigmatized h-dropping even in their most casual style (as RP speakers do; NB we are not dealing here with /h/ in unstressed pronouns.). Is there a formal style of Cockney that is distinct from EE? Tentatively, yes: Cockney is arguably the speech of the uneducated, who are unable to achieve standard grammar even where it might be called for; while EE speakers are those who can consistently use standard grammar with ease and fluency. The boundary between EE and RP is also hard to establish. Presumably it rests on the degree of localizability: EE is localizable as belonging to the southeast of England (see Coggle's impressionistic sketch-map, 1993:28), whereas RP is not. (Many of Rosewarne's comments surely relate to style or to change over time, rather than to the decline of RP, to localizability or to the Thames estuary area. Things like cheers for thank you/goodbye are surely part of contemporary casual RP/StdEng - at least I use them, and no-one has ever suggested that I am a speaker of EE! Some commentators seem not to appreciate that RP can be spoken in informal situations.) Principles of transcribing EE We need a standardized phonetic transcription for the EE accent. Although Rosewarne and Coggle have arguably done a public service by drawing attention to it, neither they nor anyone else (as far as I am aware) has attempted a serious phonetic description of it; nor indeed have they ever transcribed more than the odd sound in isolation. Once we have standardized and codified EE, we could teach it to students, ask them to do transcription exercises using it, and give phonetic dictation in it. Quite apart from its importance for EE's own native speakers and their imitators, it would furthermore attract great interest and attention among EFL teachers disenchanted with RP. Some might wish to teach it to their EFL pupils. ('Because it obscures sociolinguistic origins, "Estuary English" is attractive to many' - Rosewarne 1984.) The present document aims to highlight some of the decisions we would need to make in arriving at a standardized transcription. One basic question we must face is: how comparative should the EE transcription system be? Should we use phonetically explicit symbols, often different from those we use for RP (with the resultant risk of confusing the beginner)? Or is it more sensible to use the same symbols as for RP wherever possible, but with different conventions of interpretation? E.g., Should we write EE face as fVIs or as feIs? Should we write EE price as prAIs or as praIs? Should we write EE loaf as lVUf or as l@Uf? Should we write EE goose as g}:s or as gu:s? My view is that for the time being, at any rate, we should take a minimalist position. We should aim to make the notation as similar as possible to that used for RP.

Given a conformation, the algorithm's purpose is to produce a reduced, smoothed and 'topologically equivalent' representation in which the knotted core, i.e., the minimal chain segment that contains the knot, is sufficiently far from both chain ends for the knot type to be well defined. In Taylor's method the chain ends are kept fixed (and unconnected) throughout the whole procedure. Taylor discovered a deep figure-eight (or 41) knot (i.e. a knot for which there is no planar projection with less than four crossings) in protein acetohydroxy acid isomeroreductase (PDB ID: 1yvel) [7], which can only be removed if 70 residues are deleted from the carboxy-terminus or 245 residues are deleted from the amino-terminus. Because this knot is deep, Taylor's discovery represents a rather important contribution that actually boosted research in the field of knotted proteins. Taylor's algorithm is applied to a linear conformation and it was noticed that the final outcome may depend on the order of smoothing operations (i.e. if it starts at the N-terminus or at the C-terminus) [8]. Therefore, the initial conformation needs to be closed prior to the smoothing procedure through a closure method (reviewed in [9]). The combination of smoothing algorithms with closure methods and knot invariants provides a straightforward way to systematically scrutinize the universe of protein conformations deposited in the PDB in searching for different knots (Fig. 2). An interesting variation amongst knotted conformations is that of the slipknot, originally identified by Yeates and co-workers [10]. A slipknot is a structure that when examined in its complete form is unknotted, but becomes knotted by deletion of suitable terminal segments because-just like in a shoelace-it is the arrangement of the terminal segment that unties the knot as the chain folds back upon itself close to one of its ends (Fig. 3a). The most recent survey of the PDB found 1150 tangled proteins (including slipknots) amongst 144,554 analyzed protein entries [11]. Tangled topologies, and knotted proteins in particular, thus represent a small fraction of the folding space represented by the PDB. There are many proteins with the 31 knot in their native structure, some with the 41 knot and only a few with the 52 knot [12-14]. So far, the most complex knot type found in the PDB is the Stevedore's (or 61) knot, which was detected in protein -haloacid dehalogenase (PDB ID: 3bjx) [15]. Information on knotted proteins can be retrieved from databases that have been created along the years [13,16]. KnotProt is likely the most up-to-date collection of tangled structures that cover knotted proteins as well as slipknots [11]. Since Taylor firstly provided compelling evidence for the existence of deeply knotted proteins, a body of experimental and theoretical work has been developed that seeks to address two fundamental questions, 1) how do knotted proteins fold? and 2) what is the functional role of knots in proteins?

Papa Bouchard - as the artillery captain had the impudence to call him - did, it is true, keep a tight hand on Leontine's fortune, and would allow her only half her income, at which Leontine grumbled and incited Captain de Meneval to grumble, too. But Papa Bouchard, having full power as trustee, met their complaints and protests with a proposition to cut down their allowance to one-fourth of their income, at which the two young people grew frightened, and desisted. Now, there dwells in every masculine breast a germ of lawlessness that no discipline ever invented can wholly kill. Man or parrot, it is the same. After having been brought up in the way he should go, he longs to go it. Such was the case with Pierrot, with Pierre and with Monsieur Bouchard. It was the bird that first made a dash for liberty. After ten years of irreproachable conduct, Pierrot, on that June morning, suddenly jumped from the balcony, where he had been walking the railing in the most sedate manner, and scuttled off in the direction of the Alcazar d'Ete, the Ambassadeurs, the Moulin Rouge, and the very gayest quarter of Paris. Monsieur Bouchard was sitting on the balcony at the time. He was rather younger looking, with his clean-shaven face and wiry figure, than most men of his age, but thanks to Mademoiselle Celeste, he patronized the same tailors that had made for his father and his grandfather. Their cut and style indicated that they had been tailors to Cardinal Richelieu and others of that time, and they dressed Monsieur Bouchard in coats and trousers and waistcoats of the pliocene age of tailoring. As for his hats, they might have been dug out of Pompeii, for any modernity they had, and the result was that Monsieur Bouchard's back and legs looked about seventy-five, while his face looked little more than forty. Instead of giving the alarm when Pierrot trotted gaily off, Monsieur Bouchard felt a strange thrill of sympathy with the runaway. "Poor devil!" thought he. "No doubt he is sick of the Rue Clarisse - tired of the moral maxims - weary of the whole business. He isn't so young as he was, but there's a good deal of life in him still" - Pierrot was just scampering around the corner - "and he wants to see life." "There is a psychologic moment for everything," so Otto von Bismarck said. The parrot's escape made a psychologic moment for Monsieur Bouchard, and quietly putting on his hat, and telling Mademoiselle Bouchard that he was going to a meeting of the Society of French Antiquarians at St. Germains, and afterward for a stroll through the museum in the town, made straight for a street in the neighborhood of the Champs Elysees. He remembered seeing in that quarter a handsome new apartment house lately finished and thoroughly modern. He had for curiosity's sake entered it.

Parnell, his eyes narrowing in mock suspicion, leaned against the doorframe, the remnants of his drink casting a warm glow on his face. Parnell retorted, striding further into the room, where disarray ruled-papers scattered on the desk like fallen leaves, books stacked precariously high, and a coffee cup long forgotten, now teetering on the brink of collapse. As Parnell settled into the worn chair opposite Paul's desk, the conversations of the bar faded behind them, cloistered by the familiar walls that felt like the confines of memory itself. The old leather creaked under his weight. "What's the scoop, counselor? Paul let out a small, reluctant chuckle before leaning forward, the weight of the world pressing down on his brow. "I've been digging into the case, Parnell, you know the one. Parnell interjected with a hint of alarm. "That poor woman tangled up with a man who couldn't outwit a bargain sale. Talks of the town, it is. "Exactly," Paul continued, sensing Parnell's unease. "I need to get ahead of this. Navigate the murky waters before we drown in them. "You're talking about a web of mischief that's not easily unraveled, my friend," Parnell said, a sagacious nod punctuating his words. "They say knowledge is power, but when it's wielded carelessly, it can become a weapon against you." He leaned back, eyes glimmering with the thrill of the chase. "And who knows what lurks in the shadows, waiting for that opportunity?" "Maybe even in plain sight, disguised as a friend," Paul replied thoughtfully, an edge creeping into his voice. The tension in the room mounted, thick enough to cut with a knife. They both understood the sacrifices that lay ahead, the truths they would have to confront, and the price of loyalty amidst such turmoil. As silence settled in, and the hum of the outside world rushed on as indifferently as time itself, they found themselves caught in the storm of each other's contemplation-each man straddling the precipice of peril and possibility. And in that moment, standing at the edge of the known, they were reminded that tomorrow often bore the weight of choices made today.

But given that both types are caused by a collapse into an underground cavity and the end result - a large, potentially dangerous hole in the ground at the surface - is the same, for the sake of simplicity, let us call them all sinkholes. Certainly, anyone suffering the tragedy of having their house fall into one won't be worrying about the difference. Fatalities caused by sinkholes in this country are thankfully very rare, but a homeowner in Florida did die in exactly those circumstances only last year. Risk: Gretel Davidson feared she would have to pay around 10,000 after a sinkhole twice the height of a double-decker bus appeared in her garden in Banehurst, South-East London. The sheer size of sinkholes and their sudden appearance without warning does make them extremely hazardous. This explains why in the superstitious distant past, their appearance was often linked to misfortune. Some saw them as a direct route to Hell itself; one near Darlington that collapsed in the 12th century is called Hell Kettle and the rising groundwater in it steams in the winter. Of course, it's not the Devil but all the heavy rain that lies behind the sudden spate of sinkholes. Rainwater dissolves limestone easily because it gets acidified from carbon dioxide in the air and by passing through rotting vegetation or certain types of rock. The water dissolves rocks such as chalk, limestone and gypsum, making existing natural underground cavities bigger. It also scours fine material out of existing cavities. In addition, it makes the surface layers of soil composed of such things as clay or gravel heavier as they become waterlogged. Bit by bit, the cavity becomes a little bigger, the covering layers a little heavier until.. snap.. those covering layers no longer have the mechanical strength to span the cavity and suddenly they collapse into it, taking anything unfortunate to have been standing on the surface down with them. Concern: A 35ft wide hole appeared underneath a home in Hemel Hempstead last week, prompting the surrounding properties to be evacuated. It's no accident that sinkholes often seem to appear next to a fairly substantial piece of civil engineering, such as a house or road, rather than underneath the piece of civil engineering itself. As long as we put roofs on houses and impermeable cambers on our roads, rainwater will be thrown off the things being protected. It's often where that rainwater ends up - by the side of the road, by side of the house - that becomes vulnerable to sinkholes. Nor is it a coincidence that so many of the new sinkholes have appeared in the South-East. Not only has this part of the country endured one of its wettest winters for decades, possibly centuries, but it is also home to one of the four types of underlying soluble rock - in this case chalk - that make an area vulnerable to sinkholes.

Its sliding-scale subsidies provide at least some families on the exchanges with a strong disincentive against earning more income. And by raising the bar for what counts as acceptable private insurance, there's a real risk that it will lead to a net decrease in the number of people who have private insurance. When I envision an ideal health system, I don't doubt that it would involve insurance marketplaces where consumers can compare different policies to make informed decisions. That is what the insurance exchanges are at their best. The big problem with the Obamacare exchanges is that they don't give insurers the option of offering consumers a wide range of products suited to their needs, and they don't offer enough flexibility on pricing. Obamacare's defenders often claim that conservatives are hypocritical to oppose the law because it relies on the kind of insurance marketplaces that conservatives favor. What these critics miss is that the problem isn't having insurance marketplaces per se. Rather, Obamacare is narrowly constraining the kind of products available on the marketplaces, and in doing it is pricing a fair number of cost-conscious consumers out of the market, even after factoring in subsidies. I should also note that I don't think Republicans have great solutions for America's health care woes either. During the 2008 presidential campaign, Sen. John McCain introduced a controversial plan for coverage expansion that I greatly admired and which the Democrats fiercely attacked. Ever since then, Republicans have been extremely gun-shy about offering ambitious health reform proposals of their own. I was sympathetic to the Massachusetts coverage expansion law that passed in 2006 under then-Gov. Mitt Romney, which struck me as a reasonable solution for an affluent state with a small uninsured population. (The Massachusetts experiment hasn't turned out as well as I had hoped, but that's a story for another day.) And I've advocated a number of reforms designed to expand coverage, such as more federal funding for high-risk pools, federal and state reinsurance programs designed to make insurance more affordable and tax reforms designed to limit the health insurance tax subsidies that flow to high-income households while increasing those that flow to low- and middle-income households. None of these reforms is cheap, which is why they are opposed by the many of the same Republican lawmakers who oppose Obamacare. Eventually, the GOP is going to have to recognize that any durable health care fix is going to cost money - less than Obamacare, perhaps, but not nothing. For now, however, millions of Americans like me who don't believe that Obamacare is the right way forward for the country will have to learn to live with it.
