The twentieth century phenomena of concentrated corporate power is the result, not of industrialization itself, but of laws developed by liberal democrats equating the rights of man with the rights of corporate bodies, and the possession of property with the possession of monopolies (17) that created an environment conducive to economic concentration (14). Rather, because industrial societies are characterized by rapid innovation and change, they are incompatible with the inherently slow changing nature of authoritarian regulation (11). Rulers can only know current levels of production technology and thus can only regulate with current technology considered thereby obstructing innovation (10). Collectivists felt that the state was either necessary as protection for the people against the oppression by machines and their subsequent concentration of economic power or that only the state could fully realize the machines' potential (7). There is an inherent paradox in this return to authoritarian collectivism because it was the rolling back of this collectivism by the eighteenth century liberals that paved the way for the rise of industrialization and technological advancement. The apparatus of a politically administered economy-price and wage control, forced labor, directed production, and controlled opinion-were rejected to allow for the Industrial Revolution's onset. Since authoritarian controls existed prior to the industrial revolution and since only in their absence or reduction did industrialization occur, the assumption that only authoritarian power could manage industrial society is hardly self-evident (8-9). The hopes of collectivists are founded on the myth that omnipotence is combined with omniscience-that the power of the state could join with the knowledge of science in the Providential state (22). When we realize that governments consist only of fallible mortals, we must also realize that there are limits to the amount of planning and administration of the social order that can be achieved (24). Effective and predictable control over a social system requires vast amounts of knowledge and an intimate understanding of the minute logic guiding society's infinite interactive elements. Such knowledge and understanding is beyond man's reach (33). If a society is to be directed and planned by authorities, the members of the society must conform to the plan and dissenters must be eliminated either by violence or conversion (56). This demands an absolute state and it is thus incompatible with democracy (51). Since violence and terrorism cannot generally be maintained indefinitely, other means must be found to rid the society of dissension (57). Fascist states seek to eliminate this dissent by controlling all forms of communication and education-the media, churches, and schools-and by outlawing dissent in order to mold the minds of the masses to an acceptance of the authoritarian plan (59). The paradox of fascism is that intelligent, adventurous, and ambitious leaders must be culled from the docile masses (60). Any opportunities created to determine who will be leaders will inevitably produce dissenters also (62).

In many ant species, foragers have higher brain dopamine titer than workers of other task group (Kamhi et al., 2017; Seid and Traniello, 2005; Smith et al., 2013), although in some species this pattern appears to be reversed (Penick et al., 2014). Laboratory pharmacological studies in carpenter ants confirm a role for dopaminergic signaling in the regulation of individual foraging activity (Entler et al., 2016). In ants, dopamine is also involved in trophallaxis (Wada-Katsumata et al., 2011) and reproduction (Okada et al., 2015; Penick et al., 2014). Recent pharmacological experiments in the field have been used to examine ant behavior (Male et al., 2017), but not the biogenic amine neurophysiology of foraging. Colonies of the red harvester ant, Pogonomyrmex barbatus, forage in the desert for seeds that provide both food and water. Foragers lose water while out in the desert sun, and the rate of water loss is higher in dry conditions (Lighton and Bartholomew, 1988; Lighton and Feener, 1989). To manage the tradeoff between food accumulation and water loss, colonies adjust foraging activity to changes in ambient conditions, especially humidity (Gordon, 2013; Gordon et al., 2013; Prabhakar et al., 2012). Colony foraging activity is regulated in a distributed fashion by brief olfactory interactions when one ant assesses the cuticular hydrocarbons of the other (Greene et al., 2013; Greene and Gordon, 2003): an outgoing forager is stimulated to leave the nest by its rate of interaction with incoming foragers with food (Davidson et al., 2016; Greene et al., 2013; Pinter-Wollman et al., 2013; Pless et al., 2015). Since a forager continues to search until it finds a seed, the rate of forager return is related to food availability (Gordon, 1991). Colonies of P. barbatus significantly vary in how strongly they reduce foraging activity in dry conditions (Gordon, 1991, 2013; Gordon et al., 2011, 2013), meaning that colonies differ in their sensitivity to humidity. These behavioral differences among colonies of P. barbatus persist year after year despite total worker turnover (Gordon, 1991, 2013; Gordon et al., 2011; Gordon and Holldobler, 1987), and daughter colonies resemble their mothers in the thresholds for dry conditions that lead them to reduce foraging (Gordon, 2013). This variation among colonies of P. barbatus in foraging behavior is ecologically important and associated with differences in colony lifetime reproductive success (Gordon, 2013; Ingram et al., 2013). Colony differences in collective behavior could be due to stable colony differences in how foragers adjust their sensitivity to interactions in dry conditions (Davidson et al., 2016; Pagliara et al., 2018). Here we examine the neurophysiological basis of variation among red harvester ant colonies in how they regulate their collective foraging behavior. Because differences among P. barbatus colonies in sensitivity to humidity persist year after year, it appears that successive cohorts of nestmate foragers inherit genetic or epigenetic factors, which bias their foraging activity in dry conditions. Molecular variation among foragers from different colonies may lead to differences in individual forager decisions about whether to forage in dry conditions.

INT. SCHOOL HALLWAY - MORNING The hallway is buzzing with energy, children rushing to their classes, backpacks swinging haphazardly. Benjamin walks swiftly, trying to navigate through the throng while stealing glances at his watch. He spots a bulletin board plastered with colorful flyers. Lost pets, club sign-ups, bake sales-all the chaos of a school day. He can't help but feel like he's wandering through a maze of reminders, reminders of a life that isn't his anymore. As he approaches Dylan's classroom, he hears a voice calling out to him from behind. It's APRIL, a classmate from the PTA. "Hey there, Benjamin! How are you adjusting?" she asks, her tone too cheerful for the morning. "Oh, you know, just trying to keep my head above water," he responds, forcing a smile. April digs her manicured nails into her designer tote. "That's tough! If you ever need help with the kids or anything, don't hesitate." He nods appreciatively but already feels the pressure of her gaze lingering too long on him-like she's searching for signs of weakness. "Thanks, really, I appreciate that," he mumbles as he brushes past her into the classroom, exhaling deeply. INT. DYLAN'S CLASSROOM - MOMENTS LATER Inside, the room is abuzz with laughter and chatter. Dylan is at his desk, scribbling away, while his classmates bustle about, trading snack packs and shooting paper airplanes. "Dad!" Dylan exclaims upon seeing him. "Did you bring my lunch?" Benjamin raises the Subway bag triumphantly. "Whole wheat turkey wrap, just like you like it. And I didn't forget the extra chips this time." Dylan grins, the chaos around them fading into the background. "Awesome! See, Dad? You can do this!" He watches his son, momentarily lost in the innocence and sincerity of his gaze. Then, like a sudden splash of cold water, the impending responsibilities flood back in. "I just need to get you some milk after school, alright?" Benjamin says, his tone shifting to that of an adult, a parent. "Almond milk?" Dylan replies, brow furrowing. "I told you! I can't have real milk!" Benjamin sighs, caught in the whirlwind. "I'll make sure," he promises quickly, but his mind is already running ahead-swimming through preparations for dinner, homework checks, and fragile discussions about feelings that are still raw. But then, he catches sight of a photo taped to the board: a field trip group shot. A flash of memories-Katherine beside him, laughing, bright-eyed, the perfect moment. Suddenly, the walls feel closer, tighter. He finds himself standing there, mouth a little dry, tears prickling at the corners of his eyes. A gentle pat on his back breaks him out of the reverie. It's another parent, LUCY, a reliable presence, always well-prepared for every school event. "Don't worry too much, Benjamin. You're doing great," she encourages softly, and it's unnerving how real it feels. "Thanks, Lucy," he says, swallowing hard. "I'm just... figuring things out." "You will," she reassures him, her smile warm and knowing. Just then, the bell rings, and the classroom explodes with energy as kids grab their bags and shuffle toward the door. "See you after school, Dad!" Dylan yells over the noise, his face alight with the simplicity of being a child, carefree for now. Benjamin smiles back, the pressure momentarily lifting, if only just a bit. "Yeah, kiddo. See you." He takes a deep breath, glancing at the photo again. There's no escaping the past, but perhaps, just perhaps, there's a flicker of hope flickering dimly ahead.

The image, a stunning snapshot of the universe's ancient past, reveals a dozen or so galaxies that existed a mere 400 million years after the Big Bang. It's a cosmic family album, with each galaxy a tiny, fuzzy smudge on the canvas of space. But what's remarkable about these galaxies is that they're not just any galaxies - they're massive, with stars and gas swirling around a central, unseen anchor. That anchor, Windhorst and Yan propose, is a supermassive black hole. The finding is significant because it suggests that these ancient galaxies didn't form without a catalyst. Instead, the black holes may have played a crucial role in their creation, providing the gravitational scaffolding for stars and gas to coalesce. It's a chicken-and-egg problem, with astronomers debating whether galaxies gave birth to black holes or vice versa. But Windhorst and Yan's discovery tips the scales in favor of the latter. "This is the first direct evidence that galaxies formed around the earliest black holes," Windhorst says, his voice still buzzing with excitement. "It's a game-changer. We're no longer talking about black holes as endpoints of evolution, but as the engines that drive galaxy formation." The implications are profound. If black holes are indeed the spark that ignites galaxy formation, it means that these enigmatic objects are not just passive observers in the cosmic dance, but active participants. They're the conductors, orchestrating the movement of stars and gas to create the majestic spiral arms and elliptical shapes we see in the universe today. It's a far cry from the traditional view of black holes as destructive forces, vacuuming up matter and energy with reckless abandon. Instead, they're more like cosmic architects, shaping the very fabric of space and time. And it's not just a one-way street - the galaxies, in turn, influence the growth and evolution of their resident black holes. "This is a deeply symbiotic relationship," says Urry, who has spent years studying the connection between black holes and galaxies. "The black hole grows as the galaxy grows, and the galaxy grows because of the black hole. It's a beautiful, intricate dance that we're only just beginning to understand." As astronomers continue to probe the depths of the universe, they're uncovering more evidence of this cosmic waltz. From the majestic elliptical galaxies of the present day to the faint, distant smudges of the early universe, the fingerprints of black holes are everywhere. And at the heart of it all is the concept of co-evolution, a radical idea that's rewriting the history of the cosmos.

To them it was a pastime, a spectacle; to the Roundhead, a ceremony. The Cavaliers were mostly young men, and many of them wore mustaches curled up after the fashion of Charles I., and long love-locks. Their gay attire and bright colors contrasted strangely with the sombre costumes of the Puritans. As the hour approached for the beginning of the proceedings, the crowd grew denser, and there was much pushing and jostling among those who strove to obtain the best places of observation. Suddenly a silence fell over the multitude, and every eye was directed toward a little procession wending its way through the throng. First came two stalwart soldiers armed with muskets; then followed three magistrates, each bearing a staff of office; behind these walked the sheriff of James City County, leading a woman by the arm. She was dressed in a plain gray gown, without any ornament or trimming, and her hair hung loosely about her shoulders. Her eyes were fixed on the ground, and she seemed utterly unconscious of the gaze of the multitude. Behind this group came several constables, and last of all the minister of the parish church, a venerable man, whose flowing beard reached to his waist. He carried a Bible in his hand. When the procession reached the ducking-stool, the woman was unceremoniously lifted into the seat, and strapped firmly in place, whereupon the sheriff retired. Then the oldest magistrate advanced and read from a paper the following: "Whereas, Goody Dutton hath been accused and tried before the worshipful magistrates of James City County, Virginia Colony, for the crime of witchcraft, and hath been duly convicted thereof, and whereas the said Goody Dutton hath confessed under oath that she did most wickedly and feloniously bewitch the body of Elizabeth Carrington, daughter of the worshipful John Carrington, Esquire, whereby the said Elizabeth Carrington did suffer grievous pain of body and mind, and thereby became bedridden and unable to perform her duties, and whereas the said Goody Dutton hath further confessed that she did bewitch the bodies of certain swine belonging to the said John Carrington, Esquire, and did cause the same to die of a loathsome disease; now therefore, this being the first offence of the said Goody Dutton, it is ordered by the court that she shall be punished by the infliction of thirteen stripes, and that she shall be placed in the ducking-stool and held under the water of the pond for the space of five minutes. "It is further ordered that if the said Goody Dutton shall again commit the like offence, or other felony, she shall be put to death according to law. "God save the Commonwealth." After reading this judgment, the old magistrate handed the paper to the minister, who began to read a prayer in a loud voice. The crowd remained silent during the reading, and when he concluded, the officer who had charge of the ducking-stool pulled the rope, and the poor creature was swung out over the water. At the same instant a half-naked negro sprang forward, and with uplifted whip applied the lash to the exposed back of the prisoner. Thirteen times the cruel thongs cut the air, and each time they left a red mark across the shoulders of the victim. The cries of agony that escaped her lips only served to increase the fiendish delight of the executioner. When the task was finished, he stepped aside, and the officer let the prisoner down into the water, holding her beneath the surface until the allotted time expired.

In vitro studies on flat surface-supported membranes have shown that ESCRT-III forms spirals that are proposed to behave like springs, storing elastic energy, which deform the membrane upon release (Chiaruttini et al., 2015). The observation of this spiral structure informs the mechanical rationale for membrane deformation and scission in many of the proposed mechanisms where either a spiral (Chiaruttini and Roux, 2017), cone (Agudo-Canalejo and Lipowsky, 2018), or dome (Fabrikant et al., 2009; Rozycki et al., 2012) structure made by ESCRT-III stabilizes and subsequently drives scission of the ILV bud neck. This process is made possible by the action of the ATPase Vps4, which has been shown to catalyze ESCRT-III activity by maintaining the dynamics of complex assembly and disassembly (Mierzwa et al., 2017; Adell et al., 2017; Schoneberg et al., 2018). ESCRT-II recruits the ESCRT-III subunit Vps20 to form a complex with affinity for regions of membrane curvature (Fyfe et al., 2011). In turn, Vps20 nucleates the formation of Snf7 spirals that are capped at the growing end by a Vps24-Vps2 complex (Teis et al., 2008). Vps2 recruits the ATPase Vps4 through the interaction between its MIM (MIT-interacting motif) and the MIT (microtubule-interacting and transport) domain of Vps4 (Obita et al., 2007; Stuchell-Brereton et al., 2007). ILV formation by ESCRT-II/ESCRT-III can be reconstituted in vitro with a GUV-based bulk-phase uptake assay. The activity of a minimal ESCRT-III/Vps4 system in artificial vesicle systems was first demonstrated by Wollert et al. (Wollert et al., 2009) where ILVs were generated in GUV parent vesicles and observed by microscopy. In addition, there are examples of more minimal sets of ESCRTs inducing ILV formation in vitro, such as Vps20/Snf7 only (Avalos-Padilla et al., 2018), and some minimal activity with moderate concentrations of Snf7 alone (Marklew et al., 2018), suggesting further scope for simplification of the system in a technological context. The reconstitution of ESCRT activity in vitro opens the possibility of achieving finer control of ILV formation in artificial systems. Therefore we initially set out to investigate the relative stoichiometry of ESCRT-III components to underpin their influence on the size and number of ILVs that form within individual GUVs (Figure 1B). Interestingly, our initial experiments reveal wide variation in ILV size and number between different GUVs within an individual experiment (Figure 2A). Membrane mechanics are considered to be the likely source of these differences due to variability in tension across a single GUV population. Modulating membrane tension could therefore provide a further means to exert control over ILV formation and will also be investigated in this study. Here we report on how changing the relative stoichiometry of the ESCRT-III subunits and the mechanical properties of the membrane regulate the size and number of ILVs formed in a GUV-based bulk-phase uptake assay (Figure 1B).

"Let's skate around and around while Tom talks. That way we'll get exercise and hear all about it." "Good idea," spoke Tom. "Come along then." The four lads started off again, circling the lake at a slow pace. Tom was the only one who knew anything about the subject under discussion, and the others wanted to know all about it. "Now, where are we going to go?" asked Jack, after a few moments' silence, during which the other two members of the party were listening to Tom with rapt attention. "To the Adirondacks," replied Tom. "We're going to spend Christmas vacation in a hunters' camp, and hunt bears and deer and other game." "Oh, boy! That's fine!" cried Bert, waving his stick in the air. "When do we start?" "Right away. We leave next week." "Where do we go?" asked George. "How far is it from here?" "It isn't too far," answered Tom. "I hope you won't object to sleeping on board a train. It takes about twelve hours to reach our destination, but we'll sleep most of the time." "Sleep on the train?" echoed Bert. "I don't mind that part of it, though I'd rather be in bed, but I never slept on a train before. Will it be safe?" "Yes, perfectly safe. You see, we have a Pullman sleeper, and there are no breaks on the road between here and the Adirondacks." "Will we get there in daylight?" asked George. "No, we'll probably arrive in the night." "Then how shall we find our way to the camp?" "We won't need to. There will be a guide waiting for us at the station. Oh, yes, we'll have no trouble getting to our destination. I found the place advertised in a sporting goods store window, and wrote to the owner, Mr. Borden, asking him if he could put up four boys for a couple of weeks. He answered that he could, and gave me all sorts of information." "Is he a good sport?" asked Jack. "He certainly seems to be. He writes that he has been running a hunters' camp for five years, and knows every inch of the country roundabout. He says we can go anywhere we want to within ten miles of the camp, and he'll show us how to get back." "Did you book seats?" asked Bert. "Yes, I took care of everything. All you have to do now is to pack your clothes in a grip, and bring your guns, fishing rods, and other necessary things. If you haven't got them yet, you'd better buy 'em soon. I'm going to have mine sent home, as I left them there when I went East last summer." "Are we going to have a cook?" asked George. "No, we must do our own cooking, and make beds, and wash dishes, and take care of ourselves generally." "What fun!" cried Bert, slapping his leg. "I'll bet we'll have a great time!" "I hope so," agreed Tom. "The first thing we must do is to get our tickets. They're all booked, and I paid for them myself. Then we'll each have to pack a suitcase, and go to the station to meet the train." "I wish we could start now," said Jack. "But we'll have to wait until Tuesday morning. By that time we ought to be ready." "I guess we will be," observed Bert.

We must descend and walk; you forget we must enter unsuspected;" and Dalibard, as the carriage stopped, opened the door and let down the steps. Lucretia recoiled, then pressing one hand to her heart, she descended, without touching the arm held out to her. Dalibard bade the coachman wait, and they walked back to the house. "Yes, he may see her," exclaimed Lucretia, her face brightening. "Ah, there you have not deceived me; I see your stratagem, - I despise it; I know she loves him; she has sought this interview. He is so mild and gentle, so fearful to give pain; he has consented, from pity, - that is all. Is he not pledged to me? He, so candid, so ingenuous! There must be truth somewhere in the world. If he is false, where find truth? Dark man, must I look for it in you, - you?" "It is not my truth I require you to test; I pretend not to truth universal; I can be true to one, as you may yet discover. But I own your belief is not impossible; my interest in you may have made me rash and unjust, - what you may overhear, far from destroying, may confirm forever your happiness. Would that it may be so!" "It must be so," returned Lucretia, with a fearful gloom on her brow and in her accent; "I will interpret every word to my own salvation." Dalibard's countenance changed, despite his usual control over it. He had set all his chances upon this cast, and it was more hazardous than he had deemed. He had counted too much upon the jealousy of common natures. After all, how little to the ear of one resolved to deceive herself might pass between these two young persons, meeting not to avow attachment, but to take courage from each other! What restraint might they impose on their feelings! Still, the game must be played out. As they now neared the house, Dalibard looked carefully round, lest they should encounter Mainwaring on his way to it. He had counted on arriving before the young man could get there. "But," said Lucretia, breaking silence, with an ironical smile, - "but - for your tender anxiety for me has, no doubt, provided all means and contrivance, all necessary aids to baseness and eavesdropping, that can assure my happiness - how am I to be present at this interview?" "I have provided, as you say," answered Dalibard, in the tone of a man deeply hurt, "those means which I, who have found the world one foe and one traitor, deemed the best to distinguish falsehood from truth. I have arranged that we shall enter the house unsuspected. Mainwaring and your sister will be in the drawing-room; the room next to it will be vacant, as Mr. Fielden is from home: there is but a glass-door between the two chambers." "Enough, enough!" and Lucretia turned round and placed her hand lightly on the Provencal's arm.

Turel et al. have conjugated quinolones (ofloxacin [15], nalidixic acid [16] and cinoxacin [16]) to the Ru-arene framework with the Ru(II) -bonded to a p-cymene (p-cym) ring and -bonded to the two oxygen atoms of the chelated quinolone with the remaining site occupied by a chloride ligand. All three complexes, upon hydrolysis, rapidly and selectively form adducts with guanosine 5'-monophosphate via coordination to N7, thus providing preliminary evidence that DNA may be a potential target. It has also been suggested that electrostatic interactions and hydrogen bonding may initially play a role in DNA recognition prior to guanosine 5'-monophosphate binding. Of the three complexes, only the ofloxacin derivative demonstrated in vitro cytotoxicity and in only one of the cell lines tested (CH1 with IC50 of 18 +/- 7 1/2M) [16]. Fluoroquinolones are attractive for incorporation into metallodrugs with anti-bacterial properties since they possess a much broader spectrum of anti-bacterial activity as well as an enhanced pharmacokinetic profile when compared to quinolones. The antibiotic ciprofloxacin (Cip), a second generation orally or parentally administered fluoroquinolone, was the drug of choice to treat victims infected by anthrax in 2001 [17]. Structural optimisation of this lead drug molecule has led to derivatives with broad spectrum activities and minimal toxic side effects [18]. Metal complexes of Cip such as those of Co, Zn, Cd, Ni and Cu have also been investigated as an alternative strategy to optimise its therapeutic potential [19,20]. These complexes, in which Cip is bound via O,O'-bidentate coordination, have comparable anti-bacterial activity against several bacteria when compared to Cip itself. Interestingly, the complexes, in contrast to the ligand, are more bactericidal against stationary bacteria, a property which may be attractive for the treatment of chronic or device-related infections (e.g. catheter infections) which involve slowly metabolising bacteria in biofilm mode [21]. Vieira et al. recently reported a Pt-Cip derivative in which the antibiotic is complexed via piperazine N,N'-coordination. A positive correlation between lipophilicity, in vitro anti-tumour activity and rate of drug uptake was observed [22]. Furthermore, Azema et al. reported a structure activity study of 31 Cip derivatives investigating the correlation between lipophilicity and anti-tumour activity, with two lead candidates being identified, both demonstrating enhanced in vitro cytotoxicity in the low 1/2M range against a panel of tumour cell lines as compared to the parent Cip [23]. Of the two, the 7-(4-(decanoyl)piperazin-1-yl) derivative CipA, Fig. 2, was most potent. These derivatives, particularly CipA, have IC50 values in the low 1/2M range (3-7 1/2M in 4 cell lines tested), but were also non-toxic in an in vivo xenograft mouse model. While Cip is reported to have anti-proliferative and anti-cancer effects itself, harnessing its anti-bacterial activity in the cancer setting where significant infection risks are present due to immunosuppression, may augment its therapeutic effects.

Clouds usually cover large portions of the Earth's surface: globally cirrus clouds, the most difficult to be detected (Xu et al., 2014), are thought to cover on average about 17% of the surface with >50% in the Intertropical Convergence Zone (Kovalskyy and Roy, 2015 and references therein). Recent estimates suggested that low altitude clouds, typically non-cirrus, may co-exist with spatially overlapping cirrus clouds and that, more in general, about 30% of low clouds are overlapped by high clouds (Kovalskyy and Roy, 2015 and reference therein). Clouds largely affect the transmission of radiation between the satellite sensors and surface targets, reducing the ability to identify land covers, decreasing the accuracy of the retrieval of surface parameters, and providing misleading information on monitored surfaces (Kazantzidis et al., 2011; Lanfredi et al., 2015; Li et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2016). The multiple types of clouds and the complexity of land structures further complicate their detection due to the frequent difficulty in distinguishing clouds from the underlying landscape, even at high resolution (Hagolle et al., 2010; Jedlovec et al., 2008). Sentinel-2 MSI, even if lacks thermal bands which are included in other sensors such as Landsat and ASTER, has spectral bands useful to provide better cloud screening and compensation of atmospheric effects: Band 1 (centered at 0.443 1/2m with 60 m of spatial resolution), Band 2 (centered at 0.490 1/2m with 10 m of spatial resolution), Band 9 (centered at 0.945 1/2m with 60 m of spatial resolution), Band 10 (centered at 1.375 1/2m with 60 m of spatial resolution), and Band 12 (centered at 2.190 1/2m with 20 m of spatial resolution). In particular, Band 10 (hereafter B10) at 1.375 1/2m is based on MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and Landsat 8 OLI (Operational Land Imager) sensors design heritage and provides the possibility to examine the incidence of cirrus clouds. The opportunity to dispose of all this information, contextually acquired by the same sensor, is rather new in satellite systems primarily intended for operational services. It represents a prerequisite for establishing fundamental environmental and climate data records to obtain consistent products and harmonized time series (Berger et al., 2012; Simoniello et al., 2004). Sentinel-2 images are among the first high resolution data distributed with an associated cloud mask, followed by the VEN 1/2S (Vegetation and Environment monitoring on a New MicroSatellite) mission (French and Israeli cooperation) launched on 1 August 2017. Sentinel-2 Level-1C (L1C) products include cloud masks to simplify the user's work and to provide many useful products ready for delivery. Cloud masks identify cloudy pixels and separate them from those that are cloud-free. They include both dense clouds and cirrus clouds, by specifying the cloud type with an indicator. Overzealous in their pursuit of a secular democratic state, they inadvertently tread the same path of exclusion and short-sighted policies that led the Islamists into a corner. The secularists, eager to dismantle the remnants of the Brotherhood's influence, resort to measures that, while aimed at ensuring stability, risk alienating a substantial segment of the populace. Such tactics, mirroring the Islamists' past errors, include stifling dissenting voices that do not align with the secular narrative and marginalizing communities that bear the Brotherhood label. The polarization of the Egyptian socio-political landscape is further exacerbated by this mirrored stance, where neither side possesses the foresight or willingness to reach out and bridge the chasm. Instead, both the secularists and the Brotherhood entrench themselves deeper, much to the detriment of national cohesion and progress. The call for reconciliation, teetering on the fringes, is often drowned out by the cacophony of steadfast ideological proclamations and entrenched resentments. International actors observing from a distance are reticent to choose sides overtly, aware that any perceived favoritism could tip the delicate balance of power and influence. Rather than wield influence as a tool for productive dialogue, international involvement often manifests as perfunctory statements urging restraint, offering little in the way of substantive solutions. This lack of decisive external pressure allows the internal stalemate to fester, feeding into a cycle of distrust and antagonism. For the secularists, assuming that simply dismantling the Brotherhood's structure would lead to a seamlessly democratic society is dangerously naive. True, the Brotherhood's leadership errors are numerous and significant, yet the movement's grassroots connections and deep-seated societal influence cannot be erased through forceful suppression alone. This underestimation may lead to a resurgence not anticipated by secular proponents, one that could rally the disenchanted under a banner of resistance bolstered by portrayals of martyrdom and persecution. Concurrently, the Brotherhood faces a reflective moment, yet they remain largely resistant to critique and adaptation. Refusing internal reform, they risk becoming encapsulated in their past, unable to adapt to the shifting sands of contemporary political landscapes. Instead of seeking to evolve and engage in meaningful dialogue, the Brotherhood may find itself holding onto anachronistic ideals that fail to resonate with emerging societal aspirations for pluralism and inclusivity. The path forward demands an unprecedented courage from both parties-a courage defined by compromise, humility, and recognition of the common good. Such an endeavor necessitates dismantling walls of suspicion and embracing avenues for inclusive participation that respects both secular and religious rights and aspirations. The potential for constitutional dialogues and reforms remains untapped, buried beneath layers of ego and animosity. Thus, Egypt is presented with a choice: continue dwelling in cyclical conflict propelled by the shadows of division, or strive towards a renewed vision that truly upholds the ideals of freedom, justice, and unity. The world watches, as history waits for Egypt to define its future. The crossroads are clear, and the decision looming holds the power to not only transform a nation but to set a precedent for a region rife with similar tensions. For it is the actions taken at this juncture that will echo through the corridors of time.

Ritz nodded in assent. The teacher turned away and called: "Fritz!" The teacher was standing before Fritz, who sat on the first bench and was reading aloud. He read as follows: "A clock is an indispensable object in every household. It has the following three qualities: It shows the hours, it rings the quarters, and it strikes the half-hours." The teacher was pleased and asked: "Is the hour hand fixed?" Fritz did not know what that meant. "Can you move it yourself?" Fritz answered: "No, sir." Then the teacher said: "That is right. We call that 'stopping' or 'breaking,' and it says, 'the clock is broken.' It also strikes the quarter-hours, but it does not show them. Is that clear?" Fritz nodded. The teacher continued: "Now tell us where the hands are placed when it is twelve o'clock." Fritz showed it. The teacher went on: "What is the name of the other hand?" Fritz replied: "The minute-hand." "Right. And how many minutes are there in an hour?" "Sixty, sir." The teacher remarked: "But only fifty-nine minutes in an hour, for there are sixty seconds in a minute, and each second is smaller than a minute. If there were sixty minutes in an hour, then there would be 3600 seconds in an hour, instead of 3,600." Fritz was greatly surprised over this discovery, and it occurred to him to ask: "How many seconds are there in a day?" The teacher answered: "There are 86,400 seconds in twenty-four hours." Fritz exclaimed: "Oh, how much is that?" The teacher said: "If I counted one thousand, four hundred eighty-eight seconds per minute, and then counted one thousand, four hundred eighty-eight times forty-eight times twenty-four hours, then I should count 86,400 seconds." Fritz stared at the teacher and did not understand anything. The teacher continued: "I shall give you a riddle. There are eight letters in the word 'school.' If I write these letters in the order of their value, according to the alphabet, and add the values together, then I get the number 54. Can you solve the riddle?" Fritz shook his head. And there, between the fireplace and the window, is my book-rack, and from its shelves old friends look down upon me. The gilt titles are tarnished and worn, but I know each book by the place it occupies, and I feel that, even after the long, long years that have separated us, Tom Brown, Robinson Crusoe, and David Copperfield will speak to me again, laugh with me, cry with me, as they did in days of yore. Often has Betty, I know, swept and tidied this little room. Every article has been lifted, dusted, and carefully returned to its place. I know with what feelings of reverence the dear old soul has fingered every ornament. I am conscious of the loving care she has exercised on all my old belongings, and somehow I feel consoled and comforted, my physical weakness depresses me less, my mother's presence seems nearer me, and unbidden tears of thankfulness come to my eyes and trickle from my cheek to my pillow. This has been to me a day of great events. I have travelled by rail from Edinburgh to Elvanfoot, thence by horse-carriage to Thornhill - during the last stage driven by Charlie Walker, the 'bus Jehu I envied in my schoolboy years, and tended by my fail-me-never Betty. To her also this has been a memorable day, for when we were driving down the Dalveen Pass she told me that never before had she seen a Caledonian train, and that her last memory of Traloss dated back to a Sabbath-school trip about the year 1868. Such a long ride in a well-sprung, well-upholstered carriage was also a novelty to her, a new experience which only with great difficulty I could persuade her to enjoy to the full. She insisted on sitting forward on the extreme edge of the seat, and it was only after I had told her that her uncomfortable-looking position made me uneasy and unhappy that she sat well back, till her shoulders rested on the cushion behind. Contrary to my expectations, I am suffering neither pain nor inconvenience from my long journey; and as I lie here in my little bed, looking through the curtained window to the long, low range of the Lowther Hills, and listening to the familiar sounds in the village street below, a blissful peace which I cannot express in words possesses me, my physical and my mental organisation seem to have undergone a change, my experience of city life is blotted out and forgotten, and, strangely enough, I feel myself, as of old, a unit of the village community.

In dolphins, simultaneous same-sex sexual behavior is frequently observed among triads of primarily unrelated males and this is also the most frequent social configuration for cooperative alliances (Mann, 2006). In other species, same-sex sexual behavior mainly occurs when competition between participants is high, and it is used to attract opposite sex mates rather than to strengthen same-sex relationships (e.g. tropical fish (Poecilia mexicana), Bierbach et al., 2012). In addition to behavioral data, measures of physiological changes associated with sexual behavior provide further insights into likely functions. Of particular interest in the context of cooperation is the neuropeptide hormone oxytocin (OT), which mediates many aspects of female sexual, reproductive and social behavior (reviewed in Borrow and Cameron, 2012). OT is released centrally from hypothalamic nuclei in response to salient social stimuli, including sexual behavior (rats: Nyuyki et al., 2011; voles: Ross et al., 2009). Centrally, OT activation in social brain circuitry results in enhanced social memory, reduced fear and anxiety and activation of neural reward pathways, all of which are related to fostering selective social bonds that promote cooperation (reviewed in Gangestad and Grebe, 2017). OT can also be released peripherally via the posterior pituitary, facilitating non-invasive measurement (Crockford et al., 2014). In several species, measures of peripheral OT correlate positively with the extent of behavioral coordination and cooperation within selective social relationships, such as between mothers and offspring (humans: Feldman, 2012), monogamous mates (humans: Grewen et al., 2005; Schneiderman et al., 2012; cotton-top tamarins (Saguinus oedipus): Snowdon et al., 2010) and stable alliance partners (chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes): Crockford et al., 2013). In humans (De Dreu, 2012; Nagasawa et al., 2009) and chimpanzees (Samuni et al., 2017), there is evidence that the OT system has been co-opted outside of maternal and reproductive contexts to facilitate cooperation with a broader range of social partners (reviewed in Trumble et al., 2015). Based on this combined evidence, the link between sexual behavior and OT system activation may be strongest related to sexual behavior that facilitates additional trust and cooperation, whether this occurs within or outside of monogamous pair-bonds. We were interested in whether unrelated female bonobos exhibit increases in peripheral oxytocin associated with sexual interactions, as this may explain their unusual extent of cooperation. Bonobos are a particularly promising model for investigating different functions of sexual behavior, given that all adult females engage in same-sex sexual behavior that occurs at similar or higher rates as copulations (Hohmann and Fruth, 2000, 2003a; Ryu et al., 2015). In contrast, same-sex sexual interactions among male bonobos are relatively rare (Fruth and Hohmann, 2006; Kano, 1980; Surbeck et al., 2017b). Bonobos live in multi-male, multi-female communities characterized by fission-fusion social dynamics, female-biased dispersal and a promiscuous mating system notable for a relative lack of male coercion and a high degree of female control over sexual partners (Furuichi, 2011; Surbeck and Hohmann, 2013).

And they listened to audio recordings of Balfour's interviews with detectives, in which he repeatedly denied involvement in the murders. Defence attorney Thompson argued that the state did not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Balfour committed the crimes. She noted that no physical evidence linked him to the murders, and that none of the witnesses saw him commit them. The Middle East in biblical times was a Jewish community occupied against its will by the Roman Empire, and the message of Jesus was equally threatening to both sides: to the Romans, because he was a revolutionary, and to the establishment of Jewish priests, because he preached a new covenant and threatened the status quo. In the movie's scenes showing Jesus being condemned to death, the two main players are Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, and Caiaphas, the Jewish high priest. Both men want to keep the lid on, and while neither is especially eager to see Jesus crucified, they live in a harsh time when such a man is dangerous. Pilate is seen going through his well-known doubts before finally washing his hands of the matter and turning Jesus over to the priests, but Caiaphas, who also had doubts, is not seen as sympathetically. The critic Steven D. Greydanus, in a useful analysis of the film, writes: "The film omits the canonical line from John's gospel in which Caiaphas argues that it is better for one man to die for the people [so] that the nation be saved. As the sun dips lower, the air cools and the shadows grow longer, the animals begin to stir. The impala, sensing the approaching darkness, grow more skittish, their large brown eyes darting back and forth as they nibble on the last of the day's grasses. The wild dogs, their coats a mottled mix of brown and white, move silently through the underbrush, their ears perked up and their tails held high. They are a formidable pack, their reputation for hunting prowess preceding them like a whispered rumor. Mokwami's voice is low and smooth as he points out the various animals, his knowledge of the land and its creatures honed from years of living in the bush. "Look, the giraffe is drinking from the waterhole," he says, his eyes scanning the horizon. "And see, the elephants are making their way to the river. They'll spend the night there, feeding on the lush grasses and plants that grow along the banks." As the stars begin to twinkle in the night sky, the animals grow more restless. The impala, sensing the darkness, move closer together, their large ears flapping in the breeze. The wild dogs, too, are getting ready to strike, their paws padding softly on the ground as they stalk their prey. Mokwani's voice is a gentle whisper in our ears, guiding us through the darkness, pointing out the various animals as they go about their evening routines. We drive through the night, the Jeep's headlights casting an eerie glow over the landscape. The air is thick with the sounds of insects and animals, the rustling of leaves and snapping of twigs the only sounds that break the stillness. It's as if we're the only ones awake in the world, the only ones privy to the secrets of the night. As we drive, Mokwani tells us stories of the animals we're seeing, of the struggles they face in this harsh and unforgiving land. He speaks of the great floods that come every year, bringing with them a bounty of food and water, but also posing a threat to the very survival of the animals that call the delta home. He speaks of the droughts, too, that can last for years, leaving the animals to fight for every scrap of food and every drop of water. As the night wears on, we come across a group of hippos, their large bodies wallowing in the water, their ears and eyes above the surface, watching us with a wary eye. We drive slowly by, careful not to startle them, and Mokwani points out the different species of birds that call the delta home, their calls echoing through the night air. As the first light of dawn begins to creep over the horizon, we come to a stop at a small clearing. The animals are still moving, but the night is slowly giving way to day. Mokwani turns off the engine and we sit in silence, listening to the sounds of the delta waking up. It's a moment of perfect peace, a moment of connection to the natural world that is hard to find in our busy, modern lives. As the sun rises higher in the sky, we pack up our gear and continue on our journey, the animals of the Okavango Delta slowly emerging from the shadows, ready to face another day in this harsh and beautiful land.

We're told to conform to certain standards, to fit in, to be accepted. And I'm not saying that's all bad, because of course, we need to have some sense of belonging and connection with others. But what I am saying is that we often lose ourselves in the process. We forget what makes us unique, what makes us special, what makes us, us. And I think this is where the concept of giving yourself permission comes in. Giving yourself permission to be yourself, to be different, to be quirky, to be weird, to be whatever it is that makes you, you. Because let's be real, the world is a crazy place, and it's okay to not fit in. In fact, it's more than okay, it's necessary. Think about it, if we all fit in, if we all looked the same, if we all thought the same, where would be the creativity, where would be the innovation, where would be the progress? We need our differences, we need our quirks, we need our individuality. And yet, we're constantly being told to conform, to fit in, to be like everyone else. And it's exhausting, it's draining, it's suffocating. It's like we're living in a world where we're constantly trying to be someone we're not, instead of embracing who we are. So, giving yourself permission to be yourself is not just about being okay with being different, it's about being okay with being you. It's about embracing your quirks, your flaws, your strengths, your weaknesses. It's about accepting that you're not perfect, and that that's okay. And I know, I know, it's hard. It's hard to let go of the need to fit in, to be accepted, to be loved. It's hard to let go of the need to be someone you're not. But trust me, it's worth it. Because when you give yourself permission to be yourself, you open yourself up to a world of possibility. You open yourself up to new experiences, new connections, new opportunities. And most importantly, you open yourself up to self-love. Because when you're being yourself, you're not trying to be someone you're not, you're not trying to fit in, you're not trying to impress anyone. You're just being you, and that's where self-love comes in. Self-love is not about loving yourself because of what you do, or because of what you look like, or because of what you achieve. Self-love is about loving yourself because you are. Because you exist. Because you're a unique, special, one-of-a-kind individual, with your own strengths, your own weaknesses, your own quirks. And that, my friends, is the key to living a life of true freedom, true happiness, and true fulfillment. So, I want to leave you with a challenge today. I want to challenge you to give yourself permission to be yourself. To be different, to be quirky, to be weird, to be whatever it is that makes you, you. Because when you do, you'll find that the world is a much more beautiful, much more interesting, much more fulfilling place.

For a brief season, transient as the flash of a loon's wing on the shadow of a lake, the post was bright with the thronging of many people. The Indians pitched their wigwams on the broad meadows below the bend; the half-breeds sauntered about, flashing bright teeth and wicked dark eyes at whom it might concern; the traders gazed stolidily over their little black pipes, and uttered brief sentences through their thick black beards. Everywhere was gay sound - the fiddle, the laugh, the song; everywhere was gay color - the red sashes of the voyageurs, the beaded moccasins and leggings of the metis, the capotes of the brigade, the variegated costumes of the Crees and Ojibways. Like the wild roses around the edge of the muskegs, this brief flowering of the year passed. Again the nights were long, again the frost crept down from the eternal snow, again the wolves howled across barren wastes. Just now the girl stood ankle-deep in green grasses, a bath of sunlight falling about her, a tingle of salt wind humming up the river from the bay's offing. She was clad in gray wool, and wore no hat. Her soft hair, the color of ripe wheat, blew about her temples, shadowing eyes of fathomless black. The wind had brought to the light and delicate brown of her complexion a trace of color to match her lips whose scarlet did not fade after the ordinary and imperceptible manner into the tinge of her skin, but continued vivid to the very edge; her eyes were wide and unseeing. One hand rested idly on the breech of an ornamented bronze field-gun. McDonald, the chief trader, passed from the house to the store where his bartering with the Indians was daily carried on; the other Scotchman in the Post, Galen Albret, her father, and the head Factor of all this region, paced back and forth across the veranda of the factory, caressing his white beard; up by the stockade, young Achille Picard tuned his whistle to the note of the curlew; across the meadow from the church wandered Crane, the little Church of England missionary, peering from short-sighted pale blue eyes; beyond the coulee, Sarnier and his Indians chock-chock-chocked away at the seams of the long coast-trading bateau. The girl saw nothing, heard nothing. She was dreaming, she was trying to remember. In the lines of her slight figure, in its pose there by the old gun over the old, old river, was the grace of gentle blood, the pride of caste. Of all this region her father was the absolute lord, feared, loved, obeyed by all its human creatures. When he went abroad, he travelled in a state almost mediaeval in its magnificence; when he stopped at home, men came to him from the Albany, the Kenogami, the Missinaibe, the Mattagami, the Abitibi - from all the rivers of the North - to receive his commands.

Thus, it is crucial to consider the implications of perceived food variety and its interplay with SSS in shaping eating behaviors. The perceived variety not only influences the dynamics of hunger and meal satisfaction but also extends into broader dietary patterns and nutritional outcomes. When individuals perceive a greater variety of foods, they may experience a more prolonged engagement with the meal, indicating that our biological systems for hunger regulation can be subtly overridden by cognitive factors related to food diversity (Higgs & Woodward, 2009). Further investigation into the impact of contextual cues reveals additional layers of complexity within SSS. Contextual influences can be particularly pivotal when considering social aspects of eating. Dining in the presence of others, for example, may enhance the stimulation of taste perception, leading individuals to savor foods longer and potentially indulge more when subjects are grouped in convivial settings. This phenomenon echoes findings from social psychology, where the motivation to conform to social norms enhances consumption behaviors (Wolf & Boulanger, 2020). Moreover, the aspect of portion control is intricately linked with SSS, and thus examined under various contexts. Studies by Wansink and van Ittersum (2003) have shown that larger portions lead to increased intake without necessarily enhancing the enjoyment of the food, effectively training individuals to ignore sensory-specific signals of satiety. This suggests that the mere visual presence of food can, in some cases, overpower intrinsic sensory feedback mechanisms. Given this interplay, portion sizes become a mechanism through which food environments can manipulate eating behavior significantly. Yet, the interaction between cognition and sensory responses extends further into the realms of marketing and food presentation strategies. The notion of "food plating," where aesthetic considerations influence perceived taste and quality, ties back into SSS in practical ways. Visually appealing meals can enhance expectations and, ultimately, the motivational desire to consume larger amounts, irrespective of the actual nutritional value or sensory quality of the foods presented (Raghunathan, Naylor, & Hoyer, 2006). Interestingly, age-related variations also complicate the landscape of SSS and perceived variety. Elderly populations may experience a diminished responsiveness to SSS, which can potentially lead to unhealthy eating patterns characterized by excessive consumption of less nutrient-dense foods (Nicklaus, 2016). It is increasingly evident that age-related physiological changes, such as declines in taste sensitivity, further exacerbate this issue, compelling researchers to delve into targeted interventions that can reinvigorate interest in a variety of compelling, nutritious foods within this demographic cohort. Alongside age considerations, cultural factors undoubtedly play a pivotal role in shaping food preferences and, consequently, the dynamics of SSS. Different culinary traditions encompass a wide array of flavors, ingredients, and preparation methods that not only satisfy hunger but evoke emotional responses tied to identity, memory, and community (Havermans, 2012). Therefore, understanding the complexities of SSS necessitates a broader examination of cultural influences - including the significance attached to specific meals, the rituals surrounding food consumption, and the accumulated experiences that inform individual and collective attitudes toward eating. Ultimately, the intricate weave of sensory specific satiety reflects a convergence of biological, cognitive, social, and cultural factors that govern the multifaceted dynamics of eating behaviors. As researchers continue to unravel the mechanisms that underpin SSS, the insights gained are poised to inform better dietary guidelines, meal planning initiatives, and public health campaigns aimed at fostering healthier eating habits across diverse populations.

It was supposed that she had been captured by the enemy, but still no tidings of her capture were received. Two men belonging to her had been brought home by a Danish East-Indiaman, and shortly after the first intelligence, these men arrived in London, and gave a more particular detail of what had occurred. Sir Charles, in a state of feverish anxiety, as soon as he heard of their arrival, hastened up to town to question these men; and the result of his interrogatories fully convinced him that he was now quite bereaved and childless. This was the last blow and the most severe; it was long before he could resign himself to the unsearchable dispensations of Providence; but time and religion had at last overcome all his repining feelings, - all disposition to question the goodness or wisdom of his Heavenly Father, and he was enabled to say, with sincerity, "Not my will, but thine, be done." But although Sir Charles was thus left childless, as years passed away, he at last found that he had those near to him for whom he felt an interest, and one in particular who promised to deserve all his regard. This was his grand-nephew, Alexander Wilmot, who was the legal heir to the title and entailed property, - the son of a deceased nephew, who had fallen during the Peninsular war. On this boy Sir Charles had lavished those affections which it pleased Heaven that he should not bestow upon his own issue, and Alexander Wilmot had gradually become as dear to him as if he had been his own child. Still the loss of his wife and children was ever in his memory, and as time passed on, painful feelings of hope and doubt were occasionally raised in Sir Charles's mind, from the occasional assertions of travellers, that all those did not perish who were supposed so to do when the Grosvenor was wrecked, and that, from the reports of the natives, some of them and of their descendants were still alive. It was a paragraph in the newspaper, containing a renewal of these assertions, which had attracted the attention of Sir Charles, and which had put him in the state of agitation and uneasiness in which we have described him at the opening of this chapter. We left him in deep and painful thought, with the newspaper in his hands.

After a few more words Dolly's companion passed on, and the unfortunate Freshman wandered dolefully into her bedroom and sat down on the edge of the bed where we first saw her. As a rule, Dolly and tears were strangers, but just now poor Dolly felt unutterably miserable. Not only was she homesick, but she felt outside all the college fun and good camaraderie of the place. "I ought to unpack that trunk and take off my things," she told herself, but she felt more inclined to run out of the door, back to the depot and on board the first train bound for her home. "Well, of all the forlorn damsels I ever saw, you certainly are the worst, and I thought you looked so full of fun when I noticed you downstairs." Dolly glanced up in surprise, to see a merry face regarding her from the doorway. The newcomer was much below medium height, with a very freckled face, very red, curly hair, and a very good-natured expression. "Didn't you feel forlorn yourself last year?" retorted Dolly. The use of Jatropha curcas L. as a feedstock for biodiesel production has been extensively studied, with research focusing on the optimization of cultivation practices, oil extraction methods, and transesterification processes [30-33]. However, despite its potential, Jatropha curcas L. has several limitations, including its toxicity, water requirements, and relatively low yield compared to other oilseed crops [34,35]. As a result, researchers have continued to explore alternative non-edible oilseed crops, such as Camelina sativa, which has been shown to have a higher oil content and lower water requirements than Jatropha curcas L. [36,37]. Other crops, such as Lesquerella fendleri and Calendula officinalis, have also been identified as potential feedstocks for biodiesel production, with studies demonstrating their suitability for transesterification and engine testing [38,39]. In addition to the identification of new oilseed crops, researchers have also explored the use of waste biomass as a feedstock for biodiesel production. This approach has the advantage of reducing waste disposal costs and generating a valuable product from otherwise discarded materials [40]. For example, waste cooking oils, which are typically discarded after use in the food industry, have been shown to be suitable for biodiesel production through transesterification [41,42]. Similarly, algae-based biodiesel has gained significant attention in recent years, with studies demonstrating the potential for large-scale production of algal oils through photobioreactors and open pond systems [43,44]. The use of microorganisms, such as bacteria and yeast, has also been explored as a means of producing biodiesel through microbial lipid production [45,46]. This approach has the advantage of not competing with food crops and can utilize waste biomass as a feedstock, reducing the environmental impact of biodiesel production [47]. Furthermore, microbial lipids can be engineered to have improved properties, such as higher cetane numbers and lower viscosity, making them more suitable for use in compression ignition engines [48]. Despite the progress made in the development of alternative feedstocks for biodiesel production, several challenges remain. For example, the cost of production remains a significant barrier to widespread adoption, with biodiesel typically more expensive than fossil diesel [49]. Additionally, the scalability of alternative feedstock production and processing remains a concern, with many studies focusing on small-scale production and limited to laboratory or pilot-scale testing [50]. Furthermore, the environmental impact of large-scale biodiesel production, including land use change and water requirements, must be carefully considered to ensure that the production of alternative fuels does not result in unintended consequences [51]. In conclusion, the development of alternative feedstocks for biodiesel production is a critical step towards reducing greenhouse gas emissions and improving the sustainability of the transport sector. While significant progress has been made in the identification of new oilseed crops, waste biomass, and microbial lipids, challenges remain in terms of cost, scalability, and environmental impact. Further research is needed to overcome these challenges and ensure that the production of alternative fuels results in a sustainable reduction in greenhouse gas emissions.

Therefore, artificial intelligence approaches have become increasingly popular for Rs estimation over the past two decades. A wide range of machine learning algorithms has been proposed for Rs estimation including neural networks [113,67], support vector machines [29,82], random forest [62,127], Gaussian process regression [10,43], etc. Machine learning models have been shown to outperform empirical models in terms of prediction accuracy [121,91,23]. For example, Chen et al. [21] compared the performance of four machine learning algorithms including multilayer perceptron (MLP), radial basis function network (RBFN), generalized regression neural network (GRNN) and support vector regression (SVR) for Rs estimation in China and found that SVR had the highest accuracy. The MLP model was reported to perform better than the GRNN and RBFN models. Mubiru and Banda [81] evaluated the performances of three artificial neural networks (ANNs) including MLP, GRNN and RBFN for Rs estimation in Uganda and found that the MLP model provided the best prediction results. On the contrary, some studies showed that GRNN performed better than other ANN models [122,20]. In addition to ANNs, ensemble learning algorithms have also been widely used for Rs estimation, e.g., Adaboost [84,53], gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT) [27,42], random forests (RF) [62,54]. Ensemble learning refers to combining multiple individual learners into one predictive model to improve the generalization ability and reduce the variance of the final predictions [31,73]. According to Zhou [132], there are two main categories of ensemble learning algorithms: sequential ensemble learning and parallel ensemble learning. Sequential ensemble learning algorithms train each base learner sequentially using all training samples while the errors of previous base learners are considered when training subsequent base learners. Parallel ensemble learning algorithms train each base learner independently without considering the information of other base learners. Compared with parallel ensemble learning algorithms, sequential ensemble learning algorithms usually achieve higher prediction accuracy but require longer training time [74,104]. The most commonly used sequential ensemble learning algorithm is AdaBoost, which trains a series of weak classifiers sequentially and combines them through weighted majority voting [36,106]. The AdaBoost algorithm has been successfully used for solving classification problems in many fields, e.g., image processing [46], face recognition [57] and speech emotion recognition [44]. To deal with regression tasks, Drucker [32] extended the original AdaBoost.M1 algorithm to the AdaBoost.RT algorithm which constructs an additive model in a forward stage-wise manner by fitting a regression tree to the current residuals. The AdaBoost.RT algorithm has been demonstrated to achieve state-of-the-art performance in many regression tasks, such as electricity load forecasting [25], water quality prediction [117] and sea level prediction [116]. It should be noted that the AdaBoost.RT algorithm uses the same weight update strategy as the AdaBoost.M1 algorithm, i.e., it assigns larger weights to misclassified instances and smaller weights to correctly classified instances. However, this weight update strategy is not suitable for regression tasks because regression errors are continuous rather than binary values (0/1). To address this issue, Solomatine and Shrestha [108] proposed a modified version of AdaBoost.RT called ModAd-RtBoost which updates instance weights according to the absolute value of residual error. In addition to AdaBoost, GBDT is another well-known sequential ensemble learning algorithm which builds an ensemble of decision trees by fitting each new tree to the negative gradient of the loss function of the entire ensemble [34].

Jerry laughs, the kind of laugh that tells you he's about to say something profound but lighthearted. "But that's just it! You don't see what you do. You're the glue that holds it together." "Glue? More like the tape that keeps it from falling apart. And half the time, I'm just trying not to get squished between the turnstile and the crowd during rush hour." She smirks, but wears a mask of humility beneath her jest. Their meals arrive: a steaming tuna sandwich for Lucy and a plate of fries for Jerry, piled high like the aspirations of a city that never sleeps. She takes a bite, chewing thoughtfully. "But you really think so? Life just feels-" "Like it's running a marathon with no finish line? I know the feeling. But sometimes, it's the little things that matter, Lucy. Holding your ground, keeping the customer service voice while all you want to do is escape to a beach somewhere. I've seen you handle fussy customers at the booth; they can be downright harrowing." A chorus of laughter erupts from a group at a nearby table, the kind that reminds Lucy of more carefree days, and she shifts her gaze. Outside, the city buzzes with life. "Speaking of escape," Jerry says abruptly, "what're the plans for the holidays? You doing the whole 'family gathering' thing? Baking, carols?" Lucy sighs heavily, her thoughts gliding like a feather. "Not really. I was planning on a quiet evening in with Mel, maybe watching holiday movies... you know, the usual tussle of warmth against the bleakness of winter." Jerry chuckles, smirking. "A cat, a Christmas tree, and a few cheesy rom-coms? Sounds like a recipe for a true holiday spirit, if I've ever heard one." The honest declaration makes Lucy chuckle despite herself. "Maybe I could dress Mel up as a reindeer? Just for kicks. Who knows, it might even go viral." "Definitely. Just don't forget to include the blue spruce next time." He leans back, looking pensive. "But really, Lucy... if you ever feel like breaking away from the predictable, just let me know. The office could use a little holiday cheer, and I happen to know the best spots for that." They finish their meals, the atmosphere soaked in easy chatter and the warmth of camaraderie spilling into the gaps of the gray, city sky. Then, with the carefully masked ease of a year that has leached every ounce of color from their lives, Lucy nods contemplatively. "Alright, I'll think about it. But first..." She reaches into her purse, producing a miniature bottle of hot sauce. "I can't let another sandwich go by without giving it a kick!" Jerry snorts. "So that's the secret! Next time you'll call yourself a culinary genius." They share a laugh, the sound intertwining with the hustle of the world outside, a reminder-some days it certainly feels....

The observed correlation between force-induced unfolding of the NRR and S2 site accessibility provides a mechanistic insight into the regulation of Notch signalling. The notion that mechanical force can regulate Notch activation has significant implications for our understanding of cell-cell communication and tissue development. In addition to the canonical Notch signalling pathway, there is evidence to suggest that non-canonical Notch signalling pathways exist, which do not rely on the proteolytic cleavage cascade [27,28]. These pathways are thought to involve the direct interaction of the Notch receptor with other proteins, such as p53, and can result in the regulation of gene expression independent of the Notch intracellular domain [29,30]. The regulation of these non-canonical pathways is poorly understood and warrants further investigation. The Notch signalling pathway has been implicated in a wide range of diseases, including cancers, neurological disorders, and cardiovascular disease [3-8]. The dysregulation of Notch signalling has been linked to the development and progression of various types of cancer, including T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, breast cancer, and lung cancer [31-34]. Furthermore, mutations in Notch receptors have been identified in several human diseases, including CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy), a rare genetic disorder characterized by stroke and dementia [35]. The intricate control mechanisms that regulate Notch signalling are still not fully understood and require further investigation. The mechanical force model of Notch activation provides a new perspective on the regulation of Notch signalling and highlights the importance of considering the mechanical properties of the Notch receptor and its ligands in the signalling process. Further research is needed to fully elucidate the mechanisms of Notch signalling and to explore the potential therapeutic applications of targeting the Notch pathway in disease. In conclusion, the Notch signalling pathway is a complex and highly regulated process that plays a critical role in cell differentiation and development.
