To avoid negative backlash of this kind, CSR engagements need to be genuine and aligned with the core values of the company (Alhouti, Johnson, & Holloway, 2016; Beckman, Colwell, & Cunningham, 2009; Mazutis & Slawinski, 2015; McShane & Cunningham, 2012) - a concept recently labeled CSR authenticity (Beckman et al., 2009; McShane & Cunningham, 2012). Authenticity is particularly relevant to CSR evaluations since it captures the tensions inherent in CSR. Additionally, previous work suggests that perceived authenticity determines the acceptance and relative success of CSR engagement (Beckman et al., 2009). Consequently, perceived authenticity can mitigate unfavorable outcomes such as perceptions of window dressing or greenwashing. Although the idea of CSR authenticity has been studied from the perspective of, for example, consumers (Alhouti et al., 2016), senior business managers, consultants, and nonprofit managers in various countries (Berger, Cunningham, & Drumwright, 2007), leaders of multinational companies (MNCs) and nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) (Beckman et al., 2009), and from a theoretical perspective (Mazutis & Slawinski, 2015), the literature on authenticity in the context of CSR from the perspective of employees is scarce. Analyses of employees' evaluation of the authenticity of their organizations' CSR programs are particularly rare. To our knowledge, only McShane and Cunningham (2012) have carried out in-depth-interviews with employees that identified drivers of authenticity from their perspective. Our study contributes to this important stream of research. In this investigation, we seek to develop and empirically test a CSR authenticity model that examines the factors that influence employees' evaluation of the authenticity of their company's CSR engagement (Fig. 1). Unlike previous CSR studies that have mainly focused on external stakeholders, we focus on employees, addressing recent calls for enhanced research approaches that shed light on how employees respond to CSR programs (McShane & Cunningham, 2012; Rupp, Wright, Aryee, & Luo, 2015). Drawing from persuasion knowledge theory (Friestad & Wright, 1994), attribution theory (Kelley, 1973), and McShane and Cunningham's qualitative study on CSR authenticity from the employee perspective (2012), the roles of four important antecedents for the authenticity evaluation are analyzed: employees' evaluation of the company's CSR advertising (including affective evaluation of the advertising, message credibility and cause-company-fit), perceived fit between corporate culture and CSR engagement, and two perceived underlying CSR motives (unselfish versus selfish, noneconomic versus economic reasons). Our selection of these four antecedents reflects the results of the much-cited CSR meta-analysis by Orlitzky, Schmidt, and Rynes (2003), who identified three main research concepts related to CSR, namely, the tensions inherent in CSR between prosociality and corporate financial performance (captured in perceived underlying CSR motives), reputation building (captured in the evaluation of CSR advertising), and the internal-resources perspective (captured in perceived corporate culture fit). Since previous research indicates that involvement in CSR can either diminish or enhance the relationships between the antecedents and the evaluation of CSR engagements (Du et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2013), employees' involvement in CSR is incorporated as a moderator.

The king is more wroth than before, since tidings of Lord Warwick's restless machinations in France have soured his temper. He cannot hear thy name without threats against thy father as a secret adherent of Lancaster, and accuseth thee of witching his chamberlain, - as, in truth, thou hast. The Duchess of Bedford is more than ever under the influence of Friar Bungey, to whose spells and charms, and not to our good swords, she ascribes the marvellous flight of Warwick and the dispersion of our foes; and the friar, methinks, has fostered and yet feeds Edward's suspicions of thy harmless father. The king chides himself for having suffered poor Warner to depart unscathed, and even recalls the disastrous adventure of the mechanical, and swears that from the first thy father was in treasonable conspiracy with Margaret. Nay, sure I am, that if I dared to wed thee while his anger lasts, he would condemn thee as a sorceress, and give me up to the secret hate of my old foes the Woodvilles. But fie! be not so appalled, my Sibyll; Edward's passions, though fierce, are changeful, and patience will reward us both." "Meanwhile, thou lovest me, Hastings!" said Sibyll, with great emotion. "Oh, if thou knewest how I torment myself in thine absence! I see thee surrounded by the fairest and the loftiest, and say to myself, 'Is it possible that he can remember me?' But thou lovest me still - still - still, and ever! Dost thou not?" And Hastings said and swore. "And the Lady Bonville?" asked Sibyll, trying to smile archly, but with the faltering tone of jealous fear. "I have not seen her for months," replied the noble, with a slight change of countenance. "She is at one of their western manors. They say her lord is sorely ill; and the Lady Bonville is a devout hypocrite, and plays the tender wife. But enough of such ancient and worn-out memories. Thy father - sorrows he still for his Eureka? I can learn no trace of it." "See," said Sibyll, recalled to her filial love, and pointing to Warner as they now drew near the house, "see, he shapes another Eureka from his thoughts!" "How fares it, dear Warner?" asked the noble, taking the scholar's hand. "Ah," cried the student, roused at the sight of his powerful protector, "bringest thou tidings of IT? Thy cheerful eye tells me that - no - no - thy face changes! They have destroyed it! Oh, that I could be young once more!" "What!" said the world-wise man, astonished. "If thou hadst another youth, wouldst thou cherish the same delusion, and go again through a life of hardship, persecution, and wrong?" "My noble son," said the philosopher, "for hours when I have felt the wrong, the persecution, and the hardship, count the days and the nights when I felt only the hope and the glory and the joy!

But just as we are crossing the great overpass that joins us up with Highway 50, the engine revs up inexplicably and there's no power to the wheels. We are just coasting. Fortunately it is downhill but once momentum is gone we start slowing down. Eventually, I discover that if I turn off the engine and then restart it I can accellerate for about twenty yards before the transmission disconnects again. I hobble to an off ramp and call my insurance's 24-hour line. They say they might reimburse my towing expense but can't be sure because for some reason they could not pull up my policy. It's just after midnight and I decide to deal with it in the morning. The exit we are at is pitch dark save for the glow of the AutoMall sign in the distance so I limp the van to the next exit down. Fortunately, that's the one with about a half dozen fast food joints and diners and about as many motels. The Holiday Inn Express costs more than we have on us (no, we have no credit cards). In order to use my mother-in-laws AmEx card, she'd have to fax them a copy of her driver's license. That's more of a hassle than I'm willing to put her through. But the desk clerk gives us a line on a cheaper place: the Inns of America. That's when I discover that we don't have any reverse as well as any forward gears. I have to push the van out of the parking spot with a bad knee earned over the weekend (see previous post). Actually it only hurts when twisted not during normal pressure, so when the older teen offerst to help, I tell her to stay in the car. We make it down the road in fits and starts and it turns out that with her contribution we scrape together just enough to get us all a room. It should be a relief, and to a great degree it was. We call my mother-in-law to update her and she agrees to meet us the next morning around 9am. Sack time. However, my middle daughter gets up about a dozen times that night to the bathroom and my oldest (the one with the cash) ends up getting sick in the middle of the night. Too much stress, seafood, and probably some allergies as well. Fortunately she makes it to the toilet and there's no extra mess which is good because if I smell it, I'm compelled to add my own. But the poor thing, I felt bad for her and would've forced her to accept a hug from ol' dad if I wasn't exhausted. Next day: Girls seem well, if tired. Ma-in-law shows up promptly as I'm negotiating a tow and locating a transmission repair shop.

Today we dive into the world of online content creation, where passion meets persistence, and every upload could be a step towards success or a lesson learned. Matthew Tran, the brains behind Engineered Truth, understands this journey all too well. From navigating the murky waters of a nascent YouTube landscape to becoming a trusted voice for aspiring professionals and students alike, his story serves as a beacon for many who dare to dream. As we sit down with Matt, it becomes evident that the road wasn't paved with instant gratification. He recalls the initial struggles: "When I first hit that 'upload' button in 2011, there weren't countless tutorials or strategies. It was just me, my ideas, and a small camera." The early days saw Matt grappling with the complexities of production, from lighting to scripting, creating content that resonated with barely a handful of viewers. Yet, that didn't deter him; instead, it sparked a relentless curiosity to improve. "Every video was a lesson," he reflects, acknowledging that the technical aspects of video production were just one piece of the puzzle. What truly mattered was crafting authentic connections with his audience. He diligently studied his analytics, a tool he describes as invaluable. "Understanding who watched your content, when they watched it, and why they engaged was like finding gold." With every dip and rise in viewership, Matt adapted, learning to refine his message and spotlight the topics that resonated most. Audience engagement soon transformed into a community. Matt emphasizes, "It's not just about numbers. It's about building relationships." He recounts a pivotal moment when he decided to directly engage with his audience through comment responses and Q&A sessions. This, he notes, helped foster loyalty and trust, encouraging viewers to return and share their experiences. As the Engineered Truth brand flourished, monetization became a hot topic. "There's this misconception that if you build it, they will come," Matt explains. The reality is more nuanced. "Monetization isn't just about ad revenue; it's about diversifying your income streams." He shares tips, such as exploring affiliate marketing, merchandise, and even leveraging platforms like Patreon. "Think big! Don't box yourself into one revenue stream; that's a surefire way to limit your potential." In the midst of these discussions, we address criticism. "YouTube is a tough crowd; the internet is unforgiving," Matt admits. His approach? Embrace it. "Criticism isn't the enemy; it's feedback. Use it to evolve," he advises, sharing that constructive critiques shaped the content he eventually created. He encourages aspiring YouTubers to develop a thick skin and focus instead on how to improve. Investment also plays a critical role in his roadmap to success. "The day I saw my first paycheck, I knew I had to invest wisely. Whether it's in better equipment, courses, or even hiring help, reinvestment is key," he emphasizes. By prioritizing growth, he was able to shift focus away from manageable pain points, allowing for creative freedom and exploration of new ideas. As our conversation unfolds, Matt's enthusiasm for his craft shines brightly, illuminating the myriad possibilities available to aspiring content creators. He is a living testament to the adage that struggles breed strength, and with the right mindset, anyone can carve their niche in the digital world. So, as we embark on this journey through YouTube's complexities with Matthew Tran, buckle up. His insights may very well inspire you to turn your own hustle into transformative success. Whether you're an aspiring YouTuber or simply curious about the digital landscape, there's something to be learned from his relentless pursuit of excellence.

He said administration was never discussed while he was chairman of the club and he believed even by 2011 its debt was "manageable". The trial heard about a fraudulent attempt to buy Rangers before Craig Whyte came on the scene. Two individuals, said to have links to the brother of an English football boss, produced a letter from a Belgian bank stating they had 50m euros ( 42m) to invest. But one of the pair was found to have the same name as someone banned from being a company director in the UK. The letter was also discovered to be "fraudulent". Mike McGill, former Murray Group finance director, told the court that another offer came in and was to be funded by a Lithuanian bank. The court heard it seemed to have the "wherewithal" to complete a sale. But, Mr McGill told the court that the Murray Group became "extremely uncomfortable" dealing with the Lithuanian bank because of accusations it was involved in "organised crime and money laundering". There were also added concerns about any "furore" given the publicity surrounding the Lithuanian owners of another Scottish club. At that time, Heart of Midlothian were owned by Lithuanian tycoon Vladimir Romanov. When he took to the witness box, Craig Whyte's then lawyer, Gary Withey, admitted that he initially thought his client was part of the Whyte and Mackay whisky group. Mr Withey said that Whyte had been portrayed as "someone with substantial financial wealth", when he first showed an interest in buying Rangers. He added: "Most people in the City would have said that." When asked how much was spent investigating Craig Whyte and his business ahead of the Rangers takeover deal, a key adviser to Sir David Murray admitted it had not been a lot. In referring to the amount spent on due diligence into Craig Whyte, David Horne told the trial: "Not very much at all. I don't know. Possibly nothing." Two weeks before Craig Whyte took over Rangers, Dave King, then a director at the club, warned of a possible future police investigation into the Whyte takeover. His warning came in a letter in April 2011 to the statutory takeover panel, set up in relation to the deal. Mr King wrote of concerns about the source of Mr Whyte's funds to buy the club. Mr King said he was excluded from involvement in the takeover deal. Sir David Murray said this was not true. Craig Whyte lawyer, Gary Withey, said that before the Rangers takeover, he had told Whyte he would be "mad" to do the deal and urged him to walk away. He said he had been "shocked" about the lack of financial information that had been provided by the club's sellers. Mr Withey said Whyte responded to his concerns by laughing. Gary Withey, who was hired by Craig Whyte to see through the Rangers deal, was unable to tell the court how old he was.

As he wandered through the labyrinthine corridors, Mr. Pett's thoughts grew darker and more foreboding. The cacophony of creative energies that swirled around him was a constant reminder of the chaos that had descended upon his life since his marriage. The sound of typewriters clacking away, the rustling of pages being turned, and the occasional burst of laughter or argument all blended together to create a maddening symphony that threatened to shatter his fragile nerves. He paused in front of the door to the study, where his wife was holding court with her latest protege, a young poet named Reginald who was expounding the virtues of free verse to a rapt audience. Mr. Pett's eyes narrowed as he listened to the young man's bombastic declarations, his mind reeling with the thought of the countless hours he would have to spend editing and revising the resulting manuscript. As he turned to leave, he was confronted by the imposing figure of his wife, her eyes flashing with a fierce intensity that made him take a step back. "Peter, darling, come and meet Reginald," she exclaimed, her voice dripping with enthusiasm. "He's going to revolutionize the art of poetry!" Mr. Pett forced a smile onto his face, his mind racing with the prospect of the impending literary battles that lay ahead. He knew that his wife would not rest until she had coaxed the hidden genius out of every last one of her proteges, and he was the one who would be left to pick up the pieces when the inevitable collapse came. As he made his way back to his own study, he couldn't help but think of his first wife, Elmer Ford, who had died suddenly and unexpectedly. He had always felt a pang of regret and guilt whenever he thought of her, wondering what his life would have been like if he had married someone more... conventional. Someone who didn't have a talent for attracting a coterie of eccentric writers and artists. The thought was interrupted by the sound of his wife's voice, calling out from the study. "Peter, darling, come and join us! We're having a discussion about the merits of surrealism!" Mr. Pett sighed, his eyes rolling heavenward in a gesture of resignation. He knew that he was trapped in a world of his wife's creation, a world of artistic expression and creative chaos. And he was not sure if he would ever find his way out.

One example of multi-mode data is household travel surveys and travel diaries using CAPI or similar techniques, where participants also undertake a survey of their travel using GPS devices (Bricka, Sen, Paleti, & Bhat, 2012; Cottrill et al., 2013; Stopher, FitzGerald, & Xu, 2007). Another example is surveys on household and building characteristics that affect energy use and detailed energy use data from smart meters (Kavousian, Rajagopal, & Fischer, 2013). The Understanding Society longitudinal dataset, consisting of a core annual survey on multiple social, economic and lifecourse constructs, as well as a unique biomarker dataset on survey respondents consisting of blood samples and other physical measurements, as well as a short questionnaire on health, medications and so on, is a multi-mode survey allowing novel research on social determinants of health (Buck & McFall, 2012). There are several reasons for using a multi-mode approach to studying urban living. First, analyzing multidimensional social, economic or behavioral problems from multiple perspectives have the potential to allow research questions to be raised - and answered - beyond that which is possible by analyzing each dataset separately, and to yield a richer, perhaps more complete view of the phenomena under study (Lahat, Adali, & Jutten, 2015). Many new forms of data are also available at a finer spatial resolution, and are timely and available in real-time or close to real-time, as they are continuously and passively generated by sensor systems or actively generated by citizen participants. Such data can potentially provide information on the wider social and economic context to survey responses. The benefits of mixed-mode survey data collection are many, including cost-effectiveness and reduction in coverage bias and nonresponse error (de Leeuw, 2005), and some of these benefits also potentially accrue to situations where data are collected using entirely different systems, not just with different modes in the same survey process. Second, it helps bring together methodological expertise on data from different disciplinary and practitioner communities, e.g., communities with specialized knowledge in social surveys, sensor systems, GIS, social media or other highly unstructured data, which tend to be in different disciplines. This leads to an interdisciplinary approach to data collection and to data that are not too specific to each application. Third, urban data systems tend to be highly siloed as they are held by researchers within specific disciplines or government administrators having specific responsibilities in transportation, housing, environment and so on. Depending on the purpose of the data collection, a multi-mode approach can help address data fragmentation thereby allowing a more comprehensive, broad-based approach to addressing urban challenges relating to sustainability, social justice, resilience and other end goals. Fourth, having different sources of data on the same construct allows going beyond description, monitoring and hypothesis generation, to explanation, inference and understanding of causality in urban phenomenon. Finally, a major benefit is that there is a possibility of collecting ground truth data, to be able to compare and validate data quality in different data streams.

The astacin metalloprotease family has since been found to be ubiquitous in nematodes, with multiple members identified in C. elegans, including NAS-36, NAS-37, and NAS-38 (Hishida et al., 1996; Davis et al., 2004; Novelli et al., 2004, 2006; Suzuki et al., 2004). These enzymes have been shown to play critical roles in various biological processes, including cuticle biosynthesis, molting, and embryogenesis. In parasitic nematodes, astacin metalloproteases have been identified in species such as Haemonchus contortus and Teladorsagia circumcincta, where they are thought to play similar roles in cuticle biosynthesis and development (Laing et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013). The importance of astacin metalloproteases in nematode development and survival makes them attractive targets for the development of novel anthelmintics. Inhibitors of these enzymes could potentially disrupt cuticle biosynthesis, leading to impaired nematode development and survival. Several studies have demonstrated the potential of astacin metalloprotease inhibitors as anthelmintics, with inhibitors of the C. elegans NAS-36 enzyme showing potent activity against the parasite (Novelli et al., 2006). Furthermore, RNA interference (RNAi) studies have shown that silencing of astacin metalloprotease genes in parasitic nematodes leads to impaired development and survival (Smith et al., 2013). The development of astacin metalloprotease inhibitors as anthelmintics is an active area of research, with several approaches being explored. One approach is the use of small molecule inhibitors, which can be designed to target the active site of the enzyme and disrupt its catalytic activity. Several small molecule inhibitors have been identified, including peptide-based inhibitors and non-peptide inhibitors, which have shown potent activity against astacin metalloproteases (Novelli et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2013). Another approach is the use of RNAi-based therapies, which involve the delivery of small RNA molecules that silence the expression of astacin metalloprotease genes. This approach has shown promise in animal models, with RNAi-based therapies leading to significant reductions in nematode burdens (Smith et al., 2013). In addition to their potential as anthelmintics, astacin metalloproteases are also of interest as vaccine candidates. The enzymes are highly conserved between nematode species, making them potential targets for broad-spectrum vaccines. Furthermore, the enzymes are expressed on the surface of nematodes, making them accessible to the host immune system. Several studies have demonstrated the potential of astacin metalloprotease-based vaccines, with vaccination leading to significant protection against nematode infection (Dalton et al., 2003; Diemert et al., 2008). In conclusion, astacin metalloproteases are critical enzymes involved in nematode development and survival, making them attractive targets for the development of novel anthelmintics and vaccines. Further research is needed to fully understand the role of these enzymes in nematode biology and to develop effective inhibitors and vaccines. However, the potential of astacin metalloproteases as targets for the control of gastrointestinal nematode infections is clear, and continued research in this area is likely to lead to significant advances in the control of these debilitating diseases.

In no small measure I was tempted to abandon my quest, to seek solace instead in some cheerful tavern where the ruddy glow of local spirits mingled with the laughter of townsfolk, unburdened by the heavy mantle of historical responsibility. But duty, that most unrelenting taskmaster, pulled at my sleeve like an importunate child, imploring me to persist. I settled in at an inn decidedly lesser in elegance than the one you might favor; the only adornments were the faded portraits of anonymous dignitaries whose somber gazes seemed to inhabit a time long devoid of joy. I dined upon a dubious stew, the meat of indeterminate origin swam languidly in a broth that conveyed the impression of being both lukewarm and unwelcoming, somewhat akin to my own spirits. With each passing day, I scoured the landscape, navigating through soft meadows and dense woodland, only to be greeted with blank stares and the occasional chuckle from the locals when I inquired about Rozel Abbey. Their faces betrayed little intelligence regarding matters of the heart and stone, content instead to extol the virtues of their own more modern establishments. They directed me, more than once, to the neighbor's barn or to the baker's house, where tales of the last epidemic of animal pox or the virtues of the recent harvest seemed to hold more weight than the whispers of history ingrained in crumbling walls. Then, one auspicious afternoon, chance-a romantic of the most capricious kind-bestowed upon me a benevolent encounter. I found myself in the company of an ancient, though sprightly, local named Achille, whose bedraggled beard suggested wisdom enriched by many years of detours and diversions through life's more humorous labyrinths. He was lounging on a weather-beaten log outside a slightly better tavern than my own, and, upon hearing my plight, his eyes brightened. "Ah, Rozel Abbey!" he rasped, his voice bearing the gravelly textures of distant thunderclouds, "Why that's a girl with a dress dusty enough to hide in plain sight!" We struck up a grand conversation, his laughter punctuating the air as I shared my mission with an exuberance that seemed to breathe life into my own dire pursuits. With great flourish, Achille spun me tales of long-lost monks who roamed the Abbey's halls, their spectral forms preoccupied with divine musings while the world outside sped past in an endless blur of cobblestones and creeping brambles. His genuine delight in recounting the stories of bygone eras transformed my irritation into gentle anticipation; it was as if the very fabric of time was pulling together to allow me glimpses of wondrous history. Thus inspired, I accompanied Achille on a pilgrimage-trundling from village to village, gathering the loose threads of folklore, old parchments, and half-remembered verses that reverberated through the whispers of wind amid the trees. Each night, as the sun spilled over the horizon, I recorded every detail of our misadventures, the pulse of Rozel Abbey gradually taking form in my imagination: a tapestry of shadowy monks, echoing chants, and beams of light filtering through stained glass. How enchanting, my dear Paul, to discover that adventure often lurks in unexpected corners, patiently awaiting the daring souls who grasp it with open hands!

So that I was led to reason that colour must be washed out of hair by exposure to the weather; as perhaps in his case it was. I think that his face was almost handsome, in a rough, hard-bitten way, and he was as hairy a man as I ever saw. His short beard was like curled wire; but I can remember that long after I had grown to resent being kissed by women, being no longer a baby, I gladly climbed his knee to kiss my grandfather, though his shaven upper-lip was like a rasp. In these early days I lived with my mother in a little house of a short row that stood on a quay, in a place that was not exactly a dock, nor a wharf, nor a public thoroughfare; but where people from the dock trying to find a wharf, people from a wharf looking for the dock, and people from the public thoroughfare in anxious search of dock and wharves, used to meet and ask each other questions. It was a detached piece of Blackwall which had got adrift among locks and jetties, and was liable to be cut off from the rest of the world at any moment by the arrival of a ship and the consequent swinging of a bridge, worked by two men at a winch. So that it was a commonplace of my early childhood (though the sight never lost its interest) to observe from a window a ship, passing as it were up the street, warped into dock by the capstans on the quay. And the capstan-songs of the dockmen - Shenandore, Mexico is covered with Snow, Hurrah for the Black Ball Line, and the like - were as much my nursery rhymes as Little Boy Blue and Sing a Song o' Sixpence. These things are done differently nowadays; the cottages on the quay are gone, and the neighbourhood is a smokier place, where the work is done by engines, with no songs. My father was so much at sea that I remember little of him at all. He was a ship's officer, and at the time I am to tell of he was mate of the brig Juno, owned by Viney and Marr, one of the small shipowning firms that were common enough thirty years ago, though rarer now; the sort of firm that was made by a pushing skipper and an ambitious shipping clerk, beginning with a cheap vessel bought with money raised mainly by pawning the ship. Such concerns often did well, and sometimes grew into great lines; perhaps most of them yielded the partners no more than a comfortable subsistence; and a good few came to grief, or were kept going by questionable practices which have since become illegal - sometimes in truth by what the law called crime, even then. Viney had been a ship's officer - had indeed served under Grandfather Nat, who was an old skipper.

Moreover, as the festive season approaches, it becomes increasingly paramount that we shift our focus toward nurturing community ties and fostering connections among the elderly. Increasingly, the narrative surrounding the holidays often revolves around bustling families, festive gatherings, and shared laughter. Yet, intertwined within this celebration is the sobering truth that for a significant number of older individuals, these same days can become a solitary reminder of their isolation. Statistics reveal a chilling reality: approximately one in three older adults express feelings of loneliness that are exacerbated during the holiday season. It is imperative for local communities and social organizations to redouble their efforts in creating supportive environments for older citizens. Community outreach programs can serve as essential lifelines, enabling volunteers to deliver not only meals but also genuine companionship. The simple act of sharing a meal or engaging in conversation can act as a balm for the fraught souls who, too often, are left to grapple with their silence amidst the celebrations. Volunteer initiatives, such as community visits, home-cooked meal deliveries, or even hosting social gatherings, can forge connections and, crucially, highlight to older folks that they have not been forgotten. The simple act of a neighbor checking in can transcend mere goodwill; it can encapsulate the essence of community spirit that inherently combats the pernicious effects of loneliness. As Mr. Lamb poignantly mentioned, fostering relationships with those who live nearby is not only an act of kindness but also a vital step towards cultivating an environment where the elderly feel valued and supported. Additionally, digital engagement should not be overlooked. In an increasingly interconnected world, utilizing technology to bridge the gap between generations can provide older individuals with new avenues for interaction. Initiatives designed to teach digital literacy or set up video calls can foster intergenerational bonding, drawing lines of dialogue where none existed before. It is this dual approach-simultaneously embracing both direct social interactions and the wonders of technology-that can help diminish the harsh isolation experienced by so many. Furthermore, local councils and organizations must take proactive measures to address the dwindling resources allocated to social care. The alarming practice of 15-minute care visits must be re-evaluated. Quality over quantity is paramount; a brief encounter is unlikely to meet the emotional and social needs of individuals who depend on these visits for connection and support. Advocating for longer visitation times and more comprehensive care strategies could allow for more meaningful interactions, ensuring that care is not only adequate but also compassionate. As we circle around the festive period, let us remold our thoughts from mere contemplation of loneliness to actionable solutions. The ethos of holiday spirit ought to be shared across our communities, uniquely woven through the fabric of our interactions. In recognizing the myriad faces behind our neighbors' doors and resisting the urge to retreat into our own lives, we can fortify the societal bonds that are crucial during this season. Let this Christmas become a catalyst for change-an impetus to break the cycle of neglect. By extending the hand of friendship and active participation, we can kindle a sense of belonging among our elderly citizens that so often dims during the harsh winter months. It is through collective efforts of empathy and outreach that we can foster a society that does not just coexist but flourishes in unity, ensuring that no one faces the trials of loneliness alone.

Well, captain," he said, "what has this to do with the present evil that you seem to apprehend?" "To do with it, lad? nothing - 'xcept that it reminds me that we little know what is in store for us. Here are we becalmed - three day's sail from the coral island, where the niggers were so near converting us into cooked victuals, and I wouldn't at this minute give twopence in security for the life of any one on board the Rover." "Why, what mean you?" asked Will, with increasing perplexity. "Some of the crew are bad enough, no doubt, but many of them are evidently good men - what is it that you fear?" "Fear! why, there's everything to fear," said the captain in a suppressed but excited whisper, drawing still closer to his friend. "I've often sailed in these seas, and I know that while some of the traders sailing between these islands and South America and other parts are decentish enough, others are as great cut-throats as ever deserved to swing at the yard-arm. But that's not the point. I have overheard, of late, some of the rascals plotting to murder the officers and take this ship. But I cannot point 'em out, for though I heard their voices I couldn't see their faces. I think I know who they are, but could not swear to 'em, and it would be worse than useless to denounce them till we have some evidence to go on. I therefore want you to help me with your advice and assistance, so that we may get up a counterplot to spoil their fun - for I'm quite certain that if we fail to - hark! what's that?" Will did not answer, but both listened intently to the sound which had interrupted Captain Dall's discourse. It was evident that the officer and men of the watch had also heard it, for they, too, had ceased to walk to and fro, and their figures could be dimly seen in a listening attitude at the gangway. For several minutes they listened without hearing anything - then a hoarse, guttural shout broke the stillness of the night for a few seconds and died away. The men looked at each other, and some of the more superstitious among them grew pale. Again the cry was repeated, somewhat nearer, and again all was still. Some of the oldest hands in the watch stood transfixed and powerless with terror. They would have faced death in any form manfully, but this mysterious sound unnerved them! The officer of the watch went down to report it to Captain Blathers, who immediately came on deck. Just as he appeared, the cry was repeated and a slight splash was heard. "Some one in distress," cried Captain Blathers promptly; "a crew for the starboard quarter-boat to pick him up. Stand by to lower. Be smart, lads!"

It's got four staircases whereas the greatest of rulers at this time was usually satisfied with just one. It also does not seem to have any entrances.' A map of the Thames was found among 60,000 documents in the collection showing an interest in the country. Detailed maps were a key part of the collection and it is estimated to take around two years to catalogue. Mr Barber said one of the most unique things about the collection was that the monarch built it up and used it himself, unlike his collections of scientific instruments and books which he left to his assistants to manage. It reveals the personal side of the King - particularly in plans for a bathing machine, popular with prudish Victorians who wanted to swim in the sea without anyone seeing them. King George III ruled from 1760 to 1820. The King's bathing machine was particularly large, allowing him to bathe naked in the sea at Weymouth in his own form of private swimming pool without ever being seen. As well as the scrawled plans and legal documents the collection also contains thousands of maps, showing the interest of the ruler in the rest of the world - despite the fact he only travelled as far as Weymouth. 'He was an armchair traveller,' said Mr Barber. 'He didn't actually travel further than Weymouth but through books and maps he eagerly learnt about the rest of the world and was able to do a grand tour of Italy. 'George probably didn't travel far because he was a conscientious leader and didn't want to be away from his work for too long.' Amongst the dozens of papers are also items the monarch is likely to have inherited, such as a 'birth certificate' for New York. This was likely to have been presented to the Duke of York in 1664 after it was captured by the English from the Dutch and renamed from New Amsterdam. He also collected early images of Canada and plans for churches in East London. Some of the items produced and collected by the King are likely to have been put into the collection when he suffered episodes of mania. Mr Barber added: 'The 1780s and 1790s were very hard years for George as he had lost the American colonies and had these really very severe attacks of mental illness.

Other work suggests that these innovations could be combined to create new types of public transit services that can achieve both high ridership and financial viability (MacKenzie et al., 2014). Yet, several authors have warned of the potentially large rebound effects if people substitute walking, cycling and transit trips with automated vehicles (Brown et al., 2014; Milakis et al., 2017); while others note that automation may actually increase safety concerns for cyclists and pedestrians (Clabaux et al., 2018). In fact, several scholars have argued that the very notion of sustainability is missing from the discussion around automated vehicles, and that the focus instead seems to be on increasing convenience and comfort (Apostolopoulou and Pijanowski, 2018; Shladover, 2018). This Special Issue focuses on the role of users in shaping innovation outcomes and the future of mobility. In this section, we first define what we mean by 'users,' and then briefly outline the reasons why their choices matter. Users include all individuals who interact with a product or service, either directly or indirectly. A direct user interacts with the product/service itself, such as driving an electric car or riding in a shared automated taxi. An indirect user does not necessarily come in contact with the product/service but may still be impacted by its use. Examples include people who walk or cycle near automated vehicles, those living along the routes used by shared automated taxis, and anyone breathing polluted air emitted by cars. Users can also be segmented based on their level of adoption: non-users (those who do not currently adopt a given technology or behavior), early adopters (the first segment of the population to adopt), mainstream adopters (majority of the population), and laggards (the last group to adopt). Users also differ in terms of their personal characteristics, motivations, perceptions and preferences. These differences impact how they respond to innovations, and ultimately determine the success or failure of the innovation. Users thus play a critical role in shaping the diffusion of new products/services through the marketplace. Diffusion is commonly described using an s-shaped curve, where sales start slowly at the beginning, grow rapidly once a certain threshold is reached, and finally slow down again when saturation is approached. The exact shape of the diffusion curve depends on factors such as the price and quality of the innovation relative to existing alternatives, the ease with which users can try it out, and the strength of social norms that encourage or discourage adoption. At each stage of the diffusion process, different segments of users drive growth, with innovators and early adopters initially purchasing the innovation, followed by the majority of users, and finally the laggards.

I saw outside. We were crossing Ambala Cantt. Station. We had covered almost half of our journey. All of us got down at the platform to have some fresh air and stretch ourselves. We did not stop here for more than 15 minutes. We had to reach Shimla before evening. At around 7 PM we reached Shimla. It was dark and cold. There was not much traffic on the roads. We checked into our hotel "The Woodville Palace". This hotel has been constructed during the British era and is still maintained in the same manner. There are huge lawns, a bar, a discotheque, a billiards room, a swimming pool and a restaurant. The rooms are luxurious and comfortable. We had booked three rooms. Each room had two beds. We kept our luggage in our rooms and came out to have dinner. After having our dinner we went to the discotheque to enjoy a drink or two. The music was loud and the dance floor was crowded. There were many foreigners playing Golf. We had fun watching them play. We tried to hit a ball but failed miserably. Then we proceeded towards Chail. Chail is famous for its palace. The palace is now converted into a resort. We spent about an hour there. Then we went to Tattapani. Tattapani is famous for its sulphur springs. People come here to take bath in these springs. They believe that their diseases get cured by taking bath in these springs. On our return journey, we stopped at a place called Shogi. We had lunch at a roadside Dhabha. The food was tasty and cheap. We reached Shimla at around 5 PM. We went to the Mall Road. We bought some souvenirs for our families and friends. Later we went to the Ridge Grounds. We sat there for sometime enjoying the view of the city from above. We went to the Jakhoo Temple. This temple is situated on the highest peak of Shimla. We hired horses to climb the hill. It took us half an hour to reach the temple. The temple is dedicated to Lord Hanuman. We paid our respects to the lord and then started our descent. By the time we reached the bottom of the hill, it was already dark. We went to the hotel and changed our clothes. We had dinner at a restaurant called "Himachal Restaurant".

The postchaise rolled onward, its familiar rhythm providing a soothing backdrop to the bustling imagery that enveloped me. The twilight air was alive with the fragrance of wood-smoke and the distant murmurs of life, a tapestry woven from fading light and the soft rustle of the leaves above. It seemed as if each turn of the wheel uncovered yet another fragment of the past, like the peeling layers of an old map revealing the contours of yesteryears. Almost imperceptibly, I felt a stirring at the core of my being-a yearning that surged like the golden hues of a harvest sun dipping behind the horizon. How curious it is, this pull of nostalgia, the way it beckons us to meander along the sidewalks of memory, where every footfall is cushioned by the echoes of laughter, the sweet refrain of childhood games now grown faint but not lost. It was as though I had slipped into some alternate realm where time stood still, a pause allowed, like the stillness enveloping Gylingden as the day slipped gently into night. We turned a corner and the quaint marketplace came into sight, an assemblage of old stones and crumbling eaves, their surfaces textured with time. I could see the old baker's shop-the very place where I first tasted the warm, sugary notes of a gingerbread man, still comforting to recall. A small crowd had gathered round the window, drawn by the mouthwatering aroma that drifted through the air like a siren's call. Faded signs hung askew above their heads-remnants of past glories and bustling trade, where life seemed to overflow from each cobblestone. As we passed, my gaze was drawn to a flickering lantern hanging just beyond the square, its light a warm beacon amid the growing shadows. It illuminated the delicate stone carvings flanking the doorway of a pub, where many a tale had been spun around foaming tankards of ale. I could almost hear the raucous laughter and spirited arguments echoing through those walls, a community enmeshed in bonds of camaraderie woven over pints and stories shared. Rounding the bend, my heart leapt at the sight of the old church, with its stout tower rising defiantly against a sky that deepened into indigo. The graveyard surrounding it cradled the memories of generations, headstones standing vigil through the march of time. I recalled the whispered tales of ghostly apparitions that once made me shiver with delight, my youthful imagination stirred by the twilight tales spun by our village elders. The church, with its sturdy stone and arched windows, bore witness to the threads of life that comprised the town's tapestry. "Just a little further," I prompted the postilion, eager to traverse the threshold where contemporary life met reminiscence. I felt a soft wind caress my cheek, a gentle reminder that seasons shift relentlessly. The chill that accompanied this dusk promised the allure of fireside stories and the refuge of warm embraces. Even as the burdens of the present weighed upon my brow, I reveled in the delicate balance of remembrance and anticipation that enveloped me like a well-worn cloak. As we glided forth, the shrill call of a distant bell echoed, signaling the end of day, summoning shadows and whispers of twilight souls. In that moment, as the town unfurled before me, I knew that to wander through Gylingden was far more than just a simple journey; it was an odyssey into the unfathomable depths of my own heart, where twilight secrets danced in the embrace of burgeoning night. The evening had much to reveal, as did the paths which had led me here, their every twist and turn cradling not only memory but the very essence of longing itself.

The light from the diner's neon sign flickers rhythmically, casting erratic shadows on the stainless steel countertop. Norville stares into his lukewarm cup of coffee, its surface rippling with echoes of distant laughter from shuffling patrons. A waitress, slightly worn but sprightly, glides past him, her arms laden with greasy plates and half-hearted smiles. She doesn't pause, too busy navigating the chaos of spilled ketchup and jubilant cheers, and where's Norville's celebration? He's lost amidst the clinking of silverware and the clatter of dreams, a lone figure in a bustling tableau where everything seems to sparkle except for him. His brow furrows-a faint trace of desire mixed with dread. He still can't shake that one nagging question: "How'd I get here?" A vacant look passes across his eyes, reflecting the flickering neon above. Once, he was a harness-maker in a small town, free with the sun on his skin and laughter on his lips. Ah, the simplicity! They had no need for these fancy titles that seemed to carve out the essence of a man right down to his soul. They just wanted to connect, to laugh, to weave hands in the cosmos and create something beautiful together. But now? Now a catastrophe looms beneath the glow of local fame, and he feels like he's swallowed a whole brick of uncertainty. Could it have been that wild ambition that snagged onto his heart and led him through the glass doors of Hudsucker? He'd aimed for the stars, but somehow landed in the shadow of skyscrapers, coming up for air only to realize no one's watching anymore. He chuckles dryly, humor choking in his throat-memories flash of those boardroom faces, rigid and cold like numbing steel. Where's the warmth when the air is thick with metrics and fiscal reports? Across the diner, a pair of jazzmen erupts into harmonious life-smooth notes of brass and sax, their spirits intertwining with poetic language that Norville's too tired to grasp. They're alive, they resonate, they pulse in rhythms beyond mere statistics. Sweet harmonies soar, and for just that moment, awake from his stupor, he yearns to be part of the city's hum, the breathing machine of dreams and aspirations. But still, he remains a captive of past glories-when did the laughter dry up? When did the optimism of fresh opportunities spiral into a spiral of regret? With every tick of that mocking clock, whatever remained of youth-a time when boldness was an unshakable armor-withdraws like a tide pulling away a sandcastle. The jazzmen strut their stuff, captivating the diner, yet their magic serves only to deepen the ache in Norville's heart. He shuffles in his seat, the memory of lost camaraderie pinching him tighter. Ah, dreams, they were never meant to walk so painfully hand-in-hand with reality, were they? Suddenly he feels an itch-a spark igniting deep within, the idea forming like an ember ready to blaze forth. Damn it, he's still Norville Barnes! The boy with dreams bigger than Muncie's skyline. While the reader cannot help feeling sympathy for Rosa, he or she will also find oneself judging her actions. At one point in the book, Dash asks Rosa why she hasnt tried harder to raise her children better. She responds, "You dont know how hard it is." This response shocks the reader into realizing that Rosa Lees situation is not her fault, and yet it is. It is difficult to say whether or not Rosa Lee would have done any better had she been born to a more educated, affluent family. But there is no doubt that her situation is made worse by her lack of education and opportunity. When asked about her life, Rosa Lee says, "I never thought I could do anything else." She believes that her destiny was set for her when she was young, and that her situation was hopeless. As her own grandmother told her, "This is the way God made me and my kids." Many readers will ask if Rosa Lee is a victim of her circumstances or a product of them. But the question is misleading. Rosa Lee is neither a victim nor a product of her environment; rather, she is a combination of the two. The tragedy of Rosa Lees life is that her environment was not conducive to success. When Rosa Lee sees her friend Betty, who was raised in a stable home with supportive parents, she tells Dash, "Betty got lucky. She got out of here." But Rosa Lees situation is not merely one of bad luck. Her environment contributed heavily to her failure. Because of her own mothers low expectations, Rosa Lees future was bleak from the start. Despite this, however, Rosa Lee did have opportunities to change her life. In fact, she chose not to take advantage of those opportunities. For example, after she dropped out of school in the ninth grade, she could have gone back to get her GED. Yet she refused to do so. After dropping out, she worked for a while, but quit to have a baby. Her son died in infancy, and she went back to working. However, she soon tired of that and returned to having babies. Rosa Lee is not unique in her choices. Many women in similar situations choose not to go back to school or hold down jobs. Even though they may want to succeed, they feel they wont be able to. Rosa Lees mother once said, "Its not easy being poor. You need to be smart, and you need some kind of luck.... Its just too much for people like us." Rosa Lee believed her. Dash quotes Rosa Lee saying, "It doesnt make any difference how hard you try. You still end up getting nowhere." Her view of herself and her society were shaped by her experiences. Rosa Lee grew up believing that she was worthless, that she was doomed to fail. Her self-image is reflected in the names she gives her children: Deedee, which stands for Dont Ever Expect Anything, and Bobby, whose name means Born To Lose. Both of these beliefs were reinforced by her family members. Rosa Lees father told her, "All girls are dumb," and her mother told her, "Girls cant think." Their views of women are shared by most of her friends and relatives, and they are reinforced by popular culture, which depicts women as sex objects. Rosa Lees family and community provided few positive role models for her. They lacked any sense of hope, and they expected nothing from themselves. Their worldview is summed up by one of Rosa Lees neighbors, who says, "We all just live to die." Rosa Lees peers, who were mostly dropouts, taught her little. When she started school, she didnt know how to write her name.

A total of 30 nations sent 694 athletes to the 1952 Oslo Winter Olympics. Most of them stayed at the newly constructed Ullevaal Stadion, where the opening ceremony was held. Some events took place at the Holmenkollen Ski Jump, built in 1892 but rebuilt several times since then. Today, it hosts annual international competitions and houses the Ski Museum, which features exhibits about the history of skiing and other winter sports. The FIS World Cup Biathlon takes place each year at the Holmenkollen National Arena. Garmisch-Partenkirchen, Germany (1936) This Bavarian town hosted the last Winter Olympic Games before World War II interrupted the tradition. The games were opened by Adolf Hitler, who had already begun rebuilding Germany's military forces in violation of the Treaty of Versailles. But German athletes didn't do very well at these games, winning only three gold medals out of a possible 17. The main venue for these games was the Olympia-Schanze ski jump, which still exists today and hosts major international ski-jumping competitions every January. It also serves as a popular tourist attraction, offering spectacular views from its observation deck. Cortina d'Ampezzo, Italy (1956) With the exception of the speed skating events, all of the 1956 Winter Olympic Games events took place within walking distance of Cortina d'Ampezzo's city center. The Olympic Ice Stadium is still there, along with the original Olympic Village, which has been converted into apartments. And the ski jump is still in operation as part of the Eugenio Monti Cross Country Skiing Centre. The slopes around Cortina d'Ampezzo are still popular with winter sports enthusiasts, but the town's reputation as a fashionable resort attracts many visitors who come for the shopping rather than the skiing. Squaw Valley, California (1960) Walt Disney was responsible for designing the pageantry of the 1960 Winter Olympic Games, including the torch and cauldron for the opening ceremonies. The Squaw Valley Olympic Skating Rink is no longer operational, but the Olympic flame still burns in front of the Resort at Squaw Creek, and the ski jump tower can still be seen on High Camp. The resort hosts an annual celebration of the games in February, and you'll find memorabilia displayed throughout the lodge and shops. Innsbruck, Austria (1964 and 1976) Although the Austrian city of Innsbruck had to step in as host for the 1976 games when Denver voters rejected funding for the games, the 1964 games were originally awarded to Innsbruck. The Bergisel ski jump, which dates back to 1925, was renovated for the 2003/04 season and is now a popular tourist attraction, as is the nearby Swarovski Crystal Worlds. The Olympic Hall, which housed the closing ceremonies in 1964, was demolished in 2004 and replaced by the Tivoli Stadium Tirol, home of the FC Wacker Innsbruck soccer club. Grenoble, France (1968) For the first time, the Winter Olympic Games included a giant slalom competition. Jean-Claude Killy, one of the greatest French skiers ever, swept all three Alpine skiing gold medals in 1968. Other notable achievements include the first use of artificial snow and the first doping disqualification in the history of the Winter Games. The Stade de Glace, where the opening and closing ceremonies were held, was destroyed in 1991.

When asked to speak, PWS produce greater activity in right primary motor cortex than controls, and less activity in left primary motor cortex (De Nil et al., 2003; De Nil, Kroll, Kapur, & Houle, 2003; De Nil et al., 2008; Fox et al., 1996; Fox, Ingham, Ingham, Hirsch, Martin, Jerabek, et al., 2000; Ingham et al., 2003; Salmelin et al., 2000; Soros et al., 2008; Toyomura et al., 2011; Watkins et al., 2008; Xuan et al., 2012). The reduced activity in left primary motor cortex may contribute to the difficulties experienced when trying to produce fluent speech (Neef, Hoang, et al., 2015). There are few published studies of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) applied to people who stutter. These studies have used different electrode montages, targeted different cortical areas, and delivered tDCS either before or after speech tasks. In the first study, anodal tDCS was applied to left inferior frontal gyrus while participants performed a picture-naming task. Fluency increased significantly after stimulation compared to sham (Choo et al., 2011). In another study, anodal tDCS was applied to left inferior frontal gyrus prior to speech practice sessions. Participants were trained to use the 'easy onset' technique, and speech samples were recorded before and after each session. Stuttering decreased only in those participants receiving real tDCS (Choo et al., 2016). A third study used bilateral tDCS, placing cathodes over left and right Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal sulcus) and anodes over left and right Broca's area (left inferior frontal gyrus and right homologue) (Kronfeld-Duenias, Amir, Ezrati-Vinacour, Civier, & Ben-Shachar, 2014). All participants received both real and sham tDCS, but it was given after the speech tasks had been completed. The authors reported no significant effect of tDCS on stuttering rate. The final study used unilateral tDCS to apply cathodal stimulation to right posterior perisylvian region (Wernicke's area), while anodal stimulation was applied to left anterior perisylvian region (Broca's area). In contrast to the other studies, there was no concurrent speech task. Instead, the effects of tDCS were measured in two ways: immediately after stimulation, a test battery was administered, including a reading task. Secondly, a follow-up phone call took place one week later, to assess the longer-term effects of stimulation. No immediate effects were found, but stuttering severity ratings taken from the phone calls were lower following real tDCS than sham (Jung et al., 2016).

A noise in the hall told of the arrival of the first guest. A heavy, dragging step and a snorting breath told them who it was. The door opened, and Agricultural Counsellor von Konradi made his appearance. A rather fleshy sort of man, with glasses on his aristocratic nose, over the tops of which his eyes sought the lady of the house. His hair was dyed a fine dark shade, and envy proclaimed that this was done on account of the fair sex; for he was unmarried. His two ideals in life, however, were a good dinner and several bottles of even a better wine to go with it. Since he realized both of these ideals in the captain's house, he was fond of going there. As to the rest, he was held to be a gentleman. While he was at the critical point in a story embodying his profound grief at the arrival from his estate of a pheasant in a scandalously unripe condition, the door opened again and admitted the spouse of Captain Kahle. Of a dainty, petite figure, and with a face that seemed to belong to a gamin, she presented on the whole a graceful enough ensemble. But there were two drawbacks - her rather large mouth was wreathed in a stereotyped smile, and when she opened it it gave utterance to a voice of somewhat unpleasant, strident timbre. Three youngish men followed on her heels. The first of them was Lieutenant Pommer, who was somewhat of a general favorite because of his unaffected, frank demeanor. Occasionally it became a trifle rough or rude; but you always knew where you had him. With special ardor he saluted Frau Kahle, and it looked almost droll to watch the contrast between him, a burly, corpulent fellow, and this tiny, fragile figure that resembled a Dresden china shepherdess. The second one was Lieutenant Mueller. Those who did not know him could have guessed from his stiff, self-contained mien that he must be the regimental adjutant. Housewives dreaded him, for his appetite was Gargantuan. With stoic defiance of all warning glances he was in the habit of demolishing thrice the quantity of the daintiest eatables apportioned to each guest.

The true stakes construct themselves against a backdrop of age-old rivalries and contemporary ambitions, intricately woven into the fabric of Sri Lanka's modern identity. The echoes of colonial dominance resonate with the same clarity as the waves crashing upon its stunning shores, hinting at the island's precarious balance upon the geopolitical chessboard. The engagement with external powers, ranging from nations grappling for influence to corporations seeking profit, stirs a tempest within the island's troubled polity. Under the Rajapaksa administration, sovereignty wades through an ephemeral swamp; treacherous alliances carved in the spirit of self-preservation resonate with historical precedents. Amidst this swirling tide of foreign interests, local sentiment remains fiercely protective of national integrity. The specter of neo-colonialism, a term increasingly bandied about in political discourses, looms large over discussions regarding infrastructural projects and foreign investments, which often come saddled with burdensome debts that stifle local economies. China's expansive reach, evidenced by its substantial financial commitments to Colombo, raises the specter of dependency that haunts nations engaged in such intricate romances of power. Local opposition roars through the streets in response to infrastructural projects perceived as being built atop the bones of laborers and the sweat of the marginalized. Social fractures surface as the populace grapples with the impact of globalization heralded by these investments. Rent-seeking behaviors emerge as various stakeholders vye for the spoils of burgeoning contracts, creating a murky atmosphere within which the powerful thrive at the expense of ordinary citizens. The delicate balance between economic necessity and national pride continues to elicit sharp reactions, particularly among ethnic communities, who remain wary of any developmental agenda that may gloss over their longstanding grievances. Amid the tumult, the island's ethereal beauty persists, defying the clutter of geopolitical maneuvering. Lush, verdant hills and expansive tea plantations cradle a rich cultural heritage marred by modern conflicts, as the ghost of ethnic discord refuses to dissipate entirely. Furthermore, an increased militarization and a nationalistic narrative, propagated by the ruling elites, provide the backdrop for moments of simmering discontent that threaten to erupt at any given moment. The Tamil population, long shrouded in the injustices of a civil war that scarred an entire generation, remains a point of focal tension between the government and various international stakeholders. As ports expand and infrastructure bolsters, raising the island's profile as an emerging trade nexus, so too do the demands for accountability grow louder. The discord between the local aspiration for development and the global appetite for strategic positioning creates a cacophony of voices, each vying for acknowledgment within the broader tapestry of Sri Lanka's national narrative. The struggle persists; a battle waged not with weapons, but with ideologies, identities, and visions of what the future holds. In this contest of wills, Sri Lanka stands at the confluence of ancient maritime routes and modern-day ambitions. The promise of prosperity dances enticingly on the horizon, yet the shadows of history whisper cautionary tales, urging vigilance against repeating past mistakes. What remains to be seen is whether the island can masterfully navigate this new paradigm or if it shall find itself ensnared by the very forces it once sought to control. As strategic interests converge and diverge, the quest for an identity freestanding and unfettered may serve as both a guiding light and a daunting challenge in the years to come.

It was an unrelenting grind, a rhythm that pulsed through their bones and into their very souls. After the tumultuous days turned to restless nights, the crew found solace beneath a bleached canopy of stars, punctuated occasionally by the vast blackness of the ocean that surrounded them. Each stroke felt simultaneously like an eternity and the blink of an eye, as they pulled against nature's unforgiving currents. 'Every moment held its own kind of beauty, though' reflects Heather Rees-Gaunt, a spirited adventurer whose laugh danced over the waves like sunlight prancing on the ocean surface. 'We saw sunrises that turned the sky into a canvas of oranges and reds, and sunsets that would make even the most seasoned painters envious. Those were the moments, fleeting as they were, that brought us together in our shared struggle.' The crew's bond, forged in the crucible of hardship, flourished amidst the salty spray and the cacophony of their surroundings. Each member had their unique strengths, but together, they formed an inseparable unit. 'We became like family,' adds Cameron Bellamy, steady yet filled with laughter, as he looks around at his fellow rowers. 'Sometimes we would laugh until we cried. Other times, we'd shed tears over the struggles we faced. But, in the end, the laughter always won.' The mental challenge was relentless, requiring every ounce of stamina and spirit. Leven Brown, who held the role of navigator, recounts some of the darker moments. 'There were days of absolute despair-when nothing went right, and the sea felt more a prison than a pathway. We had these moments of doubt, but each time we faced a storm together, we emerged stronger. We learned to read each other's faces, to sense when someone was faltering.' As Wallace Dickens famously said, nothing worth having comes easily, and this expedition epitomized that adage. Each member, bearing the scars of physical exertion, understood the high cost of their ambition. Tim bore memories not just of biting winds and enormous waves, but an indomitable spirit that rallied the crew at the darkest hours. 'The ocean tried to break us down, but we found power in our unity,' he asserts firmly, even now, as they navigate the soft sands of Seychelles. Yet, upon growing accustomed to a boat that pitched and yawed with every swell, the transition to solid ground felt peculiar. 'The world is still spinning in my mind, even if I'm standing still,' says James Douglas-Hamilton, his voice tinged with both exhaustion and exhilaration. The crew was confronted with the mundane, the simple act of walking becoming an extraordinary challenge. Bodies, conditioned to the rhythm of rowing, were bewildered on dry land as they reacquainted themselves with gravity. What awaited them in the chirpy seaside towns was a carnival-warm welcomes infused with vibrancy and life-a tapestry of colors that had been absent upon the ocean. Street vendors, cheerful laughter, and local music were overwhelming delights, yet there lay a longing for the simplicity of the past weeks. 'It's strange,' Tim muses. 'I missed the sound of the waves at night and the company of my teammates, and now, I stand here amongst the crowd, and it feels foreign to me.' These emotions, complex as they are precious, weave together the story of the expedition, an odyssey of humanity's will against nature's vastness, and a collective journey through struggle, metamorphosis, and unyielding perseverance. The crew's adventure, now immortalized in their hearts, will forever echo in their minds like the ocean waves calling them home.

Recommendations such as those set in EN 12150-1:2000 [3] are often used to determine whether the optical quality of the curved plate is acceptable. These limit the amplitude of the roller wave distortion in fully toughened glass to 0.5 mm over a length of 300 mm [5]. It is currently, possible to manufacture toughened glass with significantly smaller roller wave distortion amplitudes. In fact, a limit of 0.25 mm is often prescribed for high-end applications. More information on these thermal bending methods can be found in [6-11]. Cold bending is an alternative, and relatively recent, technique of creating curved glass plates. During this process, the curvature is induced elastically at ambient conditions with a relatively small amount of equipment, thereby, making the process energy efficient and also allowing the bending to be executed on site. Cold bent glass can be used to generate either single or doubly curved forms. Single curvature/developable glass surfaces are easier to form, but they are not as popular in architectural design as doubly curved glass provide a much larger architectural freedom and can be used to create smooth, free form, transparent facades. The glass panels of various curvatures that are required in this kind of applications can be cold bent in shape without any requirement for moulds, therefore, minimising their cost and making cold bending an attractive method of creating curved glass surfaces. Cold bending involves the application of out-of-plane loads on the glass surface to create the desired shape of the glass plate, the plate is then restrained in its curved state by means of mechanical fixings or structural adhesives. The glass is therefore subjected to permanent bending stresses throughout its service life. Cold lamination bending [12,13] is another recent technique used to restrain the curved glass plate during the cold bending of laminated glass and involves: (i) bending the un-bonded unit of glass plates and interlayer(s) in the desired shape and; (ii) laminating the un-bonded bent unit in an autoclave. In this case, the interlayer preserves the shape of the glass in place though partially, since initial springback is expected when the restraints are removed after the lamination [12,13]. There is a growing interest in cold bent glass [18-23] and cold bent glass has already been used in real world applications [24-27]. Two of the most notable examples of completed projects is the 125 m long glass shell of the Strasbourg TGV train station consisting of 6 mm heat-strengthened laminated plates and the glass roof of the Victoria and Albert museum in London that covers an area of 370 m2 and consists of cold bent insulated glass units that are point fixed. Yet, to-date no guideline is available for its manufacture/design process.

Recently, the isotopic composition of Cl has been determined in lunar samples and the results show wide variation ranging from 1/2-15 to 1/2+10 (Barnes et al., 2015; Barnes et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017). The 37Cl values of Martian meteorites are also highly variable, ranging from 1/2-17 to 1/2+18 (Barnes et al., 2013; Sharp et al., 2013a; Barnes et al., 2014; Barnes et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017). Lunar and Martian apatite also display a wide range of 37Cl values, from 1/2-25 to 1/2+15 (Barnes et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017). Apatite grains from the Vesta family meteorites (e.g., Eucrites) show a narrow range of 37Cl values ( 1/2-5 to 1/20 ) (Liu et al., 2017). This suggests that apatite may be a good indicator of the 37Cl value of the parent body, although there are several factors that must be considered when interpreting these data. The purpose of this study was to determine the 37Cl values of apatite from terrestrial basalts to provide a reference dataset for comparison with other planetary bodies. Here we present new measurements of apatite 37Cl values from seven terrestrial basalts: two Icelandic tholeiitic basalts (Hekla and Torfajokull), one Hawaiian alkalic basalt (Mauna Loa), one South African kimberlite (Premier Diamond Mine), one North American kimberlite (Diavik Diamond Mine), and two Antarctic flood basalts (Lamont and McMurdo Volcanics). We also report the first 37Cl values for clinopyroxene from four of the samples. Finally, we compare our new data with previously published values for lunar apatite to assess whether or not the terrestrial apatite 37Cl values can serve as a proxy for lunar apatite 37Cl values. All samples were obtained through the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. For the Icelandic basalts, samples were collected from outcrops at Hekla and Torfajokull volcanoes. For the Hawaiian basalt, sample KIL-13 was obtained from Mauna Loa volcano. Samples from the Diavik Diamond Mine and Premier Diamond Mine were obtained from the Canadian Geological Survey. Sample MSL-1 was obtained from the Lamont volcanic province, Antarctica, while sample MDV-1 was obtained from the McMurdo volcanic province, Antarctica. All samples were crushed using a steel mortar and pestle until they were reduced to small chips ( 1/22.95) and left to settle overnight. The supernatant was decanted off and the remaining material was washed with deionized water to remove any excess sodium polytungstate solution.

In addition to the above mentioned applications, sorption cycles also show their potential in combined heat and power (CHP), micro CHP, organic rankine cycle (ORC), solar thermal energy utilisation and waste heat recovery etc., all of which are considered as the key technologies for a sustainable future [17-20]. The state-of-the-art research on sorption power generation cycle mainly focuses on the improvement of performance and expansion of application scope; however there is still lack of systematic review and comprehensive analysis of these technologies. Therefore, this paper will summarise the latest advances in sorption power generation and provide a critical discussion about its current situation and future perspectives. 2. Working principle Fig. 1 illustrates a generalised schematic diagram of a sorption power generation cycle. The process can be divided into two sub-cycles: desorption cycle and absorption cycle. During the desorption cycle, the adsorber is heated up by external heat source to drive off the adsorbate, which flows through the expander to generate power before being condensed back to liquid phase. Meanwhile, the absorbent in the absorber is cooled down to absorb the vapour generated in the evaporator and hence producing useful cooling effect. Then the whole cycle is reversed during the absorption cycle. The adsorber and absorber exchange their roles, and the adsorber is cooled down to absorb the vapour generated in the desorber, whilst the absorbent in the absorber is heated up to desorb the adsorbate which flows through the compressor to consume power. This process continues until the next desorption cycle starts again. It is worth noting that there are several variations of this basic cycle, such as resorption cycle, chemisorption cycle, sorption compression cycle and hybrid cycle, which will be discussed later in detail. Figure 1 Generalised schematic diagram of a sorption power generation cycle. 3. Classification and comparison Based on the classification methods adopted by the previous literature reviews [21,22], a new classification method is proposed in Fig. 2 according to the type of working pair, the way of power generation and the number of reactors involved. The first level divides the sorption power generation cycles into three categories: physical sorption cycle, chemical sorption cycle and hybrid sorption cycle. Physical sorption cycle uses physical sorbents and refrigerants as working pairs, e.g. zeolite/water and silica gel/water, whereas chemical sorption cycle employs chemical sorbents and refrigerants, e.g. SrBr2/NH3 and MnCl2/NH3. Hybrid sorption cycle combines both physical and chemical sorption processes, and it normally includes two chemical sorbents and one refrigerant, e.g. MgCl2-NaBr/NH3 and SrCl2-BaCl2/NH3. The second level categorises sorption power generation cycles based on the way of power generation, i.e. whether it generates power directly from the adsorbed gas or indirectly from the rejected heat. For direct power generation, the adsorbed gas flows through the expander to produce power, and for indirect power generation, the rejected heat drives an ORC or a steam turbine to produce power. The third level further classifies sorption power generation cycles according to the number of reactors involved, i.e. single reactor, double reactors and multi-reactors. Table 1 compares the advantages and disadvantages of each category, and provides examples of working pairs and references for further information.
