With ADHD exhibiting a spectrum of symptoms and manifestations across lifespan, it becomes increasingly essential to discern the nuances within the disorder. Investigating the interplay of arousal and cognitive functions may elucidate more targeted intervention strategies that address the unique arousal profiles individual patients exhibit. As research continues, it is critical to parse out aspects of impulse control, attention variability, and task engagement in relation to measured arousal states. For instance, do specific ADHD subtypes exhibit distinct physiological markers in response to various tasks, or is there a unifying pattern that transcends these classifications? Utilizing skin conductance measures in conjunction with tasks of varied complexity may provide insight into a range of cognitive functions specific to ADHD subtypes, distinguishing the more hyperactive presentations from those characterized by inattentiveness. Moreover, the role of environmental context cannot be understated in shaping arousal levels within individuals with ADHD. Task parameters such as novelty, difficulty, and sensory input can act in concert to modulate arousal, either enhancing or diminishing cognitive engagement. Preliminary findings suggest that increasing task complexity may activate latent arousal systems, enabling better performance in situations previously deemed non-rewarding or mundane (James et al., 2016). Therefore, future inquiries should aim to systematically vary contextual factors while evaluating skin conductance responses, to uncover whether a dynamic interplay exists between environmental stimuli and arousal regulation in ADHD populations. Additionally, it is crucial to consider the impact of comorbid conditions, which frequently accompany ADHD. Disorders such as anxiety and depression may contribute to altered arousal profiles and must be examined to discern their influence on the overall physiological and behavioral presentations of ADHD. For instance, heightened sympathetic nervous system activation commonly observed in anxiety disorders may complicate interpretations of skin conductance findings in individuals who present with overlapping symptoms. Therefore, adopting a comprehensive dimensional approach that considers overlapping neurophysiological patterns across comorbid conditions will enhance our understanding of ADHD and its manifestations. A further layer of complexity arises when considering developmental trajectories. ADHD does not exist in a vacuum but evolves throughout childhood into adulthood. As such, it is paramount to examine whether childhood patterns of arousal dysregulation persist, change, or even resolve with age. Longitudinal studies that incorporate repeated measures of skin conductance across different developmental stages may yield invaluable insights into the stability of arousal patterns and their implications for cognitive performance over time. The implications of these findings extend into clinical practice as well; understanding the mechanisms of arousal dysregulation can inform more nuanced treatment modalities. For instance, the application of mindfulness-based interventions may offer individuals strategies to enhance self-regulatory capacities, promoting adaptive arousal management. Furthermore, pharmacological interventions aimed at modulating arousal levels may benefit from tailoring, individualized to the specific arousal profiles captured through neurophysiological assessments. In conclusion, while our current understanding of ADHD and its associated arousal patterns is evolving, there remains a considerable deficit in knowledge. The utilization of objective measures such as skin conductance provides a promising avenue for furthering our comprehension of this multifaceted disorder. Continued exploration may unravel the intricacies of how arousal dysregulation manifests in ADHD, paving the way for improved diagnostic practices and targeted therapeutic strategies. Such investigations promise to enrich the broader discourse surrounding ADHD, contributing to a fuller appreciation of its complexities and the diverse experiences of those affected.

It echoed in his ears, tugging at the memories of his college days, when he and his teammates might slick their hair back and belt out raucous renditions of the latest pop hits after a victory. But this was no pop song; this was the shrill, riotous serenade of the old frontier, conjured by the vivid imagination of his slumbering mind. Yet, as he blinked the LAST vestiges of sleep from his hazel eyes, he recalled he was entrenched not in the dusty plains of the Wild West, but in the cramped quarters of Bannister's dormitory. The world of the sagebrush and cowpokes evaporated, leaving nothing but the musty aroma of long-overdue laundry and the faint sound of laughter drifted from the hall outside. "Sure would be nice to swap this place for a cowboy's trail," he thought, his mind still caught on the scents of gunpowder and the rush of the chase. With a shudder, he considered the six-gun strapped to his hip-well, it was merely a dream object, but it bore a weighty significance. In reality, only the heavy playbook of his football practice awaited him in his satchel. Raising his heavy frame with a groan, Butch swung his legs over the side of the bunk and scratched his tousled hair, pondering the enthrallment of his dreams. Outside, the shrieks and hollers grew louder, a chaotic symphony of unruly joy. With a grunt, he unwrapped himself from the blankets and set foot to the wooden floor, his large feet thudding softly. "Y'all better not be messin' around when I get out there!" he bellowed, half-joking, half-nurturing the typical fierce persona that he had adopted in the football field. The last remnants of the cowboy adventure flickered in his mind as he shoved open the creaky door and stepped into the corridor. There, to his utter surprise, he caught sight of several of his teammates gathered in the common room. They were fully engrossed in a raucous game of poker, their faces illuminated by the flickering glow of an old lamp. And at the center of it all, shouting his head off in delight, was none other than Slim McCoy, half-reclined against the threadbare couch, his flannel shirt unbuttoned, a wild grin plastered upon his face. "Ah! Butch! The big man awakens!" Slim hollered, launching a handful of poker chips into the air like confetti. "Come and join us-before we finish emptying out this here saloon!" "I'll take your whole pot, boys!" Butch declared with a hearty laugh, striding toward the table, the spirit of adventure clinging to him like sweat in August. Poker, unlike the pursuit of lawless outlaws, was his own brand of battleground, where bluffing was the armor and luck was the gun. He slid into a chair at the table, ready to throw in his lot against his teammates, a good-natured rivalry ready to unfold like a Louisiana get-together. As the game commenced, Butch could hardly suppress the thrill that beat within him. Poker felt a lot like the sheriffs and bandits of his fantasies. Every card held mystery; every bluff risked life, liberty, or at the very least, a spot on the dormitory couch for the night. The stakes swelled higher, as did his enthusiasm. Little did he know, their jovial revelry would soon attract the attention of uninvited guests lurking in the shadows of their carefree horizon.

Therefore, the new contribution of this paper is to provide an investigation of the outdoor ventilation conditions for real complex urban areas and provide a quantitative evaluation of the accuracy of LES and RANS (through the wind-tunnel study validation) for relevant metrics for such outdoor ventilation. It is well known that steady RANS is incapable of capturing the inherently transient behavior of separation and recirculation downstream of buildings and of von Karman vortex shedding in the wake [51,52,54,55]. Transition simulations with Large-Eddy Simulation (LES), on the other hand can provide accurate descriptions of the mean and instantaneous flow field around bluff bodies, at the expense of much larger computational requirements. However, steady RANS is still the most frequently used method for urban breathability studies based on the information provided in Table 1, since it can be very effective in terms of time and computational cost. It should be noted that earlier studies on urban ventilation have shown the significant contribution of turbulence diffusion in the air mixing between inside and above of urban canopies [5,30,39,53,56], while turbulence can act as the main mechanism controlling pollutant removal from an urban canopy layer [12,57]. Given the important influence of turbulence on outdoor ventilation, a detailed evaluation of steady RANS and LES for outdoor ventilation of complex real urban areas is in order. Furthermore, using the information provided in this paper in terms of accuracy and computational time, engineers, urban planners and researchers can easily decide which of these turbulence modeling approaches would be more beneficial. This includes both structural solutions, like insulation and renovation, and behavioral changes, such as switching off lights when not necessary. Information provision measures provide information to consumers about how to save energy and money, and where to find help if needed. The majority of existing studies focus on one type of measure and analyze its effectiveness and/or efficiency [13-18]. There is no study so far investigating the synergies among different types of measures, nor what their combined effect could be on the reduction of energy poverty. In this paper, we propose an integrated framework to assess the effectiveness of the different policy measures aimed at addressing energy poverty. We use a set of indicators to evaluate the impact of each single measure on the level of energy poverty in a specific region. Then, we combine the results obtained using all the measures to identify the optimal mix of policy instruments that best reduces energy poverty. The case study is based on the Emilia-Romagna Region in Italy, which has recently launched a regional strategy to tackle energy poverty. The analysis focuses on the city of Bologna, where data were collected through a questionnaire survey administered to 400 residents. In the European Union, more than 50 million households experience energy poverty conditions, which means they lack some of the most basic features of ordinary life: adequate warmth, cooling, lighting and energy required to power normal appliances [1]. These services are not only essential to satisfy basic human needs and guarantee a decent standard of living and health [2], but also to overcome social segregation and increase perceptions of agency [3]. Individuals who live in energy poverty are usually vulnerable consumers who have low incomes, face high-energy costs and live in energy inefficient dwellings [4]. Living in conditions of energy poverty has adverse consequences not only for physical health and for wellbeing 'with increased likelihood of obtaining or exacerbating respiratory and cardiac illnesses due to uncomfortable temperatures' but also for mental health, due to stress associated with the inability to pay energy bills [5]. Therefore, addressing energy poverty might result not only in lowering individual and governmental expenditures on health and in bettering environmental outcomes, but also and more importantly, in assuring positive results for vulnerable households in terms of comfort, wellbeing, and cost savings allowing for protection of available resources. For this reason, the European Commission has recognized tackling energy poverty as a policy priority in Europe in the 'Clean Energy for All Europeans'1 legislative package. Several initiatives promoting the exchange of good practices, such as the European2 and the Italian3 Energy Poverty Observatories, have been launched. Moreover, energy poverty has received increasing attention by scholars from different fields who have proposed new concepts, frameworks and approaches [6,7]. However, there remain few studies attempting to capture the varieties of factors affecting energy poverty in a more holistic way [8]. Additional conceptual vectors would contribute not only to understanding better, but also to addressing better, the complex combination of drivers of energy poverty.

A nurse inside a Monrovia clinic wore a camera showing his job, revealing that he worked inside a clinic with seemingly unclean conditions. Patients were lying on stretchers on floors that appear filthy, and there were open buckets lying around with objects and substances in them. The situation for caregivers across Liberia has become so dire that nurses are now are threatening to strike. Just days ago, CNN's cameras captured crowds of caregivers yelling outside Liberia's largest Ebola treatment center in Monrovia. Underscoring the serious consequences of a Liberia without health care workers, President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf arrived to try to calm the crowd. "We're trying to meet all their needs, and we'll continue to do that," she told CNN, struggling to be heard above the shouting. "I don't want to strike," one caregiver said, telling CNN that he foresees deaths increasing several thousand-fold if facilities' conditions don't improve. "But the President has to listen to the massive health care workers out there," he said. "There are angry people. You don't want to have angry people knocking on your doors during this kind of emergency situation." This weekend, The Washington Post detailed horrific conditions at a Monrovia Ebola facility where one doctor died from Ebola and another tested positive for the virus. The Post reported: "Doctors put on their protective gear in the kitchen. There is no incinerator, so a 10-foot pile of Ebola-laced garbage and excrement sits in the back yard. There is no morgue, so bodies sometimes decay outside, next to where patients sit in white lawn chairs. There are no protective hoods for the full-body medical suits," so caregivers make their own. There have also been questions about how tight security is at health care centers. In August, CNN reported that an Ebola treatment facility in Monrovia was overrun by an armed mob who stole mattresses and equipment. Ebola patients fled, local authorities said. A legacy of self-sacrifice. The mother of modern nursing, Florence Nightingale, suffered for her dedication to treating patients during the Crimea War. It's believed that she also contracted a bacterial infection as she treated the wounded, dealing the effects of the illness for much of her life. Just as Nightingale was revered as a hero, so too was Dr. Sheik Umar Khan, a top doctor from Sierra Leone who specialized in Ebola. He died in late July from the virus. He had been overseeing Ebola treatment at Kenema Government Hospital, about 185 miles east of Sierra Leone's capital city, Freetown. Doctors Without Borders was treating him.

He suggested, in the meantime, that I might become a clerk in a mercantile house, and that I might one day become a partner; but that day seemed so very far off in the perspective, that I begged he would not trouble himself about the matter, deciding rather to seek for some government appointment, either at home or abroad. "Well, Maurice, my boy, you'll become wiser as you grow older, and you'll be glad to accept the first offer made you," remarked my father. He, however, immediately wrote to Dublin, to the only friend of the family who was likely to render us assistance. This was Councillor Roacharty, who in the course of a few days replied that he would do his best; but that his friend Maurice must put his impatience under lock and key until Ireland had her rights, and Irishmen ruled their green island home. As I confidently hoped that this happy event would soon be an accomplished fact, I was content; but my father was not so well satisfied as I was with the councillor's reply. Meantime I shot, fished, hunted, and visited our neighbours, and was rapidly adopting the habits and customs of Irish squireens, when one day, returning home from shooting, just before dinner, I found my father deeply engaged in reading a foreign-looking letter. So absorbed was he in its contents that he did not perceive my entrance. Not wishing to disturb him, I retired to get rid of my muddy boots and leggings; and on my return, dinner was on the table. Visitors can revel in the charm of Casa del Horno's historic ambiance, combining old-world elegance with modern amenities. Whether basking in the sunlit courtyard or sipping artisanal coffee on a balcony overlooking the vibrant streets, visitors are encouraged to savor each moment. The district is peppered with galleries showcasing local talent and quaint artisan shops selling unique handmade crafts. Evenings are best spent at one of the lively music venues where the soulful rhythms of jazz and the infectious beats of salsa entice locals and tourists alike to dance the night away. Culinary explorers will find delight in the district's eclectic range of eateries, from cozy cafes to upscale dining establishments serving innovative takes on traditional Panamanian cuisine. A short drive from the city, the world-renowned Panama Canal awaits its visitors. Observing the engineering marvel up close is a bucket-list experience, offering insight into the canal's pivotal role in global trade and its impact on Panama's history. As day excursions conclude, returning to the city offers renewed opportunities for indulgence. Unwinding with a massage or spa treatment at one of the luxury hotels, such as the Waldorf Astoria, ensures relaxation after a day of exploration. Transportation around the city is both affordable and convenient. While taxis abound, the efficient Metro offers a budget-friendly alternative for those looking to traverse the city efficiently. Bicycle rentals and pedestrian-friendly paths further enhance the accessibility of the city's diverse neighborhoods, inviting more intimate exploration of Panama's many facets. Thus, Panama City stands as a testament to luxury without excess, where even a modest budget offers entry to the experiences cherished by world travelers. Every sunrise beckons a new opportunity to engage with the vibrant dance of everyday life in a city where culture, history, and modernity blend seamlessly. Whether indulging in the rich heritage of Casco Viejo or simply relaxing under the dappled sunlight of a tropical afternoon, Panama City promises memories that linger long after the journey ends.

Money like you wouldn't believe. It flowed in like a river of green, crashing against the shores of our ambition, eroding any sense of right or wrong with its sheer weight. It was a world sculpted by greed, yet sustained by the illusion of a dream. We lived in a bubble of opulence and self-indulgence, where everything had a price and nothing was ever out of reach. Ginger was a whirlwind, the kind of woman who could walk into a room and make time stand still. Her beauty was matched only by her boldness, a dangerous combination that could inspire both admiration and jealousy. She understood the game's mechanics, what made the wheels turn. In the glittering chaos of Vegas, she shone like a diamond under the harsh lights of the casino floor, catching everyone's eye but eluding their grasp. Yet, behind her dazzling smile, a storm brewed, threatening to unravel everything we carefully built. Nicky was the wildcard. A firebrand with a short fuse and a penchant for trouble. He was my ace in the hole, a man who commanded respect through fear and force. But even he wasn't immune to the seductive lure of power and the madness it often brings to those unequipped to wield it. I should have known from the start that our paths were on a collision course, a tragedy in the making. Yet, in the beginning, it seemed worth the gamble. Every day in Vegas wordlessly whispered another chapter of risk and reward, painted in the vibrant colors of excess and danger. As the Tangiers thrived, so did we, plunging ever deeper into a world that blurred the lines between reality and illusion. But the higher we climbed, the more precarious our balance became, teetering on the edge of a seemingly endless peak. Ginger, with her inner demons, was a harbinger of the chaos that loomed. Her need for something more, something untouchable and real, drove wedges between us. The make-believe perfection of our life was a fragile facade hiding a tangled mess of insecurities and broken promises. Watching her slip away was like witnessing a star fall from the sky-a beautiful, tragic descent I was powerless to stop. And Nicky, well, his ambition outgrew the shadows, branching into territories that were as dangerous as they were seductive. The deeper he dug into the underbelly of our empire, the more I realized our dreams were built on shifting sands. Our facade of respectability crumbled faster than I could reinforce it, each crack revealing the truth of what we really were. Hustlers. Dreamers. Fools chasing an impossible reality. Beneath the bright lights and endless nights, the real Vegas was a relentless judge, demanding payment for our transgressions. It dangled promises of immortality and invincibility, but in the end, it was simply a city of mirages, giving nothing unless it could take more in return. It was a hard lesson, one I learned too late but understood too well. I still remember the nights when everything seemed possible, and the world was our playground. But now, all I have left are memories and the echoes of dreams that never came true.

In the pursuit of cosmic understanding, our gaze is not merely directed at distant celestial bodies; it is steeped in the tantalizing prospect that we may not be alone in the vastness of the universe. The burgeoning field of exoplanet research, emboldened by the data collected from missions like Kepler, has thrust the concept of finding extraterrestrial life into the forefront of scientific inquiry. With each pulse of light detected-a rhythmic dance of stars and planets-our understanding widens, bridging the gap between myth and reality. As Howard articulates, the likelihood of discovering life-sustaining planets surrounding sun-like stars signifies a watershed moment in the history of human exploration. Each newly discovered exoplanet serves as a testament to the potential diversity of worlds that might teem with organisms, resilient and unyielding, adapting to their environments much as life on Earth has forged its path. It's an affirmation of the idea that environments, which seem inhospitable at first glance, could cradle life forms vastly different from our own. Meanwhile, the continued advancements in technology and methodologies employed to detect exoplanets bear fruit. Ground-based observatories are complementing the legacy of the Kepler mission, while the advent of space telescopes such as TESS and the forthcoming James Webb Space Telescope offer unprecedented insights into the atmospheres of distant worlds. Researchers are now poised to delve deeper into the study of spectral signatures, hunting for biomarkers that might signal the presence of water, oxygen, or even more complex organic compounds-each one a whisper of life. As we contemplate the implications of these celestial findings, it becomes evident that we are not merely observers; we are participants in a grand cosmic narrative. The notion that one in five stars may host a planet akin to our own evokes a profound reflection on our place in the universe. It propels us beyond the confines of philosophical musings into concrete actions: consolidation of international efforts in astrobiology, funding for exploratory missions, and a recommitment to fostering scientific literacy among the public. Yet, amid this optimism resides a nagging uncertainty-what constitutes life? The criteria we utilize are rooted in our terrestrial experience; we seek carbon-based life forms, reliant on water, under conditions reminiscent of Earth. However, could life as we do not know it dwell within the frigid clouds of a gas giant or beneath the jagged surfaces of ice-covered moons? Researchers are expanding their definitions, venturing into the uncharted territories of biochemistry. The search for microbial life on Mars, the ice-covered oceans of Europa, and the smog-shrouded atmosphere of Venus signifies just the beginning. Our search for extraterrestrial intelligence does not merely hinge upon solid evidence of living organisms but speaks to the very essence of humankind's quest for understanding and companionship. As we send out the Voyager probes, carrying our messages across the void, we recognize the yearning for connection, a shared existence in the galactic tapestry. Ultimately, the story of our universe is still being penned. The more we probe the cosmic depths, the more we learn, enriching our narrative with real-life encounters and the enigmas they pose. Whether the intricate dance of life is indeed a universal constant or an Earthly singularity hinges upon the revelations awaiting us among the stars, just beyond our reach yet tantalizingly close to our aspirations. In embracing this journey into the celestial unknown, we not only expand our worldly view but also venture evermore deeply into the essence of existence itself. Only time-and perhaps a well-timed cosmic revelation-will unveil the secrets that lie in wait.

Through the use of 3D printing technologies it becomes possible to place stimuli responsive materials into 3D geometries that may not be easily achievable using other fabrication methods. In this work we demonstrate the ability to utilise 3D printing techniques to create multi-material responsive systems where the stimuli-responsive material acts as a component in a larger structure. We describe how the combination of stimuli-responsive material and the geometry of the resulting structure enable us to obtain a range of different morphing behaviours. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for future research directions in the field of self-assembly and self-repair. Cellulose acetate (CA) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (purity >99%) and dissolved in acetic acid (AA) at a concentration of 20% w/w to produce the printable solution. To produce the printed samples, the CA/AA solution was loaded into a syringe barrel attached to a custom-built micro-extruder head capable of dispensing the liquid at temperatures up to 100 C. A commercially available desktop stereolithography printer (Formlabs Form 1+) was used to print the moulds for the 3D printed samples. The moulds were designed using Autodesk Inventor software and printed using a mixture of SLA resins. Once printed, the moulds were removed from the printer, washed in isopropanol and dried under vacuum before being filled with the CA/AA solution. The printed moulds were then placed onto a glass slide and heated in a hot air oven at 50 C for 30 min to allow the CA/AA solution to infiltrate the mould. After infiltration, the sample was removed from the mould and allowed to cool down to room temperature. The resultant samples had a thickness of approximately 300 1/2m. To determine the extent of hydration of the samples, the weight of the sample was measured immediately after removal from the oven and again after 24 h at ambient conditions. The percentage difference between these weights gives the approximate amount of water absorbed by the sample during the 24 h period. The dynamic deformation of the samples was studied using an optical microscope fitted with a digital camera and video capture software. Samples were held in a custom-made clamp while a glass rod was applied to the top surface of the sample. Images were captured at 10 frames per s while the glass rod was moved across the sample at a constant speed of 0.5 mm/s. The images were analysed using ImageJ software to measure the distance travelled by the glass rod and the corresponding displacement of the sample. For more information please visit [1] S. F. As the world grew increasingly volatile, the Pentagon found itself in a quagmire that demanded not just adept navigation through the labyrinth of military strategy, but also a resonant voice in the public discourse surrounding national security. The resignation of Chuck Hagel underscored the often unforgiving nature of Washington politics, particularly during periods of global upheaval. Once celebrated for his candid perspectives, Hagel had been an emblem of pragmatic political service, yet the essence of that service appeared diluted by the fierce tides of a changing geopolitical landscape. When he assumed office, the expectation was clear. Hagel was to usher in an era of fiscal prudence and strategic withdrawal, a vision that aligned with Obama's hope for a post-war military engagement. But as the wheels of history turned, what emerged was a stark contrast to those aspirations. The Islamic State's swift ascendancy and Russia's brazen annexation of Crimea confronted Hagel not only as mere operational challenges but as ideological battles that required a far more vigorous response than he was equipped or willing to provide. Here lay the crux of the debate: was Hagel a casualty of circumstances, or an unwilling participant in a game far beyond his grasp? In quiet moments at the Pentagon, the whispers of frustration grew louder. Senior officials began to speculate whether Hagel's tenure was simply a case of poor timing or if more deep-rooted deficiencies existed. As new crises unfolded, it became apparent to staffers and analysts alike that the defense secretary was struggling to articulate a coherent strategy that resonated with both the administration's aims and the broader national sentiment. Meanwhile, Congress buzzed with dissent, teetering between bipartisan frustrations and fragmented partisan viewpoints, all while Hagel attempted to recalibrate a message that felt increasingly muddled. The perspective of those within the administration painted a picture of an uphill battle that Hagel was woefully ill-equipped to fight. His knack for handling budgetary constraints and departmental management, once seen as a strong suit, ironically unfurled as a double-edged sword. While efficiency within the Pentagon was crucial, the broader narrative-one of courage, decisiveness, and visionary leadership-often beckoned for a more robust presence. Observers within the White House became increasingly convinced that Hagel had failed to embody the resolute leader that a turbulent time demanded. Yet, it was not merely Hagel's performance that came under scrutiny; it was also the prevailing environment in which he functioned. Among the myriad challenges was the ever-looming specter of a divided government, with Congress eager to assert its influence on military doctrines and budget allocations. Although the temporal resolution of fNIRS is lower than that of EEG, fNIRS uses an infant-friendly headset without any paste or gel and is a more portable system, which has better temporal resolution (10 Hz) than fMRI. fNIRS measures neuronal activity reflected in changes in concentrations of oxygenated (oxy-) Hb and deoxygenated (deoxy-) Hb and it has been used to identify various neurocognitive developmental processes in infants (Minagawa-Kawai et al., 2011; Gervain et al., 2011; Minagawa-Kawai et al., 2008). Such findings have elucidated the cerebral responses of infants to two spoken language components: phonemes and prosody (Sato et al., 2003; Arimitsu et al., 2011). Phonemic structures (e.g., vowels and consonants) tend to be processed predominantly in the left temporal area, while prosody (e.g., intonations or rhythms) activates the right side more in both children and adults. This functional hemispheric specialization is called functional cerebral laterality of the auditory cortices and it facilitates efficient processing in the cerebral cortex (Minagawa-Kawai et al., 2011; Sato et al., 2003; Arimitsu et al., 2011). Although language comprehension involves various processes, the perceptual analysis of phonemes and prosody is a crucial initial step for language acquisition in the first year of life. Indeed, perceptual analysis of phonemes deeply affects an infant's learning of their native language. Likewise, prosody is important, because it provides various cues, such as pitch changes, intensity, and rhythmic structures-all of which facilitate the infant's speech acquisition, as exemplified by infant-directed speech offering rich prosodic cues. Apart from the investigations of cognitive functions stated above, fNIRS is also one of the significant tools to examine hemodynamic physiology in infants as well as in adults. Typical hemodynamic activity of the adult cerebral cortex is characterized by an increase in oxy-Hb and a slight decrease in deoxy-Hb. This is known as the hemodynamic response function (HRF) (Boynton et al., 1996; Friston et al., 2000). However, the development of the HRF pattern in the human brain remained unclear, and some fNIRS studies reported an inverted HRF pattern for young infants in response to perceptual stimuli, whereas some studies did not (Minagawa-Kawai et al., 2008; Sato et al., 2003; Arimitsu et al., 2011). This has been a controversial issue, and evidence of its presence in preterm infants is particularly sparse, partly because the fNIRS investigation of HRF is a relatively new subject. Notably, a recent fNIRS study reported developmental changes in phase differences of oxy- and deoxy-Hb in preterm infants (Watanabe et al., 2017). Although such developmental changes in neurovascular regulation are very intriguing, these results come only from resting-state measurements; HRF patterns during perceptual or cognitive processing should also be investigated. Consequently, the present study attempts to determine developmental differences in the HRF in response to different functional speech stimuli in preterm and term infants at each PMA.

Miss Farrow sank gracefully down into her deep, comfortable chair. Again she put out her feet to the fire, for it was very cold on this 23rd of December, and she knew she had a tiring, probably a boring, evening before her. Some strangers of whom she knew nothing, and cared less, excepting that they were the friends of her friend and host, Lionel Varick, were to arrive at Wyndfell Hall in time for dinner. It was now six o'clock. "Well," she said patiently, "begin at the beginning, Pegler. I wish you'd sit down too - somehow it worries me to see you standing there. In the last twelve years Miss Farrow had several times invited her to sit down, but of course she had always refused, being one that knew her place. She had only sat in Miss Farrow's presence during the days and nights when she had nursed her mistress through a serious illness - then, of course, everything had been different, and she had had to sit down sometimes.

It was not long ere the big door was thrown wide open, and as the men and women passed by he scrutinised them as closely as possible. He was watching for one person alone, and presently he saw her walking by herself. When she had gone a short distance he followed after, and never once let her out of his sight until she came to a large house, the door of which she opened and entered. For some time the man stood outside, keeping his eyes fixed upon the building. A policeman passing by noted the man, and, mistaking him for a vagrant, ordered him away. The stranger's pale face flushed, and his hands clenched as he obeyed the command. Slowly he walked along the street with his eyes fixed upon the pavement. At length he paused, retraced his steps, and stood once more before the house into which the woman had entered. Here he remained until the clock of a nearby church struck the hour of eleven. Then, drawing himself together, the man hurried away with rapid steps. Reaching a house on a side street, he opened a door with a latch-key, and passed within. Up three flights of stairs he moved till he came to a little room on the top floor. Groping around in the dark, he lighted an oil lamp fastened to the wall. It was a humble and scantily furnished garret he had entered. In one corner was a narrow cot. At its foot stood a wash-stand, over which hung a small cracked mirror. A rough worn table occupied the centre of the room, upon which rested a well-kept violin lying by its open case. Opposite the door was an open fire-place, and as the night was chilly the man lighted a fire from several dry sticks, and threw on some soft coal. Soon a cheerful blaze was curling up the chimney, before which the man sat on the one rickety chair the room contained and warmed his numbed hands. For over half an hour he remained thus, gazing down intently into the fire. But hotter than the coals before him seemed the eyes which burned in his head. At last he aroused from his reverie and, crossing the room, opened a small grip and brought forth a carefully-folded newspaper clipping. This he unwrapped, spread it out upon the table, and drawing up his chair sat down. He fixed his eyes upon an article with the big headline, "Deposed by His Bishop." A deep flush mantled his cheeks and brow as he read for more than the thousandth time that story of disgrace and degradation. He had really no need to read it over again, for every word was seared upon his soul as with a red-hot iron. But the printed words seemed to fascinate him. The tale was all there in black and white, and the newspaper had made the most of it.

In recent years, the concept of safety cases has begun to gain traction in healthcare, with advocates suggesting that their adoption could lead to a more informed understanding of risk, thereby enhancing patient safety. Indeed, the dynamic nature of healthcare, where variability in processes and patient conditions is manifold, necessitates an adaptable yet rigorous approach to safety management. Embedding safety cases into healthcare practice may allow organizations to more accurately demonstrate that the systems and procedures in place are effectively managing risks associated with patient care. The transition toward using safety cases in healthcare is not without its challenges. Implementation requires significant cultural and procedural shifts within healthcare institutions, traditionally governed by prescriptive standards. Furthermore, many healthcare professionals may initially resist this paradigm shift, due to the perception of safety cases as overly complex or burdensome. However, proponents argue that the potential benefits - including enhanced patient outcomes and reduced incidences of harm - far outweigh these initial hurdles. In sectors such as aviation and rail transport, the adoption of safety cases has resulted in demonstrable improvements in safety performance, suggesting a promising avenue for similar advancements within healthcare. To effectively integrate safety cases within the existing healthcare framework, it is essential to cultivate an environment that prioritizes continuous learning and improvement. This involves more than just adopting new processes; it requires a shift in mindset where healthcare workers are encouraged to engage actively in identifying hazards and in developing comprehensive safety arguments grounded in empirical evidence. Education and training should emphasize the value of risk assessment and safety case development not only as a bureaucratic requirement but as a substantive component of patient care. The role of technology in this transformation cannot be overstated. Advanced data analytics, artificial intelligence, and machine learning can offer new insights into potential risks, thus providing a robust foundation for constructing a safety case. These technologies can enhance the ability to forecast adverse events and contribute to creating a more resilient healthcare system. Despite these promising aspects, the adaptation of safety cases does pose several critical questions for healthcare leaders. How can we ensure that the evidence gathered is both relevant and reliable? How do we balance the need for thorough documentation with the practical constraints faced by healthcare providers? Addressing these issues requires a thoughtful approach, one that values interdisciplinary collaboration and that fosters partnerships between clinicians, engineers, and policymakers. Ultimately, the pursuit of integrating safety cases in healthcare aligns with the broader objective of fostering a culture of safety. It positions healthcare systems to not only respond to adverse events more effectively but to anticipate them, thereby safeguarding patient well-being. As science and technology continue to advance, the potential for safety innovation within healthcare also grows. In conclusion, while the path to widespread adoption of safety cases in healthcare is fraught with complexity, it also holds immense promise. By learning from safety-critical industries and by harnessing the power of modern technology, healthcare systems can take decisive steps towards becoming safer and more reliable. To truly capitalize on this potential, healthcare leaders must be committed to driving change, ensuring that every patient encounter is underpinned by a robust understanding of safety and risk.

The daytime mixed layer develops from sunrise to sunset through the action of solar radiation heating the earth's surface and subsequent convection. In the evening, the surface cools down and the convective activity ceases, leading to the formation of the stable nocturnal boundary layer. During the night, turbulence within this layer decreases until it disappears completely. At dawn, the process starts again with a new mixed layer forming above the old one, which then becomes the residual layer. This diurnal evolution of the atmospheric boundary layer has a significant impact on the wind speed profile as illustrated in Fig. 2. The wind speed is lowest during the day and increases toward nighttime. The magnitude of the increase depends on the stability of the nocturnal boundary layer and the strength of the low-level jet. He did not speak, but the expression in his eyes told of his profound thankfulness. I placed the letter in my breast-pocket. Something seemed to be enclosed within. "Go and open the bag," he whispered, after a brief silence. I did so, and within, to my great surprise, found two huge bundles of fifty and hundred pound Bank of England notes, each packet several inches thick and tied with faded pink tape. He beckoned me to bring them to him, and when I again stood near the bed, he selected one note, and then said - "I wish you to destroy all of them - burn them there in the grate - so that I can watch you," and he gave vent to a harsh, unnatural laugh, a hideous laugh of despair. I looked at him in hesitation. The poor old fellow was surely mad. In my hands I held notes to the value of an enormous sum. And yet he wished to ruthlessly destroy them! He noticed my hesitation, and in a quick, impatient tone, asked whether I would not carry out his wishes, at the same time handing me the note he had taken, telling me that it was to pay for his interment. "As you desire," I said, with some reluctance. "But is it just - with so much distress here, in London - to deliberately destroy money like this?" "I have a reason, Mr Kemball, a very strong reason," he answered in a low tone. So I was compelled to untie the bundles, and, separating the notes, placed them in the grate and commenced a fire, which I fed on and on, until the last note had been consumed, and there remained only a grate full of blackened tinder. I confess that I found myself wishing that I had the numbers of some of the notes, in order to reclaim their equivalent from the Bank. The old man's wild eyes, full of unnatural fire, watched the flames die down, and as they did so he gave a sigh of distinct relief. Then, with difficulty, he turned to me and, putting out his hand, said - "In the bag - at the bottom - you will find a sealed cylinder of metal." I searched as he directed, and drew forth a heavy ancient cylinder of bronze, about a foot and a half long and three inches in diameter. The top had, I saw, been welded down, but a long time ago, because of the green corrosion about it. When I had carried it across to him, he looked me straight in the face with those deep-set glassy eyes, which haunted me for long afterwards, and said - "I trust you with that, Mr Kemball, because - because - I feel assured that you will act as I direct. Do not attempt to seek - to discover what is within. That secret must be withheld - from you. In this I hope - that you will respect my desire - I hope so, for - for your own sake."

The threat, made by Vice President Mohammad Reza Rahimi yesterday, drew a sharp rebuke from Washington. The narrow strait at the mouth of the Persian Gulf is crucial to the global energy market because around 15 million barrels of oil pass through it every day. That represents just under 20 per cent of the world's oil shipments - making it a far bigger bottleneck than the Suez Canal or Panama Canal. About 35 per cent of all seaborne oil shipments and 20 per cent of the world's oil supplies travel through the Strait of Hormuz. This includes crude oil that is produced in Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Iran, and other Gulf states including Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. On average, 14 supertankers traverse the Strait on their way to markets around the world. By comparison, the Suez Canal has about half of the tanker traffic, most of it headed north. The canal carries about 1.8 million barrels a day, mainly imported oil to Europe. The Suez-Mediterranean pipeline system can handle another 2 million barrels daily, but is closed. The biggest share of oil that traverses the Strait of Hormuz goes to Asia, including Japan, China, Singapore, South Korea and India. Oil moves through the strait in two-ways, both entering and exiting the Persian Gulf. Tankers from Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates typically transit the strait and their cargos offload at ports worldwide. Similarly, ships destined for Pakistan often use the same route to pick up cargoes before steaming to Karachi, Pakistan's largest port. To keep ships moving without delays, the channel has two 2-mile-wide traffic lanes for ocean-going vessels, separated by a 2-mile-wide buffer zone. The distance between the north and south boundaries of the ship channel is 21 miles. In addition, there is a 2-mile separation between inbound and outbound traffic in each traffic lane. More than 85 per cent of the crude oils exported from these countries are transported by sea. Closing the Strait of Hormuz would require Iran to take direct action against ships, likely triggering conflict, analysts say. 'The agency continues to verify the non-diversion of declared nuclear material at the nuclear facilities,' the IAEA said in a statement. As soon as anything happens, the recorder starts ticking, and records it in shorthand.

He was accompanied by his trainer and attendants, who bore his armor and javelins. A murmur of surprise greeted him, for he seemed so slight and slender beside the Spartan that few could believe him capable of sustaining a contest with the renowned athlete. The cell type-specific differences in IFN I production in response to nucleic acids are further exemplified by the distinct expression patterns of PRRs and downstream signaling molecules. For instance, plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) are renowned for their exceptional ability to produce IFN I in response to viral infections, which is attributed to their high expression of TLR7 and TLR9, as well as IRF7 (Gilliet et al., 2008). In contrast, myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs) exhibit a more limited capacity to produce IFN I, despite expressing similar levels of TLR7 and TLR9, due to the lower expression of IRF7 (Kerkmann et al., 2005). Moreover, the expression of cGAS and STING is also cell type-dependent, with cGAS being more highly expressed in hematopoietic cells, while STING is more ubiquitously expressed (Li et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013). This differential expression of PRRs and downstream signaling molecules can lead to distinct outcomes in terms of IFN I production and antiviral responses. Furthermore, the subcellular localization of PRRs can also influence the outcome of nucleic acid sensing. For example, TLR9 is localized to the endoplasmic reticulum in pDCs, whereas in mDCs, it is localized to the endosomes, which affects the recognition of CpG DNA and subsequent IFN I production (Honda et al., 2005). Similarly, the subcellular localization of cGAS and STING can also impact the detection of cytosolic DNA and the subsequent activation of the IFN I response (Wu et al., 2013). In addition to cell type-specific differences, the expression and functionality of PRRs and downstream signaling molecules can also be influenced by various factors, such as the activation status of the cell, the presence of certain cytokines, and the type of nucleic acid encountered. For instance, the expression of TLR7 and TLR9 is upregulated in activated pDCs, which enhances their ability to produce IFN I in response to viral infections (Kerkmann et al., 2005). Similarly, the presence of type I IFN can also modulate the expression and functionality of PRRs, leading to a feedback loop that amplifies the antiviral response (Honda et al., 2005). In conclusion, the production of IFN I in response to nucleic acids is a complex process that is influenced by a multitude of factors, including the cell type, the expression and functionality of PRRs and downstream signaling molecules, and the subcellular localization of these molecules. Understanding these intricacies is crucial for the development of effective therapeutic strategies that target the IFN I response to combat viral infections and other diseases.

Dr. Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, told CNN's Candy Crowley that the mandatory quarantine goes against what experts have learned about Ebola. The collie rose upon hearing his name mentioned, and thrust his nose into the boy's hand, wagging his tail and looking as though he would say, 'Come along now, do; and tell the others to come; you've played at that dangerous game long enough; let's all have a jolly scamper after rabbits!' A red cap appeared over the edge of the cliff, followed immediately by a laughing face framed in a crop of fair curly hair; then a girl scrambled on to firm ground. 'Hulloa, Reggie! are you there already?' she said. 'How many have you got?' 'Five,' said Reggie, displaying the contents of his pockets; 'an auk's, two puffin's, and two kittiwake's. Aren't they prettily marked?' 'Beauties,' replied the girl, examining the eggs. 'Better get Neil to blow them for you; he always does it the best. I have only two, and another broke as I was getting it out; but oh, it was glorious down on these ledges! I'd like to have a scramble like this every morning!' 'I daresay,' broke in an exasperated little voice; 'fine fun for you others to get up at four in the morning when the steamer isn't expected until six, and go scrambling about on the rocks, getting sea-birds' eggs, saying that you'll only be five minutes, and then stay an hour!' The child spoke in little rushes and gushes, and her eyes twinkled and looked pathetic by turns in her little dark, round face. 'An hour, Tricksy! It can't have been so long as that!' 'Indeed it was, Marjorie, because I have Reggie's watch; he left it with me, and it has been rather tiresome waiting here, when you know I mayn't climb the rocks as you do.' 'Poor Tricksy, what a shame! It's too bad of us, leaving you alone all that time. Just wait until you are a year or two older, and then your mother will let you climb like the rest of us. Who would have thought that we had been away so long! Time does go so quickly when you're scrambling about for eggs!' She looked around with bright, fearless blue eyes; a tall, slight girl of fifteen, with a face so tanned by sun and wind as almost to have lost its extreme fairness, and with the quick, free movements which speak of perfect health and an open-air life. 'Hulloa,' said Reggie suddenly; 'there's the steamer!' 'Where?' asked both the girls eagerly. 'Over there, just rounding the headland, quite in the distance; you can see the trail of smoke, She won't be in for some time yet.' For a minute or two the young people stood watching the grey line upon the horizon; then Marjorie said - 'She's coming along pretty quickly. Hadn't we better call the others and let them know?'

But, although the action is now purely mechanical, it is not always so, as we shall see if we use our story-teller's privilege and dip into his inner thoughts. Briefly rendered, they run in this wise: "Oh, this awful drought! When is it going to end? Not that it much matters, either way, now, for there's hardly a sound hoof left on the place; and, even if a good rain did come, it would only finish off the whole fever-stricken lot. Well, I'll have to clear out, that's one consolation. I've held on as long as any man could, and now I'll just have to go." His gaze wanders over the arid plain. Far away through the shimmer it rests on a multitude of white specks - a flock of Angora goats, striving in desperation to pick up what miserable subsistence it may. "There's nothing to be done with the place - nothing," he muses, bringing his hammer down upon a boulder with a despairing whack. "It won't sell even for an old song - no one will so much as touch land now, nor will they for a long time to come, and there isn't a `stone' [`Diamond' in digger parlance] on the whole farm, for I've dug and fossicked in every likely place, and unlikely one, too. No; I'll shut up shop and get away. The few miserable brutes left are not worth looking after - not worth their brand ziek [Scab-affected] skins. Yet I'll have one more search, one more crazy fool's errand, after the `Valley of the Eye,' before I trek. This 'll make the fifth - but, no matter. One may as well make an ass of oneself five times as four. I can't exactly believe old Greenway took all that trouble to dictate an infernal lie on his death-bed; and, if his yarn's true, I'm a rich man for life - if I can only find the place, that is," he adds bitterly. "And I've had four shies at it. Well, perhaps the fifth is going to be lucky." With which consoling reflection the thinker rises from his stony resting-place, revealing as he does so a tall, straight figure, admirably proportioned. Suddenly he starts, and a sallow paleness comes over the bronzed, handsome features. For he is conscious of a strange giddiness. A mist seems to float before his eyes, shutting out completely the glare of the burning veldt. "Never that cursed up-country fever again?" he murmurs, to himself, in real alarm. With the development of computer technology, many machine learning models have been proposed to predict Rs, including (1) Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) [67,84], e.g. Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) [15,48], Radial Basis Function Neural Network (RBF) [123,79], Generalized Regression Neural Networks (GRNN) [45,73] and Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) [109,87]; (2) Kernel-based algorithms [22,75], e.g. Support Vector Machine (SVM) [24,26,41,96] and Support Vector Regression (SVR) [105,98]; (3) tree-based assemble models, e.g., M5 model tree (M5Tree) [124,60], Random Forest (RF) [54] and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) [118,40]; and (4) other machine learning models, e.g. Adaptive Neuro Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) [111,132,91], Multivariate Adaptive Regression Spline (MARS) [60], Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) [48,103] and fuzzy logic models [19,102,13]. Among these machine learning models, the ANN algorithms are the most frequently used models and the kernel-based models have started to be used more frequently. However, the tree-based assemble models and other machine learning models are seldom employed. Sunshine-based empirical models are simple and easy to use in practice, but they are not necessarily able to estimate Rs accurately under climatic conditions different from those where they were developed. Given the vast land areas and diverse regional climates of China, it is necessary to calibrate different empirical models using local meteorological data and evaluate their performances in estimating Rs. For instance, Jin et al. [58] have tested the performance of sunshine-based empirical models for monthly average daily Rs estimation at 69 sites in China. It was concluded that the cubic and quadratic models were generally superior to the Angstrom-Prescott model [8,94]. Wu et al. [126] compared several sunshine-based empirical models for estimating Rs in Nanchang, southern China. They recommended the cubic model as the most accurate method for daily Rs estimation. Li et al. [69] and Liu et al. [71] tested different types of sunshine-based empirical models at four weather stations on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau of China. It was found that the Angstrom-Prescott and Bahel models exhibited similar prediction accuracy for Rs estimation. Yao et al. [129] evaluated 108 empirical models for daily Rs estimation in Shanghai of China with a subtropical monsoon climate, and found the polynomial models gave better Rs estimates. Machine learning models generally provide more accurate Rs prediction compared with empirical models, but the prediction accuracy of various types of machine learning models, particularly their computational efficiency on large-scale dataset for predicting Rs have been rarely compared in different regions of the world, especially across the whole China. For instance, Wang et al. [123] only compared three ANN models, e.g., MLP, RBF and GRNN models, for daily Rs estimation with sunshine duration and other meteorological variables at 12 stations across China in terms of prediction accuracy. It was found that the MLP and RBF models outperformed the GRNN model.

Compared with the steam Rankine Cycle, the sCO2 Joule-Brayton one allows to achieve better efficiencies at lower temperatures [8,9] and it presents lower capital and operational costs since sCO2 is several times denser than steam. This feature allows to operate with compact and simple components which would also require less maintenance [10]. Furthermore, with respect to the Rankine technologies, the sCO2 one allows a better thermal matching between the temperature glides of working fluid and hot source and, in turn, to achieve a higher 2nd law (exergy) efficiency, i.e. a better heat utilization [11]. For these reasons, simplified or more complex configurations of sCO2 power cycles are being considered for high-grade heat to power conversion application including next generation nuclear and fossil fuel power generation (500-1000 MWe) [12,13], modular nuclear power generation (300 MWe) [14-17], solar thermal power generation (10-100 MWe) [18-25], shipboard propulsion, geothermal, oxy-combustion and house power (1-100 MWe) [26-35], and industrial scale waste heat recovery (1-10 MWe) [36,37]. The technical feasibility of such systems has been so far assessed mostly at a theoretical level, and it has been focused on cycle analyses of large power plants. In particular, Kacludis et al. [38] reported an overview of several possible WHR applications for a 7.5 MWe condensing simple recuperated sCO2 power cycle, also known as sCO2 Rankine cycle. Mondal et al. [39] presented a sCO2 Brayton cycle with multi-stage intercooled compression considering as waste heat source a flue gas stream at 180 C. The number of compression stages together with the key parameters of the cycle have been optimized in order to achieve the best cycle 1st and 2nd laws efficiency. In the analysis however, optimistic values for the efficiencies of the several components have been assumed. Moreover in the temperature range considered, other heat to power conversion systems can achieve competitive performance at lower costs. Mohagheghi et al. [40] optimized simple regenerated and re-compressed layouts recovering heat from a 100 kg/s exhaust stream. The results showed that adopting the re-compression layout, which guarantees the maximization of the overall cycle efficiency, does not provide benefits in terms of net power output, which is much more relevant for energy recovery systems. A 100 MWe re-compression sCO2 power unit for nuclear applications has been analyzed also by Moisseytsev et al. [41], where the impact deriving from the introduction of re-heating and intercooling was evaluated in terms of efficiency and net power output. What has been found is that the small increase of performance does not justify the resulting increased plant complexity. A further analysis of sCO2 cycle layouts for nuclear applications has been carried out by Kulhanek et al. [42], where the simple Brayton cycle has been compared to the re-compression, pre-compression, split expansion, partial cooling and partial cooling with improved regeneration cycles.

"It's the feeling that's been in that room for days. A feeling of...of something waiting." Miss Farrow's eyebrows rose slightly, but she said nothing, encouraging Pegler to continue. "At first, I thought it was just my imagination, but last night it was different. I was getting ready for bed when I saw...I saw a shadow, ma'am. A dark shape, tall and thin, standing just inside the door. It didn't move or make a sound, but I knew it was there. I felt its presence, like a cold draft on a winter's night." Miss Farrow's expression remained skeptical, but her eyes betrayed a flicker of curiosity. "And what happened then?" she asked, her voice soft and gentle. Pegler's hands twisted together in a nervous gesture. "I tried to go to bed, ma'am, but I couldn't sleep. I kept thinking I heard whispers, faint whispers, like someone was trying to tell me something. I didn't know what to do, so I got up and came downstairs." Miss Farrow nodded thoughtfully, her eyes never leaving Pegler's face. "And what about tonight, Pegler? What made you decide you couldn't stay in that room again?" The maid's face crumpled, and she covered her mouth with her hand, as if to stifle a sob. "Tonight was worse, ma'am. Tonight, I saw its face." The words hung in the air, heavy with emotion, and Miss Farrow's expression changed, her skepticism giving way to a dawning unease. "What did you see, Pegler?" she asked, her voice barely above a whisper. Pegler's eyes closed, as if she was reliving the moment. "A face, ma'am. A face with eyes that...that seemed to see right through me. I knew then that I couldn't stay in that room, not even for you, ma'am." Miss Farrow's grip on the armchair tightened, her knuckles white with tension. She knew Pegler too well to doubt her words, and a shiver ran down her spine as she realized that she might have to confront something she had always dismissed as superstition. "Very well, Pegler," she said finally, her voice firm and resolute. "You shall not sleep in that room again. We'll make arrangements for you to stay in one of the other rooms. But I must ask you, Pegler...are you quite sure you're not just imagining things?" The maid's eyes flashed open, a spark of defiance in their depths. "I'm not imagining it, ma'am. The doors are locked and barred. A porter who lives in a lodge at some distance from the house has the key, and lets you in if he thinks proper, or shuts you out if he pleases, as is his wont. If you ask him what the name of the house is, he says "Murkley," and if you ask whose it is, he tells you "the laird's." He will not tell you whether there ever was any other name for it, nor whether any one ever lived there. He is surly, uncommunicative, and suspicious. He does not know anything, or if he does, he will not say. And yet, though nobody knows why, everybody knows that the house is called St. Leonard's, after the village church hard by, and that it belongs to Sir Patrick Maxwell, who owns half the county round, and who built the house thirty years ago, when he came home from India with a fortune and a wife. Where did he get either? Nobody knows. People used to say he got both in India, but nobody knows how. He had been a poor man, a younger son, and went away a lieutenant in the Company's service, and came back a baronet, with money enough to build the biggest house in Scotland, and buy half the land in the shire. But how he made it, nobody knows. Some people say that he married it, and others that he found it, and others again that he won it. But none of these things are known. And then he built St. Leonard's, which cost a mint of money, and he brought his young bride here, and she died, and he left the place, and never came back again. This is all that is known. For the rest, the house remains open-mouthed and staring, and nobody enters except by stealth, and the trees grow and flourish, and the grass grows green upon the terrace-walks, and the birds sing in the shrubberies, and the river flows along the edge of the park, and all the world goes by, wondering and asking questions, and getting no answer.

Perhaps best known for his version of the Kris Kristofferson song For The Good Times, a pop hit in 1970, the velvet-voiced Price was a giant among traditional country performers in the 1950s, 60s and 70s, as likely to defy a trend as he was to defend one. He helped invent the genre's honky-tonk sound early in his career, then took it in a more polished direction. Price (far right) was a pioneer of his genre, introducing the 4/4 rhythm-heavy shuffle to country on his track Crazy Arms which is used by artists to this day. He reached the Billboard Hot 100 eight times from 1958-73 and had seven No. 1 hits and more than 100 titles on the Billboard country chart from 1952 to 1989. For The Good Times was his biggest crossover hit, reaching No. 11 on the Billboard pop music singles chart. His other country hits included Crazy Arms, Release Me, The Same Old Me, Heartaches By The Number, City Lights and Too Young To Die. Price was elected to the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1996, long after he had become dissatisfied with Nashville and returned to his home state of Texas. His importance went well beyond hit singles. He was among the pioneers who popularized electric instruments and drums in country music. After helping establish the 4/4 shuffle in country music, Price angered traditionalists by breaking away from country. He gave early breaks to Nelson, Roger Miller and other major performers. His Danny Boy in the late 1960s was a heavily orchestrated version that crossed over to the pop charts. He then started touring with a string-laden 20-piece band that outraged his dancehall fans. In the 1970s he sang often with symphony orchestras - in a tuxedo and cowboy boots. Like Nelson, his good friend and contemporary, Price simply didn't care what others thought and pursued the chance to make his music the way he wanted to. 'I have fought prejudice since I got in country music and I will continue to fight it,' he said in 1981. 'A lot of people want to keep country music in the minority of people. But it belongs to the world. It's art.' In the same 1981 interview, he credited the cowboy for the popularity of country music. 'Everyone loves the cowboy. He's nice, humble and straightforward. And country music is the same thing. The kids have discovered what mom and pop told `em.' Price continued performing and recording well into his 70s. 'I have to be in the business at least five or 10 more years," Price said in 2000, when he and his band were doing 100 shows a year.

The present study aimed to address this gap by developing and validating a brief, parent-report measure of social anxiety for young children, the Social Worries Anxiety Index for Young children (SWAIY). The SWAIY was adapted from the Social Worries Questionnaire-Parent version (SWQ-P; Spence, 1995), a well-established measure of social anxiety in older children. The SWAIY was designed to assess the frequency and severity of social anxiety symptoms in children aged 4-7 years, with 30 items that capture the range of social anxiety symptoms, including worries about being embarrassed, rejected, or judged by others. The SWAIY was pilot-tested with 100 parents of young children and demonstrated good internal consistency and test-retest reliability. To validate the SWAIY, we conducted a secondary analysis of data from a larger study of preschoolers (n=200) who were assessed using the SWAIY and other measures of anxiety and social competence. Results showed that the SWAIY was significantly correlated with other measures of social anxiety and social competence, and that it distinguished between children with and without social anxiety disorder. Furthermore, the SWAIY was found to be a significant predictor of social anxiety symptoms at a 6-month follow-up assessment. The SWAIY has several potential advantages over existing measures of social anxiety in young children. First, it is a brief, easy-to-administer measure that can be completed by parents in under 10 minutes. Second, it assesses a range of social anxiety symptoms, including worries about being embarrassed, rejected, or judged by others, which are commonly reported by young children. Finally, the SWAIY can be used to screen for social anxiety disorder in young children, which is essential for early intervention and prevention efforts. In conclusion, the SWAIY is a reliable and valid measure of social anxiety in young children, and it has the potential to be a valuable tool for researchers and clinicians working with young children. Future studies should investigate the longitudinal stability and development of social anxiety in young children, as well as the efficacy of early interventions aimed at reducing social anxiety symptoms.

Further advancements in operational ocean forecasting systems hinge upon enhancing data assimilation techniques, which not only govern the integration of various observational datasets but also dictate the level of accuracy in biogeochemical modeling efforts. As the complexity of marine ecosystems escalates in tandem with anthropogenic pressures, there is an urgent need to refine our comprehension of nutrient cycles, carbon uptake, and ecosystem health (Haussermann et al., 2019; Oschlies et al., 2018). Indeed, the intricate relationships among biotic components and their abiotic environment necessitate sophisticated mathematical frameworks that can adequately capture the dynamics of these interdependencies. This evolution demands the adoption of next-generation data assimilation approaches that extend beyond traditional frameworks, thus enabling the incorporation of novel datasets such as those sourced from autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) and satellite-based biogeochemical sensors into operational practices (Chassignet et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2020). Recent developments in machine learning have also started to offer promising avenues to enhance predictive capabilities within ocean models. The intersection of machine learning and operational oceanography presents unprecedented opportunities to process vast amounts of heterogeneous data while identifying complex patterns that conventional statistical methods might overlook (Faghmous and Kumar, 2016). By training algorithms on historical datasets, researchers can enhance their models' predictive accuracy and efficiency, with particular emphasis on spatial and temporal resolutions that were previously implausible (Rasp et al., 2018). In this regard, integrating machine learning into existing ocean forecasting systems may serve as a force multiplier, significantly enriching model outputs and improving situational awareness for coastal management efforts. Moreover, the advent of high-resolution numerical models allows for finer-scale simulations and better representation of physical processes, such as upwelling and stratification, which are crucial for accurate biogeochemical predictions (Moller et al., 2018). The combination of high-performance computing capabilities and enhanced observational networks-such as the expansion of the Argo float array and the implementation of ship-based sampling protocols-enables the gathering of high-quality datasets critical for the effective calibration of these models (Kershaw et al., 2021). The challenge moving forward is to harmonize these technological advancements with traditional oceanographic practices, ensuring that model outputs can be used effectively by stakeholders including policymakers, fishermen, and conservationists. Furthermore, the communication of data within and across disciplines emerges as another significant aspect of operational ocean forecasting. Stakeholders must be equipped with user-friendly visualizations and insights derived from rigorous models to facilitate informed decision-making and to promote an understanding of the implications of ocean conditions (Rogers et al., 2018). As we endeavor to translate scientific knowledge into actionable insights, multi-disciplinary collaborations become paramount. Cross-pollinating ideas from marine biology, climate science, and socio-economics expands the potential for holistic solutions that address the multifaceted crises impacting marine environments-whether it be through mitigating climate change, restoring coastal ecosystems, or sustaining fisheries. In summary, the evolving landscape of operational ocean forecasting systems requires an ongoing commitment to improving algorithms, assimilating diverse datasets, and fostering interdisciplinary collaborations. Such efforts will not only enhance our understanding of the ocean but will also solidify our capacities to respond to the pressing challenges posed by a changing climate and increasing human activities. Within this context, the recognition and integration of diverse data sources remain foundational to the development of robust, adaptive, and sustainable ocean management strategies in the twenty-first century. Each step taken towards optimizing these systems is undoubtedly a step towards a more informed and resilient society that thrives in harmony with the oceans.
