No studies exist that analyze the role of the magnetic bias in a direct force harvester. This paper aims at filling this gap and discusses the effect of the magnetic bias in a direct force transducer made with a single Fe-Ga rod. The analysis is performed by changing the magnetic bias strength by varying the number of PMs used. A detailed characterization of the magnetic bias has been carried out by measuring the field-magnetization characteristics of the Fe-Ga rod under stress. The measured curves were then fitted using a phenomenological model, which allows extracting all the parameters necessary to describe the behaviour of the rod. The numerical simulations were then compared to experimental results. Titolo: Magnetic bias effect in a vibrational energy harvester based on Fe-Ga Autori interni: RIZZI, Giovanni Rivista: JOURNAL OF MAGNETISM AND MAGNETIC MATERIALS Abstract: Energy harvesters (EHs) represent an ideal energy supply for wireless sensors, and especially for microelectromechanical systems, since they are able to generate electric energy using sources generally untapped (i.e. the exhaust heat or the vibrations generated by an engine) [1]. Electrostatic, electrodynamic and piezoelectric harvesters are the most common vibrational energy harvesters in these applications. Wang and Yuan perform a comparison in [2], where pros and cons of each device are discussed. Otherwise, giant magnetostrictive materials, such as amorphous metallic glass Metglas (Fe81B13.5Si3.5C2) [2], crystalline alloy Terfenol-D (Tb0.3Dy0.7Fe1.9-2) [3,4] or galfenol (Fe1-xGax; x 1/2 0.20) [5], can provide a robust alternative with high power density [6]. Reference [7] illustrates an overview on recent achievements in the field of magnetostrictive energy harvesting. In particular, a comparison between galfenol and Terfenol-D [5] shows the better performances of the first one in vibrational energy harvesting applications where the mechanical excitation vibrational frequency is lower than 100 Hz. In addition, Fe-Ga provides a good compromise between magnetoelastic properties and workability. Galfenol's magnetostrictive properties have been widely analysed in literature, studying dependency on temperature [8], on stress annealing [9] and on crystalline texture [10,11]. Coupling coefficients have been discussed in [12]. In [13] and [14,15], the magnetic induction variation in a galfenol rod is studied versus the applied stress as a function of different applied magnetic biases, neglecting the preload effect and applying the stress in quasi static conditions (1) Hz). The Fe-Ga vibrational EHs are proposed both as cantilever structure and as direct force arrangement. In cantilever harvesters, the magnetic bias is provided by a permanent magnet (PM), but few papers discuss the role of this parameter and none do it extensively. In [16] and [17] the performance of a cantilever transducer is analyzed by varying the resistive load. In [18], the output voltage of a PM unimorph energy harvester is experimentally analyzed as a function of a variable magnetic bias given using 0, 1, 2 and 3 PMs. In [19] the PM of a cantilever transducer is chosen by analyzing the magnetic bias effect through a finite element approach, based on experimental field-magnetization characteristics drawn as a function of stress.

The risk-based argument is intended to demonstrate that all risks associated with a particular system have been identified, that appropriate risk controls have been put in place, and that there are appropriate processes in place to monitor the effectiveness of the risk controls and the safety performance of the system on an on-going basis. Safety cases are usually confidential, but there are publicly available safety cases (see for example the Safety Case Repository [14]). The history of safety cases and safety case legislation in high-risk industries in the UK has been closely linked to the occurrence of high profile accidents, such as the Windscale fire in 1957, which led to the Nuclear Installations Act 1959 (with revision in 1965) that introduced a licensing scheme along with the requirement for the production of a safety case. While there has been criticism of the safety case approach [15-17], the use of safety cases remains an accepted best practice in UK safety-critical industries as a means to provide rigour and structure to safety management activities. There has been some recent interest in the potential application of safety cases in healthcare [18]. However, this is limited at present to the domain of medical devices and health informatics [19,20], such as the guidance for infusion pumps issued by the US Food & Drug Administration (FDA) [21] and guidance issued by the NHS Health and Social Care Information Centre (HSCIC) on Clinical Safety Cases for health informatics products [22,23]. A systematic review of the published literature suggests that there is a lack of published empirical evidence of safety case use in healthcare, in particular at the system or service level, where safety cases have not been used at all [9]. It is far from clear whether, and if so, how safety cases might be developed and put to reasonable use at the healthcare system or service level [18,24]. The organisational and institutional context in healthcare is very different from safety-critical industries: the maturity of safety management practices in healthcare is arguably at a lower level than in traditional safety-critical industries; there does not exist a notion of acceptable levels of risk within the healthcare community; and the regulatory regime is predominantly prescriptive, relying largely on inspection and routinely collected mortality data. The aim of this paper is to describe and to reflect upon first practical experiences with the development and use of safety cases in healthcare at a service level. Two examples from a multi-site service improvement project in the NHS are presented. The paper argues that safety cases might be helpful in supporting healthcare organisations with the adoption of proactive and rigorous safety management practices. However, it is also important to consider the different professional, regulatory and cultural background in healthcare, which might require adaptations to the purpose and use of safety cases in this domain. The next section provides background to the service improvement project within which the work was undertaken.

These examples suggest that viruses may exploit cell types with a limited intracellular nucleic acid response as targets for persistence. Herpesviruses are large, enveloped DNA viruses that are characterized by their lifelong persistence following primary infection. To achieve this, herpesviruses establish a delicate balance between viral replication and immune activation (Schuren et al., 2016; Ressing et al., 2015). Activation of cGAS-STING dependent DNA sensing pathways by human herpesviruses has mostly been studied in macrophages, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells. In these cell types, infection with herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), human cytomegalovirus (HCMV), and Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) led to IFN I production (Jakobsen et al., 2013; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Ma et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013). The human -herpesviruses Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and KSHV exploit the human B cell as a reservoir for persistence. EBV's DNA genome can be sensed by TLR9 (van Gent et al., 2011) and nuclear EBV and KSHV genomes have been reported to trigger IFI16 resulting in inflammasome-mediated IL-1 maturation in B cells (Ansari et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2013). Thus far, it is unclear if and how the cGAS-STING axis contributes to cytoplasmic sensing of the dsDNA genomes of EBV or KSHV in human B cells. In this study, we therefore investigated if human B cells produce IFN I upon exposure to cytoplasmic DNA that can stimulate the cGAS-STING pathway. As herpesviruses like EBV are known to interfere with innate immunity, the unresponsiveness of JY cells to cytosolic DNA could reflect viral immune evasion. To circumvent potential inhibitory effects of EBV proteins present in the JY cells, we turned to the two EBV-negative human B cell lines 2A8 and BJAB. These cells produced the DNA sensors IFI16 and cGAS, and the signaling components TBK1 and IRF3, but lacked sufficient levels of STING protein (Fig. 2D and E). We assessed if reconstitution of STING could rescue IFN I production upon dsDNA stimulation. Murine STING (mSTING) is able to reconstitute human STING-deficient cells to respond to cyclic dinucleotides (Diner et al., 2013). To confirm that the mSTING construct we used was functional in human cells, we expressed low levels of mSTING in 293T cells. When mSTING was co-expressed with human cGAS in these cells, IFN- and ISG54 were induced as determined by qPCR analysis (Fig. 4A). Transfection of cGAS alone did not result in activation of the pathway, while high levels of mSTING did (data not shown). Having shown that the mSTING construct was functional in human cells, we introduced it into human B cells to reconstitute the cGAS-STING pathway. For this, we used lentiviral transduction, since transfection approaches to introduce genes for protein synthesis are inefficient in B cells. We introduced different amounts of C-terminally HA-tagged mSTING into 2A8 and BJAB cells and pure populations of transduced, GFP+ cells were sorted and analysed by Western blot (Fig. 4B).

"Yes, yes!" cried others. "Build a fire." "Have a jolly time." "Tell us some ghost stories." "I'm game if you fellows are," said the doctor, looking around at them. "You know I can't tell ghost stories worth a cent." "We'll sing songs," suggested one boy. "All right," replied the doctor, "but I don't know any good ones." "I know lots of 'em," put in another lad. "I'll teach you a couple, Doctor." "What shall we sing first?" asked Mr. Frankland. "How would 'The Old Oaken Bucket' do?" suggested Mr. Porter. "No, no," objected one of the boys, "we want something lively." "Lively? Well, then, how will 'Marching Through Georgia' do?" "Fine!" shouted the boys. "Fine! Fine! We'll march through Georgia every time." The camp-fire was soon blazing brightly. The boys gathered round it in a half-circle, sitting down on the ground or upon stones, with the three teachers standing behind them. When the song ended the lads gave a cheer and began to shout for more music. "Now let's hear some stories," proposed the doctor. "Who has a good story to tell?" "Doctor, won't you please tell us about the cliff-dwellers?" requested one of the boys. "I've heard you say that this canyon got its name from a discovery made here years ago. Tell us about it." "Yes, yes," chorused the other boys, "tell us about it." "Well, now, boys," responded the doctor, "I've told you that story so often that I thought you'd get tired of hearing it. But since you wish me to repeat it, I'll give it to you again." He paused for a moment, looking into the glowing coals of the fire. Then he went on: "A number of years ago, before this part of Colorado was settled, a party of hunters were out in this region after big game. One morning, just after leaving their camp, they saw what appeared to be the entrance to a cave in the face of a high cliff. They examined the opening, and finding it large enough to admit a man, determined to explore it. So one of them crawled inside. He had gone but a little distance when he stopped suddenly, exclaiming: "'My stars! Here's a dead Indian!' "His companions hurried forward to see what he had discovered. Sure enough, there lay the body of an old Indian, evidently long since dead, wrapped in skins and cloth, and tied up with thongs of rawhide. His bow and arrows were beside him. The men looked around and saw that the cave was a natural tunnel leading back into the solid rock. They followed it for some distance, and finally came to a room cut in the stone. There they found the remains of a rude table, some broken pottery, and a few other articles. Evidently the place had once been occupied as a dwelling. From the condition of everything, however, it was plain that no one had lived there for a long time. "After coming out of the cave the men took the dead Indian to their camp and buried him. This incident is supposed to have given the canyon its present name." "But why should they call it Mummy Canyon because they found a dead Indian in a cave?" queried one of the boys. "Why didn't they call it Dead Indian Canyon?" "Because the word mummy means a body preserved from decay," answered the doctor.

Under thermodynamic equilibrium, 13C and 18O in the carbonate lattice have a tendency to clump into the same carbonate ion group, leading to a relative enrichment in the abundance of the 13C18O16O22- isotopologue over that which would be expected if all isotopes were randomly distributed. The magnitude of this enrichment varies as a function of the carbonate formation temperature and can thus be used as a geothermometer. Ghosh et al. (2006) first calibrated the carbonate clumped isotope thermometer by precipitating synthetic calcites in the lab, yielding a temperature relationship of 47 = 0.0592 * 106/T2 - 0.02 (T in kelvin). Subsequently, Dennis and Schrag (2010) precipitated calcites and found a 47 temperature dependence of 47 = 0.0337 * 106/T2 + 0.247, significantly different from that of Ghosh et al. (2006). We refer to these contrasting calibrations as the Ghosh calibration line and the Dennis calibration line throughout this study. The discrepancies between these calibration lines are not resolved by converting the measured 47 values to the absolute reference frame (ARF) (Dennis et al., 2011). Recently Zaarur et al. (2013) repeated similar precipitation experiments to Ghosh et al. (2006) and found a temperature dependence close to the Ghosh calibration line for calcite and aragonite. In contrast, weaker temperature dependences of the clumped isotope thermometer in aragonite similar to the Dennis calibration line have also since been reported (Kim et al., 2010; Defliese et al., 2015). The causes of the different calibration slopes - which also exist in the calibration of some biogenic carbonates, e.g. brachiopods (Henkes et al., 2013; Came et al., 2014; Petrizzo et al., 2014) - are a matter of current debate within the clumped isotope community. It has been postulated that these inter-laboratory differences are related to differences in the analytical protocols in different labs, e.g. the extent of equilibration between the produced CO2 and the water associated with the digestion acid (Came et al., 2014; Defliese et al., 2015). Despite the complications described above, calibrations of the clumped isotope thermometer in many (although not all) biogenic carbonates appear to agree closely with the Ghosh calibration line (Came et al., 2007; Tripati et al., 2010; Thiagarajan et al., 2011; Zaarur et al., 2011; Eagle et al., 2013). However, with the exception of Eagle et al. (2013), these studies used the same analytical methods as Ghosh et al. (2006). Confidence in the application of the carbonate clumped isotope thermometer in cold-water corals increased with the finding that the relationship between their clumped isotope compositions and growth temperature was indistinguishable from the Ghosh calibration line (Thiagarajan et al., 2011). This result highlighted the possibility that the processes generating large vital effects in coral 18O and 13C did not affect clumped isotope fractionations in cold-water corals. The carbonate clumped isotope thermometer has since then been applied to the cold-water coral Desmophyllum dianthus, to explore past ocean temperatures (Thiagarajan et al., 2014).

A knock at the door interrupted his reflections. It was the maid-servant, bringing the coffee service. The cups were set on the table, and the silver spoons were counted, as was the captain's custom, to make sure that they were neither more nor less numerous than usual. The kettle was then put upon the stove, and the maid retired. "That girl will never learn to keep things clean," said the captain, as he took from the tray a cup and rubbed off a brown spot. "You must remember that she has had no experience. I am quite satisfied with her, and if you would only treat her kindly once in a while, she might do better." "I have nothing against her. Why should I treat her kindly?" "Because she is young and inexperienced, and because we are old enough to be her parents." "She is twenty-five." "Well, what does that signify?" "Nothing whatever. When she gets married, I shall present her with a silver coffee pot." "Oh!" "What do you mean by 'oh'?" "You always say that you want to get rid of her." "I don't. You know very well that I don't care much for servants, but I like this one." "But you are always finding fault with her." "That's just it. If I didn't find fault with her, how could I ever hope to improve her?" "Well, go ahead and find fault. I won't interfere." The captain glanced sharply at his wife, but seeing that she was smiling, he laughed heartily. The clock struck seven, and the bell rang. The first guest had arrived. Soon after eight o'clock all had gathered except Herr von Fritsche, whom Frau Clara had invited at her husband's request, as he was a fellow-officer and a bachelor. Captain Koenig had repeatedly urged his wife to invite this gentleman, whose acquaintance he had lately made at the club. Frau Clara had objected to doing so, because she knew that he was a boorish person, and she feared that he would offend her lady friends. Finally, however, she consented, stipulating that he should not be allowed to play cards. "No fear of that," said the captain. "He doesn't gamble." So he had been bidden, and now was awaited. He entered at half past eight. "A thousand pardons for my tardiness," he began, bowing to the ladies, and shaking hands with the gentlemen. "I went to the wrong house. I knocked at Number Seven instead of Eight." All smiled, and Frau Clara replied: "We thought perhaps you had forgotten us entirely." "No danger of that. I never forget anything. It was simply a case of absent-mindedness." Thereupon he seated himself beside the hostess, and continued to talk to her. But hardly had he begun when the servant announced dinner. They passed into the dining-room, where a long table was laid for twelve. The captain sat at the head, with his wife opposite him. On either side were six chairs, two of which remained vacant. As soon as the company was seated, the captain rose, and, lifting high his glass, proposed a toast to the Kaiser. This was followed by another to the health of the Empress Augusta Victoria. Captain Koenig believed in toasts.

Mr Farage believes the same thing could happen here. 'I am not saying I will be Prime Minister,' he says. 'But I would like to see a Conservative Government that is not shackled by the European Union, so we can have lower taxes and less regulation. If we can do that, we can make ourselves competitive again. And if we do that, then we can start growing again. 'If there is no real alternative, then people will continue to vote for us, and we will continue to grow. What we need now is for politicians to stand up and say they are opposed to the European project. That's the only way we're going to get back control of our borders, our laws, our money and our fisheries.' Mr Farage has already started work on building the new party, which he expects to launch next spring. His aim is to create a mass movement that will sweep away both the existing parties, allowing them to merge into a new centre-Right group. 'The main objective is to break the mould of British politics,' he says. 'To have a proper debate about where this country should go in the future.' To do it, Mr Farage intends to build a modern version of Margaret Thatcher's 'Broad Church', uniting all shades of Conservatism. 'We are not a narrow party,' he says. 'Our manifesto is not just anti-European, it is also about tax cuts and reducing red tape. It is a very broad church indeed.' He says he wants a party that is 'as open as possible' to supporters of other groups such as the English Democrats or the Christian Peoples Alliance. 'This is not about me. This is not about Nigel Farage. This is about the electorate wanting a choice. And we are offering that choice.' Mr Farage does not rule out the idea of working with the Liberal Democrats, whose collapse in the polls has left them facing extinction. He says: 'It depends on whether they are prepared to dump the Lib Dems' obsession with Europe. If they are, then yes. I'd consider it.' He denies the inevitable question: Is he planning to run for Parliament? 'Not until we have built up a really strong party machine. Then I might consider it. But I'm not going to parachute myself into some safe seat. I don't want to be an MP. I want to be Prime Minister.' Mr Farage is dismissive of fears that the rise of UKIP will lead to a left-wing coalition between Labour and the Lib Dems, pointing out that most of the Left has deserted Labour for the Greens. He insists that any rise in support for the Greens, who are predicted to win three seats, will be temporary, because voters will return to UKIP once they realise how far the Green Party is from mainstream politics. He adds: 'We are talking about the British people getting their own country back. There are millions of people who feel exactly the same way, but they haven't got a vehicle to express their feelings. That's why we've grown so fast.'

John continues to wait for a response, but the line remains silent. He looks around his cubicle, taking in the familiar surroundings. The drawings on the wall, the family photos, the stack of comic books on the corner of his desk. He lets out a sigh and tries again. "Hello? Are you still there?" Suddenly, a voice responds, "Yes, I'm here. Sorry about the delay, Mr. Hollar." John's eyes light up with relief. "Ah, great. Thank you. I was calling about order number 6849-49-494-8464-9494-8602. I'm still waiting on the proofs for my book." There's a pause on the other end of the line, and John can hear the sound of typing in the background. "I apologize, Mr. Hollar, but it seems there's been a mistake. Your order was cancelled due to a processing error." John's face falls. "What? That can't be right. I need those proofs for my publisher. Can you fix it?" The voice on the other end of the line is apologetic but firm. "I'm afraid not, Mr. Hollar. The order was cancelled over a week ago. You should have received an email notification." John's eyes scan his desk, searching for any sign of the email. He knows he's been busy, but he's certain he would have seen something like that. "I never got any email. Can you resend it?" The voice hesitates before responding, "I'll see what I can do, Mr. Hollar. In the meantime, you can resubmit your order and we'll expedite the process." John lets out a frustrated sigh. This is not what he needed today. He glances at the clock on his wall, realizing he's already running late for a meeting with his editor. "Fine. I'll resubmit the order. But can you at least give me a reference number so I can track it?" The voice provides the reference number, and John scribbles it down on a Post-It note. As he hangs up the phone, he can't shake the feeling that this is just the beginning of a long and frustrating day. Meanwhile, back in Ohio, Ron is still on the phone with the ambulance service, trying to get help for his mother. Don is still frozen in shock, staring at Sally's injured wrist. The curling iron lies broken on the floor, its cord still sparking. The bathroom is filling with smoke, and Ron is getting desperate. "Hello? Yes, I need an ambulance at 345 Elm Street. My mom's been electrocuted. Please hurry!" The voice on the other end of the line is calm and reassuring. "Okay, sir. Help is on the way. Can you stay on the line and keep me updated on your mom's condition?" Ron nods, even though he knows the person on the other end can't see him. "Yeah, I'll stay on. Please, just hurry." As he waits for the ambulance to arrive, Ron can't help but think about his life in New York, and how far away he is from his family in Ohio. He wonders if he'll ever be able to make it back to the city, or if he'll be stuck in this small town forever. The sound of sirens in the distance breaks his reverie, and he looks up to see the ambulance pulling into the driveway.

This her betrothed had rightly interpreted as a sign of dismissal. Sophia, after hurling this defiance at her family, gave Christos time to retreat, and then went about her daily business. Her mother had died some years before, and since her father's death she had had sole management of the house and of all his business, which was ship-building. But she had been accustomed from the time she could walk to be in and out of the building-yards with him, and the outraged clan, even in the unequalled bitterness of this moment, would have confessed that she was quite capable of managing anything. She was tall and finely made, and the sun had joined hands with the winds of the sea to mould her face with the lines of beauty and serene health. Her eyes and hair were of the South, her brow and nose of her untainted race, her mouth firm and fine. She watched Christos out of the gate with all the complete indifference her great black eyes could hold, and then set off down to the ship-yard where a new brig was to be launched that day. There she stood all morning among the workmen, bareheaded to the sun and wind, directing, and often helping with her own strong hands, and though it would have seemed that she had her eyes and all her mind at the work, she yet found time to glance through the open gate on to the pier, where she could see a talking knot of her clan gathered round the rejected Christos; and, in fact, her mind was more given over to the difficult question of what step she should next take with regard to the question of marriage than to the work on hand. For, indeed, she had no intention of marrying Christos at all. Since her father's death her work and position had become more and more absorbingly dear, and she did not propose to resign her place to a somewhat slow-minded cousin, whom, as she had candidly declared on her betrothal, she loved only as much as is usual among cousins. The question was how to make this indubitably evident.

He did not hurry, but shaved carefully, enjoying the act of shaving, enjoying his own image, enjoying the morning light. His name was John Gorman. He was forty-three years old, tall and lean, and he wore his hair cut very short and close to his head. His face was thin and high-boned, and his skin was weather-beaten and brown. There were lines in his face, but these were the lines of character rather than of age. He looked like what he was - a professional soldier, trained to kill, living by killing. He was dressed in khaki trousers, a shirt and a leather jacket, and he carried a revolver on his hip. When he finished shaving, he put away his razor and mirror and stood up. "Well," he said, "I think I'm ready for breakfast." He walked toward the fire. The men watched him come out of the shadows, moving easily, comfortably, quietly. One of the men laughed softly, and another spoke. "He is good," he said. "But we are better." The lieutenant turned to look at him. "What?" he asked. "We're better soldiers than you are." "Are you? Well, let me tell you something. We've got some men in this outfit who can shoot straighter than you can. We've got some men who know more about fieldcraft than you do. We've got some men who know more about tactics than you do. And we've got some men who can fight hand-to-hand with a knife or a club better than you can. But there isn't a man here, except myself, who knows as much about how to keep a bunch of men together and get them safely across country as I do. And there isn't a man here who can handle men and make them follow him as well as I can. That's why I'm in charge. You may be able to fight better than I can, but if you don't obey my orders, you'll never get anywhere. So just remember that. I'm going to give you your orders and you're going to carry them out. Is that understood?" "Yes, sir." "All right. Then listen while I talk. It looks to me like we're going to have to stay where we are until relief comes. If we try to move, we might run into trouble before we find our way out of this mess. We can't move anyhow, without knowing where we are. We'll hole up here and wait till somebody finds us. We'll hold the ridge line, the best we can. This place has been abandoned for months, so it should be safe enough. I want everybody to take care of his weapon. There's ammunition for every man, but no extra magazines. Take care of yours. Keep it clean and oiled. Don't lose it. The same goes for your bayonet and your belt equipment. Make sure everything is in working order. Check your first aid kit and see that you have everything you need. If you don't have anything you need, report to me and I'll fix you up. We're going to have to be careful about water. There doesn't seem to be any around here, so we'd better conserve what we have. Anybody who gets thirsty will have to drink coffee instead of water. Soft drugs are specifically designed to be active at the site of application but are rapidly metabolized into inactive compounds once absorbed into the systemic circulation. This approach minimizes systemic side effects while maintaining efficacy at the target site. Soft drug design involves incorporating easily metabolizable linkages or functional groups that are recognized by specific enzymes, ensuring inactivation occurs swiftly upon systemic entry. Our journey in developing a topical S1PR1 modulator began with identifying a suitable active compound that could be modified to fit the soft drug paradigm. We conducted extensive computational modeling and synthesized a series of candidate molecules. The aim was to retain the desired S1PR1 agonistic activity while ensuring rapid inactivation post-absorption. The challenge was balancing the molecule's stability on the skin with its ability to degrade rapidly in the bloodstream. After several iterations and in vitro testing, we identified Compound X, a promising candidate demonstrating potent S1PR1 agonistic activity in keratinocyte cultures. Compound X showed effective inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokine release and normalization of keratinocyte proliferation without cytotoxicity. Encouraged by these findings, we proceeded to in vivo studies to assess the therapeutic potential and systemic safety of Compound X. In a psoriasis mouse model, topical application of Compound X led to significant improvements in skin lesions, with reduced erythema and scaling observed. Histological analysis revealed normalization of epidermal thickness and a marked decrease in inflammatory cell infiltrate. Importantly, pharmacokinetic studies showed rapid degradation of Compound X into non-active metabolites in systemic circulation, thus minimizing concerns about potential side effects. This compelling efficacy profile, combined with favorable safety data, positioned Compound X as a viable candidate for further clinical development. We envisioned transforming patient care by providing a highly effective topical treatment that could complement existing therapies, particularly for those with mild to moderate psoriasis. Our approach promised to bridge the gap between systemic and topical therapies, offering a novel route with reduced systemic risks. Moving forward, we conducted toxicity studies and assessed the long-term stability of Compound X formulations. The results fortified our belief in its safety and effectiveness, setting the stage for phase 1 clinical trials. These trials would evaluate pharmacokinetics, safety, and preliminary efficacy in human subjects, marking a crucial milestone in our pursuit of an innovative psoriasis treatment. Feedback from the scientific community and patient advocacy groups was overwhelmingly supportive, signifying a broader recognition of the unmet need in topical psoriasis therapies. The development of a dependable topical S1PR1 modulator like Compound X could redefine treatment protocols and improve countless lives by offering relief from the burdens of chronic inflammation and skin discomfort. As we advanced towards clinical validation, our commitment to addressing patient needs remained unwavering. Combining cutting-edge science with patient-centric goals, our journey underscored the potential of innovative medicinal chemistry to revolutionize chronic disease management. While challenges undoubtedly lay ahead, our path was clear: bring Compound X to psoriasis patients worldwide, offering renewed hope and tangible improvements in their quality of life.

Stem cells for the corneal epithelium are located at the limbus (Dua and Azuara-Blanco, 2000; Osei-Bempong et al., 2013; O'Sullivan and Clynes, 2007; Yoon et al., 2014). The conjunctival epithelium is folded to form the bulbar conjunctiva and palpebral conjunctiva. The anatomic characteristics of the corneal and conjunctival epithelia are distinct (Fukuda and Nishida, 2010b; Kinoshita et al., 2001). Whereas both face the external environment, the corneal epithelium forms a tight barrier but the conjunctival epithelium does not. The cornea is also an avascular tissue, whereas the conjunctiva has an extensive vascular system. Furthermore, immune cells, such as mast cells, lymphocytes, and eosinophils, are abundant in the conjunctiva, but they are present in only low numbers in the cornea (Allansmith et al., 1978; Morgan et al., 1991). In addition, mucin-secreting (goblet) cells are present only in the conjunctival epithelium (Argueso and Gipson, 2001; Gipson, 2004). Given that the conjunctival and corneal epithelia are separated by tear fluid (Gipson, 2007), inflammatory reactions in the conjunctiva can spread to the cornea through tear fluid and vice verse (Nishida, 2010a). Tear fluid is an evolutionary adaptation to life on dry land that arose to prevent desiccation of the ocular surface. In addition, tear fluid provides a pathway for inflammatory cells and various cytokines and chemokines (Nishida, 2006). Dry eye is a multifactorial disease of tear fluid and the ocular surface that is characterized by symptoms of ocular discomfort, visual disturbance, and tear film instability and can result in damage to the ocular surface (Lemp et al., 2007). The condition of tear fluid affects that of the corneal epithelium. Conversely, the condition of the cornea and conjunctiva influences the quality of tear fluid. The cornea-tear fluid-conjunctiva axis thus plays a key role in inflammatory reactions at the ocular surface and in ocular surface disturbances. Although the surface of the cornea is continually exposed to environmental threats as a result of its anatomic location, the corneal epithelium is equipped with active repair mechanisms. In the case of most corneal epithelial injuries, the defects are resurfaced rapidly by the remaining epithelial cells at a rate of about 1 mm2/h (Hanna et al., 1961) and without serious aftereffects. Under certain conditions, however, the cornea develops various types of epithelial disorders, such as superficial punctate keratopathy, corneal erosion, and persistent corneal epithelial defects (also known as nonhealing epithelial defects). These disorders may arise as a result of changes either in the activities of epithelial cells or in conditions such as the shape of the lid margin, inflammation at the ocular surface, the amount or quality of tear fluid, or nerve activity. Furthermore, in the presence of systemic disease or a deteriorating local environment, complete repair of corneal epithelial damage is not achieved and more serious conditions can develop.

End-of-life restoration issues have been an endemic problem in many countries' for a range of land uses, notably minerals extraction, and this feeds in to social concerns about new developments. The scope for comparable risks to emerge with renewables is a further reason for examining end-of-life decisions. As the renewable energy sector in many countries begins to enter an era where initial planning consents and equipment are becoming time-expired, facilities have three key sets of end-of-life options. Firstly, to end the operation of the infrastructure, involving either removing the infrastructure through decommissioning or in some cases abandonment (although the research presented here considers whether this is likely). Secondly, to increase the operational life of the existing asset through extending the planning consent while making no material changes to the infrastructure (possibly involving a like-for-like replacement of parts). Finally, to repower the infrastructure with newer turbines, creating a material change to the site and usually involving replacing the existing turbines with fewer, larger turbines1. This paper seeks to advance our understanding of how end-of-life issues are addressed within land use planning systems. The paper seeks to understand the rate at which wind energy facilities are approaching 'end-of-life' in the UK and to answer the following research question: 'To what extent is the issue of end-of-life decision making for renewables problematised and regulated by government'. Through examining government efforts to control end-of-life decision-making and any omissions and ambit in the scope of state action it aims to understand which issues are considered to be a problem. Such a research question is shaped by dilemmas of uncertainty: how might policy-makers seek to steer situations that span from the present to the further future, in which myriad outcomes are possible? The focus is on planning control of end-of-life decisions, for which there is a significant research gap (for a review of the slightly more extensive literature on technical and economic aspects, especially from developers' perspectives, see Ziegler et al., 2018). In the electricity-generation field in the UK such time limited consents apply only to wind and solar (not nuclear, fossil or hydro), and indeed most planning permission for built structures are in perpetuity - time limitations are the exception. In providing context for the research it is important to note that the majority of wind farm sites in the UK, and particularly older sites, are commercially rather than community owned. In order to address such issues this paper examines how far onshore wind farms are moving towards end-of-life decisions and the policy framework and experiences of end-of-life procedures for England, Wales and Scotland. The three main categories of end-of-life decisions - decommissioning, repowering and asset life extension - are assessed in order to explore the nature of decision-making processes, the planning decision outcomes, challenges faced and the implications of current policy approaches.

To obtain a better damage representation in three dimensions, ultrasonic time-of-flight methods [17,18] can be employed. It provides an image which is a superimposition of the through-laminate thickness damage network but means that the overlapping damage can be difficult to distinguish and near surface damage can obscure the damage beneath. X-ray computed tomography (CT) is capable of providing 3D images of damage non-destructively, as reviewed by Withers and Preuss [19]. As a rapidly improving non-destructive evaluation (NDE) method, its capabilities to evaluate and assess composite materials and their structure are still at an early stage of development. Nevertheless, an increasing number of studies have been performed using CT to characterise composite materials, mainly for the assessment of porosity and defects [20-24]. The use of CT for the study of impact damage in composite structures has received less attention [18,25-27]. Accurate quantification of damage in carbon fibre composites to date has been limited partly by the difficulty of obtaining sufficient defect contrast (related to low contrast and insufficient spatial resolution) [26,28] and partly by the lack of sufficiently sophisticated image analysis procedures to segment and quantify the resulting low contrast images and complex geometry of the damage. The study by McCombe et al. [18] was the first to report on the through-thickness distribution of the damage, i.e. the mapping of the damage as a function of depth; in their case through a self-healing laminate. While damage was quantified for every slice in the CT volume a significant shortcoming of this methodology is that it neglects the curvature of the panel. This means that a slice in the CT volume may contain information from more than one ply. Since composite panels can be non-planar by design, or as a result of loading, a method that can take account of this is needed so that the damage can be located with respect to the underlying ply architecture. The consideration of impact damage is an important case in point. The virtual X-ray CT orthoslices in Fig. 1 clearly show the distortion in the centre of an impacted panel, resulting from an impact energy of 20 J. As a result of the out-of-plane curvature, many laminae are apparent in any one 2D CT slice (as illustrated in Fig. 1c). Consequently, the damage in any one orthoslice comes from a number of separate plies and inter-ply interfaces, hindering the interpretation of the damage levels recorded. Clearly, while 2D analysis tools maybe appropriate for pristine composite laminates they are not appropriate for the accurate quantification of complex 3D structures such as those that characterise extensive impact damage. The paper describes a novel data analysis methodology able to quantify damage in non-planar as well as flat composite laminates.

In response came the grating sound of the telegraph bell. Soon after came the whirring of the turbines. A second later the destroyer got under way. By the time she reached the outer end of the breakwater the "Reed" also was under way, following closely astern. "Just like a pair of trained dogs!" laughed Dave Darrin, as he stood gazing aft at the other destroyer. "But it isn't fair to call them dogs," protested Dan. "Dogs! Why, they're the finest pair of destroyers that ever floated!" "They seem to have the same idea about each other," chuckled Darrin. "Look!" "What boat is that?" demanded the officer in the bow of the launch. "The 'Grigsby.' And you are wanted aboard, sir." Moreover, the use of Virtual Reality (VR) in experimental settings presents unique opportunities for psychological research, particularly in the investigation of stress responses and the nuances associated with trauma processing (Aust et al., 2015; Freeman et al., 2017). As a compelling tool, VR allows researchers to create vividly realistic and emotionally charged environments, immersing participants in scenarios that can exemplify various stressful contexts (Mussap, 2009; Slater et al., 2009). This immersion, which is fundamental to the VR experience, not only increases the ecological validity of research findings but also enhances participants' engagement with the material being presented (Hale et al., 2017). It opens up the possibility of eliciting genuine emotional responses that are critical for understanding the pathways through which individuals respond to, interpret, and ultimately recover from traumatic events. Importantly, VR can also facilitate the study of individual differences in trauma response, a factor that is often overlooked in traditional methodologies (Norr et al., 2017). The customizable nature of VR environments means that research can be tailored to probe specific demographic or psychological characteristics of participants (Huang et al., 2016). For instance, one can create scenarios that vary in severity and context, allowing for a nuanced examination of how different groups (e.g., veterans, victims of accidents, or individuals with previous traumatic experiences) might interact with and perceive threats in a controlled yet realistic manner. This capacity for differentiation is vital in crafting effective therapeutic interventions, as understanding the specific triggers and coping mechanisms of diverse populations can lead to more personalized treatment options (Bennett & Geyer, 2014; Jordan et al., 2015). Furthermore, VR applications extend beyond mere exploration of stress responses; they hold therapeutic potential as well. By utilizing VR in exposure therapy, for instance, clinicians can create controlled environments where patients confront their fears or trauma-related stimuli in a safe space (Carl et al., 2016; Gerardi et al., 2010). This method not only allows for gradual exposure but also empowers patients to develop and practice coping strategies in real time, reinforcing the applicability of learned skills in their everyday lives (Panicz et al., 2018). Moreover, the interactive and immersive dimensions of VR can engender a sense of agency and control that is often lacking in traditional therapeutic settings. When individuals actively participate in shaping their VR experiences, it can lead to enhanced feelings of self-efficacy, thus promoting resilience in the face of stressors (Lindner et al., 2016). Additionally, the integration of physiological assessments with VR provides a promising avenue for elucidating the somatic aspects of stress and trauma (Dando et al., 2017; Wilmer et al., 2018). By monitoring physiological responses such as heart rate, skin conductance, or even neuroimaging while participants engage with VR scenarios, researchers can attain a multi-faceted understanding of the interplay between cognitive appraisal and physical response (Baegert et al., 2018). This convergence of data can offer insights into why certain individuals might be more vulnerable to developing PTSD or related disorders while others exhibit resilience and adaptive functioning following similar experiences (Wessa et al., 2010). Consequently, the versatility of VR not only enhances the methodological rigor of psychological research but also heralds a new era of therapeutic practices that prioritize individualized treatment and real-time response measurements. As research continues to unfold, the challenge lies in harnessing the full potential of VR and ensuring that its implementation is conducted ethically and with sensitivity towards the complexities of human experience.

Binding of EF-G-GTP to the ribosome stops the fluctuations of L1, stabilizes the R-H state and induces the formation of yet another subset of conformations, the chimeric (CHI) or intermediate (INT) states (Adio et al., 2015; Brilot et al., 2013; Ramrath et al., 2013; Ratje et al., 2010; Wasserman et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2013, 2014). GTP hydrolysis by EF-G promotes rapid movement of the tRNA-mRNAs complex into the post-translocation (POST) state accompanied by CW rotation of the ribosomal subunits into the N state (Belardinelli et al., 2016; Ermolenko and Noller, 2011; Rodnina et al., 1997; Wasserman et al., 2016). Spontaneous fluctuations between C and H or N and R states were studied by single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer FRET (smFRET) methods (Note S1 and references therein). Estimations based on smFRET measurements indicated that the spontaneous transitions toward the R-H-L1closed states are rather slow, in the range from 0.05 s-1 to 10 s-1 (Cornish et al., 2008; Fei et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2007; Munro et al., 2010a; Wasserman et al., 2016) (Note S1; Table S2). These rates are either slower or in the same range as the rates of tRNA translocation measured by ensemble kinetics and smFRET (Chen et al., 2011; Holtkamp et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2007). The effect of EF-G on this transition is difficult to estimate, because EF-G binding to PRE complexes induces rapid transition toward CHI and POST states. To overcome this limitation, the rates of the transitions toward the R-H-L1closed state were estimated on translocationally inactive complexes, i.e., without a tRNA in the A site. Also in the presence of EF-G, these rates are low and comparable to the translocation rates. These results implied that the rate of spontaneous fluctuations preceding EF-G binding may determine the global rate of EF-G binding and translocation (Munro et al., 2010a; Wang et al., 2011; Wasserman et al., 2016). In contrast, ensemble kinetics hinted at a possibility that in the presence of EF-G the N-to-R rotation rate of a PRE complex is very high (>200 s-1), although the exact rates were not determined and the rates of spontaneous fluctuations were not measured (Ermolenko and Noller, 2011; Guo and Noller, 2012). We note that it is important to study translocation on true PRE complexes with a deacylated tRNA in the P site and a peptidyl-tRNA in the A site, because the presence of an A site tRNA, or at least its anticodon-stem loop domain, is essential for translocation (Joseph and Noller, 1998) and the rate of translocation depends on the acylation state of the tRNAs (Semenkov et al., 2000). Furthermore, the rates of subunit rotations were mostly measured at conditions dictated by smFRET experiments, typically at 20 C-25 C and with buffers containing high Mg2+ or polyamine concentrations, rather than at conditions optimal for translation (Note S1).

His gray trousers made of coarse home-spun cloth, his deer-skin hunting jacket, his fox-skin cap and sturdy moccasins, all bespoke a life far removed from the busy scenes and worldly comforts of town or city. He had a bright, piercing eye, a countenance frank and winning, a voice as clear and musical as the call of the meadow-lark. He was as nimble as a squirrel. There was about his whole person an air of singular freedom, and every part of his well-shaped frame was perfectly developed by continued though not overtasking labor. The friend who stood beside him was dressed in the same unique hunter's costume. He appeared less active, but more robust than his companion. His face was ruddy, round, and freckled; his long, unkempt hair fell in reddish clusters from beneath his hunting cap. A look of thoughtful earnestness was stamped upon his features as he stood and gazed at the place where the deer had disappeared. "Probably it'll cross Rapier's Ford," said Owen, recovering from his surprise. "It has been a favorite crossing for them of late. There's no harm in trying. I would walk a week for a shot at that fellow." "All right. Let us hurry on fast," said Martin. So the two pushed on at a brisk rate toward the ford about a mile below. They posted themselves so as to cover the narrow path which approached the river, and waited in true huntsman-like silence. An hour passed, and no sound of the faithful dog could be heard. At last, far over the hills his bark was faintly audible. Then the alarm became louder, and a slight click of their rifles showed that the boys were preparing to give the deer a warm welcome. If it was far ahead of the hound, as usually happened, it might rush by them at any moment. Suddenly their attention was drawn to a spot by the rustling of leaves, and peering from behind the trees they saw a large turkey-gobbler, strutting along wholly unconscious of the danger near at hand. What a fine mark it made as it strolled deliberately by with its head erect and wings arched! Owen was the first to see it and raised his rifle to fire; but as Martin signed to him to wait he lowered his rifle and let the turkey pass by. Judging from the barking of the dog, the deer was making for the ford. Owen felt comforted for the loss of the turkey, for if the deer passed between them one or the other would certainly bring it down. "How I would like to wring the neck off that turkey!" muttered Martin to himself, for the gobbler persisted in remaining within rifle-shot, scratching among the dry leaves, and making as much noise as a whole flock of turkeys.

The traveler took a breath, his demeanor unwavering despite the belligerent tone of the man before him. "I am indeed a humble servant of peace and goodwill," he replied, his voice steady yet gentle. "I have journeyed far with the intent to spread kindness and compassion, seeking not to impose but to share in the warmth of human connection." Mr. Steele regarded him with thinly veiled disdain, the corners of his mouth curving downwards as though he had just bitten into something bitter. "And what warmth could you possibly bring?" he scoffed. "This is a hard land, where the strong survive, and the weak are left to wither. We need strength, not your flimsy ideals." The traveler shook his head softly, his expression unperturbed. "It is often the most fragile among us that carry the greatest strength- the strength of love, understanding, and unity. Would it not be a testament to fortitude to extend a hand rather than a fist?" Mr. Kerr, who had remained silent, felt a stir of indignation prickling his insides. He had long observed Mr. Steele wield his authority like a cudgel, scaring away any dissenting voice or tender spirit. The meekness of the traveler seemed a beacon of hope that made him courageous. "Perhaps," he interjected hesitantly, "the stranger deserves a chance to rest. A friendly welcome could do no harm, could it?" Steele's glare was like shards of ice. "You're soft, Kerr," he muttered. "Too easy to sway. This man is a meddler and a nuisance. He represents what is weak and submissive in this world, and I want none of it around here. We have our way of life. Conform to it or leave." Yet, the traveler continued undeterred, his tone a balm for the unyielding tension. "I ask not for allegiance to my beliefs, but rather for shelter as I tread this weary road. He took a careful step closer to the wooden gate, its paint weathered and peeling, much like the dreams of those who had crossed its threshold before. "Oh, I see! Mr. Kerr, his resolve bolstered by the traveler's earnestness, took a step forward. "I think, Mr. Steele, the man speaks truth. We are all wanderers on this earth seeking connection. "Perhaps the lesson lies in humility, in recognizing that the calloused heart can still learn from the gentleness of another's spirit. Will you not allow your Goliath to ponder the words of David?" Mr. Kerr found himself nodding, his heart compelled by the sentiment radiating from the weary traveler. "At the very least, he should have a meal and a moment to rest." For a fleeting second, a flicker of uncertainty crossed Steele's features, as if he pondered the depths of his oppositional stance, yet his pride would not relent easily.

The main limitations of these models include a static perspective, fixed production coefficients, absence of substitution between inputs and outputs, and lack of price feedbacks. On the other side, CGE models allow to account for dynamic interactions among multiple sectors of an economy, including the possibility of substituting inputs and outputs under variable prices, but they require complex calibration and validation processes, possibly leading to high computational costs. In addition, both I/O and CGE models are usually based on the assumption of constant returns to scale, which might not always hold true in real-world applications. Further, the implementation of either I/O or CGE methods requires significant data collection efforts. In particular, the construction of detailed input-output tables and/or social accounting matrices can be very demanding, especially for developing countries where statistical information may be scarce and/or unreliable. Due to the aforementioned reasons, some authors prefer to adopt alternative approaches to economic analysis of disasters. Examples include agent-based modeling [18,19], system dynamics [20], Bayesian networks [21], and stochastic frontier analysis [22]. These methodologies offer distinct advantages in terms of flexibility, adaptability and computational efficiency, but they also present certain drawbacks. Agent-based models, for example, rely heavily on assumptions regarding agents' behavior and decision-making processes, which can be difficult to validate empirically. System dynamics models suffer from similar issues, plus they typically assume linear relationships between variables, which may not accurately reflect reality. Bayesian networks provide a probabilistic framework for analyzing causal relationships among variables, yet they require substantial amounts of training data to generate reliable results. Stochastic frontier analysis allows estimating technical efficiency levels across firms or industries, however its applicability depends crucially upon having access to accurate measures of inputs and outputs. As a matter of fact, the choice of the best-suited methodology for assessing indirect economic losses due to disasters ultimately depends on several factors, including the specific characteristics of the affected area(s), the type of disaster being considered, the level of detail required by stakeholders, and the available resources (time, money, expertise). It is therefore important to carefully evaluate all options before selecting a particular approach. Disaster economics: a review F. Salzano Primo;A. PetrilloSecondo;V. FabozziUltimo In [1], disaster has been defined as the set of "consequences of a natural or man made hazard". Considering the multi-faceted nature of primary triggers and outcomes encompassed by this definition, today one of the core research areas in disaster analysis is related to the assessment of resulting spillover effects in networked systems and societies. A critical review of the nature of cascading disasters and their fallouts was proposed in [2], pointing out elements of interest such as "interdependencies, vulnerability, amplification, secondary disasters and critical infrastructure". [3] introduces a magnitude scale for classifying incidents, disasters and catastrophic events. Dominoes are sometimes subtle to forecast and unexpected in magnitude and extent, when compared with causing factors. This is also the case as far as economic losses associated to disasters are concerned. In this domain, a quantitatively precise evaluation of indirect losses remains a challenge so far, considering the complexity of many economic environments, the diverse nature of disaster contingencies, data constraints (e.g. information availability, accuracy, resolution) and restrictions intrinsic to the analytic tools in use, which are often tailored to specific hazard types, geographical areas and/or historical moments. In spite of that, economic theory has an ancient interest in the discipline of disaster impact assessment [4] and a number of principles have been determined towards sound economic loss estimation [5-10], whereas many aspects remain open for debate and further inquiry.

As the overshadowing clouds continued their capricious race across the April sky, the vicar, with a stately air befitting his office, made his way down the aisle, his gait deliberate as though he were treading sacred ground. A rustle ran through the congregation, a pulsating wave of reverence crashing over the youthful and old alike. The vicar took his place beside the imposing figure of the bishop, who was resplendent in his elaborate episcopal vestments; an array of deep reds and golds caught the drifting beams of sunlight, casting a divine glow upon his portly frame. Within the hearts of the confirmands, whispers of doubt intermingled with echoes of hope. Would the bishop's blessing grant them the grace they sought? Would the lifting of those holy hands forge an invisible bond that linked them not only to their faith but to each other in a manner as tangible as the threads woven into their capes? They were hostages to their own burgeoning self-awareness, the heady mixture of relief and anxiety swirling around in collective imagination as vividly as the colors of May's blossoming petals cascading from the trees outside. Betty, still lost in her thoughts, caught a glimpse of Timothy Wainwright, a boy from their school with tousled hair and an impish grin. He was fumbling nervously with his prayer book, trying to appear ingratiatingly earnest while the look in his eyes spoke volumes of mischief yet to be unleashed. A sharp pang of longing struck her, the sweet tug of youthful camaraderie mixing with the solemnity of the ceremony. She found herself again wishing for the past summer, where their laughter had spilled through sun-soaked fields and playful antics into evenings draped in endless twilight. In that moment, she wished for a life untouched by the restraints of expectations and fear, where innocence lingered not only in memories but in the days yet to unfold. Suddenly, the air thudded with the monumental silence that befell the church as the bishop rose, his bearing regal and the timbre of his voice resonant. He spoke in measured tones, addressing the joys and trials of faith with an eloquence that stirred the very stones of the church to flex with emotion. "Dearly beloved," he intoned, casting his gaze over the youthful line-up, "today, we affirm your commitment. Let this day mark the threshold upon which you shall step boldly and faithfully into the world, waving your banners high!" At that moment, as her heart danced in shared rhythm with the actions unfolding before her, Betty resolved to absorb every moment, to engrave the colors of the world into her memory. To carry not only the weight of the ceremony but the love and hope binding them all together as a community-a kaleidoscope of dreams that stretched far beyond the embrace of the church itself. Every flickering candle, every fervent prayer, created a tapestry she wished to hold dear, as fragile yet as eternal as the fresh blooms adorning the sacred altar.

Specifically, the excitability of the tongue motor cortex is enhanced in the left hemisphere during transitions between speech gestures in fluent speakers, but this left-lateralised enhancement of excitability is absent in PWS (Neef, Hoang, et al., 2015). The lack of left-lateralisation of motor activation in PWS is consistent with less efficient communication between the left IFC and motor cortex affecting timely planning of motor sequences. This suggestion is further supported by findings using magnetoencephalography to measure the timing of brain activity during single word reading, which showed that PWS activate left motor cortex prior to left IFC, a reversal of the timing seen in fluent speakers (Salmelin, Schnitzler, Schmitz, & Freund, 2000). One form of non-invasive brain stimulation that shows promise in the treatment of speech disorders is transcranial direct current stimulation (TDCS). TDCS modulates neuronal excitability by slightly shifting the resting membrane potential of cells (hyper- or de-polarising, depending on current direction). Variation in the placement of the positive (anode) and negative (cathode) electrodes during TDCS affects neuronal excitability and behaviour in different ways, and interacts with other factors such as the duration and intensity of stimulation. For example, placing the anode over the primary motor cortex, and the cathode over the contra-lateral supra-orbital ridge of the forehead increases neuronal excitability in the primary motor cortex (Nitsche & Paulus, 2000). Such stimulation improves motor task performance and learning (Nitsche et al., 2003; Reis et al., 2009). Furthermore, anodal stimulation outside of the motor cortex also has positive effects on targeted behaviours (Holland et al., 2011; Iyer et al., 2005). Critically, the effects of TDCS on behaviour depend upon stimulation being administered in combination with some task that itself engages the targeted brain region in that behaviour. This combination of stimulation and task is key to the promotion of long-lasting behavioural effects (Reis & Fritsch, 2011). TDCS current flow is relatively non-focal, meaning that current is likely to disperse across the targeted region as well as other regions. However, when the target region is activated by a task during TDCS, ongoing plasticity changes in this region can be reinforced by the neuromodulatory effect of TDCS (Bikson, Name, & Rahman, 2013; Reis et al., 2015; Stagg et al., 2011). Studies in healthy participants have shown that speech and language skills can be improved using anodal TDCS to the left IFC. For example, combining anodal left IFC stimulation with a single session of a "tongue-twister" task resulted in increased articulatory skills following the task (Fiori, Cipollari, Caltagirone, & Marangolo, 2014), and anodal left IFC stimulation reduced reaction times during a naming task (Holland et al., 2011). Performance on artificial grammar learning (de Vries et al., 2010) and verbal fluency (Iyer et al., 2005) also improved in healthy people, following anodal left IFC stimulation.

Second, a nuanced understanding of the pathways through which this interconnectedness operates remains elusive, particularly with respect to the mechanisms of knowledge transfer. The theory posits that the strength and nature of inter-firm relationships significantly modulate the flow of information and capabilities; thus, the configuration of a firm's supply chain network may have profound implications on its innovation outcomes (Ahuja, 2000; Lazzarini et al., 2001). The interconnectedness of suppliers can enhance collective intelligence, as firms operating within a dense network may access a broader spectrum of knowledge than isolated entities. For instance, when a firm's direct suppliers maintain active collaborations with one another, they can share insights and best practices that indirectly benefit the original firm-creating a synergistic effect that amplifies the overall knowledge diffusion process. This scenario poses a compelling question: how do the characteristics of supply chain networks contribute to the efficacy of knowledge transfer? A social network analysis approach is particularly lucrative in this context, as it enables researchers to map and quantify the relationships among firms while unveiling the latent structures that govern knowledge flows. Through network metrics-such as centrality, density, and clustering-scholars can begin to unravel how a firm's position within its supply chain alters its innovation capacity. Specifically, firms situated in hubs of activity, defined by a high degree of connectedness, may exhibit greater knowledge acquisition due to their strategic position to leverage information from various sources (Borgatti et al., 2009). Moreover, the implications extend beyond mere connections; the nature of interactions-whether transactional or collaborative-further mediates the knowledge diffusion effect. Collaborative relationships often engender trust and mutual learning, which can propel firms into higher tiers of innovation (Swan et al., 2007). Therefore, while a firm may benefit from a diverse array of suppliers, those benefits are contingent upon the depth and quality of the relationships formed. The extent to which firms engage in information sharing, joint projects, or co-development initiatives may critically alter the landscape of what constitutes productive inter-firm dynamics in supply chains. Further complicating this tapestry is the role of external entities, such as industry associations and innovation consortia, which can serve as conduits for enhancing knowledge diffusion. This speaks to the critical interplay between local knowledge networks and broader industry contexts-wherein the ability to harness knowledge from varied sources can afford firms substantial leverage in navigating the complexities of innovation. In conclusion, knowledge diffusion through buyer-supplier relations emerges as a multifaceted phenomenon, intricately woven into the fabric of inter-firm networks. The implications for practitioners and policymakers are profound, as fostering conducive environments for collaboration and interconnectedness may bolster overall industry productivity and innovation. Future research endeavors must continue to dissect these relationships, employing robust methodologies that can capture the dynamism inherent in contemporary supply chains while addressing the remaining gaps in existing literature. This will not only illuminate the pathways of knowledge transfer but ultimately offer actionable insights for firms aiming to enhance their innovation strategies amidst an ever-evolving economic landscape.

However, most people don't know that distinction, nor indeed do most geologists; so let's just stick with 'sinkhole' for now. The other thing you might notice about the recent holes is that they are mostly appearing in southern England. That makes sense, too, since this is where the chalk lies close to the surface - and it is the chalk that is causing many of the problems. In fact, much of southern England sits on top of a layer of chalk. Chalk isn't actually rock; rather it's the sedimentary remains of marine creatures such as shellfish and small fish. As it formed, the bodies were broken down and turned to limestone. Then, over millions of years, the limestone was compressed into chalk. It is porous, with tiny tunnels running through it. In some places, these tunnels can be quite large. For example, in Dorset, the chalk contains cavities known as kars or karrens. These may be tens of feet across and several storeys high. It's not uncommon to see trees growing inside them. Some of these caves are open to the public. You can visit the Kents Cavern near Torquay, Devon, or Wookey Hole in Somerset. But in many parts of Britain, the chalk is covered by clay, silt and sand. This material is deposited on top of the chalk by rivers and streams. Over time, this becomes compacted and forms a kind of concrete-like cap. Sometimes, though, water seeps into the chalk below. Because the chalk is porous, the water flows freely through it. As the water moves downwards, it dissolves the calcium carbonate that makes up the chalk. Over thousands of years, the pores become larger and eventually form underground caverns. In some cases, the roof of these caverns collapses and the resulting cave-in creates a sinkhole. Of course, these aren't the only causes of sinkholes. They can also happen when old mine workings collapse. This happens especially in Wales and the Midlands, where coal seams run close to the surface. If miners dig too close to an old working, it can give way and cause a sinkhole. But the biggest problem comes from groundwater. There's a lot of it around. Much of our drinking water is taken from aquifers. These are underground reservoirs of freshwater that lie between the soil and rocks. We rely heavily on these aquifers. About 60 per cent of our drinking water comes from them. Unfortunately, they are under threat from climate change. More frequent storms and heavier rainfall mean that aquifers are becoming saturated. So much water is being added to them that the pressure builds up. Eventually, the water will burst through the ground above. Sometimes, this results in a sinkhole. Other times, the water simply emerges as a spring. And that brings us back to the current spate of sinkholes. Heavy rains have caused the ground to become saturated. Pressure has built up and forced water through cracks in the chalk. The water has dissolved the chalk and created underground caverns. Now, it's just a matter of time before the ground above gives way. Many of the recent holes have appeared in residential areas. This is worrying. Most houses are built on shallow foundations, so they're vulnerable to subsidence. This means that anyone unlucky enough to live over an active sinkhole is at risk of seeing his property collapse. And there's another potential hazard. Sinkholes tend to occur in rural areas, where farmers grow crops. If a farmer finds himself standing in a hole, he's likely to get wet.

The representation of backward and forward linkages allowed by I/O models (see [25], Chapter 12) can serve towards the identification of key sectors, the appreciation of different sources of change and of the system's sensitivity, the comparison of economies. The immediate task for the Russian military was to quickly remove thousands of battlefield weapons such as nuclear artillery shells and land mines from other Soviet nations. These relatively compact arms posed the biggest proliferation risk and often were stored close to areas of conflict. 'The military officers who did the job were the unknown heroes,' said Alexander Golts, a Russian independent analyst. 'It's hard to imagine what might have happened if the tactical nuclear weapons had remained on the territories of the states involved in military conflicts.' They now dominate public discourse. To try to counter them without understanding the nature of framing and without having an adequate linguistic infrastructure to draw upon is to fail at the outset. So long as progressives ignore these matters, they will continue to lose on issue after issue. Let me begin with the concept of a "frame."" A frame is a conceptual structure used in thinking. We can see a simple frame in the word house: It evokes the concepts of floors, walls, ceilings, doors and windows, and a place to live. These are not literal meanings of the word house, but rather background ideas associated with the concept. Frames are part of our common sense. Frames are also physical. Though we cannot see or hear them, we know they are there because they change the way we reason. Frames exist in our neural circuitry, ready to be activated. Frames are indispensable for understanding and they shape the goals we want to achieve. Frames come in hierarchies called systems. For example, there is a system of frames surrounding the family. The basic frame in the system concerns the idealized nuclear family, with Mom and Dad married to each other with two kids, a boy and girl. The strict father model assumes this as an ideal. The nurturant parent model does not make such an assumption. The strict father frame constitutes one version of the family frame; the nurturant parent frame, another. What makes a complex frame a moral frame is a background condition specifying how the world should be and why it should be that way. For example, consider the following frame: If your child disobeys you, then you must punish him/her. Why? Because if you don't, the child will develop undisciplined habits. Undisciplined children grow up irresponsible, a drain on society. Punishment produces pain. Inflicting pain on your child hurts you emotionally, and it contradicts your childrearing principles. But your duty as a responsible parent requires inflicting that hurt. That is morality, and it trumps your emotional reaction. This is a typical strict father morality story. There is no need to say explicitly that punishment is required, since that follows from the frame. Strict father morality includes a ranked list of things that a child must be disciplined to do: Obey authority, behave properly, learn self-reliance, succeed and compete according to rules, appreciate rigid limits and boundaries, and embrace responsibility for the consequences of his actions. To teach your child discipline, you have to first teach respect for authority, and that means respecting your authority. Respect is a form of obedience. You therefore have to earn your child's respect. You earn respect by being strong, by knowing your mind, and knowing right from wrong. Strong parents set and enforce clear strict moral boundaries. Children depend on their parents and are naturally inclined to respect them. As a result, they obey their parents and remain within the moral boundaries set by their parents. This allows them to build character, that is, to become self-reliant, respectful of others, obedient to legitimate authority, and so on through the list of what it takes to be disciplined. Once they have character, they will obey strict moral authority on their own, which is good because they won't always have someone around to tell them what to do. And when they are old enough to question authority, they will have internalized their parents' strict moral authority, which will keep them on the path of righteousness. The role of the strict father is to teach the child self-discipline. This suits the child for a world of competition. Self-discipline is rewarded by success and prosperity. Prosperity implies financial prosperity. Financial prosperity implies the accumulation of wealth.

In addition, the potential costs from natural disasters are an order of magnitude greater than averages - losses from large, infrequent events which have not been experienced in recent years are extremely large. For example, a repeat of the 1923 Tokyo earthquake could cause over US$2.0 trillion in economic losses, over US$30 billion in insured losses, and over 40,000 deaths (See also Grossi et al., 2006). Considering the potential losses caused from natural hazards, DSSs help policy advisors, stakeholders and decision makers explore the options they have available in reducing the impact of these hazards on their communities. Losses due to natural disasters are expected to increase into the future: There are two main factors for this increase: The first is climate change. The 5th IPCC assessment finds that storm surge, heat stress, extreme precipitation, inland and coastal flooding, landslides, drought, aridity, water scarcity, and air pollution hazard are increasing with climate change (IPCC, 2013, 2014a, b). The second is that populations and economies continue to grow, and are increasingly concentrated in urban areas, consequently increasing exposure and vulnerability (Bouwer, 2010; Changnon et al., 2000; Kunkel et al., 1999; Neumayer and Barthel, 2011). This is aggravated by cities often developing adjacent to rivers and oceans that form the backbones of navigation/transport systems (Glaeser and Kohlhase, 2004; McGranahan et al., 2007; Small and Nicholls, 2003), and populations often congregating around fertile basins formed through alluvial flood deposition or soils of volcanic provenance. In addition, as cities grow, supply of land to facilitate growth reduces, which results in human developments using land that is more vulnerable. DSSs can help explore how risk will change in the future, and what needs to be done contemporaneously to abate these risks. Risk reduction is broadly recognised as being more effective than response and recovery: There is increasing evidence showing the benefit of pre-hazard risk-reduction (i.e. risk-reduction actions undertaken prior to a hazards event). For example, Rose et al. (2007) found that the overall benefit-cost ratio across nearly 5500 Federal Emergency Management Agency risk-reduction grants was about 4:1. The English Environment Agency tested funding strategies for maintaining existing, and investing in new, flood risk management assets across England and found that the optimal expenditure on mitigation was 25 billion over the next century with a benefit-cost ratio of about 5:1, when the costs and benefits for managing coastal, tidal and river flooding, and managing coastal erosion were considered (Environment Agency, 2014). Harper et al. (2013) investigated three risk-reduction projects in Australia for flooding, storm and bushfire risk, and found that benefit cost ratios were better than 1 and up to 9 where risk-reduction investments were made that target high-risk locations with appropriate combinations of structural and non-structural measures. Despite these benefits, risk reduction is broadly recognised to be lacking sufficient investment (Hennessy et al., 2014; Sadiq and Weible, 2010; Wood, 2004).
