There was one thing concerning Creggan's wild life that he did not care for anyone to know, not even his best friend, M'Ian the minister. And it was this: he was kind to the very poor. The fact is, that the lad was always either in pursuit of game, as he chose to call even rabbits, or fishing from his skiff or from the rocks, so that he had generally more than sufficed for his own needs and those of his guardian, whom I shall presently introduce to you. So when he appeared at the door of widow M'Donald, M'Leod, or M'Rae, as the case might be - for they were nearly all Macs thereabout, - you couldn't have guessed that he was carrying a beautiful string of codling or a "sonsy" rabbit, so carefully was it concealed in his well-worn and somewhat tattered plaid. I am quite sure that Creggan's faithful collie, whose name was Oscar, quite approved of what his master did; he always looked so pleased, and sometimes even barked for joy, when Creggan presented those welcome gifts, and while the recipients called blessings down from heaven on the boy's curly head. But not only did the poorest among the crofters, or squatters as they might have been called, love the winsome, happy-visaged boy, but many of them looked upon him with a strange mixture of superstition and awe. He was supposed to bear a kind of charmed life, because a mystery hung over his advent which might never, never be cleared up. For Creggan was an ocean-child in the truest sense of the word. When a mere infant he had been found in a small boat which was stranded on the rock-bound Isle of Kilmara, off the shores of Skye, one morning after a gale of wind. In this islet, which indeed is but little more than a sea-girt rock, he had dwelt for many years with the strange being who had picked him up half-frozen, and had wooed him back to life, and became not only a father to him but a tutor as well. A strange being indeed was old Tomnahurich, the Hermit of Kilmara, the name by which he was generally known. Only old people could remember his coming to and taking possession of the island, which probably belonged to no one in particular, although in summer-time a few sheep used to be sent to crop the scanty herbage that grew thereon. But one beautiful spring morning, - with snow-white cloudlets in the blue sky, and a light breeze rippling the Minch, till from the mainland of Skye it looked like some mighty river rolling onwards and north 'twixt the Outer and Inner Hebrides, - some fisher-lads on landing were confronted by a tall, brown-bearded stranger, dressed in seaman's clothes, and with a cast of countenance and bearing that showed he was every inch a sailor.

Lord Millefleurs resumed his life amidst the decorous company who had almost resigned themselves to accepting his absence as permanent. Yet, the prodigal's return brought not only relief but also an unfurling wave of change that was as unsettling as it was invigorating. When he walked into the drawing rooms of Lavender Hall, his entrance demanded the attention of all present, as if a delightful specter had decided to descend from its hallowed realms to entertain and be entertained by terrestrial company. Yet, Millefleurs came back not with the airs of repentance but with tales - stories woven from the vibrant fabric of life across the Atlantic. His narratives painted pictures of sweat-streaked brows striving under an unforgiving sun, the noonday lull of bustling markets, voices rising in a cacophony of bartering life into substance, and the silent symphony of an untouched wilderness. Such anecdotes enthralled his kin, who, though initially suspecting embroidery and whimsical aggrandizement, soon found themselves leaning closer, their inherited propriety momentarily cast aside in the warm glow of his curiosity and conviction. It was as if by some alchemical process, his experiences refined the diluted gold of life to its purer essence. Yet, the adjustment was not without its frictions. Overnight, Millefleurs's presence at table introduced more than just another voice; it was a torrent of perspectives and philosophies, challenging the conventional in favor of the experiential. His oft-posited thesis, that wealth without the experience of want was but half a life lived, was met with bemused skepticism. The dowagers of the family clucked their tongues, their lace-gloved hands hovering in the air as if to dust away the perceived folly of youth. Yet, beneath their reprimands lay an intrigue that belied their attempts to dismiss his ideas. Millefleurs, however, was nothing if not amenable, engaging their doubts with the patient vigor of a craftsman intrigued by recalcitrant wood. He spent long hours with his uncle, the Duke himself, whose curiosity, though more circumspectly cloaked, mirrored that of the prodigal son. Often were they found ensconced in the library, the gilt-lined shelves echoing with the rumble of discourse and debate, in which even the walls seemed interested spectators. The heir also found allies in unlikely quarters - the younger cousins who gathered, as iron filings to a magnet, around his tales of daring exploration and transformative encounters. His recitations of labor, not just physical but intellectual, sparked a yearning among them for a life beyond gilded cage experience. Slowly, Lord Millefleurs became less the subject of silent scrutiny and more the beacon whose light revealed pathways unseen and untrodden. Yet, for all his eager recounting and philosophical ponderings, Millefleurs kept certain tales untold, fragments of a journal neither spoken nor penned. Perhaps these threads were for himself alone, portions of his tapestry yet to be shown, still woven in the privacy of his good-natured soul. As Lord Millefleurs settled into his role renewed, a subtle transformation brewed beneath the patriarchal roof, tilting the axis of familial expectation toward a modern constellation of possibilities. Like a sapling taking root, his vision would grow, nourished by the fertile soil of shared understanding, and watered by the diligence of an adventure-loving heart.

I called at the prefecture while still laboring under the effect of this disappointment; the prefect, Valton, whom you know very well, received me with his usual affability; but to the questions I addressed him on the subject of the condition of the ruins which the council seemed so desirous of preserving for the admiration of its constituents, he replied with an absent smile, that his wife, who had visited these ruins on the occasion of an excursion into the country, while she was sojourning on the sea shore, could tell me a great deal more about the ruins than he possibly could himself. He invited me to dinner, and in the evening, Madame Valton, after the usual struggles of expiring modesty, showed me, in her album, some views of the famous ruins sketched with considerable taste. She became mildly excited while speaking to me of these venerable remains, situated, if she is to be believed, in the midst of an enchanting site, and, above all, particularly well suited for picnics and country excursions. A beseeching and corrupting look terminated her harangue. It seems evident to me that this worthy lady is the only person in the department who takes any real interest in that poor old abbey, and that the conscript fathers of the general council have passed their resolution authorizing an investigation out of pure gallantry. It is impossible for me, however, not to concur in their opinion; the abbey has beautiful eyes; she deserves to be classed - she shall be classed. My decision was therefore settled, from that moment, but it was still necessary to write it down and back it with some documentary evidence. Unfortunately, the local archives and libraries do not abound in traditions relative to my subject; after two days of conscientious rummaging, I had collected but a few rare and insignificant documents, which may be summed up in these two lines; "Rozel Abbey, in Rozel township, was inhabited from time immemorial by monks, who left it when it fell in ruins." That is why I resolved to go, without further delay, and ask their secret of these mysterious ruins, and to multiply, if need be, the artifices of my pencil, to make up for the compulsory conciseness of my pen. I left on Wednesday morning for the town of Vitry, which is only two or three leagues distant from the abbey. A Norman coach, complemented with a Norman coachman, jogged me about all day, like an indolent monarch, along the Norman hedges. When night came, I had traveled twelve miles and my coachman had taken twelve meals. The country is fine, though of a character somewhat uniformly rustic. Under everlasting groves is displayed an opulent and monotonous verdure, in the thickness of which contented-looking oxen ruminate.

He looked neither to right nor left as he walked briskly along the sidewalk, turning in at the entrance of the first restaurant he encountered. He entered the dining-room, seated himself at a table, ordered his meal, ate it hurriedly, paid his bill, and stepped out upon the pavement again. He stood there a moment irresolute, then turned toward the bridge, crossed the river, and started homeward. "Home" was a room in the third story of a lodging-house situated in a quiet neighborhood away from the business center. This particular lodging-house was conducted by Mrs. O'Connell, a widow who eked out her small pension by letting rooms to boarders. She had three other lodgers besides John Winthrope. One was Mr. Doolittle, a clerk in a large dry goods establishment. Another was Mr. Bollingbroke, a commercial traveler. The third was Miss Elinor Purcell, a stenographer employed by a prominent lawyer. There was also Mrs. O'Connell's son, Dennis, a lad of twelve years, who attended school, ran errands, delivered papers, sold papers, and did odd jobs about the house. These people comprised the household. They were all strangers in the city, and they were all lonely. As each one entered the front hall after the day's work was done, he would take off his wraps and hang them up in the closet near the front door, then go upstairs to his own room and stay there until supper time. After supper they would gather in the parlor, sit around in silence for awhile, read the evening paper, perhaps converse a bit, then return to their rooms and prepare for retiring. On Sundays they would go out separately to church, come back together, eat dinner, go out again to walk or visit, return home, spend an hour or so in the parlor, retire early, and sleep late next morning. Such was the life led by these people. There was no companionship, no social intercourse between them. Each one was too much engrossed in his own affairs to give heed to those of others. John Winthrope was not happy. He felt that he was growing old before his time. His thoughts were somber. He was disgusted with the monotony of his existence. He longed for something to happen to change the routine of his daily life. As he walked along the street he pictured to himself various incidents that might occur to break the dead level of dullness and wearisomeness. He saw himself called upon to perform deeds of heroism; to rescue persons from drowning; to snatch children from under the wheels of runaway teams; to save houses from burning; to catch thieves; to subdue rioters; to bring order out of chaos; to act in an emergency. He saw himself rewarded for his daring exploits by public acclaim, by medals, by money, by fame. He saw himself beloved, admired, adored, worshiped by the beautiful woman he had rescued from death, by the grateful parents whose child he had saved, by the delighted friends whose property he had preserved from destruction. He saw himself sitting beside this beautiful woman in a box at the opera, in a carriage driving through the park, in a boat drifting down the stream, in a bower listening to her sweet voice singing songs of love and praise. He saw himself surrounded by a crowd of applauding citizens, shaking hands with the mayor, receiving congratulations from the governor, bowing low before the president. He saw himself the hero of the hour, the hero of the town, the hero of the land. He saw himself the idol of the multitude.

Henry Morris, then sixteen years old, lived with his father, a farmer named John Morris, about ten miles from Albany, New York. The Morrises owned a farm of several acres, and also some land adjoining the Mohawk River, where they had built a sawmill. It may be added here that the mill did not belong entirely to them, but was run by them in partnership with an Englishman named Josiah Jamieson. This man had left England because of religious differences, and had become very friendly with John Morris, whose views on religion were somewhat similar to his own. Besides the Morrises there were living at the homestead Mrs. Morris, a kindly lady, and her two daughters, Nellie and Lucy. Nellie was fourteen and Lucy twelve. All loved Henry dearly, for he was a bright, manly lad, and always willing to lend a hand wherever it was needed. As my old readers already know, Henry had taken part in many stirring events connected with the struggle for supremacy in the New World. He had been present at the siege of Fort William Henry, and had witnessed the massacre following the surrender of that stronghold. Then he had accompanied Major Robert Rogers on his famous expedition against St. Francis, and later had gone to Canada again, to do what he could towards ending the conflict in favor of the English. While in Canada he had met his uncle, Maurice Thompson, who was a prisoner, and had aided materially in securing his release. A few weeks previous to the opening of our tale Henry had returned to his home, and he had been followed soon afterwards by his cousin Dave.

The younger brother spoke English quite fluently. He smiled at her as he handed over the change. Marjorie said good-morning and left him smiling after her. She walked quickly homeward, conscious of having spent more than she ought. But she felt better for the walk, and happier because of the thought that she would have something nice for supper. The development of Hyperspectral Imaging (HSI) technology has led to a significant advancement in the field of art analysis, offering a non-invasive and non-destructive method for the classification and mapping of paints and pigments. This technology has the potential to revolutionize the way art experts evaluate and identify artworks, particularly in the detection of counterfeits. By combining HSI with chemometrics algorithms, researchers can create a powerful tool for art authentication and restoration. One of the primary challenges in the art world is the authentication of artworks, particularly those that are rare or of high value. Connoisseurship, or the expertise of art historians and curators, is often relied upon to authenticate artworks, but this method is subjective and can be prone to error. Scientific methods, such as X-ray fluorescence and FTIR, can provide more objective results, but these methods often require the removal of sample material, which can be destructive and may not be feasible for all artworks. HSI technology offers a solution to this problem by providing a non-destructive and non-invasive method for analyzing artworks. HSI cameras capture hyperspectral data, which is then analyzed using chemometrics algorithms to identify the chemical composition of the paints and pigments used in the artwork. This information can be used to identify the artist, the date of creation, and the materials used, allowing for a more accurate authentication of the artwork. In addition to its application in art authentication, HSI technology has also been used in the restoration and conservation of paintings. By analyzing the chemical composition of the paints and pigments used in a painting, conservators can identify areas that have been restored or altered, and develop a plan for preserving the artwork. This information can also be used to create a digital copy of the painting, which can be used for conservation and preservation purposes. The potential applications of HSI technology in the art world are vast, and researchers are continuing to explore its capabilities. In addition to authentication and restoration, HSI technology can be used to analyze the condition of artworks, detect signs of damage or deterioration, and monitor the effects of environmental factors such as light and humidity. It can also be used to analyze the materials used in artworks, such as pigments, binders, and varnishes, and to identify any potential health risks associated with these materials. He knew that there he would find all the headmen to whom he had to convey the Magistrate's message, as well as other good company, and an excellent brew of beer. Thus would be afforded a most fortunate opportunity of combining business and pleasure. When Galada arrived at his destination he found the "beer-drink" in full swing. The men were all sitting in a circle before the main entrance to the cattle kraal, which was half-surrounded by a crescent of beehive-shaped huts. In the centre stood several immense earthenware pots full of the pink liquor, while several smaller pots, each with a cleft-calabash spoon floating in it, were circulating among the guests. Galada removed the saddle from his horse, let the animal loose to join the horses of the other visitors - which were being herded by a couple of boys. Then, after greeting the giver of the feast, he joined the circle of drinkers. But the Sergeant was far too sensible a man to allow pleasure to interfere with duty to his own disadvantage, so after quenching his immediate thirst by emptying one of the largest of the secondary pots, he drew Rolobele and the other headmen aside for the purpose of communicating to them the Magistrate's message, while all were yet in a state of sobriety. "This, then, is the word of Government," said he. "The people who have `the sickness' (the Kaffirs have no name for the disease of leprosy) are to be gathered together at Izolo. From there they will be sent on in wagons to Emjanyana, where they will henceforth dwell. The Magistrate tells me to warn you that this word is a word which must be listened to and obeyed." The four headmen looked at each other in silence for awhile. Then Rolobele spoke - "Yes, we knew of the coming of the word and we will obey. With the old men and women there will be no difficulty, but with the young men - the son of Makanda, for instance - he will be a difficult bull to drive into the Emjanyana kraal." "What! Makanda's son, Mangele," exclaimed Galada in a tone of surprise; "he that I saw among the drinkers; has he got it?" "Oh, yes," replied Rolobele. "The doctor was here last week and found `the sickness' in his hand and his knee. But you knew, surely, that his mother died of it three years ago." Across the heavy features of the youngest of the headmen - a man named Xaba - the ghost of a smile seemed to flit. Xaba had quite recently been appointed to the headmanship in succession to his father.

The broader 'material turn' in social theory, Barry (2015) argues, has also underplayed the 'energetic liveliness' of materials with scope for much more direct engagement with natural scientific accounts of thermodynamic relations. We are concerned with bringing those relations into play as significant and agentive within broader assemblages of heterogeneous material entities, including in bodies-at-work. Second, we are interested in working with an ontology of rhythm and polyrhythmic interrelation as a way of tracing and articulating the 'energetic liveliness' of how heat flows and has consequence in space and time. By bringing together space, time, energy and matter in a single syntax, rhythm enables us to think through their inescapable imbrication. There have been various theorisations of rhythm across different disciplinary domains (Brighenti and Karrholm, 2018, Deleuze, 2003, Adam, 1990, Desain and Windsor, 2000, Rakoff, 2002, Henriques et al., 2014). In geography, rhythmanalysis, as developed by Lefebvre and Regulier,1 has been particularly influential, worked with in relation to a growing diversity of geographical phenomena, cases and questions (Edensor and Holloway, 2008, Jones, 2011, Karrholm, 2009, Kullman and Palludan, 2011, Lager et al., 2016, Mulicek et al., 2016, Reid-Musson, 2017). For Crang (2001), Edensor (2010b) and others, rhythm provides a powerful way of thinking time and space together. Rhythms are spatiotemporal in constituting 'the multiplicity of flows that emanate from, pass through and centre upon place and contribute to its situated dynamics' (Edensor, 2010b: 3). Such flows can span the human and more-than-human and range across corporeal, social and cosmological domains (Lefebvre and Regulier, [1985] 2004). Crucially for our argument, rhythms are not only spatiotemporal but also energetic. Indeed for Lefebvre they are 'that which [connect] space, time and the energies that unfold here and there, namely rhythms' (Lefebvre, [1992] 2004: 18). This conjunction has been little acknowledged (Walker, 2016), or has been interpreted abstractly as an indicator of social force and intent (Brighenti and Karrholm, 2018). We, however, follow our interest in 'energetic liveliness' through a material and thermodynamic understanding, engaging with energy as heat, and bodies physiologically as sites of thermal interaction and consequence that are shaped by rhythms. These rhythms are 'constituted by a myriad of materialities that are not restricted to the body', given that 'the body inhabits the world through... rhythmic exchanges' (Chen, 2017: 24), from the immediate (such as metabolizing food), to the cosmic (such as being warmed by the sun). Therefore, we ask: how might the analytical vocabulary of rhythmanalysis be turned to conceptualizing how heterogeneous, multi-scaled (temporally and spatially), polyrhythmic interactions play out, as thermo-energetic flows move within and around human bodies? Bodies that, in our empirical case, seek to manage the thermal load generated by such flows, while also being variously caught up in other rhythmic structures, such as the organisation of physical labour, market demand and production targets, or logics of safety and repair.
